TheTalas on Instagram: "The 97-Year-Old Marathon Runner Who Rewrote Aging Science

When researchers studied a 97-year-old endurance runner, they expected to see the usual signs of extreme aging: sluggish energy production and failing mitochondria. Instead, they found the opposite.

His mitochondria—the power plants inside every cell—were producing energy at levels similar to a healthy 30-year-old.

No drugs.
No gene therapy.
No rare genetics.

Just one daily habit.

Mitochondria convert oxygen and nutrients into ATP, the fuel that powers muscles, organs, and brain function. With age, they usually decline, leading to fatigue, slow recovery, brain fog, and muscle loss.

But this runner’s cells showed none of that collapse.

The secret wasn’t intensity. It was consistency.

Every day, he moved at low intensity—walking, light jogging, or gentle cycling. Sometimes for 20 minutes, sometimes longer. But he always stopped before exhaustion. He never pushed into burnout.

This matters because mitochondria don’t respond best to extreme stress. They respond to repeated energy demand without damage.

Most people do the opposite. They stay inactive for days, then overtrain. That pattern creates inflammation and mitochondrial damage instead of renewal.

Researchers found that his daily movement activated mitochondrial biogenesis—the creation of new, efficient mitochondria. His cells weren’t just maintaining energy. They were rebuilding it.

Blood markers showed lower inflammation and faster cellular repair than sedentary adults decades younger.

The conclusion was clear: aging at the cellular level is less about time and more about energy neglect.

As one researcher summarized:

“Your body doesn’t age because it gets old. It ages because it stops being used.”

It wasn’t intensity.
It was daily use—without exhaustion.

Like 👍 Follow ❤️🙏🙏🙏"

TheTalas on Instagram: "The 97-Year-Old Marathon Runner Who Rewrote Aging Science

When researchers studied a 97-year-old endurance runner, they expected to see the usual signs of extreme aging: sluggish energy production and failing mitochondria. Instead, they found the opposite.

His mitochondria—the power plants inside every cell—were producing energy at levels similar to a healthy 30-year-old.

No drugs.
No gene therapy.
No rare genetics.

Just one daily habit.

Mitochondria convert oxygen and nutrients into ATP, the fuel that powers muscles, organs, and brain function. With age, they usually decline, leading to fatigue, slow recovery, brain fog, and muscle loss.

But this runner’s cells showed none of that collapse.

The secret wasn’t intensity. It was consistency.

Every day, he moved at low intensity—walking, light jogging, or gentle cycling. Sometimes for 20 minutes, sometimes longer. But he always stopped before exhaustion. He never pushed into burnout.

This matters because mitochondria don’t respond best to extreme stress. They respond to repeated energy demand without damage.

Most people do the opposite. They stay inactive for days, then overtrain. That pattern creates inflammation and mitochondrial damage instead of renewal.

Researchers found that his daily movement activated mitochondrial biogenesis—the creation of new, efficient mitochondria. His cells weren’t just maintaining energy. They were rebuilding it.

Blood markers showed lower inflammation and faster cellular repair than sedentary adults decades younger.

The conclusion was clear: aging at the cellular level is less about time and more about energy neglect.

As one researcher summarized:

“Your body doesn’t age because it gets old. It ages because it stops being used.”

It wasn’t intensity.
It was daily use—without exhaustion.

**Eliud Kipchoge**[EGH](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Golden_Heart_(Kenya) "Order of the Golden Heart (Kenya)") ([English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_language "English language"): [_ELL-ih-yood kip-CHOH-gay_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Help:Pronunciation_respelling_key "Help:Pronunciation respelling key")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-4)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-5); born 5 November 1984) is a Kenyan [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner") who competes in the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") and formerly specialized in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres"). Kipchoge is the [2016](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_marathon "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon") and [2020](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_marathon "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon") Olympic marathon champion, and was the [world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record_progression "Marathon world record progression") holder in the marathon from 2018 to 2023,[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-George_Ramsay-6) until that record was broken by [Kelvin Kiptum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin_Kiptum "Kelvin Kiptum") at the [2023 Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Chicago_Marathon "2023 Chicago Marathon"). He is widely considered to be one of the greatest marathon runners of all time.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-7)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-George_Ramsay-6)

Kipchoge claimed his first individual world championship title in 2003 by winning the junior race at the [World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2003 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") and setting a [world junior record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_junior_world_records_in_athletics "List of junior world records in athletics") for the 5000 m. At the age of eighteen, he became the senior 5000 m world champion at the [2003 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2003 World Championships in Athletics") with a championship record, then followed by an Olympic bronze for Kenya in [2004](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2004 Summer Olympics") and a bronze at the [2006 World Indoor Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships "2006 IAAF World Indoor Championships"). A five-time [World Championship 5000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres_at_the_World_Championships_in_Athletics "5000 metres at the World Championships in Athletics") finalist, Kipchoge took silver medals at the [2007 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2007 World Championships in Athletics"), [2008 Beijing Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics"), and [2010 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2010_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 2010 Commonwealth Games").

He switched to [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") in 2012 and made the second-fastest [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") debut ever, at 59:25. In his marathon debut, he won the 2013 [Hamburg Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg_Marathon "Hamburg Marathon") in a course record time. His first victory at a [World Marathon Major](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Marathon_Major "World Marathon Major") came at the [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon") in 2014, and he went on to become series champion a record five times – for 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2022. He has won the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") a record four times and also holds the record for most [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon") wins with five, his latest coming in September 2023. With 15 victories in his first 18 marathons from 2013 to 2023, Kipchoge's only losses were a second-place finish behind [Wilson Kipsang Kiprotich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kipsang_Kiprotich "Wilson Kipsang Kiprotich") at the [2013 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Berlin_Marathon "2013 Berlin Marathon"), where Kipsang broke the world record; an eighth-place finish at the [2020 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_London_Marathon "2020 London Marathon") and a sixth place in his debut at the [Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boston_Marathon "Boston Marathon") in [2023](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Boston_Marathon "2023 Boston Marathon").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-News-8)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-BBC_Sport-9)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-runningmagazine.ca-10) He has since 2024, been defeated in his last three marathons. Kipchoge's last world record run broke by 30 seconds his own 2018 world record, which was in turn a 78-second improvement over the existing best, the greatest improvement in a marathon world record time since 1967.

On 12 October 2019, Kipchoge ran the marathon distance for the [Ineos 1:59 Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ineos_1:59_Challenge "Ineos 1:59 Challenge") in [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna"), achieving a time of 1:59:40.2, becoming the first person in recorded history to do a [sub-two-hour marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sub-two-hour_marathon "Sub-two-hour marathon").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-11) The run did not count as a new marathon record, as he ran with specialized shoes, standard competition rules for pacing and fluids were not followed, and it was not an open event.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-12)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-13)[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-14)

Kipchoge was appointed [Elder of the Order of the Golden Heart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Order_of_the_Golden_Heart_(Kenya) "Order of the Golden Heart (Kenya)") by former Kenyan President [Uhuru Kenyatta](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uhuru_Kenyatta "Uhuru Kenyatta") on 20 October 2019 in recognition of his sub-two-hour marathon.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-15) He was also named the 2019 [BBC World Sport Star of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Sports_Personality_World_Sport_Star_of_the_Year "BBC Sports Personality World Sport Star of the Year"). In 2023 he was awarded the [Princess of Asturias Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Princess_of_Asturias_Award "Princess of Asturias Award") in the category "Sports".[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-Princess_of_Asturias_Award_2023-16)

Kipchoge was born on 5 November 1984 in Kapsisiywa, [Nandi County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandi_County "Nandi County"), in Kenya. He graduated from the Kaptel Secondary School in Nandi County in 1999 but did not run seriously or as a profession then.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-WAprofile-17)[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-18) He ran three kilometres (2 mi) to school on a daily basis.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-19) Kipchoge was raised by a single mother (a teacher), and only knew his father from pictures. He is the youngest of four children. He met his trainer [Patrick Sang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patrick_Sang "Patrick Sang") (a former Olympic medalist in the [steeplechase](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Steeplechase_(athletics) "Steeplechase (athletics)")) in 2001 at the age of 16.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-nytimes201809-20)

Kipchoge's wife and three children live in [Eldoret](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eldoret "Eldoret"), Kenya.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-auto1-21)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-22) He lives and trains in [Kaptagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kaptagat "Kaptagat"), 30 km (19 miles) from Eldoret.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-23) He is a devout [Catholic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Catholic_Church "Catholic Church").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-24)

Following the death of [Kelvin Kiptum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kelvin_Kiptum "Kelvin Kiptum") in 2024, Kipchoge and his family faced online threats falsely accusing him of being involved in Kiptum's death. These threats impacted his training and well-being.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-25)[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-26)

In 2002, he won at the Kenyan trials for the [2002 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2002 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") junior race. At the World Cross Country Championships, held in [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin"), Kipchoge finished fifth in the individual race and was part of the Kenyan junior team that won gold. Kipchoge also won the 5000-meter race at the Kenyan trial for the [2002 World Junior Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics "2002 World Junior Championships in Athletics") but fell ill and missed the championships. He won the junior race at the [2003 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2003 IAAF World Cross Country Championships").

He set a [world junior record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_junior_records_in_athletics "List of world junior records in athletics") in the 5000 m at the 2003 [Bislett Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bislett_Games "Bislett Games"), running a time of 12:52.61 minutes. This stood as the world and [African junior record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_African_junior_records_in_athletics "List of African junior records in athletics") until 2012, when it was improved to 12:47.53 minutes by [Hagos Gebrhiwet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hagos_Gebrhiwet "Hagos Gebrhiwet") of Ethiopia.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-27)

Kipchoge won a gold medal at the [5000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_World_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Men's_5000_metres "2003 World Championships in Athletics – Men's 5000 metres") final at the [2003 World Championships in Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2003 World Championships in Athletics"), outsprinting runner-up [Hicham El Guerrouj](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hicham_El_Guerrouj "Hicham El Guerrouj"), the world record holder in the [1500 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1500_metres "1500 metres") and [mile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mile_run "Mile run"), by four-hundredths of a second in 12:52.79.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-28)

In July, he participated in the Golden League 2004 Roma Meeting. In the 5000 m event, he dipped first among the starters with 12:46.53, which made him the sixth-fastest ever in the event.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-29)

In 2004, Kipchoge won a bronze medal in the [5000 m final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 2004 Summer Olympics – Men's 5000 metres") at the [2004 Athens Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics"), behind El Guerrouj and [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-30) He also won the [Trofeo Alasport](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trofeo_Alasport "Trofeo Alasport") cross country race earlier that season.

Kipchoge won the bronze in the 3000 metres indoor at the [2006 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships "2006 IAAF World Indoor Championships") in Moscow.

At the end of the year, Kipchoge won the [San Silvestre Vallecana](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/San_Silvestre_Vallecana "San Silvestre Vallecana") New Year's Eve 10 km road race in a time of 26:54 minutes, which beat his own course record by 40 seconds. This time was also better than the 10K road world record at the time but was run on a downhill course.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-31)

[![Image 29](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d3/Osaka07_D6A_M5000M_Heat2-2.jpg/250px-Osaka07_D6A_M5000M_Heat2-2.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Osaka07_D6A_M5000M_Heat2-2.jpg)

Kipchoge (third from the right) during the 5000 m heat at the [2007 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2007 World Championships in Athletics") in [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka"). He won a silver medal in the final.

Kipchoge won a silver medal at the 5000 m final of the [2007 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2007 World Championships in Athletics") at [Osaka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Osaka "Osaka") in 13:46.00, behind [Bernard Lagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bernard_Lagat "Bernard Lagat") (13:45.87).[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-32)

During the [2008 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics") held in Beijing, China, Kipchoge won a silver medal in the 5000 m event with a time of 13:02.80; although better than the previous Olympic record of 13:05.59, it was not enough to match Kenenisa Bekele's pace, who won the gold medal for this race.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-33) On the circuit, he won the [Great Yorkshire Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Yorkshire_Run "Great Yorkshire Run") 10K and [Campaccio](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Campaccio "Campaccio") Cross Country that year.

He failed to reach the podium at the [2009 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics"), finishing in fifth place. He also finished ninth in the 3000 m at the [2009 IAAF World Athletics Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_IAAF_World_Athletics_Final "2009 IAAF World Athletics Final").

He made his debut on the [2010 IAAF Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_IAAF_Diamond_League "2010 IAAF Diamond League") by winning the 5000 m [Qatar Athletic Super Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Qatar_Athletic_Super_Grand_Prix "Qatar Athletic Super Grand Prix") in a meet record time.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-34)

Kipchoge then entered the Carlsbad 5000 in California, United States. The Carlsbad 5 km road race is the venue for the world's best times for a 5k road race for men and women, respectively. The fastest to cover the track was Sammy Kipketer in 2000, with 12:59.52 min.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-35) Kipchoge made a world best attempt, and although he won the race, weather affected his chances, and he finished in 13:11, the fourth-fastest ever for the course up to that point in time.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-36)

In the first athletics final of the [2010 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_Commonwealth_Games "2010 Commonwealth Games"), he attempted to win the 5000 m Commonwealth title. Ugandan runner [Moses Kipsiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Kipsiro "Moses Kipsiro") held a slender lead over him in the race's final stages, and Kipchoge ended up in second place, taking the silver medal some seven-hundredths of a second behind.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-37)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-38) He flew back to Europe immediately after to take part in the [Belgrade Race through History](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgrade_Race_through_History "Belgrade Race through History") the following day. His shoe fell off in the first kilometre, and, after putting it back on, he made up much ground on the field to eventually take second place two seconds behind [Josphat Menjo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Josphat_Menjo "Josphat Menjo").[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-39)

At the start of 2011, he won the short race at the [Great Edinburgh Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Edinburgh_Cross_Country "Great Edinburgh Cross Country"), ahead of [Asbel Kiprop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asbel_Kiprop "Asbel Kiprop").[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-40) He attempted to retain his title at the Carlsbad 5000 in April but came a close second behind [Dejen Gebremeskel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dejen_Gebremeskel "Dejen Gebremeskel").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-41) In May he raced the [3000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres") (finished third) in Doha, with a time of 7:27.66 and ranked him as the 12th-fastest at the distance up to this point.[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-42) Kipchoge was chosen to represent Kenya at the [2011 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2011_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2011 World Championships in Athletics") and reached the 5000 m final for the fifth consecutive time, although he only managed seventh place on this occasion.

Kipchoge returned to the Edinburgh Cross Country in 2012, but this time he finished third behind Asbel Kiprop and Britain's [Jonathan Hay](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jonathan_Hay_(athlete) "Jonathan Hay (athlete)").[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-43) He was also third at the [Carlsbad 5000](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlsbad_5000 "Carlsbad 5000") in March.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-44) He attempted to gain a place on the 10,000 m Olympic team at the [Prefontaine Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prefontaine_Classic "Prefontaine Classic"), but fell back in the late stages of the Kenyan trial race, finishing seventh.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-45) A seventh-place finish in the Kenyan 5000 m trial race meant he would not make a third consecutive Olympic team.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-46)

He made his [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") debut in the [Lille Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lille_Half_Marathon "Lille Half Marathon").[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-47) The run was won by a new course record time of 59:05 (previously 59:36 by ilahun Regassa set in 2008) by Ezekiel Chebii (former personal_best 59:22), trailed by Bernard Koech 59:10, and Kipchoge earned a third place with 59:25. His time of 59:25 became the second fastest Half Marathon debut, only second to Moses Mosop's 59:20 in Milan in 2010.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-48)

On 6 October 2012, Kipchoge ran at the [2012 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2012_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2012 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in [Kavarna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kavarna "Kavarna"), Bulgaria. [Zersenay Tadese](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zersenay_Tadese "Zersenay Tadese") of Eritrea won in 1:00:19, and Kipchoge placed sixth in 1:01:52.[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-49)

[![Image 30](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/69/Wilson_Kipsang_Kiprotich_running_world_record_at_Berlin_marathon_2013.jpg/250px-Wilson_Kipsang_Kiprotich_running_world_record_at_Berlin_marathon_2013.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wilson_Kipsang_Kiprotich_running_world_record_at_Berlin_marathon_2013.jpg)

Wilson Kipsang (front) and Kipchoge (behind) running in the [2013 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Berlin_Marathon "2013 Berlin Marathon") in which Kipsang set the world record with 2:03:23 and Kipchoge, racing in his second marathon, finished second, 42 seconds later.

Kipchoge opened his 2013 season with a win at the [Barcelona Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona_Half_Marathon "Barcelona Half Marathon") in a time of one hour and four seconds.[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-50) Making his [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") debut in April, he demonstrated a smooth transition to the longer distance by taking the [Hamburg Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg_Marathon "Hamburg Marathon") title with a run of 2:05:30 hours (with a half marathon split time of 1:03:13 hours), beating the field by over two minutes and setting a new course record.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-51)[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-52) In August 2013, he won the Half Marathon of [Klagenfurt](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Klagenfurt "Klagenfurt") in 1:01:02 minutes.[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-53)

Then, he raced in the [2013 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_Berlin_Marathon "2013 Berlin Marathon") and finished second in 2:04:05 (with a half marathon split time of 1:01:32 hours), the fifth-fastest time in history, in his second-ever marathon,[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-54)[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-55) behind [Wilson Kipsang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wilson_Kipsang_Kiprotich "Wilson Kipsang Kiprotich"), who set a new marathon world record with 2:03:23. Third place went to [Geoffrey Kamworor](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Geoffrey_Kamworor "Geoffrey Kamworor") of Kenya with 2:06:26.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-BBC_Sport-9) This was the ninth world record set at the Berlin Marathon.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-BerlinRecords-56)

[![Image 31](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/2015-04-26_RK_London_Marathon_0137_%2819952962904%29.jpg/250px-2015-04-26_RK_London_Marathon_0137_%2819952962904%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:2015-04-26_RK_London_Marathon_0137_(19952962904).jpg)

Kipchoge races in the [2015 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_London_Marathon "2015 London Marathon").

On 2 February, Kipchoge participated in the Ras al-Khaimah Half Marathon. He placed sixth with a time of 1:00:50. The run was won by Mosinet Geremew (Ethiopia) in 1:00:05.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-57) Kipchoge ran 2:04:42 to win the [2015 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_London_Marathon "2015 London Marathon") in April. He also won the [2015 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_Berlin_Marathon "2015 Berlin Marathon") later in the year. His win and then-personal best time (2:04:00) occurred even though his shoes malfunctioned, causing his insoles to flap out of both shoes from 10 km onward; rather than risk time lost from an adjustment, he finished the race with bloodied, blistered feet.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-58)

In April, Kipchoge won the [2016 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_London_Marathon "2016 London Marathon") for the second consecutive year in a time of 2:03:05.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-59) His performance broke the course record in London and became the second-fastest marathon time in history, missing [Dennis Kimetto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dennis_Kimetto "Dennis Kimetto")'s world record by 8 seconds.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-60)

**Rio Olympic Games**

As the prerace favourite, during the [2016 Rio Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics"), Kipchoge gained a gold medal in the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics") event.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-61)[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-62)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-63) On the last day of the Olympic Games on 21 August 2016, he won in a time of 2:08:44. The runner up was Feyisa Lilesa (Ethiopia) in 2:09:54 and the bronze medal went to Galen Rupp (USA), doing his second marathon, crossing the finish line in 2:10:05. When the halfway point after 21.0975 km was reached, 37 men were within 10 seconds of the lead runner. The participants' field diminished to 3 lead runners shortly before 34 km. Kipchoge made his final move on silver medal winner Lilesa around 36 km into the race. He covered the first half of the race in 1:05:55 while doing the second half in 1:02:49, which amounts to a difference of more than 3 minutes, a negative split.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-64)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-Ingle-65) The winning gap between Kipchoge and Lilesa by 70 seconds was the largest victory margin since the [1972 Olympic marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_1972_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_marathon "Athletics at the 1972 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon").[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-66) Kipchoge's winning time of 2:08:44 was, as of August 2021, his slowest marathon time. One hundred fifty-five runners started the race, the largest field in Olympic history; 140 of them finished the race.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-67)[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-68) With this win, Kipchoge became the second Kenyan male after Sammy Wanjiru in [Beijing 2008](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics") to win an Olympic marathon gold medal. At the same Olympics, the women's marathon was won by [Jemima Sumgong](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jemima_Sumgong "Jemima Sumgong"), who became the first female Kenyan winner.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-69)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-Ingle-65)

On 20 November 2016, Kipchoge ran in the Airtel [Delhi Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delhi_Half_Marathon "Delhi Half Marathon"), winning the race, clocking a time of 59:44.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-70)

On 6 May, Kipchoge, along with Zersenay Tadese (then world record holder in the half marathon) and [Lelisa Desisa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lelisa_Desisa "Lelisa Desisa") (2-time Boston Marathon winner), attempted the first sub-two-hour assisted marathon in the Nike [Breaking2](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Breaking2 "Breaking2") project on the [Monza](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monza "Monza")[Formula 1 racetrack](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autodromo_Nazionale_Monza "Autodromo Nazionale Monza") near [Milan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Milan "Milan"), Italy. All three runners ran a test 2 months before the attempt. The target time was 1 hour for a half Marathon. Kipchoge finished first in 59:17. The course was measured at 2400 m per lap.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-71) During the 2-hour attempt, the runners were paced by a lead car and 30 supporting pacers joining in stages (both considered illegal under [IAAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF "IAAF") rules).[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-veconomist-72) The race started at 5:45h local time on the 2.4 km track. Kipchoge finished in 2:00:25, while the other two had to slow and finished far behind.[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-73) The runners planned even 14:13 5k splits to break 2 hours. His 5k splits were: 14:14, 14:07, 14:13, 14:15, 14:14, 14:17, 14:17, 14:27, and 6:20 to finish.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-74) The 5k split times from 25k and further would be world records: 25k in 1:11:03, 30k in 1:25:20, 35k in 1:39:37, 40k in 1:54:04.

On 24 September, he won the [2017 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_Berlin_Marathon "2017 Berlin Marathon") in a time of 2:03:32.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-75) In rainy conditions, he finished 14 seconds ahead of [Guye Adola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guye_Adola "Guye Adola") who ran his first marathon, and set the fastest marathon debut ever.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-76) Former marathon world record holder Wilson Kipsang and 2016 winner Kenenisa Bekele failed to finish.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-77)[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-78)

Kipchoge won the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_London_Marathon "2018 London Marathon") in a time of 2:04:17 with a half marathon split time of 1:01:00. In a time of 2:04:49 Shura Kitata (Ethiopia) came in second and [Mo Farah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mo_Farah "Mo Farah") (Great Britain) finished in 2:06:21, a British record. Kenenisa Bekele finished sixth 2:08:53 and defending champion [Daniel Wanjiru](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Daniel_Wanjiru "Daniel Wanjiru").[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-79)[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-80)[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-81)[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-82)[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-83) eighth 2:10:35.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-84) Kipchoge confirmed question on attempting to break the Marathon world record. The women's race saw a win by Vivian Cheriuyot (Kenya) with a time of 2:18:31 the 4th best time ever and Brigid Kosgei (Kenya) place second in 2:20:13.

> 
> Kipchoge's splits– 1:01:06 for the first half, a ridiculous 1:00:33 for his second half– sound made up. But they were real, and they were spectacular."

On 16 September, Kipchoge won the [2018 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Berlin_Marathon "2018 Berlin Marathon") in a time of 2:01:39, breaking the previous world record by 1 minute and 18 seconds (2:02:57 set by fellow countryman Dennis Kimetto at the Berlin Marathon in 2014). It was the greatest improvement in a marathon world record time since 1967.[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-88) He finished 4:43 min ahead of second-placed fellow Kenyan Amos Kipruto. The world record holder from 2013, Wilson Kipsang of Kenya, came in third at 2:06:48.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-89)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-90) It was the 11th world record set at the Berlin Marathon.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-BerlinRecords-56)

Following his performances in the 2018 season, Kipchoge received numerous accolades and awards. He was named [IAAF World Athlete of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Athlete_of_the_Year "IAAF World Athlete of the Year") together with [Caterine Ibargüen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caterine_Ibarg%C3%BCen "Caterine Ibargüen"), who received the female World Athlete of the Year award.[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-91) On 11 January 2019, Kipchoge was named the 2018 Sportsman of the Year at the [Kenyan Sports Personality of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenyan_Sports_Personality_of_the_Year "Kenyan Sports Personality of the Year") Awards in [Mombasa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mombasa "Mombasa"), Kenya.[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-92)

Kipchoge won the [2019 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_London_Marathon "2019 London Marathon") in a time of 2:02:37, the second fastest marathon ever at that time, behind his 2018 Berlin Marathon win.[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-93) He became the first man to win the event four times and set a new course record, beating his own 2016 London Marathon best by 28 seconds.[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-94) The lead runner passed the half marathon mark in 1:01:37.[[94]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-95)[Mosinet Geremew](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mosinet_Geremew "Mosinet Geremew") (Ethiopia) finished as the runner up in 2:02:55 and [Mule Wasihun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mule_Wasihun "Mule Wasihun") (Ethiopia) came in third place in 2:03:16.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-News-8) The British runner [Mo Farah](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mo_Farah "Mo Farah"), a four-time Olympic gold medalist and a pre-race favourite, finished 5th.[[95]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-96)

#### Ineos 1:59 Challenge

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eliud_Kipchoge&action=edit&section=15 "Edit section: Ineos 1:59 Challenge")]

[![Image 33: Wikinews logo](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/24/Wikinews-logo.svg/40px-Wikinews-logo.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Wikinews-logo.svg)

In May 2019, a few days after his London Marathon win, Kipchoge announced another take on the sub-two-hour marathon, named the [Ineos 1:59 Challenge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ineos_1:59_Challenge "Ineos 1:59 Challenge"). On 12 October 2019 in [Vienna](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vienna "Vienna")'s [Prater](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prater "Prater") park, he ran 4.4 laps of the Hauptallee in 1:59:40, becoming the first person in recorded history to break the two-hour barrier over a marathon distance.[[96]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-97)[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-98)[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-99)

The effort did not count as a new world record under IAAF rules due to the setup of the challenge. Specifically, it was not an open event; Kipchoge was handed fluids by his support team throughout; the run featured a pace car and included rotating teams of other runners pacing Kipchoge in a formation designed to reduce wind resistance and maximise efficiency.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-100)[[100]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-101) The achievement was recognised by [Guinness World Records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Guinness_World_Records "Guinness World Records") with the titles 'Fastest marathon distance (male)' and 'First marathon distance run under two hours'.[[101]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-102)[[102]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-103)

Kipchoge placed 8th in the [2020 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_London_Marathon "2020 London Marathon") in October with a time of 2:06:49, the lowest finish of his marathoning career so far.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-runningmagazine.ca-10) The race was won by Ehtopias'S Shura Itata in a time of 2:05:41. Kipchoge lost contact with the lead runner with 3 miles to go. For the first time, the run was on a 19 laps looped course and originally set for April and postponed to October due to the COVID-19 pandemic.[](https://worldathletics.org/news/report/london-marathon-2020-kitata-kosgei-kipchoge)

In preparation for the delayed [2020 Tokyo Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics"), he won the _NN Mission Marathon_, which was held at [Enschede Airport Twente](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Enschede_Airport_Twente "Enschede Airport Twente") in the Netherlands on 18 April 2021 in a time of 2:04:30. Jonathan Korir finished as the runner up with a personal best of 2:06:40.[[103]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-104)

Kipchoge successfully defended his title from the Rio Olympics by winning the gold medal in the men's marathon at the Tokyo Games in a time of 2:08:38, becoming only the third person to successfully defend their gold medal in the men's marathon, after [Abebe Bikila](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abebe_Bikila "Abebe Bikila") in 1960 and 1964, and [Waldemar Cierpinski](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Waldemar_Cierpinski "Waldemar Cierpinski") in 1976 and 1980.[[104]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-105) He was the favourite to win and attacked around the 30 km mark, looking back only once afterwards. He won by 80 seconds, the largest margin in 49 years.[[105]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-106) The silver medal went to [Abdi Nageeye](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abdi_Nageeye "Abdi Nageeye") (Netherlands), while [Bashir Abdi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bashir_Abdi "Bashir Abdi") (Belgium) came in third for a bronze medal with 2:10:00. Kipchoge was the oldest Olympic marathon winner since [Carlos Lopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Lopes "Carlos Lopes") won in 1984 at the age of 37. The run was staged 500 miles north of Tokyo in [Sapporo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sapporo "Sapporo"), with 106 runners participating.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-107) A documentary on the Ineos 1:59 Challenge, titled _[Kipchoge: The Last Milestone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kipchoge:\_The\_Last\_Milestone "Kipchoge: The Last Milestone")_, was released digitally [on-demand](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Video_on_demand "Video on demand") on 24 August 2021.

On 20 January, Kipchoge announced his desire to win all six [World Marathon Majors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Marathon_Majors "World Marathon Majors") (he had already won three, the London, Berlin, and Chicago marathons, by that time). This was followed up by an announcement on 18 February that he would be participating in the [2021 Tokyo Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2021_Tokyo_Marathon "2021 Tokyo Marathon") (which took place on 6 March 2022 due to [COVID-19](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/COVID-19 "COVID-19") restrictions in 2021) and that the majority of his recent training has been dedicated towards this goal.[[107]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-108) He won the Tokyo Marathon with a time of 2:02:40 – a course and all-comers' record. [Amos Kipruto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amos_Kipruto "Amos Kipruto") of Kenya finished second with a personal best of 2:03:13, and [Tamirat Tola](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tamirat_Tola "Tamirat Tola") from Ethiopia came in third in a time of 2:04:14.[[108]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-109)

#### 2022 Berlin and second world marathon record

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Eliud_Kipchoge&action=edit&section=19 "Edit section: 2022 Berlin and second world marathon record")]

[![Image 34](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/56/Berlin_Marathon_2022_Eliud_Kipchoge_km_14%2C5.jpg/250px-Berlin_Marathon_2022_Eliud_Kipchoge_km_14%2C5.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Berlin_Marathon_2022_Eliud_Kipchoge_km_14,5.jpg)

[![Image 35](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/01/Eliud_Kipchoge_in_Berlin.jpg/250px-Eliud_Kipchoge_in_Berlin.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Eliud_Kipchoge_in_Berlin.jpg)

On 25 September, Kipchoge won the [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Berlin_Marathon "2022 Berlin Marathon") decisively in a time of 2:01:09, beating by 30 seconds his own previous world record, which he set on the same course in 2018. With his fourth victory in Berlin, he equaled the record achievement of [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie"). He finished 4:49 min ahead of second-placed compatriot [Mark Korir](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mark_Korir "Mark Korir") while Ethiopia's Tadu Abate took third place with a time of 2:06:28. Kipchoge achieved halfway in 59:51, which, being at the time, the fastest split in marathon history, would have been a world record in the standalone half-marathon in 1993, and was only 26 seconds off his best in that distance. He slowed down later with the second half in 61:18.[[109]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-110)[[110]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-111)[[111]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-112)[[112]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-113) It was the eighth time in a row that the men's record was set in Berlin and the 12th record there overall.[[113]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-114)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-BerlinRecords-56)

At the [2023 Boston Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Boston_Marathon "2023 Boston Marathon"), Kipchoge aimed to win his fifth of the six major marathons. However, after missing his water bottle and due to a left leg problem,[[114]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-115)[[115]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-116) the 38-year-old was unable to stay with the lead group on a hilly section after the 30 km mark. He suffered the third defeat of his marathon career, finishing sixth with a time of 2:09:23. [Evans Chebet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Evans_Chebet "Evans Chebet") was the winner in 2:05:54, successfully defending his title.[[116]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-117)

At the [2023 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Berlin_Marathon "2023 Berlin Marathon"), his first race since the Boston defeat, Kipchoge won the race for a record fifth time, finishing at 2:02:42. He ran alone from 32 km (20 mi) onward after Ethiopia's Derseh Kindie dropped away, but fell short of breaking his own world record that he had set the previous year. With the victory, Kipchoge became the first man in history to win the Berlin Marathon five times, having already won in 2015, 2017, 2018, and 2022.[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_] Fellow Kenyan Vincent Kipkemoi came in third place in a time of 2:03:13. The half marathon split time was 1:00:22.[](https://worldathletics.org/news/report/tigst-assefa-world-marathon-record-berlin-kipchoge-2023)

Kipchoge failed to finish the marathon for the first time in his career when defending his gold medal at the [2024 Paris Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics"), dropping out of the race after around 30 km (19 mi), citing discomfort around his waist. He later told reporters that he would not compete at another Olympic Games. When asked about the prospects of competing in [Los Angeles in 2028](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2028_Summer_Olympics "2028 Summer Olympics"): he explained:

> "You will see me in a different way, maybe giving people motivation, but I will not run. I need to go back, sit down, try to figure my 21 years of running at high level. I need to evolve and feature in other things."[[117]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-118)

The Marathons winner was Tamirat Tola (Ethiopia) in a time of 2:06:26, an Olympic record; silver went to Bashir Abdi (Belgium) 2:06:47; and bronze to Benson Kipruto (Kenya) in 2:07:00. Kipchoge's longtime rival Kenenisa Bekele finished 2:12:24 placed 39 among 71 finishers with 10 runners not finishing.[](https://marathonhandbook.com/kenenisa-bekele-joins-eliud-kipchoge-nyc-marathon/)[](https://www.watchathletics.com/page/5867/men-s-marathon-results-paris-olympic-games-2024-athletics) Despite the performance, Kenyan President [William Ruto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_Ruto "William Ruto") still recognized Kipchoge's achievements:

> "I know how people were disappointed. Many people I know made a lot of comments, 'How could Eliud not finish?' But Eliud we celebrate you. You have held our flag high."[[118]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-119)

Kipchoge competed in the [2025 New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2025_New_York_City_Marathon "2025 New York City Marathon"), finishing 17th, thus completing all six World Marathon Major courses. After finishing, Kipchoge announced a new project known as _Eliud's Running World_, where he will run seven marathons across seven continents over a period of two years to raise awareness about sustainability and education.[[119]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-120) This would also be in an effort to raise money to build libraries in Kenya.[[120]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-121)

On 11th October 2026, Kipchoge won the Melbourne Marathon in a time of 2:09:10.[[121]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-122)

Personal information
Born 5 November 1984 (age 41)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-Paris_2024_KIPCHOGE-1)

Kapsisiywa, [Rift Valley Province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rift_Valley_Province "Rift Valley Province"), Kenya (today in [Nandi County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nandi_County "Nandi County"))[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge#cite_note-Paris_2024_KIPCHOGE-1)

Sport
Country[Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya")
Sport[Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sport_of_athletics "Sport of athletics")

**Joshua Kiprui Cheptegei** (born 12 September 1996) is a Ugandan [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). He is the current world record holder for the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres"), and once held the world-best time over the [15 kilometres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/15K_run "15K run") distance.

Cheptegei is the reigning [Olympic champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2020_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2020 Summer Olympics") in the 10000 m and three-time [World champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") in the 10,000 m. Cheptegei also won a gold medal in the 5000 m and 10,000 m at the [2018 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2018_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 2018 Commonwealth Games") and at the [2019 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2019 IAAF World Cross Country Championships"). At the [2024 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics"), Cheptegei won gold in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres"), becoming the Olympic champion and setting a new [Olympic record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") in the process.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-5)

Cheptegei is the tenth man in history to hold the 5000 m and 10,000 m world records concurrently, both set in 2020.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-7)

Cheptegei was born on 12 September 1996 in Kapsewui, [Kapchorwa District](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapchorwa_District "Kapchorwa District"), Uganda.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-CWG-2) In primary school, he first played football and tried out [long jump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long_jump "Long jump") and [triple jump](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Triple_jump "Triple jump"), but he switched to running when he discovered his talent in distance running.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-CWG-2)

Cheptegei studied procurement and logistics management in Uganda and is employed by the [Uganda National Police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda_National_Police "Uganda National Police").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-8) His coach is Addy Ruiter. In the timeframe from March to May 2020, he reduced his weekly training sessions from 12 to 8.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-FAZ202008-9)

### 2015–2019: Career beginnings

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joshua_Cheptegei&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2015–2019: Career beginnings")]

[![Image 27](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/a/aa/Spc._Paul_Chelimo_wins_silver_medal_in_5%2C000_meters_at_Rio_Olympic_Games_photos_by_Tim_Hipps%2C_IMCOM_Public_Affairs_%2829090428856%29.jpg/330px-Spc._Paul_Chelimo_wins_silver_medal_in_5%2C000_meters_at_Rio_Olympic_Games_photos_by_Tim_Hipps%2C_IMCOM_Public_Affairs_%2829090428856%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Spc._Paul_Chelimo_wins_silver_medal_in_5,000_meters_at_Rio_Olympic_Games_photos_by_Tim_Hipps,_IMCOM_Public_Affairs_(29090428856).jpg)

Cheptegei (L in yellow) races the 5000 m at the [2016 Rio Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics"), where he finished eighth.

Cheptegei competed in the 10,000 metres at the [2015 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2015 World Championships in Athletics") in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), finishing ninth.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-Beijing2015-10) He ran at the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics") in the 5000 metres and 10,000 metres, finishing eighth and sixth. respectively.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-Rio2016-5-11)[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-Rio2016-10-12) He is a silver medallist in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") at the [2017 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2017 World Championships in Athletics") in London.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-13) Cheptegei was the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and 10,000 metres champion at the [2018 Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2018_Commonwealth_Games "2018 Commonwealth Games").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-14)

Cheptegei is a four-time winner of the [Zevenheuvelenloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zevenheuvelenloop "Zevenheuvelenloop") 15 km road race in [Nijmegen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nijmegen "Nijmegen"), Netherlands. In 2018, he set the world record for a 15 km road race.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-15) Abrar Osman finished second with 42:34 and the 2017 5000 m world champion Muktar Edris placed third with 42:56.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-16) On 19 February 2022, the record was broken by Cheptegei's compatriot [Jacob Kiplimo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo "Jacob Kiplimo"), who ran a 15 km split of 40:43 min at the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah_Half_Marathon "Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-17)

Cheptegei was the winner of the senior men's race at the 2019 [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships") in [Aarhus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aarhus "Aarhus"), Denmark. He won in 31:40 on the 10.24 km course. Ugandan teammate Jacob Kiplimo finished second in 31:44, while Thomas Ayeko placed seventh and Joseph Ayeko tenth; Uganda won the team first-place title.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-18)

### 2019–2020: World records

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joshua_Cheptegei&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2019–2020: World records")]

On 1 December 2019, Cheptegei set a new [10 km road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_run "10K run") record in [Valencia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia "Valencia"), Spain. His time of 26:38 improved on the previous world record, set by [Leonard Komon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Leonard_Komon "Leonard Komon") in 2010, by 6 seconds.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-19) This mark has since been lowered to 26:24, the world record being held, as of October 2020, by [Rhonex Kipruto](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhonex_Kipruto "Rhonex Kipruto") of Kenya, who also incidentally set it in Valencia just six weeks later, on 12 January 2020.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-20)

On 16 February 2020, he set a new [5 km road race](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5K_run "5K run") world record in [Monaco](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Monaco "Monaco") with a time of 12:51. The previous ratified record was 13:22, set by Robert Keter on 9 November 2019 in [Lille](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lille "Lille"), France, and the previous fastest time ever recorded over the distance was 13:00 set by [Sammy Kipketer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Kipketer "Sammy Kipketer") on 26 March 2000 in [Carlsbad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlsbad,_California "Carlsbad, California"), USA. This record stood for nearly two years until broken by [Berihu Aregawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berihu_Aregawi "Berihu Aregawi"), who ran 12:49 at the Cursa dels Nassos meet in [Barcelona](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barcelona "Barcelona") on 31 December 2021.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-21)

On 13 August 2020, a day before the [Herculis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Herculis "Herculis") meet of the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Diamond_League "2020 Diamond League") in Monaco, Cheptegei announced that he aimed to return to the track and run his first official race in the season with a world record time in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres"), which would be more than 20 seconds faster than his personal best on a track.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-22) At the meet on the next day, with the help of expert pace-making from Roy Hoornweg, Stephen Kissa, and [Matthew Ramsden](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Matthew_Ramsden "Matthew Ramsden"), he set a [new world record in the 5000 metres with a time of 12:35.36](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres_world_record_progression "5000 metres world record progression"), which broke [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s 16-year-old record—the longest duration in the history of the event—by almost 2 seconds.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-24) His splits were 2:31.87; 5:03.77; 7:35.14 and 10:05.46. Kenenisa congratulated Cheptegei from Addis Ababa.[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-FAZ202008-9)

On 7 October 2020, in Valencia, he set a [world-record time of 26:11.00](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres_world_record_progression "10,000 metres world record progression") in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres"), which improved on [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s 15-year-old record by more than 6 seconds.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-25)

### 2021–present: Olympic medals

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Joshua_Cheptegei&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2021–present: Olympic medals")]

Cheptegei won gold in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and silver in the 10,000 metres at the [2020 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2020_Summer_Olympics "2020 Summer Olympics").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-26)

At the [2022 World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_World_Athletics_Championships "2022 World Athletics Championships"), Cheptegei won the 10,000 metres[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-27) and placed ninth in the 5000 metres.

At the [2023 World Athletics Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Athletics_Cross_Country_Championships "2023 World Athletics Cross Country Championships"), Cheptegei placed third to his countryman [Jacob Kiplimo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jacob_Kiplimo "Jacob Kiplimo") and Ethiopian [Berihu Aregawi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berihu_Aregawi "Berihu Aregawi").[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-28) Cheptegei successfully defended his 10,000 metres title at the [2023 World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_World_Athletics_Championships "2023 World Athletics Championships").[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-29) Later that year, he made his marathon debut at the [Valencia Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Valencia_Marathon "Valencia Marathon"), running 2:08:59 to place 37th.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-30)

At the [2024 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics") in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris"), Cheptegei won gold in the [10,000 metres final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres"), in a new [Olympic record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") of 26:43.14.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-31) The former Olympic record was [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s 27:01.17 set at the [2008 Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-32) Shortly after winning gold in the 10000 meter event, Cheptegei announced on Instagram that he would not be defending his 5000-metre gold medal from Tokyo, citing failure to recover from the race.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-33) Cheptegei also hinted that he will not pursue another Olympic Games on the track, and instead focus more on road racing in the future.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-34) In September 2026, Cheptegei placed third in the half marathon at the [2026 World Athletics Road Running Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2026_World_Athletics_Road_Running_Championships "2026 World Athletics Road Running Championships") in Copenhagen, Demark, in a new personal best time of 58:26.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joshua_Cheptegei#cite_note-35)

**Kenenisa Bekele Beyecha**[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-4) ([Oromo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromo_language "Oromo language"): _Qananiisaa baqqalaa_; [Amharic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amharic_language "Amharic language"): ቀነኒሳ በቀለ; born 13 June 1982) is an Ethiopian [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). He was the world record holder in both the [5,000-metre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") and [10,000-metre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10000_metres "10000 metres") from 2004 until 2020. He won the gold medal in both the [5,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's 5000 metres") and [10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres") events at the [2008 Beijing Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics"). At the [2004 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Summer_Olympics "2004 Summer Olympics"), he won the gold medal in the [10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2004 Summer Olympics – Men's 10,000 metres") and the silver medal in the [5,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2004_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_5000_metres "Athletics at the 2004 Summer Olympics – Men's 5000 metres").

He is the most successful runner in the history of the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), with six long (12 km) course and five short (4 km) course titles. He won the 10,000 m title at the [World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Championships_in_Athletics "World Championships in Athletics") in 2003, 2005, 2007 and 2009 (matching [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie")'s four in a row win streak). Kenenisa was unbeaten over 10,000 m from his debut in 2003 until 2011, when he failed to finish at the World Championships final.

At the [2009 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics") he became the first man to win both 5000 m and 10,000 m title at the same championships. Over 5000 m he has also won an Olympic silver (2004), World Championship bronze (2003), two [African Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/African_Championships_in_Athletics "African Championships in Athletics") titles and one [All-Africa Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/All-Africa_Games "All-Africa Games") gold medal. He also won the [3000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/3000_metres "3000 metres") title at the [2006 World Indoor Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships "2006 IAAF World Indoor Championships").

On 6 April 2014, he produced the sixth fastest marathon debut ever on a record-eligible course with his victory at the [Paris Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris_Marathon "Paris Marathon"), in a course record time of 2:05:04. On 25 September 2016, Kenenisa won the [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon") in a time of 2:03:03, a new personal best, then the third-fastest marathon of all time. On 29 September 2019, he again won the Berlin Marathon in a time of 2:01:41, two seconds slower than [the then world record of 2:01:39](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record_progression "Marathon world record progression") set by [Eliud Kipchoge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eliud_Kipchoge "Eliud Kipchoge") in the 2018 Berlin Marathon.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-5) Considering his accomplishments in cross country, track, and road racing, many consider him to be the greatest distance runner of all time.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-8)

Kenenisa Bekele was born in 1982 in [Bekoji](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bekoji "Bekoji") in the [Arsi Zone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Arsi_Zone "Arsi Zone") of [Oromia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromia "Oromia") Region, the same town as several other prominent long-distance runners, including the Dibaba's Daughters ([Ejegayehu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ejegayehu_Dibaba "Ejegayehu Dibaba"), [Tirunesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirunesh_Dibaba "Tirunesh Dibaba") and [Genzebe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genzebe_Dibaba "Genzebe Dibaba")) and their cousin [Derartu Tulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derartu_Tulu "Derartu Tulu").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-9) Kenenisa was born the second child to parents who made a living as [barley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barley "Barley") farmers, along with three brothers and two sisters.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:0-10)[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-11) The family practiced [Ethiopian Orthodox Christianity](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopian_Orthodox_Tewahedo_Church "Ethiopian Orthodox Tewahedo Church").[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:0-10)

Kenenisa initially aspired to a career in medicine, education, or the civil service.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:1-12) He began to train seriously in running with the encouragement of a physical education teacher, while drawing inspiration from the success of Derartu Tulu and [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:1-12) Kenenisa achieved his first medals at an international competition with second-place finishes in both the 3000 metres of the [1999 World Youth Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_World_Youth_Championships_in_Athletics "1999 World Youth Championships in Athletics") and the 5000 metres of the [2000 World Junior Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Men's_200_metres "2000 World Junior Championships in Athletics – Men's 200 metres").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:2-13) He won his first gold medal in the junior race of the [2001 World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships_%E2%80%93_Junior_men's_race "2001 IAAF World Cross Country Championships – Junior men's race").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-:2-13)[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-14) His success in running enabled him to purchase a house and to help fund his siblings' educations.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-15)
