From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Abraham Chepkirwok

[![Image 1: Abraham Chepkirwok at ISTAF 2008](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fb/Abraham_Chepkirwok.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Abraham_Chepkirwok.jpg "Abraham Chepkirwok at ISTAF 2008")
Personal information
Born 18 November 1988 (age 37)
Medal record Men's [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_(sport) "Athletics (sport)") Representing ![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Flag_of_Uganda.svg/40px-Flag_of_Uganda.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") [World Junior Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics "IAAF World Junior Championships in Athletics") ![Image 3: Bronze medal – third place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Bronze_medal_icon_%28B_initial%29.svg/20px-Bronze_medal_icon_%28B_initial%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[2006 Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics "2006 World Junior Championships in Athletics")800 m [World Athletics Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Athletics_Final "IAAF World Athletics Final") ![Image 4: Silver medal – second place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Silver_medal_icon_%28S_initial%29.svg/20px-Silver_medal_icon_%28S_initial%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[2008 Stuttgart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_IAAF_World_Athletics_Final "2008 IAAF World Athletics Final")800 m

**Abraham Chepkirwok** (born 18 November 1988) is a [Ugandan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda")[middle-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle-distance_runner "Middle-distance runner") who specializes in the [800 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/800_metres "800 metres"). He is the Ugandan record holder in this distance, with 1:43.72 minutes, achieved in July 2008 in [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid"). He is a [World Junior Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics "IAAF World Junior Championships in Athletics") bronze medalist from 2006 and [Olympic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympics "Summer Olympics") competitor from 2008.

He was born in [Kapchorwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapchorwa "Kapchorwa"). By June 2006 he had run the 800 metres in 1:45.0 minutes, at a meet in [Kampala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampala "Kampala").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-iaaf-1) With this he was the season's world leader for juniors—athletes aged nineteen and less.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-beij-2) With electronic timing his best time was 1:45.44 minutes, achieved in a meet in Heusden.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-pace-3) He competed at the [2006 World Junior Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics "2006 World Junior Championships in Athletics") in Beijing, and won the bronze medal, having led the race halfway through but been outsprinted near the end by two Kenyan runners.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-beij-2)

In the 2006–07 indoor season he ran the 800 metres in 1:46.91 minutes in Stuttgart.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-iaaf-1) This was a Ugandan indoor record.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-pace-3) He opened the outdoor season by winning the IAAF Grand Prix in Dakar. He also won the Grand Prix meet in Hengelo, and finished third at the Super Grand Prix meet in Doha, the [Golden Spike Ostrava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Spike_Ostrava "Golden Spike Ostrava") and the [Bislett Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bislett_Games "Bislett Games").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-pace-3) Then, in July 2007 he achieved a new personal best time of 1:44.78 minutes at the Grand Prix meet in Athens.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-iaaf-1) A fifth place at the [All-Africa Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2007_All-Africa_Games "Athletics at the 2007 All-Africa Games")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-pace-3) was followed by the entrance in the [2007 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2007 World Championships in Athletics"). Chepkirwok reached the final round, and in an unusually tight race, where all eight runners finished in the range of 1 minute 47 seconds, Chepkirwok finished fourth with 1:47.41. This was 0.02 seconds behind the bronze medalist, and 0.01 second ahead of the fifth placer.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-4) Rounding off the season, Chepkirwok finished seventh at the [2007 World Athletics Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_IAAF_World_Athletics_Final "2007 IAAF World Athletics Final").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-iaaf-1)

In the 2007–08 indoor season Chepkirwok competed at the [2008 World Indoor Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships_-_Men's_800_metres "2008 IAAF World Indoor Championships - Men's 800 metres"). He reached the semi-final round, finished fourth there but did not progress to the final.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-iaaf-1) During the summer he performed better. He opened with a second place in Doha, then won the [ISTAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internationales_Stadionfest "Internationales Stadionfest")[Golden League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_IAAF_Golden_League "2008 IAAF Golden League") meet in Berlin. He then finished second at the Grand Prix meets in Madrid and Athens, and won the Super Grand Prix meet in Crystal Palace, London.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-pace-3) In Madrid he had achieved a personal best time is 1:43.72 minutes,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-iaaf-1) which is also the Ugandan record.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-pace-3) Entering the [2008 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics"), then, Chepkirwok was the only middle distance runner in the Ugandan squad.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-5) In the [800 metres competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_800_metres "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's 800 metres") he did not reach the final, however. He rounded off the season with a second place at the [2008 World Athletics Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_IAAF_World_Athletics_Final "2008 IAAF World Athletics Final").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-iaaf-1) In early 2009 it was announced that Chepkirwok was a candidate for the title Ugandan Athlete of the Year.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-6) He eventually finished second runner-up for the award, behind [Moses Kipsiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Kipsiro "Moses Kipsiro") and [Benjamin Kiplagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Kiplagat "Benjamin Kiplagat").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-7)

In February 2009 he set a national indoor record in the 1000 metres, running in 2:18.18 minutes in Stuttgart.

Chepkirwok is represented by PACE Sports Management, and is coached by Ricky Simms.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-pace-3)

Abraham Chepkirwok

[![Image 1: Abraham Chepkirwok at ISTAF 2008](https://upload.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/f/fb/Abraham_Chepkirwok.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail_unscaled)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Abraham_Chepkirwok.jpg "Abraham Chepkirwok at ISTAF 2008")
Personal information
Born 18 November 1988 (age 37)
Medal record Men's [athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_(sport) "Athletics (sport)") Representing ![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Flag_of_Uganda.svg/40px-Flag_of_Uganda.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[Uganda](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda") [World Junior Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics "IAAF World Junior Championships in Athletics") ![Image 3: Bronze medal – third place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/60/Bronze_medal_icon_%28B_initial%29.svg/20px-Bronze_medal_icon_%28B_initial%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[2006 Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics "2006 World Junior Championships in Athletics")800 m [World Athletics Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Athletics_Final "IAAF World Athletics Final") ![Image 4: Silver medal – second place](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/91/Silver_medal_icon_%28S_initial%29.svg/20px-Silver_medal_icon_%28S_initial%29.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)[2008 Stuttgart](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_IAAF_World_Athletics_Final "2008 IAAF World Athletics Final")800 m

**Abraham Chepkirwok** (born 18 November 1988) is a [Ugandan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda")[middle-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle-distance_runner "Middle-distance runner") who specializes in the [800 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/800_metres "800 metres"). He is the Ugandan record holder in this distance, with 1:43.72 minutes, achieved in July 2008 in [Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Madrid "Madrid"). He is a [World Junior Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics "IAAF World Junior Championships in Athletics") bronze medalist from 2006 and [Olympic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Summer_Olympics "Summer Olympics") competitor from 2008.

He was born in [Kapchorwa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kapchorwa "Kapchorwa"). By June 2006 he had run the 800 metres in 1:45.0 minutes, at a meet in [Kampala](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampala "Kampala").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-iaaf-1) With this he was the season's world leader for juniors—athletes aged nineteen and less.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-beij-2) With electronic timing his best time was 1:45.44 minutes, achieved in a meet in Heusden.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-pace-3) He competed at the [2006 World Junior Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2006_World_Junior_Championships_in_Athletics "2006 World Junior Championships in Athletics") in Beijing, and won the bronze medal, having led the race halfway through but been outsprinted near the end by two Kenyan runners.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-beij-2)

In the 2006–07 indoor season he ran the 800 metres in 1:46.91 minutes in Stuttgart.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-iaaf-1) This was a Ugandan indoor record.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-pace-3) He opened the outdoor season by winning the IAAF Grand Prix in Dakar. He also won the Grand Prix meet in Hengelo, and finished third at the Super Grand Prix meet in Doha, the [Golden Spike Ostrava](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Spike_Ostrava "Golden Spike Ostrava") and the [Bislett Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bislett_Games "Bislett Games").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-pace-3) Then, in July 2007 he achieved a new personal best time of 1:44.78 minutes at the Grand Prix meet in Athens.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-iaaf-1) A fifth place at the [All-Africa Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2007_All-Africa_Games "Athletics at the 2007 All-Africa Games")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-pace-3) was followed by the entrance in the [2007 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2007 World Championships in Athletics"). Chepkirwok reached the final round, and in an unusually tight race, where all eight runners finished in the range of 1 minute 47 seconds, Chepkirwok finished fourth with 1:47.41. This was 0.02 seconds behind the bronze medalist, and 0.01 second ahead of the fifth placer.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-4) Rounding off the season, Chepkirwok finished seventh at the [2007 World Athletics Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2007_IAAF_World_Athletics_Final "2007 IAAF World Athletics Final").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-iaaf-1)

In the 2007–08 indoor season Chepkirwok competed at the [2008 World Indoor Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_IAAF_World_Indoor_Championships_-_Men's_800_metres "2008 IAAF World Indoor Championships - Men's 800 metres"). He reached the semi-final round, finished fourth there but did not progress to the final.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-iaaf-1) During the summer he performed better. He opened with a second place in Doha, then won the [ISTAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Internationales_Stadionfest "Internationales Stadionfest")[Golden League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_IAAF_Golden_League "2008 IAAF Golden League") meet in Berlin. He then finished second at the Grand Prix meets in Madrid and Athens, and won the Super Grand Prix meet in Crystal Palace, London.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-pace-3) In Madrid he had achieved a personal best time is 1:43.72 minutes,[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-iaaf-1) which is also the Ugandan record.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-pace-3) Entering the [2008 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics"), then, Chepkirwok was the only middle distance runner in the Ugandan squad.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-5) In the [800 metres competition](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2008_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_800_metres "Athletics at the 2008 Summer Olympics – Men's 800 metres") he did not reach the final, however. He rounded off the season with a second place at the [2008 World Athletics Final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_IAAF_World_Athletics_Final "2008 IAAF World Athletics Final").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-iaaf-1) In early 2009 it was announced that Chepkirwok was a candidate for the title Ugandan Athlete of the Year.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-6) He eventually finished second runner-up for the award, behind [Moses Kipsiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moses_Kipsiro "Moses Kipsiro") and [Benjamin Kiplagat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benjamin_Kiplagat "Benjamin Kiplagat").[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-7)

In February 2009 he set a national indoor record in the 1000 metres, running in 2:18.18 minutes in Stuttgart.

Chepkirwok is represented by PACE Sports Management, and is coached by Ricky Simms.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Abraham_Chepkirwok#cite_note-pace-3)

**John Akii-Bua** (3 December 1949 – 20 June 1997) was a [Ugandan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda")[hurdler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurdles "Hurdles") and the first [Olympic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") champion from his country Uganda.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-1) In 1986, he was a recipient of the Silver [Olympic Order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Order "Olympic Order").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-2)

Akii-Bua was raised in a family of 43 children from one father and his eight wives.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-sr-4) Akii-Bua started his athletic career as a short-distance hurdler, but failed to qualify for the 1968 Olympics.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-sr-4) Coached by British-born athletics coach [Malcolm Arnold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_Arnold_(athletics_coach) "Malcolm Arnold (athletics coach)"), he was introduced to the 400 meter hurdles.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-Inzikuru-5) Beyond the hurdles, Akii-Bua was a versatile athlete; in 1971, he set a Ugandan national record in the decathlon with 6,933 points, a record that stood for decades.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6) Following his Olympic triumph, he continued his dominance on the continent, winning gold at the 1973 All-Africa Games in Lagos. Even while his international career was being throttled by political restrictions, he managed to record a personal best of 45.82 seconds in the 400-meter flat in 1976.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6) Arnold identified that while Akii-Bua lacked raw sprinting speed, his willpower and endurance were suited for the longer distance. To prepare for the demands of the event, he adopted a grueling training regimen that included running 1,500-meter repeats over high hurdles while wearing a 25lb weighted vest. He also performed high-altitude conditioning in the hills of [Kabale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabale "Kabale"), consisting of 600-meter uphill sprints twice daily.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6)

Although he finished fourth in the 1970 [Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games "Commonwealth Games") and running the fastest time of 1971 and finishing second at the British [1972 AAA Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_AAA_Championships "1972 AAA Championships"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-9) he was not a big favourite for the [1972 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Summer_Olympics "1972 Summer Olympics") in [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich"), having limited competitive experience. Nevertheless, he won the final there, setting a world record time of 47.82 seconds despite running on the inside lane. Running in Lane 1 was considered a major disadvantage due to the tighter radius of the turn, which required more energy to maintain momentum. Despite suffering from severe pre-race nerves that prevented him from eating, Akii-Bua became the first man to break the 48-second barrier in the event. Following his victory, he famously performed a lap of honor, continuing to jump hurdles even after the race had concluded.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6) He missed the [1976 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Summer_Olympics "1976 Summer Olympics") and a showdown with United States rival [Edwin Moses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Moses "Edwin Moses") because of the boycott by Uganda and other African nations.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-sr-4) The boycott was a significant blow to Akii-Bua’s career; as the defending champion and team captain, he had already arrived in the Olympic Village in Montreal when Amin ordered the team to return home. He was forced to leave on the day of the 400m hurdles final, missing what experts predicted would be his career-defining showdown with American rival Edwin Moses.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6)

As a police officer, Akii-Bua was promoted by Ugandan president [Idi Amin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Idi_Amin "Idi Amin") and given a house as a reward for his athletic prowess. When the Amin regime was collapsing, he fled to [Kenya](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya "Kenya") with his family, fearful that he would be seen as a collaborator; this was more likely because he was a member of the [Langi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Langi_people "Langi people") tribe, many of whom were persecuted by Amin,[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-10) whereas Akii-Bua was cited by Amin as an example of a Langi who was doing well.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6) Despite being used as a propaganda tool to signal tribal unity, Akii-Bua faced significant personal danger; three of his brothers were killed by Amin’s state security forces. While he was promoted to Senior Superintendent of Police, he was frequently denied permission to compete internationally, effectively grounding his career during his athletic prime. The Amin regime’s impact on Akii-Bua’s career went beyond direct physical threats. Despite the "Golden Age" of Ugandan athletics—where the police and army provided professional coaching—Amin's increasing paranoia led to a "house arrest" style of existence for Akii-Bua.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6) He was often denied the necessary exit visas to compete in the lucrative European circuit, preventing him from gaining the tactical experience and financial security enjoyed by his rivals.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6) However, in Kenya he was put into a refugee camp. From there, he was freed by his shoe-manufacturer [Puma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puma_SE "Puma SE") and lived in [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") working for Puma for 3–4 years. He represented Uganda once again at the [1980 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics "1980 Summer Olympics").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-sr-4) Later he returned to Uganda and became a coach.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BBC-11) His escape from Uganda in 1979 involved a perilous car journey through roadblocks, eventually tailing a West German diplomatic convoy to the Kenyan border. During the flight, his wife gave birth prematurely to a child who did not survive. Upon his final return to Uganda in 1983, he found his home looted and his legacy marginalized. He famously remarked to anti-corruption officers that he had "no wealth to declare, only poverty."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6) After the [fall of Amin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Kampala "Fall of Kampala") in 1979, the institutional support for athletics in Uganda collapsed. Many of the facilities built during the 1970s fell into disrepair, and government funding was drastically reduced. Akii-Bua struggled to compete in the 1980 Moscow Olympics and the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, as he was well past his athletic prime and lacked the conditioning support required for elite performance.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6) He remained a police officer until his death, though he never received another promotion after his initial reward in 1972.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6)

Akii-Bua died a widower, at the age of 47, survived by eleven children. He was given a state funeral.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-Inzikuru-5) His nephew is international footballer [David Obua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Obua "David Obua"), and his brother [Lawrence Ogwang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Ogwang "Lawrence Ogwang") competed in the long jump and triple jump at the 1956 Olympics.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-sr-4)

The phrase "_akii-buas_" has come to colloquially mean "runs" in Uganda.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-12)

While he was promoted to Senior Superintendent of Police, he was frequently denied permission to compete internationally, effectively grounding his career during his athletic prime. The Amin regime’s impact on Akii-Bua’s career went beyond direct physical threats. Despite the "Golden Age" of Ugandan athletics—where the police and army provided professional coaching—Amin's increasing paranoia led to a "house arrest" style of existence for Akii-Bua.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6) He was often denied the necessary exit visas to compete in the lucrative European circuit, preventing him from gaining the tactical experience and financial security enjoyed by his rivals.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6) However, in Kenya he was put into a refugee camp. From there, he was freed by his shoe-manufacturer [Puma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puma_SE "Puma SE") and lived in [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") working for Puma for 3–4 years. He represented Uganda once again at the [1980 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics "1980 Summer Olympics").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-sr-4) Later he returned to Uganda and became a coach.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BBC-11) His escape from Uganda in 1979 involved a perilous car journey through roadblocks, eventually tailing a West German diplomatic convoy to the Kenyan border. During the flight, his wife gave birth prematurely to a child who did not survive. Upon his final return to Uganda in 1983, he found his home looted and his legacy marginalized. He famously remarked to anti-corruption officers that he had "no wealth to declare, only poverty."[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6) After the [fall of Amin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fall_of_Kampala "Fall of Kampala") in 1979, the institutional support for athletics in Uganda collapsed. Many of the facilities built during the 1970s fell into disrepair, and government funding was drastically reduced. Akii-Bua struggled to compete in the 1980 Moscow Olympics and the 1984 Los Angeles Olympics, as he was well past his athletic prime and lacked the conditioning support required for elite performance.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6) He remained a police officer until his death, though he never received another promotion after his initial reward in 1972.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6)

Akii-Bua died a widower, at the age of 47, survived by eleven children. He was given a state funeral.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-Inzikuru-5) His nephew is international footballer [David Obua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Obua "David Obua"), and his brother [Lawrence Ogwang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Ogwang "Lawrence Ogwang") competed in the long jump and triple jump at the 1956 Olympics.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-sr-4)

The phrase "_akii-buas_" has come to colloquially mean "runs" in Uganda.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-12)

**John Akii-Bua** (3 December 1949 – 20 June 1997) was a [Ugandan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Uganda "Uganda")[hurdler](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hurdles "Hurdles") and the first [Olympic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Games "Olympic Games") champion from his country Uganda.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-1) In 1986, he was a recipient of the Silver [Olympic Order](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olympic_Order "Olympic Order").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-2)

Akii-Bua was raised in a family of 43 children from one father and his eight wives.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-sr-4) Akii-Bua started his athletic career as a short-distance hurdler, but failed to qualify for the 1968 Olympics.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-sr-4) Coached by British-born athletics coach [Malcolm Arnold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Malcolm_Arnold_(athletics_coach) "Malcolm Arnold (athletics coach)"), he was introduced to the 400 meter hurdles.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-Inzikuru-5) Beyond the hurdles, Akii-Bua was a versatile athlete; in 1971, he set a Ugandan national record in the decathlon with 6,933 points, a record that stood for decades.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6) Following his Olympic triumph, he continued his dominance on the continent, winning gold at the 1973 All-Africa Games in Lagos. Even while his international career was being throttled by political restrictions, he managed to record a personal best of 45.82 seconds in the 400-meter flat in 1976.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6) Arnold identified that while Akii-Bua lacked raw sprinting speed, his willpower and endurance were suited for the longer distance. To prepare for the demands of the event, he adopted a grueling training regimen that included running 1,500-meter repeats over high hurdles while wearing a 25lb weighted vest. He also performed high-altitude conditioning in the hills of [Kabale](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kabale "Kabale"), consisting of 600-meter uphill sprints twice daily.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6)

Although he finished fourth in the 1970 [Commonwealth Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Commonwealth_Games "Commonwealth Games") and running the fastest time of 1971 and finishing second at the British [1972 AAA Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_AAA_Championships "1972 AAA Championships"),[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-9) he was not a big favourite for the [1972 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1972_Summer_Olympics "1972 Summer Olympics") in [Munich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Munich "Munich"), having limited competitive experience. Nevertheless, he won the final there, setting a world record time of 47.82 seconds despite running on the inside lane. Running in Lane 1 was considered a major disadvantage due to the tighter radius of the turn, which required more energy to maintain momentum. Despite suffering from severe pre-race nerves that prevented him from eating, Akii-Bua became the first man to break the 48-second barrier in the event. Following his victory, he famously performed a lap of honor, continuing to jump hurdles even after the race had concluded.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6) He missed the [1976 Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1976_Summer_Olympics "1976 Summer Olympics") and a showdown with United States rival [Edwin Moses](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edwin_Moses "Edwin Moses") because of the boycott by Uganda and other African nations.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-sr-4) The boycott was a significant blow to Akii-Bua’s career; as the defending champion and team captain, he had already arrived in the Olympic Village in Montreal when Amin ordered the team to return home. He was forced to leave on the day of the 400m hurdles final, missing what experts predicted would be his career-defining showdown with American rival Edwin Moses.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BuaDoc-6)

From there, he was freed by his shoe-manufacturer [Puma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Puma_SE "Puma SE") and lived in [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") working for Puma for 3–4 years. He represented Uganda once again at the [1980 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1980_Summer_Olympics "1980 Summer Olympics").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-sr-4) Later he returned to Uganda and became a coach.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-BBC-11) His escape from Uganda in 1979 involved a perilous car journey through roadblocks, eventually tailing a West German diplomatic convoy to the Kenyan border. He was given a state funeral.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-Inzikuru-5) His nephew is international footballer [David Obua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/David_Obua "David Obua"), and his brother [Lawrence Ogwang](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lawrence_Ogwang "Lawrence Ogwang") competed in the long jump and triple jump at the 1956 Olympics.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/John_Akii-Bua#cite_note-sr-4)

**Samuel Kamau Wanjirū** (10 November 1986 – 15 May 2011) was a Kenyan long-distance runner who won the [2008 Beijing Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") Marathon in an [Olympic record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") time of 2:06:32; becoming the first Kenyan to win the Olympic [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_medal "Gold medal") in the marathon. He became the youngest gold medallist in the marathon since 1932.

He held the 10,000m U20 World Record from 2005 until 2024 and set the half marathon world record 3 times.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-2) In 2009, he won both the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") and [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon"), running the fastest marathons ever recorded in the United Kingdom and United States, respectively. He retained his Chicago title in 2010 in a season fraught with injury.

In 2011, he died after a fall from a balcony at his home in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu") following a domestic dispute.

Samuel Wanjirū was born in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu"), [Laikipia County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laikipia_County "Laikipia County"), a town in the [Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Rift_Valley,_Kenya "Great Rift Valley, Kenya"), about 150 kilometres (93 mi) northwest of the capital, [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-huff1-3) and was brought up with his brother Simon Njoroge in poverty by his mother Hannah Wanjiru, the daughter of Samuel Kamau.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-obituary-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-5) Wanjirū took his mother's given name as a surname, because she was a single mother. He dropped out of school aged around 12 because they could not afford the school fees.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-6)

Wanjirū started running at the age of 8. In 2002, he moved to [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") and enrolled in Sendai Ikuei Gakuen High School in [Sendai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai "Sendai"). He had success on the Japanese [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") circuit, where he won the [Fukuoka International Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_International_Cross_Country "Fukuoka International Cross Country") at sixteen years old in 2003. He went on to win in both [Fukuoka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka "Fukuoka") and at the [Chiba International Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiba_International_Cross_Country "Chiba International Cross Country") consecutively in 2004 and 2005.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-7) After graduating in 2005, he joined the [Toyota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota "Toyota")[Kyūshū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ky%C5%ABsh%C5%AB "Kyūshū") athletics team, coached by 1992 Olympic marathon [silver medalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_medal "Silver medal")[Koichi Morishita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koichi_Morishita "Koichi Morishita").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-8)

Wanjirū had a [5000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") best of 13:12.40, run as a 17-year-old in April 2004 in [Hiroshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima "Hiroshima"), Japan. At age 18, Wanjirū broke the half marathon world record on 11 September 2005 in the [Rotterdam Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Half_Marathon "Rotterdam Half Marathon") with a time of 59:16 minutes, officially beating [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat")'s half-marathon record of 59:17 minutes.

This was preceded two weeks earlier by a bettering of the [10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_track_event "Long-distance track event")[U20 world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_junior_records_in_athletics "World junior records in athletics") by a margin of almost 23 seconds in the IAAF Golden League [Van Damme Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Van_Damme "Memorial Van Damme") Race on 26 August. His WJR time of 26:41.75 was good enough for third place in the race behind [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s world record, set in the same race, of 26:17.53 and [Boniface Kiprop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boniface_Kiprop "Boniface Kiprop")'s 26:39.77. It was Kiprop who held the previous world junior mark (27:04.00 minutes), set at the same meeting the previous year. The run saw 6 runners going under 27 minutes[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-10)

### World records and Olympic gold

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Wanjiru&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: World records and Olympic gold")]

Wanjiru took back the half-marathon world record, which [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie") broke in early 2006, with 58:53 minutes on 9 February 2007 at the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah_Half_Marathon "Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-11) and improved it to 58:33 on 17 March 2007 in the [City-Pier-City Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-Pier-City_Loop "City-Pier-City Loop") in [The Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague"), [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"). While improving his own record, he recorded an unofficial time of 55:31 for 20 km, which was faster than Haile Gebrselassie's world record but was never ratified due to the timing methods in the race.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-12)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Samuel_Wanjiru%2C_Marathon%2C_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg/250px-Samuel_Wanjiru%2C_Marathon%2C_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Samuel_Wanjiru,_Marathon,_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg)

Wanjiru approaching the finishing line at the [2008 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics")

Wanjiru made his marathon debut at [Fukuoka Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_Marathon "Fukuoka Marathon") on 2 December 2007, winning it impressively with a course record of 2:06:39.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-13) He started 2008 by winning the [Zayed International Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_International_Half_Marathon "Zayed International Half Marathon") and receiving a prize of US$300,000.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-14) In the 2008 [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon"), he came in second, breaking 2:06 for the first time. In the 2008 Summer Olympics, Wanjiru won the marathon gold medal in an Olympic record time of 2:06:32, smashing the previous record of 2:09:21 set by [Carlos Lopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Lopes "Carlos Lopes") of Portugal in the 1984 Olympics.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-15) He received the [AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIMS_World_Athlete_of_the_Year_Award "AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award") that year in recognition of his performances.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-16)

### London and Chicago wins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Wanjiru&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: London and Chicago wins")]

At the [Granollers Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granollers_Half_Marathon "Granollers Half Marathon") in February 2008, in which Wanjiru won, the Kenyan stated his intent for the future, saying, "in five years' time I feel capable of clocking a sub 2 hours time for the marathon."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-17) In April 2009, Wanjiru won the London Marathon in a time of 2:05:10, a new personal record and also a new course record. He was pleased with the achievement and stated that he hoped to break Haile Gebrselassie's world record in the near future.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-18) At the Rotterdam Half Marathon, Wanjiru clocked a 1:01:08 on 13 September, which was won by [Sammy Kitwara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Kitwara "Sammy Kitwara") with a time of 58:58.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-19) In October 2009, Wanjiru won the [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_winners_of_the_Chicago_Marathon "List of winners of the Chicago Marathon") in a time of 2:05:41, setting a new course record for the city and the fastest marathon time ever run in the United States.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-20) The wins in London and Chicago helped him reach the top of the [World Marathon Majors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Marathon_Majors "World Marathon Majors") rankings for 2009, earning him a jackpot of US$500,000.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-21)

He signed up to defend his title at the [2010 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_London_Marathon "2010 London Marathon"), but he encountered knee trouble at the midway point of the race and decided to drop out to avoid further injury – the first time in six marathons that he had failed to finish.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-22) He chose to run at the 2010 Chicago Marathon in October, but a stomach virus before the race had hampered his preparations and he entered the competition with the lesser aim of reaching the top three. [Tsegaye Kebede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsegaye_Kebede "Tsegaye Kebede") took the opportunity to forge a lead, but Wanjiru (despite a lack of peak physical form) persevered with the pace and caught up with the Ethiopian. He took the lead in the final 400 m to defend his title in Chicago with a time of 2:06:24. "It was the greatest surprise I have ever seen in my life", remarked his coach, Federico Rosa, on the performance.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-24)

Wanjiru married [Mary Wacera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Wacera "Mary Wacera"), a fellow long-distance runner, in 2009 and the two had a child (Ann) in 2010. He had previously married Triza Njeri in a traditional ceremony and had two children, although Wanjiru and Wacera's marriage was legally binding.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

Wanjiru began drinking alcohol when he moved to Japan, and it increased and became a major part of his life. Despite that, his marathoning career continued successfully, though his personal life became somewhat chaotic.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

In December 2010, Wanjiru was arrested by [Kenyan police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Police "Kenya Police") at his house in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu") and charged with threatening to kill his wife and illegally possessing an [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47") rifle. He denied both the accusations and claimed that he was being framed.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-28)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

Wanjiru and his wife Triza Njeri, a beautician, had a daughter Anne Wanjiru and a son Simon Njoroge.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-obituary-4)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-29) Wanjiru also had a third wife, Judy Wambui Wairimu, who was pregnant when he died and has since had a son.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-30)

Wanjiru's cousin [Joseph Riri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Riri?action=edit&redlink=1 "Joseph Riri (page does not exist)") was a world-class marathon runner,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-31) and Wanjiru's younger brother [Simon Njoroge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Njoroge?action=edit&redlink=1 "Simon Njoroge (page does not exist)") was also a long-distance runner.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-32)

On 15 May 2011, Wanjiru died from a fall off a balcony at his home in Nyahururu. Wanjiru appeared to have suffered internal injuries after the fall and was confirmed dead by doctors at a nearby hospital after attempts to revive him failed.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-bbc1-33)

Police said Wanjiru's wife, Triza Njeri, had come home to find him in bed with another woman. She locked the couple in the bedroom and ran outside. Wanjiru then died after falling from the balcony.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-huff1-3) Police were unsure if Wanjiru intended suicide or jumped out of rage, and investigated the circumstances related to Njeri and his female companion that led to his death.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-huff1-3)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-nytLongman16May2011-34)

In May 2017, while testifying during an inquest into Wanjiru's death, his mother Hannah Wanjiru said at the Milimani law court that she believes her son was murdered.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-37)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

His mother claimed at an inquest into his death that her son was murdered by six men who had conspired with his wife Trizah Njeri.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-38) During the inquest at the Milimani court that sought to establish whether Wanjiru was murdered or jumped to his death, a former chief government pathologist said he was convinced that Wanjiru was hit by a blunt object after he had jumped from the balcony of his home, landing on his legs, or that he was possibly pushed and then struck.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-39)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

**Samuel Kamau Wanjirū** (10 November 1986 – 15 May 2011) was a Kenyan long-distance runner who won the [2008 Beijing Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") Marathon in an [Olympic record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") time of 2:06:32; becoming the first Kenyan to win the Olympic [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_medal "Gold medal") in the marathon. He became the youngest gold medallist in the marathon since 1932.

He held the 10,000m U20 World Record from 2005 until 2024 and set the half marathon world record 3 times.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-2) In 2009, he won both the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") and [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon"), running the fastest marathons ever recorded in the United Kingdom and United States, respectively. He retained his Chicago title in 2010 in a season fraught with injury.

In 2011, he died after a fall from a balcony at his home in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu") following a domestic dispute.

Samuel Wanjirū was born in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu"), [Laikipia County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laikipia_County "Laikipia County"), a town in the [Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Rift_Valley,_Kenya "Great Rift Valley, Kenya"), about 150 kilometres (93 mi) northwest of the capital, [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-huff1-3) and was brought up with his brother Simon Njoroge in poverty by his mother Hannah Wanjiru, the daughter of Samuel Kamau.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-obituary-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-5) Wanjirū took his mother's given name as a surname, because she was a single mother. He dropped out of school aged around 12 because they could not afford the school fees.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-6)

Wanjirū started running at the age of 8. In 2002, he moved to [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") and enrolled in Sendai Ikuei Gakuen High School in [Sendai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai "Sendai"). He had success on the Japanese [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") circuit, where he won the [Fukuoka International Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_International_Cross_Country "Fukuoka International Cross Country") at sixteen years old in 2003. He went on to win in both [Fukuoka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka "Fukuoka") and at the [Chiba International Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiba_International_Cross_Country "Chiba International Cross Country") consecutively in 2004 and 2005.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-7) After graduating in 2005, he joined the [Toyota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota "Toyota")[Kyūshū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ky%C5%ABsh%C5%AB "Kyūshū") athletics team, coached by 1992 Olympic marathon [silver medalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_medal "Silver medal")[Koichi Morishita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koichi_Morishita "Koichi Morishita").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-8)

Wanjirū had a [5000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") best of 13:12.40, run as a 17-year-old in April 2004 in [Hiroshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima "Hiroshima"), Japan. At age 18, Wanjirū broke the half marathon world record on 11 September 2005 in the [Rotterdam Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Half_Marathon "Rotterdam Half Marathon") with a time of 59:16 minutes, officially beating [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat")'s half-marathon record of 59:17 minutes.

This was preceded two weeks earlier by a bettering of the [10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_track_event "Long-distance track event")[U20 world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_junior_records_in_athletics "World junior records in athletics") by a margin of almost 23 seconds in the IAAF Golden League [Van Damme Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Van_Damme "Memorial Van Damme") Race on 26 August. His WJR time of 26:41.75 was good enough for third place in the race behind [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s world record, set in the same race, of 26:17.53 and [Boniface Kiprop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boniface_Kiprop "Boniface Kiprop")'s 26:39.77. It was Kiprop who held the previous world junior mark (27:04.00 minutes), set at the same meeting the previous year. The run saw 6 runners going under 27 minutes[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-10)

### World records and Olympic gold

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Wanjiru&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: World records and Olympic gold")]

Wanjiru took back the half-marathon world record, which [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie") broke in early 2006, with 58:53 minutes on 9 February 2007 at the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah_Half_Marathon "Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-11) and improved it to 58:33 on 17 March 2007 in the [City-Pier-City Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-Pier-City_Loop "City-Pier-City Loop") in [The Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague"), [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"). While improving his own record, he recorded an unofficial time of 55:31 for 20 km, which was faster than Haile Gebrselassie's world record but was never ratified due to the timing methods in the race.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-12)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Samuel_Wanjiru%2C_Marathon%2C_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg/250px-Samuel_Wanjiru%2C_Marathon%2C_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Samuel_Wanjiru,_Marathon,_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg)

Wanjiru approaching the finishing line at the [2008 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics")

Wanjiru made his marathon debut at [Fukuoka Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_Marathon "Fukuoka Marathon") on 2 December 2007, winning it impressively with a course record of 2:06:39.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-13) He started 2008 by winning the [Zayed International Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_International_Half_Marathon "Zayed International Half Marathon") and receiving a prize of US$300,000.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-14) In the 2008 [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon"), he came in second, breaking 2:06 for the first time. In the 2008 Summer Olympics, Wanjiru won the marathon gold medal in an Olympic record time of 2:06:32, smashing the previous record of 2:09:21 set by [Carlos Lopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Lopes "Carlos Lopes") of Portugal in the 1984 Olympics.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-15) He received the [AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIMS_World_Athlete_of_the_Year_Award "AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award") that year in recognition of his performances.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-16)

### London and Chicago wins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Wanjiru&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: London and Chicago wins")]

At the [Granollers Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granollers_Half_Marathon "Granollers Half Marathon") in February 2008, in which Wanjiru won, the Kenyan stated his intent for the future, saying, "in five years' time I feel capable of clocking a sub 2 hours time for the marathon."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-17) In April 2009, Wanjiru won the London Marathon in a time of 2:05:10, a new personal record and also a new course record. He was pleased with the achievement and stated that he hoped to break Haile Gebrselassie's world record in the near future.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-18) At the Rotterdam Half Marathon, Wanjiru clocked a 1:01:08 on 13 September, which was won by [Sammy Kitwara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Kitwara "Sammy Kitwara") with a time of 58:58.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-19) In October 2009, Wanjiru won the [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_winners_of_the_Chicago_Marathon "List of winners of the Chicago Marathon") in a time of 2:05:41, setting a new course record for the city and the fastest marathon time ever run in the United States.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-20) The wins in London and Chicago helped him reach the top of the [World Marathon Majors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Marathon_Majors "World Marathon Majors") rankings for 2009, earning him a jackpot of US$500,000.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-21)

He signed up to defend his title at the [2010 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_London_Marathon "2010 London Marathon"), but he encountered knee trouble at the midway point of the race and decided to drop out to avoid further injury – the first time in six marathons that he had failed to finish.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-22) He chose to run at the 2010 Chicago Marathon in October, but a stomach virus before the race had hampered his preparations and he entered the competition with the lesser aim of reaching the top three. [Tsegaye Kebede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsegaye_Kebede "Tsegaye Kebede") took the opportunity to forge a lead, but Wanjiru (despite a lack of peak physical form) persevered with the pace and caught up with the Ethiopian. He took the lead in the final 400 m to defend his title in Chicago with a time of 2:06:24. "It was the greatest surprise I have ever seen in my life", remarked his coach, Federico Rosa, on the performance.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-24)

Wanjiru married [Mary Wacera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Wacera "Mary Wacera"), a fellow long-distance runner, in 2009 and the two had a child (Ann) in 2010. He had previously married Triza Njeri in a traditional ceremony and had two children, although Wanjiru and Wacera's marriage was legally binding.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

Wanjiru began drinking alcohol when he moved to Japan, and it increased and became a major part of his life. Despite that, his marathoning career continued successfully, though his personal life became somewhat chaotic.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

In December 2010, Wanjiru was arrested by [Kenyan police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Police "Kenya Police") at his house in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu") and charged with threatening to kill his wife

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Samuel_Wanjiru%2C_Marathon%2C_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg/250px-Samuel_Wanjiru%2C_Marathon%2C_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Samuel_Wanjiru,_Marathon,_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg)

Wanjiru approaching the finishing line at the [2008 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics")

Wanjiru made his marathon debut at [Fukuoka Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_Marathon "Fukuoka Marathon") on 2 December 2007, winning it impressively with a course record of 2:06:39.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-13) He started 2008 by winning the [Zayed International Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_International_Half_Marathon "Zayed International Half Marathon") and receiving a prize of US$300,000.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-14) In the 2008 [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon"), he came in second, breaking 2:06 for the first time. In the 2008 Summer Olympics, Wanjiru won the marathon gold medal in an Olympic record time of 2:06:32, smashing the previous record of 2:09:21 set by [Carlos Lopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Lopes "Carlos Lopes") of Portugal in the 1984 Olympics.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-15) He received the [AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIMS_World_Athlete_of_the_Year_Award "AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award") that year in recognition of his performances.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-16)

### London and Chicago wins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Wanjiru&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: London and Chicago wins")]

At the [Granollers Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granollers_Half_Marathon "Granollers Half Marathon") in February 2008, in which Wanjiru won, the Kenyan stated his intent for the future, saying, "in five years' time I feel capable of clocking a sub 2 hours time for the marathon."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-17) In April 2009, Wanjiru won the London Marathon in a time of 2:05:10, a new personal record and also a new course record. He was pleased with the achievement and stated that he hoped to break Haile Gebrselassie's world record in the near future.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-18) At the Rotterdam Half Marathon, Wanjiru clocked a 1:01:08 on 13 September, which was won by [Sammy Kitwara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Kitwara "Sammy Kitwara") with a time of 58:58.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-19) In October 2009, Wanjiru won the [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_winners_of_the_Chicago_Marathon "List of winners of the Chicago Marathon") in a time of 2:05:41, setting a new course record for the city and the fastest marathon time ever run in the United States.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-20) The wins in London and Chicago helped him reach the top of the [World Marathon Majors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Marathon_Majors "World Marathon Majors") rankings for 2009, earning him a jackpot of US$500,000.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-21)

He signed up to defend his title at the [2010 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_London_Marathon "2010 London Marathon"), but he encountered knee trouble at the midway point of the race and decided to drop out to avoid further injury – the first time in six marathons that he had failed to finish.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-22) He chose to run at the 2010 Chicago Marathon in October, but a stomach virus before the race had hampered his preparations and he entered the competition with the lesser aim of reaching the top three. [Tsegaye Kebede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsegaye_Kebede "Tsegaye Kebede") took the opportunity to forge a lead, but Wanjiru (despite a lack of peak physical form) persevered with the pace and caught up with the Ethiopian. He took the lead in the final 400 m to defend his title in Chicago with a time of 2:06:24. "It was the greatest surprise I have ever seen in my life", remarked his coach, Federico Rosa, on the performance.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-24)

Wanjiru married [Mary Wacera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Wacera "Mary Wacera"), a fellow long-distance runner, in 2009 and the two had a child (Ann) in 2010. He had previously married Triza Njeri in a traditional ceremony and had two children, although Wanjiru and Wacera's marriage was legally binding.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

Wanjiru began drinking alcohol when he moved to Japan, and it increased and became a major part of his life. Despite that, his marathoning career continued successfully, though his personal life became somewhat chaotic.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

In December 2010, Wanjiru was arrested by [Kenyan police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Police "Kenya Police") at his house in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu") and charged with threatening to kill his wife

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Jaap_Bakema_1966.jpg/250px-Jaap_Bakema_1966.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jaap_Bakema_1966.jpg)

Jaap Bakema in 1966

**Jacob Berend "Jaap" Bakema** (8 March 1914 – 20 February 1981) was a Dutch modernist [architect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architect "Architect"). He is notable for design of public housing and involvement in the reconstruction of [Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam "Rotterdam") after the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), and especially his work with [Jo van den Broek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_van_den_Broek "Jo van den Broek"). The firm was renamed **Van den Broek en Bakema** in 1951. Bakema is also noted for his impact on the direction of [modernist architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist_architecture "Modernist architecture").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jaap_Bakema&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Jacob Berend "Jaap" Bakema was born on 8 March 1914[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-penguin-1) in [Groningen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groningen_(city) "Groningen (city)"), Netherlands.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-curl-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

He studied at the Groningen Higher Technical College[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3) (1931–1936).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-curl-2)

After being inspired by the [Rietveld Schröder House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rietveld_Schr%C3%B6der_House "Rietveld Schröder House") in [Utrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utrecht "Utrecht"), he decided he wanted to be an architect.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3) He enrolled at the [Academy of Architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Architecture_(Amsterdam) "Academy of Architecture (Amsterdam)") in [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam"), where he studied under [Mart Stam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mart_Stam "Mart Stam"), and graduated with distinction in 1941.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-curl-2)

[![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/TerneuzenStadhuis.JPG/250px-TerneuzenStadhuis.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TerneuzenStadhuis.JPG)

Terneuzen town hall

Bakema first worked at the Amsterdam Department of Public Works, in the urban development division. While the Second World War was still on, he moved to [Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam "Rotterdam") and joined the practice of Van Tijen and Maaskant.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

After the war (which ended in 1945), he worked for the Rotterdam Public Housing Agency.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

In 1948, [Jo van den Broek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_van_den_Broek "Jo van den Broek") invited him to join his firm in Rotterdam, Brinkman and Van den Broek Architects. [Jan Brinkman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Brinkman "Jan Brinkman") died in 1949, and in 1951, the practice was renamed Van den Broek en Bakema (Van den Broek & Bakema). The practice played a leading role in Dutch post-war reconstruction rebuilding and expanding the housing in the Netherlands.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-vanes2019-4) The two architects collaborated to design landmarks and neighborhoods in Rotterdam and around the Netherlands.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-5)

[![Image 3](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Hansa4tel_4a.jpg/330px-Hansa4tel_4a.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hansa4tel_4a.jpg)

"Bakema Tower" housing in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin")'s [Hansaviertel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hansaviertel "Hansaviertel"), designed for [Interbau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interbau "Interbau") and built 1959

Van den Broek and Bakema participated in the 1957 [Interbau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interbau "Interbau") project in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"), a post-war building project in which 13 prominent international architects designed buildings for the [Hansaviertel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hansaviertel "Hansaviertel"). Although their building, known as the Bakema Tower, was not constructed until two years after the exhibition of the project opened in July 1957, the plans and models were included in the catalogue.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-7) This was regarded as one of the firm's most significant projects.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

They achieved international fame with some of their projects, including the [Lijnbaan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijnbaan "Lijnbaan") shopping centre (1949-53) and buildings for retailers [Ter Meulen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ter_Meulen "Ter Meulen"), Wassen and Van Vorst (1948-51) in Rotterdam.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Uitbreidingsplan_Pampus_-_Pampus_Expansion_Plan_%286143543120%29.jpg/250px-Uitbreidingsplan_Pampus_-_Pampus_Expansion_Plan_%286143543120%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Uitbreidingsplan_Pampus_-_Pampus_Expansion_Plan_(6143543120).jpg)

Pampus Expansion Plan (1965)

Van den Broek en Bakema was commissioned to design buildings for [Delft University of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delft_University_of_Technology "Delft University of Technology"), including the Faculty of Architecture (1959-64) and the Auditorium (1959-66). Other major projects for which they are known are [Marl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marl,_North_Rhine-Westphalia "Marl, North Rhine-Westphalia") civic centre in Germany (1958-62); [Terneuzen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terneuzen "Terneuzen") town hall in [Zeeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeeland "Zeeland"), Netherlands (1963-72); the [Kennemerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennemerland "Kennemerland") regional plan (1957-59); and the plan for a city on the artificial island [Pampus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampus "Pampus") (1965).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-9)

Van den Broek en Bakema was commissioned to design buildings for [Delft University of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delft_University_of_Technology "Delft University of Technology"), including the Faculty of Architecture (1959-64) and the Auditorium (1959-66). Other major projects for which they are known are [Marl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marl,_North_Rhine-Westphalia "Marl, North Rhine-Westphalia") civic centre in Germany (1958-62); [Terneuzen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terneuzen "Terneuzen") town hall in [Zeeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeeland "Zeeland"), Netherlands (1963-72); the [Kennemerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennemerland "Kennemerland") regional plan (1957-59); and the plan for a city on the artificial island [Pampus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampus "Pampus") (1965).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-10)

Bakema stayed on after Van den Broek left the practice in the early 1970s, working under the same name until his death in 1981.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

In 1946 Bakema began attending meetings of the [Congrès International d'Architecture Moderne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congr%C3%A8s_International_d'Architecture_Moderne "Congrès International d'Architecture Moderne"), became its secretary in 1955, and was a core member of its offshoot [Team 10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_10 "Team 10").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-curl-2)

After the war, first Van den Broek (1947) and then Bakema (1964) were appointed [extraordinary professors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extraordinary_professor "Extraordinary professor") at [Delft University of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delft_University_of_Technology "Delft University of Technology").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-vanes2019-4) In 1965 Bakema became a professor at Staatliche Hochschule in [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg"). He was also a visiting professor at [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University") in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") and [Cornell University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University") in [Ithaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ithaca,_New_York "Ithaca, New York").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

Bakema was an outspoken character, and his personality has often been described in contrast to Van den Broek's, the later analytical, pragmatic, and likened to a schoolmaster, whereas Bakema was more of an idealist, philosopher, and priest.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-vanes2019-4)

Bakema died on 20 February 1981.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-penguin-1) Van den Broek en Bakema carried on, continuing to operate today as Architectenbureau Van den Broek en Bakema.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)As of 2025 the firm continues as [Broekbakema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broekbakema?action=edit&redlink=1 "Broekbakema (page does not exist)")[[nl](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broekbakema "nl:Broekbakema")].[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-11)

Bakema left his mark on both architectural education and the atmosphere of the Department of Architecture at Delft, where he continued to teach until his death.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-vanes2019-4) The architectural practice of Van den Broek and Bakema was a significant player in the postwar reconstruction of the Netherlands, creating large housing projects and creating a new cityscape out of the bombed ruins. He is described by architectural historian Evelien van Es as "among the enthusiastic architects of the post-war period moving [modernist architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist_architecture "Modernist architecture") in a new direction".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-vanes2019-4)

Australian architect [Col James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Col_James_(architect) "Col James (architect)"), who had been influenced by reading about Team 10, spent some time working in Bakema's studio in the early 1960s.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-smhobit2013-12)

In 2000, an exhibition called _The Function of the Form – Van den Broek & Bakema Architecture and Urban Design_ was held at the [Netherlands Architecture Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands_Architecture_Institute "Netherlands Architecture Institute") in Rotterdam. The exhibition, which included original drawings and models, photographs, film footage, and audio tapes, was the largest survey of their work to date.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-13)

*   [Lijnbaan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijnbaan "Lijnbaan"), Rotterdam (1949-54)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-penguin-1)
*   Amstleven, Amsterdam (1961)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-penguin-1)
*   [Buikslotermeer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buikslotermeer "Buikslotermeer"), Amsterdam (1962)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-penguin-1)
*   [Marl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marl,_North_Rhine-Westphalia "Marl, North Rhine-Westphalia") Civic Center, Germany (1958-62)
*   [Terneuzen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terneuzen "Terneuzen") Town Hall, Netherlands (1968)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-curl-2)
*   Netherlands Pavilion, [Expo '70](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Expo_'70 "Expo '70"), Osaka (1970)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-penguin-1)
*   Psychiatric hospital, [Middelharnis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middelharnis "Middelharnis") (1973-74)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-curl-2)
