From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

[![Image 1](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/f0/Jaap_Bakema_1966.jpg/250px-Jaap_Bakema_1966.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Jaap_Bakema_1966.jpg)

Jaap Bakema in 1966

**Jacob Berend "Jaap" Bakema** (8 March 1914 – 20 February 1981) was a Dutch modernist [architect](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Architect "Architect"). He is notable for design of public housing and involvement in the reconstruction of [Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam "Rotterdam") after the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), and especially his work with [Jo van den Broek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_van_den_Broek "Jo van den Broek"). The firm was renamed **Van den Broek en Bakema** in 1951. Bakema is also noted for his impact on the direction of [modernist architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist_architecture "Modernist architecture").

## Early life and education

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Jaap_Bakema&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and education")]

Jacob Berend "Jaap" Bakema was born on 8 March 1914[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-penguin-1) in [Groningen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Groningen_(city) "Groningen (city)"), Netherlands.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-curl-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

He studied at the Groningen Higher Technical College[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3) (1931–1936).[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-curl-2)

After being inspired by the [Rietveld Schröder House](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rietveld_Schr%C3%B6der_House "Rietveld Schröder House") in [Utrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utrecht "Utrecht"), he decided he wanted to be an architect.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3) He enrolled at the [Academy of Architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Academy_of_Architecture_(Amsterdam) "Academy of Architecture (Amsterdam)") in [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam"), where he studied under [Mart Stam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mart_Stam "Mart Stam"), and graduated with distinction in 1941.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-curl-2)

[![Image 2](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/6/64/TerneuzenStadhuis.JPG/250px-TerneuzenStadhuis.JPG?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:TerneuzenStadhuis.JPG)

Terneuzen town hall

Bakema first worked at the Amsterdam Department of Public Works, in the urban development division. While the Second World War was still on, he moved to [Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam "Rotterdam") and joined the practice of Van Tijen and Maaskant.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

After the war (which ended in 1945), he worked for the Rotterdam Public Housing Agency.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

In 1948, [Jo van den Broek](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_van_den_Broek "Jo van den Broek") invited him to join his firm in Rotterdam, Brinkman and Van den Broek Architects. [Jan Brinkman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jan_Brinkman "Jan Brinkman") died in 1949, and in 1951, the practice was renamed Van den Broek en Bakema (Van den Broek & Bakema). The practice played a leading role in Dutch post-war reconstruction rebuilding and expanding the housing in the Netherlands.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-vanes2019-4) The two architects collaborated to design landmarks and neighborhoods in Rotterdam and around the Netherlands.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-5)

[![Image 3](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/44/Hansa4tel_4a.jpg/330px-Hansa4tel_4a.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hansa4tel_4a.jpg)

"Bakema Tower" housing in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin")'s [Hansaviertel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hansaviertel "Hansaviertel"), designed for [Interbau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interbau "Interbau") and built 1959

Van den Broek and Bakema participated in the 1957 [Interbau](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Interbau "Interbau") project in [Berlin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin "Berlin"), a post-war building project in which 13 prominent international architects designed buildings for the [Hansaviertel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hansaviertel "Hansaviertel"). Although their building, known as the Bakema Tower, was not constructed until two years after the exhibition of the project opened in July 1957, the plans and models were included in the catalogue.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-7) This was regarded as one of the firm's most significant projects.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

They achieved international fame with some of their projects, including the [Lijnbaan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijnbaan "Lijnbaan") shopping centre (1949-53) and buildings for retailers [Ter Meulen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ter_Meulen "Ter Meulen"), Wassen and Van Vorst (1948-51) in Rotterdam.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Uitbreidingsplan_Pampus_-_Pampus_Expansion_Plan_%286143543120%29.jpg/250px-Uitbreidingsplan_Pampus_-_Pampus_Expansion_Plan_%286143543120%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Uitbreidingsplan_Pampus_-_Pampus_Expansion_Plan_(6143543120).jpg)

Pampus Expansion Plan (1965)

Van den Broek en Bakema was commissioned to design buildings for [Delft University of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delft_University_of_Technology "Delft University of Technology"), including the Faculty of Architecture (1959-64) and the Auditorium (1959-66). Other major projects for which they are known are [Marl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marl,_North_Rhine-Westphalia "Marl, North Rhine-Westphalia") civic centre in Germany (1958-62); [Terneuzen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terneuzen "Terneuzen") town hall in [Zeeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeeland "Zeeland"), Netherlands (1963-72); the [Kennemerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennemerland "Kennemerland") regional plan (1957-59); and the plan for a city on the artificial island [Pampus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampus "Pampus") (1965).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-9)

Van den Broek en Bakema was commissioned to design buildings for [Delft University of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delft_University_of_Technology "Delft University of Technology"), including the Faculty of Architecture (1959-64) and the Auditorium (1959-66). Other major projects for which they are known are [Marl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marl,_North_Rhine-Westphalia "Marl, North Rhine-Westphalia") civic centre in Germany (1958-62); [Terneuzen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terneuzen "Terneuzen") town hall in [Zeeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeeland "Zeeland"), Netherlands (1963-72); the [Kennemerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennemerland "Kennemerland") regional plan (1957-59); and the plan for a city on the artificial island [Pampus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampus "Pampus") (1965).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-10)

Bakema stayed on after Van den Broek left the practice in the early 1970s, working under the same name until his death in 1981.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

In 1946 Bakema began attending meetings of the [Congrès International d'Architecture Moderne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congr%C3%A8s_International_d'Architecture_Moderne "Congrès International d'Architecture Moderne"), became its secretary in 1955, and was a core member of its offshoot [Team 10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_10 "Team 10").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-curl-2)

After the war, first Van den Broek (1947) and then Bakema (1964) were appointed [extraordinary professors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extraordinary_professor "Extraordinary professor") at [Delft University of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delft_University_of_Technology "Delft University of Technology").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-vanes2019-4) In 1965 Bakema became a professor at Staatliche Hochschule in [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg"). He was also a visiting professor at [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University") in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") and [Cornell University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University") in [Ithaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ithaca,_New_York "Ithaca, New York").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

Bakema was an outspoken character, and his personality has often been described in contrast to Van den Broek's, the later analytical, pragmatic, and likened to a schoolmaster, whereas Bakema was more of an idealist, philosopher, and priest.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-vanes2019-4)

Bakema died on 20 February 1981.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-penguin-1) Van den Broek en Bakema carried on, continuing to operate today as Architectenbureau Van den Broek en Bakema.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)As of 2025 the firm continues as [Broekbakema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broekbakema?action=edit&redlink=1 "Broekbakema (page does not exist)")[[nl](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broekbakema "nl:Broekbakema")].[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-11)

Bakema left his mark on both architectural education and the atmosphere of the Department of Architecture at Delft, where he continued to teach until his death.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-vanes2019-4) The architectural practice of Van den Broek and Bakema was a significant player in the postwar reconstruction of the Netherlands, creating large housing projects and creating a new cityscape out of the bombed ruins. He is described by architectural historian Evelien van Es as "among the enthusiastic architects of the post-war period moving [modernist architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist_architecture "Modernist architecture") in a new direction".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-vanes2019-4)

Australian architect [Col James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Col_James_(architect) "Col James (architect)"), who had been influenced by reading about Team 10, spent some time working in Bakema's studio in the early 1960s.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-smhobit2013-12)

In 2000, an exhibition called _The Function of the Form – Van den Broek & Bakema Architecture and Urban Design_ was held at the [Netherlands Architecture Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands_Architecture_Institute "Netherlands Architecture Institute") in Rotterdam. The exhibition, which included original drawings and models, photographs, film footage, and audio tapes, was the largest survey of their work to date.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-13)

*   [Lijnbaan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijnbaan "Lijnbaan"), Rotterdam (1949-54)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-penguin-1)
*   Amstleven, Amsterdam (1961)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-penguin-1)
*   [Buikslotermeer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Buikslotermeer "Buikslotermeer"), Amsterdam (1962)[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-penguin-1)
*   [Marl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marl,_North_Rhine-Westphalia "Marl, North Rhine-Westphalia") Civic Center, Germany (1958-62)
*   [Terneuzen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terneuzen "Terneuzen") Town Hall, Netherlands (1968)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-curl-2)

*   Psychiatric hospital, [Middelharnis](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middelharnis "Middelharnis") (1973-74)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-curl-2)

Although their building, known as the Bakema Tower, was not constructed until two years after the exhibition of the project opened in July 1957, the plans and models were included in the catalogue.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-7) This was regarded as one of the firm's most significant projects.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

They achieved international fame with some of their projects, including the [Lijnbaan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lijnbaan "Lijnbaan") shopping centre (1949-53) and buildings for retailers [Ter Meulen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ter_Meulen "Ter Meulen"), Wassen and Van Vorst (1948-51) in Rotterdam.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

[![Image 4](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/0/0b/Uitbreidingsplan_Pampus_-_Pampus_Expansion_Plan_%286143543120%29.jpg/250px-Uitbreidingsplan_Pampus_-_Pampus_Expansion_Plan_%286143543120%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Uitbreidingsplan_Pampus_-_Pampus_Expansion_Plan_(6143543120).jpg)

Pampus Expansion Plan (1965)

Van den Broek en Bakema was commissioned to design buildings for [Delft University of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delft_University_of_Technology "Delft University of Technology"), including the Faculty of Architecture (1959-64) and the Auditorium (1959-66). Other major projects for which they are known are [Marl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marl,_North_Rhine-Westphalia "Marl, North Rhine-Westphalia") civic centre in Germany (1958-62); [Terneuzen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terneuzen "Terneuzen") town hall in [Zeeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeeland "Zeeland"), Netherlands (1963-72); the [Kennemerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennemerland "Kennemerland") regional plan (1957-59); and the plan for a city on the artificial island [Pampus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampus "Pampus") (1965).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-9)

Van den Broek en Bakema was commissioned to design buildings for [Delft University of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delft_University_of_Technology "Delft University of Technology"), including the Faculty of Architecture (1959-64) and the Auditorium (1959-66). Other major projects for which they are known are [Marl](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marl,_North_Rhine-Westphalia "Marl, North Rhine-Westphalia") civic centre in Germany (1958-62); [Terneuzen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Terneuzen "Terneuzen") town hall in [Zeeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zeeland "Zeeland"), Netherlands (1963-72); the [Kennemerland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kennemerland "Kennemerland") regional plan (1957-59); and the plan for a city on the artificial island [Pampus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pampus "Pampus") (1965).[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-10)

Bakema stayed on after Van den Broek left the practice in the early 1970s, working under the same name until his death in 1981.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

In 1946 Bakema began attending meetings of the [Congrès International d'Architecture Moderne](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Congr%C3%A8s_International_d'Architecture_Moderne "Congrès International d'Architecture Moderne"), became its secretary in 1955, and was a core member of its offshoot [Team 10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Team_10 "Team 10").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-curl-2)

After the war, first Van den Broek (1947) and then Bakema (1964) were appointed [extraordinary professors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Extraordinary_professor "Extraordinary professor") at [Delft University of Technology](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Delft_University_of_Technology "Delft University of Technology").[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-vanes2019-4) In 1965 Bakema became a professor at Staatliche Hochschule in [Hamburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg "Hamburg"). He was also a visiting professor at [Columbia University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Columbia_University "Columbia University") in [New York City](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City "New York City") and [Cornell University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cornell_University "Cornell University") in [Ithaca](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ithaca,_New_York "Ithaca, New York").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)

Bakema was an outspoken character, and his personality has often been described in contrast to Van den Broek's, the later analytical, pragmatic, and likened to a schoolmaster, whereas Bakema was more of an idealist, philosopher, and priest.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-vanes2019-4)

Bakema died on 20 February 1981.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-penguin-1) Van den Broek en Bakema carried on, continuing to operate today as Architectenbureau Van den Broek en Bakema.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-team10-3)As of 2025 the firm continues as [Broekbakema](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broekbakema?action=edit&redlink=1 "Broekbakema (page does not exist)")[[nl](https://nl.wikipedia.org/wiki/Broekbakema "nl:Broekbakema")].[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-11)

Bakema left his mark on both architectural education and the atmosphere of the Department of Architecture at Delft, where he continued to teach until his death.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-vanes2019-4) The architectural practice of Van den Broek and Bakema was a significant player in the postwar reconstruction of the Netherlands, creating large housing projects and creating a new cityscape out of the bombed ruins. He is described by architectural historian Evelien van Es as "among the enthusiastic architects of the post-war period moving [modernist architecture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Modernist_architecture "Modernist architecture") in a new direction".[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-vanes2019-4)

Australian architect [Col James](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Col_James_(architect) "Col James (architect)"), who had been influenced by reading about Team 10, spent some time working in Bakema's studio in the early 1960s.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-smhobit2013-12)

In 2000, an exhibition called _The Function of the Form – Van den Broek & Bakema Architecture and Urban Design_ was held at the [Netherlands Architecture Institute](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands_Architecture_Institute "Netherlands Architecture Institute") in Rotterdam. The exhibition, which included original drawings and models, photographs, film footage, and audio tapes, was the largest survey of their work to date.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jaap_Bakema#cite_note-13)

The **Netherlands**,[[l]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-23) also informally known as **Holland**, is a country in [Northwestern Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwestern_Europe "Northwestern Europe"), with [overseas territories](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean_Netherlands "Caribbean Netherlands") in the [Caribbean](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Caribbean "Caribbean"). It is the largest of the four constituent countries of the [Kingdom of the Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_the_Netherlands "Kingdom of the Netherlands").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-24) The Netherlands consists of [twelve provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provinces_of_the_Netherlands "Provinces of the Netherlands") and three overseas special municipalities. European Netherlands has land borders with [Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germany "Germany") to the east and with [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium") to the south, and a coastline to the north and west. It shares [maritime borders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maritime_boundary "Maritime boundary") with the [United Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/United_Kingdom "United Kingdom"), Germany, and Belgium in the [North Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea "North Sea").[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-25) The official language is [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_language "Dutch language"), with [West Frisian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Frisian_language "West Frisian language") as a secondary official language in the province of [Friesland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Friesland "Friesland").[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-official-and-recognised-languages-2) Dutch, English, and [Papiamento](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Papiamento "Papiamento") are official languages in the Caribbean territories.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-official-and-recognised-languages-2) People from the Netherlands are referred to as [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_people "Dutch people").[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-26)

_Netherlands_ literally means "lower countries", in reference to its low elevation and flat topography, 26% of which is below [sea level](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Height_above_mean_sea_level "Height above mean sea level").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-schiermeier-2010-27) Most of the areas below sea level, known as [_polders_](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Polder "Polder"), are the result of [land reclamation that began in the 14th century](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Land_reclamation_in_the_Netherlands "Land reclamation in the Netherlands").[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Cavendish_2003-28) The [Dutch Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Republic "Dutch Republic") experienced major political, economic, and cultural development; this period is commonly known as the [Dutch Golden Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Golden_Age "Dutch Golden Age").[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-29) During this time, its trading companies, the [Dutch East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company "Dutch East India Company") and the [Dutch West India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_West_India_Company "Dutch West India Company"), established multiple colonies and trading posts.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-30)[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-31) While neutral in the [First World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/First_World_War "First World War"), the Netherlands was [invaded](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/German_invasion_of_the_Netherlands "German invasion of the Netherlands") and [occupied](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reichskommissariat_Niederlande "Reichskommissariat Niederlande") by [Nazi Germany](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nazi_Germany "Nazi Germany") in 1940 during the [Second World War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_World_War "Second World War"), which lasted until the end of the war in 1945.

With a population of over 18 million people, all living within a total area of 41,850 km 2 (16,160 sq mi)—of which the land area is 33,500 km 2 (12,900 sq mi)—the Netherlands is the [15th most densely populated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_and_dependencies_by_population_density "List of countries and dependencies by population density") country, with a density of 433 people per square kilometre (1,120 people/sq mi). Nevertheless, it is the world's second largest exporter of food and agricultural products by value, owing to its fertile soil, mild climate, intensive agriculture, and [inventiveness](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Dutch_inventions_and_innovations "List of Dutch inventions and innovations").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-32)[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-hollandtrade.com-33)[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-nationalgeographic.com-34) The four largest cities are [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam"), [Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam "Rotterdam"), [The Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague") and [Utrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utrecht "Utrecht").[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-35) Amsterdam is most populous city and the nominal [capital](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capital_of_the_Netherlands "Capital of the Netherlands"), though the primary national political institutions are in The Hague.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-36)

The Netherlands has been a parliamentary [constitutional monarchy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Constitutional_monarchy "Constitutional monarchy") with a [unitary structure](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Unitary_state "Unitary state") since 1848. The country has a tradition of [pillarisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pillarisation "Pillarisation") (separation of citizens into groups by religion and political beliefs) and a long record of social tolerance, having legalised [prostitution](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prostitution_in_the_Netherlands "Prostitution in the Netherlands") and [euthanasia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euthanasia_and_assisted_suicide_in_the_Netherlands "Euthanasia and assisted suicide in the Netherlands"), along with maintaining [a liberal drug policy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_policy_of_the_Netherlands "Drug policy of the Netherlands"). The Netherlands allowed women's suffrage in 1919 and was the first country to legalise [same-sex marriage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Same-sex_marriage_in_the_Netherlands "Same-sex marriage in the Netherlands") in 2001.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-37) A [developed country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Developed_country "Developed country"), its [mixed-market](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mixed_economy "Mixed economy")[advanced economy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Advanced_economy "Advanced economy") is the [18th-largest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(nominal) "List of countries by GDP (nominal)") in the world and has the [11th-highest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_countries_by_GDP_(PPP)_per_capita "List of countries by GDP (PPP) per capita") per capita income globally. The Hague holds the seat of the [States General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States_General_of_the_Netherlands "States General of the Netherlands"), [cabinet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cabinet_of_the_Netherlands "Cabinet of the Netherlands"), and [Supreme Court](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Supreme_Court_of_the_Netherlands "Supreme Court of the Netherlands").[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-38) The [Port of Rotterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Port_of_Rotterdam "Port of Rotterdam") is the [busiest in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_busiest_ports_in_Europe "List of busiest ports in Europe").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Ec.europa.eu/eurostat/web/products-eurostat-news/-/ddn-20200402-2_2021-11-25-39)[Schiphol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Airport_Schiphol "Amsterdam Airport Schiphol") is the [busiest airport in the Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_the_Netherlands "List of the busiest airports in the Netherlands") and the [fourth busiest in Europe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_the_busiest_airports_in_Europe "List of the busiest airports in Europe"). The Netherlands is a founding member of the [European Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/European_Union "European Union"), [eurozone](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eurozone "Eurozone"), [G10](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Group_of_Ten_(economics) "Group of Ten (economics)"), [NATO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/NATO "NATO"), [OECD](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/OECD "OECD"), and [World Trade Organization](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Trade_Organization "World Trade Organization"), as well as a part of the [Schengen Area](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Schengen_Area "Schengen Area") and the trilateral [Benelux Union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benelux_Union "Benelux Union"). It hosts [intergovernmental organisations](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Intergovernmental_organisation "Intergovernmental organisation") and [international courts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/International_court "International court"), many of which are in The Hague.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-40)

## Etymology

### Netherlands and the Low Countries

In most [Romance languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_languages "Romance languages"), the term "[Low Countries](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Low_Countries "Low Countries")" is officially used as the name for the Netherlands. The countries that constitute the region called the Low Countries (Netherlands, [Belgium](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Belgium "Belgium"), and [Luxembourg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Luxembourg "Luxembourg")) all have similar [toponymy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toponymy "Toponymy"). Place names with _Neder_, _Nieder_, _Nedre_, _Nether_, _Lage(r)_ or _Low(er)_ (in [Germanic languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanic_languages "Germanic languages")) and _Bas_ or _Inferior_ (in [Romance languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romance_languages "Romance languages")) are in use in low-lying places all over Europe. The [Romans](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") made a distinction between the Roman provinces of downstream [Germania Inferior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germania_Inferior "Germania Inferior") (nowadays part of Belgium and the Netherlands) and upstream [Germania Superior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germania_Superior "Germania Superior"). Thus, in the case of the Low Countries and the Netherlands, the geographical location of this _lower_ region is more or less downstream and near the sea, compared to that of the upper region of Germania Superior. The designation 'low' returned in the 10th-century Duchy of [Lower Lorraine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Lorraine "Lower Lorraine"), which covered much of the Low Countries.[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Franks_(Columbia_Encyclopedia)-41)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-42)

The [Dukes of Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dukes_of_Burgundy "Dukes of Burgundy") used the term _les pays de par deçà_ ("the lands over here") for the Low Countries.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-BlockmansPrevenier2010-43) Under [Habsburg rule](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Habsburg_Netherlands "Habsburg Netherlands"), this became _pays d'embas_ ("lands down here").[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-44) This was translated as _Neder-landen_ in contemporary Dutch official documents.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Lem-45) From a regional point of view, _Niderlant_ was also the area between the [Meuse](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meuse "Meuse") and the lower [Rhine](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rhine "Rhine") in the late Middle Ages. From the mid-16th century, the "Low Countries" and the "Netherlands" lost their original [deictic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Deixis "Deixis") meaning.

### Holland

The term _[Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holland "Holland")_ has frequently been used [informally](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Colloquialism "Colloquialism") to [refer to the whole](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pars_pro_toto "Pars pro toto") of the modern country of the Netherlands in various languages,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-MoFA-46) including [Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_language "Dutch language")[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Van_Dale-47)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-48) and English. In some languages, Holland is used as the formal name for the Netherlands. However, Holland is a region within the Netherlands that consists of the two provinces of [North](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Holland "North Holland") and [South Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/South_Holland "South Holland"). Formerly these were a single province, and earlier the [County of Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Holland "County of Holland"), which also included parts of present-day [Utrecht province](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Utrecht_(province) "Utrecht (province)"). The emphasis on Holland during the formation of the [Dutch Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Republic "Dutch Republic"), the [Eighty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighty_Years'_War "Eighty Years' War"), and the [Anglo-Dutch wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Dutch_wars "Anglo-Dutch wars") in the 17th and 18th centuries made Holland a _pars pro toto_ for the entire country.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-49)[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-50)

Many Dutch people object to the country being referred to as _Holland_ instead of _the Netherlands_, on much the same grounds as many [Welsh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Welsh_people "Welsh people") or [Scottish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Scottish_people "Scottish people") people object to the United Kingdom being referred to as England.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-51) In particular, those from regions other than Holland find it undesirable or misrepresentative to use the term Holland for the whole country,[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-MoFA-46) as the Holland region only comprises two of the twelve provinces, and 38% of Dutch citizens. As of 2019, the Dutch government officially has preferred _the Netherlands_ over _Holland_ when talking about the country _._[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-52)[[41]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-53)[[42]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-54)

Often _Holland_ or _Hollanders_ are used by the [Flemish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flemish_people "Flemish people") to refer to the Dutch in the Netherlands.[[43]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-55) The terms are used in a [derogatory](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pejorative "Pejorative") fashion [[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-ensie-2023-56)[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-nos-2017-57) by the Dutch living south of [the great rivers](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Grote_rivieren "Grote rivieren") (a natural [cultural](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Culture_of_the_Netherlands "Culture of the Netherlands"), [social](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demographics_of_the_Netherlands "Demographics of the Netherlands"), and [religious](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Religion_in_the_Netherlands "Religion in the Netherlands") boundary formed by the rivers Rhine and Meuse) to refer to the Dutch in the north.[[44]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-ensie-2023-56) In the southern province of [Limburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limburg_(Netherlands) "Limburg (Netherlands)"), the term is used for the Dutch from the other 11 provinces.[[45]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-nos-2017-57)

### Dutch

_Dutch_ is used in English as the adjective for the Netherlands, as well as the [demonym](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Demonym "Demonym"). The origins of the word go back to proto-Germanic _[*þiudiskaz](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Reconstruction:Proto-Germanic/%C3%BEiudiskaz#Proto-Germanic "wikt:Reconstruction:Proto-Germanic/þiudiskaz")_ ([Latinised](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Onomastic_Latinisation "Onomastic Latinisation") into _[Theodiscus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Theodiscus "Theodiscus")_), meaning "popular" or "of the people", the origin of [Old Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch "Old Dutch")_[*thiudisc](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/Reconstruction:Old%20Dutch/thiudisc#Old\_Dutch "wikt:Reconstruction:Old Dutch/thiudisc")_ and [Old English](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_English "Old English")_[þeodisc](https://en.wiktionary.org/wiki/%C3%BEeodisc#Old\_English "wikt:þeodisc")_, meaning "(of) the common ([Germanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanic_peoples "Germanic peoples")) people".[[46]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-58) At first, the English language used _Dutch_ to refer to any or all speakers of [West Germanic languages](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Germanic_languages "West Germanic languages"). The term gradually came to be used more narrowly to refer to the West Germanic people with whom the English had the most contact.[[47]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-59)

## History

### Prehistory (before 800 BC)

[![Image 13](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4f/5500vc_ex_leg.jpg/250px-5500vc_ex_leg.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:5500vc_ex_leg.jpg)

The Netherlands in 5500 BC

[![Image 14](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/9/99/BronzAgeElp.png/250px-BronzAgeElp.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:BronzAgeElp.png)

Bronze Age cultures in the Netherlands

The oldest human ([Neanderthal](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neanderthal "Neanderthal")) traces in the Netherlands, believed to be about 250,000 years old, were found near [Maastricht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maastricht "Maastricht").[[48]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-60) At the end of the [Ice Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weichselian_glaciation "Weichselian glaciation"), the nomadic late Upper Palaeolithic [Hamburg culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hamburg_culture "Hamburg culture") (13,000–10,000 BC) hunted [reindeer](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Reindeer "Reindeer") in the area, using spears. The later [Ahrensburg culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ahrensburg_culture "Ahrensburg culture") (11,200–9,500 BC) used [bow and arrow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bow_and_arrow "Bow and arrow"). From Mesolithic [Maglemosian-like tribes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Maglemosian_culture "Maglemosian culture") (c. 8000 BC), the world's [oldest canoe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pesse_canoe "Pesse canoe") was found in [Drenthe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drenthe "Drenthe").[[49]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-61)

Indigenous late Mesolithic hunter-gatherers from the [Swifterbant culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Swifterbant_culture "Swifterbant culture") (c. 5600 BC), related to the southern Scandinavian [Ertebølle culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erteb%C3%B8lle_culture "Ertebølle culture"), were strongly linked to rivers and open water.[[50]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Kooijmans1998-62) Between 4800 and 4500 BC, the Swifterbant people started to adopt from the neighbouring [Linear Pottery culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Linear_Pottery_culture "Linear Pottery culture") the practice of animal husbandry, and between 4300 and 4000 BC agriculture.[[51]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-63) The [Funnelbeaker culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Funnelbeaker_culture "Funnelbeaker culture") (4300–2800 BC) erected the [dolmens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dolmens "Dolmens"), large stone grave monuments found in Drenthe. There was a quick transition from the Funnelbeaker [farming culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Early_European_Farmers "Early European Farmers") to the pan-European pastoralist [Corded Ware culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Corded_Ware_culture "Corded Ware culture") (c. 2950 BC). In the southwest, the [Seine–Oise–Marne culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seine%E2%80%93Oise%E2%80%93Marne_culture "Seine–Oise–Marne culture")—related to the [Vlaardingen culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vlaardingen_culture "Vlaardingen culture") (c. 2600 BC)—survived well into the [Neolithic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Neolithic "Neolithic") period, until it too was succeeded by the Corded Ware culture.

The subsequent [Bell Beaker culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bell_Beaker_culture "Bell Beaker culture") (2700–2100 BC)[[52]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-64) introduced metalwork in copper, gold and later bronze and opened new international trade routes, reflected in [copper artefacts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chalcolithic_Europe "Chalcolithic Europe"). Finds of rare bronze objects suggest that Drenthe was a trading centre in the [Bronze Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bronze_Age_Europe "Bronze Age Europe") (2000–800 BC). The Bell Beaker culture developed locally into the Barbed-Wire Beaker culture (2100–1800 BC) and later the [Elp culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elp_culture "Elp culture") (1800–800 BC),[[53]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-65) a Middle Bronze Age culture marked by earthenware pottery. The southern region became dominated by the related [Hilversum culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hilversum_culture "Hilversum culture") (1800–800 BC).

### Celts, Germanic tribes and Romans (800 BC–410 AD)

From 800 BC onwards, the [Iron Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Iron_Age_Europe "Iron Age Europe") Celtic [Hallstatt culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hallstatt_culture "Hallstatt culture") became influential. Iron ore brought a measure of prosperity and was available throughout the country. [Smiths](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Blacksmith "Blacksmith") travelled from settlement to settlement with bronze and iron, fabricating tools on demand. The [King's grave of Oss](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vorstengraf_(Oss) "Vorstengraf (Oss)") (700 BC) was found in a burial mound, the largest of its kind in Western Europe.

The deteriorating climate in Scandinavia from 850 BC and 650 BC might have triggered the migration of [Germanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germanic_peoples "Germanic peoples") tribes from the north. By the time this migration was complete, around 250 BC, a few general cultural and linguistic groups had emerged.[[54]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-66)[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Verhaal-67) The [North Sea Germanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea_Germanic "North Sea Germanic")[Ingaevones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ingaevones "Ingaevones") inhabited the northern part of the Low Countries. They would later develop into the [Frisii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frisii "Frisii") and the early [Saxons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxons "Saxons").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Verhaal-67) The [Weser–Rhine Germanic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weser%E2%80%93Rhine_Germanic "Weser–Rhine Germanic") (or [Istvaeones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Istvaeones "Istvaeones")) extended along the middle Rhine and [Weser](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weser "Weser") and inhabited the Low Countries south of the great rivers. These tribes would eventually develop into the [Salian Franks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salian_Franks "Salian Franks").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Verhaal-67) The [Celtic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Celts "Celts")[La Tène culture](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/La_T%C3%A8ne_culture "La Tène culture") (c. 450 BC to the Roman conquest) expanded over a wide range, including the southern area of the Low Countries. Some scholars speculate that even a third ethnic identity and language, neither Germanic nor Celtic, survived in the Netherlands until the Roman period, the [Nordwestblock](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nordwestblock "Nordwestblock") culture.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-68)[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Lendering-69)

[![Image 15](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/49/Germania_70.svg/250px-Germania_70.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Germania_70.svg)

The Rhine frontier around 70 AD

The first author to describe the coast of Holland and [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Flanders "Flanders") was the geographer [Pytheas](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pytheas "Pytheas"), who notes in c. 325 BC that in these regions, "more people died in the struggle against water than in the struggle against men."[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-70) During the [Gallic Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallic_Wars "Gallic Wars"), the area south and west of the Rhine was conquered by [Roman forces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Roman_Empire "Roman Empire") under [Julius Caesar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julius_Caesar "Julius Caesar") from 57 BC to 53 BC.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Lendering-69) Caesar describes two main Celtic tribes living in what is now the southern Netherlands: the [Menapii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Menapii "Menapii") and the [Eburones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eburones "Eburones"). Under [Augustus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustus "Augustus"), the Roman Empire conquered the entirety of the modern day Netherlands, incorporating it into the province of [Germania Antiqua](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germania_Antiqua "Germania Antiqua") in 7 BC, and was repelled back across the Rhine after the [Battle of Teutoburg Forest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Teutoburg_Forest "Battle of the Teutoburg Forest") in AD 9; the Rhine became fixed as Rome's permanent northern frontier about AD 12. Notable towns at [Nijmegen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nijmegen "Nijmegen") and [Voorburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Voorburg "Voorburg") arose along the [Limes Germanicus](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Limes_Germanicus "Limes Germanicus"). In the first part of [Gallia Belgica](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gallia_Belgica "Gallia Belgica"), the area south of the Limes became part of [Germania Inferior](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Germania_Inferior "Germania Inferior"). The area to the north of the Rhine, inhabited by the Frisii, remained outside Roman rule, while the Germanic border tribes of the [Batavi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Batavi_(Germanic_tribe) "Batavi (Germanic tribe)") and [Cananefates](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cananefates "Cananefates") served in the [Roman cavalry](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ala_(Roman_allied_military_unit) "Ala (Roman allied military unit)").[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-71) The [Batavi revolted](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Revolt_of_the_Batavi "Revolt of the Batavi") in 69 and were defeated. The Batavi later merged with other tribes into the confederation of the [Salian Franks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Salian_Franks "Salian Franks"), whose identity emerged in the early 3rd century.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Previt%C3%A9-Orton-72) Salian Franks appear in Roman texts as both allies and enemies. They were forced by the confederation of the Saxons from the east to move over the Rhine into Roman territory in the 4th century. From their base in [West Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Flanders "West Flanders") and the southwest Netherlands, they were raiding the [English Channel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/English_Channel "English Channel"). Roman forces [pacified](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Pacification_(military_action) "Pacification (military action)") the region but did not expel the Franks, who continued to be feared at least until the time of [Julian the Apostate](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Julian_(emperor) "Julian (emperor)") (358) when Salian Franks were allowed to settle as _[foederati](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Foederati "Foederati")_ in [Texandria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Texandria "Texandria").[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Previt%C3%A9-Orton-72)

### Early Middle Ages (411–1000)

[![Image 16](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Frisia_716-la.svg/250px-Frisia_716-la.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Frisia_716-la.svg)

[Franks](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franks "Franks"), [Frisians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frisians "Frisians") and [Saxons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saxons "Saxons"), c. 716 AD

After the Roman government in the area collapsed around 406,[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-rietbergen-2000b-73) the Franks expanded their territories into numerous kingdoms. By the 490s, [Clovis I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Clovis_I "Clovis I") had conquered and united all these territories in the southern Netherlands in one [Frankish kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Francia "Francia") and from there continued his conquests into [Gaul](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gaul "Gaul"). During this expansion, Franks migrating to the south (modern territory of France and [Walloon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wallonia "Wallonia") part of Belgium) eventually adopted the [Vulgar Latin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vulgar_Latin "Vulgar Latin") of the local population.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Verhaal-67) A widening cultural divide grew with the Franks remaining in their original homeland in the north (i.e. the southern Netherlands and Flanders), who kept on speaking [Old Frankish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Frankish "Old Frankish"), which by the 9th century had evolved into Old Low Franconian or [Old Dutch](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Old_Dutch "Old Dutch").[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Verhaal-67) A Dutch-French language boundary hence came into existence.[[55]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Verhaal-67)[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-74)

[![Image 17](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/23/Franks_expansion.gif/250px-Franks_expansion.gif?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Franks_expansion.gif)

Frankish expansion (481 to 870 AD)

To the north of the Franks, climatic conditions improved, and during the [Migration Period](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Migration_Period "Migration Period") the [Angles](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Angles_(tribe) "Angles (tribe)"), [Jutes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jutes "Jutes"), and [Frisii](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frisii "Frisii") settled the coast.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Ethnic_Constructs_in_Antiquity-75) Many moved on to England and came to be known as [Anglo-Saxons](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anglo-Saxons "Anglo-Saxons"), but those who stayed would be referred to as [Frisians](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frisians "Frisians") and their language as [Frisian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frisian_languages "Frisian languages").[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Ethnic_Constructs_in_Antiquity-75) Frisian was spoken along the entire southern [North Sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/North_Sea "North Sea") coast. By the 7th century, a [Frisian Kingdom](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frisian_Kingdom "Frisian Kingdom") (650–734) under King [Aldegisel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Aldegisel "Aldegisel") and King [Redbad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Radbod_of_Frisia "Radbod of Frisia") emerged with [Traiectum](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Traiectum_(Utrecht) "Traiectum (Utrecht)") (Utrecht) as its centre of power,[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Ethnic_Constructs_in_Antiquity-75)[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-76) while [Dorestad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dorestad "Dorestad") was a flourishing trading place.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-77)[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Atlas-78) Between 600 and 719, the strategic cities and commercial hubs of the Rhine delta were fiercely contested by the Frisian Kingdom and the expanding Frankish Empire. In 734, at the [Battle of the Boarn](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_the_Boarn "Battle of the Boarn"), the Frisians were defeated after a [series of wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frisian%E2%80%93Frankish_wars "Frisian–Frankish wars"). With the approval of the Franks, the Anglo-Saxon missionary [Willibrord](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Willibrord "Willibrord") converted the Frisian people to Christianity and established the [Archdiocese of Utrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Diocese_of_Utrecht_(695%E2%80%931580) "Diocese of Utrecht (695–1580)"). However, his successor [Boniface](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Saint_Boniface "Saint Boniface") was murdered by the Frisians in 754.

The Frankish [Carolingian Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carolingian_Empire "Carolingian Empire") controlled much of Western Europe. In 843, it was divided into three parts—[East](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/East_Francia "East Francia"), [Middle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Middle_Francia "Middle Francia"), and [West Francia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/West_Francia "West Francia"). Most of present-day Netherlands became part of Middle Francia, which was a weak kingdom and subject to numerous partitions and annexation attempts by its stronger neighbours. It comprised territories from [Frisia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frisia "Frisia") in the north to the [Kingdom of Italy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingdom_of_Italy_(Holy_Roman_Empire) "Kingdom of Italy (Holy Roman Empire)") in the south. Around 850, [Lothair I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lothair_I "Lothair I") of Middle Francia acknowledged the Viking [Rorik of Dorestad](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rorik_of_Dorestad "Rorik of Dorestad") as ruler of most of Frisia. When Middle Francia was partitioned in 855, the lands north of the [Alps](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alps "Alps") passed to [Lothair II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lothair_II "Lothair II") and subsequently were named [Lotharingia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lotharingia "Lotharingia"). After he died in 869, Lotharingia was partitioned, into [Upper](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Lorraine "Duchy of Lorraine") and [Lower Lotharingia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lower_Lotharingia "Lower Lotharingia"), the latter comprising the Low Countries that became part of East Francia in 870. Around 879, another Viking expedition led by [Godfrid, Duke of Frisia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Godfrid,_Duke_of_Frisia "Godfrid, Duke of Frisia"), raided the Frisian lands. Resistance to the Vikings, if any, came from local nobles who gained in stature as a result, and that laid the basis for the disintegration of Lower Lotharingia into semi-independent states. One of these local nobles was [Gerolf of Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gerolf_of_Holland "Gerolf of Holland"), who assumed lordship in Frisia, and Viking rule came to an end.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-79)

### High Middle Ages (1000–1384)

[![Image 18](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/7/7a/Graftombe_Ridder_Arnold_van_der_Sluijs.jpg/250px-Graftombe_Ridder_Arnold_van_der_Sluijs.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Graftombe_Ridder_Arnold_van_der_Sluijs.jpg)

A medieval tomb of the Brabantian knight Arnold van der Sluijs

The [Holy Roman Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") ruled much of the Low Countries in the 10th and 11th century but was not able to maintain political unity. Powerful local nobles turned their cities, counties and duchies into private kingdoms that felt little sense of obligation to the emperor.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-80)[_[failed verification](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Verifiability "Wikipedia:Verifiability")_][Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Holland "County of Holland"), [Hainaut](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Hainaut "County of Hainaut"), [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Flanders "County of Flanders"), [Gelre](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Gelre "Duchy of Gelre"), [Brabant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brabant "Duchy of Brabant"), and [Utrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Prince-Bishopric_of_Utrecht "Prince-Bishopric of Utrecht") were in a state of almost continual war or paradoxically formed personal unions. As Frankish settlement progressed from Flanders and Brabant, the area became Old Low Franconian (or Old Dutch).

By the 11th century agrarian conditions started to improve which led to increase in population, reclamation of wasteland by farmers, and steady growth of trade and industry.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-rietbergen-2000b-73) Towns grew around monasteries and castles, and a mercantile middle class began to develop in these urban areas, especially in Flanders and Brabant. Wealthy cities started to buy certain [privileges for themselves](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City_rights_in_the_Low_Countries "City rights in the Low Countries") from the sovereign.

By the 12th century farmers from Flanders and Utrecht began draining and cultivating uninhabited swampy land in the western Netherlands, making the emergence of the County of Holland as the centre of power possible. The title of [Count of Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Count_of_Holland "Count of Holland") was fought over in the [Hook and Cod Wars](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hook_and_Cod_Wars "Hook and Cod Wars") between 1350 and 1490. The Cod faction consisted of the more progressive cities, while the Hook faction consisted of the conservative noblemen. These noblemen invited Duke [Philip the Good](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_the_Good "Philip the Good") of Burgundy to conquer Holland.[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-81)

### Burgundian, Habsburg and Spanish Habsburg Netherlands (1384–1581)

[![Image 19](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/d/d0/Political_map_of_the_Low_Countries_%281350%29-NL.svg/250px-Political_map_of_the_Low_Countries_%281350%29-NL.svg.png?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Political_map_of_the_Low_Countries_(1350)-NL.svg)

The Low Countries in the late 14th century

[![Image 20](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fa/William_I%2C_Prince_of_Orange_by_Adriaen_Thomasz._Key_Rijksmuseum_Amsterdam_SK-A-3148.jpg/120px-William_I%2C_Prince_of_Orange_by_Adriaen_Thomasz._Key_Rijksmuseum_Amsterdam_SK-A-3148.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:William_I,_Prince_of_Orange_by_Adriaen_Thomasz._Key_Rijksmuseum_Amsterdam_SK-A-3148.jpg)

Most of the [Imperial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Holy_Roman_Empire "Holy Roman Empire") and [French](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/France_in_the_Middle_Ages "France in the Middle Ages") fiefs in the region were united in a [personal union](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Personal_union "Personal union") by Philip the Good in 1433. The [House of Valois-Burgundy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Valois-Burgundy "House of Valois-Burgundy") and their [Habsburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/House_of_Habsburg "House of Habsburg") heirs ruled the Low Countries from 1384 to 1581. The rulers defended Dutch trading interests. The fleets of the [County of Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Holland "County of Holland") defeated the fleets of the [Hanseatic League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hanseatic_League "Hanseatic League") several times. [Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam") grew and in the 15th century became the primary trading port in Europe for grain from the [Baltic region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Baltic_region "Baltic region"). Amsterdam distributed grain to the major cities of Belgium, northern France and England. This trade was vital because Holland could no longer produce enough grain to feed itself. Land drainage had caused the [peat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peat "Peat") of the former [wetlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wetland "Wetland") to reduce to a level that was too low for drainage to be maintained.[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-82)

Under Habsburg [Charles V](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Charles_V,_Holy_Roman_Emperor "Charles V, Holy Roman Emperor"), all fiefs in the region were united into the [Seventeen Provinces](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Seventeen_Provinces "Seventeen Provinces"), which included most of present-day Belgium, Luxembourg, and parts of France and Germany. In 1568, under [Phillip II](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Spain "Philip II of Spain") the [Eighty Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Eighty_Years'_War "Eighty Years' War") between the Seventeen Provinces and their [Spanish](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire") ruler began. The level of ferocity exhibited by both sides can be gleaned from a Dutch chronicler's report:[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-83)

> On more than one occasion men were seen hanging their own brothers, who had been taken prisoners in the enemy's ranks... A Spaniard had ceased to be human in their eyes. On one occasion, a surgeon at Veer cut the heart from a Spanish prisoner, nailed it on a vessel's prow, and invited the townsmen to come and fasten their teeth in it, which many did with savage satisfaction.

The [Duke of Alba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fernando_%C3%81lvarez_de_Toledo,_3rd_Duke_of_Alba "Fernando Álvarez de Toledo, 3rd Duke of Alba") attempted to suppress the Protestant movement in the Netherlands. Netherlanders were "burned, strangled, beheaded, or buried alive" by his "[Blood Council](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Council_of_Troubles "Council of Troubles")" and Spanish soldiers. Bodies were displayed along roads to terrorise the population into submission. Alba boasted of having executed 18,600;[[72]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-84)[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-85) this figure does not include those who perished by war and famine.[[74]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-86)

The first great siege was Alba's effort to capture [Haarlem](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haarlem "Haarlem") and thereby cut Holland in half. It dragged on from December 1572 to the next summer, when Haarlemers finally surrendered on 13 July upon the promise that the city would be spared from being sacked. It was a stipulation [Don Fadrique](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fadrique_%C3%81lvarez_de_Toledo,_4th_Duke_of_Alba "Fadrique Álvarez de Toledo, 4th Duke of Alba") was unable to honour, when his soldiers mutinied, angered over pay owed and the miserable conditions of the campaign.[[75]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-87) On 4 November 1576, Spanish [tercios](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tercio "Tercio") seized [Antwerp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Antwerp "Antwerp") and [subjected it to the worst pillage](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sack_of_Antwerp "Sack of Antwerp") in the Netherlands' history. The citizens resisted but were overcome; 7,000 were killed, and 1,000 buildings were torched.[[76]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-88)

[![Image 21](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/3/35/Philip_II_of_Spain_berating_William_the_Silent_Prince_of_Orange_by_Cornelis_Kruseman.jpg/250px-Philip_II_of_Spain_berating_William_the_Silent_Prince_of_Orange_by_Cornelis_Kruseman.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Philip_II_of_Spain_berating_William_the_Silent_Prince_of_Orange_by_Cornelis_Kruseman.jpg)

[Philip II of Spain](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_II_of_Spain "Philip II of Spain") reproaches William of Orange in [Vlissingen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vlissingen "Vlissingen") upon his departure from the Netherlands in 1559.

Delegates from Catholic Brabant, Protestant Holland and Zeeland agreed to join Utrecht and [William the Silent](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_the_Silent "William the Silent") in driving out Spanish troops and forming a new government for the Netherlands. [Don Juan of Austria](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Don_Juan_of_Austria "Don Juan of Austria"), the Spanish governor, was forced to concede initially but within months returned to active hostilities. The Dutch looked for help from the Protestant [Elizabeth I](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Elizabeth_I "Elizabeth I") of England, but she initially stood by her commitments to the Spanish in the [Treaty of Bristol](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Convention_of_Nymegen "Convention of Nymegen") of 1573. When the next large-scale battle took place at [Gembloux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gembloux "Gembloux") in 1578, the Spanish forces won easily.[[77]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-89) In light of the [defeat at Gembloux](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Gembloux_(1578) "Battle of Gembloux (1578)"), the southern states of the Seventeen Provinces distanced themselves from the rebels in the north with the 1579 [Union of Arras](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_Arras "Union of Arras"). Opposing them, the northern half of the Seventeen Provinces forged the [Union of Utrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Union_of_Utrecht "Union of Utrecht") in which they committed to support each other against the Spanish.[[78]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-90) The Union of Utrecht is seen as the foundation of the modern Netherlands.[[79]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-91)

Spanish troops [sacked Maastricht in 1579](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Siege_of_Maastricht_(1579) "Siege of Maastricht (1579)"), killing over 10,000 civilians.[[80]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-92) In 1581, the northern provinces adopted the [Act of Abjuration](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Act_of_Abjuration "Act of Abjuration"), the declaration of independence in which the provinces officially deposed Philip II.[[81]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-93) Against the rebels Philip could draw on the resources of the [Spanish Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Spanish_Empire "Spanish Empire"). Elizabeth I sympathised with the Dutch struggle and sent an army of 7,600 soldiers to aid them.[[82]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-94) English forces faced the Spanish in the Netherlands under the [Duke of Parma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Farnese,_Duke_of_Parma "Alexander Farnese, Duke of Parma") in a series of largely indecisive actions that tied down significant numbers of Spanish troops and bought time for the Dutch to reorganise their defences.[[83]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-95) The war continued until 1648, when Spain under King [Philip IV](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Philip_IV_of_Spain "Philip IV of Spain") recognised the independence of the seven north-western provinces in the [Peace of Münster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Peace_of_M%C3%BCnster "Peace of Münster").[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-rietbergen-2000b-73) Parts of the southern provinces became _de facto_ colonies of the new republican-mercantile empire.[[84]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-96)

### Dutch Republic (1581–1795)

[![Image 22](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/5f/Hendrick_Avercamp_-_IJsvermaak_bij_een_stad.jpg/250px-Hendrick_Avercamp_-_IJsvermaak_bij_een_stad.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Hendrick_Avercamp_-_Winterlandschap_met_schaatsers_bij_de_stad_Kampen.jpg)

_Winter landscape with skaters near the city of [Kampen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kampen,\_Overijssel "Kampen, Overijssel")_ by [Hendrick Avercamp](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hendrick_Avercamp "Hendrick Avercamp") (1620s)

After the declaration of independence, the provinces of [Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Holland "County of Holland"), [Zeeland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Zeeland "County of Zeeland"), [Groningen](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lordship_of_Groningen "Lordship of Groningen"), [Friesland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lordship_of_Friesland "Lordship of Friesland"), [Utrecht](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lordship_of_Utrecht "Lordship of Utrecht"), [Overijssel](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lordship_of_Overijssel "Lordship of Overijssel"), and [Gelderland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Gelderland "Duchy of Gelderland") entered into a confederation. All these duchies, lordships and counties enjoyed a significant degree of autonomy and were governed by their own administrative bodies known as the [States-Provincial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Provincial_council_(Netherlands) "Provincial council (Netherlands)"). The confederal government, known as the [States General](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/States_General_of_the_Netherlands "States General of the Netherlands"), was headquartered in The Hague and comprised representatives from each of the seven provinces. The sparsely populated region of Drenthe was part of the republic, albeit not considered a province in its own right. Moreover, during the Eighty Years' War, the republic came to occupy [Generality Lands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Generality_Lands "Generality Lands") in [Flanders](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/County_of_Flanders "County of Flanders"), [Brabant](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Brabant "Duchy of Brabant") and [Limburg](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Duchy_of_Limburg "Duchy of Limburg"). These areas were primarily inhabited by Roman Catholics and lacked a distinct governmental structure of their own. They were used as a buffer zone between the republic and the Spanish-controlled [Southern Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Southern_Netherlands "Southern Netherlands").[[85]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-97)

[![Image 23](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/2/2a/Johannes_Lingelbach_001.jpg/250px-Johannes_Lingelbach_001.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Johannes_Lingelbach_001.jpg)

[Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam "Amsterdam")'s [Dam Square](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dam_Square "Dam Square") in 1656 by [Johannes Lingelbach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Johannes_Lingelbach "Johannes Lingelbach")

During the [Dutch Golden Age](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Golden_Age "Dutch Golden Age") of the 17th century, the [Dutch Republic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Republic "Dutch Republic") grew to become one of the major seafaring and economic powers. Dutch science, military and art (especially [painting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Golden_Age_painting "Dutch Golden Age painting")) were among the most acclaimed in the world. By 1650, the Dutch owned 16,000 merchant ships.[[86]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-98) The [Dutch East India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_India_Company "Dutch East India Company") and the [Dutch West India Company](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_West_India_Company "Dutch West India Company") established colonies and [trading posts](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Trading_post "Trading post") all over the world. The [Dutch settlement in North America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Netherland "New Netherland") began with the formation of [New Amsterdam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Amsterdam "New Amsterdam") in 1624. In South Africa, the Dutch settled the [Cape Colony](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cape_Colony "Cape Colony") in 1652. [Dutch colonies in South America](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_colonisation_of_the_Guianas "Dutch colonisation of the Guianas") were established along the many rivers in the fertile [Guyana plains](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Guianas "The Guianas"), among them [Colony of Surinam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Surinam_(Dutch_colony) "Surinam (Dutch colony)"). In Asia, the Dutch established a presence in [India](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_India "Dutch India"), the [Dutch East Indies](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_East_Indies "Dutch East Indies") (now [Indonesia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Indonesia "Indonesia")), [Formosa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Formosa "Dutch Formosa") (now [Taiwan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Taiwan "Taiwan")), and the only western trading post in Japan, [Dejima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dejima "Dejima").[[87]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-99) During the period of [proto-industrialisation](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Proto-industrialisation "Proto-industrialisation"), the empire received 50% of textiles and 80% of silks import from India's [Mughal Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mughal_Empire "Mughal Empire").[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-tong-100)[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-esposito-101)[[90]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-102)[[91]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Prakash-103)

[![Image 24](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/fd/Storck%2C_Four_Days_Battle.jpg/250px-Storck%2C_Four_Days_Battle.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Storck,_Four_Days_Battle.jpg)

The [Four Days' Battle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Four_Days'_Battle "Four Days' Battle") during the [Second Anglo-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Second_Anglo-Dutch_War "Second Anglo-Dutch War"), 1–4 June 1666

Many economic historians regard the Netherlands as the first thoroughly [capitalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Capitalism "Capitalism") country. In early modern Europe, it had the wealthiest trading city in Amsterdam and the first full-time [stock exchange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Euronext_Amsterdam "Euronext Amsterdam"). The inventiveness of the traders led to insurance and retirement funds as well as phenomena such as the [boom-bust cycle](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Business_cycle "Business cycle"), the world's first [asset-inflation bubble](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asset_price_inflation "Asset price inflation"), the [tulip mania](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tulip_mania "Tulip mania") of 1636–1637, and the world's first [bear raider](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bear_raid "Bear raid"), [Isaac Le Maire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Isaac_Le_Maire "Isaac Le Maire").[[92]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-104) In 1672 – known in Dutch history as the [Rampjaar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rampjaar "Rampjaar") (Disaster Year) – the Dutch Republic was attacked by France, England and two German bishoprics simultaneously, in what would become known as the [Franco-Dutch War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Franco-Dutch_War "Franco-Dutch War"). [At sea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Third_Anglo-Dutch_War "Third Anglo-Dutch War"), it could successfully prevent the English and French navies from blockading the western shores. On land the republic was almost overrun by the advancing French and German armies from the east, but the Dutch managed to turn the tide by [inundating parts of Holland](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dutch_Waterline "Dutch Waterline").[[93]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands#cite_note-Rowman_&_Littlefield-105)

[![Image 25](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/e8/Nederlandse_troepen_tijdens_de_Slag_bij_Malplaquet_%28cropped%29.jpg/250px-Nederlandse_troepen_tijdens_de_Slag_bij_Malplaquet_%28cropped%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Nederlandse_troepen_tijdens_de_Slag_bij_Malplaquet_(cropped).jpg)

Dutch troops at the [Battle of Malplaquet](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Battle_of_Malplaquet "Battle of Malplaquet"), 11 September 1709

From 1672 to 1712 the republic, led by [William III of Orange](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/William_III_of_England "William III of England") and [Anthonie Heinsius](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anthonie_Heinsius "Anthonie Heinsius"), would regularly clash with France in what some historians call the _Forty Years' War_. In the [Nine Years' War](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nine_Years'_War "Nine Years' War") and the [War of the Spanish Succession](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/War_of_the_Spanish_Succession "War of the Spanish Succession"), the republic was at the centre of anti-French coalitions.
