**Samuel Kamau Wanjirū** (10 November 1986 – 15 May 2011) was a Kenyan long-distance runner who won the [2008 Beijing Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") Marathon in an [Olympic record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") time of 2:06:32; becoming the first Kenyan to win the Olympic [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_medal "Gold medal") in the marathon. He became the youngest gold medallist in the marathon since 1932.

He held the 10,000m U20 World Record from 2005 until 2024 and set the half marathon world record 3 times.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-2) In 2009, he won both the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") and [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon"), running the fastest marathons ever recorded in the United Kingdom and United States, respectively. He retained his Chicago title in 2010 in a season fraught with injury.

In 2011, he died after a fall from a balcony at his home in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu") following a domestic dispute.

Samuel Wanjirū was born in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu"), [Laikipia County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laikipia_County "Laikipia County"), a town in the [Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Rift_Valley,_Kenya "Great Rift Valley, Kenya"), about 150 kilometres (93 mi) northwest of the capital, [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-huff1-3) and was brought up with his brother Simon Njoroge in poverty by his mother Hannah Wanjiru, the daughter of Samuel Kamau.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-obituary-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-5) Wanjirū took his mother's given name as a surname, because she was a single mother. He dropped out of school aged around 12 because they could not afford the school fees.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-6)

Wanjirū started running at the age of 8. In 2002, he moved to [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") and enrolled in Sendai Ikuei Gakuen High School in [Sendai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai "Sendai"). He had success on the Japanese [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") circuit, where he won the [Fukuoka International Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_International_Cross_Country "Fukuoka International Cross Country") at sixteen years old in 2003. He went on to win in both [Fukuoka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka "Fukuoka") and at the [Chiba International Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiba_International_Cross_Country "Chiba International Cross Country") consecutively in 2004 and 2005.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-7) After graduating in 2005, he joined the [Toyota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota "Toyota")[Kyūshū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ky%C5%ABsh%C5%AB "Kyūshū") athletics team, coached by 1992 Olympic marathon [silver medalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_medal "Silver medal")[Koichi Morishita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koichi_Morishita "Koichi Morishita").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-8)

Wanjirū had a [5000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") best of 13:12.40, run as a 17-year-old in April 2004 in [Hiroshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima "Hiroshima"), Japan. At age 18, Wanjirū broke the half marathon world record on 11 September 2005 in the [Rotterdam Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Half_Marathon "Rotterdam Half Marathon") with a time of 59:16 minutes, officially beating [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat")'s half-marathon record of 59:17 minutes.

This was preceded two weeks earlier by a bettering of the [10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_track_event "Long-distance track event")[U20 world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_junior_records_in_athletics "World junior records in athletics") by a margin of almost 23 seconds in the IAAF Golden League [Van Damme Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Van_Damme "Memorial Van Damme") Race on 26 August. His WJR time of 26:41.75 was good enough for third place in the race behind [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s world record, set in the same race, of 26:17.53 and [Boniface Kiprop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boniface_Kiprop "Boniface Kiprop")'s 26:39.77. It was Kiprop who held the previous world junior mark (27:04.00 minutes), set at the same meeting the previous year. The run saw 6 runners going under 27 minutes[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-10)

### World records and Olympic gold

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Wanjiru&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: World records and Olympic gold")]

Wanjiru took back the half-marathon world record, which [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie") broke in early 2006, with 58:53 minutes on 9 February 2007 at the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah_Half_Marathon "Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-11) and improved it to 58:33 on 17 March 2007 in the [City-Pier-City Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-Pier-City_Loop "City-Pier-City Loop") in [The Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague"), [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"). While improving his own record, he recorded an unofficial time of 55:31 for 20 km, which was faster than Haile Gebrselassie's world record but was never ratified due to the timing methods in the race.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-12)

[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Samuel_Wanjiru%2C_Marathon%2C_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg/250px-Samuel_Wanjiru%2C_Marathon%2C_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Samuel_Wanjiru,_Marathon,_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg)

Wanjiru approaching the finishing line at the [2008 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics")

Wanjiru made his marathon debut at [Fukuoka Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_Marathon "Fukuoka Marathon") on 2 December 2007, winning it impressively with a course record of 2:06:39.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-13) He started 2008 by winning the [Zayed International Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_International_Half_Marathon "Zayed International Half Marathon") and receiving a prize of US$300,000.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-14) In the 2008 [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon"), he came in second, breaking 2:06 for the first time. In the 2008 Summer Olympics, Wanjiru won the marathon gold medal in an Olympic record time of 2:06:32, smashing the previous record of 2:09:21 set by [Carlos Lopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Lopes "Carlos Lopes") of Portugal in the 1984 Olympics.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-15) He received the [AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIMS_World_Athlete_of_the_Year_Award "AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award") that year in recognition of his performances.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-16)

### London and Chicago wins

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Wanjiru&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: London and Chicago wins")]

At the [Granollers Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granollers_Half_Marathon "Granollers Half Marathon") in February 2008, in which Wanjiru won, the Kenyan stated his intent for the future, saying, "in five years' time I feel capable of clocking a sub 2 hours time for the marathon."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-17) In April 2009, Wanjiru won the London Marathon in a time of 2:05:10, a new personal record and also a new course record. He was pleased with the achievement and stated that he hoped to break Haile Gebrselassie's world record in the near future.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-18) At the Rotterdam Half Marathon, Wanjiru clocked a 1:01:08 on 13 September, which was won by [Sammy Kitwara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Kitwara "Sammy Kitwara") with a time of 58:58.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-19) In October 2009, Wanjiru won the [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_winners_of_the_Chicago_Marathon "List of winners of the Chicago Marathon") in a time of 2:05:41, setting a new course record for the city and the fastest marathon time ever run in the United States.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-20) The wins in London and Chicago helped him reach the top of the [World Marathon Majors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Marathon_Majors "World Marathon Majors") rankings for 2009, earning him a jackpot of US$500,000.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-21)

He signed up to defend his title at the [2010 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_London_Marathon "2010 London Marathon"), but he encountered knee trouble at the midway point of the race and decided to drop out to avoid further injury – the first time in six marathons that he had failed to finish.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-22) He chose to run at the 2010 Chicago Marathon in October, but a stomach virus before the race had hampered his preparations and he entered the competition with the lesser aim of reaching the top three. [Tsegaye Kebede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsegaye_Kebede "Tsegaye Kebede") took the opportunity to forge a lead, but Wanjiru (despite a lack of peak physical form) persevered with the pace and caught up with the Ethiopian. He took the lead in the final 400 m to defend his title in Chicago with a time of 2:06:24. "It was the greatest surprise I have ever seen in my life", remarked his coach, Federico Rosa, on the performance.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-24)

Wanjiru married [Mary Wacera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Wacera "Mary Wacera"), a fellow long-distance runner, in 2009 and the two had a child (Ann) in 2010. He had previously married Triza Njeri in a traditional ceremony and had two children, although Wanjiru and Wacera's marriage was legally binding.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

Wanjiru began drinking alcohol when he moved to Japan, and it increased and became a major part of his life. Despite that, his marathoning career continued successfully, though his personal life became somewhat chaotic.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

In December 2010, Wanjiru was arrested by [Kenyan police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Police "Kenya Police") at his house in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu") and charged with threatening to kill his wife and illegally possessing an [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47") rifle. He denied both the accusations and claimed that he was being framed.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-28)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

Wanjiru and his wife Triza Njeri, a beautician, had a daughter Anne Wanjiru and a son Simon Njoroge.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-obituary-4)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-29) Wanjiru also had a third wife, Judy Wambui Wairimu, who was pregnant when he died and has since had a son.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-30)

Wanjiru's cousin [Joseph Riri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Riri?action=edit&redlink=1 "Joseph Riri (page does not exist)") was a world-class marathon runner,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-31) and Wanjiru's younger brother [Simon Njoroge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Njoroge?action=edit&redlink=1 "Simon Njoroge (page does not exist)") was also a long-distance runner.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-32)

On 15 May 2011, Wanjiru died from a fall off a balcony at his home in Nyahururu. Wanjiru appeared to have suffered internal injuries after the fall and was confirmed dead by doctors at a nearby hospital after attempts to revive him failed.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-bbc1-33)

Police said Wanjiru's wife, Triza Njeri, had come home to find him in bed with another woman. She locked the couple in the bedroom and ran outside. Wanjiru then died after falling from the balcony.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-huff1-3) Police were unsure if Wanjiru intended suicide or jumped out of rage, and investigated the circumstances related to Njeri and his female companion that led to his death.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-huff1-3)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-nytLongman16May2011-34)

In May 2017, while testifying during an inquest into Wanjiru's death, his mother Hannah Wanjiru said at the Milimani law court that she believes her son was murdered.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-37)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

His mother claimed at an inquest into his death that her son was murdered by six men who had conspired with his wife Trizah Njeri.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-38) During the inquest at the Milimani court that sought to establish whether Wanjiru was murdered or jumped to his death, a former chief government pathologist said he was convinced that Wanjiru was hit by a blunt object after he had jumped from the balcony of his home, landing on his legs, or that he was possibly pushed and then struck.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-39)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

Eliud Kipchoge EGH (English: /ˈɛlɪjud kɪpˈtʃoʊɡeɪ/ ELL-ih-yood kip-CHOH-gay[3][4]; born 5 November 1984) is a Kenyan long-distance runner who competes in the marathon and formerly specialized in the 5000 metres. Kipchoge is the 2016 and 2020 Olympic marathon champion, and was the world record holder in the marathon from 2018 to 2023,[5] until that record was broken by Kelvin Kiptum at the 2023 Chicago Marathon. He is widely considered to be one of the greatest marathon runners of all time.[6][5]

Kipchoge claimed his first individual world championship title in 2003 by winning the junior race at the World Cross Country Championships and setting a world junior record for the 5000 m. At the age of eighteen, he became the senior 5000 m world champion at the 2003 World Championships with a championship record, then followed by an Olympic bronze for Kenya in 2004 and a bronze at the 2006 World Indoor Championships. A five-time World Championship 5000 m finalist, Kipchoge took silver medals at the 2007 World Championships, 2008 Beijing Olympics, and 2010 Commonwealth Games.

He switched to road running in 2012 and made the second-fastest half marathon debut ever, at 59:25. In his marathon debut, he won the 2013 Hamburg Marathon in a course record time. His first victory at a World Marathon Major came at the Chicago Marathon in 2014, and he went on to become series champion a record five times – for 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2022. He has won the London Marathon a record four times and also holds the record for most Berlin Marathon wins with five, his latest coming in September 2023. With 15 victories in his first 18 marathons from 2013 to 2023, Kipchoge's only losses were a second-place finish behind Wilson Kipsang Kiprotich at the 2013 Berlin Marathon, where Kipsang broke the world record; an eighth-place finish at the 2020 London Marathon and a sixth place in his debut at the Boston Marathon in 2023.[7][8][9] He has since 2024, been defeated in his last three marathons. Kipchoge's last world record run broke by 30 seconds his own 2018 world record, which was in turn a 78-second improvement over the existing best, the greatest improvement in a marathon world record time since 1967.

On 12 October 2019, Kipchoge ran the marathon distance for the Ineos 1:59 Challenge in Vienna, achieving a time of 1:59:40.2, becoming the first person in recorded history to do a sub-two-hour marathon.[10] The run did not count as a new marathon record, as he ran with specialized shoes, standard competition rules for pacing and fluids were not followed, and it was not an open event.[11][12][13]

Kipchoge was appointed Elder of the Order of the Golden Heart by former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta on 20 October 2019 in recognition of his sub-two-hour marathon.[14] He was also named the 2019 BBC World Sport Star of the Year. In 2023 he was awarded the Princess of Asturias Award in the category "Sports".[15]

Personal lifeedit

Kipchoge was born on 5 November 1984 in Kapsisiywa, Nandi County, in Kenya. He graduated from the Kaptel Secondary School in Nandi County in 1999 but did not run seriously or as a profession then.[16][17] He ran three kilometres (2 mi) to school on a daily basis.[18] Kipchoge was raised by a single mother (a teacher), and only knew his father from pictures. He is the youngest of four children. He met his trainer Patrick Sang (a former Olympic medalist in the steeplechase) in 2001 at the age of 16.[19]

Kipchoge's wife and three children live in Eldoret, Kenya.[20][21] He lives and trains in Kaptagat, 30 km (19 miles) from Eldoret.[22] He is a devout Catholic.[23]

Following the death of Kelvin Kiptum in 2024, Kipchoge and his family faced online threats falsely accusing him of being involved in Kiptum's death. These threats impacted his training and well-being.[24][25]

Careeredit
2002–2004edit

In 2002, he won at the Kenyan trials for the 2002 IAAF World Cross Country Championships junior race. At the World Cross Country Championships, held in Dublin, Kipchoge finished fifth in the individual race and was part of the Kenyan junior team that won gold. Kipchoge also won the 5000-meter race at the Kenyan trial for the 2002 World Junior Championships in Athletics but fell ill and missed the championships. He won the junior race at the 2003 IAAF World Cross Country Championships.

He set a world junior record in the 5000 m at the 2003 Bislett Games, running a time of 12:52.61 minutes. This stood as the world and African junior record until 2012, when it was improved to 12:47.53 minutes by Hagos Gebrhiwet of Ethiopia.[26]

Kipchoge won a gold medal at the 5000 m final at the 2003 World Championships in Paris, outsprinting runner-up Hicham El Guerrouj, the world record holder in the 1500 metres and mile, by four-hundredths of a second in 12:52.79.[27]

In July, he participated in the Golden League 2004 Roma Meeting. In the 5000 m event, he dipped first among the starters with 12:46.53, which made him the sixth-fastest ever in the event.[28]

In 2004, Kipchoge won a bronze medal in the 5000 m final at the 2004 Athens Olympics, behind El Guerrouj and Kenenisa Bekele.[29] He also won the Trofeo Alasport cross country race earlier that season.

2006–2009edit

Kipchoge won the bronze in the 3000 metres indoor at the 2006 World Championships in Moscow.

At the end of the year, Kipchoge won the San Silvestre Vallecana New Year's Eve 10 km road race in a time of 26:54 minutes, which beat his own course record by 40 seconds. This time was also better than the 10K road world record at the time but was run on a downhill course.[30]

Kipchoge (third from the right) during the 5000 m heat at the 2007 World Championships in Osaka. He won a silver medal in the final.

Kipchoge won a silver medal at the 5000 m final of the 2007 World Championships at Osaka in 13:46.00, behind Bernard Lagat (13:45.87).[31]

During the 2008 Olympics held in Beijing, China, Kipchoge won a silver medal in the 5000 m event with a time of 13:02.80; although better than the previous Olympic record of 13:05.59, it was not enough to match Kenenisa Bekele's pace, who won the gold medal for this race.[32] On the circuit, he won the Great Yorkshire Run 10K and Campaccio Cross Country that year.

He failed to reach the podium at the 2009 World Championships in Athletics, finishing in fifth place. He also finished ninth in the 3000 m at the 2009 IAAF World Athletics Final.

2010–2011edit

He made his debut on the 2010 IAAF Diamond League by winning the 5000 m Qatar Athletic Super Grand Prix in a meet record time.[33]

Kipchoge then entered the Carlsbad 5000 in California, United States. The Carlsbad 5 km road race is the venue for the world's best times for a 5k road race for men and women, respectively. The fastest to cover the track was Sammy Kipketer in 2000, with 12:59.52 min.[34] Kipchoge made a world best attempt, and although he won the race, weather affected his chances, and he finished in 13:11, the fourth-fastest ever for the course up to that point in time.[35]

In the first athletics final of the 2010 Commonwealth Games, he attempted to win the 5000 m Commonwealth title. Ugandan runner Moses Kipsiro held a slender lead over him in the race's final stages, and Kipchoge ended up in second place, taking the silver medal some seven-hundredths of a second behind.[36][37] He flew back to Europe immediately after to take part in the Belgrade Race through History the following day. His shoe fell off in the first kilometre, and, after putting it back on, he made up much ground on the field to eventually take second place two seconds behind Josphat Menjo.[38]

At the start of 2011, he won the short race at the Great Edinburgh Cross Country, ahead of Asbel Kiprop.[39] He attempted to retain his title at the Carlsbad 5000 in April but came a close second behind Dejen Gebremeskel.[40] In May he raced the 3000 metres (finished third) in Doha, with a time of 7:27.66 and ranked him as the 12th-fastest at the distance up to this point.[41] Kipchoge was chosen to represent Kenya at the 2011 World Championships in Athletics and reached the 5000 m final for the fifth consecutive time, although he only managed seventh place on this occasion.

2012edit

Kipchoge returned to the Edinburgh Cross Country in 2012, but this time he finished third behind Asbel Kiprop and Britain's Jonathan Hay.[42] He was also third at the Carlsbad 5000 in March.[43] He attempted to gain a place on the 10,000 m Olympic team at the Prefontaine Classic, but fell back in the late stages of the Kenyan trial race, finishing seventh.[44] A seventh-place finish in the Kenyan 5000 m trial race meant he would not make a third consecutive Olympic team.[45]

He made his half marathon debut in the Lille Half Marathon.[46] The run was won by a new course record time of 59:05 (previously 59:36 by ilahun Regassa set in 2008) by Ezekiel Chebii (former personal_best 59:22), trailed by Bernard Koech 59:10, and Kipchoge earned a third place with 59:25. His time of 59:25 became the second fastest Half Marathon debut, only second to Moses Mosop's 59:20 in Milan in 2010.[47]

On 6 October 2012, Kipchoge ran at the 2012 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships in Kavarna, Bulgaria. Zersenay Tadese of Eritrea won in 1:00:19, and Kipchoge placed sixth in 1:01:52.[48]

Wilson Kipsang (front) and Kipchoge (behind) running in the 2013 Berlin Marathon in which Kipsang set the world record with 2:03:23 and Kipchoge, racing in his second marathon, finished second, 42 seconds later.
2013edit

Kipchoge opened his 2013 season with a win at the Barcelona Half Marathon in a time of one hour and four seconds.[49] Making his marathon debut in April, he demonstrated a smooth transition to the longer distance by taking the Hamburg Marathon title with a run of 2:05:30 hours (with a half marathon split time of 1:03:13 hours), beating the field by over two minutes and setting a new course record.[50][51] In August 2013, he won the Half Marathon of Klagenfurt in 1:01:02 minutes.[52]

Then, he raced in the 2013 Berlin Marathon and finished second in 2:04:05 (with a half marathon split time of 1:01:32 hours), the fifth-fastest time in history, in his second-ever marathon,[53][54] behind Wilson Kipsang, who set a new marathon world record with 2:03:23. Third place went to Geoffrey Kamworor of Kenya with 2:06:26.[8] This was the ninth world record set at the Berlin Marathon.[55]

2015edit
Kipchoge races in the 2015 London Marathon.

On 2 February, Kipchoge participated in the Ras al-Khaimah Half Marathon. He placed sixth with a time of 1:00:50. The run was won by Mosinet Geremew (Ethiopia) in 1:00:05.[56] Kipchoge ran 2:04:42 to win the 2015 London Marathon in April. He also won the 2015 Berlin Marathon later in the year. His win and then-personal best time (2:04:00) occurred even though his shoes malfunctioned, causing his insoles to flap out of both shoes from 10 km onward; rather than risk time lost from an adjustment, he finished the race with bloodied, blistered feet.[57]

2016edit

In April, Kipchoge won the 2016 London Marathon for the second consecutive year in a time of 2:03:05.[58] His performance broke the course record in London and became the second-fastest marathon time in history, missing Dennis Kimetto's world record by 8 seconds.[59]

Rio Olympic Games

As the prerace favourite, during the 2016 Rio Summer Olympics, Kipchoge gained a gold medal in the marathon event.[60][61][62] On the last day of the Olympic Games on 21 August 2016, he won in a time of 2:08:44. The runner up was Feyisa Lilesa (Ethiopia) in 2:09:54 and the bronze medal went to Galen Rupp (USA), doing his second marathon, crossing the finish line in 2:10:05. When the halfway point after 21.0975 km was reached, 37 men were within 10 seconds of the lead runner. The participants' field diminished to 3 lead runners shortly before 34 km. Kipchoge made his final move on silver medal winner Lilesa around 36 km into the race. He covered the first half of the race in 1:05:55 while doing the second half in 1:02:49, which amounts to a difference of more than 3 minutes, a negative split.[63][64] The winning gap between Kipchoge and Lilesa by 70 seconds was the largest victory margin since the 1972 Olympic marathon.[65] Kipchoge's winning time of 2:08:44 was, as of August 2021, his slowest marathon time. One hundred fifty-five runners started the race, the largest field in Olympic history; 140 of them finished the race.[66][67] With this win, Kipchoge became the second Kenyan male after Sammy Wanjiru in Beijing 2008 to win an Olympic marathon gold medal. At the same Olympics, the women's marathon was won by Jemima Sumgong, who became the first female Kenyan winner.[68][64]

On 20 November 2016, Kipchoge ran in the Airtel Delhi Half Marathon, winning the race, clocking a time of 59:44.[69]

2017edit
Further information: Breaking2

On 6 May, Kipchoge, along with Zersenay Tadese (then world record holder in the half marathon) and Lelisa Desisa (2-time Boston Marathon winner), attempted the first sub-two-hour assisted marathon in the Nike Breaking2 project on the Monza Formula 1 racetrack near Milan, Italy. All three runners ran a test 2 months before the attempt. The target time was 1 hour for a half Marathon. Kipchoge finished first in 59:17. The course was measured at 2400 m per lap.[70] During the 2-hour attempt, the runners were paced by a lead car and 30 supporting pacers joining in stages (both considered illegal under IAAF rules).[71] The race started at 5:45h local time on the 2.4 km track. Kipchoge finished in 2:00:25, while the other two had to slow and finished far behind.[72] The runners planned even 14:13 5k splits to break 2 hours. His 5k splits were: 14:14, 14:07, 14:13, 14:15, 14:14, 14:17, 14:17, 14:27, and 6:20 to finish.[73] The 5k split times from 25k and further would be world records: 25k in 1:11:03, 30k in 1:25:20, 35k in 1:39:37, 40k in 1:54:04.

On 24 September, he won the 2017 Berlin Marathon in a time of 2:03:32.[74] In rainy conditions, he finished 14 seconds ahead of Guye Adola who ran his first marathon, and set the fastest marathon debut ever.[75] Former marathon world record holder Wilson Kipsang and 2016 winner Kenenisa Bekele failed to finish.[76][77]

2018edit

Kipchoge won the London Marathon in a time of 2:04:17 with a half marathon split time of 1:01:00. In a time of 2:04:49 Shura Kitata (Ethiopia) came in second and Mo Farah (Great Britain) finished in 2:06:21, a British record. Kenenisa Bekele finished sixth 2:08:53 and defending champion Daniel Wanjiru.[78][79][80][81][82] eighth 2:10:35.[83] Kipchoge confirmed question on attempting to break the Marathon world record. The women's race saw a win by Vivian Cheriuyot (Kenya) with a time of 2:18:31 the 4th best time ever and Brigid Kosgei (Kenya) place second in 2:20:13.

It was a performance so far superior to anything we've seen before that comparing it to another marathon feels inadequate. This was Wilt Chamberlain's 100-point game in basketball, Usain Bolt's 9.58 in the 100-meter dash.

Kipchoge's splits – 1:01:06 for the first half, a ridiculous 1:00:33 for his second half – sound made up. But they were real, and they were spectacular."

On 16 September, Kipchoge won the 2018 Berlin Marathon in a time of 2:01:39, breaking the previous world record by 1 minute and 18 seconds (2:02:57 set by fellow countryman Dennis Kimetto at the Berlin Marathon in 2014). It was the greatest improvement in a marathon world record time since 1967.[87] He finished 4:43 min ahead of second-placed fellow Kenyan Amos Kipruto. The world record holder from 2013, Wilson Kipsang of Kenya, came in third at 2:06:48.[88][89] It was the 11th world record set at the Berlin Marathon.[55]

2018 accoladesedit

Following his performances in the 2018 season, Kipchoge received numerous accolades and awards. He was named IAAF World Athlete of the Year together with Caterine Ibargüen, who received the female World Athlete of the Year award.[90] On 11 January 2019, Kipchoge was named the 2018 Sportsman of the Year at the Kenyan Sports Personality of the Year Awards in Mombasa, Kenya.[91]

2019edit

Kipchoge won the 2019 London Marathon in a time of 2:02:37, the second fastest marathon ever at that time, behind his 2018 Berlin Marathon win.[92] He became the first man to win the event four times and set a new course record, beating his own 2016 London Marathon best by 28 seconds.[93] The lead runner passed the half marathon mark in 1:01:37.[94] Mosinet Geremew (Ethiopia) finished as the runner up in 2:02:55 and Mule Wasihun (Ethiopia) came in third place in 2:03:16.[7] The British runner Mo Farah, a four-time Olympic gold medalist and a pre-race favourite, finished 5th.[95]

Ineos 1:59 Challengeedit
Further information: Ineos 1:59 Challenge
Wikinews has related news:
Eliud Kipchoge of Kenya runs marathon under two hours

In May 2019, a few days after his London Marathon win, Kipchoge announced another take on the sub-two-hour marathon, named the Ineos 1:59 Challenge. On 12 October 2019 in Vienna's Prater park, he ran 4.4 laps of the Hauptallee in 1:59:40, becoming the first person in recorded history to break the two-hour barrier over a marathon distance.[96][97][98]

The effort did not count as a new world record under IAAF rules due to the setup of the challenge. Specifically, it was not an open event; Kipchoge was handed fluids by his support team throughout; the run featured a pace car and included rotating teams of other runners pacing Kipchoge in a formation designed to reduce wind resistance and maximise efficiency.[99][100] The achievement was recognised by Guinness World Records with the titles 'Fastest marathon distance (male)' and 'First marathon distance run under two hours'.[101][102]

2020edit

Kipchoge placed 8th in the 2020 London Marathon in October with a time of 2:06:49, the lowest finish of his marathoning career so far.[9] The race was won by Ehtopias'S Shura Itata in a time of 2:05:41. Kipchoge lost contact with the lead runner with 3 miles to go. For the first time, the run was on a 19 laps looped course and originally set for April and postponed to October due to the COVID-19 pandemic.

2021edit

In preparation for the delayed 2020 Tokyo Olympic Games, he won the NN Mission Marathon, which was held at Enschede Airport Twente in the Netherlands on 18 April 2021 in a time of 2:04:30. Jonathan Korir finished as the runner up with a personal best of 2:06:40.[103]

Kipchoge successfully defended his title from the Rio Olympics by winning the gold medal in the men's marathon at the Tokyo Games in a time of 2:08:38, becoming only the third person to successfully defend their gold medal in the men's marathon, after Abebe Bikila in 1960 and 1964, and Waldemar Cierpinski in 1976 and 1980.[104] He was the favourite to win and attacked around the 30 km mark, looking back only once afterwards. He won by 80 seconds, the largest margin in 49 years.[105] The silver medal went to Abdi Nageeye (Netherlands), while Bashir Abdi (Belgium) came in third for a bronze medal with 2:10:00. Kipchoge was the oldest Olympic marathon winner since Carlos Lopes won in 1984 at the age of 37. The run was staged 500 miles north of Tokyo in Sapporo, with 106 runners participating.[106] A documentary on the Ineos 1:59 Challenge, titled Kipchoge: The Last Milestone, was released digitally on-demand on 24 August 2021.

2022edit

On 20 January, Kipchoge announced his desire to win all six World Marathon Majors (he had already won three, the London, Berlin, and Chicago marathons, by that time). This was followed up by an announcement on 18 February that he would be participating in the 2021 Tokyo Marathon (which took place on 6 March 2022 due to COVID-19 restrictions in 2021) and that the majority of his recent training has been dedicated towards this goal.[107] He won the Tokyo Marathon with a time of 2:02:40 – a course and all-comers' record. Amos Kipruto of Kenya finished second with a personal best of 2:03:13, and Tamirat Tola from Ethiopia came in third in a time of 2:04:14.[108]

2022 Berlin and second world marathon recordedit
Kipchoge (back center) about 14.5 km (9.0 mi) into the race, behind pacemakers (in striped gear).
Eliud at the 2022 Berlin Marathon.

On 25 September, Kipchoge won the Berlin Marathon decisively in a time of 2:01:09, beating by 30 seconds his own previous world record, which he set on the same course in 2018. With his fourth victory in Berlin, he equaled the record achievement of Haile Gebrselassie. He finished 4:49 min ahead of second-placed compatriot Mark Korir while Ethiopia's Tadu Abate took third place with a time of 2:06:28. Kipchoge achieved halfway in 59:51, which, being at the time, the fastest split in marathon history, would have been a world record in the standalone half-marathon in 1993, and was only 26 seconds off his best in that distance. He slowed down later with the second half in 61:18.[109][110][111][112] It was the eighth time in a row that the men's record was set in Berlin and the 12th record there overall.[113][55]

2023–presentedit

At the 2023 Boston Marathon, Kipchoge aimed to win his fifth of the six major marathons. However, after missing his water bottle and due to a left leg problem,[114][115] the 38-year-old was unable to stay with the lead group on a hilly section after the 30 km mark. He suffered the third defeat of his marathon career, finishing sixth with a time of 2:09:23. Evans Chebet was the winner in 2:05:54, successfully defending his title.[116]

At the 2023 Berlin Marathon, his first race since the Boston defeat, Kipchoge won the race for a record fifth time, finishing at 2:02:42. He ran alone from 32 km (20 mi) onward after Ethiopia's Derseh Kindie dropped away, but fell short of breaking his own world record that he had set the previous year. With the victory, Kipchoge became the first man in history to win the Berlin Marathon five times, having already won in 2015, 2017, 2018, and 2022.[citation needed] Fellow Kenyan Vincent Kipkemoi came in third place in a time of 2:03:13. The half marathon split time was 1:00:22.




Kipchoge failed to finish the marathon for the first time in his career when defending his gold medal at the 2024 Paris Olympics, dropping out of the race after around 30 km (19 mi), citing discomfort around his waist. He later told reporters that he would not compete at another Olympic Games. When asked about the prospects of competing in Los Angeles in 2028: he explained:

"You will see me in a different way, maybe giving people motivation, but I will not run. I need to go back, sit down, try to figure my 21 years of running at high level. I need to evolve and feature in other things."[117]

The Marathons winner was Tamirat Tola (Ethiopia) in a time of 2:06:26, an Olympic record; silver went to Bashir Abdi (Belgium) 2:06:47; and bronze to Benson Kipruto (Kenya) in 2:07:00. Kipchoge's longtime rival Kenenisa Bekele finished 2:12:24 placed 39 among 71 finishers with 10 runners not finishing. Despite the performance, Kenyan President William Ruto still recognized Kipchoge's achievements:

"I know how people were disappointed. Many people I know made a lot of comments, 'How could Eliud not finish?' But Eliud we celebrate you. You have held our flag high."[118]

Kipchoge competed in the 2025 New York City Marathon, finishing 17th, thus completing all six World Marathon Major courses. After finishing, Kipchoge announced a new project known as Eliud's Running World, where he will run seven marathons across seven continents over a period of two years to raise awareness about sustainability and education.[119] This would also be in an effort to raise money to build libraries in Kenya.[120]

On 11th October 2026, Kipchoge won the Melbourne Marathon in a time of 2:09:10.[121]

**Samuel Kamau Wanjirū** (10 November 1986 – 15 May 2011) was a Kenyan long-distance runner who won the [2008 Beijing Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics") Marathon in an [Olympic record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Olympic_records_in_athletics "List of Olympic records in athletics") time of 2:06:32; becoming the first Kenyan to win the Olympic [gold](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Gold_medal "Gold medal") in the marathon. He became the youngest gold medallist in the marathon since 1932.
He held the 10,000m U20 World Record from 2005 until 2024 and set the half marathon world record 3 times.[[1]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-1)[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-2) In 2009, he won both the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") and [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon"), running the fastest marathons ever recorded in the United Kingdom and United States, respectively. He retained his Chicago title in 2010 in a season fraught with injury.
In 2011, he died after a fall from a balcony at his home in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu") following a domestic dispute.

Samuel Wanjirū was born in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu"), [Laikipia County](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laikipia_County "Laikipia County"), a town in the [Rift Valley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Rift_Valley,_Kenya "Great Rift Valley, Kenya"), about 150 kilometres (93 mi) northwest of the capital, [Nairobi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nairobi "Nairobi").[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-huff1-3) and was brought up with his brother Simon Njoroge in poverty by his mother Hannah Wanjiru, the daughter of Samuel Kamau.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-obituary-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-5) Wanjirū took his mother's given name as a surname, because she was a single mother. He dropped out of school aged around 12 because they could not afford the school fees.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-6)

Wanjirū started running at the age of 8. In 2002, he moved to [Japan](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Japan "Japan") and enrolled in Sendai Ikuei Gakuen High School in [Sendai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sendai "Sendai"). He had success on the Japanese [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") circuit, where he won the [Fukuoka International Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_International_Cross_Country "Fukuoka International Cross Country") at sixteen years old in 2003. He went on to win in both [Fukuoka](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka "Fukuoka") and at the [Chiba International Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chiba_International_Cross_Country "Chiba International Cross Country") consecutively in 2004 and 2005.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-7) After graduating in 2005, he joined the [Toyota](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Toyota "Toyota")[Kyūshū](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ky%C5%ABsh%C5%AB "Kyūshū") athletics team, coached by 1992 Olympic marathon [silver medalist](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Silver_medal "Silver medal")[Koichi Morishita](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Koichi_Morishita "Koichi Morishita").[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-8)

Wanjirū had a [5000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") best of 13:12.40, run as a 17-year-old in April 2004 in [Hiroshima](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hiroshima "Hiroshima"), Japan. At age 18, Wanjirū broke the half marathon world record on 11 September 2005 in the [Rotterdam Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Half_Marathon "Rotterdam Half Marathon") with a time of 59:16 minutes, officially beating [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat")'s half-marathon record of 59:17 minutes.
This was preceded two weeks earlier by a bettering of the [10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_track_event "Long-distance track event")[U20 world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_junior_records_in_athletics "World junior records in athletics") by a margin of almost 23 seconds in the IAAF Golden League [Van Damme Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Van_Damme "Memorial Van Damme") Race on 26 August. His WJR time of 26:41.75 was good enough for third place in the race behind [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s world record, set in the same race, of 26:17.53 and [Boniface Kiprop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boniface_Kiprop "Boniface Kiprop")'s 26:39.77. It was Kiprop who held the previous world junior mark (27:04.00 minutes), set at the same meeting the previous year. The run saw 6 runners going under 27 minutes[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-9)[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-10)

### World records and Olympic gold
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Wanjiru&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: World records and Olympic gold")]
Wanjiru took back the half-marathon world record, which [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie") broke in early 2006, with 58:53 minutes on 9 February 2007 at the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah_Half_Marathon "Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-11) and improved it to 58:33 on 17 March 2007 in the [City-Pier-City Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-Pier-City_Loop "City-Pier-City Loop") in [The Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague"), [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"). While improving his own record, he recorded an unofficial time of 55:31 for 20 km, which was faster than Haile Gebrselassie's world record but was never ratified due to the timing methods in the race.[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-12)
[![Image 9](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/f/ff/Samuel_Wanjiru%2C_Marathon%2C_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg/250px-Samuel_Wanjiru%2C_Marathon%2C_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Samuel_Wanjiru,_Marathon,_2008_Summer_Olympics.jpg)
Wanjiru approaching the finishing line at the [2008 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Summer_Olympics "2008 Summer Olympics")

chunks.text:
### World records and Olympic gold
Wanjiru made his marathon debut at [Fukuoka Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_Marathon "Fukuoka Marathon") on 2 December 2007, winning it impressively with a course record of 2:06:39.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-13) He started 2008 by winning the [Zayed International Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_International_Half_Marathon "Zayed International Half Marathon") and receiving a prize of US$300,000.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-14) In the 2008 [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon"), he came in second, breaking 2:06 for the first time. In the 2008 Summer Olympics, Wanjiru won the marathon gold medal in an Olympic record time of 2:06:32, smashing the previous record of 2:09:21 set by [Carlos Lopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Lopes "Carlos Lopes") of Portugal in the 1984 Olympics.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-15) He received the [AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIMS_World_Athlete_of_the_Year_Award "AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award") that year in recognition of his performances.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-16)

### London and Chicago wins
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Samuel_Wanjiru&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: London and Chicago wins")]
headings: ### London and Chicago wins

chunks.text:
### London and Chicago wins
At the [Granollers Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granollers_Half_Marathon "Granollers Half Marathon") in February 2008, in which Wanjiru won, the Kenyan stated his intent for the future, saying, "in five years' time I feel capable of clocking a sub 2 hours time for the marathon."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-17) In April 2009, Wanjiru won the London Marathon in a time of 2:05:10, a new personal record and also a new course record. He was pleased with the achievement and stated that he hoped to break Haile Gebrselassie's world record in the near future.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-18) At the Rotterdam Half Marathon, Wanjiru clocked a 1:01:08 on 13 September, which was won by [Sammy Kitwara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Kitwara "Sammy Kitwara") with a time of 58:58.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-19) In October 2009, Wanjiru won the [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_winners_of_the_Chicago_Marathon "List of winners of the Chicago Marathon") in a time of 2:05:41, setting a new course record for the city and the fastest marathon time ever run in the United States.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-20) The wins in London and Chicago helped him reach the top of the [World Marathon Majors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Marathon_Majors "World Marathon Majors") rankings for 2009, earning him a jackpot of US$500,000.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-21)

### London and Chicago wins
He signed up to defend his title at the [2010 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_London_Marathon "2010 London Marathon"), but he encountered knee trouble at the midway point of the race and decided to drop out to avoid further injury – the first time in six marathons that he had failed to finish.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-22) He chose to run at the 2010 Chicago Marathon in October, but a stomach virus before the race had hampered his preparations and he entered the competition with the lesser aim of reaching the top three. [Tsegaye Kebede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsegaye_Kebede "Tsegaye Kebede") took the opportunity to forge a lead, but Wanjiru (despite a lack of peak physical form) persevered with the pace and caught up with the Ethiopian. He took the lead in the final 400 m to defend his title in Chicago with a time of 2:06:24. "It was the greatest surprise I have ever seen in my life", remarked his coach, Federico Rosa, on the performance.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-24)
Wanjiru married [Mary Wacera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Wacera "Mary Wacera"), a fellow long-distance runner, in 2009 and the two had a child (Ann) in 2010. He had previously married Triza Njeri in a traditional ceremony and had two children, although Wanjiru and Wacera's marriage was legally binding.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

Wanjiru began drinking alcohol when he moved to Japan, and it increased and became a major part of his life. Despite that, his marathoning career continued successfully, though his personal life became somewhat chaotic.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)
In December 2010, Wanjiru was arrested by [Kenyan police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Police "Kenya Police") at his house in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu") and charged with threatening to kill his wife and illegally possessing an [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47") rifle. He denied both the accusations and claimed that he was being framed.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-28)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)
Wanjiru and his wife Triza Njeri, a beautician, had a daughter Anne Wanjiru and a son Simon Njoroge.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-obituary-4)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-29) Wanjiru also had a third wife, Judy Wambui Wairimu, who was pregnant when he died and has since had a son.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-30)

Wanjiru's cousin [Joseph Riri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Joseph_Riri?action=edit&redlink=1 "Joseph Riri (page does not exist)") was a world-class marathon runner,[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-31) and Wanjiru's younger brother [Simon Njoroge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Simon_Njoroge?action=edit&redlink=1 "Simon Njoroge (page does not exist)") was also a long-distance runner.[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-32)
On 15 May 2011, Wanjiru died from a fall off a balcony at his home in Nyahururu. Wanjiru appeared to have suffered internal injuries after the fall and was confirmed dead by doctors at a nearby hospital after attempts to revive him failed.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-bbc1-33)
Police said Wanjiru's wife, Triza Njeri, had come home to find him in bed with another woman. She locked the couple in the bedroom and ran outside. Wanjiru then died after falling from the balcony.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-huff1-3) Police were unsure if Wanjiru intended suicide or jumped out of rage, and investigated the circumstances related to Njeri and his female companion that led to his death.[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-huff1-3)[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-nytLongman16May2011-34)

In May 2017, while testifying during an inquest into Wanjiru's death, his mother Hannah Wanjiru said at the Milimani law court that she believes her son was murdered.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-35)[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-37)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)
His mother claimed at an inquest into his death that her son was murdered by six men who had conspired with his wife Trizah Njeri.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-38) During the inquest at the Milimani court that sought to establish whether Wanjiru was murdered or jumped to his death, a former chief government pathologist said he was convinced that Wanjiru was hit by a blunt object after he had jumped from the balcony of his home, landing on his legs, or that he was possibly pushed and then struck.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-39)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

From Wikipedia, the free encyclopedia

Ethiopian long-distance runner (born 1991)

This article is about a person whose name includes a [patronymic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Patronymic "Patronymic"). The article properly refers to the person by her given name, Almaz, and not as Ayana.

**Almaz Ayana Eba** ([Oromo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromo_language "Oromo language"): _Almaaz Ayyanaa Eebbaa_; [Amharic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amharic_language "Amharic language"): አልማዝ አያና ኤባ, born 21 November 1991[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-WAprofile-4)) is an Ethiopian [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). She won the gold medal in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") and bronze in the [5,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") at the [2016 Rio Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics"). Almaz is a four-time [World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") medallist earning a bronze for the 5,000m in [2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2013 World Championships in Athletics"), gold at the event in [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2015 World Championships in Athletics") as well as gold in the 10,000m and silver in the 5,000m in [2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2017 World Championships in Athletics").

She broke the 10,000 metres world record, set in 1993, while winning the gold medal at the Rio Olympics and held it until 2021. At the 2017 World Championships in London, Almaz won the title in the 10,000m, finishing 46 seconds ahead of the runner-up. She finished third in both the 5,000m and 10,000m on the respective world all-time lists. In 2016, she was voted [IAAF](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics "World Athletics")[Female World Athlete of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athlete_of_the_Year "World Athlete of the Year").

Almaz set the fastest ever women's marathon debut at the 2022 [Amsterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Marathon "Amsterdam Marathon").

## Early life and background

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and background")]

Almaz Ayana was born in [Wenbera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wenbera "Wenbera"), [Benishangul-Gumuz Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benishangul-Gumuz_Region "Benishangul-Gumuz Region"), Ethiopia.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-aips_media-5) Born the seventh youngest of nine siblings, she started running at local school around age 13–14.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-6) Like other notable athletes such as [Fatuma Roba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatuma_Roba "Fatuma Roba") and [Derartu Tulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derartu_Tulu "Derartu Tulu"), Almaz is also Oromo descent.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-7) In addition to her native [Oromo language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromo_language "Oromo language"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-8) she also speaks [Amharic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amharic "Amharic").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-9) The name Almaz means 'diamond' in Amharic.

Almaz is married to her childhood friend and longtime partner, Soressa Fida.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-aips_media-5) She is a devout Christian.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-aips_media-5)

## Career

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=2 "Edit section: Career")]

### 2013–2014: World 5000 m bronze in Moscow

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=3 "Edit section: 2013–2014: World 5000 m bronze in Moscow")]

At age 21, Almaz won a bronze medal in the [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_5000_metres "2013 World Championships in Athletics – Women's 5000 metres") at the [2013 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2013 World Championships in Athletics") held in [Moscow](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Moscow "Moscow"), Russia.

At the [2014 African Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_African_Championships_in_Athletics "2014 African Championships in Athletics") in [Marrakesh](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marrakesh "Marrakesh"), she defeated favourite [Genzebe Dibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genzebe_Dibaba "Genzebe Dibaba") to take the title in a championship record time of 15:32.72.[[10]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-10) One month later at the [Continental Cup](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2014_IAAF_Continental_Cup "2014 IAAF Continental Cup") also held in Marrakesh, she won the 5000 m by over 24 seconds.[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-11)

### 2015: World 5000 m champion in Beijing

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=4 "Edit section: 2015: World 5000 m champion in Beijing")]

[![Image 46](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/e/ec/Almaz_Ayana_at_Beijing_2015.jpg/250px-Almaz_Ayana_at_Beijing_2015.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Almaz_Ayana_at_Beijing_2015.jpg)

At the [2015 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2015 World Championships in Athletics") in [Beijing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Beijing "Beijing"), Almaz won her first world title with a 5000 m victory.

In May 2015, Almaz ran a personal best of 14:14.32 over 5000 m at the [Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_IAAF_Diamond_League "2015 IAAF Diamond League") meeting in [Shanghai](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Shanghai_Golden_Grand_Prix "Shanghai Golden Grand Prix"), China, improving significantly upon her previous personal best of 14:25.84 set in 2013 in [Paris](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paris "Paris").[[12]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-12)[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-WAprofile-4) This made her the [third fastest](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres#Women "5000 metres") female athlete over that distance, behind compatriots [Tirunesh Dibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tirunesh_Dibaba "Tirunesh Dibaba"), the world record holder, and [Meseret Defar](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Meseret_Defar "Meseret Defar"). At the [Beijing World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2015 World Championships in Athletics") in August, she put on a stunning display of front-running to win the [5000 m final](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_5000_metres "2015 World Championships in Athletics – Women's 5000 metres") with a time of 14:26.83, setting a new championship record in the process and beating silver medalist [Senbere Teferi](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Senbere_Teferi "Senbere Teferi") by more than 17 seconds with [Genzebe Dibaba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Genzebe_Dibaba "Genzebe Dibaba") in third.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-13) Her win was named the Performance of the Championships by World Athletics.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-14) In her final race of the season, Almaz set a new 3000 m meeting record of 8:22.34 to beat Tirunesh Dibaba at the [Zurich Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weltklasse "Weltklasse").[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-15)

### 2016: Rio Olympic 10,000 m champion with a world record, bronze at 5000 m

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: 2016: Rio Olympic 10,000 m champion with a world record, bronze at 5000 m")]

Almaz opened her season by winning over 3000 m at the [Doha Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Doha_Diamond_League "Doha Diamond League") on the 6 May, running a time of 8:23.11 which narrowly missed her personal best.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-16) On 2 June 2016, Almaz set a new personal best in the 5000 m in a time of 14:12.59 at the [Rome](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Golden_Gala "Golden Gala")[Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_IAAF_Diamond_League "2016 IAAF Diamond League"). This made her the second fastest woman ever at this distance, behind only Tirunesh Dibaba's world record of 14:11.15, and established a new circuit record. Later that month, she ran the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") competitively for the first time at the Ethiopian Olympic trials in [Hengelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengelo "Hengelo"), Netherlands.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-17) She posted the fastest ever debut time of 30:07.00, defeating Tirunesh Dibaba and moving up to eighth on the world all-time list.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-18)

[![Image 47](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/4/4e/Provas_de_Atletismo_nas_Olimp%C3%ADadas_Rio_2016_%2829109535365%29.jpg/250px-Provas_de_Atletismo_nas_Olimp%C3%ADadas_Rio_2016_%2829109535365%29.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Provas_de_Atletismo_nas_Olimp%C3%ADadas_Rio_2016_(29109535365).jpg)

Almaz (in second) on her way to 10,000 m gold at the [2016 Rio Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2016_Summer_Olympics "2016 Summer Olympics").

At the [2016 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics") held in August in [Rio de Janeiro](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rio_de_Janeiro "Rio de Janeiro"), Almaz set a world record of 29:17.45 in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Women's_10,000_metres "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics – Women's 10,000 metres"), topping Chinese athlete [Wang Junxia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wang_Junxia "Wang Junxia")'s 23-year-old world record by 14 seconds.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-19)[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-Guardian_report-20) No one previously had run within 22 seconds of Wang's record.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-21) The 10,000 metres was already an extremely fast race when Ayana broke away with 12 laps to go. Second-placed [Vivian Cheruiyot](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Vivian_Cheruiyot "Vivian Cheruiyot") of Kenya finished just a second shy of Wang's record and double Olympic 10,000 metres champion Tirunesh Dibaba earned the bronze medal with a 12 seconds improvement on her personal best and the fourth fastest time in history. Multiple national records were set, and eighteen competitors set personal bests.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-22) The lax [drug testing](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Drug_testing "Drug testing") regime in Ethiopia[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-23) and the doping scandals that embroiled athletics before the Rio Olympics caused some to question whether Almaz had been doping.[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-538_discussion-24) British commentators [Brendan Foster](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brendan_Foster "Brendan Foster") and [Paula Radcliffe](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe "Paula Radcliffe"), both former world record holders in distance events, were skeptical about Almaz's performance.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-Guardian_report-20) Fellow competitors reported that before the race, the Ethiopian was coughing and did not seem well.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-AW_report-25) In her post-race press conference, Almaz said her time was purely the outcome of hard training.[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-26) On 9 September, in her first race since the Olympics, Almaz attempted to break Tirunesh Dibaba's 2008 5000 m world record of 14:11.15 at the [Brussels Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_van_Damme "Memorial van Damme").[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-27) Despite a strong start, she fell short of breaking the record but did set a meeting record of 14:18.99.[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-28)

### 2017: 10,000 m gold and 5000 m silver at the London World Championships

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=6 "Edit section: 2017: 10,000 m gold and 5000 m silver at the London World Championships")]

[![Image 48](https://thumb.wikimedia.org/wikipedia/commons/thumb/5/50/Almaz_Ayana_London_2017.jpg/250px-Almaz_Ayana_London_2017.jpg?utm_source=en.wikipedia.org&utm_campaign=parser&utm_content=thumbnail)](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/File:Almaz_Ayana_London_2017.jpg)

Almaz celebrates her 10,000 m win at the [2017 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2017 World Championships in Athletics") in London.

On 5 August 2017, Almaz secured a dominant victory as she won over 10,000 metres at the [World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2017 World Championships in Athletics") in London with a world-leading 30:16.32,[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-29)[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-30) She ran her final 5,000 m in 14:24.94, a time that would've placed her seventh on the [all-time 5,000 m lists](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres#Women_(outdoor) "5000 metres") at the time.[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-Letsrun-31) Her win set the record for the biggest margin of victory over 10,000 m at a World Championship and was described as "one of the finest displays in women’s distance running history" by [Letsrun](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Letsrun.com "Letsrun.com").[[31]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-Letsrun-31) She went on to add a silver for the 5,000 metres eight days later, having run a time of 14:40.35 to finish behind Kenya's [Hellen Obiri](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hellen_Obiri "Hellen Obiri") (14:34.86).[[32]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-32) Almaz made her debut over the [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") at the [New Delhi Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_Delhi_Half_Marathon "New Delhi Half Marathon") winning in a time of 1:07:12.[[33]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-33)

### 2018–present: Injuries, motherhood and comeback

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2018–present: Injuries, motherhood and comeback")]

The Ethiopian distance running star took almost three years off due to injury problems and pregnancy. Her only race during this time was at the [2019 Prefontaine Classic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2019_Prefontaine_Classic "2019 Prefontaine Classic") where she placed 18th over 3,000 m in a time of 8:57.16.[[34]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-34) Almaz started regularly competing again from April 2022.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-WAprofile-4)

Almaz made her return to the track at the 2022 [FBK Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fanny_Blankers-Koen_Games "Fanny Blankers-Koen Games") in [Hengelo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hengelo "Hengelo"), placing seventh over the 10,000 m in 30:48.48. She also placed sixth over 5,000 m at the [Oslo Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Bislett_Games "2022 Bislett Games") in 14:32.17.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-35)

On 16 October 2022, the 30-year-old made the fastest ever women's [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") debut of 2:17:20 at the [Amsterdam Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amsterdam_Marathon "Amsterdam Marathon") to win the race and defeat her old-time rival Genzebe Dibaba by 45 seconds. Almaz beat the course record by almost 40 seconds, setting a Dutch all-comers' record (best performance on country's soil) and putting her seventh on the [world all-time list](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon#All-time_individual_top_25 "Marathon") at the time.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-36)[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-37)

In 2023, Almaz opened her season by winning the [Lisbon Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lisbon_Half_Marathon "Lisbon Half Marathon") in a course record of 1:05:30.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-38) On 17 September, Almaz competed over the [10 mile](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10-mile_run "10-mile run") distance for the first time by placing third at the [Dam tot Damloop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dam_tot_Damloop "Dam tot Damloop") in [Zaandam](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zaandam "Zaandam") in 52:23.[[39]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-39) She set a new personal best for the marathon of 2:16:20 in finishing second behind [Worknesh Degefa](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Worknesh_Degefa "Worknesh Degefa") at the [Valencia Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2023_Valencia_Marathon "2023 Valencia Marathon").[[40]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-40)
