### World records and Olympic gold
Wanjiru made his marathon debut at [Fukuoka Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fukuoka_Marathon "Fukuoka Marathon") on 2 December 2007, winning it impressively with a course record of 2:06:39.[[13]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-13) He started 2008 by winning the [Zayed International Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Zayed_International_Half_Marathon "Zayed International Half Marathon") and receiving a prize of US$300,000.[[14]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-14) In the 2008 [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon"), he came in second, breaking 2:06 for the first time. In the 2008 Summer Olympics, Wanjiru won the marathon gold medal in an Olympic record time of 2:06:32, smashing the previous record of 2:09:21 set by [Carlos Lopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Lopes "Carlos Lopes") of Portugal in the 1984 Olympics.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-15) He received the [AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIMS_World_Athlete_of_the_Year_Award "AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award") that year in recognition of his performances.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-16)

Wanjiru took back the half-marathon world record, which [Haile Gebrselassie](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie "Haile Gebrselassie") broke in early 2006, with 58:53 minutes on 9 February 2007 at the [Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ras_Al_Khaimah_Half_Marathon "Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon")[[11]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-11) and improved it to 58:33 on 17 March 2007 in the [City-Pier-City Loop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/City-Pier-City_Loop "City-Pier-City Loop") in [The Hague](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/The_Hague "The Hague"), [Netherlands](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Netherlands "Netherlands"). At age 18, Wanjirū broke the half marathon world record on 11 September 2005 in the [Rotterdam Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Rotterdam_Half_Marathon "Rotterdam Half Marathon") with a time of 59:16 minutes, officially beating [Paul Tergat](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paul_Tergat "Paul Tergat")'s half-marathon record of 59:17 minutes.
This was preceded two weeks earlier by a bettering of the [10,000 m](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_track_event "Long-distance track event")[U20 world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_junior_records_in_athletics "World junior records in athletics") by a margin of almost 23 seconds in the IAAF Golden League [Van Damme Memorial](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Memorial_Van_Damme "Memorial Van Damme") Race on 26 August. His WJR time of 26:41.75 was good enough for third place in the race behind [Kenenisa Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele "Kenenisa Bekele")'s world record, set in the same race, of 26:17.53 and [Boniface Kiprop](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Boniface_Kiprop "Boniface Kiprop")'s 26:39.77. It was Kiprop who held the previous world junior mark (27:04.00 minutes), set at the same meeting the previous year. In the 2008 Summer Olympics, Wanjiru won the marathon gold medal in an Olympic record time of 2:06:32, smashing the previous record of 2:09:21 set by [Carlos Lopes](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Carlos_Lopes "Carlos Lopes") of Portugal in the 1984 Olympics.[[15]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-15) He received the [AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIMS_World_Athlete_of_the_Year_Award "AIMS World Athlete of the Year Award") that year in recognition of his performances.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-16)

He signed up to defend his title at the [2010 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_London_Marathon "2010 London Marathon"), but he encountered knee trouble at the midway point of the race and decided to drop out to avoid further injury – the first time in six marathons that he had failed to finish.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-22) He chose to run at the 2010 Chicago Marathon in October, but a stomach virus before the race had hampered his preparations and he entered the competition with the lesser aim of reaching the top three. [Tsegaye Kebede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsegaye_Kebede "Tsegaye Kebede") took the opportunity to forge a lead, but Wanjiru (despite a lack of peak physical form) persevered with the pace and caught up with the Ethiopian. He took the lead in the final 400 m to defend his title in Chicago with a time of 2:06:24. "It was the greatest surprise I have ever seen in my life", remarked his coach, Federico Rosa, on the performance.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-24)
Wanjiru married [Mary Wacera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Wacera "Mary Wacera"), a fellow long-distance runner, in 2009 and the two had a child (Ann) in 2010. He had previously married Triza Njeri in a traditional ceremony and had two children, although Wanjiru and Wacera's marriage was legally binding.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

He signed up to defend his title at the [2010 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2010_London_Marathon "2010 London Marathon"), but he encountered knee trouble at the midway point of the race and decided to drop out to avoid further injury – the first time in six marathons that he had failed to finish.[[22]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-22) He chose to run at the 2010 Chicago Marathon in October, but a stomach virus before the race had hampered his preparations and he entered the competition with the lesser aim of reaching the top three. [Tsegaye Kebede](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tsegaye_Kebede "Tsegaye Kebede") took the opportunity to forge a lead, but Wanjiru (despite a lack of peak physical form) persevered with the pace and caught up with the Ethiopian. He took the lead in the final 400 m to defend his title in Chicago with a time of 2:06:24. "It was the greatest surprise I have ever seen in my life", remarked his coach, Federico Rosa, on the performance.[[23]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-23)[[24]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-24)
Wanjiru married [Mary Wacera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Mary_Wacera "Mary Wacera"), a fellow long-distance runner, in 2009 and the two had a child (Ann) in 2010. He had previously married Triza Njeri in a traditional ceremony and had two children, although Wanjiru and Wacera's marriage was legally binding.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-25)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)

### London and Chicago wins
At the [Granollers Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Granollers_Half_Marathon "Granollers Half Marathon") in February 2008, in which Wanjiru won, the Kenyan stated his intent for the future, saying, "in five years' time I feel capable of clocking a sub 2 hours time for the marathon."[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-17) In April 2009, Wanjiru won the London Marathon in a time of 2:05:10, a new personal record and also a new course record. He was pleased with the achievement and stated that he hoped to break Haile Gebrselassie's world record in the near future.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-18) At the Rotterdam Half Marathon, Wanjiru clocked a 1:01:08 on 13 September, which was won by [Sammy Kitwara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Kitwara "Sammy Kitwara") with a time of 58:58.[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-19) In October 2009, Wanjiru won the [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_winners_of_the_Chicago_Marathon "List of winners of the Chicago Marathon") in a time of 2:05:41, setting a new course record for the city and the fastest marathon time ever run in the United States.[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-20) The wins in London and Chicago helped him reach the top of the [World Marathon Majors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Marathon_Majors "World Marathon Majors") rankings for 2009, earning him a jackpot of US$500,000.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-21)

In December 2010, Wanjiru was arrested by [Kenyan police](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenya_Police "Kenya Police") at his house in [Nyahururu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Nyahururu "Nyahururu") and charged with threatening to kill his wife and illegally possessing an [AK-47](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AK-47 "AK-47") rifle. He denied both the accusations and claimed that he was being framed.[[27]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-27)[[28]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-28)[[26]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-drinking-26)
Wanjiru and his wife Triza Njeri, a beautician, had a daughter Anne Wanjiru and a son Simon Njoroge.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-obituary-4)[[29]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-29) Wanjiru also had a third wife, Judy Wambui Wairimu, who was pregnant when he died and has since had a son.[[30]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Samuel_Wanjiru#cite_note-30)

Kipchoge claimed his first individual world championship title in 2003 by winning the junior race at the World Cross Country Championships and setting a world junior record for the 5000 m. At the age of eighteen, he became the senior 5000 m world champion at the 2003 World Championships with a championship record, then followed by an Olympic bronze for Kenya in 2004 and a bronze at the 2006 World Indoor Championships. A five-time World Championship 5000 m finalist, Kipchoge took silver medals at the 2007 World Championships, 2008 Beijing Olympics, and 2010 Commonwealth Games.
He switched to road running in 2012 and made the second-fastest half marathon debut ever, at 59:25. In his marathon debut, he won the 2013 Hamburg Marathon in a course record time. His first victory at a World Marathon Major came at the Chicago Marathon in 2014, and he went on to become series champion a record five times – for 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2022. He has won the London Marathon a record four times and also holds the record for most Berlin Marathon wins with five, his latest coming in September 2023. With 15 victories in his first 18 marathons from 2013 to 2023, Kipchoge's only losses were a second-place finish behind Wilson Kipsang Kiprotich at the 2013 Berlin Marathon, where Kipsang broke the world record; an eighth-place finish at the 2020 London Marathon and a sixth place in his debut at the Boston Marathon in 2023.[7][8][9] He has since 2024, been defeated in his last three marathons. Kipchoge's last world record run broke by 30 seconds his own 2018 world record, which was in turn a 78-second improvement over the existing best, the greatest improvement in a marathon world record time since 1967.

Eliud Kipchoge EGH (English: /ˈɛlɪjud kɪpˈtʃoʊɡeɪ/ ELL-ih-yood kip-CHOH-gay[3][4]; born 5 November 1984) is a Kenyan long-distance runner who competes in the marathon and formerly specialized in the 5000 metres. Kipchoge is the 2016 and 2020 Olympic marathon champion, and was the world record holder in the marathon from 2018 to 2023,[5] until that record was broken by Kelvin Kiptum at the 2023 Chicago Marathon. He is widely considered to be one of the greatest marathon runners of all time.[6][5]
state.next_chunk:
On 12 October 2019, Kipchoge ran the marathon distance for the Ineos 1:59 Challenge in Vienna, achieving a time of 1:59:40.2, becoming the first person in recorded history to do a sub-two-hour marathon.[10] The run did not count as a new marathon record, as he ran with specialized shoes, standard competition rules for pacing and fluids were not followed, and it was not an open event.[11][12][13]
Kipchoge was appointed Elder of the Order of the Golden Heart by former Kenyan President Uhuru Kenyatta on 20 October 2019 in recognition of his sub-two-hour marathon.[14] He was also named the 2019 BBC World Sport Star of the Year. In 2023 he was awarded the Princess of Asturias Award in the category "Sports".[15]
Personal lifeedit
Kipchoge was born on 5 November 1984 in Kapsisiywa, Nandi County, in Kenya. He graduated from the Kaptel Secondary School in Nandi County in 1999 but did not run seriously or as a profession then.[16][17] He ran three kilometres (2 mi) to school on a daily basis.[18] Kipchoge was raised by a single mother (a teacher), and only knew his father from pictures. He is the youngest of four children. He met his trainer Patrick Sang (a former Olympic medalist in the steeplechase) in 2001 at the age of 16.[19]
Kipchoge's wife and three children live in Eldoret, Kenya.[20][21] He lives and trains in Kaptagat, 30 km (19 miles) from Eldoret.[22] He is a devout Catholic.[23]
Following the death of Kelvin Kiptum in 2024, Kipchoge and his family faced online threats falsely accusing him of being involved in Kiptum's death. These threats impacted his training and well-being.[24][25]
Careeredit

Kipchoge claimed his first individual world championship title in 2003 by winning the junior race at the World Cross Country Championships and setting a world junior record for the 5000 m. At the age of eighteen, he became the senior 5000 m world champion at the 2003 World Championships with a championship record, then followed by an Olympic bronze for Kenya in 2004 and a bronze at the 2006 World Indoor Championships. A five-time World Championship 5000 m finalist, Kipchoge took silver medals at the 2007 World Championships, 2008 Beijing Olympics, and 2010 Commonwealth Games.
He switched to road running in 2012 and made the second-fastest half marathon debut ever, at 59:25. In his marathon debut, he won the 2013 Hamburg Marathon in a course record time. His first victory at a World Marathon Major came at the Chicago Marathon in 2014, and he went on to become series champion a record five times – for 2016, 2017, 2018, 2019 and 2022. He has won the London Marathon a record four times and also holds the record for most Berlin Marathon wins with five, his latest coming in September 2023. With 15 victories in his first 18 marathons from 2013 to 2023, Kipchoge's only losses were a second-place finish behind Wilson Kipsang Kiprotich at the 2013 Berlin Marathon, where Kipsang broke the world record; an eighth-place finish at the 2020 London Marathon and a sixth place in his debut at the Boston Marathon in 2023.[7][8][9] He has since 2024, been defeated in his last three marathons. Kipchoge's last world record run broke by 30 seconds his own 2018 world record, which was in turn a 78-second improvement over the existing best, the greatest improvement in a marathon world record time since 1967.

2023–presentedit
At the 2023 Boston Marathon, Kipchoge aimed to win his fifth of the six major marathons. However, after missing his water bottle and due to a left leg problem,[114][115] the 38-year-old was unable to stay with the lead group on a hilly section after the 30 km mark. He suffered the third defeat of his marathon career, finishing sixth with a time of 2:09:23. Evans Chebet was the winner in 2:05:54, successfully defending his title.[116]
At the 2023 Berlin Marathon, his first race since the Boston defeat, Kipchoge won the race for a record fifth time, finishing at 2:02:42. He ran alone from 32 km (20 mi) onward after Ethiopia's Derseh Kindie dropped away, but fell short of breaking his own world record that he had set the previous year. With the victory, Kipchoge became the first man in history to win the Berlin Marathon five times, having already won in 2015, 2017, 2018, and 2022.[citation needed] Fellow Kenyan Vincent Kipkemoi came in third place in a time of 2:03:13. The half marathon split time was 1:00:22.
Kipchoge failed to finish the marathon for the first time in his career when defending his gold medal at the 2024 Paris Olympics, dropping out of the race after around 30 km (19 mi), citing discomfort around his waist. He later told reporters that he would not compete at another Olympic Games. When asked about the prospects of competing in Los Angeles in 2028: he explained:
"You will see me in a different way, maybe giving people motivation, but I will not run. I need to go back, sit down, try to figure my 21 years of running at high level. I need to evolve and feature in other things."[117]
state.previous_chunk:
On 20 January, Kipchoge announced his desire to win all six World Marathon Majors (he had already won three, the London, Berlin, and Chicago marathons, by that time). This was followed up by an announcement on 18 February that he would be participating in the 2021 Tokyo Marathon (which took place on 6 March 2022 due to COVID-19 restrictions in 2021) and that the majority of his recent training has been dedicated towards this goal.[107] He won the Tokyo Marathon with a time of 2:02:40 – a course and all-comers' record. Amos Kipruto of Kenya finished second with a personal best of 2:03:13, and Tamirat Tola from Ethiopia came in third in a time of 2:04:14.[108]
2022 Berlin and second world marathon recordedit  
Kipchoge (back center) about 14.5 km (9.0 mi) into the race, behind pacemakers (in striped gear).  
Eliud at the 2022 Berlin Marathon.
On 25 September, Kipchoge won the Berlin Marathon decisively in a time of 2:01:09, beating by 30 seconds his own previous world record, which he set on the same course in 2018. With his fourth victory in Berlin, he equaled the record achievement of Haile Gebrselassie. He finished 4:49 min ahead of second-placed compatriot Mark Korir while Ethiopia's Tadu Abate took third place with a time of 2:06:28. Kipchoge achieved halfway in 59:51, which, being at the time, the fastest split in marathon history, would have been a world record in the standalone half-marathon in 1993, and was only 26 seconds off his best in that distance. He slowed down later with the second half in 61:18.[109][110][111][112] It was the eighth time in a row that the men's record was set in Berlin and the 12th record there overall.[113][55]
state.next_chunk:
The Marathons winner was Tamirat Tola (Ethiopia) in a time of 2:06:26, an Olympic record; silver went to Bashir Abdi (Belgium) 2:06:47; and bronze to Benson Kipruto (Kenya) in 2:07:00. Kipchoge's longtime rival Kenenisa Bekele finished 2:12:24 placed 39 among 71 finishers with 10 runners not finishing. Despite the performance, Kenyan President William Ruto still recognized Kipchoge's achievements:
"I know how people were disappointed. Many people I know made a lot of comments, 'How could Eliud not finish?' But Eliud we celebrate you. You have held our flag high."[118]
Kipchoge competed in the 2025 New York City Marathon, finishing 17th, thus completing all six World Marathon Major courses. After finishing, Kipchoge announced a new project known as Eliud's Running World, where he will run seven marathons across seven continents over a period of two years to raise awareness about sustainability and education.[119] This would also be in an effort to raise money to build libraries in Kenya.[120]
On 11th October 2026, Kipchoge won the Melbourne Marathon in a time of 2:09:10.[121]

2023–presentedit
At the 2023 Boston Marathon, Kipchoge aimed to win his fifth of the six major marathons. However, after missing his water bottle and due to a left leg problem,[114][115] the 38-year-old was unable to stay with the lead group on a hilly section after the 30 km mark. He suffered the third defeat of his marathon career, finishing sixth with a time of 2:09:23. Evans Chebet was the winner in 2:05:54, successfully defending his title.[116]
At the 2023 Berlin Marathon, his first race since the Boston defeat, Kipchoge won the race for a record fifth time, finishing at 2:02:42. He ran alone from 32 km (20 mi) onward after Ethiopia's Derseh Kindie dropped away, but fell short of breaking his own world record that he had set the previous year. With the victory, Kipchoge became the first man in history to win the Berlin Marathon five times, having already won in 2015, 2017, 2018, and 2022.[citation needed] Fellow Kenyan Vincent Kipkemoi came in third place in a time of 2:03:13. The half marathon split time was 1:00:22.
Kipchoge failed to finish the marathon for the first time in his career when defending his gold medal at the 2024 Paris Olympics, dropping out of the race after around 30 km (19 mi), citing discomfort around his waist. He later told reporters that he would not compete at another Olympic Games. When asked about the prospects of competing in Los Angeles in 2028: he explained:
"You will see me in a different way, maybe giving people motivation, but I will not run. I need to go back, sit down, try to figure my 21 years of running at high level. I need to evolve and feature in other things."[117]

# Almaz Ayana
**Almaz Ayana Eba** ([Oromo](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromo_language "Oromo language"): _Almaaz Ayyanaa Eebbaa_; [Amharic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amharic_language "Amharic language"): አልማዝ አያና ኤባ, born 21 November 1991[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-WAprofile-4)) is an Ethiopian [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running"). She won the gold medal in the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") and bronze in the [5,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres") at the [2016 Rio Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2016_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2016 Summer Olympics"). Almaz is a four-time [World Athletics Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") medallist earning a bronze for the 5,000m in [2013](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2013_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2013 World Championships in Athletics"), gold at the event in [2015](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2015 World Championships in Athletics") as well as gold in the 10,000m and silver in the 5,000m in [2017](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2017_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2017 World Championships in Athletics").

## Early life and background
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=1 "Edit section: Early life and background")]
Almaz Ayana was born in [Wenbera](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wenbera "Wenbera"), [Benishangul-Gumuz Region](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Benishangul-Gumuz_Region "Benishangul-Gumuz Region"), Ethiopia.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-aips_media-5) Born the seventh youngest of nine siblings, she started running at local school around age 13–14.[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-6) Like other notable athletes such as [Fatuma Roba](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Fatuma_Roba "Fatuma Roba") and [Derartu Tulu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Derartu_Tulu "Derartu Tulu"), Almaz is also Oromo descent.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-7) In addition to her native [Oromo language](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oromo_language "Oromo language"),[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-8) she also speaks [Amharic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amharic "Amharic").[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-9) The name Almaz means 'diamond' in Amharic.
Almaz is married to her childhood friend and longtime partner, Soressa Fida.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-aips_media-5) She is a devout Christian.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-aips_media-5)

[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Almaz_Ayana&action=edit&section=7 "Edit section: 2018–present: Injuries, motherhood and comeback")]

She also placed sixth over 5,000 m at the [Oslo Diamond League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_Bislett_Games "2022 Bislett Games") in 14:32.17.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Almaz_Ayana#cite_note-35)

The record lasted for three and a half years, being broken by [Augustine Choge](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Augustine_Choge "Augustine Choge") with a run of 7:28.78 minutes.[[16]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-16) In December 2000 and 2001 Kenenisa won the 15k roadrace Montferland Run in the Netherlands.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WA-17) For five years in a row, from 2002 (at the age of 19) through 2006, he took both short (4 km) and long (12 km) races at the [IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "IAAF World Cross Country Championships"), a feat no other runner has accomplished even once.[[18]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-18) After the IAAF eliminated the short course race in 2007, Kenenisa won a final long course race in 2008, bringing his World Cross Country medal totals to 11 senior individual gold medals (6 long course, 5 short course), 1 senior silver medal (2001), 1 junior gold medal (2001), 2 team gold medals (2004, 2005), 3 team silver medals (2002, 2003, & 2008), and 1 team bronze medal (2006) for a grand total of 19 medals.[[17]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WA-17)

### 2001 – 2003: Early career
In 2004, Kenenisa broke the world records for the indoor 5000 m, outdoor 5000 m and outdoor 10,000 m (both in a timeframe of 9 days).[[19]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-19) He won the short and long course world cross country titles, leading Ethiopia to the senior men's team title. He also won a gold medal in the men's 10,000 metres and a silver medal in the men's 5000 metres in the 2004 Olympic Games in [Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athens "Athens").[[20]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-20)
On 4 January 2005, Kenenisa's fiancée, 18-year-old Alem Techale, died of an apparent heart attack while on a training run with him. Although it was initially stated that no [autopsy](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Autopsy "Autopsy") was performed, Alem's and Kenenisa's manager [Jos Hermens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jos_Hermens "Jos Hermens") later said that an autopsy had revealed nothing conclusive about Techale's death. She was the [2003 World Youth Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2003_World_Youth_Championships_in_Athletics "2003 World Youth Championships in Athletics") in the [1500 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1500_metres "1500 metres") and in excellent physical condition.[[21]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-21)

At the end of 2005 Kenenisa was voted the _[Track & Field News](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track\_&\_Field\_News "Track & Field News")_ magazine athlete of the year for the second year in a row.[[25]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-25)

### 2009: Berlin World Championships
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Kenenisa_Bekele&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2009: Berlin World Championships")]
Kenenisa Bekele won two gold medals at the [2009 World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics"), held in Berlin. His double victories in 5000m (13:17.09) and 10,000m (26:46.31 – a World Championships Record) were unprecedented and by doing this became the first man to take both the long-distance track gold medals at the same World Championships.[[35]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-35) His talent combination of endurance and speed has made it nearly impossible to defeat Kenenisa when he is at full strength. ### 2011 World Championships and 2012 Olympics
The 41-year-old Kenenisa competed in the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_London_Marathon "2024 London Marathon") on 21 April 2024, where he finished second behind [Alexander Munyao](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Alexander_Mutiso_Munyao "Alexander Mutiso Munyao") breaking his own Masters record by 4 seconds running 2:04:15.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-64) Kenenisa was selected to represent Ethiopia in the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2024_Summer_Olympics_%E2%80%93_Men's_marathon "Athletics at the 2024 Summer Olympics – Men's marathon") at the [2024 Summer Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2024_Summer_Olympics "2024 Summer Olympics"). At 41 years of age, it was his fourth Olympic appearance and first time competing at the event since the 2012 London Olympics.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-65) Kenenisa ended up finishing in 39th place with a time of 2:12:24[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-66)
On 18 November 2007, Kenenisa married [Ethiopian](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Ethiopians "Ethiopians") film actress Danawit Gebregziabher in Addis Ababa.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-67) Kenenisa has one younger brother, [Tariku Bekele](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Tariku_Bekele "Tariku Bekele"), who is also an accomplished world-class distance runner.

2022 - 2023  
In September, he placed third at the Great North Run half marathon in a time of 1:01:01.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-WAprofile-2) The next month, Kenenisa competed in the [2022 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2022_London_Marathon "2022 London Marathon"), finishing fifth in 2:05:53 to set a masters world record in age 40 group.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kenenisa_Bekele#cite_note-63) In April, he took part in the London Marathon but withdrew from the race after 25k mark. Then, in October, he announced on Instagram that he had departed from the NN running team and transitioned his sponsorship from Nike to Anta, a Chinese sports brand. In December, Kenenisa took part in the Valencia Marathon. Although he fell behind the leading group before reaching the 15 km mark, he managed to finish fourth in a M40 Master World Record with a time of 2:04:19. This achievement solidifies him as the first athlete aged over 40 to complete a marathon in sub 2:05 clocking.

He lost his first half marathon in Den Haag (14 March 2009), when he was beaten by [Sammy Kitwara](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Sammy_Kitwara "Sammy Kitwara") (59:47 for Kitwara, 59:50 for Haile).[_[citation needed](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Citation\_needed "Wikipedia:Citation needed")_]

In 2010, he tried to attack his world record for the third consecutive time at the Dubai Marathon 2010. Although he won the race with a time of 2:06:09, he failed to break his 18-month world record. In a post-race interview, Haile revealed that he had suffered back pain, requiring intensive pre-race physiotherapy, resulting from having slept in a bad position.[[36]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-36) His problems continued at the NYC Half Marathon, where he pulled up mid-race visibly uncomfortable in his running.[[37]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-37) He had an easy victory in the inaugural edition of the [10K de Madrid](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10K_de_Madrid "10K de Madrid") in April.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-World_Athletics-38) He scored his third victory at the Great Manchester Run the following month, although he missed out on Micah Kogo's course record.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-World_Athletics-38) He followed this with his first win at the [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run") in September, finishing the half marathon in a time of 59:33 minutes.[[38]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-World_Athletics-38)

### 2004 Athens Olympics
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paula_Radcliffe&action=edit&section=8 "Edit section: 2004 Athens Olympics")]
Radcliffe did not compete in the London Marathon in 2004, but was the favourite to win a gold medal in the marathon at the [Olympic Games in Athens](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2004_Olympic_Games "2004 Olympic Games"). This had an adverse effect on her [stomach](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Stomach "Stomach"), hindering food absorption. She ended up withdrawing from the race after 36 km (22 mi). The race is remembered for a notorious moment towards the end when Radcliffe, hindered by [runner's diarrhoea](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Runner's_diarrhoea "Runner's diarrhoea") and in need for a toilet break, stopped and [defecated](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Defecated "Defecated") on the side of the road in view of the crowd and TV cameras which broadcast the incident live.[[88]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-88) After the race, she apologised to viewers and explained what happened, "I was losing time because I was having stomach cramps and I thought 'I just need to go and I'll be fine'. ... I didn't really want to resort to that in front of hundreds of thousands of people.[[89]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-89) Basically I needed to go. I started feeling it between 15 and 16 miles (26 km) and probably carried on too long before stopping. I must have eaten too much beforehand". ### 2008–09: Beijing Olympics and fitness problems
Radcliffe won the 2008 [New York City Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Marathon "New York City Marathon"), making it her third victory at the competition with a time of 2:23:56. Russian [Lyudmila Petrova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Lyudmila_Petrova "Lyudmila Petrova") came in second, and American [Kara Goucher](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kara_Goucher "Kara Goucher") took third.[[97]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-97)
Following the New York Marathon, Radcliffe suffered more injury setbacks: she had to withdraw from the [2009 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_London_Marathon "2009 London Marathon") due to a fractured toe. In March that year, she had a [bunion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bunion "Bunion") removed which doctors believed was the root cause of her other injuries at that time.[[98]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-98) She did not run competitively for almost 10 months, but made herself available for inclusion in the [2009 British team](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "Great Britain at the 2009 World Championships in Athletics") for the [World Championships in Athletics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2009_World_Championships_in_Athletics "2009 World Championships in Athletics"). She announced that the [New York City Half Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_City_Half_Marathon "New York City Half Marathon") would be a testing ground for her fitness before the competition.[[99]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-99)

### 2008–09: Beijing Olympics and fitness problems
Following a 19-month layoff that included the birth of her second child, Radcliffe returned to action at the Bupa London 10 km (6 mi), where she finished third, 55 seconds behind the winner, [Jo Pavey](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jo_Pavey "Jo Pavey"). She did not perform well and was comfortably beaten by the Ethiopian, while she crossed the line with a time of 72:03.[[106]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-106)

## Anti-doping activity
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paula_Radcliffe&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Anti-doping activity")]
Radcliffe has frequently made high-profile condemnations of the [use of performance-enhancing drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Use_of_performance-enhancing_drugs_in_sport "Use of performance-enhancing drugs in sport") in athletics. Radcliffe and teammate [Hayley Tullett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayley_Tullett "Hayley Tullett") caused controversy when, in the heats of the 5,000 metres at the 2001 World Athletics Championships in [Edmonton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonton "Edmonton"), they held up a sign protesting against the reinstatement of Russian athlete [Olga Yegorova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olga_Yegorova "Olga Yegorova") after Yegorova had tested positive for the banned substance [EPO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erythropoietin "Erythropoietin"). The sign was made by Radcliffe's husband and read 'EPO Cheats Out'.

## Anti-doping activity
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paula_Radcliffe&action=edit&section=14 "Edit section: Anti-doping activity")]
Radcliffe has frequently made high-profile condemnations of the [use of performance-enhancing drugs](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Use_of_performance-enhancing_drugs_in_sport "Use of performance-enhancing drugs in sport") in athletics. Radcliffe and teammate [Hayley Tullett](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hayley_Tullett "Hayley Tullett") caused controversy when, in the heats of the 5,000 metres at the 2001 World Athletics Championships in [Edmonton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Edmonton "Edmonton"), they held up a sign protesting against the reinstatement of Russian athlete [Olga Yegorova](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Olga_Yegorova "Olga Yegorova") after Yegorova had tested positive for the banned substance [EPO](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Erythropoietin "Erythropoietin"). The sign was made by Radcliffe's husband and read 'EPO Cheats Out'.

Radcliffe has advocated a system where first time offenders are banned for four years and any future offence for life. ## Anti-doping activity
In 2015, in the wake of revelations of widespread doping in athletics,[[134]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-ST_report_suppressed-134) Radcliffe said that, unlike some other prominent British athletes, she would not be releasing her blood-test history, and discouraged other athletes from doing so.[[135]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-135) She was later indirectly identified as a suspected doper by MP [Jesse Norman](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Jesse_Norman "Jesse Norman") during a parliamentary inquiry into blood doping.[[136]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-Graun_parliament-136)[[137]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-Radcliffe_fighting_back-137) In response, Radcliffe issued a statement in which she "categorically denied" cheating in any form and said she has "nothing to hide".[[138]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-Radcliffe_response-138) Shortly afterwards, her three suspect test results were leaked, though Radcliffe still refused to release her complete blood-test history.[[139]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-Indie_bloods_leak-139) In late November 2015, the IAAF declared that the accusations were "based on the gross misinterpretation of incomplete data". The [UK Anti Doping Agency](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/UK_Anti-Doping "UK Anti-Doping"), having received Radcliffe's blood test history via the IAAF, stated that "UKAD has come to the same conclusion as the IAAF review that there is no case to answer".[[140]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-140)

Radcliffe has advocated a system where first time offenders are banned for four years and any future offence for life. However, she felt that in cases like that of [Christine Ohuruogu](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Christine_Ohuruogu "Christine Ohuruogu"), who missed three out-of-competition drugs tests, that she should be allowed to compete in the Olympics, as the BOA does not allow anyone who has served a doping ban to compete.[[130]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-130) However, when Ohuruogu admitted to not trying to get to the tests, Radcliffe expressed her disappointment and hoped that it was a lesson learned.[[131]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-131) When [Marion Jones](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marion_Jones "Marion Jones") admitted to steroid use, Radcliffe stated that it was good for the sport that Jones was caught and that they had to keep testing and that people being caught is a big deterrent to would-be cheats.[[129]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-Jones-129)

Radcliffe is a former world champion in the marathon, [half marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Half_marathon "Half marathon") and [cross country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running"). She has also been European champion over [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") and in cross country. On the [track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_running "Track running"), Radcliffe won the 10,000 metres silver medal at the [1999 World Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1999_World_Championships_in_Athletics "1999 World Championships in Athletics")[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-3) and was the [2002 Commonwealth champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2002_Commonwealth_Games "Athletics at the 2002 Commonwealth Games") at [5000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/5000_metres "5000 metres"). She represented [Great Britain at the Olympics](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_Britain_at_the_Olympics "Great Britain at the Olympics") in four consecutive games (1996 to 2008), although she never won an Olympic medal.

to race over 1,500 metres in Barcelona.[[56]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-56) In her first race since the World Cross Country, Radcliffe finished 11th.[[57]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-57) At the London Grand Prix, Radcliffe finished second, one second outside of her British record, in only her second track race of the season.[[58]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-58) At the [Weltklasse Zürich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Weltklasse_Z%C3%BCrich "Weltklasse Zürich")[IAAF Golden League](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_Golden_League "IAAF Golden League") meeting Radcliffe competed in the 3,000 metres and finished in fourth place.[[59]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-59) At the UK trials won the 5,000 metres title.[[60]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-60) The [British Grand Prix](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/British_Grand_Prix_(athletics) "British Grand Prix (athletics)") saw Radcliffe race over 3000 metres, where once again she finished third.[[61]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-61) At the [2000 Olympic Games](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Athletics_at_the_2000_Summer_Olympics "Athletics at the 2000 Summer Olympics") in Sydney, Radcliffe finished sixth in her 10,000 metres heat to qualify for the final.[[62]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-62) In the final Radcliffe set a new British record,

but crossed the line in fourth and was highly disappointed to miss out on a medal.[[63]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-63) Radcliffe returned to action by winning the BUPA Ireland five-mile race.[[64]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-64) At the [Great North Run](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Run "Great North Run"), Radcliffe ran a new European record for the half marathon, as she won the race in a time of 67 minutes and 7 seconds.[[65]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-65) Radcliffe was then selected for the [2000 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2000_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2000 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships") in Mexico.[[66]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-66) Radcliffe won her first World title, despite suffering a panic attack when her nose tape, designed to help her breathe, fell off halfway round.[[67]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-67) The good run of form came to an end, when she turned her attention to the Cross Country events and finished third in Brussels.[[68]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-68) Radcliffe confirmed that her last race of the year would be the [Great North Cross Country](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Great_North_Cross_Country "Great North Cross Country").[[69]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-69) There Radcliffe defeated Tulu by seventy-five seconds,[[70]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-70) in eight inches of snow.[[71]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-71)

**Paula Jane Radcliffe** (born 17 December 1973) is a British former [long-distance runner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_runner "Long-distance runner"). She is a three-time winner of the [London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/London_Marathon "London Marathon") (2002, 2003, 2005), three-time [New York Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/New_York_Marathon "New York Marathon") champion (2004, 2007, 2008), the 2002 [Chicago Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Chicago_Marathon "Chicago Marathon") winner, and the [2005 World Champion in the marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2005_World_Championships_in_Athletics_%E2%80%93_Women's_marathon "2005 World Championships in Athletics – Women's marathon"). She was previously the fastest female [marathoner](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathoner "Marathoner") of all time, and held the [women's marathon world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record_progression "Marathon world record progression") with a time of 2:15:25 for 16 years from 2003 to 2019, when it was broken by [Brigid Kosgei](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Brigid_Kosgei "Brigid Kosgei").[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-2)

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe

She won back-to-back titles in the 2000 and 2001 [IAAF World Half Marathon Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "IAAF World Half Marathon Championships"), winning a third title in 2003.

#### Cross country champion
[[edit](https://en.wikipedia.org/w/index.php?title=Paula_Radcliffe&action=edit&section=5 "Edit section: Cross country champion")]

Held in March in [Dublin](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Dublin "Dublin"), Radcliffe defended her title in the Women's Long Race when she won the [2002 IAAF World Cross Country Championships](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2002_IAAF_World_Cross_Country_Championships "2002 IAAF World Cross Country Championships") title for a second year. She won in 26:46.[[73]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-73)

**Haile Gebrselassie** ([Amharic](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Amharic_language "Amharic language"): ኀይሌ ገብረ ሥላሴ, [romanized](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Romanization_of_Amharic "Romanization of Amharic"):_Haylē Gebre Silassē_; born 18 April 1973) is an Ethiopian former [long-distance](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Long-distance_running "Long-distance running")[track](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Track_running "Track running"), [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") athlete, and businessman.[[2]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-2)[[3]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-3) He won two Olympic gold medals and four [World Championship](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Championships "World Athletics Championships") titles over the [10,000 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/10,000_metres "10,000 metres") and won the [Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Berlin_Marathon "Berlin Marathon") on four consecutive occasions between 2006 and 2009. He also earned four [world titles indoors](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/World_Athletics_Indoor_Championships "World Athletics Indoor Championships") and was the [2001 World Half Marathon Champion](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2001_IAAF_World_Half_Marathon_Championships "2001 IAAF World Half Marathon Championships"). He is considered to be one of the greatest long-distance runners of all time.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-4)

Haile had major competition wins at distances between [1,500 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/1500_metres "1500 metres") and the [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon"), moving from outdoor, indoor and [cross country running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cross_country_running "Cross country running") to [road running](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Road_running "Road running") in the latter part of his career. He broke 61 [Ethiopian national records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_Ethiopian_records_in_athletics "List of Ethiopian records in athletics"), ranging from [800 metres](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/800_metres "800 metres") to the marathon, set 27 [world records](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/List_of_world_records_in_athletics "List of world records in athletics"), and is regarded as one of the greatest long-distance runners in history.[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-5)[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-6)[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-7)[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-8)[[9]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Haile_Gebrselassie#cite_note-9) He won the [2008 Berlin Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2008_Berlin_Marathon "2008 Berlin Marathon") with a [world record time of 2:03:59](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon_world_record_progression "Marathon world record progression"), breaking his own world record by 27 seconds. The record stood for three years. Haile's 10,000 m [Masters age group world record](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Masters_Athletics_World_Records "Masters Athletics World Records") remains unchallenged since 2008. Due to his various achievements on track & road running events, many called him as the "Emperor of the Distance Running".

Source: https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe
Chunks: 15,16
Her running has earned her a number of accolades including the [BBC Sports Personality of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/BBC_Sports_Personality_of_the_Year "BBC Sports Personality of the Year"), [Laureus World Comeback of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Laureus_Awards "Laureus Awards"), [IAAF World Athlete of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/IAAF_World_Athlete_of_the_Year "IAAF World Athlete of the Year"), [AIMS World Athlete of the Year](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/AIMS_World_Athlete_of_the_Year "AIMS World Athlete of the Year") (three times) and a [Member of the Order of the British Empire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Member_of_the_Order_of_the_British_Empire "Member of the Order of the British Empire") (MBE). She has also been nominated for World Sportswoman of the year on several occasions. In 2010, she was inducted into the [England Athletics Hall of Fame](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/England_Athletics_Hall_of_Fame "England Athletics Hall of Fame"). She was inducted into the [Loughborough University](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Loughborough_University "Loughborough University") Hall of Fame in 2015.[[4]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-4)[[5]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-5)
Radcliffe ended her competitive running career at the [2015 London Marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/2015_London_Marathon "2015 London Marathon"),[[6]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-6) although she later entered the 2025 editions of the Tokyo and Boston marathons.

Radcliffe was born on 17 December 1973 in [Davenham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Davenham "Davenham") near [Northwich](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Northwich "Northwich"), [Cheshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Cheshire "Cheshire"). Her family then moved to nearby [Barnton](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Barnton,_Cheshire "Barnton, Cheshire") where she attended Little Leigh Primary School.[[7]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-7) Despite suffering from [asthma](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Asthma "Asthma") and [anaemia](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Anaemia "Anaemia"), she took up running at the age of seven, influenced by her father who was a keen amateur [marathon](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Marathon "Marathon") runner and joined [Frodsham](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Frodsham "Frodsham") Athletic Club. Her family later moved to [Kingsley](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Kingsley,_Cheshire "Kingsley, Cheshire").
When Radcliffe was aged 12, the family moved to [Oakley, Bedfordshire](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Oakley,_Bedfordshire "Oakley, Bedfordshire") and she became a member of Bedford & County Athletics Club. Her joining the club coincided with a talented and dedicated coach, Alex Stanton, building the women's and girls' sections into one of the strongest in the country, in spite of [Bedford](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Bedford "Bedford")'s relatively small size.
Radcliffe's father became club vice-chairman and her mother, a fun-runner, managed the women's cross-country team.[[8]](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Paula_Radcliffe#cite_note-historic_Rad-8) Her first race at a national level came as a 12-year-old in 1986 when she placed 299th out of around 600 in the girls' race of the English Schools Cross Country Championships. She finished fourth in the same race one year later.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oR4p!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd75638f2-b86c-4b84-89d8-b1116f800b8d_995x689.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oR4p!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd75638f2-b86c-4b84-89d8-b1116f800b8d_995x689.png)
Apologies for not sending out an edition of the newsletter last week. I was a bit tied up working on a project for _Sports Illustrated_ that required a bit more time than anticipated.

Since the last newsletter, I can share how that one-mile time trial went at the Bakline x Trial of Miles meet in Jersey City. I unfortunately did not achieve my goal of breaking five minutes. However, I’m super thankful for the opportunity to experience a legitimate race for the first time in seven months and walking away with a four-second personal best. I ran 5:09.87 but really tried to give myself the best chance to get under my goal through 1,000 meters and then it got tough. Still have some work to do. I’m trusting the training and hopefully giving it another go soon.

Also, it felt great to get back behind the mic for some commentary and play-by-play for the first time in SIX years. Shout-out to my friend Ryan Welsh for an awesome debut. [You can re-watch the entire meet on Youtube (if you go to the 1:02:36 mark our best call was definitely the women’s B heat of the 5,000m](https://youtu.be/RYmjNLptdYA)).

Here’s a highlight video from the meet, including my shortcomings :( :

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dSKTAUbLnkk)

I’m in Chicago from Oct. 18 to Nov. 18 so if anyone knows of any opportunities to race in the area, let your boy know!

PS: [If you like the “Future is Female Coaches” shirt from Bakline that I’m rocking. You can get it here and use code CITIUS for 15% off](https://www.bakline.nyc/collections/running/graphic_future-is-female).

Onto this week’s latest news from the running world...

Somehow, there’s a global championship taking place in 2020 as international stars descend upon Gdynia, Poland for Saturday’s World Half Marathon Championships. To my understanding, a lot of the CITIUS MAG readers are based in the United States and Canada so unfortunately there won’t be any local athletes to root for since their respective governing bodies have decided not to send teams due to concerns with the coronavirus. There are still some incredible matchups to watch for.

**MEN’S RACE:** Since the last newsletter, Uganda’s Joshua Cheptegei added another world record to his resume by clocking a 26:11:02 for 10,000 meters in Valencia, Spain. He’s three for three with wins and world records in his three races of the year. Can he go four for four? That will be hard. The half marathon world record is 58:01 by Geoffrey Kamworor from Copenhagen last September. Kamworor is the reigning three-time champion but will not race on Saturday as he continues to recover from an injury sustained when he got hit by a motorcyclist in June. Cheptegei has never raced a half marathon. The longest race I was able to find on his athletic profile was a 10-miler in 45:15 from Zaandam, the Netherlands in Sept. 2018. There’s no denying whatever Cheptegei runs will be fast and he’s certainly the favorite.

We can pinpoint his toughest competition to three men. Kenya’s Kibiwott Kandie is the fastest man on paper with his 58:38 personal best from the Prague Half in September. That time puts him at No. 6 on the all-time list behind Kamworor, Abraham Kiptum (later busted for doping), Zersenay Tadese, Sammy Wanjiru and Jemal Yimer. The Kenyan championship streak could rest on his shoulders or Bernard Ngeno, who ran 59:07 for second place at the 2019 Valencia Half.

Cheptegei’s compatriot Jacob Kiplimo is just 19 years old but has electrified the track circuit with a 12:48 for 5,000 meters and 7:26 for 3,000 meters earlier this summer. The lone half marathon on his record is a 61:53 in Kampala in November 2019.

Ethiopia has five men entered with sub-60 personal bests so keep an eye out on their contingent led by Andamlak Belihu and his 59:10 personal best.

_Prediction: No one is beating Joshua Cheptegei in 2020_

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4MIN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4e075165-85ea-45af-a636-429615e10fc1_600x374.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4MIN!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4e075165-85ea-45af-a636-429615e10fc1_600x374.gif)
**WOMEN’S RACE:** Remember how hyped up the world was for the clash between Kipchoge and Bekele only to get let down when Bekele pulled out of the race? Let’s bring some of that excitement to a showdown between two world record holders and a title defense by Netsanet Gudeta.

In one corner, we have Kenya’s Peres Jepchirchir. She set the women’s-only half marathon world record of 65:35 in Prague in September and recently had it ratified by World Athletics. Jepchirchir has proven that she can win at the championship stage with her world half marathon title from 2016.

In the other corner, we’ve got Ethiopia’s Ababel Yeshaneh. She is one of only six women to have run faster than Jepchirchir with her 64:31 at the Ras Al Khaimah Half in February. It’s her lone race of the year and she beat marathon world record holder/London Marathon champion Brigid Kosgei by 18 seconds.

Because of how fast the women’s half marathon has been in recent years, Joyciline Jepkosgei has been bumped down to No. 3 on the all-time list and hasn’t run a half marathon since the NYC Half in March 2019. The last time many of us heard of her was when she won the 2019 New York City Marathon in 2:22:38 in a Central Park sprint against Mary Keitany. Just don’t be surprised if she’s in the mix for the win and tries to improve upon her world half marathon championships silver medal from two years ago.

For those wondering where’s Sifan Hassan after her one-hour record and after she ran 29:36.67 for a European Record in the 10,000 meters in Hengelo last week: Hassan scratched from the race saying that she has opted “to give myself some rest and focus for next year.”

_Prediction: I’m going with Peres Jepchirchir for the win over Ababel Yeshaneh simply due to the recency of their standout performances and her experience on the championship stage._

So how can you watch it? The races will be broadcast live on The Olympic Channel from 5:00 a.m. to 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time.[Catch me on Twitter](http://twitter.com/ChrisChavez) at that time with a few live updates.

Mark your calendars! The [NCAA has announced](http://on.ncaa.com/NCAAHost) the following locations for upcoming NCAA Division I Cross Country Championships: 2022 in Stillwater, OK hosted by Oklahoma State; 2023 in Charlottesville, VA hosted by Virginia; 2024 in Madison, WI hosted by Wisconsin 2025 in Columbia, MO hosted by Mizzou. A reminder that the 2020 NCAA Division I Cross Country Championships will be contested on March 15, 2021 in Stillwater and the 2021 NCAA Division I Cross Country Championships remain on schedule for next November in Tallahassee, Florida. It’s going to make for awkward anniversaries later on for those respective champions.

If you enjoy college track then plan on many more visits to Hayward Field with the Ducks slated to host the 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 NCAA Championships. Austin, Texas will host in 2023 after doing a good job in 2019.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sGGo!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff6ac4240-022c-4d9c-ba7a-265aaff2ed3a_2048x1151.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sGGo!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff6ac4240-022c-4d9c-ba7a-265aaff2ed3a_2048x1151.jpeg)
I’ve always said to friends of mine that Ekiden races should be more popular in the United States. For those unfamiliar with the ekiden, it’s a multi-person and multi-distance relay race. There’s no set distance or set number or team members. Each runner hands off a sash called the Tasuki.

Last year, I ran the Tokyo Marathon and then paid a visit to Hakone. That’s the site of the finish for one of Japan’s biggest ekiden. They have a museum that has all the sashes, uniforms and race highlights from past races. From watching old videos (and I recommend doing this on YouTube) you can see the hype is real when they mention that more people turn out and watch the Hakone Ekiden than people watch the Super Bowl in the United States. Thrilled to see what comes next as Hansons-Brooks Original Distance Project [announced the MICHIGAN PRO EKIDEN](https://www.instagram.com/p/CGAeYRVndbk/) will take place on Oct. 21.

Our own Jesse Squire will be on hand to cover the race. The teams committed include the Atlanta Track Club, the Hansons-Brooks Original Distance Project, Rots Running, Bowerman Track Club, Team Boulder, Minnesota Distance Elite and Northern Arizona Elite.

I’ve also been told by people to watch the “Run With The Wind” anime series to get even more excited for this so I’ve got some time to do that.

David Melly [wrote a short post on his experience competing in the Izumo Ekiden](https://citiusmag.com/bringing-ekiden-racing-to-america/) as a member of the Ivy League team. He said, “I’ve never seen anything like it.”

Kudos again to Josh Cox and Ben Rosario for their efforts to put together another star-studded marathon to the United States before the year is up. The Marathon Project, which I mentioned in the last newsletter, will now also include Sara Hall – fresh off that 2:22:01 second-place finish at the London Marathon. Hall just loves racing and this shouldn’t come as much of a surprise to us. [I wrote about her for](https://www.si.com/edge/2019/08/06/sara-hall-berlin-new-york-city-marathon-double-2019)_[Sports Illustrated](https://www.si.com/edge/2019/08/06/sara-hall-berlin-new-york-city-marathon-double-2019)_ last year on why she chooses to double up on marathons in such a short time span.

Cam Levins, who told the media that he was in great shape before the London Marathon but ultimately dropped out due to the cold conditions, will chase the Olympic standard to try and get a spot on Canada’s team for Tokyo.

Fan favorites Beverly Ramos, Diane Nukuri, Noah Droddy and Alexi Pappas have also been added to the fields. You can find the [women’s accepted entries](https://themarathonproject.com/accepted-entries-women/) and [men’s accepted entries here](https://t.co/wjWBrC5dqs).

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fbLT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F91240049-cbf1-40d5-bcb5-de2462c158ad_1080x607.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fbLT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F91240049-cbf1-40d5-bcb5-de2462c158ad_1080x607.jpeg)
The CITIUS MAG Podcast Network is pleased to bring on Emma Zimmerman and the [Social Sport Podcast](https://www.instagram.com/socialsportpod/) to our lineup of shows.

In the past couple of months, the show popped onto my radar and I’ve listened to several episodes. I was impressed with Emma’s careful research and care into amplifying and telling the stories of these people with strong passions for social change across all endurance sports. I know a lot of people who follow CITIUS MAG do so for our running coverage but I think there’s a place for these conversations with our audience, especially since it’s been made clear that there’s no line between sports and activism in 2020. Athletes know and embrace that sports are their stage to call for change that they want to see in the world. I think this podcast does a great job of addressing the issues and possible solutions with notable people.

For runners looking to get into the show, you’ll have several episodes featuring [Amir M. Figueroa](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-8-amir-m-figueroa-on-harlem-run-public-health/id1505320511?i=1000474228816) of Harlem Run in New York City, [Jacqueline Alnes, Ph.D.](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-11-jacqueline-alnes-mind-being-tinyart-on-elevating/id1505320511?i=1000477165922) (whose TinyArt drawings are an Instagram hit), [Alison Wade of the Fast Women](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-17-alison-wade-fast-women-newsletter-on-running/id1505320511?i=1000480120675) newsletter, [Kamilah Journet](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-18-kamilah-journ%C3%A9t-powerful-voice-for-anti/id1505320511?i=1000481775957) (now the Tracksmith Marketing Manager), and [Therese Haiss](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-25-therese-haiss-on-authentic-conversation/id1505320511?i=1000487658240) (former professional runner and now coach) to go back and listen to. Those are just some of the runners featured but [the whole archive of episodes is great](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/social-sport/id1505320511).

[In the most recent episode](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/social-sport-podcast-running-to-protest-movement-nyc-running-community/), Emma catches up with Coffey ([a guest on the Runners of NYC Podcast in May](http://citiusmag.com/runners-of-nyc-podcast-coffey/)) about his work in starting the [Running to Protest movement in New York City](https://www.instagram.com/runningtoprotest/). I’ve personally attended three of the protest runs and it’s moving to see 700+ people shut down the Brooklyn Bridge and call for justice regarding the murder of Breonna Taylor or listening to first-hand accounts of mistreatment with police in the city. I come on in the second half of the show to share some of my observations and thoughts about the power protesting has through running.

[Subscribe to Social Sport now.](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/social-sport/id1505320511) | [Follow Social Sport on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/socialsportpod/).

In recent editions of this newsletter, I’ve provided a few updates on the efforts to save the University of Minnesota’s men’s track and field team from being cut. The decision was left to a vote by members of the Board of Regents last week. The proposal to eliminate men's indoor track and field, men's tennis and men's gymnastics teams at the end of the 2020-21 school year [was passed on a 7-5 vote](https://www.si.com/olympics/2020/10/09/minnesota-indoor-track-and-field-gymnastics-tennis-eliminated-board-of-regents-vote-results). Men’s outdoor track and field was kept after a revised proposal was submitted on Friday and approved. It was still a very heavy day for members of the Gopher community because this puts them in a very weird spot. [I decided to chat with Obsa Ali](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast-obsa-ali-save-minnesota-track/), the 2018 NCAA steeplechase champion, about his feelings regarding the decision, what challenges this presents for recruiting and the women’s team as well as what happens next.

You can catch the latest episode of the [podcast on iTunes so subscribe and leave a five-star review](https://itunes.apple.com/us/podcast/id1204506559). We are also on [Stitcher,](https://www.stitcher.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast)[Google Play](https://play.google.com/music/listen?u=0#/ps/Iadq5oufkygxq6jwxblxx5ljhlq) and [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/70eINNmXl67VqorbTsMOaH?si=ikhzVGlDQ_igRjaOBykDFA)!

[Full show notes and quotes can be found here.](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast-obsa-ali-save-minnesota-track/)

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!CaSg!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7f46b9ec-a0cd-4cda-9a0c-b5e4ffd67072_723x723.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!CaSg!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7f46b9ec-a0cd-4cda-9a0c-b5e4ffd67072_723x723.jpeg)
– On Runners of NYC, [Leigh Anne Sharek and I spoke with Lenny Grullon](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/runners-of-nyc-podcast-lenny-grullon-boogie-down-bronx/). He is one of the founders of the [Boogie Down Bronx Runners](https://www.instagram.com/boogiedownbronxrunners/). If you’ve ever run the New York City Marathon, there’s a part when you cross into the Bronx and you’re greeted with some super loud cheers from a running crew decked out in black and white. That’s his group and it wasn’t always that loud on that part of the course. When Lenny decided to start the group, no one showed up for the first run. However, he kept at it and wanted to get the Bronx community active and it’s paid off. [Listen to his whole story here](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/runners-of-nyc-podcast-lenny-grullon-boogie-down-bronx/).

– [Just wanted to give a quick shout-out to Joshua and Aaron Potts for having me on Two Black Runners](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/ep-27-chris-chavez-how-to-chase-your-dreams-sports/id1486031415?i=1000494598108). If you’re not familiar with their show, they’ve brought on some pretty high-profile guests from the pro running circuit on their podcast over the past six months. They bring the type of energy to the sport that you’d get from watching ESPN analysts debate over NFL and NBA performances. We discussed some of the 2020 track season but also the lack of diversity in the track and field media landscape. Love what these guys are doing and I’m looking forward to sharing the mixed zone with them at the 2021 U.S. Olympic Trials.

That’s all from me this week. If you enjoyed this edition of CITIUS MAG and think your friend would too, forward it to them encourage them to subscribe. Let me know if you have any comments, feedback or thoughts on anything discussed.

Enjoy your weekend!

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oR4p!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd75638f2-b86c-4b84-89d8-b1116f800b8d_995x689.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oR4p!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd75638f2-b86c-4b84-89d8-b1116f800b8d_995x689.png)
Apologies for not sending out an edition of the newsletter last week. I was a bit tied up working on a project for _Sports Illustrated_ that required a bit more time than anticipated.

Since the last newsletter, I can share how that one-mile time trial went at the Bakline x Trial of Miles meet in Jersey City. I unfortunately did not achieve my goal of breaking five minutes. However, I’m super thankful for the opportunity to experience a legitimate race for the first time in seven months and walking away with a four-second personal best. I ran 5:09.87 but really tried to give myself the best chance to get under my goal through 1,000 meters and then it got tough. Still have some work to do. I’m trusting the training and hopefully giving it another go soon.

Also, it felt great to get back behind the mic for some commentary and play-by-play for the first time in SIX years. Shout-out to my friend Ryan Welsh for an awesome debut. [You can re-watch the entire meet on Youtube (if you go to the 1:02:36 mark our best call was definitely the women’s B heat of the 5,000m](https://youtu.be/RYmjNLptdYA)).

Here’s a highlight video from the meet, including my shortcomings :( :

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dSKTAUbLnkk)

I’m in Chicago from Oct. 18 to Nov. 18 so if anyone knows of any opportunities to race in the area, let your boy know!

PS: [If you like the “Future is Female Coaches” shirt from Bakline that I’m rocking. You can get it here and use code CITIUS for 15% off](https://www.bakline.nyc/collections/running/graphic_future-is-female).

Onto this week’s latest news from the running world...

Somehow, there’s a global championship taking place in 2020 as international stars descend upon Gdynia, Poland for Saturday’s World Half Marathon Championships. To my understanding, a lot of the CITIUS MAG readers are based in the United States and Canada so unfortunately there won’t be any local athletes to root for since their respective governing bodies have decided not to send teams due to concerns with the coronavirus. There are still some incredible matchups to watch for.

**MEN’S RACE:** Since the last newsletter, Uganda’s Joshua Cheptegei added another world record to his resume by clocking a 26:11:02 for 10,000 meters in Valencia, Spain. He’s three for three with wins and world records in his three races of the year. Can he go four for four? That will be hard. The half marathon world record is 58:01 by Geoffrey Kamworor from Copenhagen last September. Kamworor is the reigning three-time champion but will not race on Saturday as he continues to recover from an injury sustained when he got hit by a motorcyclist in June. Cheptegei has never raced a half marathon. The longest race I was able to find on his athletic profile was a 10-miler in 45:15 from Zaandam, the Netherlands in Sept. 2018. There’s no denying whatever Cheptegei runs will be fast and he’s certainly the favorite.

We can pinpoint his toughest competition to three men. Kenya’s Kibiwott Kandie is the fastest man on paper with his 58:38 personal best from the Prague Half in September. That time puts him at No. 6 on the all-time list behind Kamworor, Abraham Kiptum (later busted for doping), Zersenay Tadese, Sammy Wanjiru and Jemal Yimer. The Kenyan championship streak could rest on his shoulders or Bernard Ngeno, who ran 59:07 for second place at the 2019 Valencia Half.

Cheptegei’s compatriot Jacob Kiplimo is just 19 years old but has electrified the track circuit with a 12:48 for 5,000 meters and 7:26 for 3,000 meters earlier this summer. The lone half marathon on his record is a 61:53 in Kampala in November 2019.

Ethiopia has five men entered with sub-60 personal bests so keep an eye out on their contingent led by Andamlak Belihu and his 59:10 personal best.

_Prediction: No one is beating Joshua Cheptegei in 2020_
