**WOMEN’S RACE:** Remember how hyped up the world was for the clash between Kipchoge and Bekele only to get let down when Bekele pulled out of the race? Let’s bring some of that excitement to a showdown between two world record holders and a title defense by Netsanet Gudeta.

In one corner, we have Kenya’s Peres Jepchirchir. She set the women’s-only half marathon world record of 65:35 in Prague in September and recently had it ratified by World Athletics. Jepchirchir has proven that she can win at the championship stage with her world half marathon title from 2016.

In the other corner, we’ve got Ethiopia’s Ababel Yeshaneh. She is one of only six women to have run faster than Jepchirchir with her 64:31 at the Ras Al Khaimah Half in February. It’s her lone race of the year and she beat marathon world record holder/London Marathon champion Brigid Kosgei by 18 seconds.

Because of how fast the women’s half marathon has been in recent years, Joyciline Jepkosgei has been bumped down to No. 3 on the all-time list and hasn’t run a half marathon since the NYC Half in March 2019. The last time many of us heard of her was when she won the 2019 New York City Marathon in 2:22:38 in a Central Park sprint against Mary Keitany. Just don’t be surprised if she’s in the mix for the win and tries to improve upon her world half marathon championships silver medal from two years ago.

For those wondering where’s Sifan Hassan after her one-hour record and after she ran 29:36.67 for a European Record in the 10,000 meters in Hengelo last week: Hassan scratched from the race saying that she has opted “to give myself some rest and focus for next year.”

_Prediction: I’m going with Peres Jepchirchir for the win over Ababel Yeshaneh simply due to the recency of their standout performances and her experience on the championship stage._

So how can you watch it? The races will be broadcast live on The Olympic Channel from 5:00 a.m. to 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time.[Catch me on Twitter](http://twitter.com/ChrisChavez) at that time with a few live updates.

Mark your calendars! The [NCAA has announced](http://on.ncaa.com/NCAAHost) the following locations for upcoming NCAA Division I Cross Country Championships: 2022 in Stillwater, OK hosted by Oklahoma State; 2023 in Charlottesville, VA hosted by Virginia; 2024 in Madison, WI hosted by Wisconsin 2025 in Columbia, MO hosted by Mizzou. A reminder that the 2020 NCAA Division I Cross Country Championships will be contested on March 15, 2021 in Stillwater and the 2021 NCAA Division I Cross Country Championships remain on schedule for next November in Tallahassee, Florida. It’s going to make for awkward anniversaries later on for those respective champions.

If you enjoy college track then plan on many more visits to Hayward Field with the Ducks slated to host the 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 NCAA Championships. Austin, Texas will host in 2023 after doing a good job in 2019.

I’ve always said to friends of mine that Ekiden races should be more popular in the United States. For those unfamiliar with the ekiden, it’s a multi-person and multi-distance relay race. There’s no set distance or set number or team members. Each runner hands off a sash called the Tasuki.

Last year, I ran the Tokyo Marathon and then paid a visit to Hakone. That’s the site of the finish for one of Japan’s biggest ekiden. They have a museum that has all the sashes, uniforms and race highlights from past races. From watching old videos (and I recommend doing this on YouTube) you can see the hype is real when they mention that more people turn out and watch the Hakone Ekiden than people watch the Super Bowl in the United States. Thrilled to see what comes next as Hansons-Brooks Original Distance Project [announced the MICHIGAN PRO EKIDEN](https://www.instagram.com/p/CGAeYRVndbk/) will take place on Oct. 21.

Our own Jesse Squire will be on hand to cover the race. The teams committed include the Atlanta Track Club, the Hansons-Brooks Original Distance Project, Rots Running, Bowerman Track Club, Team Boulder, Minnesota Distance Elite and Northern Arizona Elite.

I’ve also been told by people to watch the “Run With The Wind” anime series to get even more excited for this so I’ve got some time to do that.

David Melly [wrote a short post on his experience competing in the Izumo Ekiden](https://citiusmag.com/bringing-ekiden-racing-to-america/) as a member of the Ivy League team. He said, “I’ve never seen anything like it.”

Kudos again to Josh Cox and Ben Rosario for their efforts to put together another star-studded marathon to the United States before the year is up. The Marathon Project, which I mentioned in the last newsletter, will now also include Sara Hall – fresh off that 2:22:01 second-place finish at the London Marathon. Hall just loves racing and this shouldn’t come as much of a surprise to us. [I wrote about her for](https://www.si.com/edge/2019/08/06/sara-hall-berlin-new-york-city-marathon-double-2019)_[Sports Illustrated](https://www.si.com/edge/2019/08/06/sara-hall-berlin-new-york-city-marathon-double-2019)_ last year on why she chooses to double up on marathons in such a short time span.

Cam Levins, who told the media that he was in great shape before the London Marathon but ultimately dropped out due to the cold conditions, will chase the Olympic standard to try and get a spot on Canada’s team for Tokyo.

Fan favorites Beverly Ramos, Diane Nukuri, Noah Droddy and Alexi Pappas have also been added to the fields. You can find the [women’s accepted entries](https://themarathonproject.com/accepted-entries-women/) and [men’s accepted entries here](https://t.co/wjWBrC5dqs).

PS: [If you like the “Future is Female Coaches” shirt from Bakline that I’m rocking. You can get it here and use code CITIUS for 15% off](https://www.bakline.nyc/collections/running/graphic_future-is-female).

Onto this week’s latest news from the running world...

Somehow, there’s a global championship taking place in 2020 as international stars descend upon Gdynia, Poland for Saturday’s World Half Marathon Championships. To my understanding, a lot of the CITIUS MAG readers are based in the United States and Canada so unfortunately there won’t be any local athletes to root for since their respective governing bodies have decided not to send teams due to concerns with the coronavirus. There are still some incredible matchups to watch for.

**MEN’S RACE:** Since the last newsletter, Uganda’s Joshua Cheptegei added another world record to his resume by clocking a 26:11:02 for 10,000 meters in Valencia, Spain. He’s three for three with wins and world records in his three races of the year. Can he go four for four? That will be hard. The half marathon world record is 58:01 by Geoffrey Kamworor from Copenhagen last September. Kamworor is the reigning three-time champion but will not race on Saturday as he continues to recover from an injury sustained when he got hit by a motorcyclist in June. Cheptegei has never raced a half marathon. The longest race I was able to find on his athletic profile was a 10-miler in 45:15 from Zaandam, the Netherlands in Sept. 2018. There’s no denying whatever Cheptegei runs will be fast and he’s certainly the favorite.

We can pinpoint his toughest competition to three men. Kenya’s Kibiwott Kandie is the fastest man on paper with his 58:38 personal best from the Prague Half in September. That time puts him at No. 6 on the all-time list behind Kamworor, Abraham Kiptum (later busted for doping), Zersenay Tadese, Sammy Wanjiru and Jemal Yimer. The Kenyan championship streak could rest on his shoulders or Bernard Ngeno, who ran 59:07 for second place at the 2019 Valencia Half.

Cheptegei’s compatriot Jacob Kiplimo is just 19 years old but has electrified the track circuit with a 12:48 for 5,000 meters and 7:26 for 3,000 meters earlier this summer. The lone half marathon on his record is a 61:53 in Kampala in November 2019.

Ethiopia has five men entered with sub-60 personal bests so keep an eye out on their contingent led by Andamlak Belihu and his 59:10 personal best.

_Prediction: No one is beating Joshua Cheptegei in 2020_

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4MIN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4e075165-85ea-45af-a636-429615e10fc1_600x374.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4MIN!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4e075165-85ea-45af-a636-429615e10fc1_600x374.gif)
**WOMEN’S RACE:** Remember how hyped up the world was for the clash between Kipchoge and Bekele only to get let down when Bekele pulled out of the race? Let’s bring some of that excitement to a showdown between two world record holders and a title defense by Netsanet Gudeta.

In one corner, we have Kenya’s Peres Jepchirchir. She set the women’s-only half marathon world record of 65:35 in Prague in September and recently had it ratified by World Athletics. Jepchirchir has proven that she can win at the championship stage with her world half marathon title from 2016.

In the other corner, we’ve got Ethiopia’s Ababel Yeshaneh. She is one of only six women to have run faster than Jepchirchir with her 64:31 at the Ras Al Khaimah Half in February. It’s her lone race of the year and she beat marathon world record holder/London Marathon champion Brigid Kosgei by 18 seconds.

Because of how fast the women’s half marathon has been in recent years, Joyciline Jepkosgei has been bumped down to No. 3 on the all-time list and hasn’t run a half marathon since the NYC Half in March 2019. The last time many of us heard of her was when she won the 2019 New York City Marathon in 2:22:38 in a Central Park sprint against Mary Keitany. Just don’t be surprised if she’s in the mix for the win and tries to improve upon her world half marathon championships silver medal from two years ago.

For those wondering where’s Sifan Hassan after her one-hour record and after she ran 29:36.67 for a European Record in the 10,000 meters in Hengelo last week: Hassan scratched from the race saying that she has opted “to give myself some rest and focus for next year.”

_Prediction: I’m going with Peres Jepchirchir for the win over Ababel Yeshaneh simply due to the recency of their standout performances and her experience on the championship stage._

So how can you watch it? The races will be broadcast live on The Olympic Channel from 5:00 a.m. to 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time.[Catch me on Twitter](http://twitter.com/ChrisChavez) at that time with a few live updates.

Mark your calendars! The [NCAA has announced](http://on.ncaa.com/NCAAHost) the following locations for upcoming NCAA Division I Cross Country Championships: 2022 in Stillwater, OK hosted by Oklahoma State; 2023 in Charlottesville, VA hosted by Virginia; 2024 in Madison, WI hosted by Wisconsin 2025 in Columbia, MO hosted by Mizzou. A reminder that the 2020 NCAA Division I Cross Country Championships will be contested on March 15, 2021 in Stillwater and the 2021 NCAA Division I Cross Country Championships remain on schedule for next November in Tallahassee, Florida. It’s going to make for awkward anniversaries later on for those respective champions.

If you enjoy college track then plan on many more visits to Hayward Field with the Ducks slated to host the 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 NCAA Championships. Austin, Texas will host in 2023 after doing a good job in 2019.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sGGo!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff6ac4240-022c-4d9c-ba7a-265aaff2ed3a_2048x1151.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sGGo!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff6ac4240-022c-4d9c-ba7a-265aaff2ed3a_2048x1151.jpeg)
I’ve always said to friends of mine that Ekiden races should be more popular in the United States. For those unfamiliar with the ekiden, it’s a multi-person and multi-distance relay race. There’s no set distance or set number or team members. Each runner hands off a sash called the Tasuki.

Last year, I ran the Tokyo Marathon and then paid a visit to Hakone. That’s the site of the finish for one of Japan’s biggest ekiden. They have a museum that has all the sashes, uniforms and race highlights from past races. From watching old videos (and I recommend doing this on YouTube) you can see the hype is real when they mention that more people turn out and watch the Hakone Ekiden than people watch the Super Bowl in the United States. Thrilled to see what comes next as Hansons-Brooks Original Distance Project [announced the MICHIGAN PRO EKIDEN](https://www.instagram.com/p/CGAeYRVndbk/) will take place on Oct. 21.

Our own Jesse Squire will be on hand to cover the race. The teams committed include the Atlanta Track Club, the Hansons-Brooks Original Distance Project, Rots Running, Bowerman Track Club, Team Boulder, Minnesota Distance Elite and Northern Arizona Elite.

I’ve also been told by people to watch the “Run With The Wind” anime series to get even more excited for this so I’ve got some time to do that.

David Melly [wrote a short post on his experience competing in the Izumo Ekiden](https://citiusmag.com/bringing-ekiden-racing-to-america/) as a member of the Ivy League team. He said, “I’ve never seen anything like it.”

Kudos again to Josh Cox and Ben Rosario for their efforts to put together another star-studded marathon to the United States before the year is up. The Marathon Project, which I mentioned in the last newsletter, will now also include Sara Hall – fresh off that 2:22:01 second-place finish at the London Marathon. Hall just loves racing and this shouldn’t come as much of a surprise to us. [I wrote about her for](https://www.si.com/edge/2019/08/06/sara-hall-berlin-new-york-city-marathon-double-2019)_[Sports Illustrated](https://www.si.com/edge/2019/08/06/sara-hall-berlin-new-york-city-marathon-double-2019)_ last year on why she chooses to double up on marathons in such a short time span.

Cam Levins, who told the media that he was in great shape before the London Marathon but ultimately dropped out due to the cold conditions, will chase the Olympic standard to try and get a spot on Canada’s team for Tokyo.

Fan favorites Beverly Ramos, Diane Nukuri, Noah Droddy and Alexi Pappas have also been added to the fields. You can find the [women’s accepted entries](https://themarathonproject.com/accepted-entries-women/) and [men’s accepted entries here](https://t.co/wjWBrC5dqs).

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fbLT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F91240049-cbf1-40d5-bcb5-de2462c158ad_1080x607.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fbLT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F91240049-cbf1-40d5-bcb5-de2462c158ad_1080x607.jpeg)
The CITIUS MAG Podcast Network is pleased to bring on Emma Zimmerman and the [Social Sport Podcast](https://www.instagram.com/socialsportpod/) to our lineup of shows.

In the past couple of months, the show popped onto my radar and I’ve listened to several episodes. I was impressed with Emma’s careful research and care into amplifying and telling the stories of these people with strong passions for social change across all endurance sports. I know a lot of people who follow CITIUS MAG do so for our running coverage but I think there’s a place for these conversations with our audience, especially since it’s been made clear that there’s no line between sports and activism in 2020. Athletes know and embrace that sports are their stage to call for change that they want to see in the world. I think this podcast does a great job of addressing the issues and possible solutions with notable people.

For runners looking to get into the show, you’ll have several episodes featuring [Amir M. Figueroa](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-8-amir-m-figueroa-on-harlem-run-public-health/id1505320511?i=1000474228816) of Harlem Run in New York City, [Jacqueline Alnes, Ph.D.](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-11-jacqueline-alnes-mind-being-tinyart-on-elevating/id1505320511?i=1000477165922) (whose TinyArt drawings are an Instagram hit), [Alison Wade of the Fast Women](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-17-alison-wade-fast-women-newsletter-on-running/id1505320511?i=1000480120675) newsletter, [Kamilah Journet](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-18-kamilah-journ%C3%A9t-powerful-voice-for-anti/id1505320511?i=1000481775957) (now the Tracksmith Marketing Manager), and [Therese Haiss](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-25-therese-haiss-on-authentic-conversation/id1505320511?i=1000487658240) (former professional runner and now coach) to go back and listen to. Those are just some of the runners featured but [the whole archive of episodes is great](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/social-sport/id1505320511).

[In the most recent episode](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/social-sport-podcast-running-to-protest-movement-nyc-running-community/), Emma catches up with Coffey ([a guest on the Runners of NYC Podcast in May](http://citiusmag.com/runners-of-nyc-podcast-coffey/)) about his work in starting the [Running to Protest movement in New York City](https://www.instagram.com/runningtoprotest/). I’ve personally attended three of the protest runs and it’s moving to see 700+ people shut down the Brooklyn Bridge and call for justice regarding the murder of Breonna Taylor or listening to first-hand accounts of mistreatment with police in the city. I come on in the second half of the show to share some of my observations and thoughts about the power protesting has through running.

[Subscribe to Social Sport now.](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/social-sport/id1505320511) | [Follow Social Sport on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/socialsportpod/).

In recent editions of this newsletter, I’ve provided a few updates on the efforts to save the University of Minnesota’s men’s track and field team from being cut. The decision was left to a vote by members of the Board of Regents last week. The proposal to eliminate men's indoor track and field, men's tennis and men's gymnastics teams at the end of the 2020-21 school year [was passed on a 7-5 vote](https://www.si.com/olympics/2020/10/09/minnesota-indoor-track-and-field-gymnastics-tennis-eliminated-board-of-regents-vote-results). Men’s outdoor track and field was kept after a revised proposal was submitted on Friday and approved. It was still a very heavy day for members of the Gopher community because this puts them in a very weird spot. [I decided to chat with Obsa Ali](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast-obsa-ali-save-minnesota-track/), the 2018 NCAA steeplechase champion, about his feelings regarding the decision, what challenges this presents for recruiting and the women’s team as well as what happens next.

### [Three-Time World Half Marathon Champion Geoffrey Kamworor Shares Seven Treadmill Training Tips](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=5967)

[![Image 2](https://katarunningretreat.com/cdn/shop/files/ChatGPT_Image_May_8_2026_05_55_04_PM.png?v=1778288140&width=300)](https://katarunningretreat.com/products/my-best-runs-supporter)

Three-time world half marathon champion and two-time world cross country gold medalist[Geoffrey Kamworor](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor) is among the finest endurance runners of his generation. During lockdown the Kenyan star began using a treadmill at home and has continued to do so as part of his rehabilitation from a recent injury he suffered after a motorbike knocked him to the ground during an early morning run in June. Here the two-time New York Marathon winner offers his seven top treadmill training tips.

Take time to practice:

![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/a2141b72260b614e3afb668a9d79aeae0047d1fcf71ddc123f1cd39293071d84.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

Kamworor urges novice treadmill runners to be patient in order to become accustomed to running on the machine before engaging in any intense sessions.

“It takes take time for people to adjust and learn how to run on a treadmill,” he explains. “I learned pretty quickly how to do so, but for others it can take a little longer.”

![Image 4](https://mybestruns.com/street/bda5a4aaa3b6117c54fc2a4ac8d923ca01a654d2a76881f6832c37de0c233ef5.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

Warm up properly:

When jumping on the treadmill it should be treated no differently to running outside in that it requires a thorough warm up.

“Run slowly at first,” he says. “The good thing with a treadmill you can easily set the pace. Maybe start at a walking pace, then slowly increasing the speed to running pace.”

Embrace its versatility:

Kamworor believes the treadmill can be used for many different types of sessions, from tempo runs to fartlek and even speed sessions. A favourite fartlek session of his is three minutes of fast running at a speed of between 20-22kmph followed by one minute of jogging at 10kmph, then repeated.

“I set the calculations into the machine so 10 seconds before I’m scheduled to run at full speed again this allows the machine to gradually adjust to full speed.”

Speed sessions:

While acknowledging it is a little trickier to replicate track speed sessions on the treadmill he insists it is far from impossible.

“It is not something easy because it requires a lot of calculations but this is something you can learn over time, and, for me, it works perfectly. Normally, I would train on the track in a group but the treadmill allows me to do the speed session alone if necessary.”

Flat gradient:

Some treadmill users emphasise the importance of always running at a slight gradient but as many of Kamworor’s quicker sessions are run on the flat he prefers to replicate this with a 0.0 % gradient during many of his treadmill sessions.

“The option is there, though, to run on a slight incline or decline if you want to,” he adds.

Visualize a route:

Kamworor personally prefers not to listen to music when treadmill running, because he likes to stay fully concentrated. He does, however, suggest to any treadmill runners to visualize a running route when on the treadmill.

“Whether you are on a speed session or tempo run it is importance to visualize, even if you are visualizing a competition. It is important to think positively about running.”

Cool down:

Like on any run, Geoffrey says it is important not to neglect the cool down on the treadmill. “It is important to reduce the speed to 10kmph or less,” he says. “Twenty minutes is a nice cool down time.”

### [2027 Could Bring Unprecedented Heat, Raising New Concerns for Marathon Runners Worldwide](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15441)

The global running community could face a formidable challenge in [2027](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2027), as forecasts of a potentially powerful El Niño raise concerns about rising temperatures and the impact of extreme heat on marathon performances.

![Image 7](https://mybestruns.com/street/21525fef106f0f5e518948f3b7ac7c7a59c2dc7f609cbf843c1a3df2621fa9d4.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

With long-distance runners increasingly chasing personal bests on the world's biggest stages, the prospect of another exceptionally warm year has placed race-day weather firmly in the spotlight. For marathoners, even a modest rise in temperature can make the difference between a record-breaking performance and a difficult battle to reach the finish line.

![Image 8](https://mybestruns.com/street/c649899eb4ea226a094d35c54188897ee0ecd5f22a51cbcb024dd442b8785c9e.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

At the centre of the concern is the [Pacific Ocean](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Pacific+Ocean), where developing El Niño conditions could influence global temperatures. Forecasts have raised the possibility of an unusually strong event, although its eventual intensity and the precise effects on temperatures around the world remain uncertain.

El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon characterised by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures across parts of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. It can alter weather patterns across different regions, while its warming influence can contribute to higher global temperatures. The full impact depends on the strength of the event and how it interacts with other climate factors.

![Image 9](https://mybestruns.com/street/d0a9667bdea6ce04007f6323709b90066c76c7bf750a06efd1f2fbddbd1d21b0.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

The timing is particularly important. Global temperatures have often responded strongly in the year following a major El Niño, meaning 2027 could face an increased risk of challenging heat. However, whether it ultimately surpasses the existing global temperature record will depend on evolving ocean conditions, atmospheric patterns and human-caused climate change.

![Image 10](https://mybestruns.com/street/46b631cd0e12734e6118d1811afa82002a59f6f038f8de1a680ce25c9ce4a1e2.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

For marathon runners, the implications are significant. Scientific research has repeatedly shown that warmer conditions can reduce endurance performance, increase physiological strain and make it more difficult to maintain a planned race pace over 42.195 kilometres.

An analysis of seven North American marathons illustrates how substantially conditions can influence elite performances. Researchers found that leading male runners finished approximately 1.7 per cent slower relative to course records under the coolest conditions examined. In the warmest category, that difference increased to around 4.5 per cent.

For an athlete capable of running a marathon in 2:05:00, a slowdown of that magnitude could translate into several additional minutes on the clock. At the elite level, where races are frequently decided by seconds, such a difference can determine whether a runner achieves a personal best, secures a podium finish or misses a major performance target.

The consequences can be even more noticeable among recreational athletes, who often spend considerably longer exposed to the conditions.

A separate analysis by researchers at the University of Chicago, examining approximately 4.7 million marathon finishing times, highlighted the substantial effect of temperature on runners across different ability levels. The findings suggested that the typical participant could lose roughly 19 minutes when racing in temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, compared with conditions in the 40s. In the 80s Fahrenheit, the estimated time penalty rose to approximately 33 minutes.

These figures underline why marathon preparation involves much more than mileage, speed sessions and strength training. Temperature, humidity, direct sunlight and the body's ability to regulate heat can all influence how effectively a runner sustains an effort over the full distance.

Many marathon performances are achieved in cool conditions, with temperatures of approximately 4°C to 10°C often considered favourable for endurance running. As temperatures climb beyond that range, the body must devote more resources to cooling itself, potentially increasing cardiovascular strain and making a previously comfortable pace harder to maintain.

However, there is no universal temperature at which every marathon runner begins to slow down. Individual fitness, acclimatisation, humidity, wind, course exposure and race strategy all influence performance. A cool, overcast morning can produce very different outcomes from a sunny, humid day, even when the thermometer shows similar readings.

### [Cancer Survivor Brandon Throop Returns To Toronto Marathon In Hospital Gown For Third World Record Bid](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15440)

For [Brandon Throop](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Brandon+Throop), running a marathon in a hospital gown is about far more than chasing a place in the [Guinness World Records](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Guinness+World+Records). It is a deeply personal tribute to the medical team that helped save his life, a celebration of survival, and an opportunity to give back to the institution that stood beside him during one of the darkest chapters of his life.

![Image 13](https://mybestruns.com/street/f29108f8a11d11c189a98e7ad107e25370003868a0c2a06a0f60240f82ca748e.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

In 2022, Throop was 35 years old, a father of two, and facing a life-changing diagnosis of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. His journey soon led him to [Princess Margaret Cancer Centre](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Princess+Margaret+Cancer+Centre) in Toronto, Canada, where he underwent chemotherapy and began a difficult battle against the disease.

![Image 14](https://mybestruns.com/street/544aaad28b469831ffc670d6b1f0afed09ba7cece4e33f54484abd893edf14de.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

The treatment that helped him fight cancer also left him physically weakened. For someone who had spent much of his life running, even the simplest movements became unexpectedly challenging. After completing treatment, climbing a single flight of stairs could leave him coughing and struggling to catch his breath.

However, rather than allowing the experience to define the limits of his future, Throop began rebuilding his strength one small step at a time. He started by running once around his neighbourhood block before gradually increasing the distance as his body recovered. What began as a modest attempt to regain his fitness eventually developed into an extraordinary mission with a purpose extending far beyond the finish line.

![Image 15](https://mybestruns.com/street/609ed787d02e0efaf2f9b8e1f2b60b1718ea68e0b9bbf56ffa21a91b509d4949.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

Now, more than three years after becoming cancer-free, Throop is preparing to return to the [TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=TCS+Toronto+Waterfront+Marathon) on Sunday, October 18, 2026, for another attempt at the Guinness World Record for the fastest marathon completed while wearing a hospital gown.

This will be his third attempt to claim the record, following two determined performances in previous editions of the Toronto race. In 2023, he completed the marathon in 2:55:59 before returning in 2024 to improve his time to 2:55:01. Despite his progress, the record remained just out of reach.

Every kilometre he covers in the distinctive hospital gown carries a message of gratitude to the people who cared for him and hope for patients whose journeys are only beginning. For Throop, choosing Toronto has never been simply about finding the fastest course on which to break a record. ### [From $1 To $358: How The New York City Marathon Became A Global Running Phenomenon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15437)

What began as a modest race through Central Park, with a handful of determined runners and a budget of just $1,000, has evolved into one of the most prestigious and sought-after marathons in the world. More than five decades later, the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) tells a remarkable story of how distance running has grown from a grassroots sporting event into a global spectacle.

![Image 34](https://mybestruns.com/street/bacec4114b3d54670c15a184e950b0e7ddb43de9849a87f97fe568b1a68fdecf.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

When the inaugural New York City Marathon took place in 1970, the entry fee was just $1. Organised by the New York Road Runners, the race was held entirely within Central Park, far removed from the enormous crowds, international attention and commercial scale that define the event today.

![Image 35](https://mybestruns.com/street/cb333999ed07e06d10edcf37e5452882364cbb7336ebf8347871bb079ae7bfbf.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

Of the 127 registered participants, only 55 completed the race. Yet, despite its modest beginnings, the event laid the foundation for a marathon that would eventually capture the imagination of runners from every corner of the world.

The first champion was Gary Muhrcke, a New York City firefighter whose victory remains one of the most memorable stories from the race's early years. According to accounts of the inaugural edition, Muhrcke had finished a night shift before entering the competition shortly before the start. He went on to win in approximately 2:31, securing his place in the marathon's history.

The inaugural race also featured Nina Kuscsik, the only woman in the field. She started the event but withdrew after becoming ill, meaning no woman finished that first edition. Kuscsik would later become an important figure in the campaign for women's inclusion in competitive distance running.

Over the years, the New York City Marathon expanded beyond Central Park, eventually developing into the iconic five-borough journey that takes runners through Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Manhattan. Its transformation helped turn the race into a celebration of athletic achievement, community spirit and the extraordinary diversity of New York City.

Today, the marathon attracts elite athletes chasing victories and records, recreational runners pursuing personal milestones, charity participants raising funds for important causes, and thousands of international visitors eager to experience one of running's most celebrated events.

### [Three-Time World Half Marathon Champion Geoffrey Kamworor Shares Seven Treadmill Training Tips](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=5967)

[![Image 2](https://katarunningretreat.com/cdn/shop/files/ChatGPT_Image_May_8_2026_05_55_04_PM.png?v=1778288140&width=300)](https://katarunningretreat.com/products/my-best-runs-supporter)

Three-time world half marathon champion and two-time world cross country gold medalist[Geoffrey Kamworor](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor) is among the finest endurance runners of his generation. During lockdown the Kenyan star began using a treadmill at home and has continued to do so as part of his rehabilitation from a recent injury he suffered after a motorbike knocked him to the ground during an early morning run in June. Here the two-time New York Marathon winner offers his seven top treadmill training tips.

Take time to practice:

![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/a2141b72260b614e3afb668a9d79aeae0047d1fcf71ddc123f1cd39293071d84.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

Kamworor urges novice treadmill runners to be patient in order to become accustomed to running on the machine before engaging in any intense sessions.

“It takes take time for people to adjust and learn how to run on a treadmill,” he explains. “I learned pretty quickly how to do so, but for others it can take a little longer.”

![Image 8](https://mybestruns.com/street/c649899eb4ea226a094d35c54188897ee0ecd5f22a51cbcb024dd442b8785c9e.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon characterised by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures across parts of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. It can alter weather patterns across different regions, while its warming influence can contribute to higher global temperatures. The full impact depends on the strength of the event and how it interacts with other climate factors.

![Image 10](https://mybestruns.com/street/46b631cd0e12734e6118d1811afa82002a59f6f038f8de1a680ce25c9ce4a1e2.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

Researchers found that leading male runners finished approximately 1.7 per cent slower relative to course records under the coolest conditions examined. In the warmest category, that difference increased to around 4.5 per cent.

At the elite level, where races are frequently decided by seconds, such a difference can determine whether a runner achieves a personal best, secures a podium finish or misses a major performance target.

Every kilometre he covers in the distinctive hospital gown carries a message of gratitude to the people who cared for him and hope for patients whose journeys are only beginning. His challenge transforms a gruelling 42.195-kilometre race into a public expression of appreciation for the doctors, nurses, researchers and other healthcare professionals working to improve the lives of people affected by cancer.

The timing of this year's marathon makes the occasion even more meaningful. The race falls just days from the anniversary of his first chemotherapy session in 2022, bringing him back to a period that profoundly changed his life. Returning to the streets of Toronto now, healthy enough to pursue another marathon, offers a powerful reminder of how far he has travelled since those difficult days.

For Throop, choosing Toronto has never been simply about finding the fastest course on which to break a record. Although other marathons might offer different racing conditions, the Toronto Waterfront Marathon holds a significance that no alternative venue could easily replace. The course takes him past Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, the institution where he received treatment, while family members and friends who supported him throughout his illness are there to witness his journey.

It is a route that connects his past to his present: the hospital where he fought for his health, the streets where he now tests his endurance, and the people who helped him keep moving forward when the road ahead was uncertain.

His hospital gown is therefore much more than an unusual racing outfit. It is a symbol of the vulnerability he experienced as a patient, the strength he rediscovered through running, and his determination to turn a deeply personal struggle into something that benefits others.

As he prepares for his third record attempt, the challenge remains considerable. The existing mark of 2:50:12 demands an average pace of approximately four minutes per kilometre, a formidable task even without the physical discomfort and practical challenges of racing in a hospital gown.

Nevertheless, Throop has already demonstrated that his mission can make a difference regardless of the result on the clock. His previous attempts brought attention to cancer care, while his ongoing fundraising efforts have generated substantial support for the foundation that represents an important part of his personal story.

On Sunday, he will once again take his place among thousands of runners, carrying a message that reaches well beyond the marathon course. Whether he finally breaks the world record or falls short for a third time, his presence will stand as a reminder that recovery can open doors to remarkable achievements and that gratitude can become a powerful force for helping others.

For Brandon Throop, the finish line represents more than a sporting ambition. It is an opportunity to honour the people who helped him survive, support the research that may give other families more time together, and show what can be possible after a life-altering diagnosis.

The record is still waiting. But with more than $137,000 already raised toward his fundraising goal, Throop has another reason to consider his mission a success before the starting gun even sounds.

On the streets of Toronto, the hospital gown is returning with a purpose: to celebrate survival, give back to the people who helped save a life, and turn every step into hope for someone else.

[![Image 2](https://katarunningretreat.com/cdn/shop/files/ChatGPT_Image_May_8_2026_05_55_04_PM.png?v=1778288140&width=300)](https://katarunningretreat.com/products/my-best-runs-supporter)

Three-time world half marathon champion and two-time world cross country gold medalist[Geoffrey Kamworor](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor) is among the finest endurance runners of his generation. During lockdown the Kenyan star began using a treadmill at home and has continued to do so as part of his rehabilitation from a recent injury he suffered after a motorbike knocked him to the ground during an early morning run in June. Here the two-time New York Marathon winner offers his seven top treadmill training tips.

Take time to practice:

![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/a2141b72260b614e3afb668a9d79aeae0047d1fcf71ddc123f1cd39293071d84.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

Kamworor urges novice treadmill runners to be patient in order to become accustomed to running on the machine before engaging in any intense sessions.

“It takes take time for people to adjust and learn how to run on a treadmill,” he explains. “I learned pretty quickly how to do so, but for others it can take a little longer.”

![Image 4](https://mybestruns.com/street/bda5a4aaa3b6117c54fc2a4ac8d923ca01a654d2a76881f6832c37de0c233ef5.jpg?i=1792160482&t=1792160482)

Warm up properly:

When jumping on the treadmill it should be treated no differently to running outside in that it requires a thorough warm up.

“Run slowly at first,” he says. “The good thing with a treadmill you can easily set the pace. Maybe start at a walking pace, then slowly increasing the speed to running pace.”

Embrace its versatility:

Kamworor believes the treadmill can be used for many different types of sessions, from tempo runs to fartlek and even speed sessions. A favourite fartlek session of his is three minutes of fast running at a speed of between 20-22kmph followed by one minute of jogging at 10kmph, then repeated.

“I set the calculations into the machine so 10 seconds before I’m scheduled to run at full speed again this allows the machine to gradually adjust to full speed.”

Speed sessions:

While acknowledging it is a little trickier to replicate track speed sessions on the treadmill he insists it is far from impossible.

“It is not something easy because it requires a lot of calculations but this is something you can learn over time, and, for me, it works perfectly. Normally, I would train on the track in a group but the treadmill allows me to do the speed session alone if necessary.”

Flat gradient:

Some treadmill users emphasise the importance of always running at a slight gradient but as many of Kamworor’s quicker sessions are run on the flat he prefers to replicate this with a 0.0 % gradient during many of his treadmill sessions.

“The option is there, though, to run on a slight incline or decline if you want to,” he adds.

Visualize a route:

Kamworor personally prefers not to listen to music when treadmill running, because he likes to stay fully concentrated. He does, however, suggest to any treadmill runners to visualize a running route when on the treadmill.

“Whether you are on a speed session or tempo run it is importance to visualize, even if you are visualizing a competition. It is important to think positively about running.”

Cool down:

Like on any run, Geoffrey says it is important not to neglect the cool down on the treadmill. “It is important to reduce the speed to 10kmph or less,” he says. “Twenty minutes is a nice cool down time.”

This will be his third attempt to claim the record, following two determined performances in previous editions of the Toronto race. In 2023, he completed the marathon in 2:55:59 before returning in 2024 to improve his time to 2:55:01. Despite his progress, the record remained just out of reach.

The current benchmark stands at 2:50:12, established by Evan Ubene at the same Toronto Waterfront Marathon in 2022. To make history this time, Throop will need to improve significantly on his previous performances and take more than five minutes off his best hospital-gown marathon.

Yet the significance of Sunday's race cannot be measured by finishing time alone.

Throop's larger objective is to raise funds for the Princess Margaret Cancer Foundation, supporting the cancer research and care that played such an important role in his own recovery. He has already raised more than $137,000 toward his $150,000 fundraising target, bringing him within reach of a goal that could help support further advances in cancer treatment.

Every kilometre he covers in the distinctive hospital gown carries a message of gratitude to the people who cared for him and hope for patients whose journeys are only beginning. His challenge transforms a gruelling 42.195-kilometre race into a public expression of appreciation for the doctors, nurses, researchers and other healthcare professionals working to improve the lives of people affected by cancer.

The timing of this year's marathon makes the occasion even more meaningful. The race falls just days from the anniversary of his first chemotherapy session in 2022, bringing him back to a period that profoundly changed his life. Returning to the streets of Toronto now, healthy enough to pursue another marathon, offers a powerful reminder of how far he has travelled since those difficult days.

For Throop, choosing Toronto has never been simply about finding the fastest course on which to break a record. Although other marathons might offer different racing conditions, the Toronto Waterfront Marathon holds a significance that no alternative venue could easily replace. The course takes him past Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, the institution where he received treatment, while family members and friends who supported him throughout his illness are there to witness his journey.

It is a route that connects his past to his present: the hospital where he fought for his health, the streets where he now tests his endurance, and the people who helped him keep moving forward when the road ahead was uncertain.

His hospital gown is therefore much more than an unusual racing outfit. It is a symbol of the vulnerability he experienced as a patient, the strength he rediscovered through running, and his determination to turn a deeply personal struggle into something that benefits others.

As he prepares for his third record attempt, the challenge remains considerable. The existing mark of 2:50:12 demands an average pace of approximately four minutes per kilometre, a formidable task even without the physical discomfort and practical challenges of racing in a hospital gown.

Nevertheless, Throop has already demonstrated that his mission can make a difference regardless of the result on the clock. His previous attempts brought attention to cancer care, while his ongoing fundraising efforts have generated substantial support for the foundation that represents an important part of his personal story.

On Sunday, he will once again take his place among thousands of runners, carrying a message that reaches well beyond the marathon course. Whether he finally breaks the world record or falls short for a third time, his presence will stand as a reminder that recovery can open doors to remarkable achievements and that gratitude can become a powerful force for helping others.

For Brandon Throop, the finish line represents more than a sporting ambition. It is an opportunity to honour the people who helped him survive, support the research that may give other families more time together, and show what can be possible after a life-altering diagnosis.

On the streets of Toronto, the hospital gown is returning with a purpose: to celebrate survival, give back to the people who helped save a life, and turn every step into hope for someone else.

**COPENHAGEN (20-Sep)** — Agnes Ngetich absolutely destroyed a high-class field in the half-marathon this morning at the second World Athletics Road Running Championships. The 25 year-old Kenyan, who already earned a world title earlier this year at the World Athletics Cross Country Championships, ran alone through the streets of the Danish capital to a women’s only world record of 1:05:15. She won by a hefty 50 seconds, and became the first woman in history to win both the world cross country and half-marathon titles in the same year.

But Ngetich endured a painful final 400 meters. She had the gold medal in the bag, but she wasn’t sure if she could eclipse Peres Jepchirchir’s women-only world record of 1:05:16. With the sun at her back, she gave it everything she had in the final push to the line.

“I thought I missed the world record by two seconds or three seconds,” Ngetich told Race Results Weekly while wrapped in a Kenyan flag. “It’s me alone and a strong wind coming to us. I was like, let me just try.”

Her one-second margin over Jepchirchir’s record was worth a USD 50,000 bonus from World Athletics which will be added to her first place prize money of USD 30,000 (she will surely receive an additional bonus from her kit sponsor, adidas). Winning the race was more important, she said, but getting the record was a nice bonus.

“If I don’t get it, it’s OK; I have a medal already,” Ngetich recalled telling herself in those final meters. “I’m so happy because I still got the world record.”

Ngetich used the same simple strategy today that she employed to become world cross country champion in Tallahassee last January: push right from the gun. She split the first kilometer in three minutes flat, and went through 5K in 15:12. She already had a ten-second gap on her nearest chaser by that point, Florence Niyonkuru of Rwanda, a gap which would grow to 26 seconds by 10K (30:39). The athletes in the chase pack –eight women strong– quickly began to focus on each other, instead. Ngetich was just too far ahead.

“I noticed Agnes taking off but I knew I had to stick to my own pace,” said Ngetich’s teammate Veronica Loleo. “She was going too fast from the very beginning. So I decided to go with the pack.”

Unaware of how far ahead she was, Ngetich kept pressing. She stayed focused on her splits, and imagined what it would be like to earn another gold medal.

“Adding another medal to my gallery, I’m so happy,” she said. “I’m so grateful.”

The battle for the silver and bronze medals was intense. That chase pack of eight women at 10K dwindled to just three by 20K: Niyonkuru, Loleo, and another Kenyan, Daisilah Jerono. Americans Emma Grace Hurley, Weini Kelati, and Jess McClain were just a few seconds back (as a team they were in the silver medal position behind Kenya). In the final 100 meters before the finish, Loleo was able to sprint away from Niyonkuru to take the silver in 1:06:05. Niyonkuru was already clear of Jerono, and got the bronze in a national record 1:06:08.

“I didn’t expect to be on the podium, so for me I’m very happy,” said Loleo. “It is my first championships. This first championship medal I will award to my family and coach.”

Hurley, who is training for her marathon debut at the Bank of America Chicago Marathon on October 11, finished an impressive fifth in 1:06:23. Her mark was not only a personal best, but also a USA national record for an all-women’s race. Kelati, the USA open record holder, ran 1:06:35 for sixth, and McClain got seventh in a personal best 1:06:53.

“I’m very excited,” said Hurley, who also owns the national record for 8K on the roads. “I was super-focused on being in the top 10 today, and it’s exciting to come away with a women’s record as well. I have been so happy all week just to be here, and I was so excited for the opportunity to race against the best of the best.”

Remarkably, both Hurley and McClain were in danger of being left off the team after they were misdirected off course while leading at the national half-marathon championships last March in Atlanta which was used as the team selection race. But thanks to behind-the-scenes work by USATF, the United States was allowed to enter a larger team for these championships where Hurley, McClain and Ednah Kurgat (the three misdirected athletes) could join the other women who were selected based on the official order of finish (Team USATF was still limited to four athletes who were eligible to score).

“It was really important to us to send the strongest possible team to compete against the best in the world here today,” said Jay Holder, USATF’s communications chief. He continued: “We wanted to send our strongest team, but we wanted to honor our selection process. So, we worked hand-in-hand with World Athletics, and they worked really hard to help us achieve those goals.”

The official team results had Kenya with the gold medal (3:17:33 total time for their best three finishers), USA second (3:19:51), and Ethiopia third (3:22:40).

**ALMGREN OUTLASTS KIPKORIR FOR MEN’S GOLD**

The men’s race was a closely-contested affair between four athletes: Andreas Almgren of Sweden, Nicholas Kipkorir of Kenya, Joshua Cheptegei of Uganda and Tadese Worku of Ethiopia. They were the final survivors of an early break made possible by a from-the-gun surge by American record holder Conner Mantz, then incessant pushing by Kipkorir. The quartet went through 15K in 41:47, and over the next five kilometers Worku was dropped (he would finish fourth in a personal best 58:35).

Kipkorir thought that a fast pace was his best strategy.

“I decided to push because there was a strong team in the field,” Kipkorir told Race Results Weekly, referring to his competitors. “It was not easy, that is why I decided to push to make a smaller group to go to finishing.”

In the final six kilometers, Cheptegei struggled to stay in contact with Kipkorir and Almgren. The two-time Olympic gold medalist would gain a stride, then lose a stride, and managed to get to 20-K with both of his opponents. But in the final kilometer, when Kipkorir picked up the pace again, Cheptegei fell back. The three-time world 10,000m champion who won the world marathon title in 2020 would finish third in 58:26, a personal best.

“The race was really, really good and I’m so happy to be in the podium again,” Cheptegei told reporters. “After three years of not running in my national colors, it felt really good to fight for position. I’m grateful for third place today.”

The battle for gold came down to the final 100 meters. Kipkorir surged several times, but Almgren –the European 10,000m champion– covered every move. Finally as the pair crossed the 21K mark just before the finish, Almgren launched an all-out sprint and put a five-second gap on Kipkorir by the finish. Almgren, who will make his marathon debut in New York on November 1, ran a European record 58:06 and became the first European world half-marathon champion since Italy’s Stefano Baldini in 1996.

“It means so much,” said Almgren, who appeared to be in a state of disbelief. “I’ve had quite a few problems in my career, a lot of fourth places in the Europeans and I got a bronze at the World last year (in the 10,000m), and I was like, now I need to start getting the gold medals. To get the gold medal first in Birmingham in the 10K (at the European Championships) and be world champion in the half-marathon means so much.”

Kipkorir was upbeat and genuinely pleased with his silver medal.

“I’m feeling great for securing the silver medal in the world road championship 2026,” said Kipkorir. “I am proud to have the silver. That was my prayers: to be a bronze, silver or gold.”

Mantz, who spent most of 2026 recovering from two sacral stress fractures, finished 12th in 1:00:08 and helped Team USATF secure the bronze medal in a total time of 3:01:34 (Kenya got the gold in 2:56:30 and Ethiopia the silver in 2:59:47). He was happy to be back at the top level of the sport.

“Last night my coach (Ed Eyestone) called me and talked through the game plan,” Mantz said. “The game plan was just to be grateful out there. Be grateful to be in the race again. Felt grateful through 10K (his split was 27:55), but by the time I was running three-minute kilometers it was less gratitude and more regret for thinking I could get a medal today. My workouts are going well, but that doesn’t mean I’m in peak fitness.”

Mantz, the USA marathon record holder with a 2:04:43 personal best, will run the TCS New York City Marathon in November.

**

This was the 26th edition of the World Half-Marathon championships which was rolled into the World Athletics Road Running Championships (along with the mile and 5K) for the first time in Riga, Latvia, in 2023. This is the second time that the World Half-Marathon Championships was held in Copenhagen. The first time was in 2014 and it was at that event that the elite races were married with a mass-participation event for the first time. Today, some 45,000 runners competed in the mass race behind the elites.

**PHOTO**: Agnes Ngetich of Kenya just after winning the 2026 world-half-marathon championships in a women-only world record of 1:05:15 (photo by Jane Monti for Race Results Weekly)

The two-time Olympic gold medalist would gain a stride, then lose a stride, and managed to get to 20-K with both of his opponents. But in the final kilometer, when Kipkorir picked up the pace again, Cheptegei fell back. The three-time world 10,000m champion who won the world marathon title in 2020 would finish third in 58:26, a personal best.

“The race was really, really good and I’m so happy to be in the podium again,” Cheptegei told reporters. “After three years of not running in my national colors, it felt really good to fight for position. I’m grateful for third place today.”

The battle for gold came down to the final 100 meters. Kipkorir surged several times, but Almgren –the European 10,000m champion– covered every move. Finally as the pair crossed the 21K mark just before the finish, Almgren launched an all-out sprint and put a five-second gap on Kipkorir by the finish. Almgren, who will make his marathon debut in New York on November 1, ran a European record 58:06 and became the first European world half-marathon champion since Italy’s Stefano Baldini in 1996.

“It means so much,” said Almgren, who appeared to be in a state of disbelief. “I’ve had quite a few problems in my career, a lot of fourth places in the Europeans and I got a bronze at the World last year (in the 10,000m), and I was like, now I need to start getting the gold medals. To get the gold medal first in Birmingham in the 10K (at the European Championships) and be world champion in the half-marathon means so much.”

Kipkorir was upbeat and genuinely pleased with his silver medal.

“I’m feeling great for securing the silver medal in the world road championship 2026,” said Kipkorir. “I am proud to have the silver. That was my prayers: to be a bronze, silver or gold.”

Mantz, who spent most of 2026 recovering from two sacral stress fractures, finished 12th in 1:00:08 and helped Team USATF secure the bronze medal in a total time of 3:01:34 (Kenya got the gold in 2:56:30 and Ethiopia the silver in 2:59:47). He was happy to be back at the top level of the sport.

“Last night my coach (Ed Eyestone) called me and talked through the game plan,” Mantz said. “The game plan was just to be grateful out there. Be grateful to be in the race again. Felt grateful through 10K (his split was 27:55), but by the time I was running three-minute kilometers it was less gratitude and more regret for thinking I could get a medal today. My workouts are going well, but that doesn’t mean I’m in peak fitness.”

Mantz, the USA marathon record holder with a 2:04:43 personal best, will run the TCS New York City Marathon in November.

**

This was the 26th edition of the World Half-Marathon championships which was rolled into the World Athletics Road Running Championships (along with the mile and 5K) for the first time in Riga, Latvia, in 2023. This is the second time that the World Half-Marathon Championships was held in Copenhagen. The first time was in 2014 and it was at that event that the elite races were married with a mass-participation event for the first time. Today, some 45,000 runners competed in the mass race behind the elites.

**PHOTO**: Agnes Ngetich of Kenya just after winning the 2026 world-half-marathon championships in a women-only world record of 1:05:15 (photo by Jane Monti for Race Results Weekly)

## What is a half marathon?

A half marathon is a road running event where athletes race to finish in the fastest time. As the name suggests, a half marathon is exactly half the length of a marathon, at 13.1094 miles or 21.0975km.

The half marathon is not part of the World Athletics Championships or Olympic programmes. However, it is contested as part of the World Athletics Road Running Championships, which replaced the World Half Marathon Championships in 2023.

*   Race organisers created the half marathon in the 1950s as an alternative to the standard marathon distance

*   Half marathons have grown in popularity considerably since then, with thousands of events now taking place globally every year

*   Many athletes use the half marathon as a stepping stone towards competing in full marathons

*   The half marathon is not an Olympic event

*   The first World Athletics Road Running Championships was in Riga in 2023 and the next will be in San Diego in 2025

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=ExXzWLTg48I)

### Women’s half marathon world record

While a half marathon is exactly half the distance of a full marathon, it still requires a level of endurance and determination that can only be achieved through dedicated and prolonged training.

There are two women’s world records – one set in women-only races and the other set in mixed races, where women run alongside men.

The women-only world record-holder is Kenya’s Peres Jepchirchir, who ran 1:05:16 at the World Athletics Half Marathon Championships in Gdynia in 2020.

Ethiopian athlete Letesenbet Gidey set the world record for a mixed race of 1:02:52 in Valencia in October 2021. Overall, Kenya and Ethiopia have been to the fore in women’s half marathon running.

### Men’s half marathon world record

The first men’s half marathon world best, as listed by the sport’s governing body, was set by Ron Hill, who clocked 1:05:44 in Freckleton in 1965. Interestingly however, Abebe Bikila’s half-way split of 1:04:28 from the 1964 Tokyo Olympics was quicker.

The first time a male athlete ran a half marathon in under one hour was in 1993, when Moses Tanui achieved a time of 59:47.

The current world record-holder is Ugandan athlete Jacob Kiplimo, with 57:31 run in November 2021. This broke the former record held by Kenyan runner Kibiwott Kandie by just one second.

![Image 1](https://media.aws.iaaf.org/media/Original/65e2bbf4-c69d-418f-8425-7a0269d8dc38.jpg)

## Elite half marathon runners

As well as world record-holders Jacob Kiplimo, Letesenbet Gidey and Peres Jepchirchir, other notable half marathon runners include world champion Sabastian Sawe, 2010 world gold medallist Florence Kiplagat, three-time world champion Lornah Kiplagat and five-time world champion Zersenay Tadese. Added to this, Geoffrey Kamworor of Kenya is one of the great modern half marathon runners. He secured a hat-trick of world half marathon titles between 2014 and 2018.

Mo Farah, a four-time Olympic and six-time world champion on the track, also contested some half marathons during his career. He won the Great North Run half marathon six times.

## Half marathon training

Because running a half marathon puts a great deal of strain on the mind and body, runners should gradually build up their distance and aim to train for a minimum of 12 weeks.

Training for a half marathon can be difficult, especially if you’re new to long-distance running. However, the distance can be picked up by anyone with enough time and dedication.

*   To begin with, you should aim to run every other day, taking a rest in between training sessions to allow your body to recover

*   You should attempt to increase the distance you run every week until you are comfortable that you can run 21km (13 miles) continuously

*   Build endurance by altering your speed while you train

*   If possible, run different routes to help keep your mind engaged

*   Build strength training into your fitness routine

*   Always do warm-up and cool-down activities to get the blood pumping and help reduce the risk of injury

*   Eat a healthy and balanced diet

*   Make sure you wear comfortable, good-quality footwear

*   Always keep properly hydrated

## How to pace for a half marathon

One of the keys to successfully running a half marathon is setting a steady and manageable pace to avoid burnout. Elite men’s half marathon runners will maintain a pace of between 4:30 and 5:00 minutes per mile (2:48 to 3:06 per kilometre). Meanwhile, elite women’s half marathon runners will maintain a pace of about 5:00 minutes per mile (3:06 per kilometre).

One effective way to pace the race is to split it into chunks, e.g., 13 x 1 mile sections. Help set the pace by running each individual mile in a similar time, which you can track using a GPS watch. You should train at your target pace but listen to your body and don’t push yourself unnecessarily, as this can cause your pace to slow.

## Half marathon FAQs

### How to prepare for a half marathon

You should spend at least 12 weeks preparing for a half marathon. However, the longer you spend training, the more prepared you’ll be. You should aim to train four times per week, making sure to rest in between training sessions to allow your body to rest and recover. Over time, gradually increase the distance you run but set realistic and achievable goals based on your knowledge of your body. You should also make sure to build your strength by using weights and eating a healthy and nutritionally balanced diet.

### What to eat the night before a half marathon

At least three hours before you go to bed the night before a half marathon, you should eat a nutrient balanced meal that contains carbohydrates and protein but is low in fat and fibre. You should eat foods you’re familiar with and you should try to limit spices and processed foods to prevent digestive issues. A meal such as chicken and vegetables or pasta with a tomato-based sauce is usually a good place to start.

### What to eat after a half marathon

After completing a half marathon it’s important to replace the energy your body has lost and start its recovery. Eat a small snack, such as a banana or protein bar, about half an hour after the race. Your next meal should be high in protein and carbohydrates, such as a sandwich on whole grain bread or chicken with vegetables. You should wash this down with water or an electrolyte-rich sports drink to replace lost fluids. You can help reduce inflammation and boost recovery by eating healthy fats such as nuts or seeds.

### How long to rest after half marathon

After completing a half marathon, you should rest for at least a few days. Ideally, you should do minimal exercise for a week. However, this can depend on your overall fitness levels, and you may benefit from very light exercise during this time, such as walking or gentle yoga. You should also prioritise rest, including getting plenty of sleep, to give your body the best chance of a fast recovery.

### How many steps are in a half marathon

A half marathon is 13.1094 miles or 21.0975km, which translates to approximately 26,200 steps.

## Half marathon events

THREE-TIME WORLD CHAMPION KAMWOROR AND FORMER WORLD RECORD HOLDER YESHANEH LEAD ELITE FIELDS AT THE RAS AL KHAIMAH HALF MARATHON
Registration Open at[**rakhalfmarathon.com**](http://ses.prsts.de/CL0/http:%2F%2Frakhalfmarathon.com%2F/1/0102019c40c57d60-4e7e31d6-51d1-4f99-966d-6f567c30cd73-000000/nEeD6XacM5VymQCxKsAosGKlQAHb4ywFcxaabVZezrU=443)
Ras Al Khaimah, UAE, 9 February 2026: The 19th Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon, to be staged on Saturday (February 14), will feature a powerful elite field led by three-time World Champion Geoffrey Kamworor of Kenya and former Women’s World Record holder Ababel Yeshaneh from Ethiopia – both former Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon winners in 2013 and 2020 respectively.
The Kenyan is among the greatest half marathon runners of all time achieving a hat-trick of gold medals at the World Half Marathon Championships in 2014, 2016 and 2018, winning the highly competitive World Cross Country title twice, and claiming victory in the New York Marathon on two occasions (2017 and 2019).
Kamworor achieved his breakthrough when he won the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon in 2013, smashing his personal best by over half a minute with 58:54. Six years later he broke the half marathon world record with a personal best of 58:01 in Copenhagen, which makes him the eighth fastest half marathon runner of all time and the fastest on the Ras Al Khaimah start list.

![Image 1](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Geoffrey-Kamworor-Wins-RAK-2013.jpeg)

Ras Al Khaimah 15/02/2013 2013 RAK Half Marathon nella foto: Geoffrey Kipsang Kamworor vincitore della RAK Half Marathon – Foto di Victor Sailer/A.G.Giancarlo Colombo
Like Kamworor, Ethiopia’s Ababel Yeshaneh is another world-class athlete. She ran a spectacular 64:31 world record in the 2020 Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon, leaving behind a world-class field and improving the former record by 20 seconds.
She launched her international career as a 19 year-old back in 2011 when she competed for the military. She took ninth place in the 10,000m final at the 2013 World Championships in Moscow and finished 14th in the Olympic 5,000m final in 2016.
Besides the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon, she has also won half marathons in Istanbul and Buenos Aires and achieved podium finishes at marathons in Boston, Chicago and New York. Following her world record-breaking performance six years ago, Yeshaneh returned to Ras Al Khaimah twice more – recording a non-finish in 2022 before finishing runner-up in 2024 with a fast time of 65:44.
First staged in 2007, the Ras Al Khaimah race has proved to be one of the fastest half marathons on the international circuit and this year the event will again feature four different race distances held exclusively on Al Marjan Island.

![Image 2](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Ababel-Yeshaneh-Wins-in-RAK-2020.jpg)

Ras al-Khaima 21 /02/2020 Al Ras Khaimah , Half Marathon, Al Marjan Island, nella foto: Ababel Yeshaneh Brihane Record del mondo nella mezza Maratona – foto di Giancarlo Colombo/A.G.Giancarlo Colombo
In addition to elite superstars like Kamworor and Yeshaneh in the headline race, the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon will also see participants coming together for the associated 2km, 5km and 10km events. Registration for all four races is open at[**rakhalfmarathon.com**](http://ses.prsts.de/CL0/http:%2F%2Frakhalfmarathon.com%2F/2/0102019c40c57d60-4e7e31d6-51d1-4f99-966d-6f567c30cd73-000000/Cf9eH3HaS_4wjg-yWTNtoD9M6Hv5vflHvlNg_IYld5s=443)**.**
The 2026 Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon is also sponsored by ASICS, Channel 4 Radio Network. ITP Media Group, Bisleri and Vitamin Well.
Ends
Notes to Editors
[**About Ras Al Khaimah Tourism Development Authority (RAKTDA)**](https://ses.prsts.de/CL0/https:%2F%2Fvisitrasalkhaimah.com%2F/1/0102019c40c57d60-4e7e31d6-51d1-4f99-966d-6f567c30cd73-000000/82ABbWLG5R2AeaOJmBvP28uYLWgwSdM1fVAG4WU5DVY=443)
The Ras Al Khaimah Tourism Development Authority (RAKTDA) was established in May 2011 under the government of Ras Al Khaimah. Ras Al Khaimah, UAE, 9 February 2026: The 19th Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon, to be staged on Saturday (February 14), will feature a powerful elite field led by three-time World Champion Geoffrey Kamworor of Kenya and former Women’s World Record holder Ababel Yeshaneh from Ethiopia – both former Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon winners in 2013 and 2020 respectively.
The Kenyan is among the greatest half marathon runners of all time achieving a hat-trick of gold medals at the World Half Marathon Championships in 2014, 2016 and 2018, winning the highly competitive World Cross Country title twice, and claiming victory in the New York Marathon on two occasions (2017 and 2019).
Kamworor achieved his breakthrough when he won the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon in 2013, smashing his personal best by over half a minute with 58:54. Six years later he broke the half marathon world record with a personal best of 58:01 in Copenhagen, which makes him the eighth fastest half marathon runner of all time and the fastest on the Ras Al Khaimah start list.

![Image 1](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Geoffrey-Kamworor-Wins-RAK-2013.jpeg)

Ras Al Khaimah 15/02/2013 2013 RAK Half Marathon nella foto: Geoffrey Kipsang Kamworor vincitore della RAK Half Marathon – Foto di Victor Sailer/A.G.Giancarlo Colombo
Like Kamworor, Ethiopia’s Ababel Yeshaneh is another world-class athlete. She ran a spectacular 64:31 world record in the 2020 Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon, leaving behind a world-class field and improving the former record by 20 seconds.
She launched her international career as a 19 year-old back in 2011 when she competed for the military. She took ninth place in the 10,000m final at the 2013 World Championships in Moscow and finished 14th in the Olympic 5,000m final in 2016.
Besides the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon, she has also won half marathons in Istanbul and Buenos Aires and achieved podium finishes at marathons in Boston, Chicago and New York. Following her world record-breaking performance six years ago, Yeshaneh returned to Ras Al Khaimah twice more – recording a non-finish in 2022 before finishing runner-up in 2024 with a fast time of 65:44.
First staged in 2007, the Ras Al Khaimah race has proved to be one of the fastest half marathons on the international circuit and this year the event will again feature four different race distances held exclusively on Al Marjan Island.

![Image 2](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/02/Ababel-Yeshaneh-Wins-in-RAK-2020.jpg)

Visualize a route:

Kamworor personally prefers not to listen to music when treadmill running, because he likes to stay fully concentrated. He does, however, suggest to any treadmill runners to visualize a running route when on the treadmill.

“Whether you are on a speed session or tempo run it is importance to visualize, even if you are visualizing a competition. It is important to think positively about running.”

Cool down:

Like on any run, Geoffrey says it is important not to neglect the cool down on the treadmill. “It is important to reduce the speed to 10kmph or less,” he says. “Twenty minutes is a nice cool down time.”

At the centre of the concern is the [Pacific Ocean](link_6), where developing El Niño conditions could influence global temperatures. Forecasts have raised the possibility of an unusually strong event, although its eventual intensity and the precise effects on temperatures around the world remain uncertain.

El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon characterised by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures across parts of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. It can alter weather patterns across different regions, while its warming influence can contribute to higher global temperatures. The full impact depends on the strength of the event and how it interacts with other climate factors.

However, there is no universal temperature at which every marathon runner begins to slow down. Individual fitness, acclimatisation, humidity, wind, course exposure and race strategy all influence performance. A cool, overcast morning can produce very different outcomes from a sunny, humid day, even when the thermometer shows similar readings.

What began as a modest attempt to regain his fitness eventually developed into an extraordinary mission with a purpose extending far beyond the finish line.

Now, more than three years after becoming cancer-free, Throop is preparing to return to the [TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon](link_12) on Sunday, October 18, 2026, for another attempt at the Guinness World Record for the fastest marathon completed while wearing a hospital gown.

This will be his third attempt to claim the record, following two determined performances in previous editions of the Toronto race. In 2023, he completed the marathon in 2:55:59 before returning in 2024 to improve his time to 2:55:01. Despite his progress, the record remained just out of reach.

### Women’s half marathon world record

While a half marathon is exactly half the distance of a full marathon, it still requires a level of endurance and determination that can only be achieved through dedicated and prolonged training.

There are two women’s world records – one set in women-only races and the other set in mixed races, where women run alongside men.

The women-only world record-holder is Kenya’s Peres Jepchirchir, who ran 1:05:16 at the World Athletics Half Marathon Championships in Gdynia in 2020.

### How long to rest after half marathon

After completing a half marathon, you should rest for at least a few days. Ideally, you should do minimal exercise for a week. However, this can depend on your overall fitness levels, and you may benefit from very light exercise during this time, such as walking or gentle yoga. You should also prioritise rest, including getting plenty of sleep, to give your body the best chance of a fast recovery.

### How many steps are in a half marathon

A half marathon is 13.1094 miles or 21.0975km, which translates to approximately 26,200 steps.
