### [Tigst Assefa, Rosemary Wanjiru And Gabriel Geay Headline A Star-Studded Berlin Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15325)

With just three days remaining until the [BMW Berlin Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=BMW+Berlin+Marathon), anticipation is building for another spectacular edition of one of the world’s fastest marathon races.

![Image 48](https://mybestruns.com/street/19320f7fea7434a43d8c554d44743a3253dd9181e08fd3e55cb66d7f46be26fc.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

The 52nd edition of the race will take place on Sunday, September 27, with a deep international field set to take on the famously fast streets of the German capital.

![Image 49](https://mybestruns.com/street/261ea8904ad42000ce5edd4446b5a635a9cd3b6363010f462be489c29c4806ca.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

Tanzania’s [Gabriel Geay](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Gabriel+Geay) is among the leading names in the men’s race, bringing a personal best of 2:03:00 to Berlin. His mark, set in Valencia in 2022, places him among the fastest marathoners in the elite field. However, Ethiopia’s legendary [Kenenisa Bekele](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Kenenisa+Bekele) has since been added to the field with a 2:01:41 personal best, meaning Geay is not the fastest entrant on paper.

The men’s field also features Getaneh Molla (2:03:34), Guye Adola (2:03:46), Shura Kitata (2:03:59), Kenya’s Erick Sang (2:04:30) and Olympic 10,000m champion Selemon Barega (2:05:00), setting the stage for an exceptionally deep contest.

For Bekele, however, this return to Berlin carries a significance that goes far beyond the start list. The last time the Ethiopian legend stood on the Berlin start line was in 2019, when he ran 2:01:41—just two seconds outside the then-world record of 2:01:39. Had he gone two seconds faster, Bekele would have become the only athlete in history to simultaneously hold the world records for the 5,000 metres, 10,000 metres and marathon.

![Image 50](https://mybestruns.com/street/b3fa86d8d738154c6b2764c3d5b94547fc1ac6ecc53dae90fc78db5bddf2af86.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

Bekele returns to Berlin on Sunday at the age of 44. His most recent race was the New York City Marathon in November, where he did not finish. Berlin, however, holds a special place in his marathon career. He claimed his first Berlin Marathon victory in 2016 and has won the race twice. He also owns the masters world record of 2:04:15, set in London last year.

He will not be the favourite in this year’s race, particularly after Sabastian Sawe was ruled out with a stress fracture. Adola, Molla, Kitata and Geay lead the field on paper, but Bekele’s presence adds another layer of intrigue to a race already packed with established marathon talent.

For Bekele, Berlin is more than another marathon. It is the course where he came closer than anyone to achieving a piece of distance-running history that remains untouched. Some athletes retire from the sport. Some retire toward one course. Bekele is running the second kind of retirement.

![Image 51](https://mybestruns.com/street/4be03cb14e3dd0328f98a3077e606f8f55c0af21f11d9005d99c38fcd0d3c24b.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

In the women’s race, all eyes will be on [Tigst Assefa](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Tigst+Assefa) as the Ethiopian superstar returns to the course where she produced one of the most remarkable marathon performances in history. Assefa clocked 2:11:53 in Berlin in 2023, setting a world record at the time and establishing a course record that still stands.

![Image 52](https://mybestruns.com/street/eca84645e3b691369c59e2575e7ed009b803461b94e5c40fd19ca6be92c7cbaa.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

Assefa, a two-time Berlin Marathon champion, will face defending champion [Rosemary Wanjiru](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Rosemary+Wanjiru), who returns to the German capital looking to retain her title. Wanjiru won the 2025 edition in 2:21:05 after previously finishing second in Berlin in 2022 in 2:18:00. Her personal best of 2:16:14 came at the 2023 Tokyo Marathon.

Wanjiru’s challenge will be particularly intriguing given the depth of the Ethiopian contingent. Bedatu Hirpa enters with a 2:18:27 personal best, followed by Dera Dida at 2:18:32, Zeineba Yimer at 2:18:47, Bosena Mulatie at 2:19:00, Misgane Alemayehu at 2:19:08 and Bekelech Gudeta at 2:19:39.

Kenya will also have another strong presence through Evaline Chirchir, whose 2:20:33 personal best places her among the leading women on the start list.

The Berlin Marathon’s reputation for producing fast times adds another layer of intrigue to an already stacked field. With a flat course, long stretches of uninterrupted running and a history of world records, the German capital has consistently provided elite athletes with the ideal conditions to test the limits of marathon performance.

Beyond the headline names, the race will also offer an opportunity for several contenders to make their mark on one of the biggest stages in road running. With experienced marathoners and ambitious challengers sharing the start line, the battle for the podium is expected to unfold at a demanding pace from the opening kilometres through the final stages of the race.

With Assefa returning to the scene of her historic 2023 run, Wanjiru arriving as the defending champion and a deep international cast lining up across both races, Berlin is once again set for a weekend of world-class marathon racing.

Three days out, the stage is set. The fast Berlin streets are waiting.

### [New York City Marathon Makes First Course Change in 15 Years](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15322)

The [TCS New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=TCS+New+York+City+Marathon) is set for a small but significant change to its iconic 26.2-mile course, with runners facing a revised section in the [Bronx](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Bronx) between Miles 20 and 21.

![Image 56](https://mybestruns.com/street/1936f9c4ddcb81f2a6318668a43f8a3258c6e4f5dedf2d2dac5807d0770bcefc.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

For 15 years, every New York City Marathon runner passed through the exact same stretch of the Bronx around Mile 20, navigating a short loop that surrounded a neighborhood supermarket and a 24-hour laundromat for much of race day. This November, that familiar loop will disappear.

![Image 57](https://mybestruns.com/street/07436f3fad13077b64b5db3e62de1d38e3117daf68206f1199d03f5681bbcbaf.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

New York Road Runners (NYRR) is making its first course change to the marathon in 15 years. Instead of looping near East 140th Street, runners will head north on Alexander Avenue, turn onto Third Avenue and then cut south on 138th Street toward the Madison Avenue Bridge.

The adjustment removes two turns from the Bronx section, reducing the number from seven to five. While that may sound insignificant for a race covering 26.2 miles, the change comes at a point when runners are already deep into the marathon and every turn, road surface and change in rhythm can become more noticeable.

![Image 58](https://mybestruns.com/street/dee421746c00314bfab71315f1f23f5cb01e237877ad3c36a10fa4f29ea4a7ba.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

However, the primary reason for the change is not to make the course faster or help runners shave seconds from their finishing times.

Bronx resident Jennifer Alicea told The New York Times that the previous route made it extremely difficult to reach her only nearby grocery store on marathon day. NYRR's Metellus, who grew up in the Bronx, described the affected blocks as food deserts and saw the course's required recertification as an opportunity to address the problem.

The timing also carries added significance. This year marks 50 years since the New York City Marathon expanded beyond Central Park in 1976, becoming the five-borough race that has since grown into one of the world's most famous marathons.

The route will still cover the same 26.2 miles through New York's five boroughs, but the Bronx experience will be slightly different. For elite athletes, two fewer turns could mean a smoother rhythm during the crucial closing stages. For thousands of recreational runners, the bigger difference may be felt by the communities living along the course rather than on the race clock.

The New York City Marathon has long been celebrated not only for its elite competition but also for the connection between the race and the communities it passes through. The latest adjustment reflects that relationship, showing how even an established course can evolve while preserving the character of the event.

So, two fewer turns, the same five boroughs and the same 26.2 miles — but potentially one less headache for residents of the Bronx.

For runners taking on New York this November, the question remains: will you even notice those two fewer turns when you reach Mile 20?

The [United States](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=United+States) enjoyed a remarkable day at the [2026 World Athletics Road Running Championships](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2026+World+Athletics+Road+Running+Championships) in [Copenhagen](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Copenhagen), [Denmark](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Denmark), securing team medals in both the men’s and women’s half marathon competitions.

![Image 62](https://mybestruns.com/street/943d5a596687ea246f204c79fa6f1dceb09f9858e072a4b81655c3e156cce3bd.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

The American men claimed bronze in the team standings, while the women produced a historic performance to win silver and secure Team USA’s first-ever women’s team medal at the World Road Running Championships.

Leading the way for the American men was Conner Mantz, who finished 12th individually in 1:00:08, clocking a season’s best to spearhead the American challenge over the 21.1-kilometre distance.

For Mantz, the performance carried added significance as he continues his comeback from injury. His 1:00:08 season’s best provided a strong return to championship-level competition and an important tune-up as he prepares to take on the New York City Marathon in November.

Mantz’s performance also proved crucial to Team USA’s team medal effort, with his 12th-place finish providing the foundation for the Americans to secure bronze in the men’s standings.

Ahmed Muhumed followed closely in 13th place, crossing the finish line in 1:00:15. The performance marked a significant breakthrough for Muhumed, who lowered his previous best by 48 seconds in a major championship setting.

![Image 63](https://mybestruns.com/street/f98a092b06b269b3f9b1005c7367099c88183ce2efbfd95f803a7cf39f84cbb8.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

Wesley Kiptoo completed the American scoring trio, placing 23rd in 1:01:11. Kiptoo also produced a season’s best, contributing another important performance to the United States’ team effort.

The combined performances of Mantz, Muhumed and Kiptoo were enough to place the United States third in the men’s team standings, securing a hard-earned bronze medal in Copenhagen.

For Muhumed, the race was one of the biggest breakthroughs of the day, with his 1:00:15 representing a 48-second improvement on his previous best. Kiptoo’s season-best 1:01:11 further strengthened the American challenge and helped convert three individual performances into a place on the global podium.

![Image 64](https://mybestruns.com/street/93e930c8c25a53879b56444f3f74c1199d9b253fc7b22bf1904aa8172988b09e.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

On the women’s side, Team USA made history by placing three athletes inside the top seven, earning its first-ever women’s team medal at the World Road Running Championships.

![Image 65](https://mybestruns.com/street/52511e2c9c39685e4972e22c14e69f95b41ddd5130a349a91d8cb42f4039a544.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

Hurley also finished as the first American across the line, delivering one of the standout performances of the championship for the United States.

Weini Kelati Frezghi followed in sixth place, clocking 1:06:35 and ensuring that Team USA had two athletes inside the top six. Jessica McClain completed the scoring trio in seventh, stopping the clock at 1:06:53.

McClain’s performance represented another major breakthrough. She entered Copenhagen with a half marathon personal best of 1:08:37 but improved that mark by nearly two minutes, producing a remarkable 1:06:53 and moving to No. 6 on the U.S. all-time list.

With Hurley, Kelati Frezghi and McClain all finishing inside the top seven, the American women combined their individual performances to secure a historic team silver medal.

The achievement gave Team USA a remarkable double podium finish in the half marathon team competitions, with the men taking bronze and the women claiming silver.

Beyond the medals, Copenhagen provided a showcase of individual breakthroughs for the American distance runners. Hurley moved into the top three on the U.S. all-time list, while McClain made an equally significant leap into sixth, as Mantz added another season’s best during his return from injury.

For Mantz, the Copenhagen race now serves as an important stepping stone toward the New York City Marathon in November, giving him a competitive test and a confidence-building performance as he continues his return to top-level racing.

It was a memorable championship outing for Team USA, with strong individual performances translating into two team medals and a landmark first for the American women at the World Road Running Championships.

### [Andreas Almgren Times His Move To Perfection For World Half Marathon Gold In Copenhagen](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15305)

Sweden’s [Andreas Almgren](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Andreas+Almgren) produced a breathtaking finish on the streets of [Copenhagen](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Copenhagen), unleashing a perfectly timed late surge to win the men’s half marathon title at the 2026 [World Athletics Road Running Championships](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=World+Athletics+Road+Running+Championships) in 58:06.

![Image 68](https://mybestruns.com/street/a587031fffb10fdebbacd5e8bf5f14ef21273adb27364ff193c37928b153cdc9.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

The Swedish star waited patiently through the decisive stages of the race before making his move with roughly 200 metres remaining, accelerating away from the field and producing a devastating sprint down the final straight.

![Image 69](https://mybestruns.com/street/0878cb9572cf77b09971c450d5d88858c04ddebca24e99939b1ca8164f9b19f1.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

[Nicholas Kipkorir](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Nicholas+Kipkorir) had controlled much of the race, dictating the pace and keeping the leading contenders under pressure. Almgren, however, remained close throughout, carefully conserving enough energy for the moment that would ultimately decide the world title.

When the race entered its final stretch, Almgren made his move. The Swede surged hard over the final 200 metres and then outsprinted Kipkorir over the last 100 metres, powering clear to cross the line first in 58:06.

![Image 70](https://mybestruns.com/street/718270565b440c619d6995ec36b0ff04cc5334ca1c985ea3b6ce9416d1d6cd11.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

For much of the race, Kipkorir appeared to have control, but Almgren refused to be separated from the Kenyan. His patience proved decisive as the race entered its final kilometres, allowing him to remain within striking distance before producing the acceleration that ultimately settled the contest.

Behind the leading pair, Uganda’s [Joshua Cheptegei](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Joshua+Cheptegei) endured a gruelling battle to hold on to third position. The Olympic and world champion was pushed relentlessly in the closing stages and had to dig extremely deep to preserve his place on the podium. Despite the intense pressure from the athletes behind him, Cheptegei held firm to secure the bronze medal in a personal best of 58:26.

Ethiopia’s Tadese Worku also produced a personal best of 58:35 to finish fourth, while Kenya’s Gideon Kipkertich Rono followed in fifth in 58:57. The depth of the field was reflected by the fact that six athletes broke the 59-minute barrier, underlining the exceptional quality of the championship race.

For Almgren, the Copenhagen triumph also provides an intriguing glimpse ahead to his next challenge. With his New York City Marathon debut now on the horizon, the world half marathon title represents an important statement as he prepares to make the transition to the marathon. After demonstrating that he can handle the demands of championship racing over 21.1 kilometres while still possessing the speed to produce a decisive late surge, Almgren now turns his attention toward an entirely new distance.

The victory marks Almgren’s first global title, completing a remarkable transformation from European record-holder and leading continental distance runner into a world champion.

It also adds another spectacular chapter to an already outstanding 2026 season. Almgren has consistently demonstrated an exceptional combination of endurance, speed and tactical intelligence, and Copenhagen provided the perfect stage for all three qualities to come together.

With the clock showing 58:06, Almgren not only conquered the world championship field but also rewrote the European record books. His perfectly timed attack in the final 200 metres delivered Sweden a historic world road-running title and created one of the most dramatic finishes of the Copenhagen championships.

### [Sifan Hassan Returns To New York With Experience, Recovery And A Point To Prove](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15296)

[Sifan Hassan](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Sifan+Hassan) will return to the streets of New York City on November 1 with something she did not have during her difficult debut last year — experience of one of the most demanding marathon courses in the world.

![Image 74](https://mybestruns.com/street/a3cb71e98e019d48509afa0f67fa9f0b5f218f7f41c3483ebd7fc17a3061a08c.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

The Dutch Olympic marathon champion is set to make her second appearance at the [TCS New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=TCS+New+York+City+Marathon), where she will face another formidable international field led by defending champion Hellen Obiri, fellow Kenyan Sheila Chepkirui and former world champion Edna Kiplagat.

Hassan's first encounter with New York in 2025 proved to be a far tougher assignment than the three-time Olympic champion might have hoped. She finished sixth in 2:24:43 after struggling during the second half of the race, with her New York debut coming only weeks after her victory at the Sydney Marathon.

The demanding schedule left Hassan facing a difficult recovery, and New York's succession of bridges, climbs and sharp changes in rhythm exposed the challenge of arriving at the race without enough marathon-specific preparation.

This time, however, the circumstances are different.

![Image 75](https://mybestruns.com/street/2cd6ef054f71e9d7902bf555e97f4d9369e681242cd998135aa61c1ce82a260c.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

Hassan has had considerably more time to recover and prepare for the marathon, while she has also been managing an Achilles problem that disrupted her 2026 season. Rather than rushing back into competition, she has used the year to recover and build towards her longer-term goals.

Most importantly, Hassan now knows what awaits her when the race moves through New York's five boroughs.

She has already experienced the relentless bridges, the demanding climbs and the atmosphere created by huge crowds lining the streets. That knowledge could prove valuable when the race enters its decisive stages, particularly on a course where pacing and patience are just as important as raw marathon speed.

Hassan will also arrive with one of the fastest personal bests in the field. Her 2:13:44 national record makes her the quickest woman entered for the 2026 race, although New York's challenging layout means personal-best times do not necessarily tell the whole story.

Standing across the starting line will be a powerful Kenyan challenge.

### [From Shark Attack Survivor to New York City Marathon Finisher: Ali Truwit's Extraordinary Journey of Courage and Resilience](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14896)

Some victories are measured by finish times. Others are defined by the obstacles overcome simply to reach the starting line.

For American Paralympic swimmer [Ali Truwit](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Ali+Truwit), completing the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) represented far more than covering 26.2 miles. It was the culmination of an extraordinary journey of survival, resilience, and unwavering determination that began with a life-altering shark attack just two years earlier.

![Image 129](https://mybestruns.com/street/8112546f7a444a2f5eee29dc55aa5cb262179b96de95ea565d789400f564a403.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

On a crisp November morning in 2025, Truwit crossed the iconic finish line wearing a carbon-fibre running blade, fulfilling a promise she had made while recovering in a hospital bed after losing her lower left leg. The emotional milestone marked another remarkable chapter in one of the most inspiring comeback stories in modern sport.

The road to that unforgettable finish began only days after Truwit celebrated a major personal achievement. In May 2023, she completed her first marathon in Copenhagen alongside her mother. Just ten days later, while enjoying a graduation trip to Turks and Caicos with former Yale swimming teammate Sophie Pilkinton, tragedy struck.

While the pair were snorkelling, a shark attacked Truwit, severely injuring her left leg. Displaying remarkable courage, the two swam approximately 55 metres back to their boat, where Pilkinton—then a medical student—quickly applied a tourniquet that stopped the bleeding and ultimately saved Truwit's life.

Doctors were forced to amputate her lower left leg on her 23rd birthday.

![Image 130](https://mybestruns.com/street/60182ea28dcbec09b201b2c96b35b47844e8b704ee2161e222ca8662ac6351b0.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

Even in the darkest moments of recovery, Truwit's determination never disappeared. Reflecting on having recently completed her first marathon, she joked with one of the first responders that at least she had managed to run a marathon before the attack. The responder's simple but powerful reply would remain with her throughout rehabilitation: "You'll run another one."

Those words became a source of hope during the long and demanding road back.

![Image 131](https://mybestruns.com/street/8453df5e269fa1e38d0c2decf96df3c87ee036f4a16018159372af4552595ba9.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

Only weeks after surgery, Truwit began learning to walk on a prosthetic limb before gradually returning to the swimming pool. The process was anything but straightforward. The water that had once been her sanctuary became a source of painful memories, yet she refused to allow fear to define her future.

Her relentless work ethic soon produced extraordinary results.

Less than 16 months after the attack, Truwit represented the United States at the Paris 2024 Paralympic Games, producing a sensational performance to claim both silver and bronze medals. Standing on the Paralympic podium was a powerful reminder of how far she had come in such a short period, and she dedicated those achievements to everyone who had helped save her life.

Still, another dream remained unfinished.

The New York City Marathon carried deep personal significance. It was not merely another endurance event but a symbolic return to the city where her life had changed forever. On November 2, 2025, she lined up in Staten Island accompanied by 13 family members and close friends, all proudly representing her nonprofit foundation, Stronger Than You Think. Among them was Pilkinton, the friend whose quick thinking had preserved her life on that unforgettable day in the Caribbean.

Together, they covered every mile of the marathon before celebrating an emotional finish that Truwit later described as being "over the moon."

Completing a marathon on a carbon-fibre running blade presents challenges far beyond those faced by able-bodied runners. The prosthetic demands greater strength from the hips, core, and remaining leg while requiring exceptional balance, coordination, and endurance. Truwit's preparation combined months of disciplined training, patience, and mental resilience as she effectively taught herself how to run again.

Her story extends well beyond medals and marathon finishes.

Inspired by her own recovery, Truwit founded Stronger Than You Think, a nonprofit organisation dedicated to helping individuals overcome physical and financial barriers following limb loss. Recognising that sports prosthetics can cost tens of thousands of dollars and are often not covered by insurance, the foundation provides financial assistance for prosthetic devices, supports water-safety education, and promotes opportunities within Paralympic sport.

The organisation has already helped provide more than 11 prosthetic limbs, delivered nearly $200,000 in direct support, and funded over 4,000 hours of water-safety lessons benefiting more than 700 young people.

Throughout her journey, Truwit has remained refreshingly honest about the emotional challenges that continue to accompany recovery. She has openly acknowledged that healing is an ongoing process and that grief can still come in waves. Rather than portraying an effortless comeback, she has demonstrated that resilience is built through persistence, even on the hardest days.

Her remarkable transformation resonates far beyond elite sport. While few people will ever experience the trauma she endured, countless runners and athletes understand the frustration of injury, disappointment, or rebuilding after adversity. Truwit's journey serves as a powerful reminder that recovery is rarely linear and that courage is often measured by the willingness to keep moving forward despite uncertainty.

![Image 221](https://mybestruns.com/street/31fd23f24578a76f6fc0580d9093e935c038cda98d42eefe81cdfdd0126b8ac7.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

Their dominance has been so complete, and so sustained, that it has been described as“the greatest geographical concentration of achievement in the annals of sport.”And it is hard to argue otherwise.

From the Rift Valley to the World Stage

Most elite Kalenjin runners come from Kenya’s Rift Valley region, particularly areas such as Nandi, Elgeyo-Marakwet, Uasin Gishu, and Baringo, where elevations range from 2,000 to 2,400 meters (6,500–8,000 feet)above sea level.

Here, running is not a hobby—it is part of daily life.

Children grow up walking and running long distances, often on dirt roads. Training at altitude is the norm, not a strategy. And success stories are local and visible, creating a powerful cycle of belief and opportunity.

Champions Across Eras

The Kalenjin impact on global athletics stretches back more than half a century.

Kipchoge Keino, one of the pioneers of Kenyan distance running, won Olympic gold in the 1500 meters at the 1968 Mexico City Games and the 3000-meter steeplechase in 1972, helping place Kenyan runners on the world map.

Since then, Kenyan athletes—many of them Kalenjin—have dominated:

• The 3000-meter steeplechase, winning Olympic gold in nearly every Games since 1968

• The 5,000 meters and 10,000 meters at World Championships

• The marathon, particularly at the World Marathon Majors

Masters of the Marathon

Perhaps nowhere is this dominance more visible than in the marathon.

Kalenjin runners have repeatedly won and controlled races such as:

• Berlin Marathon

• London Marathon

• Chicago Marathon

• Boston Marathon

• New York City Marathon

These victories are not isolated moments—they are part of a long, uninterrupted pattern.

At the center of it all stands Eliud Kipchoge, widely regarded as the greatest marathon runner in history. A member of the Kalenjin community, Kipchoge has:

• Won two Olympic marathon gold medals(2016, 2021)

• Set a world record of 2:01:09 at the Berlin Marathon

• Become the first human to run 26.2 miles in under two hours

He is not an exception. He is the most refined expression of a system that has been producing champions for generations.

Why This One Tribe?

No single explanation tells the whole story, but several factors come together in the Rift Valley:

• Geography:High altitude, rolling terrain, and ideal training conditions

• Physiology:Exceptional running economy and efficient biomechanics

• Culture:Running as a respected path to success and opportunity

• Environment:Group training, competition, and long-term development from a young age

Together, these elements have created something unmatched in sport.

A Phenomenon Without Parallel

Great athletes come from everywhere. But nowhere else has such a small, specific populationproduced such sustained global dominance across events, generations, and decades.

Not sprinting.

Not swimming.

Not cycling.

Not soccer.

Only distance running.

From the highland paths of the Rift Valley to Olympic podiums and marathon finish lines around the world, the story of the Kalenjin remains one of the most extraordinary achievements in human performance.

And it is still being written.

### [At 91, Koichi Kitabatake Will Be the Oldest Runner in the 2025 New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=13965)

When Koichi Kitabatake steps onto the starting line of the 2025 TCS New York City Marathon on November 2, he will make history as the oldest competitor in the field — at 91 years old.

The runner from Kanagawa, Japan, didn’t start running until long after most people retire. In fact, he only took up the sport at age 74, after finishing a long career as a telecommunications specialist. Four years later, at 78, he ran his first marathon — and he hasn’t stopped since.

![Image 254](https://mybestruns.com/street/d607ca06fe1d2de35df8b6bd48ea213e63d82e9444e18d9683c6c2262b77a650.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

This year’s race will mark his 34th marathon, including two previous finishes in New York City. Kitabatake has flown across the world to participate in marathons on nearly every continent, proving that passion and discipline know no age limits.

Running Into His 90s

![Image 255](https://mybestruns.com/street/3ab25a75abc9eaf4b26f6e9578ceb610fb81fb7584b30cb8eaa1b933cf6d6266.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

As he prepares for the 26.2-mile journey through all five boroughs of New York City, Kitabatake shared with the Daily Mail some of his daily habits that keep him strong — both physically and mentally — well into his 90s.

“I do a short workout and stretching every morning for about half an hour,” he said. “Then I run four to six miles twice a week, depending on how I feel.”

It’s a simple but powerful routine — one that underscores his belief in consistency over intensity.

Beyond the physical benefits, Kitabatake says running has transformed his outlook on life.

“Running has changed how I see things,” he told the Daily Mail. “It helps me stay positive and keeps my mind healthy.”

A Source of Inspiration

Kitabatake’s story has inspired countless others, especially those who feel it’s “too late” to start something new. His steady approach, humility, and unwavering commitment to movement highlight the broader spirit of the marathon itself — endurance, courage, and the celebration of life at every age.

As thousands line up in Staten Island to begin the 2025 TCS New York City Marathon, Kitabatake will stand among them — proof that age is just a number, and that the human spirit, when fueled by purpose, can keep running forever.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)

Long before he conquered world cross-country championships, dominated the half-marathon distance and lifted the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) trophy, [Geoffrey Kamworor](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor) was a young Kenyan student with an ambitious dream that had little to do with running: becoming a [lawyer](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=lawyer).

![Image 2](https://mybestruns.com/street/de57be259ad5f2aa804935a23c35ae7bb6b49b6ec295d0ed68325e1b13b71303.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

Growing up in Keiyo South, Kamworor developed the discipline that would later define his extraordinary athletic career. His daily routine involved running approximately five kilometres to school and another five kilometres back home. What might have seemed like an ordinary journey for a schoolboy was quietly laying the foundation for a future in international distance running.

![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/808283ce83ea90fb69283ae3a63fb6cc12becf4782bc79b9156f109324db53df.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

He attended Chepsamo Primary School before proceeding to Lelboinet Secondary School, where he combined his education with a growing passion for athletics. At the time, his ambitions extended beyond the track and roads. He wanted to pursue a career in law, and that dream eventually brought him an opportunity to study at a college in the United States.

However, the young Kenyan faced a defining decision: follow the academic path he had envisioned or commit himself fully to the sport that was beginning to reveal his remarkable potential. Kamworor chose athletics, a decision that would ultimately place his name among the most accomplished distance runners of his generation.

![Image 4](https://mybestruns.com/street/a94c34052d38330fd293c08402206cd4d7a39c33946639bdb76ca84e0ab123e7.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

His transformation from a promising schoolboy into an international contender began gathering momentum in 2010, when he joined the GSC training camp in Kaptagat. His development accelerated rapidly, and within a short period, an opportunity to compete in Finland exposed him to a higher level of international competition.

Still only 17, he reportedly competed nine times during that trip, demonstrating an impressive ability to adapt to the demands of competitive racing. Breaking the eight-minute barrier for 3,000 metres was an early indication of the talent that would eventually carry him to the highest levels of distance running.

![Image 5](https://mybestruns.com/street/84282c8c1c650ab6ffe7062ef243eacc858a034f27f3ff8005541232e23d4bd3.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

His breakthrough on the international stage followed in March 2011, when he captured the junior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Punta Umbría, Spain. That victory announced the arrival of a young athlete whose future would extend far beyond the junior ranks.

Kamworor was not simply a runner with speed. He possessed the endurance, tactical intelligence and competitive determination required to succeed across different distances and racing surfaces. As his career developed, those qualities became the hallmarks of an athlete capable of challenging the world's best.

Cross country became one of the foundations of Kamworor's international success. In 2015, he won the senior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Guiyang, China, confirming his status as one of the leading distance runners in the world. Two years later, he returned to the top of the podium in Kampala, Uganda, defending his senior world cross-country crown in front of a home crowd. Winning consecutive senior world titles placed him in an elite category and demonstrated his remarkable command of the demanding discipline.

On the roads, however, Kamworor established an equally impressive legacy. He won the World Half Marathon Championships in Copenhagen in 2014, Cardiff in 2016 and Valencia in 2018, becoming a three-time champion at the distance. His achievements reflected a rare combination of strength, speed and race management, enabling him to prevail against formidable international opposition.

The half marathon became one of his signature events, but Kamworor's ambitions were never confined to a single discipline. He continued to demonstrate his versatility on the track, winning silver in the men's 10,000 metres at the 2015 World Athletics Championships in Beijing, China. From the grass of cross-country courses to the roads of major international races and the track of a global championship, he repeatedly demonstrated that his talent could flourish wherever the competition took him.

Among Kamworor's most memorable achievements are his victories at the New York City Marathon in 2017 and 2019. Winning one of the world's most celebrated marathons requires exceptional endurance, but winning it twice demands much more: tactical patience, resilience and the ability to navigate a demanding course against a deep international field.

Kamworor demonstrated those qualities in both victories, establishing a special connection with the New York race and adding the marathon to an already remarkable collection of honours. His success in the American city also illustrated his ability to move successfully between distances. An athlete celebrated for his cross-country and half-marathon dominance had shown that he could also conquer the 42.195-kilometre marathon, one of the most demanding challenges in road racing.

Now, as he sets his sights on another New York campaign, the Kenyan star has an opportunity to strengthen his legacy further. A third men's open-division victory would place him among a very select group of athletes to have won the prestigious race three times. Such a milestone would be more than another addition to his trophy cabinet; it would reinforce the story of a runner whose competitive range has extended across nearly every major discipline in distance running.

Behind Kamworor's achievements lies a training environment built around discipline, consistency and high-level competition. Working under the guidance of renowned coach Patrick Sang, he has trained alongside some of Kenya's most celebrated athletes, including marathon great Eliud Kipchoge and middle- and long-distance superstar Faith Kipyegon.

Sharing a training environment with athletes of such calibre provides a demanding daily standard. Yet Kamworor has built his own identity through a career defined by major championship victories and sustained success across different racing distances. His journey has also included difficult periods and setbacks, reminding the running world that even the most accomplished champions must continually work to return to their best. His longevity at the elite level reflects the importance of patience, dedication and the willingness to keep pursuing new goals.

For aspiring athletes in Kenya, his story offers an important lesson: extraordinary achievements are often built through ordinary routines repeated consistently over many years. Those five-kilometre journeys to school and back were not glamorous. They did not come with cheering crowds, television cameras or medals. Yet they formed part of the foundation of a career that would eventually take him to the world's biggest running stages.

Kamworor's story is ultimately about a choice that changed the direction of his life. The young student who once imagined himself arguing cases in a courtroom instead built his reputation by answering the toughest questions on the running track and roads. His achievements speak for themselves: world cross-country titles, three world half-marathon crowns, a global 10,000-metre silver medal and two New York City Marathon victories.

He may never have pursued the legal career he once envisioned, but his athletic record tells a compelling story of ambition, sacrifice and extraordinary accomplishment. His pursuit of another New York triumph offers a fresh chapter in a career that has already crossed the boundaries between cross country, track and road racing.

For Geoffrey Kamworor, the courtroom was a dream he left behind. The world of distance running became the stage on which he built his name. And while the law lost a prospective lawyer, athletics gained a champion whose achievements have helped define an era of Kenyan distance running.

### [From $1 To $358: How The New York City Marathon Became A Global Running Phenomenon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15437)

What began as a modest race through Central Park, with a handful of determined runners and a budget of just $1,000, has evolved into one of the most prestigious and sought-after marathons in the world. More than five decades later, the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) tells a remarkable story of how distance running has grown from a grassroots sporting event into a global spectacle.

![Image 9](https://mybestruns.com/street/bacec4114b3d54670c15a184e950b0e7ddb43de9849a87f97fe568b1a68fdecf.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

When the inaugural New York City Marathon took place in 1970, the entry fee was just $1. Organised by the New York Road Runners, the race was held entirely within Central Park, far removed from the enormous crowds, international attention and commercial scale that define the event today.

![Image 10](https://mybestruns.com/street/cb333999ed07e06d10edcf37e5452882364cbb7336ebf8347871bb079ae7bfbf.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

Of the 127 registered participants, only 55 completed the race. Yet, despite its modest beginnings, the event laid the foundation for a marathon that would eventually capture the imagination of runners from every corner of the world.

The first champion was Gary Muhrcke, a New York City firefighter whose victory remains one of the most memorable stories from the race's early years. According to accounts of the inaugural edition, Muhrcke had finished a night shift before entering the competition shortly before the start. He went on to win in approximately 2:31, securing his place in the marathon's history.

The inaugural race also featured Nina Kuscsik, the only woman in the field. She started the event but withdrew after becoming ill, meaning no woman finished that first edition. Kuscsik would later become an important figure in the campaign for women's inclusion in competitive distance running.

Over the years, the New York City Marathon expanded beyond Central Park, eventually developing into the iconic five-borough journey that takes runners through Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Manhattan. Its transformation helped turn the race into a celebration of athletic achievement, community spirit and the extraordinary diversity of New York City.

Today, the marathon attracts elite athletes chasing victories and records, recreational runners pursuing personal milestones, charity participants raising funds for important causes, and thousands of international visitors eager to experience one of running's most celebrated events.

### [Sifan Hassan Withdraws From 2026 New York City Marathon As Illness Disrupts Her Preparation](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15434)

Olympic marathon champion [Sifan Hassan](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Sifan+Hassan) of [the Netherlands](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=the+Netherlands) has officially withdrawn from the [2026 TCS New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2026+TCS+New+York+City+Marathon) after illness disrupted her preparations, ending hopes of seeing the versatile distance-running star return to one of the world’s most prestigious road races this autumn.

![Image 14](https://mybestruns.com/street/ff056ddb48590d9d5770aeba39b2968d8cbf9e31921bf90d9e503fe24646ab1c.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

Hassan announced her decision on social media, explaining that sickness had slowed her training and left her short of the level of preparation she had hoped to achieve ahead of the November 1 race. The withdrawal is a setback for the Dutch star, who had been looking forward to returning stronger after her previous appearance in New York.

“I was so excited to come back stronger, but a sickness slowed down my training and I’m not where I wanted to be. Sometimes, things just don’t go as planned,” Hassan wrote.

Despite her disappointment, the Olympic champion also sent her best wishes to the athletes preparing to compete in New York, demonstrating her support for the wider running community even as she steps away from the competition.

Hassan, who holds a personal best of 2:13:44, ranks fifth on the women’s all-time marathon list. Her extraordinary range across track and road running has established her as one of the most versatile athletes of her generation, capable of competing at the highest level from shorter distances to the marathon.

![Image 15](https://mybestruns.com/street/ef554feb696cb3fe2c211d5312650a678a574b1ad394f3e13678ec6ed3f56cfc.jpg?i=1792160795&t=1792160795)

Her marathon career has already produced several memorable achievements. Hassan has won the London Marathon and Chicago Marathon, claimed victory at the Sydney Marathon, and secured Olympic marathon gold at the Paris 2024 Games. Those accomplishments underline her ability to adapt to different courses, race conditions and competitive challenges.

The withdrawal from New York follows another interruption to her 2026 campaign. Hassan previously pulled out of the London Marathon because of an Achilles injury, and the latest illness has further disrupted her plans for the season. With her training affected, stepping aside from New York allows her to prioritise her recovery rather than compete without the preparation she considers necessary.

Hassan’s absence will be a significant talking point in the build-up to the New York City Marathon, which takes runners through all five boroughs of the city before finishing in Central Park. The demanding course and deep international field regularly produce compelling racing, and her withdrawal creates an opportunity for other leading contenders to strengthen their ambitions.

Although the precise implications for the women’s elite field will depend on the final start list, the race remains an important opportunity for leading East African athletes and top American runners to challenge for victory. Without Hassan on the starting line, attention will turn to the athletes capable of taking advantage of the opportunity and delivering a memorable performance on the streets of New York.

For Hassan, however, the priority is no longer the immediate challenge of another marathon. The Dutch star has built her reputation through resilience, adaptability and a willingness to take on some of the toughest challenges in distance running. Recovering fully and returning to structured training will be essential as she considers her next competitive objectives.

At 33, Hassan already has an exceptional record that includes Olympic glory and victories at some of the world's most prestigious marathons. While her withdrawal is disappointing for fans who hoped to see her compete in New York again, it does not diminish the achievements that have made her one of the defining distance runners of her era.

The running world will now wait for news of her recovery and next racing plans. For the moment, Hassan’s message is clear: sometimes, even the best-laid preparations do not go according to plan, and knowing when to step back is part of an athlete’s journey.

The 2026 TCS New York City Marathon is scheduled for November 1. Hassan’s withdrawal removes one of the most accomplished names from the anticipated women’s field, but the race will continue to bring together elite athletes from around the world for another major contest over the five-borough course.

content:
**Steve Prefontaine** is an American icon. He was an early employee at the fledgling company NIKE, working for **Geoff Hollister** in the tiny sports marketing department. He was a brilliant cross-country runner, a gutty indoor track racer, and a focused outdoor distance runner. Among Steve’s legacies while at Nike was sending a pair of NIKE Boston’s with a handwritten note to **Bill Rodgers,** who would wear them to win his first Boston in April 1975.

![Image 1](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/06/007_3-1.jpeg)

Steve Prefontaine racing indoors, circa 1974, photo by Jeff Johnson, curated by Walt Chadwick

**Steve Prefontaine** died on **May 30, 1975**, coming home from a party after a track meet, where he had run a 5,000 meters. Steve had set up a small meet series in Oregon, hoping to race top Europeans, especially Lasse Viren, in front of his home crowds. Steve had helped organize the series and was disappointed when Viren canceled before the races.

Steve was killed in an auto accident, inaccurately called a single-car accident. Much of the story is written about by the late, great Kenny Moore in[**Bowerman and the Men of Oregon,**](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/592821/bowerman-and-the-men-of-oregon-by-kenny-moore/) but I fear the true story will never be told.

In the end, Steve Prefontaine died much earlier than he should have. Many, like me, still idolize him, and I must say that, way back in 2008, one of my favorite projects was distributing a huge poster of Steve Prefontaine from NIKE (developed by Weiden & Kennedy), celebrating his life. I still have a few of them in my storage units.

I wanted to celebrate his life today. So, here, in no order, are **Six Lessons** that I have learned from the **life and times of Steve Prefontaine:**

1.   **Summer running is a great thing.**After he did not make the Oregon state meet in track and field during his sophomore year, Steve Prefontaine trained all summer furiously, coming into his junior year fit and ready to race. It is partially why RunBlogRun posts (and has since 2007) daily Summer Mileage programs for high school and junior high athletes. ![Image 2](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/iY4uJUqAQtWwtjkGlq61-3338891188.jpg)

Steve Prefontaine, during the summer of his sophomore year in high school, photo courtesy of Marshfield High School/TFN News

2.   **Consistency is the secret sauce of distance running.**During Steve’s time at Oregon, his coach was 1964 Olympic bronze medalist**Bill Dellinger,**an Oregon grad and a great coach and advisor to generations. Bill Dellinger mentioned to me, more than once, in coaches’ clinics and interviews, that one of the most incredible things about Steve Prefontaine was that Steve never missed a scheduled workout during his four years at the University of Oregon. ![Image 3](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/2251952a-1f29-42af-9235-4a6567ba1282-eug_041422_Prefontaine_12.webp)

Steve Prefontaine, post-workout with Coach Bill Dellinger, photo courtesy of The Eugene Register-Guard

3.   **Learn from your tough experiences.**Steve Prefontaine put so much pressure on himself at the 1972 Munich Olympics. The 5,000-meter race in Munich was one of the greatest five-thousand-meter races of all time. Lasse Viren, Mohammed Ghammoudi, Ian Stewart, and David Bedford were some of the finest distance runners in the world, and Prefontaine took them on, finishing fourth, being caught near the finish by Ian Stewart. Prefontaine was devastated. David Bedford told me a story about Steve and him having more than a few beers after the race. After that, Steve, according to his friends, changed a bit; he relaxed but stayed focused on being the best distance runner he could be. ![Image 4](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/John-Walker-Steve-Prefontaine-Rod-Dixon-by-Don-Chadez-.jpeg)

John Walker, Steve Prefontaine, Rod Dixon, racing indoors, photo by Don Chadez

4.   **Take on challenges**. **Dave Wottle**, the 1972 Olympic gold medalist at the 800 meters, told me, this past November, at the Heroes and Youth Gala on Staten Island, about racing Steve in front of HIS crowd at Hayward Field, June 20, 1973, at the **Hayward Restoration Meet.**In that race, Dave Wottle told me, again, fifty years plus late, how Steve gave Dave no quarter, no breaks, and battled him until the very end. Wottle won in 3:53.3, then ran the 3rd-fastest mile of all time. Steve finished in 3:54.6, having led most of the race, putting him, in 1973, among the fastest milers in the world! And at the time, Steve Prefontaine was known as a 5,000-meter racer! I will never forget Dave Wottle’s face as he told me the story; his respect for Steve had endured fifty-two years! ![Image 5](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Nike-Oregon-waffle-1024x570-1.jpg)

This is a photo of the NIKE Waffle racers that Steve Prefontaine used in 1974-75. They were sold at Sotheby’s for much more than the suggested retail price, photo Sotheby’s.

5.   **Do good things.**In Tom Jordan’s classic book, a must-read, [**Pre!**,](https://www.abebooks.co.uk/book-search/title/pre/author/tom-jordan/) Tom writes about Steve spending time at an Oregon prison, where he helped prisoners develop a running program. Even after Steve’s death, prisoners continued to run, including a group that ran a marathon within the prison. Steve did not have to volunteer, but he did anyway. ![Image 6](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Kenny-and-pre.jpeg)

Kenny Moore with Steve Prefontaine, photo by Jeff Johnson, curated by Walt Chadwick

6.   **Enjoy your friends.**I have been fortunate to have grown up in a generation near **Steve Prefontaine**. Several of my friends have told me stories about having a good time with Steve after races, and his sense of humor. In the book of stories [**Best Efforts**](https://www.abebooks.com/9780915297108/Best-Efforts-Moore-Kenny-0915297108/plp), by the late Kenny Moore, 1972 Olympic gold medalist (1976 silver medalist), Steve Prefontaine is described as follows: “consider at Satyr.” Steve was a complicated 25-year-old who was a few years from his very best when he died. ![Image 7](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Elite-Runner_Group-Photo_600.png)

Cooper Institute, 1975, photo by Cooper Institute

Top Row L-R Dr. Mike Pollock, Kenny Moore, Steve Prefontaine, Jim Crawford, Ted Casteneda, Philip Ndoo, Unidentified, Dr. Kenneth Cooper. Middle Row: Jeff Galloway, Doug Brown, Russell Pate, Perry Pittman, Gary Tuttle, Richard Pettigrew, Mike Manley. Bottom Row: Unidentified, Ron Wayne, Jim Johnson, Paul Geis, Don Kardong, Unidentified, Frank Shorter, from Frank Shorter

*   ![Image 8](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/14100376_10206212504540943_272549162852983311_n.jpg) Larry Eder has had a 52-year involvement in the sport of athletics. Larry has experienced the sport as an athlete, coach, magazine publisher, and now, journalist and blogger. His first article, on Don Bowden, America's first sub-4 minute miler, was published in RW in 1983. Larry has published several magazines on athletics, from American Athletics to the U.S. version of Spikes magazine. He currently manages the content and marketing development of the RunningNetwork, The Shoe Addicts, and RunBlogRun. Of RunBlogRun, his daily pilgrimage with the sport, Larry says: "I have to admit, I love traveling to far away meets, writing about the sport I love, and the athletes I respect, for my readers at runblogrun.com, the most of anything I have ever done, except, maybe running itself." Also does some updates for BBC Sports at key events, which he truly enjoys.

Theme song: Greg Allman, " I'm no Angel."

Steve Prefontaine racing indoors, circa 1974, photo by Jeff Johnson, curated by Walt Chadwick

**Steve Prefontaine** died on **May 30, 1975**, coming home from a party after a track meet, where he had run a 5,000 meters. Steve had set up a small meet series in Oregon, hoping to race top Europeans, especially Lasse Viren, in front of his home crowds. Steve had helped organize the series and was disappointed when Viren canceled before the races.

Steve was killed in an auto accident, inaccurately called a single-car accident. Much of the story is written about by the late, great Kenny Moore in[**Bowerman and the Men of Oregon,**](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/books/592821/bowerman-and-the-men-of-oregon-by-kenny-moore/) but I fear the true story will never be told.

In the end, Steve Prefontaine died much earlier than he should have. Many, like me, still idolize him, and I must say that, way back in 2008, one of my favorite projects was distributing a huge poster of Steve Prefontaine from NIKE (developed by Weiden & Kennedy), celebrating his life. I still have a few of them in my storage units.

I wanted to celebrate his life today. So, here, in no order, are **Six Lessons** that I have learned from the **life and times of Steve Prefontaine:**

1.   **Summer running is a great thing.**After he did not make the Oregon state meet in track and field during his sophomore year, Steve Prefontaine trained all summer furiously, coming into his junior year fit and ready to race. It is partially why RunBlogRun posts (and has since 2007) daily Summer Mileage programs for high school and junior high athletes. ![Image 2](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/iY4uJUqAQtWwtjkGlq61-3338891188.jpg)

Steve Prefontaine, during the summer of his sophomore year in high school, photo courtesy of Marshfield High School/TFN News

2.   **Consistency is the secret sauce of distance running.**During Steve’s time at Oregon, his coach was 1964 Olympic bronze medalist**Bill Dellinger,**an Oregon grad and a great coach and advisor to generations. Bill Dellinger mentioned to me, more than once, in coaches’ clinics and interviews, that one of the most incredible things about Steve Prefontaine was that Steve never missed a scheduled workout during his four years at the University of Oregon. ![Image 3](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/07/2251952a-1f29-42af-9235-4a6567ba1282-eug_041422_Prefontaine_12.webp)

Steve Prefontaine, post-workout with Coach Bill Dellinger, photo courtesy of The Eugene Register-Guard

3.   **Learn from your tough experiences.**Steve Prefontaine put so much pressure on himself at the 1972 Munich Olympics. The 5,000-meter race in Munich was one of the greatest five-thousand-meter races of all time. Lasse Viren, Mohammed Ghammoudi, Ian Stewart, and David Bedford were some of the finest distance runners in the world, and Prefontaine took them on, finishing fourth, being caught near the finish by Ian Stewart. Prefontaine was devastated. David Bedford told me a story about Steve and him having more than a few beers after the race. After that, Steve, according to his friends, changed a bit; he relaxed but stayed focused on being the best distance runner he could be. ![Image 4](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/John-Walker-Steve-Prefontaine-Rod-Dixon-by-Don-Chadez-.jpeg)

John Walker, Steve Prefontaine, Rod Dixon, racing indoors, photo by Don Chadez

4.   **Take on challenges**. **Dave Wottle**, the 1972 Olympic gold medalist at the 800 meters, told me, this past November, at the Heroes and Youth Gala on Staten Island, about racing Steve in front of HIS crowd at Hayward Field, June 20, 1973, at the **Hayward Restoration Meet.**In that race, Dave Wottle told me, again, fifty years plus late, how Steve gave Dave no quarter, no breaks, and battled him until the very end. Wottle won in 3:53.3, then ran the 3rd-fastest mile of all time. Steve finished in 3:54.6, having led most of the race, putting him, in 1973, among the fastest milers in the world! And at the time, Steve Prefontaine was known as a 5,000-meter racer! I will never forget Dave Wottle’s face as he told me the story; his respect for Steve had endured fifty-two years! ![Image 5](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2024/04/Nike-Oregon-waffle-1024x570-1.jpg)

This is a photo of the NIKE Waffle racers that Steve Prefontaine used in 1974-75. They were sold at Sotheby’s for much more than the suggested retail price, photo Sotheby’s.

5.   **Do good things.**In Tom Jordan’s classic book, a must-read, [**Pre!**,](https://www.abebooks.co.uk/book-search/title/pre/author/tom-jordan/) Tom writes about Steve spending time at an Oregon prison, where he helped prisoners develop a running program. Even after Steve’s death, prisoners continued to run, including a group that ran a marathon within the prison. Steve did not have to volunteer, but he did anyway. ![Image 6](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Kenny-and-pre.jpeg)

Kenny Moore with Steve Prefontaine, photo by Jeff Johnson, curated by Walt Chadwick

6.   **Enjoy your friends.**I have been fortunate to have grown up in a generation near **Steve Prefontaine**. Several of my friends have told me stories about having a good time with Steve after races, and his sense of humor. In the book of stories [**Best Efforts**](https://www.abebooks.com/9780915297108/Best-Efforts-Moore-Kenny-0915297108/plp), by the late Kenny Moore, 1972 Olympic gold medalist (1976 silver medalist), Steve Prefontaine is described as follows: “consider at Satyr.” Steve was a complicated 25-year-old who was a few years from his very best when he died. ![Image 7](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/Elite-Runner_Group-Photo_600.png)

Cooper Institute, 1975, photo by Cooper Institute

Top Row L-R Dr. Mike Pollock, Kenny Moore, Steve Prefontaine, Jim Crawford, Ted Casteneda, Philip Ndoo, Unidentified, Dr. Kenneth Cooper. Middle Row: Jeff Galloway, Doug Brown, Russell Pate, Perry Pittman, Gary Tuttle, Richard Pettigrew, Mike Manley. Bottom Row: Unidentified, Ron Wayne, Jim Johnson, Paul Geis, Don Kardong, Unidentified, Frank Shorter, from Frank Shorter

*   ![Image 8](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/14100376_10206212504540943_272549162852983311_n.jpg) Larry Eder has had a 52-year involvement in the sport of athletics. Larry has experienced the sport as an athlete, coach, magazine publisher, and now, journalist and blogger. His first article, on Don Bowden, America's first sub-4 minute miler, was published in RW in 1983. Larry has published several magazines on athletics, from American Athletics to the U.S. version of Spikes magazine. He currently manages the content and marketing development of the RunningNetwork, The Shoe Addicts, and RunBlogRun. Of RunBlogRun, his daily pilgrimage with the sport, Larry says: "I have to admit, I love traveling to far away meets, writing about the sport I love, and the athletes I respect, for my readers at runblogrun.com, the most of anything I have ever done, except, maybe running itself." Also does some updates for BBC Sports at key events, which he truly enjoys.

Theme song: Greg Allman, " I'm no Angel."

**Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce: The race to make Paris Olympics in one piece**

When sprinting legend Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce used her wealth of experience to pass through the baton to Sashalee Forbes while running the second leg of the 4x100m at the 2023 World Athletics Championships in Budapest, the Jamaican picked up an injury on her right leg with around 15m to go. It brought a bit of trepidation amongst her fans, who felt she had copped another long-term injury. It was later revealed she had aggravated the knee she recovered from prior to going into the world championships.

![Image 1](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2023/08/w100m-medalists-scaled-e1692721129406.jpg)

Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce, Sha’Carri Richardson, Shericka Jackson, 100m medalists, photo by Getty Images for World Athletics

Now, ahead of her last Olympic games in Paris next year, there are indications that her body will begin to get crocked up. By no means does this make her less of a legend, but rather, it’s an indication of how time eventually catches up with everyone. And Fraser-Pryce is not left out. The Jamaican sprint sensation has already etched her name in the annals of Olympic history, but as she embarks on her next major conquest, she carries not just a legacy but a dream. A dream of capturing her third individual Olympic gold in the women’s 100m, a feat that would no doubt make her the undisputed greatest female sprinter.

Yet, this quest is not without its challenges. Fraser-Pryce, who will be 37 when she competes in Paris, faces an uphill battle after a season marred by injuries. But if there’s one thing that history has taught us, it’s that you should never count out the “Pocket Rocket.”

![Image 2](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/08/Jackson-FraserPryce-R-Worlds22.jpg)

Shericka Jaskson and Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce, 200 meters, photo by Kevin Morris

Fraser-Pryce first burst onto the global scene at the 2008 Beijing Olympics when she claimed her maiden Olympic gold in the 100 meters. At just 21, she became not only the first Jamaican woman to win the event but also one of the youngest sprinters to capture Olympic gold. This victory marked the beginning of a remarkable journey that would see her ascend to the pinnacle of sprinting.

In the years that followed, Fraser-Pryce’s career was studded with accolades and records. She became the first woman to win Olympic gold in the 100m in consecutive Games, defending her title in London 2012. Her explosive starts and powerful strides left a trail of vanquished opponents and awestruck fans. Despite all her achievements, it wasn’t until 2022 that she got the full worth of what has been a glowing career, culminating in the Laureaus Award Sports Woman of the Year.

![Image 3](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/SAFP-scaled-e1683827341156.jpg)

Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce is the five time world champion at the 100 meters. photo by Weltklasse Zurich DL.

But, like every human, the prospect of wanting more will always be there. Fraser-Pryce surely will be licking her lips at the prospect of a third individual Olympic Gold in the 100m is on the horizon. The chance to etch her name alongside legendary sprinters like Usain Bolt, who had achieved the same feat, should be more than a motivation. But the road to Paris 2024 would not be a cakewalk.

In 2023, Fraser-Pryce faced a season marred by injuries. It was a stark reminder of the physical toll that sprinting takes on an athlete’s body, especially as they age. Niggling injuries and setbacks threatened to derail her campaign. The explosive power required to accelerate from the blocks and the relentless drive to maintain top-end speed to the finish line can push even the most accomplished athletes to their limits.

![Image 4](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/07/FraserPryce-ShellyAnne-FV-Worlds22.jpg)

Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce, 100 meters, World Athletics Championships

Eugene, Oregon, USA

July15-26, 2022, photo by Kevin Morris

For Fraser-Pryce, the path to Paris was beset with challenges, but it was also marked by a resolute spirit. She understood that injury setbacks were an unfortunate part of an athlete’s journey and had a history of bouncing back stronger. Her unwavering determination and her ability to defy the odds had already earned her the moniker “Mommy Rocket” after she returned to the track following the birth of her son, Zyon, in 2017.

Fraser-Pryce’s injury-laden season in 2023 was a test of her resolve. The Jamaican has only raced nine times this year. Excluding qualifiers, it boils down to five times. That’s the least number of times she has raced in a year since she started running professionally. How much her body is willing to take on leading up to Paris remains to be seen, but there is a huge possibility that she doesn’t run as much as she did leading up to the world championships in Budapest this year.

![Image 5](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/09/Shelly-Ann-Fraser-Pryce--750x536.jpg)

Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce, photo by Diamond League AG

In an era where sprinting is increasingly dominated by younger athletes, Fraser-Pryce’s quest is a testament to the enduring power of experience and the age-defying spirit of determination. At 37, she knows that Paris might be her last Olympic hurrah, and she is determined to make it count. Her body might have a different response to this mindset, but the Jamaican is more than just an athlete; she is an icon, a symbol of what the human spirit can achieve when it refuses to be bound by age or adversity.

Her journey is a beacon of inspiration, a reminder that age is just a number and that dreams can be realized at any stage of life. In her pursuit of a third Olympic Gold, Fraser-Pryce is not just chasing history; she is creating it. Either she defies age and time, or it catches up to her.

![Image 6](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/05/SAFP.jpeg)

Shelly-Ann Fraser-Pryce and the media, May 2022, photo by KIP KEINO CLASSIC

*   ![Image 7](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/userpic-147-100x100-1.png) Deji Ogeyingbo is one of Nigeria’s leading Track and Field Journalists as he has worked in various capacities as a writer, content creator, and reporter for radio and TV stations in the country and Africa. Deji has covered varying degrees of Sporting competitions within and outside Nigeria which includes, African Championships and World Junior Championships. Also, he founded one of Nigeria’s leading Sports PR and Branding company in Nikau Sports in 2020, a company that aims to change the narrative of how athletes are perceived in Nigeria while looking to grow their image to the highest possible level.

**Steve Prefontaine** died on **May 30, 1975**, coming home from a party after a track meet, where he had run a 5,000 meters. Steve had set up a small meet series in Oregon, hoping to race top Europeans, especially Lasse Viren, in front of his home crowds. Steve had helped organize the series and was disappointed when Viren canceled before the races.

Steve was killed in an auto accident, inaccurately called a single-car accident. Much of the story is written about by the late, great Kenny Moore in[**Bowerman and the Men of Oregon,**](link_0) but I fear the true story will never be told.

In the end, Steve Prefontaine died much earlier than he should have. Many, like me, still idolize him, and I must say that, way back in 2008, one of my favorite projects was distributing a huge poster of Steve Prefontaine from NIKE (developed by Weiden & Kennedy), celebrating his life. I still have a few of them in my storage units.

I wanted to celebrate his life today. So, here, in no order, are **Six Lessons** that I have learned from the **life and times of Steve Prefontaine:**

Bill Dellinger mentioned to me, more than once, in coaches’ clinics and interviews, that one of the most incredible things about Steve Prefontaine was that Steve never missed a scheduled workout during his four years at the University of Oregon. ![Image 3](link_1)

Steve Prefontaine, post-workout with Coach Bill Dellinger, photo courtesy of The Eugene Register-Guard

3.   **Learn from your tough experiences.**Steve Prefontaine put so much pressure on himself at the 1972 Munich Olympics. The 5,000-meter race in Munich was one of the greatest five-thousand-meter races of all time. Lasse Viren, Mohammed Ghammoudi, Ian Stewart, and David Bedford were some of the finest distance runners in the world, and Prefontaine took them on, finishing fourth, being caught near the finish by Ian Stewart. ### Book Description![Image 27](https://www.penguinrandomhouse.com/wp-content/themes/penguinrandomhouse/images/chevron-up.svg)

 Bowerman and the Men of Oregon

No man has affected more runners in more ways than Bill Bowerman. During his 24-year tenure as track coach at the University of Oregon, he won four national team titles and his athletes set 13 world and 22 American records. He also ignited the jogging boom, invented the waffle-sole running shoe that helped establish Nike, and coached the US track and field team at the 1972 Munich Olympic Games

With the full cooperation of the Bowerman family and Nike, plus years of taped interviews with friends, relatives, students, and competitors, two-time Olympic marathoner Kenny Moore – himself one of Bowerman’s champion athletes – brilliantly re-creates the legendary track coach’s life.

**Running News Daily** is edited by Bob Anderson and team. Send your news items to bob@mybestruns.com Advertising opportunities available.

[![Image 1](https://mybestruns.com/street/tho/03cbdf871fb9c8ad411152e92c945dfaba662c31005035ca1093e248b24f19d5.jpg?i=15441&t=1792160870)](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php#pok15441)

### [2027 Could Bring Unprecedented Heat, Raising New Concerns for Marathon Runners Worldwide](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15441)

The global running community could face a formidable challenge in [2027](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2027), as forecasts of a potentially powerful El Niño raise concerns about rising temperatures and the impact of extreme heat on marathon performances.

![Image 2](https://mybestruns.com/street/21525fef106f0f5e518948f3b7ac7c7a59c2dc7f609cbf843c1a3df2621fa9d4.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

With long-distance runners increasingly chasing personal bests on the world's biggest stages, the prospect of another exceptionally warm year has placed race-day weather firmly in the spotlight. For marathoners, even a modest rise in temperature can make the difference between a record-breaking performance and a difficult battle to reach the finish line.

![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/c649899eb4ea226a094d35c54188897ee0ecd5f22a51cbcb024dd442b8785c9e.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

At the centre of the concern is the [Pacific Ocean](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Pacific+Ocean), where developing El Niño conditions could influence global temperatures. Forecasts have raised the possibility of an unusually strong event, although its eventual intensity and the precise effects on temperatures around the world remain uncertain.

El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon characterised by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures across parts of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. It can alter weather patterns across different regions, while its warming influence can contribute to higher global temperatures. The full impact depends on the strength of the event and how it interacts with other climate factors.

![Image 4](https://mybestruns.com/street/d0a9667bdea6ce04007f6323709b90066c76c7bf750a06efd1f2fbddbd1d21b0.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

The timing is particularly important. Global temperatures have often responded strongly in the year following a major El Niño, meaning 2027 could face an increased risk of challenging heat. However, whether it ultimately surpasses the existing global temperature record will depend on evolving ocean conditions, atmospheric patterns and human-caused climate change.

![Image 5](https://mybestruns.com/street/46b631cd0e12734e6118d1811afa82002a59f6f038f8de1a680ce25c9ce4a1e2.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

For marathon runners, the implications are significant. Scientific research has repeatedly shown that warmer conditions can reduce endurance performance, increase physiological strain and make it more difficult to maintain a planned race pace over 42.195 kilometres.

An analysis of seven North American marathons illustrates how substantially conditions can influence elite performances. Researchers found that leading male runners finished approximately 1.7 per cent slower relative to course records under the coolest conditions examined. In the warmest category, that difference increased to around 4.5 per cent.

For an athlete capable of running a marathon in 2:05:00, a slowdown of that magnitude could translate into several additional minutes on the clock. At the elite level, where races are frequently decided by seconds, such a difference can determine whether a runner achieves a personal best, secures a podium finish or misses a major performance target.

The consequences can be even more noticeable among recreational athletes, who often spend considerably longer exposed to the conditions.

A separate analysis by researchers at the University of Chicago, examining approximately 4.7 million marathon finishing times, highlighted the substantial effect of temperature on runners across different ability levels. The findings suggested that the typical participant could lose roughly 19 minutes when racing in temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, compared with conditions in the 40s. In the 80s Fahrenheit, the estimated time penalty rose to approximately 33 minutes.

These figures underline why marathon preparation involves much more than mileage, speed sessions and strength training. Temperature, humidity, direct sunlight and the body's ability to regulate heat can all influence how effectively a runner sustains an effort over the full distance.

Many marathon performances are achieved in cool conditions, with temperatures of approximately 4°C to 10°C often considered favourable for endurance running. As temperatures climb beyond that range, the body must devote more resources to cooling itself, potentially increasing cardiovascular strain and making a previously comfortable pace harder to maintain.

However, there is no universal temperature at which every marathon runner begins to slow down. Individual fitness, acclimatisation, humidity, wind, course exposure and race strategy all influence performance. A cool, overcast morning can produce very different outcomes from a sunny, humid day, even when the thermometer shows similar readings.
