### [Cancer Survivor Brandon Throop Returns To Toronto Marathon In Hospital Gown For Third World Record Bid](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15440)

For [Brandon Throop](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Brandon+Throop), running a marathon in a hospital gown is about far more than chasing a place in the [Guinness World Records](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Guinness+World+Records). It is a deeply personal tribute to the medical team that helped save his life, a celebration of survival, and an opportunity to give back to the institution that stood beside him during one of the darkest chapters of his life.

![Image 8](https://mybestruns.com/street/f29108f8a11d11c189a98e7ad107e25370003868a0c2a06a0f60240f82ca748e.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

In 2022, Throop was 35 years old, a father of two, and facing a life-changing diagnosis of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. His journey soon led him to [Princess Margaret Cancer Centre](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Princess+Margaret+Cancer+Centre) in Toronto, Canada, where he underwent chemotherapy and began a difficult battle against the disease.

![Image 9](https://mybestruns.com/street/544aaad28b469831ffc670d6b1f0afed09ba7cece4e33f54484abd893edf14de.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

The treatment that helped him fight cancer also left him physically weakened. For someone who had spent much of his life running, even the simplest movements became unexpectedly challenging. After completing treatment, climbing a single flight of stairs could leave him coughing and struggling to catch his breath.

However, rather than allowing the experience to define the limits of his future, Throop began rebuilding his strength one small step at a time. He started by running once around his neighbourhood block before gradually increasing the distance as his body recovered. What began as a modest attempt to regain his fitness eventually developed into an extraordinary mission with a purpose extending far beyond the finish line.

![Image 10](https://mybestruns.com/street/609ed787d02e0efaf2f9b8e1f2b60b1718ea68e0b9bbf56ffa21a91b509d4949.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

Now, more than three years after becoming cancer-free, Throop is preparing to return to the [TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=TCS+Toronto+Waterfront+Marathon) on Sunday, October 18, 2026, for another attempt at the Guinness World Record for the fastest marathon completed while wearing a hospital gown.

This will be his third attempt to claim the record, following two determined performances in previous editions of the Toronto race. In 2023, he completed the marathon in 2:55:59 before returning in 2024 to improve his time to 2:55:01. Despite his progress, the record remained just out of reach.

The current benchmark stands at 2:50:12, established by Evan Ubene at the same Toronto Waterfront Marathon in 2022. To make history this time, Throop will need to improve significantly on his previous performances and take more than five minutes off his best hospital-gown marathon.

Yet the significance of Sunday's race cannot be measured by finishing time alone.

Throop's larger objective is to raise funds for the Princess Margaret Cancer Foundation, supporting the cancer research and care that played such an important role in his own recovery. He has already raised more than $137,000 toward his $150,000 fundraising target, bringing him within reach of a goal that could help support further advances in cancer treatment.

Every kilometre he covers in the distinctive hospital gown carries a message of gratitude to the people who cared for him and hope for patients whose journeys are only beginning. His challenge transforms a gruelling 42.195-kilometre race into a public expression of appreciation for the doctors, nurses, researchers and other healthcare professionals working to improve the lives of people affected by cancer.

The timing of this year's marathon makes the occasion even more meaningful. The race falls just days from the anniversary of his first chemotherapy session in 2022, bringing him back to a period that profoundly changed his life. Returning to the streets of Toronto now, healthy enough to pursue another marathon, offers a powerful reminder of how far he has travelled since those difficult days.

For Throop, choosing Toronto has never been simply about finding the fastest course on which to break a record. Although other marathons might offer different racing conditions, the Toronto Waterfront Marathon holds a significance that no alternative venue could easily replace. The course takes him past Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, the institution where he received treatment, while family members and friends who supported him throughout his illness are there to witness his journey.

It is a route that connects his past to his present: the hospital where he fought for his health, the streets where he now tests his endurance, and the people who helped him keep moving forward when the road ahead was uncertain.

What began as a modest race through Central Park, with a handful of determined runners and a budget of just $1,000, has evolved into one of the most prestigious and sought-after marathons in the world. More than five decades later, the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) tells a remarkable story of how distance running has grown from a grassroots sporting event into a global spectacle.

![Image 29](https://mybestruns.com/street/bacec4114b3d54670c15a184e950b0e7ddb43de9849a87f97fe568b1a68fdecf.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

When the inaugural New York City Marathon took place in 1970, the entry fee was just $1. Organised by the New York Road Runners, the race was held entirely within Central Park, far removed from the enormous crowds, international attention and commercial scale that define the event today.

![Image 30](https://mybestruns.com/street/cb333999ed07e06d10edcf37e5452882364cbb7336ebf8347871bb079ae7bfbf.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

Of the 127 registered participants, only 55 completed the race. Yet, despite its modest beginnings, the event laid the foundation for a marathon that would eventually capture the imagination of runners from every corner of the world.

The first champion was Gary Muhrcke, a New York City firefighter whose victory remains one of the most memorable stories from the race's early years. According to accounts of the inaugural edition, Muhrcke had finished a night shift before entering the competition shortly before the start. He went on to win in approximately 2:31, securing his place in the marathon's history.

The inaugural race also featured Nina Kuscsik, the only woman in the field. She started the event but withdrew after becoming ill, meaning no woman finished that first edition. Kuscsik would later become an important figure in the campaign for women's inclusion in competitive distance running.

Over the years, the New York City Marathon expanded beyond Central Park, eventually developing into the iconic five-borough journey that takes runners through Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Manhattan. Its transformation helped turn the race into a celebration of athletic achievement, community spirit and the extraordinary diversity of New York City.

Today, the marathon attracts elite athletes chasing victories and records, recreational runners pursuing personal milestones, charity participants raising funds for important causes, and thousands of international visitors eager to experience one of running's most celebrated events.

### [Five Years On, Agnes Tirop’s Light Still Shines in the World of Athletics](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15428)

Five years after the tragic death of [Agnes Jebet Tirop](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Agnes+Jebet+Tirop), the Kenyan distance-running star remains a powerful symbol of sporting excellence, unfulfilled potential and the urgent fight against gender-based violence.

![Image 74](https://mybestruns.com/street/5ffa31af8295f395e0aff49642712e51130387366364addc2bf2c316bd3b7edc.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

On [October 13](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=October+13), [2021](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2021), the athletics world was plunged into mourning following the death of Tirop, who was found at her home in Iten, Kenya, at just 25 years old. Her life was cut short at a time when her career was flourishing, leaving behind a legacy that continues to resonate with athletes, fans and the wider community.

For Kenya, a country whose identity is deeply intertwined with distance-running success, Tirop represented a remarkable generation of female athletes taking the sport to new heights. Her achievements on the track, across country and on the roads had already secured her place among the country's outstanding distance runners.

![Image 75](https://mybestruns.com/street/f77fa5828a0aeb325862244b31913486d927b332f71bf5f757228761f9169abf.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

Five years later, the sadness of her loss remains inseparable from the extraordinary story of what she accomplished in her short but memorable career.

A Champion Who Rose to the Top at 19

Tirop announced herself on the global stage in spectacular fashion at the 2015 World Athletics Cross Country Championships in Guiyang, China. At only 19, she won the senior women's race, becoming the youngest champion in the event since Zola Budd in 1985.

Her victory demonstrated not only her natural ability but also the composure and determination that would become defining features of her running career.

She subsequently established herself among the world's leading track athletes, winning bronze medals in the women's 10,000 metres at the 2017 World Athletics Championships in London and the 2019 edition in Doha.

Those back-to-back podium finishes confirmed her consistency at the highest level and underlined her ability to compete against the strongest distance runners in the world.

Tirop also demonstrated considerable versatility at the Tokyo 2020 Olympic Games, held in 2021, where she finished fourth in the women's 5,000 metres. Although she narrowly missed the podium, her performance reinforced her reputation as one of Kenya's most accomplished emerging distance-running talents.

A World Record That Made History

Just weeks before her death, Tirop delivered one of the defining performances of her career.

![Image 76](https://mybestruns.com/street/c78d43c7e9431cc77d4c0c7a69212a2bb6f64a57b712e93e9359780084f1438e.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

On September 12, 2021, she clocked an astonishing 30:01 to win the women's 10km road race at the adizero Road to Records event in Herzogenaurach, Germany.

Her performance broke the then women's-only world record by 28 seconds, establishing a new benchmark for the distance. The record was subsequently ratified by World Athletics. It was aremarkable achievement that placed her name among the legends of distance running. Although her record has since been broken, the greatness of her achievement remains untouched, and no change in the record books can diminish the extraordinary talent, courage and determination she displayed that day. Time may bring new champions and faster performances, but it can never erase the mark she left on athletics.

In a race that demanded patience, tactical awareness and an exceptional finishing effort, Tirop broke away from compatriot Sheila Chepkirui during the closing stages and powered towards the finish line.

The performance was a remarkable demonstration of her endurance and competitive instinct. It also offered a glimpse of what might have followed had she been given more years to develop her career.

Her final competitive appearance came on October 3, 2021, when she finished second in a 10km race in Geneva, Switzerland. Ten days later, the world learned of her death.

The timing made the tragedy particularly difficult to comprehend: an athlete who had just rewritten the record books and was still competing at the highest level was suddenly gone.

![Image 77](https://mybestruns.com/street/96776c2a38ffe92e203c98190e24001e4c1d47d376c5bd46c7feef1ad83b81ce.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

A Tragedy That Reached Far Beyond Sport

Tirop's death was not simply the loss of an elite athlete. It also brought renewed international attention to violence against women and the need to create safer environments in which women and girls can live, train and pursue their ambitions.

Her story became a painful reminder that medals, records and international recognition cannot shield someone from violence in their private life.

In the years since her death, her name has continued to feature in efforts to promote women's empowerment, athlete welfare and the prevention of gender-based violence. Initiatives associated with her legacy, including Agnes Tirop Angels, reflect the continuing determination to transform grief into meaningful action.

Her story remains especially significant within athletics, where the pursuit of excellence must go hand in hand with respect for athletes' safety, dignity and wellbeing.

Five Years Later, Her Legacy Endures

For young runners who dream of representing Kenya on the international stage, Tirop's career remains an example of what dedication, talent and courage can achieve.

She rose from a promising young athlete to a world champion, a two-time World Championships medallist and a world-record holder. She excelled across different distances and surfaces, leaving an impressive body of achievements before reaching her 26th birthday.

Yet her legacy cannot be measured by statistics alone. It also lies in the conversations her death continues to inspire, the women whose safety must be protected and the determination to ensure that sporting success is never separated from human dignity.

Five years on, Agnes Tirop is remembered not only for the records she set or the medals she won, but also for the future that was taken from her.

Her achievements remain part of Kenya's rich athletics history, while her story continues to call for a world in which women can pursue their dreams without fear of violence.

Agnes Tirop's life was tragically short, but her impact reaches far beyond the finish line. Her achievements will remain in the record books, her memory will endure in the hearts of athletics fans, and her legacy will continue to inspire generations to come.

### [Getting Into a World Marathon Major May Be Harder Than Running One](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15404)

For many marathoners, crossing the finish line of a World Marathon Major is the ultimate dream. But before you can worry about surviving 42.195 kilometres, there is another challenge: actually getting onto the starting line.

![Image 184](https://mybestruns.com/street/5d4dc1de5763b06ea3b94d885ebb3beb7a42c46fdce18c4925b726d66d79e60b.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

The six [Abbott World Marathon Majors](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Abbott+World+Marathon+Majors) — [Boston](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Boston), [London](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=London), [Berlin](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Berlin), [Chicago](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Chicago), [New York](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York) and [Tokyo](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Tokyo) — do not use the same entry system, and some are considerably more difficult to access than others.

Boston is arguably the clearest example of how running fast does not always guarantee a place. Unlike the other majors, the Boston Marathon is built around qualifying standards. However, meeting the published standard only gives a runner the opportunity to apply. Because demand is so high, the fastest qualifiers are accepted first. This means a runner can achieve the official qualifying time and still miss out when the cut-off moves faster than expected.

![Image 185](https://mybestruns.com/street/f43cbba0c0a711c3a231a45db4e08fb49d7ffb83dc86bd3092f391b075c9c8ca.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

London presents a completely different challenge. Its famous ballot is a random draw, making luck a major part of the process. However, runners have other avenues, including Good for Age, charity places and international tour operators. Even the Good for Age route can be highly competitive, with places allocated according to performance when demand exceeds the number of available spots.

New York City is another race where demand is enormous. The TCS New York City Marathon offers a general drawing alongside several guaranteed-entry routes, including qualifying times, charity places, international tour operators and other eligibility programmes. For serious runners, achieving the appropriate qualifying standard can be one of the most dependable ways to secure a place.

Chicago gives runners several ways to avoid relying entirely on the lottery. The Bank of America Chicago Marathon has a non-guaranteed drawing, but runners can also gain guaranteed entry through qualifying times, charity, tour operators and other eligible routes. For fast runners, meeting the published standard can provide a much more certain path to the start line.

Berlin is also heavily sought after. The BMW Berlin Marathon uses a lottery for the majority of runners, while qualifying performances can provide another route into the race. With its fast course and reputation for producing world-class times, demand remains enormous every year.

Tokyo adds another layer of difficulty, particularly for international runners. The race has a lottery as well as several other entry routes, including charity and performance-based options. International runners can also use official tour operators, although these packages generally cost more because they are tied to travel arrangements.

For runners chasing the Six Star Medal, the biggest lesson is simple: do not depend on the lottery alone.

Look closely at every possible route. Good-for-age standards, qualifying performances, charity programmes and official tour operators can all provide alternatives when the ballot does not go your way.

And then there is the reality every marathoner eventually discovers: sometimes getting rejected from a major marathon hurts almost as much as the race itself.

When that rejection email arrives, remember that parkrun is still free, happens every Saturday and does not require a lottery.

So, which World Marathon Major have you already completed — and which one is still at the top of your bucket list?

### [Three Years On, Kelvin Kiptum’s Historic Chicago Masterpiece Still Echoes](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15401)

Three years ago today, [Kelvin Kiptum](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Kelvin+Kiptum) delivered a marathon performance that changed the sport forever.

![Image 193](https://mybestruns.com/street/5035b48bdb0f1f56076db2ee6bffafca777ba460aff5bca001f387749cbd66d4.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

On October 8, 2023, the 23-year-old Kenyan arrived at the [Bank of America Chicago Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Bank+of+America+Chicago+Marathon) as one of the most exciting young talents in distance running. By the finish, he had rewritten the history books with a breathtaking world record of 2:00:35.

Kiptum improved Eliud Kipchoge’s previous world record by 34 seconds, becoming the first athlete in history to officially break the 2:01 barrier in a record-eligible marathon.

![Image 194](https://mybestruns.com/street/eacc796a55e9a32d214d97a136a77187518c7b402af8cfcb4c3cf4cf85977904.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

But the most remarkable aspect of the performance was not simply the finishing time. It was the way Kiptum produced it.

He reached halfway in 1:00:48, before covering the second half in an astonishing 59:47. Rather than struggling as the race entered its final stages, Kiptum accelerated, producing a negative split at a pace that seemed almost impossible to sustain.

![Image 195](https://mybestruns.com/street/225136d87ffb781fe257f7cb7053c718e7664bc764aea955ed3c0f70f7a2305f.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

His final kilometres became a masterclass in marathon racing. With every stride, the young Kenyan moved further away from the field and closer to sporting immortality.

And remarkably, Chicago was only his third marathon.

Kiptum had announced himself on the global stage by winning the 2022 Valencia Marathon in 2:01:53, before lowering the course record at the 2023 London Marathon with 2:01:25. Seven months later, he produced something even more extraordinary in Chicago.

At just 23, Kiptum had already established himself among the very best marathoners in the world.

His Chicago triumph was more than another victory. It was a glimpse of what appeared to be an extraordinary future — a future in which Kiptum seemed destined to push the limits of the marathon even further.

Tragically, that future would never unfold.

On February 11, 2024, just four months after his historic Chicago victory, Kiptum died in a road accident in Kenya alongside his Rwandan coach, Gervais Hakizimana. He was only 24 years old.

The loss sent shockwaves through the athletics world.

Today, three years after that unforgettable October morning in Chicago, 2:00:35 remains far more than a number on a record list.

It represents the extraordinary talent of a young athlete who appeared to be only at the beginning of his journey. It represents courage, ambition and a fearless approach to the marathon. And, perhaps most poignantly, it represents a chapter of greatness that ended far too soon.

Kelvin Kiptum gave the world one of the greatest marathon performances ever witnessed.

Three years later, the memory of that incredible morning remains alive.

Gone far too soon, but never forgotten.

The change is more than a simple adjustment to the racing calendar. Early October, once synonymous with crisp autumn temperatures in Minnesota, has increasingly brought challenging heat. In recent years, organisers have had to contend with conditions that can place additional stress on marathon runners and increase demands on medical and public-safety teams.

![Image 233](https://mybestruns.com/street/12413240599ee9c1859b7b3b7f7fa683f7e05a7c9997d36e865c0052b7fa2888.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

The inaugural Twin Cities Marathon was held on October 3, 1982, attracting 4,563 entrants. What began as a relatively young marathon has since developed into one of the most recognisable road races in the United States, growing alongside the running communities of Minneapolis and St. Paul.

The course itself has long been one of the event's defining features. Runners travel through Minneapolis, pass the city's famous chain of lakes and follow a scenic route toward St. Paul before finishing near the Minnesota State Capitol. The combination of major urban landmarks, parkways, waterways and autumn scenery has helped give the race its distinctive identity.

The 2026 edition continued that long tradition, with roughly 30,000 runners taking part across the various events of Marathon Weekend. The marathon also featured defending champions Will Norris and Jane Bareikis, while favourable temperatures provided runners with much more comfortable conditions than some of the warmer editions in recent years.

Yet even with favourable weather this year, the decision to move the race reflects a longer-term concern. Organisers are looking beyond a single race morning and considering how changing weather patterns could affect the event in the years ahead.

For runners, the move could eventually become one of the most important changes in the marathon's modern history. A later October date offers the possibility of cooler racing conditions while preserving the course, the atmosphere and the traditions that have made Twin Cities Marathon a fixture on the American running calendar.

For more than four decades, the first Sunday of October provided a familiar date for thousands of runners preparing to take on the Twin Cities course.

That tradition has now reached its final chapter.

From 2027, the Twin Cities Marathon will arrive later in the fall — opening a new era for a race whose history remains firmly connected to the streets of Minneapolis and St. Paul.

### [7 Packing Tips for Your First Time Traveling For a Race](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15391)

Traveling for a race is the perfect excuse to turn a running weekend into an adventure. Perhaps you’re heading to the [Tokyo Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/TokyoMarathon?b=prz&details=Y)⁠ and already thinking about the sushi and ramen you’ll enjoy afterward. Or maybe your next finish line is beside the beach.

Between training, booking a hotel and planning what to explore, packing can become an afterthought. Then race morning arrives, and your favorite socks are still at home, your race information is buried in your suitcase and your water bottle is nowhere to be found.

A little organization before departure can make the entire trip smoother. These seven packing tips will help you arrive ready to run and enjoy the weekend.

1. Pack Your Race-Day Outfit in Your Carry-On

Keep your race-day clothing and essentials in your carry-on. Pack your running top, shorts or tights, socks, sports bra if needed, and the small items you depend on during a race. If your checked luggage is delayed, your key gear will still be with you.

![Image 240](https://mybestruns.com/street/5c6a74501acac9b0ede92d94316cdfa0b4cdf306eb1a8ff130a06ab99f4b0028.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

Fold your race outfit together or place it in a packing pouch so everything is easy to find. A smaller zip pouch can hold accessories. Knowing exactly where your race kit is means one less thing to worry about when you arrive.

2. Wear Your Running Shoes on the Plane

Your running shoes deserve the same attention as your race outfit. Wearing them on the plane keeps them out of checked luggage and leaves more room in your suitcase.

Choose a familiar pair you have already used in training. Race weekend is not the time to discover that new shoes rub or fit differently than expected. If you prefer to travel in another pair, keep your race shoes in your carry-on.

![Image 241](https://mybestruns.com/street/e69995b49a9f8387df3a425267e0e7bfdd5cf1fd3f9dcf4c2ee037e9c24fb131.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

3. Bring a Spacious Bag for Your Gear

A race trip often requires more than running clothes. Add a jacket, recovery clothes, snacks and accessories, and your packing list grows quickly. A spacious duffel with sturdy handles and useful pockets can keep those extras organized and serve as a day bag at your destination.

Think about what you’ll do beyond race day. A hike may call for trail shoes and a light layer. If pickleball is part of your plans, you may want a paddle and extra clothes.

The same thinking applies when choosing your bag. If you’re planning a few games on the court during the trip, consider [pickleball tour and duffel bags](https://pickleballnation.com/collections/pickleball-bags-and-backpacks)⁠. A backpack may be more practical for hiking or exploring on foot. Choose a bag that suits your itinerary, and check your airline’s size and weight limits before packing.

4. Organize Your Bib and Race Documents

Keep your identification, registration confirmation and race instructions together. A slim document pouch works well for paper copies, while a dedicated folder on your phone can keep digital information easy to access.

Download important details before leaving home, including the race map, confirmation email and packet pickup instructions. Save copies you can open without an internet connection.

If you already have your bib, keep it flat and protected. Otherwise, check where and when you need to collect it and what identification the organizer requires. Handling these details in advance helps keep the pre-race scramble to a minimum.

5. Take Familiar Snacks with You

Race travel can disrupt your usual eating routine. Your preferred breakfast may be unavailable, and the hotel buffet may not offer what you normally eat before a run.

Bring the bars, gels and electrolyte products you have already used in training. Your [runner’s diet](https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/runners-diet)⁠ shouldn’t become a vacation guessing game.

Count what you’ll need for travel and race day, then pack a little extra. Keep some familiar snacks in your carry-on and bring enough race fuel for your planned strategy. Check destination rules before carrying food across international borders.

6. Always Have a Water Bottle

Busy travel days can make it easy to forget your usual drinking habits. A reusable water bottle is a simple item that deserves a place on your packing list.

Carry it empty through airport security, then fill it where drinking water is available. Keep it handy during your journey and when heading out for packet pickup or other race activities.

Staying hydrated is also part of [caring for your body while traveling](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php/7021)⁠. If an electrolyte mix is already part of your routine, pack your usual product. Having familiar supplies nearby makes it easier to maintain your normal habits while traveling.

7. Pack Layers for Changing Weather

A mild forecast doesn’t always reflect how it will feel while waiting at the starting line early in the morning. Pack a lightweight layer you have already worn while running.

A zip jacket or long-sleeve top can help you stay comfortable before the start. Decide in advance whether you’ll carry it during the race or leave it at an official bag check, following the organizer’s instructions.

For colder conditions, familiar gloves and other tested gear can help. Review this guide to [running in cold weather](https://mybestruns.com/What_to_Wear_for_Running_in_Cold_Weather.html)⁠, then check the forecast again before departure and once more before race morning so you can make any final adjustments.

Thoughtful packing helps you get more out of a destination race. Keep essential gear close, choose a bag that works for your plans and organize your documents before you leave. With those details handled, you can spend less time searching through your suitcase and more time enjoying the run—and everything that comes afterward.

### [2027 Could Bring Unprecedented Heat, Raising New Concerns for Marathon Runners Worldwide](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15441)

The global running community could face a formidable challenge in [2027](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2027), as forecasts of a potentially powerful El Niño raise concerns about rising temperatures and the impact of extreme heat on marathon performances.

![Image 2](https://mybestruns.com/street/21525fef106f0f5e518948f3b7ac7c7a59c2dc7f609cbf843c1a3df2621fa9d4.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

With long-distance runners increasingly chasing personal bests on the world's biggest stages, the prospect of another exceptionally warm year has placed race-day weather firmly in the spotlight. For marathoners, even a modest rise in temperature can make the difference between a record-breaking performance and a difficult battle to reach the finish line.

![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/c649899eb4ea226a094d35c54188897ee0ecd5f22a51cbcb024dd442b8785c9e.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

At the centre of the concern is the [Pacific Ocean](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Pacific+Ocean), where developing El Niño conditions could influence global temperatures. Forecasts have raised the possibility of an unusually strong event, although its eventual intensity and the precise effects on temperatures around the world remain uncertain.

El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon characterised by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures across parts of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. It can alter weather patterns across different regions, while its warming influence can contribute to higher global temperatures. The full impact depends on the strength of the event and how it interacts with other climate factors.

![Image 4](https://mybestruns.com/street/d0a9667bdea6ce04007f6323709b90066c76c7bf750a06efd1f2fbddbd1d21b0.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

The timing is particularly important. Global temperatures have often responded strongly in the year following a major El Niño, meaning 2027 could face an increased risk of challenging heat. However, whether it ultimately surpasses the existing global temperature record will depend on evolving ocean conditions, atmospheric patterns and human-caused climate change.

![Image 5](https://mybestruns.com/street/46b631cd0e12734e6118d1811afa82002a59f6f038f8de1a680ce25c9ce4a1e2.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

For marathon runners, the implications are significant. Scientific research has repeatedly shown that warmer conditions can reduce endurance performance, increase physiological strain and make it more difficult to maintain a planned race pace over 42.195 kilometres.

An analysis of seven North American marathons illustrates how substantially conditions can influence elite performances. Researchers found that leading male runners finished approximately 1.7 per cent slower relative to course records under the coolest conditions examined. In the warmest category, that difference increased to around 4.5 per cent.

For an athlete capable of running a marathon in 2:05:00, a slowdown of that magnitude could translate into several additional minutes on the clock. At the elite level, where races are frequently decided by seconds, such a difference can determine whether a runner achieves a personal best, secures a podium finish or misses a major performance target.

The consequences can be even more noticeable among recreational athletes, who often spend considerably longer exposed to the conditions.

A separate analysis by researchers at the University of Chicago, examining approximately 4.7 million marathon finishing times, highlighted the substantial effect of temperature on runners across different ability levels. The findings suggested that the typical participant could lose roughly 19 minutes when racing in temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, compared with conditions in the 40s. In the 80s Fahrenheit, the estimated time penalty rose to approximately 33 minutes.

These figures underline why marathon preparation involves much more than mileage, speed sessions and strength training. Temperature, humidity, direct sunlight and the body's ability to regulate heat can all influence how effectively a runner sustains an effort over the full distance.

Many marathon performances are achieved in cool conditions, with temperatures of approximately 4°C to 10°C often considered favourable for endurance running. As temperatures climb beyond that range, the body must devote more resources to cooling itself, potentially increasing cardiovascular strain and making a previously comfortable pace harder to maintain.

However, there is no universal temperature at which every marathon runner begins to slow down. Individual fitness, acclimatisation, humidity, wind, course exposure and race strategy all influence performance. A cool, overcast morning can produce very different outcomes from a sunny, humid day, even when the thermometer shows similar readings.

### [Cancer Survivor Brandon Throop Returns To Toronto Marathon In Hospital Gown For Third World Record Bid](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15440)

For [Brandon Throop](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Brandon+Throop), running a marathon in a hospital gown is about far more than chasing a place in the [Guinness World Records](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Guinness+World+Records). It is a deeply personal tribute to the medical team that helped save his life, a celebration of survival, and an opportunity to give back to the institution that stood beside him during one of the darkest chapters of his life.

![Image 8](https://mybestruns.com/street/f29108f8a11d11c189a98e7ad107e25370003868a0c2a06a0f60240f82ca748e.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

In 2022, Throop was 35 years old, a father of two, and facing a life-changing diagnosis of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. His journey soon led him to [Princess Margaret Cancer Centre](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Princess+Margaret+Cancer+Centre) in Toronto, Canada, where he underwent chemotherapy and began a difficult battle against the disease.

![Image 9](https://mybestruns.com/street/544aaad28b469831ffc670d6b1f0afed09ba7cece4e33f54484abd893edf14de.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

The treatment that helped him fight cancer also left him physically weakened. For someone who had spent much of his life running, even the simplest movements became unexpectedly challenging. After completing treatment, climbing a single flight of stairs could leave him coughing and struggling to catch his breath.

However, rather than allowing the experience to define the limits of his future, Throop began rebuilding his strength one small step at a time. He started by running once around his neighbourhood block before gradually increasing the distance as his body recovered. What began as a modest attempt to regain his fitness eventually developed into an extraordinary mission with a purpose extending far beyond the finish line.

![Image 10](https://mybestruns.com/street/609ed787d02e0efaf2f9b8e1f2b60b1718ea68e0b9bbf56ffa21a91b509d4949.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

Now, more than three years after becoming cancer-free, Throop is preparing to return to the [TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=TCS+Toronto+Waterfront+Marathon) on Sunday, October 18, 2026, for another attempt at the Guinness World Record for the fastest marathon completed while wearing a hospital gown.

This will be his third attempt to claim the record, following two determined performances in previous editions of the Toronto race. In 2023, he completed the marathon in 2:55:59 before returning in 2024 to improve his time to 2:55:01. Despite his progress, the record remained just out of reach.

The current benchmark stands at 2:50:12, established by Evan Ubene at the same Toronto Waterfront Marathon in 2022. To make history this time, Throop will need to improve significantly on his previous performances and take more than five minutes off his best hospital-gown marathon.

Yet the significance of Sunday's race cannot be measured by finishing time alone.

Throop's larger objective is to raise funds for the Princess Margaret Cancer Foundation, supporting the cancer research and care that played such an important role in his own recovery. He has already raised more than $137,000 toward his $150,000 fundraising target, bringing him within reach of a goal that could help support further advances in cancer treatment.

Every kilometre he covers in the distinctive hospital gown carries a message of gratitude to the people who cared for him and hope for patients whose journeys are only beginning. His challenge transforms a gruelling 42.195-kilometre race into a public expression of appreciation for the doctors, nurses, researchers and other healthcare professionals working to improve the lives of people affected by cancer.

The timing of this year's marathon makes the occasion even more meaningful. The race falls just days from the anniversary of his first chemotherapy session in 2022, bringing him back to a period that profoundly changed his life. Returning to the streets of Toronto now, healthy enough to pursue another marathon, offers a powerful reminder of how far he has travelled since those difficult days.

For Throop, choosing Toronto has never been simply about finding the fastest course on which to break a record. Although other marathons might offer different racing conditions, the Toronto Waterfront Marathon holds a significance that no alternative venue could easily replace. The course takes him past Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, the institution where he received treatment, while family members and friends who supported him throughout his illness are there to witness his journey.

It is a route that connects his past to his present: the hospital where he fought for his health, the streets where he now tests his endurance, and the people who helped him keep moving forward when the road ahead was uncertain.

His hospital gown is therefore much more than an unusual racing outfit. It is a symbol of the vulnerability he experienced as a patient, the strength he rediscovered through running, and his determination to turn a deeply personal struggle into something that benefits others.

As he prepares for his third record attempt, the challenge remains considerable. The existing mark of 2:50:12 demands an average pace of approximately four minutes per kilometre, a formidable task even without the physical discomfort and practical challenges of racing in a hospital gown.

Nevertheless, Throop has already demonstrated that his mission can make a difference regardless of the result on the clock. His previous attempts brought attention to cancer care, while his ongoing fundraising efforts have generated substantial support for the foundation that represents an important part of his personal story.

On Sunday, he will once again take his place among thousands of runners, carrying a message that reaches well beyond the marathon course. Whether he finally breaks the world record or falls short for a third time, his presence will stand as a reminder that recovery can open doors to remarkable achievements and that gratitude can become a powerful force for helping others.

For Brandon Throop, the finish line represents more than a sporting ambition. It is an opportunity to honour the people who helped him survive, support the research that may give other families more time together, and show what can be possible after a life-altering diagnosis.

The record is still waiting. But with more than $137,000 already raised toward his fundraising goal, Throop has another reason to consider his mission a success before the starting gun even sounds.

On the streets of Toronto, the hospital gown is returning with a purpose: to celebrate survival, give back to the people who helped save a life, and turn every step into hope for someone else.

### [2027 Could Bring Unprecedented Heat, Raising New Concerns for Marathon Runners Worldwide](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15441)

The global running community could face a formidable challenge in [2027](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2027), as forecasts of a potentially powerful El Niño raise concerns about rising temperatures and the impact of extreme heat on marathon performances.

![Image 2](https://mybestruns.com/street/21525fef106f0f5e518948f3b7ac7c7a59c2dc7f609cbf843c1a3df2621fa9d4.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

With long-distance runners increasingly chasing personal bests on the world's biggest stages, the prospect of another exceptionally warm year has placed race-day weather firmly in the spotlight. For marathoners, even a modest rise in temperature can make the difference between a record-breaking performance and a difficult battle to reach the finish line.

![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/c649899eb4ea226a094d35c54188897ee0ecd5f22a51cbcb024dd442b8785c9e.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

At the centre of the concern is the [Pacific Ocean](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Pacific+Ocean), where developing El Niño conditions could influence global temperatures. Forecasts have raised the possibility of an unusually strong event, although its eventual intensity and the precise effects on temperatures around the world remain uncertain.

El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon characterised by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures across parts of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. It can alter weather patterns across different regions, while its warming influence can contribute to higher global temperatures. The full impact depends on the strength of the event and how it interacts with other climate factors.

![Image 4](https://mybestruns.com/street/d0a9667bdea6ce04007f6323709b90066c76c7bf750a06efd1f2fbddbd1d21b0.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

The timing is particularly important. Global temperatures have often responded strongly in the year following a major El Niño, meaning 2027 could face an increased risk of challenging heat. However, whether it ultimately surpasses the existing global temperature record will depend on evolving ocean conditions, atmospheric patterns and human-caused climate change.

![Image 5](https://mybestruns.com/street/46b631cd0e12734e6118d1811afa82002a59f6f038f8de1a680ce25c9ce4a1e2.jpg?i=1792160870&t=1792160870)

For marathon runners, the implications are significant. Scientific research has repeatedly shown that warmer conditions can reduce endurance performance, increase physiological strain and make it more difficult to maintain a planned race pace over 42.195 kilometres.

An analysis of seven North American marathons illustrates how substantially conditions can influence elite performances. Researchers found that leading male runners finished approximately 1.7 per cent slower relative to course records under the coolest conditions examined. In the warmest category, that difference increased to around 4.5 per cent.

For an athlete capable of running a marathon in 2:05:00, a slowdown of that magnitude could translate into several additional minutes on the clock. At the elite level, where races are frequently decided by seconds, such a difference can determine whether a runner achieves a personal best, secures a podium finish or misses a major performance target.

The consequences can be even more noticeable among recreational athletes, who often spend considerably longer exposed to the conditions.

A separate analysis by researchers at the University of Chicago, examining approximately 4.7 million marathon finishing times, highlighted the substantial effect of temperature on runners across different ability levels. The findings suggested that the typical participant could lose roughly 19 minutes when racing in temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, compared with conditions in the 40s. In the 80s Fahrenheit, the estimated time penalty rose to approximately 33 minutes.

These figures underline why marathon preparation involves much more than mileage, speed sessions and strength training. Temperature, humidity, direct sunlight and the body's ability to regulate heat can all influence how effectively a runner sustains an effort over the full distance.

Many marathon performances are achieved in cool conditions, with temperatures of approximately 4°C to 10°C often considered favourable for endurance running. As temperatures climb beyond that range, the body must devote more resources to cooling itself, potentially increasing cardiovascular strain and making a previously comfortable pace harder to maintain.

However, there is no universal temperature at which every marathon runner begins to slow down. Individual fitness, acclimatisation, humidity, wind, course exposure and race strategy all influence performance. A cool, overcast morning can produce very different outcomes from a sunny, humid day, even when the thermometer shows similar readings.

In 2022, Throop was 35 years old, a father of two, and facing a life-changing diagnosis of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. His journey soon led him to [Princess Margaret Cancer Centre](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Princess+Margaret+Cancer+Centre) in Toronto, Canada, where he underwent chemotherapy and began a difficult battle against the disease.

This will be his third attempt to claim the record, following two determined performances in previous editions of the Toronto race. In 2023, he completed the marathon in 2:55:59 before returning in 2024 to improve his time to 2:55:01. Despite his progress, the record remained just out of reach.

Throop's larger objective is to raise funds for the Princess Margaret Cancer Foundation, supporting the cancer research and care that played such an important role in his own recovery. The timing of this year's marathon makes the occasion even more meaningful. The race falls just days from the anniversary of his first chemotherapy session in 2022, bringing him back to a period that profoundly changed his life. Returning to the streets of Toronto now, healthy enough to pursue another marathon, offers a powerful reminder of how far he has travelled since those difficult days.

For Throop, choosing Toronto has never been simply about finding the fastest course on which to break a record. Although other marathons might offer different racing conditions, the Toronto Waterfront Marathon holds a significance that no alternative venue could easily replace. The course takes him past Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, the institution where he received treatment, while family members and friends who supported him throughout his illness are there to witness his journey.

It is a route that connects his past to his present: the hospital where he fought for his health, the streets where he now tests his endurance, and the people who helped him keep moving forward when the road ahead was uncertain.

His hospital gown is therefore much more than an unusual racing outfit. It is a symbol of the vulnerability he experienced as a patient, the strength he rediscovered through running, and his determination to turn a deeply personal struggle into something that benefits others.

As he prepares for his third record attempt, the challenge remains considerable. The existing mark of 2:50:12 demands an average pace of approximately four minutes per kilometre, a formidable task even without the physical discomfort and practical challenges of racing in a hospital gown.

Nevertheless, Throop has already demonstrated that his mission can make a difference regardless of the result on the clock. His previous attempts brought attention to cancer care, while his ongoing fundraising efforts have generated substantial support for the foundation that represents an important part of his personal story.

On Sunday, he will once again take his place among thousands of runners, carrying a message that reaches well beyond the marathon course. Whether he finally breaks the world record or falls short for a third time, his presence will stand as a reminder that recovery can open doors to remarkable achievements and that gratitude can become a powerful force for helping others.

For Brandon Throop, the finish line represents more than a sporting ambition. It is an opportunity to honour the people who helped him survive, support the research that may give other families more time together, and show what can be possible after a life-altering diagnosis.

The record is still waiting. But with more than $137,000 already raised toward his fundraising goal, Throop has another reason to consider his mission a success before the starting gun even sounds.

On the streets of Toronto, the hospital gown is returning with a purpose: to celebrate survival, give back to the people who helped save a life, and turn every step into hope for someone else.

_I wrote this piece on Abby Steiner and her Twitter comments about social media interest on her salary and such. This is how I saw it:_

The word began to hit the social media airwaves this weekend.

Last Friday, July 1, when it was announced that Abby Steiner had given up her college eligibility to pursue a

career as a professional athlete, the social media monster started rising.

On Monday, July 4, 2022, I posted a tweet congratulating Abby Steiner on going pro and signing with PUMA Running. I also quoted that reports were that she was getting $ 2 million a year, but that no brand would corroborate such a figure.

The response was quick. Abby Steiner, the NCAA and USATF 200m champ, wrote a thoughtful response to the social media furor:

“I have been subjected to a few different social media narratives this year. Just because I don’t speak on it does not mean that I do not see it. I work very hard on my mental health with the sport of track & field and am proud of the progress that I have made. However, people who have tried to leak my deal and my contract with my sponsor have been some of the most invasive and bothersome narratives that I have seen.

As a reporter, it is your job to fact-check. As a consumer of social media and news, it is also your job to fact-check. It is common knowledge that contracts are not public. My income is not on public record, and nor should it be reported as such. Any reporter should know this, and reporting this is extremely harmful, in a time period of life that is already stressful.

Please keep in mind that athletes are human. We are worth more than attempts to get social media likes. A simple DM to me could have prevented false narratives in our social media community. As reporters, former athletes, and coaches, who should understand the pressures that athletes face, I urge you to be mindful of this for the next athlete.”

Abby Steiner (link to original:[https://twitter.com/abbysteiner1/status/1544334260437483520/photo/1](https://twitter.com/abbysteiner1/status/1544334260437483520/photo/1)

Abby Steiner has a point. In my 45 years in the sport, I have never seen a running brand confirm a salary with an athlete. They have told me when salary comments are way too high (often), but never will confirm a figure.

Abby Steiner is new to this. She has had the accolades and poor comments as an NCAA athlete, and now, she may have to deal with them as a professional athlete.

I hope not. Social media can be a good thing, but it also is a chance to be terribly negative in an anonymous fashion.

Good luck Abby Steiner, and congrats on the contract with PUMA. You are right, your salary is private.

Abby Steiner holds PBs of 10.90 for the 100 meters and 21.77, which she set while winning the USATF Title on June 26, 2022.

*   ![Image 1](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2022/06/14100376_10206212504540943_272549162852983311_n.jpg) Larry Eder has had a 52-year involvement in the sport of athletics. Larry has experienced the sport as an athlete, coach, magazine publisher, and now, journalist and blogger. His first article, on Don Bowden, America's first sub-4 minute miler, was published in RW in 1983. Larry has published several magazines on athletics, from American Athletics to the U.S. version of Spikes magazine. He currently manages the content and marketing development of the RunningNetwork, The Shoe Addicts, and RunBlogRun. Of RunBlogRun, his daily pilgrimage with the sport, Larry says: "I have to admit, I love traveling to far away meets, writing about the sport I love, and the athletes I respect, for my readers at runblogrun.com, the most of anything I have ever done, except, maybe running itself." Also does some updates for BBC Sports at key events, which he truly enjoys.

Theme song: Greg Allman, " I'm no Angel."

_I wrote this piece on Abby Steiner and her Twitter comments about social media interest on her salary and such. This is how I saw it:_

The word began to hit the social media airwaves this weekend.

Last Friday, July 1, when it was announced that Abby Steiner had given up her college eligibility to pursue a

career as a professional athlete, the social media monster started rising.

On Monday, July 4, 2022, I posted a tweet congratulating Abby Steiner on going pro and signing with PUMA Running. I also quoted that reports were that she was getting $ 2 million a year, but that no brand would corroborate such a figure.

The response was quick. Abby Steiner, the NCAA and USATF 200m champ, wrote a thoughtful response to the social media furor:

“I have been subjected to a few different social media narratives this year. Just because I don’t speak on it does not mean that I do not see it. I work very hard on my mental health with the sport of track & field and am proud of the progress that I have made. However, people who have tried to leak my deal and my contract with my sponsor have been some of the most invasive and bothersome narratives that I have seen.

As a reporter, it is your job to fact-check. As a consumer of social media and news, it is also your job to fact-check. It is common knowledge that contracts are not public. My income is not on public record, and nor should it be reported as such. Any reporter should know this, and reporting this is extremely harmful, in a time period of life that is already stressful.

Please keep in mind that athletes are human. We are worth more than attempts to get social media likes. A simple DM to me could have prevented false narratives in our social media community. As reporters, former athletes, and coaches, who should understand the pressures that athletes face, I urge you to be mindful of this for the next athlete.”

Abby Steiner (link to original:[https://twitter.com/abbysteiner1/status/1544334260437483520/photo/1](https://twitter.com/abbysteiner1/status/1544334260437483520/photo/1)

Abby Steiner has a point. In my 45 years in the sport, I have never seen a running brand confirm a salary with an athlete. They have told me when salary comments are way too high (often), but never will confirm a figure.

Abby Steiner is new to this. She has had the accolades and poor comments as an NCAA athlete, and now, she may have to deal with them as a professional athlete.

I hope not. Social media can be a good thing, but it also is a chance to be terribly negative in an anonymous fashion.

Good luck Abby Steiner, and congrats on the contract with PUMA. You are right, your salary is private.

**Editor’s note:**_I have to admit that the European Indoors are one of my favorite events on the calendar. Speaking with the fans, athletes, coaches, and European media is a big part of it. The track’s proximity and visiting Europe are two other factors. The meets tend to be in mid-sized cities, and travel is cheaper than going to Eugene, Oregon, or one of the big US marathons. I encourage you to check Valencia out!_

![Image 9](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/04/Mujinga-Kambundji-60m--scaled.jpg)

Mujinga Kambundji, European Athletics Indoors, Apeldoorn 2025, photo by European Athletics

**Timetable for Valencia 2027**

VALENCIA (ESP): **The timetable for the 2027 European Indoor Championships in Valencia from 4-7 March** has been finalized. The championships begin at 5.15pm CET on Thursday (4) with a session of heats and qualifying, including women’s triple jump qualifying, expected to feature reigning champion and home favorite Ana Peleteiro-Compaore.

![Image 10](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/10/Valencia-2027-.jpg)

Valencia 2027, the European Athletics, Indoor Championships, art by European Athletics

Friday will feature the women’s 60 m hurdles final, and Saturday will feature the men’s 60 m final and the mixed 4×400 m. The program concludes on Sunday (7) evening with 10 finals, culminating in the men’s 60m hurdles final at 9.10pm.

![Image 11](https://www.runblogrun.com/wp-content/uploads/2025/03/Mens-60-meters-scaled.jpg)

Men’s 60-meter final, Apeldoorn2025 European Indoors, photo by European Athletics

**Timetable for Valencia 2027**

VALENCIA (ESP): **The timetable for the 2027 European Indoor Championships in Valencia from 4-7 March** has been finalized. The championships begin at 5.15pm CET on Thursday (4) with a session of heats and qualifying, including women’s triple jump qualifying, expected to feature reigning champion and home favorite Ana Peleteiro-Compaore.

### Deji Ogeyingbo

Deji Ogeyingbo is one of Nigeria’s leading Track and Field Journalists as he has worked in various capacities as a writer, content creator, and reporter for radio and TV stations in the country and Africa. Deji has covered varying degrees of Sporting competitions within and outside Nigeria which includes, African Championships and World Junior Championships. Paperback. Condition: Fair. The story of America's greatest running legend. For five years, no American runner could beat him at any distance over a mile. But at the age of 24, with his best years still ahead, long-distance runner Steve Prefontaine finally lost. Driving alone at night after a party, Prefontaine crashed his sports car, putting a tragic, shocking end to the life and career of one of the most influential, accomplished runners of our time. More than 20 years later, Pre continues to influence the running world. From his humble origins in Coos Bay, Oregon, Pre became the first person to win four NCAA titles in one event. Since the last newsletter, I can share how that one-mile time trial went at the Bakline x Trial of Miles meet in Jersey City. I unfortunately did not achieve my goal of breaking five minutes. However, I’m super thankful for the opportunity to experience a legitimate race for the first time in seven months and walking away with a four-second personal best. I ran 5:09.87 but really tried to give myself the best chance to get under my goal through 1,000 meters and then it got tough. Still have some work to do. I’m trusting the training and hopefully giving it another go soon.

Also, it felt great to get back behind the mic for some commentary and play-by-play for the first time in SIX years. Shout-out to my friend Ryan Welsh for an awesome debut. [You can re-watch the entire meet on Youtube (if you go to the 1:02:36 mark our best call was definitely the women’s B heat of the 5,000m](https://youtu.be/RYmjNLptdYA)).

Here’s a highlight video from the meet, including my shortcomings :( :

[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dSKTAUbLnkk)

I’m in Chicago from Oct. 18 to Nov. 18 so if anyone knows of any opportunities to race in the area, let your boy know!

PS: [If you like the “Future is Female Coaches” shirt from Bakline that I’m rocking. You can get it here and use code CITIUS for 15% off](https://www.bakline.nyc/collections/running/graphic_future-is-female).

Onto this week’s latest news from the running world...

Somehow, there’s a global championship taking place in 2020 as international stars descend upon Gdynia, Poland for Saturday’s World Half Marathon Championships. To my understanding, a lot of the CITIUS MAG readers are based in the United States and Canada so unfortunately there won’t be any local athletes to root for since their respective governing bodies have decided not to send teams due to concerns with the coronavirus. There are still some incredible matchups to watch for.

**MEN’S RACE:** Since the last newsletter, Uganda’s Joshua Cheptegei added another world record to his resume by clocking a 26:11:02 for 10,000 meters in Valencia, Spain. He’s three for three with wins and world records in his three races of the year. Can he go four for four? That will be hard. The half marathon world record is 58:01 by Geoffrey Kamworor from Copenhagen last September. Kamworor is the reigning three-time champion but will not race on Saturday as he continues to recover from an injury sustained when he got hit by a motorcyclist in June. Cheptegei has never raced a half marathon. The longest race I was able to find on his athletic profile was a 10-miler in 45:15 from Zaandam, the Netherlands in Sept. 2018. There’s no denying whatever Cheptegei runs will be fast and he’s certainly the favorite.

We can pinpoint his toughest competition to three men. Kenya’s Kibiwott Kandie is the fastest man on paper with his 58:38 personal best from the Prague Half in September. That time puts him at No. 6 on the all-time list behind Kamworor, Abraham Kiptum (later busted for doping), Zersenay Tadese, Sammy Wanjiru and Jemal Yimer. The Kenyan championship streak could rest on his shoulders or Bernard Ngeno, who ran 59:07 for second place at the 2019 Valencia Half.

Cheptegei’s compatriot Jacob Kiplimo is just 19 years old but has electrified the track circuit with a 12:48 for 5,000 meters and 7:26 for 3,000 meters earlier this summer. The lone half marathon on his record is a 61:53 in Kampala in November 2019.

Ethiopia has five men entered with sub-60 personal bests so keep an eye out on their contingent led by Andamlak Belihu and his 59:10 personal best.

_Prediction: No one is beating Joshua Cheptegei in 2020_

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4MIN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4e075165-85ea-45af-a636-429615e10fc1_600x374.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4MIN!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4e075165-85ea-45af-a636-429615e10fc1_600x374.gif)
**WOMEN’S RACE:** Remember how hyped up the world was for the clash between Kipchoge and Bekele only to get let down when Bekele pulled out of the race? Let’s bring some of that excitement to a showdown between two world record holders and a title defense by Netsanet Gudeta.

In one corner, we have Kenya’s Peres Jepchirchir. She set the women’s-only half marathon world record of 65:35 in Prague in September and recently had it ratified by World Athletics. Jepchirchir has proven that she can win at the championship stage with her world half marathon title from 2016.

In the other corner, we’ve got Ethiopia’s Ababel Yeshaneh. She is one of only six women to have run faster than Jepchirchir with her 64:31 at the Ras Al Khaimah Half in February. It’s her lone race of the year and she beat marathon world record holder/London Marathon champion Brigid Kosgei by 18 seconds.

Because of how fast the women’s half marathon has been in recent years, Joyciline Jepkosgei has been bumped down to No. 3 on the all-time list and hasn’t run a half marathon since the NYC Half in March 2019. The last time many of us heard of her was when she won the 2019 New York City Marathon in 2:22:38 in a Central Park sprint against Mary Keitany. Just don’t be surprised if she’s in the mix for the win and tries to improve upon her world half marathon championships silver medal from two years ago.

For those wondering where’s Sifan Hassan after her one-hour record and after she ran 29:36.67 for a European Record in the 10,000 meters in Hengelo last week: Hassan scratched from the race saying that she has opted “to give myself some rest and focus for next year.”

_Prediction: I’m going with Peres Jepchirchir for the win over Ababel Yeshaneh simply due to the recency of their standout performances and her experience on the championship stage._

So how can you watch it? The races will be broadcast live on The Olympic Channel from 5:00 a.m. to 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time.[Catch me on Twitter](http://twitter.com/ChrisChavez) at that time with a few live updates.

Mark your calendars! The [NCAA has announced](http://on.ncaa.com/NCAAHost) the following locations for upcoming NCAA Division I Cross Country Championships: 2022 in Stillwater, OK hosted by Oklahoma State; 2023 in Charlottesville, VA hosted by Virginia; 2024 in Madison, WI hosted by Wisconsin 2025 in Columbia, MO hosted by Mizzou. A reminder that the 2020 NCAA Division I Cross Country Championships will be contested on March 15, 2021 in Stillwater and the 2021 NCAA Division I Cross Country Championships remain on schedule for next November in Tallahassee, Florida. It’s going to make for awkward anniversaries later on for those respective champions.

If you enjoy college track then plan on many more visits to Hayward Field with the Ducks slated to host the 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 NCAA Championships. Austin, Texas will host in 2023 after doing a good job in 2019.

[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sGGo!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff6ac4240-022c-4d9c-ba7a-265aaff2ed3a_2048x1151.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sGGo!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff6ac4240-022c-4d9c-ba7a-265aaff2ed3a_2048x1151.jpeg)
I’ve always said to friends of mine that Ekiden races should be more popular in the United States. For those unfamiliar with the ekiden, it’s a multi-person and multi-distance relay race. There’s no set distance or set number or team members. Each runner hands off a sash called the Tasuki.

Last year, I ran the Tokyo Marathon and then paid a visit to Hakone. That’s the site of the finish for one of Japan’s biggest ekiden. They have a museum that has all the sashes, uniforms and race highlights from past races. From watching old videos (and I recommend doing this on YouTube) you can see the hype is real when they mention that more people turn out and watch the Hakone Ekiden than people watch the Super Bowl in the United States. Thrilled to see what comes next as Hansons-Brooks Original Distance Project [announced the MICHIGAN PRO EKIDEN](https://www.instagram.com/p/CGAeYRVndbk/) will take place on Oct. 21.

Our own Jesse Squire will be on hand to cover the race. The teams committed include the Atlanta Track Club, the Hansons-Brooks Original Distance Project, Rots Running, Bowerman Track Club, Team Boulder, Minnesota Distance Elite and Northern Arizona Elite.

I’ve also been told by people to watch the “Run With The Wind” anime series to get even more excited for this so I’ve got some time to do that.

David Melly [wrote a short post on his experience competing in the Izumo Ekiden](https://citiusmag.com/bringing-ekiden-racing-to-america/) as a member of the Ivy League team. He said, “I’ve never seen anything like it.”

Kudos again to Josh Cox and Ben Rosario for their efforts to put together another star-studded marathon to the United States before the year is up. The Marathon Project, which I mentioned in the last newsletter, will now also include Sara Hall – fresh off that 2:22:01 second-place finish at the London Marathon. Hall just loves racing and this shouldn’t come as much of a surprise to us. [I wrote about her for](https://www.si.com/edge/2019/08/06/sara-hall-berlin-new-york-city-marathon-double-2019)_[Sports Illustrated](https://www.si.com/edge/2019/08/06/sara-hall-berlin-new-york-city-marathon-double-2019)_ last year on why she chooses to double up on marathons in such a short time span.

Cam Levins, who told the media that he was in great shape before the London Marathon but ultimately dropped out due to the cold conditions, will chase the Olympic standard to try and get a spot on Canada’s team for Tokyo.

Fan favorites Beverly Ramos, Diane Nukuri, Noah Droddy and Alexi Pappas have also been added to the fields. You can find the [women’s accepted entries](https://themarathonproject.com/accepted-entries-women/) and [men’s accepted entries here](https://t.co/wjWBrC5dqs).

[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fbLT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F91240049-cbf1-40d5-bcb5-de2462c158ad_1080x607.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fbLT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F91240049-cbf1-40d5-bcb5-de2462c158ad_1080x607.jpeg)
The CITIUS MAG Podcast Network is pleased to bring on Emma Zimmerman and the [Social Sport Podcast](https://www.instagram.com/socialsportpod/) to our lineup of shows.

In the past couple of months, the show popped onto my radar and I’ve listened to several episodes. I was impressed with Emma’s careful research and care into amplifying and telling the stories of these people with strong passions for social change across all endurance sports. I know a lot of people who follow CITIUS MAG do so for our running coverage but I think there’s a place for these conversations with our audience, especially since it’s been made clear that there’s no line between sports and activism in 2020. Athletes know and embrace that sports are their stage to call for change that they want to see in the world. I think this podcast does a great job of addressing the issues and possible solutions with notable people.

For runners looking to get into the show, you’ll have several episodes featuring [Amir M. Figueroa](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-8-amir-m-figueroa-on-harlem-run-public-health/id1505320511?i=1000474228816) of Harlem Run in New York City, [Jacqueline Alnes, Ph.D.](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-11-jacqueline-alnes-mind-being-tinyart-on-elevating/id1505320511?i=1000477165922) (whose TinyArt drawings are an Instagram hit), [Alison Wade of the Fast Women](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-17-alison-wade-fast-women-newsletter-on-running/id1505320511?i=1000480120675) newsletter, [Kamilah Journet](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-18-kamilah-journ%C3%A9t-powerful-voice-for-anti/id1505320511?i=1000481775957) (now the Tracksmith Marketing Manager), and [Therese Haiss](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-25-therese-haiss-on-authentic-conversation/id1505320511?i=1000487658240) (former professional runner and now coach) to go back and listen to. Those are just some of the runners featured but [the whole archive of episodes is great](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/social-sport/id1505320511).

[In the most recent episode](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/social-sport-podcast-running-to-protest-movement-nyc-running-community/), Emma catches up with Coffey ([a guest on the Runners of NYC Podcast in May](http://citiusmag.com/runners-of-nyc-podcast-coffey/)) about his work in starting the [Running to Protest movement in New York City](https://www.instagram.com/runningtoprotest/). I’ve personally attended three of the protest runs and it’s moving to see 700+ people shut down the Brooklyn Bridge and call for justice regarding the murder of Breonna Taylor or listening to first-hand accounts of mistreatment with police in the city. I come on in the second half of the show to share some of my observations and thoughts about the power protesting has through running.

[Subscribe to Social Sport now.](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/social-sport/id1505320511) | [Follow Social Sport on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/socialsportpod/).

[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!O4il!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff1cdd916-f5eb-40a5-b11d-9804139800ec_2059x2059.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!O4il!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff1cdd916-f5eb-40a5-b11d-9804139800ec_2059x2059.jpeg)
In recent editions of this newsletter, I’ve provided a few updates on the efforts to save the University of Minnesota’s men’s track and field team from being cut. The decision was left to a vote by members of the Board of Regents last week. The proposal to eliminate men's indoor track and field, men's tennis and men's gymnastics teams at the end of the 2020-21 school year [was passed on a 7-5 vote](https://www.si.com/olympics/2020/10/09/minnesota-indoor-track-and-field-gymnastics-tennis-eliminated-board-of-regents-vote-results). Men’s outdoor track and field was kept after a revised proposal was submitted on Friday and approved. It was still a very heavy day for members of the Gopher community because this puts them in a very weird spot. [I decided to chat with Obsa Ali](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast-obsa-ali-save-minnesota-track/), the 2018 NCAA steeplechase champion, about his feelings regarding the decision, what challenges this presents for recruiting and the women’s team as well as what happens next.

You can catch the latest episode of the [podcast on iTunes so subscribe and leave a five-star review](https://itunes.apple.com/us/podcast/id1204506559). We are also on [Stitcher,](https://www.stitcher.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast)[Google Play](https://play.google.com/music/listen?u=0#/ps/Iadq5oufkygxq6jwxblxx5ljhlq) and [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/70eINNmXl67VqorbTsMOaH?si=ikhzVGlDQ_igRjaOBykDFA)!

[Full show notes and quotes can be found here.](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast-obsa-ali-save-minnesota-track/)

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!CaSg!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7f46b9ec-a0cd-4cda-9a0c-b5e4ffd67072_723x723.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!CaSg!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7f46b9ec-a0cd-4cda-9a0c-b5e4ffd67072_723x723.jpeg)
– On Runners of NYC, [Leigh Anne Sharek and I spoke with Lenny Grullon](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/runners-of-nyc-podcast-lenny-grullon-boogie-down-bronx/). He is one of the founders of the [Boogie Down Bronx Runners](https://www.instagram.com/boogiedownbronxrunners/). If you’ve ever run the New York City Marathon, there’s a part when you cross into the Bronx and you’re greeted with some super loud cheers from a running crew decked out in black and white. That’s his group and it wasn’t always that loud on that part of the course. When Lenny decided to start the group, no one showed up for the first run. However, he kept at it and wanted to get the Bronx community active and it’s paid off. [Listen to his whole story here](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/runners-of-nyc-podcast-lenny-grullon-boogie-down-bronx/).

– [Just wanted to give a quick shout-out to Joshua and Aaron Potts for having me on Two Black Runners](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/ep-27-chris-chavez-how-to-chase-your-dreams-sports/id1486031415?i=1000494598108). If you’re not familiar with their show, they’ve brought on some pretty high-profile guests from the pro running circuit on their podcast over the past six months. They bring the type of energy to the sport that you’d get from watching ESPN analysts debate over NFL and NBA performances. We discussed some of the 2020 track season but also the lack of diversity in the track and field media landscape. Love what these guys are doing and I’m looking forward to sharing the mixed zone with them at the 2021 U.S. Olympic Trials.

That’s all from me this week. If you enjoyed this edition of CITIUS MAG and think your friend would too, forward it to them encourage them to subscribe. Let me know if you have any comments, feedback or thoughts on anything discussed.

Enjoy your weekend!

It’s going to make for awkward anniversaries later on for those respective champions.

If you enjoy college track then plan on many more visits to Hayward Field with the Ducks slated to host the 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 NCAA Championships. Austin, Texas will host in 2023 after doing a good job in 2019.

I’ve always said to friends of mine that Ekiden races should be more popular in the United States. For those unfamiliar with the ekiden, it’s a multi-person and multi-distance relay race. There’s no set distance or set number or team members. Each runner hands off a sash called the Tasuki.
