Thrilled to see what comes next as Hansons-Brooks Original Distance Project [announced the MICHIGAN PRO EKIDEN](https://www.instagram.com/p/CGAeYRVndbk/) will take place on Oct. 21.
Our own Jesse Squire will be on hand to cover the race. The teams committed include the Atlanta Track Club, the Hansons-Brooks Original Distance Project, Rots Running, Bowerman Track Club, Team Boulder, Minnesota Distance Elite and Northern Arizona Elite.
I’ve also been told by people to watch the “Run With The Wind” anime series to get even more excited for this so I’ve got some time to do that.
David Melly [wrote a short post on his experience competing in the Izumo Ekiden](https://citiusmag.com/bringing-ekiden-racing-to-america/) as a member of the Ivy League team. He said, “I’ve never seen anything like it.”
Kudos again to Josh Cox and Ben Rosario for their efforts to put together another star-studded marathon to the United States before the year is up. Hall just loves racing and this shouldn’t come as much of a surprise to us. [I wrote about her for](https://www.si.com/edge/2019/08/06/sara-hall-berlin-new-york-city-marathon-double-2019)_[Sports Illustrated](https://www.si.com/edge/2019/08/06/sara-hall-berlin-new-york-city-marathon-double-2019)_ last year on why she chooses to double up on marathons in such a short time span.

Cam Levins, who told the media that he was in great shape before the London Marathon but ultimately dropped out due to the cold conditions, will chase the Olympic standard to try and get a spot on Canada’s team for Tokyo.
Fan favorites Beverly Ramos, Diane Nukuri, Noah Droddy and Alexi Pappas have also been added to the fields. You can find the [women’s accepted entries](https://themarathonproject.com/accepted-entries-women/) and [men’s accepted entries here](https://t.co/wjWBrC5dqs).
[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fbLT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F91240049-cbf1-40d5-bcb5-de2462c158ad_1080x607.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fbLT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F91240049-cbf1-40d5-bcb5-de2462c158ad_1080x607.jpeg)  
The CITIUS MAG Podcast Network is pleased to bring on Emma Zimmerman and the [Social Sport Podcast](https://www.instagram.com/socialsportpod/) to our lineup of shows.

In the past couple of months, the show popped onto my radar and I’ve listened to several episodes. I was impressed with Emma’s careful research and care into amplifying and telling the stories of these people with strong passions for social change across all endurance sports. I know a lot of people who follow CITIUS MAG do so for our running coverage but I think there’s a place for these conversations with our audience, especially since it’s been made clear that there’s no line between sports and activism in 2020. Athletes know and embrace that sports are their stage to call for change that they want to see in the world. I think this podcast does a great job of addressing the issues and possible solutions with notable people.

For runners looking to get into the show, you’ll have several episodes featuring [Amir M. Figueroa](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-8-amir-m-figueroa-on-harlem-run-public-health/id1505320511?i=1000474228816) of Harlem Run in New York City, [Jacqueline Alnes, Ph.D.](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-11-jacqueline-alnes-mind-being-tinyart-on-elevating/id1505320511?i=1000477165922) (whose TinyArt drawings are an Instagram hit), [Alison Wade of the Fast Women](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-17-alison-wade-fast-women-newsletter-on-running/id1505320511?i=1000480120675) newsletter, [Kamilah Journet](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-18-kamilah-journ%C3%A9t-powerful-voice-for-anti/id1505320511?i=1000481775957) (now the Tracksmith Marketing Manager), and [Therese Haiss](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-25-therese-haiss-on-authentic-conversation/id1505320511?i=1000487658240) (former professional runner and now coach) to go back and listen to. Those are just some of the runners featured but [the whole archive of episodes is great](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/social-sport/id1505320511).

[In the most recent episode](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/social-sport-podcast-running-to-protest-movement-nyc-running-community/), Emma catches up with Coffey ([a guest on the Runners of NYC Podcast in May](http://citiusmag.com/runners-of-nyc-podcast-coffey/)) about his work in starting the [Running to Protest movement in New York City](https://www.instagram.com/runningtoprotest/). I’ve personally attended three of the protest runs and it’s moving to see 700+ people shut down the Brooklyn Bridge and call for justice regarding the murder of Breonna Taylor or listening to first-hand accounts of mistreatment with police in the city. I come on in the second half of the show to share some of my observations and thoughts about the power protesting has through running.
[Subscribe to Social Sport now.](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/social-sport/id1505320511) | [Follow Social Sport on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/socialsportpod/).
[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!O4il!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff1cdd916-f5eb-40a5-b11d-9804139800ec_2059x2059.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!O4il!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff1cdd916-f5eb-40a5-b11d-9804139800ec_2059x2059.jpeg)

In recent editions of this newsletter, I’ve provided a few updates on the efforts to save the University of Minnesota’s men’s track and field team from being cut. The decision was left to a vote by members of the Board of Regents last week. The proposal to eliminate men's indoor track and field, men's tennis and men's gymnastics teams at the end of the 2020-21 school year [was passed on a 7-5 vote](https://www.si.com/olympics/2020/10/09/minnesota-indoor-track-and-field-gymnastics-tennis-eliminated-board-of-regents-vote-results). Men’s outdoor track and field was kept after a revised proposal was submitted on Friday and approved. It was still a very heavy day for members of the Gopher community because this puts them in a very weird spot. [I decided to chat with Obsa Ali](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast-obsa-ali-save-minnesota-track/), the 2018 NCAA steeplechase champion, about his feelings regarding the decision, what challenges this presents for recruiting and the women’s team as well as what happens next.
You can catch the latest episode of the [podcast on iTunes so subscribe and leave a five-star review](https://itunes.apple.com/us/podcast/id1204506559). We are also on [Stitcher,](https://www.stitcher.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast)[Google Play](https://play.google.com/music/listen?u=0#/ps/Iadq5oufkygxq6jwxblxx5ljhlq) and [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/70eINNmXl67VqorbTsMOaH?si=ikhzVGlDQ_igRjaOBykDFA)!
[Full show notes and quotes can be found here.](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast-obsa-ali-save-minnesota-track/)

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!CaSg!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7f46b9ec-a0cd-4cda-9a0c-b5e4ffd67072_723x723.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!CaSg!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7f46b9ec-a0cd-4cda-9a0c-b5e4ffd67072_723x723.jpeg)  
– On Runners of NYC, [Leigh Anne Sharek and I spoke with Lenny Grullon](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/runners-of-nyc-podcast-lenny-grullon-boogie-down-bronx/). He is one of the founders of the [Boogie Down Bronx Runners](https://www.instagram.com/boogiedownbronxrunners/). If you’ve ever run the New York City Marathon, there’s a part when you cross into the Bronx and you’re greeted with some super loud cheers from a running crew decked out in black and white. That’s his group and it wasn’t always that loud on that part of the course. When Lenny decided to start the group, no one showed up for the first run. However, he kept at it and wanted to get the Bronx community active and it’s paid off. [Listen to his whole story here](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/runners-of-nyc-podcast-lenny-grullon-boogie-down-bronx/).

– [Just wanted to give a quick shout-out to Joshua and Aaron Potts for having me on Two Black Runners](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/ep-27-chris-chavez-how-to-chase-your-dreams-sports/id1486031415?i=1000494598108). If you’re not familiar with their show, they’ve brought on some pretty high-profile guests from the pro running circuit on their podcast over the past six months. They bring the type of energy to the sport that you’d get from watching ESPN analysts debate over NFL and NBA performances. We discussed some of the 2020 track season but also the lack of diversity in the track and field media landscape. Love what these guys are doing and I’m looking forward to sharing the mixed zone with them at the 2021 U.S. Olympic Trials.
That’s all from me this week. If you enjoyed this edition of CITIUS MAG and think your friend would too, forward it to them encourage them to subscribe. Let me know if you have any comments, feedback or thoughts on anything discussed.
Enjoy your weekend!

Apologies for not sending out an edition of the newsletter last week. I was a bit tied up working on a project for _Sports Illustrated_ that required a bit more time than anticipated.
Since the last newsletter, I can share how that one-mile time trial went at the Bakline x Trial of Miles meet in Jersey City. I unfortunately did not achieve my goal of breaking five minutes. However, I’m super thankful for the opportunity to experience a legitimate race for the first time in seven months and walking away with a four-second personal best. I ran 5:09.87 but really tried to give myself the best chance to get under my goal through 1,000 meters and then it got tough. Still have some work to do. I’m trusting the training and hopefully giving it another go soon.

Also, it felt great to get back behind the mic for some commentary and play-by-play for the first time in SIX years. Shout-out to my friend Ryan Welsh for an awesome debut. [You can re-watch the entire meet on Youtube (if you go to the 1:02:36 mark our best call was definitely the women’s B heat of the 5,000m](https://youtu.be/RYmjNLptdYA)).
Here’s a highlight video from the meet, including my shortcomings :( :
[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dSKTAUbLnkk)
I’m in Chicago from Oct. 18 to Nov. 18 so if anyone knows of any opportunities to race in the area, let your boy know!
PS: [If you like the “Future is Female Coaches” shirt from Bakline that I’m rocking. You can get it here and use code CITIUS for 15% off](https://www.bakline.nyc/collections/running/graphic_future-is-female).
Onto this week’s latest news from the running world...
Somehow, there’s a global championship taking place in 2020 as international stars descend upon Gdynia, Poland for Saturday’s World Half Marathon Championships. To my understanding, a lot of the CITIUS MAG readers are based in the United States and Canada so unfortunately there won’t be any local athletes to root for since their respective governing bodies have decided not to send teams due to concerns with the coronavirus. There are still some incredible matchups to watch for.

**MEN’S RACE:** Since the last newsletter, Uganda’s Joshua Cheptegei added another world record to his resume by clocking a 26:11:02 for 10,000 meters in Valencia, Spain. He’s three for three with wins and world records in his three races of the year. Can he go four for four? That will be hard. The half marathon world record is 58:01 by Geoffrey Kamworor from Copenhagen last September. Kamworor is the reigning three-time champion but will not race on Saturday as he continues to recover from an injury sustained when he got hit by a motorcyclist in June. Cheptegei has never raced a half marathon. The longest race I was able to find on his athletic profile was a 10-miler in 45:15 from Zaandam, the Netherlands in Sept. 2018. There’s no denying whatever Cheptegei runs will be fast and he’s certainly the favorite.
We can pinpoint his toughest competition to three men. Kenya’s Kibiwott Kandie is the fastest man on paper with his 58:38 personal best from the Prague Half in September. That time puts him at No. 6 on the all-time list behind Kamworor, Abraham Kiptum (later busted for doping), Zersenay Tadese, Sammy Wanjiru and Jemal Yimer. The Kenyan championship streak could rest on his shoulders or Bernard Ngeno, who ran 59:07 for second place at the 2019 Valencia Half.
Cheptegei’s compatriot Jacob Kiplimo is just 19 years old but has electrified the track circuit with a 12:48 for 5,000 meters and 7:26 for 3,000 meters earlier this summer. The lone half marathon on his record is a 61:53 in Kampala in November 2019.
Ethiopia has five men entered with sub-60 personal bests so keep an eye out on their contingent led by Andamlak Belihu and his 59:10 personal best.
_Prediction: No one is beating Joshua Cheptegei in 2020_

**WOMEN’S RACE:** Remember how hyped up the world was for the clash between Kipchoge and Bekele only to get let down when Bekele pulled out of the race? Let’s bring some of that excitement to a showdown between two world record holders and a title defense by Netsanet Gudeta.
In one corner, we have Kenya’s Peres Jepchirchir. She set the women’s-only half marathon world record of 65:35 in Prague in September and recently had it ratified by World Athletics. Jepchirchir has proven that she can win at the championship stage with her world half marathon title from 2016.
In the other corner, we’ve got Ethiopia’s Ababel Yeshaneh. She is one of only six women to have run faster than Jepchirchir with her 64:31 at the Ras Al Khaimah Half in February. It’s her lone race of the year and she beat marathon world record holder/London Marathon champion Brigid Kosgei by 18 seconds.

Because of how fast the women’s half marathon has been in recent years, Joyciline Jepkosgei has been bumped down to No. 3 on the all-time list and hasn’t run a half marathon since the NYC Half in March 2019. The last time many of us heard of her was when she won the 2019 New York City Marathon in 2:22:38 in a Central Park sprint against Mary Keitany. Just don’t be surprised if she’s in the mix for the win and tries to improve upon her world half marathon championships silver medal from two years ago.
For those wondering where’s Sifan Hassan after her one-hour record and after she ran 29:36.67 for a European Record in the 10,000 meters in Hengelo last week: Hassan scratched from the race saying that she has opted “to give myself some rest and focus for next year.”
_Prediction: I’m going with Peres Jepchirchir for the win over Ababel Yeshaneh simply due to the recency of their standout performances and her experience on the championship stage._
So how can you watch it? The races will be broadcast live on The Olympic Channel from 5:00 a.m. to 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time.[Catch me on Twitter](http://twitter.com/ChrisChavez) at that time with a few live updates.
Mark your calendars! It’s going to make for awkward anniversaries later on for those respective champions.

If you enjoy college track then plan on many more visits to Hayward Field with the Ducks slated to host the 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 NCAA Championships. Austin, Texas will host in 2023 after doing a good job in 2019.

I’ve personally attended three of the protest runs and it’s moving to see 700+ people shut down the Brooklyn Bridge and call for justice regarding the murder of Breonna Taylor or listening to first-hand accounts of mistreatment with police in the city. I come on in the second half of the show to share some of my observations and thoughts about the power protesting has through running.

[![Image 1](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oR4p!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd75638f2-b86c-4b84-89d8-b1116f800b8d_995x689.png)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!oR4p!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Fd75638f2-b86c-4b84-89d8-b1116f800b8d_995x689.png)  
Apologies for not sending out an edition of the newsletter last week. I was a bit tied up working on a project for _Sports Illustrated_ that required a bit more time than anticipated.
Since the last newsletter, I can share how that one-mile time trial went at the Bakline x Trial of Miles meet in Jersey City. I unfortunately did not achieve my goal of breaking five minutes. However, I’m super thankful for the opportunity to experience a legitimate race for the first time in seven months and walking away with a four-second personal best. I ran 5:09.87 but really tried to give myself the best chance to get under my goal through 1,000 meters and then it got tough. Still have some work to do. I’m trusting the training and hopefully giving it another go soon.

Also, it felt great to get back behind the mic for some commentary and play-by-play for the first time in SIX years. Shout-out to my friend Ryan Welsh for an awesome debut. [You can re-watch the entire meet on Youtube (if you go to the 1:02:36 mark our best call was definitely the women’s B heat of the 5,000m](https://youtu.be/RYmjNLptdYA)).
Here’s a highlight video from the meet, including my shortcomings :( :
[Video 3](https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=dSKTAUbLnkk)
I’m in Chicago from Oct. 18 to Nov. 18 so if anyone knows of any opportunities to race in the area, let your boy know!
PS: [If you like the “Future is Female Coaches” shirt from Bakline that I’m rocking. You can get it here and use code CITIUS for 15% off](https://www.bakline.nyc/collections/running/graphic_future-is-female).
Onto this week’s latest news from the running world...
Somehow, there’s a global championship taking place in 2020 as international stars descend upon Gdynia, Poland for Saturday’s World Half Marathon Championships. To my understanding, a lot of the CITIUS MAG readers are based in the United States and Canada so unfortunately there won’t be any local athletes to root for since their respective governing bodies have decided not to send teams due to concerns with the coronavirus. There are still some incredible matchups to watch for.

**MEN’S RACE:** Since the last newsletter, Uganda’s Joshua Cheptegei added another world record to his resume by clocking a 26:11:02 for 10,000 meters in Valencia, Spain. He’s three for three with wins and world records in his three races of the year. Can he go four for four? That will be hard. The half marathon world record is 58:01 by Geoffrey Kamworor from Copenhagen last September. Kamworor is the reigning three-time champion but will not race on Saturday as he continues to recover from an injury sustained when he got hit by a motorcyclist in June. Cheptegei has never raced a half marathon. The longest race I was able to find on his athletic profile was a 10-miler in 45:15 from Zaandam, the Netherlands in Sept. 2018. There’s no denying whatever Cheptegei runs will be fast and he’s certainly the favorite.
We can pinpoint his toughest competition to three men. Kenya’s Kibiwott Kandie is the fastest man on paper with his 58:38 personal best from the Prague Half in September. That time puts him at No. 6 on the all-time list behind Kamworor, Abraham Kiptum (later busted for doping), Zersenay Tadese, Sammy Wanjiru and Jemal Yimer. The Kenyan championship streak could rest on his shoulders or Bernard Ngeno, who ran 59:07 for second place at the 2019 Valencia Half.
Cheptegei’s compatriot Jacob Kiplimo is just 19 years old but has electrified the track circuit with a 12:48 for 5,000 meters and 7:26 for 3,000 meters earlier this summer. The lone half marathon on his record is a 61:53 in Kampala in November 2019.
Ethiopia has five men entered with sub-60 personal bests so keep an eye out on their contingent led by Andamlak Belihu and his 59:10 personal best.
_Prediction: No one is beating Joshua Cheptegei in 2020_

[![Image 2](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4MIN!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4e075165-85ea-45af-a636-429615e10fc1_600x374.gif)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!4MIN!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F4e075165-85ea-45af-a636-429615e10fc1_600x374.gif)  
**WOMEN’S RACE:** Remember how hyped up the world was for the clash between Kipchoge and Bekele only to get let down when Bekele pulled out of the race? Let’s bring some of that excitement to a showdown between two world record holders and a title defense by Netsanet Gudeta.
In one corner, we have Kenya’s Peres Jepchirchir. She set the women’s-only half marathon world record of 65:35 in Prague in September and recently had it ratified by World Athletics. Jepchirchir has proven that she can win at the championship stage with her world half marathon title from 2016.
In the other corner, we’ve got Ethiopia’s Ababel Yeshaneh. She is one of only six women to have run faster than Jepchirchir with her 64:31 at the Ras Al Khaimah Half in February. It’s her lone race of the year and she beat marathon world record holder/London Marathon champion Brigid Kosgei by 18 seconds.

Because of how fast the women’s half marathon has been in recent years, Joyciline Jepkosgei has been bumped down to No. 3 on the all-time list and hasn’t run a half marathon since the NYC Half in March 2019. The last time many of us heard of her was when she won the 2019 New York City Marathon in 2:22:38 in a Central Park sprint against Mary Keitany. Just don’t be surprised if she’s in the mix for the win and tries to improve upon her world half marathon championships silver medal from two years ago.
For those wondering where’s Sifan Hassan after her one-hour record and after she ran 29:36.67 for a European Record in the 10,000 meters in Hengelo last week: Hassan scratched from the race saying that she has opted “to give myself some rest and focus for next year.”
_Prediction: I’m going with Peres Jepchirchir for the win over Ababel Yeshaneh simply due to the recency of their standout performances and her experience on the championship stage._
So how can you watch it? The races will be broadcast live on The Olympic Channel from 5:00 a.m. to 8:00 a.m. Eastern Time.[Catch me on Twitter](http://twitter.com/ChrisChavez) at that time with a few live updates.
Mark your calendars! The [NCAA has announced](http://on.ncaa.com/NCAAHost) the following locations for upcoming NCAA Division I Cross Country Championships: 2022 in Stillwater, OK hosted by Oklahoma State; 2023 in Charlottesville, VA hosted by Virginia; 2024 in Madison, WI hosted by Wisconsin 2025 in Columbia, MO hosted by Mizzou. A reminder that the 2020 NCAA Division I Cross Country Championships will be contested on March 15, 2021 in Stillwater and the 2021 NCAA Division I Cross Country Championships remain on schedule for next November in Tallahassee, Florida. It’s going to make for awkward anniversaries later on for those respective champions.

If you enjoy college track then plan on many more visits to Hayward Field with the Ducks slated to host the 2024, 2025, 2026 and 2027 NCAA Championships. Austin, Texas will host in 2023 after doing a good job in 2019.
[![Image 3](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sGGo!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff6ac4240-022c-4d9c-ba7a-265aaff2ed3a_2048x1151.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!sGGo!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff6ac4240-022c-4d9c-ba7a-265aaff2ed3a_2048x1151.jpeg)  
I’ve always said to friends of mine that Ekiden races should be more popular in the United States. For those unfamiliar with the ekiden, it’s a multi-person and multi-distance relay race. There’s no set distance or set number or team members. Each runner hands off a sash called the Tasuki.

Last year, I ran the Tokyo Marathon and then paid a visit to Hakone. That’s the site of the finish for one of Japan’s biggest ekiden. They have a museum that has all the sashes, uniforms and race highlights from past races. From watching old videos (and I recommend doing this on YouTube) you can see the hype is real when they mention that more people turn out and watch the Hakone Ekiden than people watch the Super Bowl in the United States. Thrilled to see what comes next as Hansons-Brooks Original Distance Project [announced the MICHIGAN PRO EKIDEN](https://www.instagram.com/p/CGAeYRVndbk/) will take place on Oct. 21.
Our own Jesse Squire will be on hand to cover the race. The teams committed include the Atlanta Track Club, the Hansons-Brooks Original Distance Project, Rots Running, Bowerman Track Club, Team Boulder, Minnesota Distance Elite and Northern Arizona Elite.
I’ve also been told by people to watch the “Run With The Wind” anime series to get even more excited for this so I’ve got some time to do that.
David Melly [wrote a short post on his experience competing in the Izumo Ekiden](https://citiusmag.com/bringing-ekiden-racing-to-america/) as a member of the Ivy League team. He said, “I’ve never seen anything like it.”
Kudos again to Josh Cox and Ben Rosario for their efforts to put together another star-studded marathon to the United States before the year is up. The Marathon Project, which I mentioned in the last newsletter, will now also include Sara Hall – fresh off that 2:22:01 second-place finish at the London Marathon. Hall just loves racing and this shouldn’t come as much of a surprise to us. [I wrote about her for](https://www.si.com/edge/2019/08/06/sara-hall-berlin-new-york-city-marathon-double-2019)_[Sports Illustrated](https://www.si.com/edge/2019/08/06/sara-hall-berlin-new-york-city-marathon-double-2019)_ last year on why she chooses to double up on marathons in such a short time span.

Cam Levins, who told the media that he was in great shape before the London Marathon but ultimately dropped out due to the cold conditions, will chase the Olympic standard to try and get a spot on Canada’s team for Tokyo.
Fan favorites Beverly Ramos, Diane Nukuri, Noah Droddy and Alexi Pappas have also been added to the fields. You can find the [women’s accepted entries](https://themarathonproject.com/accepted-entries-women/) and [men’s accepted entries here](https://t.co/wjWBrC5dqs).
[![Image 4](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fbLT!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F91240049-cbf1-40d5-bcb5-de2462c158ad_1080x607.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!fbLT!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F91240049-cbf1-40d5-bcb5-de2462c158ad_1080x607.jpeg)  
The CITIUS MAG Podcast Network is pleased to bring on Emma Zimmerman and the [Social Sport Podcast](https://www.instagram.com/socialsportpod/) to our lineup of shows.

In the past couple of months, the show popped onto my radar and I’ve listened to several episodes. I was impressed with Emma’s careful research and care into amplifying and telling the stories of these people with strong passions for social change across all endurance sports. I know a lot of people who follow CITIUS MAG do so for our running coverage but I think there’s a place for these conversations with our audience, especially since it’s been made clear that there’s no line between sports and activism in 2020. Athletes know and embrace that sports are their stage to call for change that they want to see in the world. I think this podcast does a great job of addressing the issues and possible solutions with notable people.

For runners looking to get into the show, you’ll have several episodes featuring [Amir M. Figueroa](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-8-amir-m-figueroa-on-harlem-run-public-health/id1505320511?i=1000474228816) of Harlem Run in New York City, [Jacqueline Alnes, Ph.D.](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-11-jacqueline-alnes-mind-being-tinyart-on-elevating/id1505320511?i=1000477165922) (whose TinyArt drawings are an Instagram hit), [Alison Wade of the Fast Women](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-17-alison-wade-fast-women-newsletter-on-running/id1505320511?i=1000480120675) newsletter, [Kamilah Journet](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-18-kamilah-journ%C3%A9t-powerful-voice-for-anti/id1505320511?i=1000481775957) (now the Tracksmith Marketing Manager), and [Therese Haiss](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-25-therese-haiss-on-authentic-conversation/id1505320511?i=1000487658240) (former professional runner and now coach) to go back and listen to. Those are just some of the runners featured but [the whole archive of episodes is great](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/social-sport/id1505320511).

[In the most recent episode](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/social-sport-podcast-running-to-protest-movement-nyc-running-community/), Emma catches up with Coffey ([a guest on the Runners of NYC Podcast in May](http://citiusmag.com/runners-of-nyc-podcast-coffey/)) about his work in starting the [Running to Protest movement in New York City](https://www.instagram.com/runningtoprotest/). I’ve personally attended three of the protest runs and it’s moving to see 700+ people shut down the Brooklyn Bridge and call for justice regarding the murder of Breonna Taylor or listening to first-hand accounts of mistreatment with police in the city. I come on in the second half of the show to share some of my observations and thoughts about the power protesting has through running.
[Subscribe to Social Sport now.](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/social-sport/id1505320511) | [Follow Social Sport on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/socialsportpod/).

In recent editions of this newsletter, I’ve provided a few updates on the efforts to save the University of Minnesota’s men’s track and field team from being cut. The decision was left to a vote by members of the Board of Regents last week. The proposal to eliminate men's indoor track and field, men's tennis and men's gymnastics teams at the end of the 2020-21 school year [was passed on a 7-5 vote](https://www.si.com/olympics/2020/10/09/minnesota-indoor-track-and-field-gymnastics-tennis-eliminated-board-of-regents-vote-results). Men’s outdoor track and field was kept after a revised proposal was submitted on Friday and approved. It was still a very heavy day for members of the Gopher community because this puts them in a very weird spot. [I decided to chat with Obsa Ali](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast-obsa-ali-save-minnesota-track/), the 2018 NCAA steeplechase champion, about his feelings regarding the decision, what challenges this presents for recruiting and the women’s team as well as what happens next.
You can catch the latest episode of the [podcast on iTunes so subscribe and leave a five-star review](https://itunes.apple.com/us/podcast/id1204506559). We are also on [Stitcher,](https://www.stitcher.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast)[Google Play](https://play.google.com/music/listen?u=0#/ps/Iadq5oufkygxq6jwxblxx5ljhlq) and [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/70eINNmXl67VqorbTsMOaH?si=ikhzVGlDQ_igRjaOBykDFA)!
[Full show notes and quotes can be found here.](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast-obsa-ali-save-minnesota-track/)

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!CaSg!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7f46b9ec-a0cd-4cda-9a0c-b5e4ffd67072_723x723.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!CaSg!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7f46b9ec-a0cd-4cda-9a0c-b5e4ffd67072_723x723.jpeg)  
– On Runners of NYC, [Leigh Anne Sharek and I spoke with Lenny Grullon](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/runners-of-nyc-podcast-lenny-grullon-boogie-down-bronx/). He is one of the founders of the [Boogie Down Bronx Runners](https://www.instagram.com/boogiedownbronxrunners/). If you’ve ever run the New York City Marathon, there’s a part when you cross into the Bronx and you’re greeted with some super loud cheers from a running crew decked out in black and white. That’s his group and it wasn’t always that loud on that part of the course. When Lenny decided to start the group, no one showed up for the first run. However, he kept at it and wanted to get the Bronx community active and it’s paid off. [Listen to his whole story here](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/runners-of-nyc-podcast-lenny-grullon-boogie-down-bronx/).

– [Just wanted to give a quick shout-out to Joshua and Aaron Potts for having me on Two Black Runners](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/ep-27-chris-chavez-how-to-chase-your-dreams-sports/id1486031415?i=1000494598108). If you’re not familiar with their show, they’ve brought on some pretty high-profile guests from the pro running circuit on their podcast over the past six months. They bring the type of energy to the sport that you’d get from watching ESPN analysts debate over NFL and NBA performances. We discussed some of the 2020 track season but also the lack of diversity in the track and field media landscape. Love what these guys are doing and I’m looking forward to sharing the mixed zone with them at the 2021 U.S. Olympic Trials.
That’s all from me this week. If you enjoyed this edition of CITIUS MAG and think your friend would too, forward it to them encourage them to subscribe. Let me know if you have any comments, feedback or thoughts on anything discussed.
Enjoy your weekend!

Figueroa](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-8-amir-m-figueroa-on-harlem-run-public-health/id1505320511?i=1000474228816) of Harlem Run in New York City, [Jacqueline Alnes, Ph.D.](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-11-jacqueline-alnes-mind-being-tinyart-on-elevating/id1505320511?i=1000477165922) (whose TinyArt drawings are an Instagram hit), [Alison Wade of the Fast Women](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-17-alison-wade-fast-women-newsletter-on-running/id1505320511?i=1000480120675) newsletter, [Kamilah Journet](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-18-kamilah-journ%C3%A9t-powerful-voice-for-anti/id1505320511?i=1000481775957) (now the Tracksmith Marketing Manager), and [Therese Haiss](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/episode-25-therese-haiss-on-authentic-conversation/id1505320511?i=1000487658240) (former professional runner and now coach) to go back and listen to. Those are just some of the runners featured but [the whole archive of episodes is great](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/social-sport/id1505320511).

[In the most recent episode](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/social-sport-podcast-running-to-protest-movement-nyc-running-community/), Emma catches up with Coffey ([a guest on the Runners of NYC Podcast in May](http://citiusmag.com/runners-of-nyc-podcast-coffey/)) about his work in starting the [Running to Protest movement in New York City](https://www.instagram.com/runningtoprotest/). I’ve personally attended three of the protest runs and it’s moving to see 700+ people shut down the Brooklyn Bridge and call for justice regarding the murder of Breonna Taylor or listening to first-hand accounts of mistreatment with police in the city. I come on in the second half of the show to share some of my observations and thoughts about the power protesting has through running.
[Subscribe to Social Sport now.](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/social-sport/id1505320511) | [Follow Social Sport on Instagram](https://www.instagram.com/socialsportpod/).
[![Image 5](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!O4il!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff1cdd916-f5eb-40a5-b11d-9804139800ec_2059x2059.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!O4il!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2Ff1cdd916-f5eb-40a5-b11d-9804139800ec_2059x2059.jpeg)  

In recent editions of this newsletter, I’ve provided a few updates on the efforts to save the University of Minnesota’s men’s track and field team from being cut. The decision was left to a vote by members of the Board of Regents last week. The proposal to eliminate men's indoor track and field, men's tennis and men's gymnastics teams at the end of the 2020-21 school year [was passed on a 7-5 vote](https://www.si.com/olympics/2020/10/09/minnesota-indoor-track-and-field-gymnastics-tennis-eliminated-board-of-regents-vote-results). Men’s outdoor track and field was kept after a revised proposal was submitted on Friday and approved. It was still a very heavy day for members of the Gopher community because this puts them in a very weird spot. [I decided to chat with Obsa Ali](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast-obsa-ali-save-minnesota-track/), the 2018 NCAA steeplechase champion, about his feelings regarding the decision, what challenges this presents for recruiting and the women’s team as well as what happens next.
You can catch the latest episode of the [podcast on iTunes so subscribe and leave a five-star review](https://itunes.apple.com/us/podcast/id1204506559). We are also on [Stitcher,](https://www.stitcher.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast)[Google Play](https://play.google.com/music/listen?u=0#/ps/Iadq5oufkygxq6jwxblxx5ljhlq) and [Spotify](https://open.spotify.com/show/70eINNmXl67VqorbTsMOaH?si=ikhzVGlDQ_igRjaOBykDFA)!
[Full show notes and quotes can be found here.](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/citius-mag-podcast-obsa-ali-save-minnesota-track/)

[![Image 6](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!CaSg!,w_1456,c_limit,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7f46b9ec-a0cd-4cda-9a0c-b5e4ffd67072_723x723.jpeg)](https://substackcdn.com/image/fetch/$s_!CaSg!,f_auto,q_auto:good,fl_progressive:steep/https%3A%2F%2Fbucketeer-e05bbc84-baa3-437e-9518-adb32be77984.s3.amazonaws.com%2Fpublic%2Fimages%2F7f46b9ec-a0cd-4cda-9a0c-b5e4ffd67072_723x723.jpeg)  
– On Runners of NYC, [Leigh Anne Sharek and I spoke with Lenny Grullon](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/runners-of-nyc-podcast-lenny-grullon-boogie-down-bronx/). He is one of the founders of the [Boogie Down Bronx Runners](https://www.instagram.com/boogiedownbronxrunners/). If you’ve ever run the New York City Marathon, there’s a part when you cross into the Bronx and you’re greeted with some super loud cheers from a running crew decked out in black and white. That’s his group and it wasn’t always that loud on that part of the course. When Lenny decided to start the group, no one showed up for the first run. However, he kept at it and wanted to get the Bronx community active and it’s paid off. [Listen to his whole story here](http://citiusmag.com/podcast/runners-of-nyc-podcast-lenny-grullon-boogie-down-bronx/).

– [Just wanted to give a quick shout-out to Joshua and Aaron Potts for having me on Two Black Runners](https://podcasts.apple.com/us/podcast/ep-27-chris-chavez-how-to-chase-your-dreams-sports/id1486031415?i=1000494598108). If you’re not familiar with their show, they’ve brought on some pretty high-profile guests from the pro running circuit on their podcast over the past six months. They bring the type of energy to the sport that you’d get from watching ESPN analysts debate over NFL and NBA performances. We discussed some of the 2020 track season but also the lack of diversity in the track and field media landscape. Love what these guys are doing and I’m looking forward to sharing the mixed zone with them at the 2021 U.S. Olympic Trials.
That’s all from me this week. If you enjoyed this edition of CITIUS MAG and think your friend would too, forward it to them encourage them to subscribe. Let me know if you have any comments, feedback or thoughts on anything discussed.
Enjoy your weekend!

**Running News Daily** is edited by Bob Anderson and team. Send your news items to bob@mybestruns.com Advertising opportunities available.

Articles tagged **#Geoffrey Kamworor**

[Today's Running News](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php)

[![Image 1](https://mybestruns.com/street/tho/d93f69a130b82c1ee4b97d85505dbe4cc603bd116ae70e229f8e74f55b806361.jpg?i=15439&t=1792160904)](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor#pok15439)

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)

Long before he conquered world cross-country championships, dominated the half-marathon distance and lifted the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) trophy, [Geoffrey Kamworor](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor) was a young Kenyan student with an ambitious dream that had little to do with running: becoming a [lawyer](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=lawyer).

![Image 2](https://mybestruns.com/street/de57be259ad5f2aa804935a23c35ae7bb6b49b6ec295d0ed68325e1b13b71303.jpg?i=1792160904&t=1792160904)

Growing up in Keiyo South, Kamworor developed the discipline that would later define his extraordinary athletic career. His daily routine involved running approximately five kilometres to school and another five kilometres back home. What might have seemed like an ordinary journey for a schoolboy was quietly laying the foundation for a future in international distance running.

![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/808283ce83ea90fb69283ae3a63fb6cc12becf4782bc79b9156f109324db53df.jpg?i=1792160904&t=1792160904)

He attended Chepsamo Primary School before proceeding to Lelboinet Secondary School, where he combined his education with a growing passion for athletics. At the time, his ambitions extended beyond the track and roads. He wanted to pursue a career in law, and that dream eventually brought him an opportunity to study at a college in the United States.

However, the young Kenyan faced a defining decision: follow the academic path he had envisioned or commit himself fully to the sport that was beginning to reveal his remarkable potential. Kamworor chose athletics, a decision that would ultimately place his name among the most accomplished distance runners of his generation.

![Image 4](https://mybestruns.com/street/a94c34052d38330fd293c08402206cd4d7a39c33946639bdb76ca84e0ab123e7.jpg?i=1792160904&t=1792160904)

His transformation from a promising schoolboy into an international contender began gathering momentum in 2010, when he joined the GSC training camp in Kaptagat. His development accelerated rapidly, and within a short period, an opportunity to compete in Finland exposed him to a higher level of international competition.

Still only 17, he reportedly competed nine times during that trip, demonstrating an impressive ability to adapt to the demands of competitive racing. Breaking the eight-minute barrier for 3,000 metres was an early indication of the talent that would eventually carry him to the highest levels of distance running.

![Image 5](https://mybestruns.com/street/84282c8c1c650ab6ffe7062ef243eacc858a034f27f3ff8005541232e23d4bd3.jpg?i=1792160904&t=1792160904)

His breakthrough on the international stage followed in March 2011, when he captured the junior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Punta Umbría, Spain. That victory announced the arrival of a young athlete whose future would extend far beyond the junior ranks.

Kamworor was not simply a runner with speed. He possessed the endurance, tactical intelligence and competitive determination required to succeed across different distances and racing surfaces. As his career developed, those qualities became the hallmarks of an athlete capable of challenging the world's best.

Cross country became one of the foundations of Kamworor's international success. In 2015, he won the senior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Guiyang, China, confirming his status as one of the leading distance runners in the world. Two years later, he returned to the top of the podium in Kampala, Uganda, defending his senior world cross-country crown in front of a home crowd. Winning consecutive senior world titles placed him in an elite category and demonstrated his remarkable command of the demanding discipline.

On the roads, however, Kamworor established an equally impressive legacy. He won the World Half Marathon Championships in Copenhagen in 2014, Cardiff in 2016 and Valencia in 2018, becoming a three-time champion at the distance. His achievements reflected a rare combination of strength, speed and race management, enabling him to prevail against formidable international opposition.

The half marathon became one of his signature events, but Kamworor's ambitions were never confined to a single discipline. He continued to demonstrate his versatility on the track, winning silver in the men's 10,000 metres at the 2015 World Athletics Championships in Beijing, China. From the grass of cross-country courses to the roads of major international races and the track of a global championship, he repeatedly demonstrated that his talent could flourish wherever the competition took him.

Among Kamworor's most memorable achievements are his victories at the New York City Marathon in 2017 and 2019. Winning one of the world's most celebrated marathons requires exceptional endurance, but winning it twice demands much more: tactical patience, resilience and the ability to navigate a demanding course against a deep international field.

Kamworor demonstrated those qualities in both victories, establishing a special connection with the New York race and adding the marathon to an already remarkable collection of honours. His success in the American city also illustrated his ability to move successfully between distances. An athlete celebrated for his cross-country and half-marathon dominance had shown that he could also conquer the 42.195-kilometre marathon, one of the most demanding challenges in road racing.

Now, as he sets his sights on another New York campaign, the Kenyan star has an opportunity to strengthen his legacy further. A third men's open-division victory would place him among a very select group of athletes to have won the prestigious race three times. Such a milestone would be more than another addition to his trophy cabinet; it would reinforce the story of a runner whose competitive range has extended across nearly every major discipline in distance running.

Behind Kamworor's achievements lies a training environment built around discipline, consistency and high-level competition. Working under the guidance of renowned coach Patrick Sang, he has trained alongside some of Kenya's most celebrated athletes, including marathon great Eliud Kipchoge and middle- and long-distance superstar Faith Kipyegon.

Sharing a training environment with athletes of such calibre provides a demanding daily standard. Yet Kamworor has built his own identity through a career defined by major championship victories and sustained success across different racing distances. His journey has also included difficult periods and setbacks, reminding the running world that even the most accomplished champions must continually work to return to their best. His longevity at the elite level reflects the importance of patience, dedication and the willingness to keep pursuing new goals.

For aspiring athletes in Kenya, his story offers an important lesson: extraordinary achievements are often built through ordinary routines repeated consistently over many years. Those five-kilometre journeys to school and back were not glamorous. They did not come with cheering crowds, television cameras or medals. Yet they formed part of the foundation of a career that would eventually take him to the world's biggest running stages.

Kamworor's story is ultimately about a choice that changed the direction of his life. The young student who once imagined himself arguing cases in a courtroom instead built his reputation by answering the toughest questions on the running track and roads. His achievements speak for themselves: world cross-country titles, three world half-marathon crowns, a global 10,000-metre silver medal and two New York City Marathon victories.

He may never have pursued the legal career he once envisioned, but his athletic record tells a compelling story of ambition, sacrifice and extraordinary accomplishment. His pursuit of another New York triumph offers a fresh chapter in a career that has already crossed the boundaries between cross country, track and road racing.

For Geoffrey Kamworor, the courtroom was a dream he left behind. The world of distance running became the stage on which he built his name. And while the law lost a prospective lawyer, athletics gained a champion whose achievements have helped define an era of Kenyan distance running.

### [From 1:07:01 To 56:51: The Extraordinary Evolution Of The Half Marathon World Record](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15206)

The history of the men’s half marathon world record is a remarkable journey through more than six decades of distance running, tracing the sport’s transformation from club-level competition to an era of extraordinary professional speed.

![Image 8](https://mybestruns.com/street/bd5a26a33db4a2d8ed2cbd743ded1cfe1cee000d1eff9a864a704e344f805fe2.jpg?i=1792160904&t=1792160904)

The story began in the spring of 1960 in Romford, Essex, where British club runner [Brian Hill-Cottingham](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Brian+Hill-Cottingham) ran 21.0975 kilometres in 1:07:01, setting the fastest officially recorded time at the distance at the time.

For years, the record progressed slowly. British and American runners dominated much of the early history, with improvements often measured in seconds rather than dramatic leaps. Ron Hill lowered the mark to 1:05:44 in 1965, while Derek Clayton took it down to 1:03:22 in 1967. Through the 1970s and 1980s, the barrier continued to fall as athletes from different nations gradually pushed the limits of what was possible over 21.1 kilometres.

![Image 9](https://mybestruns.com/street/771750874dc9c2c8cf891cee9b0d935da907514fb9b5d5491c6fcf1c1a60e802.jpg?i=1792160904&t=1792160904)

Then came the breakthrough that changed the character of the event.

In 1993, Kenya’s Moses Tanui became the first man to break the one-hour barrier, running 59:47 in Milan. It was a landmark moment for road running. The half marathon was no longer simply another distance on the racing calendar; it had become an event worthy of specialised preparation and elite-level ambition.

Kenya subsequently established a remarkable presence in the record progression. Paul Tergat lowered the record to 59:17 in 1998 before eventually pushing it below 59 minutes with a 59:06 mark later that year. Eritrea’s Zersenay Tadese and Kenya’s Sammy Wanjiru continued the progression in the 2000s, with Wanjiru taking the record to 58:33 in 2007.

![Image 10](https://mybestruns.com/street/93c7f1a16e92e419561fe193bd2aaef6688c31742a3f30214d15fe9587cba55c.jpg?i=1792160904&t=1792160904)

Tadese reclaimed the record in 2010 with 58:23, but the most dramatic developments were still to come.

In 2018, Kenya’s Abraham Kiptum ran 58:18, only for countryman Geoffrey Kamworor to lower the standard to 58:01 in 2019. A year later, another Kenyan, Kibiwott Kandie, produced one of the greatest breakthroughs in the event’s history, becoming the first man to break 58 minutes with 57:32 in Valencia.

Uganda’s Jacob Kiplimo then entered the record books, running 57:31 in Lisbon in 2021. Ethiopia’s [Yomif Kejelcha](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Yomif+Kejelcha) lowered it by another second to 57:30 in Valencia in 2024.

And then, in 2026, the record progression became a breathtaking battle between two of the finest distance runners of their generation.

Kiplimo reclaimed the world record in Lisbon with 57:20, taking 10 seconds from Kejelcha’s mark. But Kejelcha responded with an extraordinary performance in Buenos Aires on 23 August 2026, stopping the clock at 56:51.

The improvement was staggering—29 seconds faster than Kiplimo’s previous record.

Kejelcha’s 56:51 means he averaged approximately 2:42 per kilometre for the entire 21.0975-kilometre distance, a pace that would have seemed almost unimaginable when Hill-Cottingham first established the record at 1:07:01 in 1960.

From 1:07:01 to 56:51, the progression tells the story of an event that has undergone a remarkable transformation. Training has become more sophisticated, competition has intensified, courses have become faster, and generations of athletes have continued to challenge the boundaries of human endurance and speed.

What began as a record set by a British club runner on a spring day in Essex has evolved into one of the most fiercely contested records in modern distance running.

And with Kiplimo and Kejelcha pushing each other to unprecedented heights, the question is no longer whether the half marathon can go faster.

The question is: how low can the world record ultimately go?

### [Geoffrey Kamworor Eyes New York Hat-Trick as Kenyan Star Chases Another Major Triumph](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15139)

Two-time [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) champion [Geoffrey Kamworor](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor) is set for another assault on the Big Apple, with the Kenyan distance-running star targeting a historic third victory when the Abbott World Marathon Majors race returns on November 1.

![Image 12](https://mybestruns.com/street/31355a57b550c210d3d83d94d9c4e883c1218b63d915be940720de44aa01910a.jpg?i=1792160904&t=1792160904)

For Kamworor, New York represents much more than another marathon. It is a course where he has already enjoyed some of the defining moments of his illustrious career, and where he will now seek to add another prestigious title to a remarkable collection of achievements.

The 33-year-old has developed a special relationship with the New York course since making his debut there in 2015. On that occasion, he finished runner-up in 2:10:48 behind compatriot Stanley Biwott, who won in 2:10:34.

![Image 13](https://mybestruns.com/street/6b59a7d5bff852d724afea3068075771894accc93519e913c4adb66868b69f07.jpg?i=1792160904&t=1792160904)

Two years later, Kamworor went one step further.

In 2017, he produced a composed performance to claim his first New York Marathon crown, crossing the finish line in 2:10:53. He held off fellow Kenyan and former world record-holder Wilson Kipsang, who finished just three seconds behind in 2:10:56, while Ethiopia's Lelisa Desisa took third in 2:11:32.

![Image 14](https://mybestruns.com/street/7aff6bfca948a07b46e2c18c5b7c108e7661ce7239f394530996551073ac3899.jpg?i=1792160904&t=1792160904)

Kamworor returned the following year hoping to defend his title but had to settle for third place. Desisa triumphed in 2:05:59, ahead of Shura Kitata in 2:06:01, while Kamworor clocked 2:06:26.

But the Kenyan refused to stay away from the top for long.

In 2019, he reclaimed the New York crown in emphatic fashion, winning in 2:08:13. Albert Korir followed in second in 2:08:36, with Ethiopia's Girma Bekele completing the podium in 2:08:38.

Those two victories remain Kamworor's only Abbott World Marathon Majors titles, making New York a particularly significant venue in his career.

His latest appearance in the race, however, ended without another podium finish. Returning in 2024, Kamworor placed fifth in 2:08:50 as the Netherlands' Abdi Nageeye won in 2:07:39. Kenya's Evans Chebet was second in 2:07:45, while Albert Korir took third in 2:08:00.

Now, Kamworor is eager to return to the city where he has already tasted victory twice.

“I am very excited to be going back to New York,” Kamworor said, expressing his anticipation ahead of another demanding battle through the streets of the world's most famous city.

For the Kenyan star, the race offers a unique combination of sporting pressure and an atmosphere unlike any other.

“It's always an incredible experience to run the biggest marathon in the world. I'm really looking forward to feeling the energy of the crowd again,” he added.

Kamworor's challenge will be to arrive in New York at his best after a mixed campaign in 2026.

He began the year in spectacular fashion, winning the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon on February 14. The Kenyan clocked an impressive 58:14, finishing ahead of Bahrain's Birhanu Balew, who ran 58:23, and compatriot Gideon Rono, who crossed the line in 58:38.

![Image 15](https://mybestruns.com/street/875eca9d427f26a3faadbd28e5eb8004e1a2a496b75bb9a93e2f049e1ef9706d.jpg?i=1792160904&t=1792160904)

His London Marathon campaign on April 26 proved considerably tougher. Kamworor finished eighth in 2:05:38 in a historic race dominated by Sebastian Sawe, who produced a sensational 1:59:30 to become the first man to break the two-hour barrier in a marathon. Ethiopia's Yomif Kejelcha was second in 1:59:41, while Uganda's Jacob Kiplimo finished third in 2:00:28.

Kamworor will therefore arrive in New York with both experience and motivation on his side. He knows exactly what the course demands, having already navigated its hills, turns and relentless closing stages on multiple occasions.

Beyond the marathon, his career is decorated with major international honours across several disciplines.

Kamworor is a three-time world half marathon champion, winning his first title in Copenhagen in 2014 before successfully defending his crown in Cardiff in 2016 and completing his remarkable hat-trick in Valencia in 2018.

He has also established himself as one of Kenya's finest cross-country runners. He won the world junior cross-country title in Punta Umbria in 2011 before becoming a senior world champion in Guiyang in 2015 and Kampala in 2017. He added a bronze medal at the 2019 World Cross Country Championships in Aarhus.

That versatility has long been one of Kamworor's greatest strengths. From cross country to the half marathon and now the marathon, he has repeatedly demonstrated the endurance, tactical intelligence and competitive resilience required to succeed at the highest level.

Yet New York remains unfinished business.

With two victories already secured and another opportunity waiting on November 1, Kamworor has a chance to strengthen his legacy on one of the sport's most iconic stages.

A third triumph would not only give him a coveted New York hat-trick but would further cement his status as one of Kenya's most accomplished distance runners of his generation.

The Big Apple has already given Kamworor some of the proudest moments of his career. Now, the Kenyan star is returning with one clear ambition — to conquer New York once again.

Uganda’s world record-holder Kiplimo, Kenya’s world champion Sawe and his Kenyan compatriot Isaia Lasoi were all in contention in the closing stages, but Sawe had the strongest finish. He managed to get a gap on Kiplimo with the finish line in sight and won in a PB of 58:05, four seconds ahead of Kiplimo. Lasoi was one second further back in a PB of 58:10.

![Image 99](https://mybestruns.com/street/a382a5e77a0f852e59cee955278bb2531829f32c2cd57598ca8b04e6172fa153.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Kenya’s world half marathon silver medallist Kipkemboi was joined by her compatriots Judy Kemboi, Catherine Reline Amanang'ole and Sheila Chelangat plus Ethiopia’s Ftaw Zeray through 10km but she left her rivals behind during the second half of the race to win by more than half a minute in 1:05:11. Kemboi was second in a PB of 1:05:43 and Amanang'ole, the world half marathon bronze medallist behind Kipkemboi, was third in a PB of 1:06:09.The men’s race also featured Norway's Olympic and world 5000m champion Jakob Ingebrigtsen, making his half marathon debut just two days after winning the Diamond League 1500m title in Brussels.

He formed part of a large lead men’s group that passed 5km in 13:53, but that pack quickly whittled down to six – pacemaker Berihu Aregawi, the 5000m champion in Brussels two days ago, leading ahead of Kiplimo, Sawe, Lasoi, Amos Kurgat, Kennedy Kimutai and Ingebrigtsen.

But Ingebrigtsen couldn’t maintain that pace and he pulled up at 10km, reached in 27:27 – a national record for the Norwegian on the roads. His rivals strode ahead and although he stopped a couple more times, Ingebrigtsen did continue to the finish and clocked 1:03:13.

After letting Sawe take the lead for a spell, Kiplimo was back in front at 15km, passed in 41:17. From there it was a battle between the trio of Kiplimo, Sawe and Lasoi. They were together through 20km in 55:13, before Sawe took control in the closing stages and went on to win in a time that improves his own world lead and is just four seconds off the race record, which was a world record when it was set by Geoffrey Kamworor in 2019.

Having won his world half marathon title in Riga last year, Sawe will have the opportunity to return to Copenhagen in 2026, when the city hosts the World Athletics Road Running Championships.

Another athlete who could be there is his compatriot Kipkemboi, who secured silver in Riga. This time in Copenhagen she ran as part of a group that reached 5km in 15:22 and she had Kemboi, Amanang'ole, Chelangat and Zeray for company through 10km in 30:52. The race was down to Kipkemboi and Kemboi by 15km, which they reached in 46:14, 15 seconds ahead of Amanang'ole.

Kipkemboi then made her break and ran the final section of the race alone, getting to the 20km mark in 1:01:42 and extending her advantage to win in 1:05:11.

“There’s no place like New York, and I am so ready to defend my title,” said Obiri. “I have been racing very well on the roads in the US, and I hope I can have another good day that sees me in contention once we enter the final stages in Central Park.”

The Kenyan delegation will also include 2010 champion Edna Kiplagat, four-time Olympic medallist Vivian Cheruiyot, and Sheila Chepkirui, who owns the fastest personal best in the field.

Ethiopia’s Tirunesh Dibaba will make her New York City Marathon debut and is one of the world’s most accomplished long-distance runners as a three-time Olympic and 16-time world champion. She will be joined by compatriot Senbere Teferi.

Dakotah Lindwurm, the top US finisher in the marathon at the Paris Olympics, will lead the US contingent.

### [Antrim Coast Half Marathon: Yehualaw returns despite 2021 world record blow](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=12525)

[Yalemzerf Yehualaw](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Yalemzerf+Yehualaw) returns to the Antrim Coast Half Marathon a year after seemingly breaking the women's world record only to learn weeks later that the course had been 54 metres short.

Race director James McIlroy is guaranteeing there will be no repeat of last year's hiccup which meant the Ethiopian's time could not be ratified.

"You don't want to blame Covid but it certainly was a factor," says McIlroy.

![Image 112](https://mybestruns.com/street/f4d38fe3b91fc555721d8a1a7abed8c06ffb4787cd1e74c3b9a7f1bd73911d46.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

"The protocol is to measure the course twice but we were unable to do that."

"We couldn't get anyone to fly here before the race to do the measurement [because of the Covid situation] so we had to do it post the race.

![Image 113](https://mybestruns.com/street/e7856c195519b2dc4619e41ac0f428b209c00cee666c519655a9294d58fb5e44.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

"The frustration is that with 50 metres short, if you add 10 seconds on, 65% of the elite race would still have run a personal best and Yalemzerf would still have been the first woman to run under 64 minutes.

"But she's back again in good shape and the course is ratified and measured correctly."

Course even faster this year - McIlroy

Indeed, McIlroy believes course tweaks this year could lead to Yalemzerf going even faster than the 63 minutes and 44 seconds she clocked last year - although the 23-year-old will have to go some to break the world mark of 62:52 set by compatriot Letesenbet Gidey in Valencia last October.

Yalemzerf's own time of 63:51 set as she finished runner-up that day remains the second fastest time in history but the 59 seconds to Gidey's world mark is a huge amount - even in half marathon terms.

McIlroy admits the UK all-comers half marathon record of 65:52 set by Kenyan Edith Chelimo in Cardiff five years ago will be a more realistic target for Yalemzerf and several of other leading ladies.

"We think we've made the course even faster," added former Great Britain Olympic 800m athlete McIlroy.

"We've taken out the section in the harbour so we've taken out one tight turn and going around the roundabout clockwise instead of anti-clockwise should also help the athletes."

While Yalemzerf, 23, will be a strong favourite, the presence of her compatriots and training partners Tsehay Gemechu [PB 65:08] and Gete Alemayehu [PB 66:37] should ensure that she has competitive company in the early stages as opposed to merely her male pacemakers.

Last year, Yehualaw finished more than six minutes ahead of Kenyan runner-up Vane Nyanamba.

2021 men's winner Jemal Yimer is also back in the Larne field and will again be the man to beat give his outstanding personal best of 58:33 set in 2018, which is 49 seconds quicker than the next fastest competitor, compatriot Tesfahun Akalnew.

Yimer was three seconds outside Sir Mo Farah's course record of 60:27 set in 2020 when he triumphed 12 months ago.

Akalnew finished one second behind his compatriot 12 months ago and is again back in the field along with last year's third placer Shadrack Kimining of Kenya.

With the field also including sub-60 minute men Ethiopians Huseydin Mohamed and Gizealew Ayana, organiser McIlroy is very optimistic that the one-hour barrier will be broken for the first time on Irish soil, with Geoffrey Kamworor's UK all-comers mark of 59:10 from 2016 possibly also in danger.

Englishman Marc Scott finished only five seconds behind Yimer in fourth spot 12 months ago and will be joined in the field by fellow British Olympian Callum Hawkins, whose has a half marathon best of exactly 60 minutes.

With Ireland's Tokyo competitor Stephen Scullion a late withdrawal from Sunday's race, Irish male hopefuls David Mansfield and Paul O'Donnell will both be aiming to improve their respective personal best of 63:23 and 63:37.

The women's event could see a good domestic battle for top-10 finishes between Emma Mitchell, Fionnuala Ross and Northern Ireland Commonwealth Games competitor this summer, Hannah Irwin.

The Eamonn Christie-coached Mitchell is the fifth fastest in the women's field on lifetime bests behind the African contingent with a 72:28 mark set in Valencia in 2019, while Ross has clocked 73:08 and Irwin 73:23.

The mass race in the event which starts and finishes in Larne will have around 6,000 competitors with McIlroy delighted to report "entrants from 19 countries this year".

The 2021 Boston Marathon champion [Benson Kipruto](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Benson+Kipruto) is targeting a podium finish at Sunday’s Tokyo Marathon.

Kipruto trains in his backyard in Kapsabet, Nandi County, ahead of the much-awaited, starstudded showdown in the Japanese capital.

![Image 148](https://mybestruns.com/street/3ed4a1a9f5fdf0c7c3e333033702af0de7171092a6e663b531e2d91d8af9681c.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

“My training and preparations for the Tokyo Marathon have been going on very well. I hope my hard training will yield great results,” said Kipruto, the 2016 Athens Classic Marathon silver medalist.

![Image 149](https://mybestruns.com/street/7dfc9a4edad15aadff530cac24159718efb613d213c865eecbc96f5915081fc9.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Kipruto was a surprise 2022 Chicago Marathon winner and silver medallist a year later­— behind the late Kelvin Kiptum, who set the world record of 2:00:35.

He said Tokyo was a a late destination after initially settling on a return to Boston.

“I was to compete at the Boston Marathon but I had to change to Tokyo since it gives me enough time to prepare for the Olympics Games,” said the 2017 Gongju Dong-A Marathon silver medalist.

He is unfazed by the calibre of competition.

“I have prepared well enough to run finish on the podium as well as lower my personal best,” said Kipruto.

Kipruto is also looking forward to representing the country at the Paris Olympic Games.

He was named in the provisional marathon team to Paris alongside Kipruto former world record holder Eliud Kipchoge, Vincent Kipkemoi, Timothy Kiplagat, Bernard Koech, Geoffrey Kamworor, Cyprian Kotut, Amos Kipruto, Titus Kipruto and the late Kelvin Kiptum.

“I have never represented my country in any competition and making the team to Paris would be a dream come true,” said Kipruto.

Meanwhile, Ugandan Victor Kiplang’at said he is well prepared for Tokyo.

Kiplangat, who has already hit the qualifying time for the Paris Olympic Games, told Xinhua that he has put in a lot of work during preparations as he seeks to improve on his time.

“I have trained well under coach Addy Ruiter and I can’t wait to go and prove a point in Japan,” said Kiplang’at.

The Tokyo Marathon is a good platform for his preparations for the Olympic Games in France in August.

Kiplang’at, who will follow Ugandan pace-setter Abel Boniface, said competing against Kipchoge will be a tough but great challenge.

### [RAS AL KHAIMAH HALF MARATHON IS ON SATURDAY AND IT SHOUlD BE A FAST ONE](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11682)

New regime, new course, but with Olympic and world champions and the usual array of speedsters, Saturday’s Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon is virtually assured of the sort of fast times that have been a feature of the event throughout its 17 year history, including three women’s world records.

Pride of place both on the start list and at this morning’s press conference in one of the smaller emirates in the UAE were Olympic marathon and three time world half-marathon champion, Peres Jepchirchir of Kenya, and keeping the balance in the long-term East African distance running rivalry, world marathon champion Tamirat Tola of Ethiopia heads the men’s entry. The wild card, hoping to gatecrash the party is Konstanze Klosterhalfen of Germany, who surprised the East Africans when she beat a dozen of them to win her debut half-marathon in Valencia in 2022.

![Image 152](https://mybestruns.com/street/7b1974a2fc307844683badc5fd9274dffaab0191850135a7be15af2e4fa7921f.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Jepchirchir may neither be the fastest marathoner or half-marathoner among current women long distance runners, but she knows how to win races, an asset far more valuable than fast times. In the seven months between late August 2021 and mid-April 2022, she won the Olympic, New York and Boston Marathons, a rare collective achievement. In her comeback marathon following an injury, she finished third in last year’s London Marathon. And she has won 12 of her 16 half-marathons. She is loath to admit her plans yet, but this RAK ‘half’ is perfectly scheduled as a springboard, to going back to London in April, to upgrade that third place.

Tola was similarly annoyed that an injury preventing him successfully defending his 2022 world marathon title in Budapest last summer, but a speedy recovery saw him break the long-standing New York Marathon record with 2.04.58 three months later. He is one of the few elites to be making his debut in the RAK ‘half’ and the scale of his task may be judged by the fact that on paper there are 15 men faster than his best of 59.37 set seven years ago in Prague. But he suggested that is due for drastic revision. ‘I’d like to think I can do under 59 minutes if the race turns out to be fast,’ he said at the press conference. Fastest man in the field is Daniel Mateiko of Kenya with 58.26, but his colleague Benard(sic) Kibet has the advantage of having won last year in 58.45.

Klosterhalfen, ‘Koko’ to her pals may prove to be not only the wild card, but the joker in the pack in the women’s race. A world bronze medallist on the track and European 5000 metres champion, the German called a halt to her summer season last year when a foot injury caused her to reassess her career. She had changed her shoe sponsor, left her coach and long-term training venue in the USA already. She then switched again and has teamed up with Gary Lough, latter-day coach to Mo Farah and spouse of former world record holder Paula Radcliffe (here in RAK as a TV commentator). Klosterhalfen has also switched her altitude training venue to Addis Ababa, where she has just spent six weeks, coming directly to here. ‘Road running is still a bit of an adventure for me’, she said this morning. ‘I still want to run on the track, but I want to more road races’.

![Image 153](https://mybestruns.com/street/65fa168c357023389dbd75a033bee8d3f4f0605944e8db1109e7d2f01beb5f92.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

The roll-call of winners since the race began in 2007 is a ‘Who’s Who’ of distance running over the last two decades; beginning with Sammy Wanjiru and Berhane Adere in the inaugural race, via luminaries such as Patrick Makau, Geoffrey Mutai, Elvan Abeylegesse, Mary Keitany, Geoffrey Kamworor, Lelisa Desisa, Samson Kandie and Hellen Obiri. Add to that Jepchirchir herself who won in 2017 in a then world record of 65min 06sec.

The promoters of the successful marathon down the road in Dubai have been invited this year to give the RAK ‘half’ a makeover, and they began by introducing a 10k race for locals and altering the half-marathon course. ‘It’s faster and better than any route before here in Ras Al Khaimah; we’ve cut out some of the sharp turns,’ said race director Peter Connerton, ‘so we’re hoping for at least similar times and hopefully better. But with a couple of good races into the bargain’.
