### [2027 Could Bring Unprecedented Heat, Raising New Concerns for Marathon Runners Worldwide](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15441)

The global running community could face a formidable challenge in [2027](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2027), as forecasts of a potentially powerful El Niño raise concerns about rising temperatures and the impact of extreme heat on marathon performances.

![Image 2](https://mybestruns.com/street/21525fef106f0f5e518948f3b7ac7c7a59c2dc7f609cbf843c1a3df2621fa9d4.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

With long-distance runners increasingly chasing personal bests on the world's biggest stages, the prospect of another exceptionally warm year has placed race-day weather firmly in the spotlight. For marathoners, even a modest rise in temperature can make the difference between a record-breaking performance and a difficult battle to reach the finish line.

![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/c649899eb4ea226a094d35c54188897ee0ecd5f22a51cbcb024dd442b8785c9e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

At the centre of the concern is the [Pacific Ocean](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Pacific+Ocean), where developing El Niño conditions could influence global temperatures. Forecasts have raised the possibility of an unusually strong event, although its eventual intensity and the precise effects on temperatures around the world remain uncertain.

El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon characterised by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures across parts of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. It can alter weather patterns across different regions, while its warming influence can contribute to higher global temperatures. The full impact depends on the strength of the event and how it interacts with other climate factors.

![Image 4](https://mybestruns.com/street/d0a9667bdea6ce04007f6323709b90066c76c7bf750a06efd1f2fbddbd1d21b0.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

The timing is particularly important. Global temperatures have often responded strongly in the year following a major El Niño, meaning 2027 could face an increased risk of challenging heat. However, whether it ultimately surpasses the existing global temperature record will depend on evolving ocean conditions, atmospheric patterns and human-caused climate change.

![Image 5](https://mybestruns.com/street/46b631cd0e12734e6118d1811afa82002a59f6f038f8de1a680ce25c9ce4a1e2.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

For marathon runners, the implications are significant. Scientific research has repeatedly shown that warmer conditions can reduce endurance performance, increase physiological strain and make it more difficult to maintain a planned race pace over 42.195 kilometres.

An analysis of seven North American marathons illustrates how substantially conditions can influence elite performances. Researchers found that leading male runners finished approximately 1.7 per cent slower relative to course records under the coolest conditions examined. In the warmest category, that difference increased to around 4.5 per cent.

For an athlete capable of running a marathon in 2:05:00, a slowdown of that magnitude could translate into several additional minutes on the clock. At the elite level, where races are frequently decided by seconds, such a difference can determine whether a runner achieves a personal best, secures a podium finish or misses a major performance target.

The consequences can be even more noticeable among recreational athletes, who often spend considerably longer exposed to the conditions.

A separate analysis by researchers at the University of Chicago, examining approximately 4.7 million marathon finishing times, highlighted the substantial effect of temperature on runners across different ability levels. The findings suggested that the typical participant could lose roughly 19 minutes when racing in temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, compared with conditions in the 40s. In the 80s Fahrenheit, the estimated time penalty rose to approximately 33 minutes.

These figures underline why marathon preparation involves much more than mileage, speed sessions and strength training. Temperature, humidity, direct sunlight and the body's ability to regulate heat can all influence how effectively a runner sustains an effort over the full distance.

Many marathon performances are achieved in cool conditions, with temperatures of approximately 4°C to 10°C often considered favourable for endurance running. As temperatures climb beyond that range, the body must devote more resources to cooling itself, potentially increasing cardiovascular strain and making a previously comfortable pace harder to maintain.

However, there is no universal temperature at which every marathon runner begins to slow down. Individual fitness, acclimatisation, humidity, wind, course exposure and race strategy all influence performance. A cool, overcast morning can produce very different outcomes from a sunny, humid day, even when the thermometer shows similar readings.

### [Cancer Survivor Brandon Throop Returns To Toronto Marathon In Hospital Gown For Third World Record Bid](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15440)

For [Brandon Throop](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Brandon+Throop), running a marathon in a hospital gown is about far more than chasing a place in the [Guinness World Records](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Guinness+World+Records). It is a deeply personal tribute to the medical team that helped save his life, a celebration of survival, and an opportunity to give back to the institution that stood beside him during one of the darkest chapters of his life.

![Image 8](https://mybestruns.com/street/f29108f8a11d11c189a98e7ad107e25370003868a0c2a06a0f60240f82ca748e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

In 2022, Throop was 35 years old, a father of two, and facing a life-changing diagnosis of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. His journey soon led him to [Princess Margaret Cancer Centre](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Princess+Margaret+Cancer+Centre) in Toronto, Canada, where he underwent chemotherapy and began a difficult battle against the disease.

![Image 9](https://mybestruns.com/street/544aaad28b469831ffc670d6b1f0afed09ba7cece4e33f54484abd893edf14de.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

The treatment that helped him fight cancer also left him physically weakened. For someone who had spent much of his life running, even the simplest movements became unexpectedly challenging. After completing treatment, climbing a single flight of stairs could leave him coughing and struggling to catch his breath.

However, rather than allowing the experience to define the limits of his future, Throop began rebuilding his strength one small step at a time. He started by running once around his neighbourhood block before gradually increasing the distance as his body recovered. What began as a modest attempt to regain his fitness eventually developed into an extraordinary mission with a purpose extending far beyond the finish line.

![Image 10](https://mybestruns.com/street/609ed787d02e0efaf2f9b8e1f2b60b1718ea68e0b9bbf56ffa21a91b509d4949.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Now, more than three years after becoming cancer-free, Throop is preparing to return to the [TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=TCS+Toronto+Waterfront+Marathon) on Sunday, October 18, 2026, for another attempt at the Guinness World Record for the fastest marathon completed while wearing a hospital gown.

This will be his third attempt to claim the record, following two determined performances in previous editions of the Toronto race. In 2023, he completed the marathon in 2:55:59 before returning in 2024 to improve his time to 2:55:01. Despite his progress, the record remained just out of reach.

The current benchmark stands at 2:50:12, established by Evan Ubene at the same Toronto Waterfront Marathon in 2022. To make history this time, Throop will need to improve significantly on his previous performances and take more than five minutes off his best hospital-gown marathon.

Yet the significance of Sunday's race cannot be measured by finishing time alone.

Throop's larger objective is to raise funds for the Princess Margaret Cancer Foundation, supporting the cancer research and care that played such an important role in his own recovery. He has already raised more than $137,000 toward his $150,000 fundraising target, bringing him within reach of a goal that could help support further advances in cancer treatment.

Every kilometre he covers in the distinctive hospital gown carries a message of gratitude to the people who cared for him and hope for patients whose journeys are only beginning. His challenge transforms a gruelling 42.195-kilometre race into a public expression of appreciation for the doctors, nurses, researchers and other healthcare professionals working to improve the lives of people affected by cancer.

The timing of this year's marathon makes the occasion even more meaningful. The race falls just days from the anniversary of his first chemotherapy session in 2022, bringing him back to a period that profoundly changed his life. Returning to the streets of Toronto now, healthy enough to pursue another marathon, offers a powerful reminder of how far he has travelled since those difficult days.

For Throop, choosing Toronto has never been simply about finding the fastest course on which to break a record. Although other marathons might offer different racing conditions, the Toronto Waterfront Marathon holds a significance that no alternative venue could easily replace. The course takes him past Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, the institution where he received treatment, while family members and friends who supported him throughout his illness are there to witness his journey.

It is a route that connects his past to his present: the hospital where he fought for his health, the streets where he now tests his endurance, and the people who helped him keep moving forward when the road ahead was uncertain.

His hospital gown is therefore much more than an unusual racing outfit. It is a symbol of the vulnerability he experienced as a patient, the strength he rediscovered through running, and his determination to turn a deeply personal struggle into something that benefits others.

As he prepares for his third record attempt, the challenge remains considerable. The existing mark of 2:50:12 demands an average pace of approximately four minutes per kilometre, a formidable task even without the physical discomfort and practical challenges of racing in a hospital gown.

Nevertheless, Throop has already demonstrated that his mission can make a difference regardless of the result on the clock. His previous attempts brought attention to cancer care, while his ongoing fundraising efforts have generated substantial support for the foundation that represents an important part of his personal story.

On Sunday, he will once again take his place among thousands of runners, carrying a message that reaches well beyond the marathon course. Whether he finally breaks the world record or falls short for a third time, his presence will stand as a reminder that recovery can open doors to remarkable achievements and that gratitude can become a powerful force for helping others.

For Brandon Throop, the finish line represents more than a sporting ambition. It is an opportunity to honour the people who helped him survive, support the research that may give other families more time together, and show what can be possible after a life-altering diagnosis.

The record is still waiting. But with more than $137,000 already raised toward his fundraising goal, Throop has another reason to consider his mission a success before the starting gun even sounds.

On the streets of Toronto, the hospital gown is returning with a purpose: to celebrate survival, give back to the people who helped save a life, and turn every step into hope for someone else.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)

Long before he conquered world cross-country championships, dominated the half-marathon distance and lifted the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) trophy, [Geoffrey Kamworor](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor) was a young Kenyan student with an ambitious dream that had little to do with running: becoming a [lawyer](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=lawyer).

![Image 14](https://mybestruns.com/street/de57be259ad5f2aa804935a23c35ae7bb6b49b6ec295d0ed68325e1b13b71303.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Growing up in Keiyo South, Kamworor developed the discipline that would later define his extraordinary athletic career. His daily routine involved running approximately five kilometres to school and another five kilometres back home. What might have seemed like an ordinary journey for a schoolboy was quietly laying the foundation for a future in international distance running.

![Image 15](https://mybestruns.com/street/808283ce83ea90fb69283ae3a63fb6cc12becf4782bc79b9156f109324db53df.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

He attended Chepsamo Primary School before proceeding to Lelboinet Secondary School, where he combined his education with a growing passion for athletics. At the time, his ambitions extended beyond the track and roads. He wanted to pursue a career in law, and that dream eventually brought him an opportunity to study at a college in the United States.

However, the young Kenyan faced a defining decision: follow the academic path he had envisioned or commit himself fully to the sport that was beginning to reveal his remarkable potential. Kamworor chose athletics, a decision that would ultimately place his name among the most accomplished distance runners of his generation.

![Image 16](https://mybestruns.com/street/a94c34052d38330fd293c08402206cd4d7a39c33946639bdb76ca84e0ab123e7.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

His transformation from a promising schoolboy into an international contender began gathering momentum in 2010, when he joined the GSC training camp in Kaptagat. His development accelerated rapidly, and within a short period, an opportunity to compete in Finland exposed him to a higher level of international competition.

Still only 17, he reportedly competed nine times during that trip, demonstrating an impressive ability to adapt to the demands of competitive racing. Breaking the eight-minute barrier for 3,000 metres was an early indication of the talent that would eventually carry him to the highest levels of distance running.

![Image 17](https://mybestruns.com/street/84282c8c1c650ab6ffe7062ef243eacc858a034f27f3ff8005541232e23d4bd3.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

His breakthrough on the international stage followed in March 2011, when he captured the junior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Punta Umbría, Spain. That victory announced the arrival of a young athlete whose future would extend far beyond the junior ranks.

Kamworor was not simply a runner with speed. He possessed the endurance, tactical intelligence and competitive determination required to succeed across different distances and racing surfaces. As his career developed, those qualities became the hallmarks of an athlete capable of challenging the world's best.

Cross country became one of the foundations of Kamworor's international success. In 2015, he won the senior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Guiyang, China, confirming his status as one of the leading distance runners in the world. Two years later, he returned to the top of the podium in Kampala, Uganda, defending his senior world cross-country crown in front of a home crowd. Winning consecutive senior world titles placed him in an elite category and demonstrated his remarkable command of the demanding discipline.

On the roads, however, Kamworor established an equally impressive legacy. He won the World Half Marathon Championships in Copenhagen in 2014, Cardiff in 2016 and Valencia in 2018, becoming a three-time champion at the distance. His achievements reflected a rare combination of strength, speed and race management, enabling him to prevail against formidable international opposition.

The half marathon became one of his signature events, but Kamworor's ambitions were never confined to a single discipline. He continued to demonstrate his versatility on the track, winning silver in the men's 10,000 metres at the 2015 World Athletics Championships in Beijing, China. From the grass of cross-country courses to the roads of major international races and the track of a global championship, he repeatedly demonstrated that his talent could flourish wherever the competition took him.

Among Kamworor's most memorable achievements are his victories at the New York City Marathon in 2017 and 2019. Winning one of the world's most celebrated marathons requires exceptional endurance, but winning it twice demands much more: tactical patience, resilience and the ability to navigate a demanding course against a deep international field.

Kamworor demonstrated those qualities in both victories, establishing a special connection with the New York race and adding the marathon to an already remarkable collection of honours. His success in the American city also illustrated his ability to move successfully between distances. An athlete celebrated for his cross-country and half-marathon dominance had shown that he could also conquer the 42.195-kilometre marathon, one of the most demanding challenges in road racing.

Now, as he sets his sights on another New York campaign, the Kenyan star has an opportunity to strengthen his legacy further. A third men's open-division victory would place him among a very select group of athletes to have won the prestigious race three times. Such a milestone would be more than another addition to his trophy cabinet; it would reinforce the story of a runner whose competitive range has extended across nearly every major discipline in distance running.

Behind Kamworor's achievements lies a training environment built around discipline, consistency and high-level competition. Working under the guidance of renowned coach Patrick Sang, he has trained alongside some of Kenya's most celebrated athletes, including marathon great Eliud Kipchoge and middle- and long-distance superstar Faith Kipyegon.

Sharing a training environment with athletes of such calibre provides a demanding daily standard. Yet Kamworor has built his own identity through a career defined by major championship victories and sustained success across different racing distances. His journey has also included difficult periods and setbacks, reminding the running world that even the most accomplished champions must continually work to return to their best. His longevity at the elite level reflects the importance of patience, dedication and the willingness to keep pursuing new goals.

For aspiring athletes in Kenya, his story offers an important lesson: extraordinary achievements are often built through ordinary routines repeated consistently over many years. Those five-kilometre journeys to school and back were not glamorous. They did not come with cheering crowds, television cameras or medals. Yet they formed part of the foundation of a career that would eventually take him to the world's biggest running stages.

Kamworor's story is ultimately about a choice that changed the direction of his life. The young student who once imagined himself arguing cases in a courtroom instead built his reputation by answering the toughest questions on the running track and roads. His achievements speak for themselves: world cross-country titles, three world half-marathon crowns, a global 10,000-metre silver medal and two New York City Marathon victories.

He may never have pursued the legal career he once envisioned, but his athletic record tells a compelling story of ambition, sacrifice and extraordinary accomplishment. His pursuit of another New York triumph offers a fresh chapter in a career that has already crossed the boundaries between cross country, track and road racing.

For Geoffrey Kamworor, the courtroom was a dream he left behind. The world of distance running became the stage on which he built his name. And while the law lost a prospective lawyer, athletics gained a champion whose achievements have helped define an era of Kenyan distance running.

### [Five Years On, Agnes Tirop’s Light Still Shines in the World of Athletics](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15428)

Five years after the tragic death of [Agnes Jebet Tirop](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Agnes+Jebet+Tirop), the Kenyan distance-running star remains a powerful symbol of sporting excellence, unfulfilled potential and the urgent fight against gender-based violence.

![Image 74](https://mybestruns.com/street/5ffa31af8295f395e0aff49642712e51130387366364addc2bf2c316bd3b7edc.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Her life was cut short at a time when her career was flourishing, leaving behind a legacy that continues to resonate with athletes, fans and the wider community.

For Kenya, a country whose identity is deeply intertwined with distance-running success, Tirop represented a remarkable generation of female athletes taking the sport to new heights. Her achievements on the track, across country and on the roads had already secured her place among the country's outstanding distance runners.

![Image 75](https://mybestruns.com/street/f77fa5828a0aeb325862244b31913486d927b332f71bf5f757228761f9169abf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Five years later, the sadness of her loss remains inseparable from the extraordinary story of what she accomplished in her short but memorable career.

A Champion Who Rose to the Top at 19

Tirop announced herself on the global stage in spectacular fashion at the 2015 World Athletics Cross Country Championships in Guiyang, China. At only 19, she won the senior women's race, becoming the youngest champion in the event since Zola Budd in 1985.

Her victory demonstrated not only her natural ability but also the composure and determination that would become defining features of her running career.

She subsequently established herself among the world's leading track athletes, winning bronze medals in the women's 10,000 metres at the 2017 World Athletics Championships in London and the 2019 edition in Doha.

Those back-to-back podium finishes confirmed her consistency at the highest level and underlined her ability to compete against the strongest distance runners in the world.

Tirop also demonstrated considerable versatility at the Tokyo 2020 Olympic Games, held in 2021, where she finished fourth in the women's 5,000 metres. Although she narrowly missed the podium, her performance reinforced her reputation as one of Kenya's most accomplished emerging distance-running talents.

A World Record That Made History

Just weeks before her death, Tirop delivered one of the defining performances of her career.

![Image 76](https://mybestruns.com/street/c78d43c7e9431cc77d4c0c7a69212a2bb6f64a57b712e93e9359780084f1438e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

On September 12, 2021, she clocked an astonishing 30:01 to win the women's 10km road race at the adizero Road to Records event in Herzogenaurach, Germany.

Her performance broke the then women's-only world record by 28 seconds, establishing a new benchmark for the distance. The record was subsequently ratified by World Athletics. It was aremarkable achievement that placed her name among the legends of distance running. Although her record has since been broken, the greatness of her achievement remains untouched, and no change in the record books can diminish the extraordinary talent, courage and determination she displayed that day. Time may bring new champions and faster performances, but it can never erase the mark she left on athletics.

In a race that demanded patience, tactical awareness and an exceptional finishing effort, Tirop broke away from compatriot Sheila Chepkirui during the closing stages and powered towards the finish line.

The performance was a remarkable demonstration of her endurance and competitive instinct. It also offered a glimpse of what might have followed had she been given more years to develop her career.

Her final competitive appearance came on October 3, 2021, when she finished second in a 10km race in Geneva, Switzerland. Ten days later, the world learned of her death.

The timing made the tragedy particularly difficult to comprehend: an athlete who had just rewritten the record books and was still competing at the highest level was suddenly gone.

![Image 77](https://mybestruns.com/street/96776c2a38ffe92e203c98190e24001e4c1d47d376c5bd46c7feef1ad83b81ce.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

A Tragedy That Reached Far Beyond Sport

Tirop's death was not simply the loss of an elite athlete. It also brought renewed international attention to violence against women and the need to create safer environments in which women and girls can live, train and pursue their ambitions.

Her story became a painful reminder that medals, records and international recognition cannot shield someone from violence in their private life.

In the years since her death, her name has continued to feature in efforts to promote women's empowerment, athlete welfare and the prevention of gender-based violence. Initiatives associated with her legacy, including Agnes Tirop Angels, reflect the continuing determination to transform grief into meaningful action.

Her story remains especially significant within athletics, where the pursuit of excellence must go hand in hand with respect for athletes' safety, dignity and wellbeing.

Five Years Later, Her Legacy Endures

For young runners who dream of representing Kenya on the international stage, Tirop's career remains an example of what dedication, talent and courage can achieve.

She rose from a promising young athlete to a world champion, a two-time World Championships medallist and a world-record holder. She excelled across different distances and surfaces, leaving an impressive body of achievements before reaching her 26th birthday.

Yet her legacy cannot be measured by statistics alone. It also lies in the conversations her death continues to inspire, the women whose safety must be protected and the determination to ensure that sporting success is never separated from human dignity.

Five years on, Agnes Tirop is remembered not only for the records she set or the medals she won, but also for the future that was taken from her.

Her achievements remain part of Kenya's rich athletics history, while her story continues to call for a world in which women can pursue their dreams without fear of violence.

Agnes Tirop's life was tragically short, but her impact reaches far beyond the finish line. Her achievements will remain in the record books, her memory will endure in the hearts of athletics fans, and her legacy will continue to inspire generations to come.

### [Getting Into a World Marathon Major May Be Harder Than Running One](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15404)

For many marathoners, crossing the finish line of a World Marathon Major is the ultimate dream. But before you can worry about surviving 42.195 kilometres, there is another challenge: actually getting onto the starting line.

![Image 184](https://mybestruns.com/street/5d4dc1de5763b06ea3b94d885ebb3beb7a42c46fdce18c4925b726d66d79e60b.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

The six [Abbott World Marathon Majors](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Abbott+World+Marathon+Majors) — [Boston](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Boston), [London](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=London), [Berlin](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Berlin), [Chicago](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Chicago), [New York](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York) and [Tokyo](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Tokyo) — do not use the same entry system, and some are considerably more difficult to access than others.

Boston is arguably the clearest example of how running fast does not always guarantee a place. Unlike the other majors, the Boston Marathon is built around qualifying standards. However, meeting the published standard only gives a runner the opportunity to apply. Because demand is so high, the fastest qualifiers are accepted first. This means a runner can achieve the official qualifying time and still miss out when the cut-off moves faster than expected.

![Image 185](https://mybestruns.com/street/f43cbba0c0a711c3a231a45db4e08fb49d7ffb83dc86bd3092f391b075c9c8ca.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

London presents a completely different challenge. Its famous ballot is a random draw, making luck a major part of the process. However, runners have other avenues, including Good for Age, charity places and international tour operators. Even the Good for Age route can be highly competitive, with places allocated according to performance when demand exceeds the number of available spots.

New York City is another race where demand is enormous. The TCS New York City Marathon offers a general drawing alongside several guaranteed-entry routes, including qualifying times, charity places, international tour operators and other eligibility programmes. For serious runners, achieving the appropriate qualifying standard can be one of the most dependable ways to secure a place.

Chicago gives runners several ways to avoid relying entirely on the lottery. The Bank of America Chicago Marathon has a non-guaranteed drawing, but runners can also gain guaranteed entry through qualifying times, charity, tour operators and other eligible routes. For fast runners, meeting the published standard can provide a much more certain path to the start line.

Berlin is also heavily sought after. The BMW Berlin Marathon uses a lottery for the majority of runners, while qualifying performances can provide another route into the race. With its fast course and reputation for producing world-class times, demand remains enormous every year.

Tokyo adds another layer of difficulty, particularly for international runners. The race has a lottery as well as several other entry routes, including charity and performance-based options. International runners can also use official tour operators, although these packages generally cost more because they are tied to travel arrangements.

For runners chasing the Six Star Medal, the biggest lesson is simple: do not depend on the lottery alone.

Look closely at every possible route. Good-for-age standards, qualifying performances, charity programmes and official tour operators can all provide alternatives when the ballot does not go your way.

And then there is the reality every marathoner eventually discovers: sometimes getting rejected from a major marathon hurts almost as much as the race itself.

When that rejection email arrives, remember that parkrun is still free, happens every Saturday and does not require a lottery.

So, which World Marathon Major have you already completed — and which one is still at the top of your bucket list?

![Image 222](https://mybestruns.com/street/370218f70d026a908a79f9ff9103e597025929cac7e1cbc7b9f82dbe8a222a3e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

The relationship between the two goes far beyond the traditional athlete-coach partnership. Giuliano, a former Italian middle- and long-distance runner, has guided his daughter throughout her career, helping her develop from a promising young talent into one of the leading figures in international distance running.

![Image 223](https://mybestruns.com/street/f433c05ab81ebd63af554cf37624e75e4e381352c2f91bc84c2d42674e52b844.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Under his guidance, Nadia has risen to the biggest stages in the sport, becoming an Olympic and World Championships silver medallist while establishing herself as a formidable presence over both track and road distances.

What makes their partnership particularly special is the understanding that comes from spending a lifetime together. Giuliano knows his daughter not simply as an athlete chasing faster times and bigger victories, but as a person — understanding her character, emotions and the demands that come with competing at the highest level.

![Image 224](https://mybestruns.com/street/a163dc0c1eb07a166f8bf26aad2f1d5aee7a2e1cebef4b0c2eaf86e4708d4ce5.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Nadia has previously made it clear that she cannot imagine her career without her father in the coaching role.

“Dad has been my coach all the way. I don't know what it would be like to have another coach, and I wouldn't see another figure in his place.”

That connection is visible in the everyday details of her training. Giuliano remains closely involved in her preparation, often riding a bicycle alongside Nadia during demanding sessions and sharing the long, difficult kilometres that form the foundation of her success.

Their story is also deeply rooted in a family sporting tradition. Nadia's mother, Jawhara Saddougui, was an accomplished middle-distance runner who represented Morocco in the 800 metres. Running, therefore, was not simply introduced into Nadia's life as a career choice — it was part of the environment in which she grew up.

But the success Nadia enjoys today has been built through years of patience, sacrifice and trust. Long before the Olympic stadiums and World Championships, there were ordinary training days, difficult workouts and countless kilometres shared between a father and his daughter.

That makes their partnership one of the more compelling stories in modern athletics. The same person who helped Nadia take her first steps in the sport has remained beside her as she has progressed onto the world's biggest stages.

In elite sport, where athletes often change coaches as their careers evolve, the Battocletti partnership stands apart. It is built on something that cannot easily be replicated: decades of knowing, understanding and believing in one another.

For Nadia Battocletti, the journey to the top has never been a solo effort. Through every demanding session, breakthrough performance and major championship, her father has been there — not only as her coach, but as the person who has known her longer than anyone else.

Sometimes, the most important person in an athlete's corner is also the one who has been there since the beginning.

### [Twin Cities Marathon Turns the Page as Iconic Race Moves to Mid-October in 2027](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15393)

The [Twin Cities Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Twin+Cities+Marathon) has closed the chapter on one of the longest-running traditions in American marathon racing, with the event set to leave its familiar early-October slot and move to mid-October beginning in 2027.

![Image 231](https://mybestruns.com/street/576a8caa96e1558e17836251b6dd208e91299ab942e1fcc3416edc3b2e811dac.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

The 2026 edition marked the final time the race would be held in its traditional early-October window, bringing an end to a calendar tradition that has defined the event for more than four decades.

![Image 232](https://mybestruns.com/street/c17c648a6b8400bbeb6d8519e3fa1e61fde3ef919778c6973281fe610cd1e68a.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Beginning in 2027, Twin Cities Marathon Weekend will move to a mid-October date. The decision follows growing concerns over warmer and increasingly unpredictable conditions during the race's traditional weekend, with organisers seeking a better environment for runners, spectators and volunteers.

The change is more than a simple adjustment to the racing calendar. Early October, once synonymous with crisp autumn temperatures in Minnesota, has increasingly brought challenging heat. In recent years, organisers have had to contend with conditions that can place additional stress on marathon runners and increase demands on medical and public-safety teams.

![Image 233](https://mybestruns.com/street/12413240599ee9c1859b7b3b7f7fa683f7e05a7c9997d36e865c0052b7fa2888.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

The inaugural Twin Cities Marathon was held on October 3, 1982, attracting 4,563 entrants. What began as a relatively young marathon has since developed into one of the most recognisable road races in the United States, growing alongside the running communities of Minneapolis and St. Paul.

The course itself has long been one of the event's defining features. Runners travel through Minneapolis, pass the city's famous chain of lakes and follow a scenic route toward St. Paul before finishing near the Minnesota State Capitol. The combination of major urban landmarks, parkways, waterways and autumn scenery has helped give the race its distinctive identity.

The 2026 edition continued that long tradition, with roughly 30,000 runners taking part across the various events of Marathon Weekend. The marathon also featured defending champions Will Norris and Jane Bareikis, while favourable temperatures provided runners with much more comfortable conditions than some of the warmer editions in recent years.

Yet even with favourable weather this year, the decision to move the race reflects a longer-term concern. Organisers are looking beyond a single race morning and considering how changing weather patterns could affect the event in the years ahead.

For runners, the move could eventually become one of the most important changes in the marathon's modern history. A later October date offers the possibility of cooler racing conditions while preserving the course, the atmosphere and the traditions that have made Twin Cities Marathon a fixture on the American running calendar.

For more than four decades, the first Sunday of October provided a familiar date for thousands of runners preparing to take on the Twin Cities course.

That tradition has now reached its final chapter.

From 2027, the Twin Cities Marathon will arrive later in the fall — opening a new era for a race whose history remains firmly connected to the streets of Minneapolis and St. Paul.

For Yugeta, the finish line simply took longer to reach.

Forty-three years after running her first marathon, she finally turned a lifelong ambition into a piece of running history — proving that sometimes the most extraordinary victories are the ones that take the longest to arrive.

### [7 Packing Tips for Your First Time Traveling For a Race](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15391)

Traveling for a race is the perfect excuse to turn a running weekend into an adventure. Perhaps you’re heading to the [Tokyo Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/TokyoMarathon?b=prz&details=Y)⁠ and already thinking about the sushi and ramen you’ll enjoy afterward. Or maybe your next finish line is beside the beach.

Between training, booking a hotel and planning what to explore, packing can become an afterthought. Then race morning arrives, and your favorite socks are still at home, your race information is buried in your suitcase and your water bottle is nowhere to be found.

A little organization before departure can make the entire trip smoother. These seven packing tips will help you arrive ready to run and enjoy the weekend.

1. Pack Your Race-Day Outfit in Your Carry-On

Keep your race-day clothing and essentials in your carry-on. Pack your running top, shorts or tights, socks, sports bra if needed, and the small items you depend on during a race. If your checked luggage is delayed, your key gear will still be with you.

![Image 240](https://mybestruns.com/street/5c6a74501acac9b0ede92d94316cdfa0b4cdf306eb1a8ff130a06ab99f4b0028.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Fold your race outfit together or place it in a packing pouch so everything is easy to find. A smaller zip pouch can hold accessories. Knowing exactly where your race kit is means one less thing to worry about when you arrive.

2. Wear Your Running Shoes on the Plane

Your running shoes deserve the same attention as your race outfit. Wearing them on the plane keeps them out of checked luggage and leaves more room in your suitcase.

Choose a familiar pair you have already used in training. Race weekend is not the time to discover that new shoes rub or fit differently than expected. If you prefer to travel in another pair, keep your race shoes in your carry-on.

![Image 241](https://mybestruns.com/street/e69995b49a9f8387df3a425267e0e7bfdd5cf1fd3f9dcf4c2ee037e9c24fb131.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

3. Bring a Spacious Bag for Your Gear

A race trip often requires more than running clothes. Add a jacket, recovery clothes, snacks and accessories, and your packing list grows quickly. A spacious duffel with sturdy handles and useful pockets can keep those extras organized and serve as a day bag at your destination.

Think about what you’ll do beyond race day. A hike may call for trail shoes and a light layer. If pickleball is part of your plans, you may want a paddle and extra clothes.

The same thinking applies when choosing your bag. If you’re planning a few games on the court during the trip, consider [pickleball tour and duffel bags](https://pickleballnation.com/collections/pickleball-bags-and-backpacks)⁠. A backpack may be more practical for hiking or exploring on foot. Choose a bag that suits your itinerary, and check your airline’s size and weight limits before packing.

4. Organize Your Bib and Race Documents

Keep your identification, registration confirmation and race instructions together. A slim document pouch works well for paper copies, while a dedicated folder on your phone can keep digital information easy to access.

Download important details before leaving home, including the race map, confirmation email and packet pickup instructions. Save copies you can open without an internet connection.

If you already have your bib, keep it flat and protected. Otherwise, check where and when you need to collect it and what identification the organizer requires. Handling these details in advance helps keep the pre-race scramble to a minimum.

5. Take Familiar Snacks with You

Race travel can disrupt your usual eating routine. Your preferred breakfast may be unavailable, and the hotel buffet may not offer what you normally eat before a run.

Bring the bars, gels and electrolyte products you have already used in training. Your [runner’s diet](https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/runners-diet)⁠ shouldn’t become a vacation guessing game.

Count what you’ll need for travel and race day, then pack a little extra. Keep some familiar snacks in your carry-on and bring enough race fuel for your planned strategy. Check destination rules before carrying food across international borders.

6. Always Have a Water Bottle

Busy travel days can make it easy to forget your usual drinking habits. A reusable water bottle is a simple item that deserves a place on your packing list.

Carry it empty through airport security, then fill it where drinking water is available. Keep it handy during your journey and when heading out for packet pickup or other race activities.

Staying hydrated is also part of [caring for your body while traveling](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php/7021)⁠. If an electrolyte mix is already part of your routine, pack your usual product. Having familiar supplies nearby makes it easier to maintain your normal habits while traveling.

7. Pack Layers for Changing Weather

A mild forecast doesn’t always reflect how it will feel while waiting at the starting line early in the morning. Pack a lightweight layer you have already worn while running.

A zip jacket or long-sleeve top can help you stay comfortable before the start. Decide in advance whether you’ll carry it during the race or leave it at an official bag check, following the organizer’s instructions.

For colder conditions, familiar gloves and other tested gear can help. Review this guide to [running in cold weather](https://mybestruns.com/What_to_Wear_for_Running_in_Cold_Weather.html)⁠, then check the forecast again before departure and once more before race morning so you can make any final adjustments.

Thoughtful packing helps you get more out of a destination race. Keep essential gear close, choose a bag that works for your plans and organize your documents before you leave. With those details handled, you can spend less time searching through your suitcase and more time enjoying the run—and everything that comes afterward.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
Long before he conquered world cross-country championships, dominated the half-marathon distance and lifted the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) trophy, [Geoffrey Kamworor](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor) was a young Kenyan student with an ambitious dream that had little to do with running: becoming a [lawyer](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=lawyer).
![Image 2](https://mybestruns.com/street/de57be259ad5f2aa804935a23c35ae7bb6b49b6ec295d0ed68325e1b13b71303.jpg?i=1792160904&t=1792160904)
Growing up in Keiyo South, Kamworor developed the discipline that would later define his extraordinary athletic career. His daily routine involved running approximately five kilometres to school and another five kilometres back home. What might have seemed like an ordinary journey for a schoolboy was quietly laying the foundation for a future in international distance running.
![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/808283ce83ea90fb69283ae3a63fb6cc12becf4782bc79b9156f109324db53df.jpg?i=1792160904&t=1792160904)
He attended Chepsamo Primary School before proceeding to Lelboinet Secondary School, where he combined his education with a growing passion for athletics. At the time, his ambitions extended beyond the track and roads. He wanted to pursue a career in law, and that dream eventually brought him an opportunity to study at a college in the United States.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
However, the young Kenyan faced a defining decision: follow the academic path he had envisioned or commit himself fully to the sport that was beginning to reveal his remarkable potential. Kamworor chose athletics, a decision that would ultimately place his name among the most accomplished distance runners of his generation.
![Image 4](https://mybestruns.com/street/a94c34052d38330fd293c08402206cd4d7a39c33946639bdb76ca84e0ab123e7.jpg?i=1792160904&t=1792160904)
His transformation from a promising schoolboy into an international contender began gathering momentum in 2010, when he joined the GSC training camp in Kaptagat. His development accelerated rapidly, and within a short period, an opportunity to compete in Finland exposed him to a higher level of international competition.
Still only 17, he reportedly competed nine times during that trip, demonstrating an impressive ability to adapt to the demands of competitive racing. “In Cardiff, it was wet and I slipped at the start,” Kamworor recalled. “Nobody tripped me. It was hard running through the crowd, but the fall made me more determined.”
That determination would be tested even further. In 2020, during the isolation of the COVID-19 pandemic, Kamworor’s career was nearly derailed when he was struck from behind by a motorcycle while training in Eldoret.
“I fractured my tibia and couldn’t run for six months,” he said. “When I started running again, my body was still out of balance and I kept getting injured. It took me over three years to be able to run properly.”

### [Tola and Obiri lead elite fields for New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=12607)
Organisers of the 2024 TCS New York City Marathon have revealed a world-class line up for this year’s World Athletics Platinum Label road race on 3 November, led by defending champions Tamirat Tola and Hellen Obiri.
Since winning last year in a course record of 2:04:58, Tola won the Olympic title in Paris in a Games record of 2:06:26. What made his feat all the more impressive is that he was only drafted into the Ethiopian team two weeks before the Games, having initially been named as a reserve.
![Image 106](https://mybestruns.com/street/79a0fa58be6d45820b6427523fe76bf575ccf966b335c091dde5a518ca94d4e5.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
“I’m excited to defend my title in New York, especially coming off an Olympic-record marathon performance,” said Tola. “The hilly course and crowds in Paris definitely prepared me well for the bridges and spectators in New York, where maybe I can go even faster this year.”
Two-time Olympic medallist Bashir Abdi will also be one to watch; the Belgian earned silver at the recent Olympics, having taken bronze at the Tokyo Olympics in 2021 and at the 2022 World Championships.
Three past winners – all from Kenya – are also in the field: 2022 champion Evans Chebet, 2021 winner Albert Korir, and 2019 and 2017 victor Geoffrey Kamworor. Chebet has twice won the Boston Marathon, and has finished first or second in 13 marathons. Kamworor has made it on to the podium in all four of his New York Marathon appearances.
Fellow Kenyan Abel Kipchumba, who won this year’s NYC Half Marathon, will be making his New York City Marathon debut.

### [Tola and Obiri lead elite fields for New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=12607)
The US charge is led by Conner Mantz and Clayton Young, who finished eighth and ninth respectively in the Paris Olympic marathon.
Women’s Open Division
Obiri is a three-time Olympic medallist and seven-time world medallist. Last year the Kenyan became the first woman in 34 years to win both Boston and New York in the same calendar year. So far this year, she retained her Boston Marathon title and went on to earn bronze in the Olympic marathon.
“There’s no place like New York, and I am so ready to defend my title,” said Obiri. “I have been racing very well on the roads in the US, and I hope I can have another good day that sees me in contention once we enter the final stages in Central Park.”
Fellow Kenyan Sharon Lokedi, the 2022 NYC Marathon winner, will return after finishing third last year and fourth in the Olympic marathon in Paris. The Kenyan delegation will also include 2010 champion Edna Kiplagat, four-time Olympic medallist Vivian Cheruiyot, and Sheila Chepkirui, who owns the fastest personal best in the field.
Ethiopia’s Tirunesh Dibaba will make her New York City Marathon debut and is one of the world’s most accomplished long-distance runners as a three-time Olympic and 16-time world champion. She will be joined by compatriot Senbere Teferi.
Dakotah Lindwurm, the top US finisher in the marathon at the Paris Olympics, will lead the US contingent.

### [Antrim Coast Half Marathon: Yehualaw returns despite 2021 world record blow](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=12525)
[Yalemzerf Yehualaw](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Yalemzerf+Yehualaw) returns to the Antrim Coast Half Marathon a year after seemingly breaking the women's world record only to learn weeks later that the course had been 54 metres short.
Race director James McIlroy is guaranteeing there will be no repeat of last year's hiccup which meant the Ethiopian's time could not be ratified.
"You don't want to blame Covid but it certainly was a factor," says McIlroy.
![Image 112](https://mybestruns.com/street/f4d38fe3b91fc555721d8a1a7abed8c06ffb4787cd1e74c3b9a7f1bd73911d46.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
"The protocol is to measure the course twice but we were unable to do that."
"We couldn't get anyone to fly here before the race to do the measurement [because of the Covid situation] so we had to do it post the race.
![Image 113](https://mybestruns.com/street/e7856c195519b2dc4619e41ac0f428b209c00cee666c519655a9294d58fb5e44.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
"The frustration is that with 50 metres short, if you add 10 seconds on, 65% of the elite race would still have run a personal best and Yalemzerf would still have been the first woman to run under 64 minutes.
"But she's back again in good shape and the course is ratified and measured correctly."
Course even faster this year - McIlroy

### [Antrim Coast Half Marathon: Yehualaw returns despite 2021 world record blow](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=12525)
Indeed, McIlroy believes course tweaks this year could lead to Yalemzerf going even faster than the 63 minutes and 44 seconds she clocked last year - although the 23-year-old will have to go some to break the world mark of 62:52 set by compatriot Letesenbet Gidey in Valencia last October.
Yalemzerf's own time of 63:51 set as she finished runner-up that day remains the second fastest time in history but the 59 seconds to Gidey's world mark is a huge amount - even in half marathon terms.
McIlroy admits the UK all-comers half marathon record of 65:52 set by Kenyan Edith Chelimo in Cardiff five years ago will be a more realistic target for Yalemzerf and several of other leading ladies.
"We think we've made the course even faster," added former Great Britain Olympic 800m athlete McIlroy.
"We've taken out the section in the harbour so we've taken out one tight turn and going around the roundabout clockwise instead of anti-clockwise should also help the athletes."
While Yalemzerf, 23, will be a strong favourite, the presence of her compatriots and training partners Tsehay Gemechu [PB 65:08] and Gete Alemayehu [PB 66:37] should ensure that she has competitive company in the early stages as opposed to merely her male pacemakers.
Last year, Yehualaw finished more than six minutes ahead of Kenyan runner-up Vane Nyanamba.
2021 men's winner Jemal Yimer is also back in the Larne field and will again be the man to beat give his outstanding personal best of 58:33 set in 2018, which is 49 seconds quicker than the next fastest competitor, compatriot Tesfahun Akalnew.
Yimer was three seconds outside Sir Mo Farah's course record of 60:27 set in 2020 when he triumphed 12 months ago.

### [Antrim Coast Half Marathon: Yehualaw returns despite 2021 world record blow](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=12525)
Akalnew finished one second behind his compatriot 12 months ago and is again back in the field along with last year's third placer Shadrack Kimining of Kenya.
With the field also including sub-60 minute men Ethiopians Huseydin Mohamed and Gizealew Ayana, organiser McIlroy is very optimistic that the one-hour barrier will be broken for the first time on Irish soil, with Geoffrey Kamworor's UK all-comers mark of 59:10 from 2016 possibly also in danger.
Englishman Marc Scott finished only five seconds behind Yimer in fourth spot 12 months ago and will be joined in the field by fellow British Olympian Callum Hawkins, whose has a half marathon best of exactly 60 minutes.
With Ireland's Tokyo competitor Stephen Scullion a late withdrawal from Sunday's race, Irish male hopefuls David Mansfield and Paul O'Donnell will both be aiming to improve their respective personal best of 63:23 and 63:37.
The women's event could see a good domestic battle for top-10 finishes between Emma Mitchell, Fionnuala Ross and Northern Ireland Commonwealth Games competitor this summer, Hannah Irwin.
The Eamonn Christie-coached Mitchell is the fifth fastest in the women's field on lifetime bests behind the African contingent with a 72:28 mark set in Valencia in 2019, while Ross has clocked 73:08 and Irwin 73:23.
The mass race in the event which starts and finishes in Larne will have around 6,000 competitors with McIlroy delighted to report "entrants from 19 countries this year".

### [Antrim Coast Half Marathon: Yehualaw returns despite 2021 world record blow](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=12525)
[Yalemzerf Yehualaw](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Yalemzerf+Yehualaw) returns to the Antrim Coast Half Marathon a year after seemingly breaking the women's world record only to learn weeks later that the course had been 54 metres short.
Race director James McIlroy is guaranteeing there will be no repeat of last year's hiccup which meant the Ethiopian's time could not be ratified.
"You don't want to blame Covid but it certainly was a factor," says McIlroy.
![Image 112](https://mybestruns.com/street/f4d38fe3b91fc555721d8a1a7abed8c06ffb4787cd1e74c3b9a7f1bd73911d46.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
"The protocol is to measure the course twice but we were unable to do that."
"We couldn't get anyone to fly here before the race to do the measurement [because of the Covid situation] so we had to do it post the race.
![Image 113](https://mybestruns.com/street/e7856c195519b2dc4619e41ac0f428b209c00cee666c519655a9294d58fb5e44.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
"The frustration is that with 50 metres short, if you add 10 seconds on, 65% of the elite race would still have run a personal best and Yalemzerf would still have been the first woman to run under 64 minutes.
"But she's back again in good shape and the course is ratified and measured correctly."
Course even faster this year - McIlroy

### [Antrim Coast Half Marathon: Yehualaw returns despite 2021 world record blow](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=12525)
Indeed, McIlroy believes course tweaks this year could lead to Yalemzerf going even faster than the 63 minutes and 44 seconds she clocked last year - although the 23-year-old will have to go some to break the world mark of 62:52 set by compatriot Letesenbet Gidey in Valencia last October.
Yalemzerf's own time of 63:51 set as she finished runner-up that day remains the second fastest time in history but the 59 seconds to Gidey's world mark is a huge amount - even in half marathon terms.
McIlroy admits the UK all-comers half marathon record of 65:52 set by Kenyan Edith Chelimo in Cardiff five years ago will be a more realistic target for Yalemzerf and several of other leading ladies.
"We think we've made the course even faster," added former Great Britain Olympic 800m athlete McIlroy.
"We've taken out the section in the harbour so we've taken out one tight turn and going around the roundabout clockwise instead of anti-clockwise should also help the athletes."
While Yalemzerf, 23, will be a strong favourite, the presence of her compatriots and training partners Tsehay Gemechu [PB 65:08] and Gete Alemayehu [PB 66:37] should ensure that she has competitive company in the early stages as opposed to merely her male pacemakers.
Last year, Yehualaw finished more than six minutes ahead of Kenyan runner-up Vane Nyanamba.
2021 men's winner Jemal Yimer is also back in the Larne field and will again be the man to beat give his outstanding personal best of 58:33 set in 2018, which is 49 seconds quicker than the next fastest competitor, compatriot Tesfahun Akalnew.
Yimer was three seconds outside Sir Mo Farah's course record of 60:27 set in 2020 when he triumphed 12 months ago.

### [Antrim Coast Half Marathon: Yehualaw returns despite 2021 world record blow](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=12525)
Akalnew finished one second behind his compatriot 12 months ago and is again back in the field along with last year's third placer Shadrack Kimining of Kenya.
With the field also including sub-60 minute men Ethiopians Huseydin Mohamed and Gizealew Ayana, organiser McIlroy is very optimistic that the one-hour barrier will be broken for the first time on Irish soil, with Geoffrey Kamworor's UK all-comers mark of 59:10 from 2016 possibly also in danger.
Englishman Marc Scott finished only five seconds behind Yimer in fourth spot 12 months ago and will be joined in the field by fellow British Olympian Callum Hawkins, whose has a half marathon best of exactly 60 minutes.
With Ireland's Tokyo competitor Stephen Scullion a late withdrawal from Sunday's race, Irish male hopefuls David Mansfield and Paul O'Donnell will both be aiming to improve their respective personal best of 63:23 and 63:37.
The women's event could see a good domestic battle for top-10 finishes between Emma Mitchell, Fionnuala Ross and Northern Ireland Commonwealth Games competitor this summer, Hannah Irwin.
The Eamonn Christie-coached Mitchell is the fifth fastest in the women's field on lifetime bests behind the African contingent with a 72:28 mark set in Valencia in 2019, while Ross has clocked 73:08 and Irwin 73:23.
The mass race in the event which starts and finishes in Larne will have around 6,000 competitors with McIlroy delighted to report "entrants from 19 countries this year".

Ethiopian long-distance running legend [Kenenisa Bekele](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=kenenisa+Bekele) has voiced doubts about his potential success in the upcoming London Marathon following his seventh-place finish at the New York Half Marathon on Sunday.
Bekele clocked 1:03:59 for seventh place in a race won by Kenya’s Abel Kipchumba, who timed 1:00:25, with Morocco’s Zouhair Talbi (1:00:41) and Ethiopian Yemane Haileselassie (1:01:37) completing the podium.

The race was part of Bekele’s pre-London preparations but he looked to have bitten more than he could chew in the streets of New York.
Reflecting on the challenges encountered during the New York race, Bekele acknowledged the demanding nature of the course and emphasised the need for additional preparation to assess his fitness levels.

### [Hope for Geoffrey Kamworor and Alexander Mutiso as Kenenisa Bekele expresses London Marathon uncertainty](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11795)
![Image 137](https://mybestruns.com/street/2ac200258c237688e51d116126152c73a0dce49a72f0335e6570bffadd5a1a15.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
"The course was tough. This race was important to see how my shape is so I think I need more preparations,"Bekele remarked.
Despite his determination to excel in the London Marathon on April 21, Bekele admitted that he is still in the process of building up his form and fitness for the upcoming challenge.
"I am still on the build-up because my big goal is success in London but this race was important to see my shape so I think I need more preparations,"he explained.
Acknowledging the importance of both time and positioning in the London Marathon, Bekele emphasised his commitment to being fully prepared for the prestigious event.
"Not only time but the position is really important in London. I think I will be ready. I have a couple of weeks to prepare and try to be ready to do something,"he asserted optimistically, despite his reservations.
As Bekele looks ahead to the London Marathon, he faces the challenge of fine-tuning his preparation and performance to meet the high expectations set for himself.
The Ethiopian great will be up against a formidable cast in London that includes Kenya’s Geoffrey Kamworor, two-time New York Marathon champion and second in London last year, and Alexander Mutiso, who finished second in Valencia last year.
He also has Ethiopian compatriots Tamirat Tola, the New York Marathon champion, and Mosinet Geremew, the seventh-fastest man in history.
This is also part of the two-time Berlin Marathon champion’s preparations towards the Olympics although he still not sure if he will make Ethiopia’s marathon team to the Paris Games.
“They can select based on time, and position is also very important,”Bekele said when asked about his chances of making the Olympics team.

### [Hope for Geoffrey Kamworor and Alexander Mutiso as Kenenisa Bekele expresses London Marathon uncertainty](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11795)
“It will depend on the competitors and they have their own method of selection. There are many Ethiopian marathoners so they have their own plan. I think my chance is 50-50 so I have to try my best.”
Bekele has been to London six times, managing second place in 2017 after third a year earlier, but could only finish sixth in 2018 and fifth in 2022. He, however, had a setback in 2020, when he was forced to withdraw with a calf injury, before failing to finish last year’s race.

Collapsing over the line with a rueful smile, Cheptegei made it clear that his objective had been achieved.
He knew that his preparation for the event had been far from perfect. It started with pulling out of the Wanda Diamond League final due to a reaction to wearing spikes in defending his world 10,000m crown in Budapest. Once he did return, the weeks that followed saw his usual runs around the rolling hills of Kapchorwa deemed too dangerous due to constant deluges.
Cheptegei never ran more than 160km a week – which, by the standards of most current marathon specialists, was a light schedule.
Yet in Valencia, he still chose to go with the pace. Many would expect little else from a world 5000m and 10,000m record holder consistently pushing the margins of the possible.
For many fans, their first clear memory of Cheptegei at a senior level was his performance at the 2017 World Cross Country Championships on home soil in Kampala.
That day, the 2016 Olympic 10,000m sixth-place finisher ripped the senior race apart, striding away through the middle section and building a huge lead into the final kilometer.
The Ugandan fans chasing him in bursts around the course almost went as far as to hand over the red, yellow and black flag.
As the commentators proclaimed his title, Cheptegei had pushed himself to the limit, a smooth stride rolling to a wayward struggle.

Veteran athletics coach Julius Kirwa has revealed how he faced a difficult time narrowing down to 20 athletes who will represent Kenya at the Paris 2024 Olympics.
![Image 164](https://mybestruns.com/street/7523d61468571aaefc122c3c93d3a3a9cd9458d19a7f7928336d4a7f3917e74e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Athletics Kenya (AK) named a provisional squad of 20 (10 men and as many women) with marathon great Eliud Kipchoge, world record holder Kelvin Kiptum, Boston and New York Marathon champion Hellen Obiri as well as three-time world half marathon champion Peres Jepchirchir among the big names included.
While the selection was based heavily on world ranking and athletes’ performances in major marathons, Kirwa admits it was a herculean task given the many good runners in the country.
![Image 165](https://mybestruns.com/street/e9c7a6468355cbcc9b46f9cfbde92cd25d11daf71bbaae08b263d4d9426b628a.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
“We are selecting them based on their time and world ranking. We are allowed to field three athletes only and in Kenya, we have about 120 athletes who are capable of representing the country,”said Kirwa.

### [Athletics coach explains the headache he faced selecting Kenya’s marathon team for Paris Olympics](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11324)
“Other countries have a few to pick from but here, it has not been easy. I have taken a lot of time monitoring and some are still coming up like Alexander Mutiso ran very well in Valencia [finished second in 2:03:11 on Sunday] but it was too late to put in someone.
“We followed the world ranking and in Kenya we have Kiptum leading then Eliud so there was no need of jumping. We follow that way unless someone withdraws and you go to the next best ranked runner.”
Besides Kipchoge and Kiptum, Vincent Ngetich, second at the Berlin Marathon this year, Rotterdam Marathon runners-up Timothy Kiplagat, former Chicago and Boston Marathon champion Benson Kipruto, Bernard Koech, two-time New York Marathon champion Geoffrey Kamworor, Cyprian Kotut, 2022 London Marathon champion Amos Kipruto and Titus Kipruto also made the list.
The women’s team has Obiri and Jepchirchir as well as former world record holder Brigid Kosgei, Tokyo Marathon champion Rosemary Wanjiru, former world champion Marathon Ruth Chepng’etich, former world half marathon record holder Joycilline Jepkosgei, Sheila Chepkirui, Judith Jeptum Korir, Selly Chepyego and Sharon Lokedi.
However, world ranking was not the only consideration given Joshua Belet and Ronald Korir, who who are ahead of Kamworor on the rankings, missed out same as Dorcas Chepchirchir and Jackline Chelal.
AK explained that they also looked at consistency, championship mentality and the attitude of the athletes before setting on the squad.

### [2023 NYC Marathon Men’s Preview](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11149)
This year’s TCS New York City Marathon fields are very different. The women’s race is absolutely stacked — the best in race history and one of the greatest assembled in the history of the sport. If you haven’t read our women’s preview yet,go ahead and do it right now. The men’s race is more of a typical NYC field — a large diversity of nationalities with some premium East African talent at the top.
Initially, the headline showdown on the men’s side was going to be the battle betweeen 2022 champ Evans Chebet and 2017/2019 champ Geoffrey Kamworor, but both withdrew last month. Instead, the field is led by Ethiopians Tamirat Tola(the 2022 world champ) and Shura Kitata, who has twice finished as runner-up in NYC but never won. Throw in a rising Cam Levins and the debut of Edward Cheserek, and there will still be some intrigue on the men’s side, but this is without a doubt the shallowest men’s major of 2023. Here are the men to watch in Sunday’s field.
The Three Guys Who Have Won Majors Before
Tamirat Tola, Ethiopia, 2:03:39 pb (2021 Amsterdam), 32 years oldSignficant wins: 2017 Dubai, 2021 Amsterdam, 2022 Worlds
![Image 176](https://mybestruns.com/street/f4460c88366bf6db0a70f2ebe82d18930c8155e31ce7fe2cfb7af6823383a4bf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

### [2023 NYC Marathon Men’s Preview](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11149)
Albert Korir, Kenya, 2:08:03 pb (2019 Ottawa), 29 years oldSignificant wins: 2019 Houston, 2021 New York
When looking for a winner, the first place to start is the runners who have won a major before. Seven of the last 10 NYC men’s winners had already won a major when they won New York. Tola, Kitata, and Korir all fit that criteria, with Tola and Kitata particularly worth of note (though Korir is the only one of the trio to have won NYC before).
![Image 177](https://mybestruns.com/street/fcdf8c58e6bdce6fa69ab0b680f2c3c7092bedb87ae5476a38612f8d00d1df3b.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The world champion last year, Tola ran 2:03:40 in Valencia in December, then finished 3rd in London in April. He did drop out of his most recent marathon at Worlds in August, but it’s worth noting he was in 3rd at 37k and dropped out in the final 5k once he was no longer in medal position. He quickly rebounded to win the Great North Run on September 10 by more than a minute in 59:58. Tola has some experience in NYC, but has had the least success of the trio in New York — Tolas was 4th in his two previous appearances in 2018 and 2019. Tola has won 3 of his career 16 marathons.

### [2023 NYC Marathon Men’s Preview](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11149)
Kitata was second in NYC a year ago and was also second in 2018, when he ran 2:06:01 — the third-fastest time ever in NYC. When he’s on his game, he’s one of the best in the world — he broke Eliud Kipchoge‘s long win streak by winning the 2020 London Marathon. But Kitata is coming off one of the worst marathons of his career as he was only 14th in Boston in April. Kitata has won 3 of his 18 career marathons.
Korir won NYC in 2021 — granted, against a very watered-down field that included just one man with a pb under 2:07– and was 2nd in 2019, beating both Tola and Kitata in the process. A grinder, he most recently finished a solid 4th in Boston in 2:08:01 and will be a contender again on Sunday. Korir has won 5 of his career 15 marathons.
In my mind, there’s a roughly a 65% chance one of these guys is your winner on Sunday, with the remaining 35% split between a few slightly longer shots. Let’s get to them.
The Global Medalists
Abdi Nageeye, Netherlands, 2:04:56 pb (2022 Rotterdam), 34 years old
Maru Teferi, Israel, 2:06:43 pb (2022 Fukuoka), 31 years old
Nageeye and Teferi have a lot in common. Both moved from East Africa to Europe as children (Nageeye from Somalia to the Netherlands when he was 6, Teferi from Ethiopia to Israel when he was 14). Both have earned global medals (2021 Olympic silver for Nageeye, 2023 World silver for Teferi). Both won a famous marathon in 2022 (Rotterdam for Nageeye, Fukuoka for Teferi). One more similarity: neither has won a World Marathon Major.

### [2023 NYC Marathon Men’s Preview](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11149)
But if you’ve medalled at the Olympics/Worlds and won Rotterdam/Fukuoka, you’re pretty damn close to winning a major. Both are coming off the World Championship marathon in August, where Teferi took silver and Nageeye dropped out after 25k.
It would be a pretty cool story if either man won as it took both of them a while to reach their current level: Nageeye did not break 2:10 until his sixth marathon; Teferi did not do it until marathon #10! New York will be career marathon #20 for Nageeye (and he’s only won 1 of them) and #19 for Teferi (and he’s only won 2 of them), and runners almost never win their first major that deep into their careers. But Nageeye and Teferi have also continued to improve throughout their careers. They have a shot.
The Former NCAA Stars
Cam Levins, Canada, 2:05:36 pb (2023 Tokyo)
Edward Cheserek, Kenya, debut.
Though Levins was an NCAA champion on the track at Southern Utah — he actually beat out future Olympic medalist Paul Chelimo to win the 5,000 in 2012 — his triple sessions and mega-miles (170+ per week) suggested his body was built to withstand the pounding of the marathon. It took a few years, but Levins is now world-class, running a 2+ minute pb of 2:07:09 to finish 4th at Worlds last year, and following that up with another huge pb, 2:05:36 in Tokyo in March. He’s run faster than any North American athlete in history.
