### [2023 NYC Marathon Men’s Preview](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11149)
Kitata was second in NYC a year ago and was also second in 2018, when he ran 2:06:01 — the third-fastest time ever in NYC. When he’s on his game, he’s one of the best in the world — he broke Eliud Kipchoge‘s long win streak by winning the 2020 London Marathon. But Kitata is coming off one of the worst marathons of his career as he was only 14th in Boston in April. Kitata has won 3 of his 18 career marathons.
Korir won NYC in 2021 — granted, against a very watered-down field that included just one man with a pb under 2:07– and was 2nd in 2019, beating both Tola and Kitata in the process. A grinder, he most recently finished a solid 4th in Boston in 2:08:01 and will be a contender again on Sunday. Korir has won 5 of his career 15 marathons.
In my mind, there’s a roughly a 65% chance one of these guys is your winner on Sunday, with the remaining 35% split between a few slightly longer shots. Let’s get to them.
The Global Medalists
Abdi Nageeye, Netherlands, 2:04:56 pb (2022 Rotterdam), 34 years old
Maru Teferi, Israel, 2:06:43 pb (2022 Fukuoka), 31 years old
Nageeye and Teferi have a lot in common. Both moved from East Africa to Europe as children (Nageeye from Somalia to the Netherlands when he was 6, Teferi from Ethiopia to Israel when he was 14). Both have earned global medals (2021 Olympic silver for Nageeye, 2023 World silver for Teferi). Both won a famous marathon in 2022 (Rotterdam for Nageeye, Fukuoka for Teferi). One more similarity: neither has won a World Marathon Major.

### [2023 NYC Marathon Men’s Preview](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11149)
But if you’ve medalled at the Olympics/Worlds and won Rotterdam/Fukuoka, you’re pretty damn close to winning a major. Both are coming off the World Championship marathon in August, where Teferi took silver and Nageeye dropped out after 25k.
It would be a pretty cool story if either man won as it took both of them a while to reach their current level: Nageeye did not break 2:10 until his sixth marathon; Teferi did not do it until marathon #10! New York will be career marathon #20 for Nageeye (and he’s only won 1 of them) and #19 for Teferi (and he’s only won 2 of them), and runners almost never win their first major that deep into their careers. But Nageeye and Teferi have also continued to improve throughout their careers. They have a shot.
The Former NCAA Stars
Cam Levins, Canada, 2:05:36 pb (2023 Tokyo)
Edward Cheserek, Kenya, debut.
Though Levins was an NCAA champion on the track at Southern Utah — he actually beat out future Olympic medalist Paul Chelimo to win the 5,000 in 2012 — his triple sessions and mega-miles (170+ per week) suggested his body was built to withstand the pounding of the marathon. It took a few years, but Levins is now world-class, running a 2+ minute pb of 2:07:09 to finish 4th at Worlds last year, and following that up with another huge pb, 2:05:36 in Tokyo in March. He’s run faster than any North American athlete in history.

### [2023 NYC Marathon Men’s Preview](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11149)
No Canadian has ever won New York, and Levins will need an off day or two by the big guns if he is to break that drought. But Levins was only 14 seconds off the win in Tokyo in March, and he may not be done improving. Of the three men seeded above him in NYC, two are coming off DNFs (Tola and Nageeye) and the other is coming off a poor showing in Boston (Kitata). If Sharon Lokedi can win NY, why can’t Levins?
Speaking of Loked, her partner Edward Cheserek is making his marathon debut on Sunday — something that is suddenly much more exciting after Cheserek took down 2:04 marathoner Bernard Koech to win the Copenhagen Half on September 17 in 59:11. While Cheserek has had a few standout performances since graduating from the University of Oregon since 2017 (3:49 mile, 27:23 10k), his professional career has largely been one of frustration following 17 NCAA titles in Eugene. In six pro seasons, Cheserek has competed in just two Diamond Leagues (finishing 15th and 7th) and never run at a global championship.
Throughout that time, Cheserek’s desire had been to stay on the track, which was one of the reasons he split with coach Stephen Haas to reunite with his college coach Andy Powell.Based on what he had seen in training, Haas believed Cheserek was better suited for the marathon and told him as much. Now, after spending time training in Kenya — 2022 NYC champ Evans Chebet is a friend and occasional training partner — Cheserek has decided to make the leap.
“A lot of people have probably got in his ear and said, look you can be really good at this if you commited to it and trained for it,” said Haas, who remains Cheserek’s agent. “…He’s going really, really well. I was super impressed with him when I was over in Kenya, his long runs, his ability to up his volume…I really think this is where he’s gonna find himself as a pro runner and I think he’s got a lot of years, a lot of races to come as a marathoner.”

### [2023 NYC Marathon Men’s Preview](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11149)
What is he capable of his first time out? New York is a tough course on which to debut, but Cheserek is an intriguing wild card. In the last two years, we’ve seen unheralded former NCAA stars hang around far longer than anyone expected on the women’s side, with Viola Cheptoo almost stealing the race in 2021 and Lokedi winning it last year. The men’s races have played out somewhat differently, but if this race goes slower and Cheserek is able to weather with the surges of the lead pack, he could be dangerous over the final miles.
Promising Talents that Would Need a Breakthrough to Win
Zouhair Talbi, Morocco, 2:08:35 pb (2023 Boston), 28 years old
Jemal Yimer, Ethiopia, 2:08:58 pb (2022 Boston), 27 years old
Based on what they’ve done in the marathon so far, both of these guys need to step up a level to actually win a major. But both have intriguing potential with Yimer being the much more likely winner.
Yimer formerly held the Ethiopian half marathon record at 58:33 and just finished 4th at the World Half. He’s only finished 2 of his 4 career marathons, however. But he’s in good form. Earlier in the year, he racked up good showings on the US road scene – winning Bloomsday in May, finishing 4th at Peachtree and winning the Utica Boilermaker in July before running 58:38 in the half in August. Most recently he was fourth (59:22) at the World half a month ago.
Talbi, the former NAIA star for Oklahoma City who has run 13:18 and 27:20 on the track,was 5th in his debut in Boston in April, running 2:08:35 in against a strong field.
The Americans
Elkanah Kibet, USA, 2:09:07 pb (2022 Boston), 40 years old

### [2023 NYC Marathon Men’s Preview](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11149)
Futsum Zienasellassie, USA, 2:09:40 pb (2023 Rotterdam), 30 years old.
There are a few other US men in New York, including 2:10 guys Nathan Martin and Reed Fischer, but Kibet and Zienasellassie are the most intriguing. Kibet is 40 years old but has churned out a number of solid results recently — 4th at ’21 NYC, 2:09:07 pb at ’22 Boston, 2:10:43 at ’23 Prague. Zienasellassie, meanwhile, has run two strong races to open his marathon career: 2:11:01 to win 2022 CIM, then 2:09:40 in April to finish 11th in Rotterdam.
Ben Rosario, executive director of Zienasellassie’s NAZ Elite team, told LetsRun Zienasellassie is running New York in part because his idol, fellow Eritrean-American Meb Keflezighi, has a deep connection to the race, winning it in 2009. The other reason? To challenge himself in terms of his in-race decision making and get some reps in an unpaced race before the Olympic Trials.

We are less than three weeks away from[Cam Levins](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Cam+Levins), Canada’s marathon record holder, toeing the start line at the 2023 TCS New York City Marathon on Nov. 5. If you have not been following his Strava workouts or recent races,you might be surprised to find out that he might be in the best shape of his life.
The 34-year-old athlete is in the final few weeks of peak training before tapering for the NYC Marathon. On Oct. 12, he threw down an impressive one-kilometer workout, maintaining an average pace of two minutes and 45 seconds per kilometer for 12 reps, with only one minute’s rest between reps.
![Image 184](https://mybestruns.com/street/e99cdf3bda1eb314587629e039e992b45aca4b7070ce2a1ce1e8d3391ffa2697.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

This workout is specifically designed for those training for a half-marathon or marathon, with short rest periods to acclimatize them to a faster pace. Levins pushed his limits during this session, clocking his fastest rep at 2:40 per kilometer and his slowest at 2:51 per kilometer, resulting in an astonishing 2:45 per kilometer average pace. This pace equates to an incredible 58 minutes for a half-marathon. (His Canadian record is 60:18.)
In his last two marathon outings, Levins achieved something historic for Canada, breaking the national record on both occasions. He also secured a top-five finish at both the 2022 World Championships and the 2023 Tokyo Marathon.
Levins chose to race the New York Marathon in his build-up to the 2024 Paris Olympic Games. The marathon course in Paris has a challenging elevation gain of more than 400 meters across 42.2 kilometers.
Of the six Abbott World Marathon Majors, New York and Boston are considered the most challenging. New York’s difficulty is attributed primarily to the four bridges participants must cross as they wind through the city’s five boroughs, with the Verrazzano-Narrows and Queensboro Bridges both extending to a distance of more than one kilometer each.
With the recent announcement that the 2022 NYC champion,Evans Chebet,and the two-time NYC champion,Geoffrey Kamworor, have both withdrawn due to injury, the 2023 race will see a new champion crowned in Central Park on Nov. 5. ### [Kenya’s Alfred Kipchirchir is set to debut at TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11038)
Kenya’s [Alfred Kipchirchir](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Alfred+Kipchirchir) makes his marathon debut on October 15 at the TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon and he hopes it goes as well as that registered by one of his training partners.
Kipchirchir, 29, trains in a group which includes Vincent Ngetich who chased two-time Olympic champion Eliud Kipchoge along the streets of Berlin last weekend, eventually finishing second in the famed Berlin Marathon in 2:03:13. It was a stunning performance and one that has inspired Kipchirchir.
![Image 188](https://mybestruns.com/street/0ffa954b3a7c343d90557607148490f0aaa9f8fd3343007de5d92f3ffeb3046d.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
“I am looking forward to running 2:05 or 2:04 in Toronto,” he reveals. “My training is going well. We run between 180 and 210km in a week.”
According to Coach Peter Bii these two star athletes trained together right up until the last two weeks with Kipchirchir running step for step with Ngetich. Of course, the latter had to back off training to prepare for the Berlin Marathon.
![Image 189](https://mybestruns.com/street/9c0ec3bc79a9643be04baee8e7a7e5e6b3ae472ec3dc1aea822900c4417b0feb.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

### [Kenya’s Alfred Kipchirchir is set to debut at TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11038)
“I want to debut in Toronto because I like what I have heard about the city from Enock Onchari,” says Kipchirchir. A year ago Onchari, another member of the group, finished 4th in Toronto Waterfront.
“We know it’s very cold (in Toronto) from when Onchari was there. I have no information about the course,” he continues.
Kipchirchir has dipped under 60 minutes for the half marathon distance three times in the past three years with his best 59:43 set in the 2021 Madrid Half Marathon. With his current training going well, it is not unreasonable for him to have very high expectations.
All of his life the village of Kapkenu has been his home. It’s about 80 Kilometres from the famed ‘runners’ town’ of Iten. As a young boy he admired the achievements of his neighbour Geoffrey Kamworor who won both the world half marathon and world cross country championships three times and was twice winner of the New York City Marathon. But it was a family member who pushed him to become a runner in his youth.
“My brother introduced me to running. He works as the manager of the High Altitude Training Centre run by Lorna Kiplagat in Iten,” he reveals.
Like many Kenyan athletes, he leaves home every Monday morning and travels to the group’s training camp where he will remain until the following Saturday. He doesn’t own a car and relies upon a ‘matatu’, a publicly shared minibus. Sometimes his brother will drive him though. It’s a sacrifice he is prepared to make to ensure he achieves his running potential.
At the training camp there is much camaraderie. The shared sense of commitment and sacrifice he finds builds mental fortitude which he hopes to translate into a superb performance in Toronto. But there is also time to relax.
“I like to listen to music, Kalenjin (tribal) songs, when I am home and at camp,” he says. “And I watch football. I am a Manchester United supporter.”

### [Kenya’s Alfred Kipchirchir is set to debut at TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11038)
Both he and Coach Peter laugh heartily when the interviewer shakes his head at the current disruption at the club. Among the group there are Tottenham Hotspur, Chelsea and Manchester City fans says Peter.
Earnings from Kipchirchir’s running career have helped him take care of his immediate family, his wife Rhoda Jepkemboi Mukche and his 14-month-old daughter Praise Jepkorir.
“I have already bought a small farm,” he says. “It’s two acres. I grow maize and I have goats. My family members are at my home and they look after the farm when I am away at camp.”
The TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon course record is 2:05:00 held by Philemon Rono since 2019. On that occasion three runners came home within thirteen seconds of Rono, once again demonstrating fast times can be achieved here.
The transition to the marathon sometimes proves difficult for even some of the best distance runners in the world. But something in his preparation and attitude reveals Kipchirchir will have a memorable debut in Toronto.

### [Lessons from the long run: with Kipyegon, Kipchoge and Sang](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11032)
The long run, for elite and amateurs alike, forms an integral part of distance runners’ training.
In the west of Kenya, 20km to the south-east of Eldoret, that weekly ritual takes place early on a Thursday morning.
At 6am sharp the first runners make their way out of the gates of the Global Sports Communications Camp in Kaptagat to join some local runners who will try to keep them company.
In the pitch-black late June morning, the runners have already woken up half an hour or so before to get dressed, take some sips of water and go to the toilet.
![Image 192](https://mybestruns.com/street/9619d676e82cfadc4eca7b90aca42a7badd2d3b3eb0f4de91ac94a1d424ab47c.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The 30 or so athletes do not eat beforehand. They have determined that there are benefits to running fasted, the most prominent being training your body to get better accustomed to taking energy from your body’s fat reserves, something that may be important when carbohydrates sources are depleted towards the end of a marathon.
Of course, these are experienced athletes. For the double Olympic champion making his way to the group, he has spent 20 years building up and adapting his body to such challenges.
What is possible for Eliud Kipchoge would be simply unsustainable, and even ill-advised, for athletes new to the sport.
![Image 193](https://mybestruns.com/street/0bfa96acaee3597ce7e01e7d8ef234d8b767dfc97c9b3d42f33b33e50fc5f0e8.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

### [Lessons from the long run: with Kipyegon, Kipchoge and Sang](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11032)
This particular morning, coach Patrick Sang has assigned the ‘Boston loop’ – an undulating route with far more elevation than its namesake marathon, eventually finishing high on the escarpment a few hundred meters higher than the 2200m starting elevation at Kaptagat.
For the Global Sports group, it is simply 40km straight out; the minibuses and pick-up trucks following them picking them up after to drive them home.
Most of Sang’s athletes training for an autumn marathon are expected to complete the full distance, among them three-time world cross-country champion Geoffrey Kamworor, fellow 2:04 marathon-man Kaan Kigen Özbilen, Kipchoge and a collection of five others all boasting either sub-60-minute half marathon or sub-2:07 marathon bests.
World and Olympic medalist Linet Masai and 2:20 marathon runner Selly Chepyego, setting off 15 minutes beforehand, have also been set that distance goal.
For world and Olympic champion and multiple world record-holder Faith Kipyegon, today’s task is 30km. Despite being on the longer end of what might be expected from a 1500m runner, Kipyegon is insistent that this run is her favorite type of training.

### [Kenya’s Alfred Kipchirchir is set to debut at TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=11038)
Both he and Coach Peter laugh heartily when the interviewer shakes his head at the current disruption at the club. Among the group there are Tottenham Hotspur, Chelsea and Manchester City fans says Peter.

The TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon course record is 2:05:00 held by Philemon Rono since 2019. On that occasion three runners came home within thirteen seconds of Rono, once again demonstrating fast times can be achieved here.
The transition to the marathon sometimes proves difficult for even some of the best distance runners in the world. But something in his preparation and attitude reveals Kipchirchir will have a memorable debut in Toronto.

Last year, Ethiopia’s Tigist Assefa, a 2016 Olympian in the 800-meter run, entered the race as an untested marathon (with a PR of 2:34:01) and surprised everyone with her 2:15:37 victory in the third-fastest time ever.The 26-year-old is back this year but hasn’t run any races because she’s been sidelined with a few nagging injuries.

### [Focus shifts from track as road racing season heats up](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=10953)
As the international outdoor track and field season draws to a close, we now look forward to the feast of top-class road racing that will be on offer throughout the final four months of the year.
In just 11 days’ time, the focus of the sport will be on the World Athletics Road Running Championships Riga 23, where the best distance runners on the planet will compete for global honours in the mile, 5km and half marathon.
![Image 195](https://mybestruns.com/street/06f5a932bd973dc98d57dfeed9b2ab4867bd12d12e4ccd86aa4f014707c20a61.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The likes of world champion Faith Kipyegon, world record-holder Berihu Aregawi and Olympic champion Peres Jepchirchir are among the stars set to compete in the Latvian capital. Recreational runners from around the world, meanwhile, will run on the same courses as the greats when they take to the streets of Riga for the associated mass races.
There are also eight Platinum Label road races between September and December, the first of which was held last weekend with Betsy Saina and Othmane El Goumri winning the Blackmores Sydney Marathon. Of the seven other upcoming Platinum events, three of them form part of the Abbott World Marathon Majors (WMM) series: the BMW Berlin Marathon, the Bank of America Chicago Marathon and the TCS New York Marathon.
Platinum Label road races, Sep-Dec 2023
8 Oct – Chicago Marathon (WMM)
15 Oct – Amsterdam Marathon
5 Nov – New York Marathon (WMM)
26 Nov – Shanghai Marathon
3 Dec – Valencia Marathon
17 Dec – Bang Saen Half Marathon
The Chicago Marathon two weeks later will be highlighted by a clash between defending champion Ruth Chepngetich and London Marathon winner Sifan Hassan.

### [Focus shifts from track as road racing season heats up](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=10953)
Two-time Tokyo Marathon champion Birhanu Legese, the fourth-fastest marathon runner of all time, headlines the men’s field for the Amsterdam Marathon. Defending champion Evans Chebet will take on two-time winner Geoffrey Kamworor at the New York City Marathon in November.
For the first time since the Covid-19 pandemic, the Shanghai Marathon in late November will welcome an international elite field.
Just one week later, multiple global champion and world record-holder Joshua Cheptegei will make his long-awaited marathon debut in Valencia. In recent years the event has established itself as one of the highest-quality marathons in the world, and this year’s edition will surely be no exception.
Towards the end of the year, the Thai coastal area of Bang Saen will host one of the newest additions to the Platinum Label calendar, the Bangsaen21 Half Marathon. Since the pandemic, it has been largely a domestic affair, but it will be back with a bang this year with a high-quality elite line-up.
Hundreds of road races each year are granted a World Athletics Label, ranging from ‘Platinum’, for the top tier of road events, to Gold, Elite and Label. There are still more than 100 World Athletics Label road races due to take place between now and the end of 2023.

The race, which starts at 9:15 A.M. local time (or 3:15 A.M. ET in the U.S.), will be broadcast worldwide by several TV partners, but not in North America. However, several websites offer live streaming so people can watch the Berlin Marathon from anywhere in the world, especially if you’re a VPN subscriber. Watch Athletics will be broadcasting the race online in real time for free, while FloTrack’s livestream requires a subscription ($29.99 for one month) in order to view their livestream. Runners can be tracked via the Berlin Marathon website’s Results page, or via the BMW Berlin Marathon App app available on Apple or Google Play.
Race day begins with the elite handbike division at 8:50 A.M., followed by the wheelchair and handcycle divisions at 8:57 A.M. Runners are sent off in four waves beginning at 9:15 A.M., starting with the men’s and women’s elite waves. The race has a strict time limit of 6 hours, 15 minutes as well as course closure times at the 33K/20.5-mile mark (3:50 P.M.) and 38K/23.6-mile mark (4:35 P.M.). Runners who have not reached those points by those times can continue on the sidewalks alongside the course or get a ride on the course-sweeping bus.
Entry to the 2024 Berlin Marathon, which is slated for September 29, 2024, will be done via a lottery that will open in October. You can enter the lottery as a solo runner or as a team consisting of two or three people. (If the team is drawn, all persons from the team are included.) Lottery dates for 2024 have not yet been announced, but the draw for the 2023 edition took place in December 2022.

### [10 Things to Know About the 2023 Berlin Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=10946)
If you’re selected, the registration fee will be about $160 euros. You can also secure a guaranteed spot in the race based on previous marathon times. In 2023, female runners up to 44 years old qualified if they ran faster than 3:00; female runners up to 59 years old qualified if they ran under 3:20; and female runners over 60 years qualified if they ran under 4:10. For men, the qualifying times were 2:45 (up to 44 years old), 2:55 (46-59 years old), 3:25 (60 and older.)

![Image 209](https://mybestruns.com/street/d5140feba2ee9474515dac7113ffee6dcc4f6e2feca7738b206749c798d4b4f9.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The field has six past event champions, including Chebet, two-time champion Geoffrey Kamworor, and World Championships medalist Maru Teferi.

### [Loaded men's field for 2023 New York City Marathon announced](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=10824)
Challenging Chebet will be Kamworor, an Olympian and three-time half marathon world champion who is looking to become only the third athlete to win three TCS New York City Marathon men’s open division titles. He won in both 2019 and 2017 and has made the podium in all four of his appearances.
The newly crowned World marathon silver medallist Teferi, two-time World silver medallist Mosinet Geremew of Ethiopia, Olympic silver medalist Abdi Nageeye of the Netherlands, and the 2021 TCS New York City Marathon champion Albert Korir of Kenya will also be in the mix to stop Chebet from winning back-to-back titles.
Two-time TCS New York City Marathon runner-up Shura Kitata of Ethiopia, North America’s marathon record-holder Cam Levins of Canada, and 2023 United Airlines NYC Half podium finisher Zouahir Talbi of Morocco will also toe the line.
Edward Cheserek, the most decorated athlete in NCAA history, will make his 26.2-mile debut, while the American contingent will be led by 2022 USATF Marathon champion Futsum Zienasellaissie and 2021 TCS New York City Marathon fourth-place finisher Elkanah Kibet.
Meanwhile, along with the previously announced TCS New York City women’s field, last year’s runner-up and two-time Olympian Lonah Chemtai Salpeter of Israel and Gotytom Gebreslase of Ethiopia will be back.
Kenyans Edna Kiplagat and Olympian Viola Cheptoo will also return. Letesenbet Gidey and Yalemzerf Yehualaw will also line up for the first time.

### [2027 Could Bring Unprecedented Heat, Raising New Concerns for Marathon Runners Worldwide](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15441)
The global running community could face a formidable challenge in [2027](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2027), as forecasts of a potentially powerful El Niño raise concerns about rising temperatures and the impact of extreme heat on marathon performances.
![Image 2](https://mybestruns.com/street/21525fef106f0f5e518948f3b7ac7c7a59c2dc7f609cbf843c1a3df2621fa9d4.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
With long-distance runners increasingly chasing personal bests on the world's biggest stages, the prospect of another exceptionally warm year has placed race-day weather firmly in the spotlight. For marathoners, even a modest rise in temperature can make the difference between a record-breaking performance and a difficult battle to reach the finish line.
![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/c649899eb4ea226a094d35c54188897ee0ecd5f22a51cbcb024dd442b8785c9e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
At the centre of the concern is the [Pacific Ocean](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Pacific+Ocean), where developing El Niño conditions could influence global temperatures. Forecasts have raised the possibility of an unusually strong event, although its eventual intensity and the precise effects on temperatures around the world remain uncertain.
El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon characterised by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures across parts of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. It can alter weather patterns across different regions, while its warming influence can contribute to higher global temperatures. The full impact depends on the strength of the event and how it interacts with other climate factors.

The timing is particularly important. Global temperatures have often responded strongly in the year following a major El Niño, meaning 2027 could face an increased risk of challenging heat. However, whether it ultimately surpasses the existing global temperature record will depend on evolving ocean conditions, atmospheric patterns and human-caused climate change.
![Image 5](https://mybestruns.com/street/46b631cd0e12734e6118d1811afa82002a59f6f038f8de1a680ce25c9ce4a1e2.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
For marathon runners, the implications are significant. Scientific research has repeatedly shown that warmer conditions can reduce endurance performance, increase physiological strain and make it more difficult to maintain a planned race pace over 42.195 kilometres.
An analysis of seven North American marathons illustrates how substantially conditions can influence elite performances. Researchers found that leading male runners finished approximately 1.7 per cent slower relative to course records under the coolest conditions examined. In the warmest category, that difference increased to around 4.5 per cent.
For an athlete capable of running a marathon in 2:05:00, a slowdown of that magnitude could translate into several additional minutes on the clock. At the elite level, where races are frequently decided by seconds, such a difference can determine whether a runner achieves a personal best, secures a podium finish or misses a major performance target.
The consequences can be even more noticeable among recreational athletes, who often spend considerably longer exposed to the conditions.

A separate analysis by researchers at the University of Chicago, examining approximately 4.7 million marathon finishing times, highlighted the substantial effect of temperature on runners across different ability levels. The findings suggested that the typical participant could lose roughly 19 minutes when racing in temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, compared with conditions in the 40s. In the 80s Fahrenheit, the estimated time penalty rose to approximately 33 minutes.
These figures underline why marathon preparation involves much more than mileage, speed sessions and strength training. Temperature, humidity, direct sunlight and the body's ability to regulate heat can all influence how effectively a runner sustains an effort over the full distance.
Many marathon performances are achieved in cool conditions, with temperatures of approximately 4°C to 10°C often considered favourable for endurance running. As temperatures climb beyond that range, the body must devote more resources to cooling itself, potentially increasing cardiovascular strain and making a previously comfortable pace harder to maintain.
However, there is no universal temperature at which every marathon runner begins to slow down. Individual fitness, acclimatisation, humidity, wind, course exposure and race strategy all influence performance. A cool, overcast morning can produce very different outcomes from a sunny, humid day, even when the thermometer shows similar readings.

### [Cancer Survivor Brandon Throop Returns To Toronto Marathon In Hospital Gown For Third World Record Bid](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15440)
For [Brandon Throop](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Brandon+Throop), running a marathon in a hospital gown is about far more than chasing a place in the [Guinness World Records](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Guinness+World+Records). It is a deeply personal tribute to the medical team that helped save his life, a celebration of survival, and an opportunity to give back to the institution that stood beside him during one of the darkest chapters of his life.
![Image 8](https://mybestruns.com/street/f29108f8a11d11c189a98e7ad107e25370003868a0c2a06a0f60240f82ca748e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
In 2022, Throop was 35 years old, a father of two, and facing a life-changing diagnosis of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. His journey soon led him to [Princess Margaret Cancer Centre](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Princess+Margaret+Cancer+Centre) in Toronto, Canada, where he underwent chemotherapy and began a difficult battle against the disease.
![Image 9](https://mybestruns.com/street/544aaad28b469831ffc670d6b1f0afed09ba7cece4e33f54484abd893edf14de.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The treatment that helped him fight cancer also left him physically weakened. For someone who had spent much of his life running, even the simplest movements became unexpectedly challenging. After completing treatment, climbing a single flight of stairs could leave him coughing and struggling to catch his breath.

### [Cancer Survivor Brandon Throop Returns To Toronto Marathon In Hospital Gown For Third World Record Bid](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15440)
However, rather than allowing the experience to define the limits of his future, Throop began rebuilding his strength one small step at a time. He started by running once around his neighbourhood block before gradually increasing the distance as his body recovered. What began as a modest attempt to regain his fitness eventually developed into an extraordinary mission with a purpose extending far beyond the finish line.
![Image 10](https://mybestruns.com/street/609ed787d02e0efaf2f9b8e1f2b60b1718ea68e0b9bbf56ffa21a91b509d4949.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Now, more than three years after becoming cancer-free, Throop is preparing to return to the [TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=TCS+Toronto+Waterfront+Marathon) on Sunday, October 18, 2026, for another attempt at the Guinness World Record for the fastest marathon completed while wearing a hospital gown.
This will be his third attempt to claim the record, following two determined performances in previous editions of the Toronto race. In 2023, he completed the marathon in 2:55:59 before returning in 2024 to improve his time to 2:55:01. Despite his progress, the record remained just out of reach.
The current benchmark stands at 2:50:12, established by Evan Ubene at the same Toronto Waterfront Marathon in 2022. To make history this time, Throop will need to improve significantly on his previous performances and take more than five minutes off his best hospital-gown marathon.
Yet the significance of Sunday's race cannot be measured by finishing time alone.

For Throop, choosing Toronto has never been simply about finding the fastest course on which to break a record. Although other marathons might offer different racing conditions, the Toronto Waterfront Marathon holds a significance that no alternative venue could easily replace. The course takes him past Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, the institution where he received treatment, while family members and friends who supported him throughout his illness are there to witness his journey.
It is a route that connects his past to his present: the hospital where he fought for his health, the streets where he now tests his endurance, and the people who helped him keep moving forward when the road ahead was uncertain.
His hospital gown is therefore much more than an unusual racing outfit. It is a symbol of the vulnerability he experienced as a patient, the strength he rediscovered through running, and his determination to turn a deeply personal struggle into something that benefits others.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
Long before he conquered world cross-country championships, dominated the half-marathon distance and lifted the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) trophy, [Geoffrey Kamworor](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor) was a young Kenyan student with an ambitious dream that had little to do with running: becoming a [lawyer](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=lawyer).
![Image 14](https://mybestruns.com/street/de57be259ad5f2aa804935a23c35ae7bb6b49b6ec295d0ed68325e1b13b71303.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Growing up in Keiyo South, Kamworor developed the discipline that would later define his extraordinary athletic career. His daily routine involved running approximately five kilometres to school and another five kilometres back home. What might have seemed like an ordinary journey for a schoolboy was quietly laying the foundation for a future in international distance running.
![Image 15](https://mybestruns.com/street/808283ce83ea90fb69283ae3a63fb6cc12becf4782bc79b9156f109324db53df.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
He attended Chepsamo Primary School before proceeding to Lelboinet Secondary School, where he combined his education with a growing passion for athletics. At the time, his ambitions extended beyond the track and roads. He wanted to pursue a career in law, and that dream eventually brought him an opportunity to study at a college in the United States.

However, the young Kenyan faced a defining decision: follow the academic path he had envisioned or commit himself fully to the sport that was beginning to reveal his remarkable potential. Kamworor chose athletics, a decision that would ultimately place his name among the most accomplished distance runners of his generation.
![Image 16](https://mybestruns.com/street/a94c34052d38330fd293c08402206cd4d7a39c33946639bdb76ca84e0ab123e7.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
His transformation from a promising schoolboy into an international contender began gathering momentum in 2010, when he joined the GSC training camp in Kaptagat. His development accelerated rapidly, and within a short period, an opportunity to compete in Finland exposed him to a higher level of international competition.
Still only 17, he reportedly competed nine times during that trip, demonstrating an impressive ability to adapt to the demands of competitive racing. Breaking the eight-minute barrier for 3,000 metres was an early indication of the talent that would eventually carry him to the highest levels of distance running.
![Image 17](https://mybestruns.com/street/84282c8c1c650ab6ffe7062ef243eacc858a034f27f3ff8005541232e23d4bd3.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
His breakthrough on the international stage followed in March 2011, when he captured the junior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Punta Umbría, Spain. That victory announced the arrival of a young athlete whose future would extend far beyond the junior ranks.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
Kamworor was not simply a runner with speed. He possessed the endurance, tactical intelligence and competitive determination required to succeed across different distances and racing surfaces. As his career developed, those qualities became the hallmarks of an athlete capable of challenging the world's best.
Cross country became one of the foundations of Kamworor's international success. In 2015, he won the senior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Guiyang, China, confirming his status as one of the leading distance runners in the world. Two years later, he returned to the top of the podium in Kampala, Uganda, defending his senior world cross-country crown in front of a home crowd. Winning consecutive senior world titles placed him in an elite category and demonstrated his remarkable command of the demanding discipline.
On the roads, however, Kamworor established an equally impressive legacy. He won the World Half Marathon Championships in Copenhagen in 2014, Cardiff in 2016 and Valencia in 2018, becoming a three-time champion at the distance. His achievements reflected a rare combination of strength, speed and race management, enabling him to prevail against formidable international opposition.
The half marathon became one of his signature events, but Kamworor's ambitions were never confined to a single discipline. He continued to demonstrate his versatility on the track, winning silver in the men's 10,000 metres at the 2015 World Athletics Championships in Beijing, China. From the grass of cross-country courses to the roads of major international races and the track of a global championship, he repeatedly demonstrated that his talent could flourish wherever the competition took him.
Among Kamworor's most memorable achievements are his victories at the New York City Marathon in 2017 and 2019. Winning one of the world's most celebrated marathons requires exceptional endurance, but winning it twice demands much more: tactical patience, resilience and the ability to navigate a demanding course against a deep international field.

His success in the American city also illustrated his ability to move successfully between distances. An athlete celebrated for his cross-country and half-marathon dominance had shown that he could also conquer the 42.195-kilometre marathon, one of the most demanding challenges in road racing.
Now, as he sets his sights on another New York campaign, the Kenyan star has an opportunity to strengthen his legacy further. A third men's open-division victory would place him among a very select group of athletes to have won the prestigious race three times. Such a milestone would be more than another addition to his trophy cabinet; it would reinforce the story of a runner whose competitive range has extended across nearly every major discipline in distance running.
Behind Kamworor's achievements lies a training environment built around discipline, consistency and high-level competition. Working under the guidance of renowned coach Patrick Sang, he has trained alongside some of Kenya's most celebrated athletes, including marathon great Eliud Kipchoge and middle- and long-distance superstar Faith Kipyegon.
Sharing a training environment with athletes of such calibre provides a demanding daily standard. Yet Kamworor has built his own identity through a career defined by major championship victories and sustained success across different racing distances. His journey has also included difficult periods and setbacks, reminding the running world that even the most accomplished champions must continually work to return to their best. His longevity at the elite level reflects the importance of patience, dedication and the willingness to keep pursuing new goals.
For aspiring athletes in Kenya, his story offers an important lesson: extraordinary achievements are often built through ordinary routines repeated consistently over many years. Those five-kilometre journeys to school and back were not glamorous. They did not come with cheering crowds, television cameras or medals. Yet they formed part of the foundation of a career that would eventually take him to the world's biggest running stages.

### [Geofry Kipchumba Returns To Defend Amsterdam Crown As World-Class Men’s And Women’s Fields Target History](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15438)
The [TCS Amsterdam Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=TCS+Amsterdam+Marathon) is set for an exciting showdown on Sunday, 18 October, with an outstanding international field preparing to challenge the course records, pursue personal bests and compete for victory on one of Europe’s most prestigious marathon stages.
![Image 21](https://mybestruns.com/street/eb8d3816a3274868be8a924326614ca1afe06b6de1ebe40127097ccfa48aa227.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The 2026 edition promises compelling competition in both the men’s and women’s races. Kenya and Ethiopia will feature prominently among the leading contenders, with experienced champions, emerging talents and athletes making their marathon debuts all bringing ambitious targets to Amsterdam.
In the men’s race, defending champion [Geofry Toroitich Kipchumba](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geofry+Toroitich+Kipchumba) returns with the course record firmly in his sights after producing a remarkable performance last year.
![Image 22](https://mybestruns.com/street/90ce64981bbdcc2ceba4696ee36703519b485ead3ee05d4dded9478724ace50d.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Kipchumba stormed to victory in 2:03:30 at the 50th edition of the race, establishing a new Amsterdam course record and the fastest marathon time ever recorded on Dutch soil. His return offers an opportunity to improve on that achievement, although a formidable field stands between him and another memorable victory.

### [Geofry Kipchumba Returns To Defend Amsterdam Crown As World-Class Men’s And Women’s Fields Target History](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15438)
The Kenyan is not the only athlete arriving with the potential to challenge the record. Ethiopia’s Haymanot Alew has a marathon personal best of 2:03:31, recorded in Berlin, leaving him just one second outside the existing course record. The 2026 Egmond Half Marathon winner will be among the athletes hoping to turn that narrow gap into history on Amsterdam’s streets.
Another major contender is Ethiopia’s Tsegaye Getachew, a two-time Amsterdam champion who won the race in 2022 and 2024 before finishing second in 2025 with a personal best of 2:04:18. His familiarity with the course and previous success make him an important presence in a race expected to feature an intense battle among the leading men.
The depth of the field is underlined by the presence of 10 athletes who have recorded marathon times below 2:05, according to the race organisers. With several runners capable of sustaining an exceptional pace, the contest could develop into a demanding tactical battle in which positioning, endurance and the ability to respond to late-race attacks will prove decisive.
Kenya’s Isaia Kipkoech Lasoi is another athlete attracting attention ahead of the race, although his challenge comes with a different question. The half-marathon specialist will make his marathon debut after establishing an impressive personal best of 58:10 over 21.0975 kilometres.
His speed over the half-marathon distance provides an intriguing indication of his potential, but the full marathon presents an entirely different test. How effectively he manages his energy beyond the halfway point and adapts to the demands of 42.195 kilometres will be among the most interesting aspects of his first appearance at the distance.

Meanwhile, compatriot Buze Diriba arrives with a best of 2:19:34, ensuring that the Ethiopian challenge extends well beyond the two former Amsterdam champions.
The international depth continues with Bahrain’s Desi Jisa Mokonin, Ethiopia’s Yeshi Kalayu Chekole and Eritrea’s Nazret Weldu Gebrehiwet, all of whom have recorded performances close to the two-hour-and-20-minute barrier.
Sweden’s Abeba Aregawi, a former world champion over 1,500 metres, adds another fascinating dimension to the contest. Aregawi set a Swedish marathon record of 2:23:12 on her debut earlier this year and will now face another major test as she continues her transition from track running to the marathon.
With the women’s course record standing at 2:16:52, the question is whether the leading contenders can produce the performance required to challenge it. Desta’s personal best of 2:17:37 already places her within striking distance, while Belete, Fikir and Diriba will be looking to turn their own ambitions into competitive results.

Beyond the elite fields, the athletes’ comments at the pre-race press conference have provided a glimpse into the different approaches they will bring to Sunday’s contest.
Kenya’s Nicholas Kipkorir expressed confidence in his return to Amsterdam, describing the city as a second home and believing that his familiarity with the environment could help him deliver his best performance.

“I love Amsterdam. It feels like my second home, and I know that will help me run my best time,” Kipkorir said.
His compatriot Geofry Kipchumba has set his sights on achieving another personal best while also fighting for victory. His ambition reflects the competitive spirit surrounding the men’s race, where the defending champion and several challengers are expected to target fast times.
“I’m going for another personal best and the win,” Kipchumba said.
Ethiopia’s Aynalem Desta is equally determined to build on her previous success in Amsterdam. Having won last year’s race in a personal best of 2:17:37, she will be aiming to deliver another strong performance against a deep women’s field.
“I love the TCS Amsterdam Marathon. I’m happy with the race I ran here last year, and I want to perform even better this year,” Desta explained.
Fellow Ethiopian Mestawut Fikir Truneh emphasised the importance of patience and perseverance, qualities that often determine the outcome of a marathon when fatigue begins to affect even the strongest runners.
“A marathon requires patience. You must not give up hope until the very last moment. Keep going and never give up,” Fikir said.
Among the Dutch athletes, Mikky Keetels has established a clear objective: breaking the two-hour-and-30-minute barrier, with hopes of going even faster if conditions allow.
“I really want to run under 2:30, and secretly maybe even a little faster,” Keetels revealed.
Fellow Dutch runner Noah Schutte is concentrating on the closing stages of the race, when maintaining pace and fighting through fatigue can make the difference between achieving a target and falling short.
“I especially want to give everything in the final kilometres and keep fighting,” Schutte said.
For Khalid Choukoud, the race presents an opportunity to improve his personal best while continuing to demonstrate his competitiveness at the age of 40. Breaking 2:10 would represent a particularly significant achievement for the experienced Dutch marathoner.

“It would be great to improve my personal best. But if I run under 2:10 at the age of 40, that would be a great achievement too,” Choukoud said.
All these ambitions will converge on Sunday, when the athletes take on the streets of Amsterdam before finishing inside the iconic Olympic Stadium.
The defending champions will be under pressure to retain their titles, record holders will be challenged by determined rivals, and debutants will have the opportunity to discover what they can achieve over the full marathon distance.
For Kipchumba, the immediate target is to defend his crown and potentially lower the 2:03:30 course record. For Alew, it is an opportunity to bridge the one-second gap separating his personal best from the mark. Getachew will be seeking another victory, while Lasoi faces the challenge of translating his exceptional half-marathon speed into marathon success.
In the women’s race, Desta will attempt to defend her title against a field featuring former champions, major-marathon performers and several athletes capable of producing personal bests. With the 2:16:52 course record in sight, the leading women could also make a serious attempt to rewrite the record books.
One start line will unite these athletes, but their objectives are different. Some are pursuing victory, others are targeting personal records, and a select few have their sights set on history.
When the gun fires on 18 October, the preparation will be over and the real test will begin. Amsterdam is ready for a day of world-class marathon racing, with the possibility of new records adding even greater anticipation to an already compelling contest.

### [From $1 To $358: How The New York City Marathon Became A Global Running Phenomenon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15437)
What began as a modest race through Central Park, with a handful of determined runners and a budget of just $1,000, has evolved into one of the most prestigious and sought-after marathons in the world. More than five decades later, the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) tells a remarkable story of how distance running has grown from a grassroots sporting event into a global spectacle.
![Image 29](https://mybestruns.com/street/bacec4114b3d54670c15a184e950b0e7ddb43de9849a87f97fe568b1a68fdecf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
When the inaugural New York City Marathon took place in 1970, the entry fee was just $1. Organised by the New York Road Runners, the race was held entirely within Central Park, far removed from the enormous crowds, international attention and commercial scale that define the event today.
![Image 30](https://mybestruns.com/street/cb333999ed07e06d10edcf37e5452882364cbb7336ebf8347871bb079ae7bfbf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Of the 127 registered participants, only 55 completed the race. Yet, despite its modest beginnings, the event laid the foundation for a marathon that would eventually capture the imagination of runners from every corner of the world.

### [From $1 To $358: How The New York City Marathon Became A Global Running Phenomenon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15437)
The first champion was Gary Muhrcke, a New York City firefighter whose victory remains one of the most memorable stories from the race's early years. According to accounts of the inaugural edition, Muhrcke had finished a night shift before entering the competition shortly before the start. He went on to win in approximately 2:31, securing his place in the marathon's history.
The inaugural race also featured Nina Kuscsik, the only woman in the field. She started the event but withdrew after becoming ill, meaning no woman finished that first edition. Kuscsik would later become an important figure in the campaign for women's inclusion in competitive distance running.
Over the years, the New York City Marathon expanded beyond Central Park, eventually developing into the iconic five-borough journey that takes runners through Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Manhattan. Its transformation helped turn the race into a celebration of athletic achievement, community spirit and the extraordinary diversity of New York City.
Today, the marathon attracts elite athletes chasing victories and records, recreational runners pursuing personal milestones, charity participants raising funds for important causes, and thousands of international visitors eager to experience one of running's most celebrated events.

### [Frankfurt Assembles Fastest-Ever Men’s Field as Former Champion Meskerem Assefa Returns](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15436)
The 43rd Mainova Frankfurt Marathon is set for a fast edition on October 25, with the deepest men’s field in race history and the return of 2018 women’s champion Meskerem Assefa.
For the first time, four men on the start list have personal bests under 2:05, with another four having broken 2:07. German record-holder Amanal Petros leads the field at 2:04:03, setting up a showdown featuring three of Germany’s leading marathoners.
The women’s race also promises strong competition. Five entrants have run under 2:22, making it the second-deepest women’s field in Frankfurt history by that measure, behind only the 2025 edition, which featured six.
“Overall this is surely the fastest elite field we have ever assembled for the Mainova Frankfurt Marathon. I am very pleased that the German men are playing a major role and I expect a thrilling top-class race,” said Jo Schindler, who is in his 25th year as race director.
German Stars Lead the Men’s Challenge
European champion Petros tops the entry list, but the competition is close. Ethiopia’s Andualem Belay brings a personal best of 2:04:44, followed by Germany’s Samuel Fitwi at 2:04:45 and Richard Ringer at 2:04:47.
With just 44 seconds separating the personal bests of the four fastest entrants, the race offers the prospect of a competitive battle at the front.
Kenya’s Benard Biwott, who has run 2:05:25, leads the next group of contenders. Israel’s Haimro Alame and Ethiopians Antenayehu Dagnachew and Jiregna Geleta round out the eight men with personal bests under 2:07.
Assefa Returns to Face Yimer and Saina
Meskerem Assefa’s return adds a former champion to an already strong women’s field. Her participation had been uncertain because of visa requirements, but organizers have now secured the visa needed for her trip to Germany.

### [South Korean Running Influencer Yoo Ji-Won, 25, Dies After Collapsing Just 500 Metres From Seoul Half Marathon Finish](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15435)
The running community is mourning the heartbreaking death of [South Korean running influencer Yoo Ji-won](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=South+Korean+running+influencer+Yoo+Ji-won), who passed away after collapsing during the half marathon at the [2026 Seoul Race](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2026+Seoul+Race) on Sunday, October 11. The 25-year-old was approaching the final stretch of the race when tragedy struck, cutting short a life filled with ambition, talent and promise.
![Image 36](https://mybestruns.com/street/a3d0147af9a05de82fc0febbf8f334c8a41992e0374bf8d58b7fd5e658d63c22.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The Seoul Race, a major city-centre running event, brought approximately 12,000 participants onto the streets of downtown Seoul. For thousands of runners, the occasion was an opportunity to challenge themselves and celebrate their shared passion for the sport. However, the event ended in tragedy following the incident involving Ji-won, whose death has sent shockwaves through South Korea's running community.
According to reports, Ji-won collapsed shortly before 9 a.m. at the 20.6-kilometre mark along Cheonggyecheon-ro, approximately 500 metres from the finish line of the 21.1-kilometre race. She was reportedly running near the front of the women's half marathon field when she suddenly fell.

A race official discovered her and immediately contacted emergency services. Cardiopulmonary resuscitation (CPR) was administered at the scene before she was transported to hospital for further medical attention. Despite the emergency response, Ji-won never regained consciousness and was subsequently pronounced dead. The cause of her death has not been officially confirmed.
Her passing has left a profound sense of sorrow among runners, particularly those who admired her performances and followed her journey in the sport. The circumstances surrounding the incident have also prompted renewed reflection on athlete safety and the importance of emergency preparedness at mass-participation running events.
![Image 38](https://mybestruns.com/street/ac1d7c031f2decf872923529891b5414a79e7ff9f845d2ed711f4ebb28f1962a.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Within South Korea's running community, Ji-won was recognised as one of the country's fastest women competing at a purely amateur level. Despite not being a professional athlete, she had achieved impressive performances over the marathon and half marathon distances, establishing herself as a formidable recreational runner.
Her personal best in the marathon stood at an impressive 2:56, while she had recorded approximately 1:22 for the half marathon. Those performances reflected a high level of dedication, disciplined training and a strong commitment to improving her abilities on the road.

Ji-won was also known for sharing aspects of her running journey with a wider audience, helping bring attention to the ambitions and achievements of amateur athletes. Her story demonstrated that the pursuit of excellence in running extends far beyond the professional ranks, with dedicated recreational athletes continually pushing their limits and setting increasingly challenging goals.
Earlier this year, she appeared on a running-focused YouTube channel, where she discussed her ambitions for the future. Among the targets she hoped to achieve was a half marathon time of 1:19, a goal that would have represented a significant improvement on her previous performance.
That ambition makes her passing particularly heartbreaking. At just 25, she was still developing as a runner, with more milestones to pursue and new challenges ahead. Away from running, Ji-won was pursuing a master's degree at the Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST), one of South Korea's leading institutions for science and technology research. “I was so excited to come back stronger, but a sickness slowed down my training and I’m not where I wanted to be. Sometimes, things just don’t go as planned,” Hassan wrote.
Despite her disappointment, the Olympic champion also sent her best wishes to the athletes preparing to compete in New York, demonstrating her support for the wider running community even as she steps away from the competition.
Hassan, who holds a personal best of 2:13:44, ranks fifth on the women’s all-time marathon list. Botswana’s sprint sensation [Letsile Tebogo](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Letsile+Tebogo) has achieved something few athletes can ever imagine: seeing his sporting legacy celebrated beyond the stadium and onto the nation’s currency.
![Image 46](https://mybestruns.com/street/d3d681e99653acd0f0d64564b71017491d3e637358a5a08133a21ecdc69cc48a.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The Olympic 200m champion has been featured on Botswana’s commemorative [50-pula banknote](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=50-pula+banknote), a powerful tribute to a young athlete whose remarkable achievements have elevated his country’s profile on the global athletics stage.
Tebogo made history at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games, storming to victory in the men’s 200 metres in an astonishing 19.46 seconds to claim Botswana’s first-ever Olympic gold medal. In doing so, he also became the first African man to win Olympic gold in the 200m, marking a landmark moment for African sprinting.
![Image 47](https://mybestruns.com/street/7a42424e1dbd3d37e2c7625b920999bdc1c5b5b62729820253ac3c3fec1559ce.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

From the Olympic track to the nation’s currency, Letsile Tebogo has become a powerful symbol of Botswana’s ambition, pride and sporting progress. His remarkable 19.46-second performance in Paris will forever remain a landmark in Olympic history, while his growing legacy continues to inspire athletes and fans far beyond his homeland.

### [Chicago Strangers Turn Ethan Woodhead’s Marathon Into an Unforgettable Homecoming After 4,000-Mile Journey](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15432)
For 24-year-old [Ethan Woodhead](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Ethan+Woodhead), travelling from [Guernsey](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Guernsey) in the [United Kingdom](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=United+Kingdom) to [Chicago](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Chicago) to run a marathon was already an adventure. What he did not anticipate was that thousands of kilometres from home, a city full of strangers would make him feel as though he had brought his entire support network with him.
![Image 50](https://mybestruns.com/street/d4e0ba7d2d3f345e2182d3175fe03ef3b9bd7a93418c2b2c1aafa6e8cd3b5d86.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Woodhead travelled more than 6,400 kilometres (approximately 4,000 miles) to compete in the Chicago Marathon, expecting to tackle the demanding 42.195-kilometre distance without friends or family members lining the streets to cheer him on. However, thanks to a thoughtful initiative from his uncle, Phil Woodhead, his race turned into an extraordinary story of community spirit and the power of running to bring people together.
Knowing that his nephew would be running far from home, Phil took to Facebook with a simple request to Chicago spectators: keep an eye out for Ethan, wearing bib number 2024, and give him some encouragement along the course.

Woodhead, who had hoped to finish the marathon in approximately 2 hours and 30 minutes, could hardly have anticipated the emotional impact of the reception awaiting him along the route.
The experience left him “lost for words,” as he described the overwhelming support as a truly special experience. Hearing so many people call out his name was something he had never expected when he set off from Guernsey for the American city.

Runners hoping to secure a place in the 2027 edition must submit their applications before the ballot closes on Tuesday, October 19, 2026, at 10:00 a.m. Australian Eastern Daylight Time (AEDT).
Unlike a conventional first-come, first-served registration system, the marathon uses a random ballot to allocate places. This means applicants have an equal opportunity in the draw, regardless of when they submit their applications during the ballot period.
Athletes are therefore encouraged to complete their applications before the deadline, ensure that their contact details are accurate and familiarise themselves with the event's important dates.
![Image 65](https://mybestruns.com/street/751a12c9c888eadc832acafc3a61bdec32d5a6558efd44848ca7126f6fa66d75.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Runners should ensure that the email addresses provided during registration are correct and check their junk or spam folders if they cannot find the notification.
The organisers have also clarified that they will not respond to individual enquiries about ballot application status between the opening of the ballot and the announcement of results. All ballot outcomes are final, and applicants are encouraged to consult the official frequently asked questions for further guidance.
Duo teams and participants competing in non-elite racing wheelchairs are subject to separate application procedures and should not apply through the general ballot.

With the ballot now open, runners have the opportunity to begin planning for an event that brings together international participation, personal achievement and the excitement of marathon racing in a world-famous destination.

[Chelsea Clinton](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Chelsea+Clinton), the daughter of former United States President [Bill Clinton](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Bill+Clinton) and former Secretary of State [Hillary Clinton](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Hillary+Clinton), completed the [2026 Chicago Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2026+Chicago+Marathon) in [3:47:55](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=3%3A47%3A55) on Sunday, combining a major endurance challenge with her commitment to supporting maternal health.
![Image 69](https://mybestruns.com/street/d721a5945034c6c17bcecda54928bcc610a5bdd2fcdc00bb09afb3d1742a8c77.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The 46-year-old joined her friend [Jen Koss](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Jen+Koss) for the 42.195-kilometre race, maintaining a consistent rhythm throughout the streets of Chicago. Clinton reached the halfway point in 1:53:10 before covering the second half in 1:54:45, demonstrating impressive pacing on her way to the finish.
However, beyond the clock and the physical demands of one of the world's most prestigious marathons, her participation carried a deeper purpose. Clinton ran to support [Every Mother Counts](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Every+Mother+Counts), a nonprofit organisation dedicated to making pregnancy and childbirth safer for mothers around the world. Through her marathon effort, she helped raise funds and awareness for maternal health, turning every kilometre into an opportunity to advance a cause close to her heart.

### [Five Years On, Agnes Tirop’s Light Still Shines in the World of Athletics](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15428)
Five years after the tragic death of [Agnes Jebet Tirop](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Agnes+Jebet+Tirop), the Kenyan distance-running star remains a powerful symbol of sporting excellence, unfulfilled potential and the urgent fight against gender-based violence.
![Image 74](https://mybestruns.com/street/5ffa31af8295f395e0aff49642712e51130387366364addc2bf2c316bd3b7edc.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
On [October 13](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=October+13), [2021](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2021), the athletics world was plunged into mourning following the death of Tirop, who was found at her home in Iten, Kenya, at just 25 years old. Her life was cut short at a time when her career was flourishing, leaving behind a legacy that continues to resonate with athletes, fans and the wider community.
For Kenya, a country whose identity is deeply intertwined with distance-running success, Tirop represented a remarkable generation of female athletes taking the sport to new heights. Her achievements on the track, across country and on the roads had already secured her place among the country's outstanding distance runners.
![Image 75](https://mybestruns.com/street/f77fa5828a0aeb325862244b31913486d927b332f71bf5f757228761f9169abf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Five years later, the sadness of her loss remains inseparable from the extraordinary story of what she accomplished in her short but memorable career.

chunks.text:
### [Five Years On, Agnes Tirop’s Light Still Shines in the World of Athletics](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15428)
A Champion Who Rose to the Top at 19
Tirop announced herself on the global stage in spectacular fashion at the 2015 World Athletics Cross Country Championships in Guiyang, China. At only 19, she won the senior women's race, becoming the youngest champion in the event since Zola Budd in 1985.
Her victory demonstrated not only her natural ability but also the composure and determination that would become defining features of her running career.
She subsequently established herself among the world's leading track athletes, winning bronze medals in the women's 10,000 metres at the 2017 World Athletics Championships in London and the 2019 edition in Doha.
Those back-to-back podium finishes confirmed her consistency at the highest level and underlined her ability to compete against the strongest distance runners in the world.
Tirop also demonstrated considerable versatility at the Tokyo 2020 Olympic Games, held in 2021, where she finished fourth in the women's 5,000 metres. Although she narrowly missed the podium, her performance reinforced her reputation as one of Kenya's most accomplished emerging distance-running talents.
A World Record That Made History
Just weeks before her death, Tirop delivered one of the defining performances of her career.
![Image 76](https://mybestruns.com/street/c78d43c7e9431cc77d4c0c7a69212a2bb6f64a57b712e93e9359780084f1438e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
On September 12, 2021, she clocked an astonishing 30:01 to win the women's 10km road race at the adizero Road to Records event in Herzogenaurach, Germany.

chunks.text:
### [Five Years On, Agnes Tirop’s Light Still Shines in the World of Athletics](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15428)
Her performance broke the then women's-only world record by 28 seconds, establishing a new benchmark for the distance. The record was subsequently ratified by World Athletics. It was aremarkable achievement that placed her name among the legends of distance running. Although her record has since been broken, the greatness of her achievement remains untouched, and no change in the record books can diminish the extraordinary talent, courage and determination she displayed that day. Time may bring new champions and faster performances, but it can never erase the mark she left on athletics.
In a race that demanded patience, tactical awareness and an exceptional finishing effort, Tirop broke away from compatriot Sheila Chepkirui during the closing stages and powered towards the finish line.
The performance was a remarkable demonstration of her endurance and competitive instinct. It also offered a glimpse of what might have followed had she been given more years to develop her career.
Her final competitive appearance came on October 3, 2021, when she finished second in a 10km race in Geneva, Switzerland. Ten days later, the world learned of her death.
The timing made the tragedy particularly difficult to comprehend: an athlete who had just rewritten the record books and was still competing at the highest level was suddenly gone.
![Image 77](https://mybestruns.com/street/96776c2a38ffe92e203c98190e24001e4c1d47d376c5bd46c7feef1ad83b81ce.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
A Tragedy That Reached Far Beyond Sport
Tirop's death was not simply the loss of an elite athlete. It also brought renewed international attention to violence against women and the need to create safer environments in which women and girls can live, train and pursue their ambitions.
Her story became a painful reminder that medals, records and international recognition cannot shield someone from violence in their private life.

### [Five Years On, Agnes Tirop’s Light Still Shines in the World of Athletics](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15428)
In the years since her death, her name has continued to feature in efforts to promote women's empowerment, athlete welfare and the prevention of gender-based violence. Initiatives associated with her legacy, including Agnes Tirop Angels, reflect the continuing determination to transform grief into meaningful action.
Her story remains especially significant within athletics, where the pursuit of excellence must go hand in hand with respect for athletes' safety, dignity and wellbeing.
Five Years Later, Her Legacy Endures
For young runners who dream of representing Kenya on the international stage, Tirop's career remains an example of what dedication, talent and courage can achieve.
She rose from a promising young athlete to a world champion, a two-time World Championships medallist and a world-record holder. She excelled across different distances and surfaces, leaving an impressive body of achievements before reaching her 26th birthday.
Yet her legacy cannot be measured by statistics alone. It also lies in the conversations her death continues to inspire, the women whose safety must be protected and the determination to ensure that sporting success is never separated from human dignity.
Five years on, Agnes Tirop is remembered not only for the records she set or the medals she won, but also for the future that was taken from her.
Her achievements remain part of Kenya's rich athletics history, while her story continues to call for a world in which women can pursue their dreams without fear of violence.
Agnes Tirop's life was tragically short, but her impact reaches far beyond the finish line. Her achievements will remain in the record books, her memory will endure in the hearts of athletics fans, and her legacy will continue to inspire generations to come.

Kenyan distance running enjoyed a successful outing in the Netherlands on Sunday as [Davis Kiplangat](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Davis+Kiplangat) and [Lidya Cheruto](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Lidya+Cheruto) claimed victories at the [Eindhoven Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Eindhoven+Marathon), delivering impressive performances over the classic 42.195-kilometre distance.
![Image 80](https://mybestruns.com/street/917e4059a7996b041a4e4f1d11cd52abc6a7297be01eba8d2f78dbfe593094e8.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Kiplangat secured the men's title in 2:07:41, while compatriot Cheruto won the women's race in 2:32:46, ensuring Kenya celebrated victories in both categories at the Dutch road-running event.
The men's race was led by Kiplangat, who produced the fastest performance of the day to cross the finish line in 2:07:41. His victory highlighted his strength over the marathon distance and placed him ahead of a competitive international field.
![Image 81](https://mybestruns.com/street/de713eccd90ce29a6641d9aed845aee7f8bb4f88fee0bd68eae6a6a694bde7c8.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Kenya's Asbel Kipkorir finished second in 2:10:25, completing a strong performance behind the winner. Although he could not match Kiplangat's pace, Kipkorir secured the runner-up position with a time of 2:10:25.
Uganda's Levi Chelangat claimed third place in 2:16:34, giving the East African region two nationalities on the men's podium. His performance ensured that the leading three finishers represented Kenya and Uganda.
Belgium's Diego van Looy finished fourth in 2:18:17, making him the highest-placed Belgian athlete in the men's overall standings shown in the results. He followed the leading trio across the line after a demanding marathon contest.
The men's results also featured Tim Calliauw of Belgium, who recorded 2:20:23 in the men's 40–49 age category. His performance was among the age-group results published alongside the leading overall finishers.

In the women's race, Kenya's Lidya Cheruto delivered another important victory, crossing the finish line in 2:32:46 to secure the title. Her performance placed her ahead of Belgium's Valentine Mathy, who finished second in 2:35:03.
Mathy's runner-up finish was followed by compatriot Elisa Vancolen, who clocked 2:37:44 to claim third place. The result gave Belgium two athletes on the women's podium behind the Kenyan winner.

Belgium's Karen van Proeyen finished fourth in 2:40:31, adding another strong result for the host country's neighbouring European running nation. Her time also appeared among the women's age-group results, where she was the leading finisher in the 40–49 category.
The women's podium therefore featured Kenya and Belgium, with Cheruto taking the overall honours ahead of Mathy and Vancolen. Their performances provided a clear picture of the leading competition in the women's marathon.
The published results also recorded Pawel Wojcik of Poland in the men's 50–59 category with 2:34:39. France's Willie Nijsten finished the men's 60–69 category in 2:57:24, while Gijs van den Hurk, also listed under France, recorded 3:24:44 in the men's 70-plus category.
In the women's age groups, Norway's Helle Blak recorded 2:59:55 in the 50–59 category, while Belgium's Silvia Lenaerts finished in 3:32:04 in the 60–69 category.
The results underline the international character of the Eindhoven Marathon, which brings together elite competitors, experienced club runners and athletes competing across a wide range of age categories.

### [From Kipchoge’s Impossible Dream to Sawe’s Historic Reality: Kenya Redefines Marathon Running](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15425)
Seven years after [Eliud Kipchoge](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Eliud+Kipchoge) challenged the limits of human endurance in [Vienna](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Vienna), fellow Kenyan [Sabastian Sawe](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Sabastian+Sawe) has transformed that extraordinary vision into a landmark achievement in competitive marathon running, becoming the first man to complete the 42.195-kilometre distance in under two hours under record-eligible race conditions.
![Image 91](https://mybestruns.com/street/09c936b4feb8e8614298bb63445b51428263e957b2269c10f6e670ba58231820.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
On October 12, 2019, Kipchoge etched his name into sporting history when he completed the [INEOS 1:59 Challenge](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=INEOS+1%3A59+Challenge) in Vienna, Austria, in an astonishing 1:59:40.2. Although the performance could not be recognised as an official world record because of the controlled conditions under which it was staged, it demonstrated that the seemingly impossible barrier was within human reach.
Kipchoge’s achievement carried a powerful message that resonated far beyond athletics: “[No human is limited](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=No+human+is+limited).” His words became a symbol of determination, ambition and the courage to challenge established boundaries.
However, the dream of breaking two hours in an official marathon remained unfinished.
