### [2027 Could Bring Unprecedented Heat, Raising New Concerns for Marathon Runners Worldwide](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15441)
The global running community could face a formidable challenge in [2027](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2027), as forecasts of a potentially powerful El Niño raise concerns about rising temperatures and the impact of extreme heat on marathon performances.
![Image 2](https://mybestruns.com/street/21525fef106f0f5e518948f3b7ac7c7a59c2dc7f609cbf843c1a3df2621fa9d4.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
With long-distance runners increasingly chasing personal bests on the world's biggest stages, the prospect of another exceptionally warm year has placed race-day weather firmly in the spotlight. For marathoners, even a modest rise in temperature can make the difference between a record-breaking performance and a difficult battle to reach the finish line.
![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/c649899eb4ea226a094d35c54188897ee0ecd5f22a51cbcb024dd442b8785c9e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
At the centre of the concern is the [Pacific Ocean](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Pacific+Ocean), where developing El Niño conditions could influence global temperatures. Forecasts have raised the possibility of an unusually strong event, although its eventual intensity and the precise effects on temperatures around the world remain uncertain.
El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon characterised by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures across parts of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. It can alter weather patterns across different regions, while its warming influence can contribute to higher global temperatures. The full impact depends on the strength of the event and how it interacts with other climate factors.

### [2027 Could Bring Unprecedented Heat, Raising New Concerns for Marathon Runners Worldwide](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15441)
![Image 4](https://mybestruns.com/street/d0a9667bdea6ce04007f6323709b90066c76c7bf750a06efd1f2fbddbd1d21b0.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The timing is particularly important. Global temperatures have often responded strongly in the year following a major El Niño, meaning 2027 could face an increased risk of challenging heat. However, whether it ultimately surpasses the existing global temperature record will depend on evolving ocean conditions, atmospheric patterns and human-caused climate change.
![Image 5](https://mybestruns.com/street/46b631cd0e12734e6118d1811afa82002a59f6f038f8de1a680ce25c9ce4a1e2.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
For marathon runners, the implications are significant. Scientific research has repeatedly shown that warmer conditions can reduce endurance performance, increase physiological strain and make it more difficult to maintain a planned race pace over 42.195 kilometres.
An analysis of seven North American marathons illustrates how substantially conditions can influence elite performances. Researchers found that leading male runners finished approximately 1.7 per cent slower relative to course records under the coolest conditions examined. In the warmest category, that difference increased to around 4.5 per cent.
For an athlete capable of running a marathon in 2:05:00, a slowdown of that magnitude could translate into several additional minutes on the clock. At the elite level, where races are frequently decided by seconds, such a difference can determine whether a runner achieves a personal best, secures a podium finish or misses a major performance target.
The consequences can be even more noticeable among recreational athletes, who often spend considerably longer exposed to the conditions.

### [2027 Could Bring Unprecedented Heat, Raising New Concerns for Marathon Runners Worldwide](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15441)
A separate analysis by researchers at the University of Chicago, examining approximately 4.7 million marathon finishing times, highlighted the substantial effect of temperature on runners across different ability levels. The findings suggested that the typical participant could lose roughly 19 minutes when racing in temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, compared with conditions in the 40s. In the 80s Fahrenheit, the estimated time penalty rose to approximately 33 minutes.
These figures underline why marathon preparation involves much more than mileage, speed sessions and strength training. Temperature, humidity, direct sunlight and the body's ability to regulate heat can all influence how effectively a runner sustains an effort over the full distance.
Many marathon performances are achieved in cool conditions, with temperatures of approximately 4°C to 10°C often considered favourable for endurance running. As temperatures climb beyond that range, the body must devote more resources to cooling itself, potentially increasing cardiovascular strain and making a previously comfortable pace harder to maintain.
However, there is no universal temperature at which every marathon runner begins to slow down. Individual fitness, acclimatisation, humidity, wind, course exposure and race strategy all influence performance. A cool, overcast morning can produce very different outcomes from a sunny, humid day, even when the thermometer shows similar readings.

### [Cancer Survivor Brandon Throop Returns To Toronto Marathon In Hospital Gown For Third World Record Bid](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15440)
For [Brandon Throop](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Brandon+Throop), running a marathon in a hospital gown is about far more than chasing a place in the [Guinness World Records](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Guinness+World+Records). It is a deeply personal tribute to the medical team that helped save his life, a celebration of survival, and an opportunity to give back to the institution that stood beside him during one of the darkest chapters of his life.
![Image 8](https://mybestruns.com/street/f29108f8a11d11c189a98e7ad107e25370003868a0c2a06a0f60240f82ca748e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

### [Five Years On, Agnes Tirop’s Light Still Shines in the World of Athletics](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15428)
A Champion Who Rose to the Top at 19
Tirop announced herself on the global stage in spectacular fashion at the 2015 World Athletics Cross Country Championships in Guiyang, China. At only 19, she won the senior women's race, becoming the youngest champion in the event since Zola Budd in 1985.
Her victory demonstrated not only her natural ability but also the composure and determination that would become defining features of her running career.
She subsequently established herself among the world's leading track athletes, winning bronze medals in the women's 10,000 metres at the 2017 World Athletics Championships in London and the 2019 edition in Doha.
Those back-to-back podium finishes confirmed her consistency at the highest level and underlined her ability to compete against the strongest distance runners in the world.
Tirop also demonstrated considerable versatility at the Tokyo 2020 Olympic Games, held in 2021, where she finished fourth in the women's 5,000 metres. Although she narrowly missed the podium, her performance reinforced her reputation as one of Kenya's most accomplished emerging distance-running talents.
A World Record That Made History
Just weeks before her death, Tirop delivered one of the defining performances of her career.

Ugandan distance-running star [Jacob Kiplimo](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Jacob+Kiplimo) has revealed that a hamstring problem disrupted his race at the [2026 Chicago Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2026+Chicago+Marathon), forcing him to abandon his ambitions of defending his title and settle for fourth place after a challenging final 12 kilometres.

![Image 87](https://mybestruns.com/street/bcddaa50798e533b22b96c84aa404c05c5d8075c35d5a281daa97d3265dadcb8.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
In a statement reflecting on his performance, the Ugandan star explained that his body had been responding well until the problem emerged. The setback significantly changed the nature of his race, leaving him to fight through the remaining distance rather than pursue the victory he had targeted.

### [Jacob Kiplimo Reveals Hamstring Injury After Chicago Marathon Struggle, Vows to Return Stronger](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15426)
![Image 88](https://mybestruns.com/street/6cf96d582c33def15b6d42d8b0621202c4f8b3c8e09608945a1f3199cb8c7c8d.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Despite the pain and disappointment, Kiplimo refused to abandon the contest. He battled through the closing kilometres, drawing on his resilience to reach the finish line, although his time was not enough to secure a place on the podium.
“Finishing fourth as the defending champion is not the result I came to Chicago for,” Kiplimo acknowledged, while emphasising the determination required to complete the race after his hamstring problem developed.
The race was ultimately won by Kenya’s Amos Kipruto, who delivered an impressive performance to claim victory in 2:01:09. Ethiopia’s Tadese Bikila finished second in 2:02:56, followed by compatriot Milkesa Mengesha, who secured third place in 2:03:46. Kiplimo completed the top four in 2:04:18.
For the Ugandan star, the immediate priority is now recovery rather than competition. He indicated that he intends to take time away from the demands of professional racing, focus on his rehabilitation and enjoy valuable moments with his family before returning to training and competition.
“This is not the end of the story,” Kiplimo declared, striking a determined tone despite the setback. He added that he would allow himself time to recover before returning to work, expressing confidence that he and his team would come back stronger and be prepared for the next challenge.
Although missing out on the title was undoubtedly disappointing, Kiplimo’s response underlines his determination to move forward rather than allow one difficult race to define his season. His recovery will now be an important factor in determining when he can resume full training and prepare for his next competitive assignment.

### [Jacob Kiplimo Reveals Hamstring Injury After Chicago Marathon Struggle, Vows to Return Stronger](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15426)

### [From Kipchoge’s Impossible Dream to Sawe’s Historic Reality: Kenya Redefines Marathon Running](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15425)
Seven years after [Eliud Kipchoge](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Eliud+Kipchoge) challenged the limits of human endurance in [Vienna](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Vienna), fellow Kenyan [Sabastian Sawe](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Sabastian+Sawe) has transformed that extraordinary vision into a landmark achievement in competitive marathon running, becoming the first man to complete the 42.195-kilometre distance in under two hours under record-eligible race conditions.
![Image 91](https://mybestruns.com/street/09c936b4feb8e8614298bb63445b51428263e957b2269c10f6e670ba58231820.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
On October 12, 2019, Kipchoge etched his name into sporting history when he completed the [INEOS 1:59 Challenge](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=INEOS+1%3A59+Challenge) in Vienna, Austria, in an astonishing 1:59:40.2. Although the performance could not be recognised as an official world record because of the controlled conditions under which it was staged, it demonstrated that the seemingly impossible barrier was within human reach.
Kipchoge’s achievement carried a powerful message that resonated far beyond athletics: “[No human is limited](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=No+human+is+limited).” His words became a symbol of determination, ambition and the courage to challenge established boundaries.
However, the dream of breaking two hours in an official marathon remained unfinished.

### [From Kipchoge’s Impossible Dream to Sawe’s Historic Reality: Kenya Redefines Marathon Running](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15425)
![Image 92](https://mybestruns.com/street/e8210b623c02520bd4eb6f1bc77879c8ebdf440eab102589d400d651b0cff86e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
That changed on April 26, 2026, when Sawe delivered a breathtaking performance at the TCS London Marathon, stopping the clock at 1:59:30 to claim victory and establish a new men's marathon world record. The Kenyan took an astonishing 65 seconds off the previous record of 2:00:35, set by the late Kelvin Kiptum at the 2023 Chicago Marathon.
Sawe’s achievement was historic not simply because he ran faster than Kipchoge’s celebrated Vienna time, but because he accomplished the feat in an official, competitive marathon eligible for world-record recognition. The distinction elevated his performance into an entirely new chapter of distance-running history.
Remarkably, Sawe was not the only athlete to challenge the two-hour barrier that day. Ethiopia’s Yomif Kejelcha finished second in 1:59:41, becoming the second man to run under two hours in a competitive marathon. Uganda’s Jacob Kiplimo completed the podium in 2:00:28, also finishing inside Kiptum’s previous world record.
The extraordinary results underlined how dramatically the boundaries of marathon running have shifted in a sport where even a few seconds can separate an athlete from immortality.
For Kenya, Sawe’s triumph represents another defining moment in a remarkable tradition of distance-running excellence. From the groundbreaking achievements of Kipchoge to Kiptum’s world-record performance and now Sawe’s sub-two-hour marathon, Kenyan athletes have continued to shape the evolution of the sport.

### [From Kipchoge’s Impossible Dream to Sawe’s Historic Reality: Kenya Redefines Marathon Running](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15425)
Yet the connection between Kipchoge and Sawe goes beyond nationality. Kipchoge demonstrated that the marathon distance could be covered in less than two hours under specially controlled conditions. Sawe carried that vision into open competition, where the challenge had to be conquered within the demands of an official race.
Their achievements tell a compelling story of how sporting dreams can inspire future generations to pursue what once appeared unattainable.
On October 12, 2026, exactly seven years after Kipchoge’s landmark run in Vienna, the anniversary offers a powerful opportunity to reflect on how far marathon running has progressed. What began as a demonstration of human potential has become an officially recognised world-record achievement.
Kipchoge opened the door to a new era of possibility. Sawe ran through it and changed marathon history forever.
One dream. Two Kenyan legends. A new definition of human endurance.
The message remains as powerful as ever: No human is limited.

### [90-Year-Old Bill Schwarz Runs His First Marathon, Turning a Lifetime of Running Into an Extraordinary Achievement](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15424)
[Bill Schwarz](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Bill+Schwarz) has been running since high school, but it took until the age of 90 for the retired engineer from Mesa, Arizona, to take on the ultimate endurance challenge of his running journey: a full marathon.
![Image 95](https://mybestruns.com/street/eb0597f2722e4b334bf4e7d8891d150992fbfd61ee7555e221265b0660f937a8.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Schwarz made his marathon debut at the Rock ’n’ Roll San Diego Marathon in [California](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=California), completing the demanding 26.2-mile (42.195-kilometre) distance in just over nine hours. His achievement has captured attention as a powerful example of determination, resilience and the willingness to pursue new goals, even in the later stages of life.
For Schwarz, the marathon was never about chasing a fast finishing time or competing against younger runners. His objective was much simpler: to cover the entire distance and reach the finish line.
“The objective is to finish the race. Time is not important,” he said before the start.
And that is precisely what he did. Even after the official race clock had stopped, Schwarz continued until his sports watch confirmed that he had covered the full marathon distance, remaining committed to completing what he had set out to achieve.
His decision to attempt the marathon emerged from an unexpected source of inspiration. At 89, Schwarz completed a 60-mile hike along Spain’s famous Camino de Santiago pilgrimage route. The demanding adventure left him feeling stronger than he had anticipated, prompting him to reconsider what he might still accomplish physically.

### [90-Year-Old Bill Schwarz Runs His First Marathon, Turning a Lifetime of Running Into an Extraordinary Achievement](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15424)
Rather than treating the experience as the culmination of his endurance adventures, he saw it as an opportunity to set himself a new challenge. The marathon, a distance he had never previously attempted, became his next major goal.
Schwarz’s professional background also makes his story particularly fascinating. A retired engineer who once worked on components for the Apollo rocket programme, he approached the challenge with the practical mindset of someone accustomed to solving complex problems. His preparation combined physical conditioning, careful planning and the use of modern technology to help him manage the demands of a long-distance race.
In the 12 months leading up to his marathon debut, Schwarz completed five half marathons while incorporating strength training, Pilates and mobility exercises into his routine. These activities helped him prepare for the physical demands of running 26.2 miles, a distance that requires not only endurance but also patience, discipline and a well-managed race strategy.
He also turned to artificial intelligence for assistance with one of the most important aspects of marathon preparation: nutrition and hydration. Using ChatGPT, Schwarz developed a fueling plan based on taking approximately 16 ounces of fluid and one energy gel per hour. Information from his fitness watch helped inform his approach, illustrating how technology can support athletes as they prepare for demanding endurance challenges.
However, his journey to the starting line was shaped by more than physical ambition. After the death of his wife, Janice, Schwarz faced a deeply personal period of grief. Running became part of his effort to navigate that loss and find renewed purpose in life.
Over time, he channelled that experience into pursuing meaningful challenges rather than withdrawing from them. His journey also included a new chapter in his personal life, as he found love again with his now-wife, Tammy. Together with his renewed commitment to running and adventure, these experiences helped shape the outlook that ultimately led him to attempt his first marathon.
The road to San Diego was therefore about far more than completing a particular distance. It represented a personal journey of rediscovery, demonstrating how a difficult chapter in life can become the starting point for new ambitions and experiences.

### [90-Year-Old Bill Schwarz Runs His First Marathon, Turning a Lifetime of Running Into an Extraordinary Achievement](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15424)
Completing a marathon is a significant achievement at any age. The 42.195-kilometre distance tests the limits of physical endurance and mental resilience, demanding careful preparation and the determination to keep moving when fatigue sets in. For a 90-year-old first-time marathoner, simply reaching the starting line after months of preparation was already a noteworthy milestone.
Schwarz went further, completing the distance and inspiring spectators and fellow participants along the route. His performance was a reminder that the meaning of a marathon extends well beyond finishing times, elite rankings and personal records. For many runners, the greatest victory is accomplishing something they once thought might remain beyond their reach.
His story also offers an important perspective on ageing. While physical abilities and training requirements change over time, Schwarz’s experience demonstrates the value of staying active, setting realistic goals and approaching new challenges with determination. His journey is not a guarantee that everyone can safely undertake the same feat, but it is a compelling example of what sustained preparation and personal motivation can make possible.
After crossing the finish line, Schwarz had fulfilled the promise he made before the race: to finish, regardless of the time. And, having committed himself to the challenge, he had every reason to enjoy a well-earned rest afterwards.
At 90, Bill Schwarz has completed a milestone that eluded him throughout decades of running. His first marathon was not about proving that age does not matter, but about showing that a person's ambitions need not end simply because another birthday arrives.
From running in high school to completing 26.2 miles for the first time nine decades into his life, Schwarz has written an extraordinary new chapter in his personal running story.
His achievement sends a message to runners and non-runners alike: sometimes, the most meaningful finish line is the one you never imagined you would reach. And sometimes, the perfect time to attempt your first marathon is 90 years old.

For many marathoners, crossing the finish line of a World Marathon Major is the ultimate dream. But before you can worry about surviving 42.195 kilometres, there is another challenge: actually getting onto the starting line.

The six [Abbott World Marathon Majors](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Abbott+World+Marathon+Majors) — [Boston](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Boston), [London](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=London), [Berlin](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Berlin), [Chicago](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Chicago), [New York](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York) and [Tokyo](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Tokyo) — do not use the same entry system, and some are considerably more difficult to access than others.
Boston is arguably the clearest example of how running fast does not always guarantee a place. Unlike the other majors, the Boston Marathon is built around qualifying standards. However, meeting the published standard only gives a runner the opportunity to apply. Because demand is so high, the fastest qualifiers are accepted first. This means a runner can achieve the official qualifying time and still miss out when the cut-off moves faster than expected.

Tokyo adds another layer of difficulty, particularly for international runners. The race has a lottery as well as several other entry routes, including charity and performance-based options. ### [7 Packing Tips for Your First Time Traveling For a Race](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15391)
Traveling for a race is the perfect excuse to turn a running weekend into an adventure. Perhaps you’re heading to the [Tokyo Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/TokyoMarathon?b=prz&details=Y)⁠ and already thinking about the sushi and ramen you’ll enjoy afterward. Or maybe your next finish line is beside the beach.
Between training, booking a hotel and planning what to explore, packing can become an afterthought. Then race morning arrives, and your favorite socks are still at home, your race information is buried in your suitcase and your water bottle is nowhere to be found.
A little organization before departure can make the entire trip smoother. These seven packing tips will help you arrive ready to run and enjoy the weekend.
1. Pack Your Race-Day Outfit in Your Carry-On
Keep your race-day clothing and essentials in your carry-on. Pack your running top, shorts or tights, socks, sports bra if needed, and the small items you depend on during a race. If your checked luggage is delayed, your key gear will still be with you.
![Image 240](https://mybestruns.com/street/5c6a74501acac9b0ede92d94316cdfa0b4cdf306eb1a8ff130a06ab99f4b0028.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Fold your race outfit together or place it in a packing pouch so everything is easy to find. A smaller zip pouch can hold accessories. Knowing exactly where your race kit is means one less thing to worry about when you arrive.
2. Wear Your Running Shoes on the Plane
Your running shoes deserve the same attention as your race outfit. Wearing them on the plane keeps them out of checked luggage and leaves more room in your suitcase.
Choose a familiar pair you have already used in training. Race weekend is not the time to discover that new shoes rub or fit differently than expected. If you prefer to travel in another pair, keep your race shoes in your carry-on.

### [7 Packing Tips for Your First Time Traveling For a Race](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15391)
![Image 241](https://mybestruns.com/street/e69995b49a9f8387df3a425267e0e7bfdd5cf1fd3f9dcf4c2ee037e9c24fb131.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
3. Bring a Spacious Bag for Your Gear
A race trip often requires more than running clothes. Add a jacket, recovery clothes, snacks and accessories, and your packing list grows quickly. A spacious duffel with sturdy handles and useful pockets can keep those extras organized and serve as a day bag at your destination.
Think about what you’ll do beyond race day. A hike may call for trail shoes and a light layer. If pickleball is part of your plans, you may want a paddle and extra clothes.
The same thinking applies when choosing your bag. If you’re planning a few games on the court during the trip, consider [pickleball tour and duffel bags](https://pickleballnation.com/collections/pickleball-bags-and-backpacks)⁠. A backpack may be more practical for hiking or exploring on foot. Choose a bag that suits your itinerary, and check your airline’s size and weight limits before packing.
4. Organize Your Bib and Race Documents
Keep your identification, registration confirmation and race instructions together. A slim document pouch works well for paper copies, while a dedicated folder on your phone can keep digital information easy to access.
Download important details before leaving home, including the race map, confirmation email and packet pickup instructions. Save copies you can open without an internet connection.
If you already have your bib, keep it flat and protected. Otherwise, check where and when you need to collect it and what identification the organizer requires. Handling these details in advance helps keep the pre-race scramble to a minimum.
5. Take Familiar Snacks with You
Race travel can disrupt your usual eating routine. Your preferred breakfast may be unavailable, and the hotel buffet may not offer what you normally eat before a run.

### [7 Packing Tips for Your First Time Traveling For a Race](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15391)
Bring the bars, gels and electrolyte products you have already used in training. Your [runner’s diet](https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/runners-diet)⁠ shouldn’t become a vacation guessing game.
Count what you’ll need for travel and race day, then pack a little extra. Keep some familiar snacks in your carry-on and bring enough race fuel for your planned strategy. Check destination rules before carrying food across international borders.
6. Always Have a Water Bottle
Busy travel days can make it easy to forget your usual drinking habits. A reusable water bottle is a simple item that deserves a place on your packing list.
Carry it empty through airport security, then fill it where drinking water is available. Keep it handy during your journey and when heading out for packet pickup or other race activities.
Staying hydrated is also part of [caring for your body while traveling](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php/7021)⁠. If an electrolyte mix is already part of your routine, pack your usual product. Having familiar supplies nearby makes it easier to maintain your normal habits while traveling.
7. Pack Layers for Changing Weather
A mild forecast doesn’t always reflect how it will feel while waiting at the starting line early in the morning. Pack a lightweight layer you have already worn while running.
A zip jacket or long-sleeve top can help you stay comfortable before the start. Decide in advance whether you’ll carry it during the race or leave it at an official bag check, following the organizer’s instructions.
For colder conditions, familiar gloves and other tested gear can help. Review this guide to [running in cold weather](https://mybestruns.com/What_to_Wear_for_Running_in_Cold_Weather.html)⁠, then check the forecast again before departure and once more before race morning so you can make any final adjustments.
Thoughtful packing helps you get more out of a destination race. Keep essential gear close, choose a bag that works for your plans and organize your documents before you leave. With those details handled, you can spend less time searching through your suitcase and more time enjoying the run—and everything that comes afterward.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)

Long before he conquered world cross-country championships, dominated the half-marathon distance and lifted the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) trophy, [Geoffrey Kamworor](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor) was a young Kenyan student with an ambitious dream that had little to do with running: becoming a [lawyer](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=lawyer).

![Image 2](https://mybestruns.com/street/de57be259ad5f2aa804935a23c35ae7bb6b49b6ec295d0ed68325e1b13b71303.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Growing up in Keiyo South, Kamworor developed the discipline that would later define his extraordinary athletic career. His daily routine involved running approximately five kilometres to school and another five kilometres back home. What might have seemed like an ordinary journey for a schoolboy was quietly laying the foundation for a future in international distance running.

![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/808283ce83ea90fb69283ae3a63fb6cc12becf4782bc79b9156f109324db53df.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

He attended Chepsamo Primary School before proceeding to Lelboinet Secondary School, where he combined his education with a growing passion for athletics. At the time, his ambitions extended beyond the track and roads. He wanted to pursue a career in law, and that dream eventually brought him an opportunity to study at a college in the United States.

However, the young Kenyan faced a defining decision: follow the academic path he had envisioned or commit himself fully to the sport that was beginning to reveal his remarkable potential. Kamworor chose athletics, a decision that would ultimately place his name among the most accomplished distance runners of his generation.

![Image 4](https://mybestruns.com/street/a94c34052d38330fd293c08402206cd4d7a39c33946639bdb76ca84e0ab123e7.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

His transformation from a promising schoolboy into an international contender began gathering momentum in 2010, when he joined the GSC training camp in Kaptagat. His development accelerated rapidly, and within a short period, an opportunity to compete in Finland exposed him to a higher level of international competition.

Still only 17, he reportedly competed nine times during that trip, demonstrating an impressive ability to adapt to the demands of competitive racing. Breaking the eight-minute barrier for 3,000 metres was an early indication of the talent that would eventually carry him to the highest levels of distance running.

![Image 5](https://mybestruns.com/street/84282c8c1c650ab6ffe7062ef243eacc858a034f27f3ff8005541232e23d4bd3.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

His breakthrough on the international stage followed in March 2011, when he captured the junior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Punta Umbría, Spain. That victory announced the arrival of a young athlete whose future would extend far beyond the junior ranks.

Kamworor was not simply a runner with speed. He possessed the endurance, tactical intelligence and competitive determination required to succeed across different distances and racing surfaces. As his career developed, those qualities became the hallmarks of an athlete capable of challenging the world's best.

Cross country became one of the foundations of Kamworor's international success. In 2015, he won the senior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Guiyang, China, confirming his status as one of the leading distance runners in the world. Two years later, he returned to the top of the podium in Kampala, Uganda, defending his senior world cross-country crown in front of a home crowd. Winning consecutive senior world titles placed him in an elite category and demonstrated his remarkable command of the demanding discipline.

On the roads, however, Kamworor established an equally impressive legacy. He won the World Half Marathon Championships in Copenhagen in 2014, Cardiff in 2016 and Valencia in 2018, becoming a three-time champion at the distance. His achievements reflected a rare combination of strength, speed and race management, enabling him to prevail against formidable international opposition.

The half marathon became one of his signature events, but Kamworor's ambitions were never confined to a single discipline. He continued to demonstrate his versatility on the track, winning silver in the men's 10,000 metres at the 2015 World Athletics Championships in Beijing, China. From the grass of cross-country courses to the roads of major international races and the track of a global championship, he repeatedly demonstrated that his talent could flourish wherever the competition took him.

Among Kamworor's most memorable achievements are his victories at the New York City Marathon in 2017 and 2019. Winning one of the world's most celebrated marathons requires exceptional endurance, but winning it twice demands much more: tactical patience, resilience and the ability to navigate a demanding course against a deep international field.

Kamworor demonstrated those qualities in both victories, establishing a special connection with the New York race and adding the marathon to an already remarkable collection of honours. His success in the American city also illustrated his ability to move successfully between distances. An athlete celebrated for his cross-country and half-marathon dominance had shown that he could also conquer the 42.195-kilometre marathon, one of the most demanding challenges in road racing.

Now, as he sets his sights on another New York campaign, the Kenyan star has an opportunity to strengthen his legacy further. A third men's open-division victory would place him among a very select group of athletes to have won the prestigious race three times. Such a milestone would be more than another addition to his trophy cabinet; it would reinforce the story of a runner whose competitive range has extended across nearly every major discipline in distance running.

Behind Kamworor's achievements lies a training environment built around discipline, consistency and high-level competition. Working under the guidance of renowned coach Patrick Sang, he has trained alongside some of Kenya's most celebrated athletes, including marathon great Eliud Kipchoge and middle- and long-distance superstar Faith Kipyegon.

Sharing a training environment with athletes of such calibre provides a demanding daily standard. Yet Kamworor has built his own identity through a career defined by major championship victories and sustained success across different racing distances. His journey has also included difficult periods and setbacks, reminding the running world that even the most accomplished champions must continually work to return to their best. His longevity at the elite level reflects the importance of patience, dedication and the willingness to keep pursuing new goals.

For aspiring athletes in Kenya, his story offers an important lesson: extraordinary achievements are often built through ordinary routines repeated consistently over many years. Those five-kilometre journeys to school and back were not glamorous. They did not come with cheering crowds, television cameras or medals. Yet they formed part of the foundation of a career that would eventually take him to the world's biggest running stages.

Kamworor's story is ultimately about a choice that changed the direction of his life. The young student who once imagined himself arguing cases in a courtroom instead built his reputation by answering the toughest questions on the running track and roads. His achievements speak for themselves: world cross-country titles, three world half-marathon crowns, a global 10,000-metre silver medal and two New York City Marathon victories.

He may never have pursued the legal career he once envisioned, but his athletic record tells a compelling story of ambition, sacrifice and extraordinary accomplishment. His pursuit of another New York triumph offers a fresh chapter in a career that has already crossed the boundaries between cross country, track and road racing.

For Geoffrey Kamworor, the courtroom was a dream he left behind. The world of distance running became the stage on which he built his name. And while the law lost a prospective lawyer, athletics gained a champion whose achievements have helped define an era of Kenyan distance running.

### [From $1 To $358: How The New York City Marathon Became A Global Running Phenomenon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15437)

What began as a modest race through Central Park, with a handful of determined runners and a budget of just $1,000, has evolved into one of the most prestigious and sought-after marathons in the world. More than five decades later, the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) tells a remarkable story of how distance running has grown from a grassroots sporting event into a global spectacle.

![Image 9](https://mybestruns.com/street/bacec4114b3d54670c15a184e950b0e7ddb43de9849a87f97fe568b1a68fdecf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

When the inaugural New York City Marathon took place in 1970, the entry fee was just $1. Organised by the New York Road Runners, the race was held entirely within Central Park, far removed from the enormous crowds, international attention and commercial scale that define the event today.

![Image 10](https://mybestruns.com/street/cb333999ed07e06d10edcf37e5452882364cbb7336ebf8347871bb079ae7bfbf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Of the 127 registered participants, only 55 completed the race. Yet, despite its modest beginnings, the event laid the foundation for a marathon that would eventually capture the imagination of runners from every corner of the world.

The first champion was Gary Muhrcke, a New York City firefighter whose victory remains one of the most memorable stories from the race's early years. According to accounts of the inaugural edition, Muhrcke had finished a night shift before entering the competition shortly before the start. He went on to win in approximately 2:31, securing his place in the marathon's history.

The inaugural race also featured Nina Kuscsik, the only woman in the field. She started the event but withdrew after becoming ill, meaning no woman finished that first edition. Kuscsik would later become an important figure in the campaign for women's inclusion in competitive distance running.

Over the years, the New York City Marathon expanded beyond Central Park, eventually developing into the iconic five-borough journey that takes runners through Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Manhattan. Its transformation helped turn the race into a celebration of athletic achievement, community spirit and the extraordinary diversity of New York City.

Today, the marathon attracts elite athletes chasing victories and records, recreational runners pursuing personal milestones, charity participants raising funds for important causes, and thousands of international visitors eager to experience one of running's most celebrated events.

### [Sifan Hassan Withdraws From 2026 New York City Marathon As Illness Disrupts Her Preparation](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15434)

Olympic marathon champion [Sifan Hassan](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Sifan+Hassan) of [the Netherlands](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=the+Netherlands) has officially withdrawn from the [2026 TCS New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2026+TCS+New+York+City+Marathon) after illness disrupted her preparations, ending hopes of seeing the versatile distance-running star return to one of the world’s most prestigious road races this autumn.

![Image 14](https://mybestruns.com/street/ff056ddb48590d9d5770aeba39b2968d8cbf9e31921bf90d9e503fe24646ab1c.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Hassan announced her decision on social media, explaining that sickness had slowed her training and left her short of the level of preparation she had hoped to achieve ahead of the November 1 race. The withdrawal is a setback for the Dutch star, who had been looking forward to returning stronger after her previous appearance in New York.

“I was so excited to come back stronger, but a sickness slowed down my training and I’m not where I wanted to be. Sometimes, things just don’t go as planned,” Hassan wrote.

Despite her disappointment, the Olympic champion also sent her best wishes to the athletes preparing to compete in New York, demonstrating her support for the wider running community even as she steps away from the competition.

Hassan, who holds a personal best of 2:13:44, ranks fifth on the women’s all-time marathon list. Her extraordinary range across track and road running has established her as one of the most versatile athletes of her generation, capable of competing at the highest level from shorter distances to the marathon.

![Image 15](https://mybestruns.com/street/ef554feb696cb3fe2c211d5312650a678a574b1ad394f3e13678ec6ed3f56cfc.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Her marathon career has already produced several memorable achievements. Hassan has won the London Marathon and Chicago Marathon, claimed victory at the Sydney Marathon, and secured Olympic marathon gold at the Paris 2024 Games. Those accomplishments underline her ability to adapt to different courses, race conditions and competitive challenges.

The withdrawal from New York follows another interruption to her 2026 campaign. Hassan previously pulled out of the London Marathon because of an Achilles injury, and the latest illness has further disrupted her plans for the season. With her training affected, stepping aside from New York allows her to prioritise her recovery rather than compete without the preparation she considers necessary.

Hassan’s absence will be a significant talking point in the build-up to the New York City Marathon, which takes runners through all five boroughs of the city before finishing in Central Park. The demanding course and deep international field regularly produce compelling racing, and her withdrawal creates an opportunity for other leading contenders to strengthen their ambitions.

Although the precise implications for the women’s elite field will depend on the final start list, the race remains an important opportunity for leading East African athletes and top American runners to challenge for victory. Without Hassan on the starting line, attention will turn to the athletes capable of taking advantage of the opportunity and delivering a memorable performance on the streets of New York.

For Hassan, however, the priority is no longer the immediate challenge of another marathon. The Dutch star has built her reputation through resilience, adaptability and a willingness to take on some of the toughest challenges in distance running. Recovering fully and returning to structured training will be essential as she considers her next competitive objectives.

At 33, Hassan already has an exceptional record that includes Olympic glory and victories at some of the world's most prestigious marathons. While her withdrawal is disappointing for fans who hoped to see her compete in New York again, it does not diminish the achievements that have made her one of the defining distance runners of her era.

The running world will now wait for news of her recovery and next racing plans. For the moment, Hassan’s message is clear: sometimes, even the best-laid preparations do not go according to plan, and knowing when to step back is part of an athlete’s journey.

The 2026 TCS New York City Marathon is scheduled for November 1. Hassan’s withdrawal removes one of the most accomplished names from the anticipated women’s field, but the race will continue to bring together elite athletes from around the world for another major contest over the five-borough course.

She has also taken on the New York City Marathon four times, building a considerable record of participation in some of the world's most celebrated long-distance races.

Although her 3:47:55 finish in Chicago was not a personal best, the result marked another successful completion of the marathon distance while reinforcing the role running can play in supporting charitable causes.

For Clinton, the Chicago Marathon was about more than reaching the finish line. It was an opportunity to challenge herself physically, share the experience with a friend, celebrate a family moment and contribute to a mission aimed at improving maternal health.

### [Getting Into a World Marathon Major May Be Harder Than Running One](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15404)

For many marathoners, crossing the finish line of a World Marathon Major is the ultimate dream. But before you can worry about surviving 42.195 kilometres, there is another challenge: actually getting onto the starting line.

![Image 24](https://mybestruns.com/street/5d4dc1de5763b06ea3b94d885ebb3beb7a42c46fdce18c4925b726d66d79e60b.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

The six [Abbott World Marathon Majors](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Abbott+World+Marathon+Majors) — [Boston](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Boston), [London](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=London), [Berlin](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Berlin), [Chicago](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Chicago), [New York](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York) and [Tokyo](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Tokyo) — do not use the same entry system, and some are considerably more difficult to access than others.

Boston is arguably the clearest example of how running fast does not always guarantee a place. Unlike the other majors, the Boston Marathon is built around qualifying standards. However, meeting the published standard only gives a runner the opportunity to apply. Because demand is so high, the fastest qualifiers are accepted first. This means a runner can achieve the official qualifying time and still miss out when the cut-off moves faster than expected.

![Image 25](https://mybestruns.com/street/f43cbba0c0a711c3a231a45db4e08fb49d7ffb83dc86bd3092f391b075c9c8ca.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

London presents a completely different challenge. Its famous ballot is a random draw, making luck a major part of the process. However, runners have other avenues, including Good for Age, charity places and international tour operators. Even the Good for Age route can be highly competitive, with places allocated according to performance when demand exceeds the number of available spots.

New York City is another race where demand is enormous. ### [New York City Marathon Makes First Course Change in 15 Years](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15322)

The [TCS New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=TCS+New+York+City+Marathon) is set for a small but significant change to its iconic 26.2-mile course, with runners facing a revised section in the [Bronx](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Bronx) between Miles 20 and 21.

![Image 56](https://mybestruns.com/street/1936f9c4ddcb81f2a6318668a43f8a3258c6e4f5dedf2d2dac5807d0770bcefc.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

For 15 years, every New York City Marathon runner passed through the exact same stretch of the Bronx around Mile 20, navigating a short loop that surrounded a neighborhood supermarket and a 24-hour laundromat for much of race day. This November, that familiar loop will disappear.

![Image 57](https://mybestruns.com/street/07436f3fad13077b64b5db3e62de1d38e3117daf68206f1199d03f5681bbcbaf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

New York Road Runners (NYRR) is making its first course change to the marathon in 15 years. Instead of looping near East 140th Street, runners will head north on Alexander Avenue, turn onto Third Avenue and then cut south on 138th Street toward the Madison Avenue Bridge.

The adjustment removes two turns from the Bronx section, reducing the number from seven to five. While that may sound insignificant for a race covering 26.2 miles, the change comes at a point when runners are already deep into the marathon and every turn, road surface and change in rhythm can become more noticeable.

![Image 58](https://mybestruns.com/street/dee421746c00314bfab71315f1f23f5cb01e237877ad3c36a10fa4f29ea4a7ba.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

However, the primary reason for the change is not to make the course faster or help runners shave seconds from their finishing times.

Bronx resident Jennifer Alicea told The New York Times that the previous route made it extremely difficult to reach her only nearby grocery store on marathon day. NYRR's Metellus, who grew up in the Bronx, described the affected blocks as food deserts and saw the course's required recertification as an opportunity to address the problem.

The timing also carries added significance. This year marks 50 years since the New York City Marathon expanded beyond Central Park in 1976, becoming the five-borough race that has since grown into one of the world's most famous marathons.

The route will still cover the same 26.2 miles through New York's five boroughs, but the Bronx experience will be slightly different. For elite athletes, two fewer turns could mean a smoother rhythm during the crucial closing stages. For thousands of recreational runners, the bigger difference may be felt by the communities living along the course rather than on the race clock.

The New York City Marathon has long been celebrated not only for its elite competition but also for the connection between the race and the communities it passes through. The latest adjustment reflects that relationship, showing how even an established course can evolve while preserving the character of the event.

So, two fewer turns, the same five boroughs and the same 26.2 miles — but potentially one less headache for residents of the Bronx.

For runners taking on New York this November, the question remains: will you even notice those two fewer turns when you reach Mile 20?

![Image 79](https://mybestruns.com/street/e0005200a822997cbe8454cfd4dcabc063f9e9744f68de4a5248c065db574fd9.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Today, she returns to the same Australian city as something far greater — an Olympic champion, four-time world champion, world cross-country champion, London Marathon winner, Laureus Sportswoman of the Year and one of Kenya’s most accomplished distance runners.

At 42, Cheruiyot will line up for the TCS Sydney Marathon on Sunday, August 30, completing an extraordinary full circle in a career that has stretched across more than two decades and transformed her from a teenage Olympian into one of the defining figures of her generation.

When Cheruiyot first competed in Sydney at the 2000 Olympic Games, few could have imagined the heights she would eventually reach. Still only 17, she advanced to the 5000m final and finished 14th — an experience that became the first chapter of an Olympic journey that would eventually span four Games.

The years that followed brought an extraordinary collection of victories.

Cheruiyot became world 5000m champion in 2009, then produced one of the greatest championship performances of her career in Daegu in 2011, winning both the 5000m and 10,000m titles while also claiming World Cross Country gold earlier that year. She added another world 10,000m title in Beijing in 2015, taking her tally to four senior world championships.

“I said I want to win,” Cheruiyot recalled after that historic victory. “This was my fourth Olympics and I’ve been dreaming about this since the very start.”

Her brilliance was not confined to the track.

After moving into marathon running, Cheruiyot established herself among the world’s best over 42.195km. She finished fourth in her London Marathon debut in 2017 before returning the following year to produce a stunning victory in 2:18:31 — a performance that placed her fourth on the world all-time list at the time and remains her marathon personal best.

She also finished runner-up in the New York City Marathon in 2018 and second in London in 2019, further demonstrating that her extraordinary competitive instinct had successfully followed her from the track to the roads.

Away from competition, Cheruiyot’s story has also evolved with her life. She became a mother, welcomed her daughter Arielle in 2021 and returned to competitive racing in 2023. In 2024, she claimed third place at the New York City Marathon, followed by fifth at the 2025 London Marathon.

Now Sydney offers her another opportunity to write her name into the city’s sporting history.

“I look back on my career with pride. I was able to win almost everything and have been at the top for a long time,” Cheruiyot said ahead of her return.

She also remembers the extraordinary generation in which she competed — an era that included global icons such as Usain Bolt, Tirunesh Dibaba and Meseret Defar.

“I was running in a great era and had a close-up view of athletes like Usain Bolt setting the world alight,” she reflected.

Yet perhaps the most remarkable aspect of Cheruiyot’s return is not simply the passage of time, but her willingness to keep challenging herself.

She arrives in Sydney having put considerable work into rebuilding her fitness, knowing that the marathon demands something entirely different from the explosive championship races that defined her track career.

“I am very excited to go back to Sydney,” she said. “It has been 26 years since I was there, and a lot has changed in my life since then. I hope to have a good run — I have put in a lot of work to regain fitness and hope my body will stand up to the 42km.”

Twenty-six years ago, Sydney introduced the world to a fearless Kenyan teenager chasing an Olympic dream.

Now, the same city welcomes back a woman who went on to conquer the track, cross country and marathon — and to leave an indelible mark on Kenyan athletics.

From teenage Olympian to Olympic champion. From world champion to marathon winner. From rising talent to mother and enduring icon.

Vivian Cheruiyot has come full circle — and Sydney is once again the stage.

### [From an Unplanned Marathon to Immortality: The Incredible Story of Grete Waitz's Nine New York City Marathon Victories](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14822)

When [Grete Waitz](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Grete+Waitz) boarded a flight to New York in October 1978 with her husband, Jack, becoming one of the greatest marathon runners in history was the last thing on her mind.

At just 25 years old, the Norwegian schoolteacher was an accomplished middle-distance athlete and a two-time Olympian over 1,500 metres. She had never raced a marathon, and the furthest she had ever run was only 10 miles in training. The journey to the United States was intended to be more of a holiday than a sporting mission.

Privately, he believed her lack of endurance experience would eventually catch up with her and that she would likely fade in the second half of the race. Instead, he unknowingly invited a future legend.

The evening before the marathon reflected just how little pressure Waitz placed on the race. She and Jack enjoyed an elegant dinner in Manhattan, complete with shrimp cocktail, filet mignon, ice cream, and red wine. It was hardly the meal most would associate with preparing for a world-class marathon, but for the couple, the trip was simply another adventure.

Even on race morning, Waitz admitted she barely knew where Central Park was.

Wearing bib 1173, she settled into the race with no expectations. As the miles unfolded, however, the Norwegian newcomer grew stronger while others began to struggle. In the second half, she surged into the lead and never looked back.

When she crossed the finish line in 2:32:30, the athletics world was left in disbelief.

Her remarkable victory transformed her career. Inspired by what she had achieved, Waitz left her teaching profession in Norway and dedicated herself fully to long-distance running. What began as a one-time experience evolved into one of the greatest careers the marathon has ever witnessed.

Geoffrey Kamworor proved once again that champions are defined not by setbacks, but by their response to them. Thirteen years after his breakthrough senior victory at the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon, the Kenyan legend returned to the same roads and delivered a masterclass performance, winning in 58:14—40 seconds faster than his winning time in 2013.

At 33, Kamworor was the oldest athlete in the elite field, yet he controlled the race with the authority of a runner in his prime. Neither the passage of time nor the devastating motorbike accident in 2020, which shattered his tibia and threatened his career, has diminished his competitive fire. Instead, his victory in Ras Al Khaimah confirmed that he remains one of the world’s most formidable distance runners.

![Image 203](https://mybestruns.com/street/e596ad71299533c0c9e862d1ca59dfd357ea084ccd69fdd6d1b63f23eb375bdd.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

From the gun, Kamworor executed a precise and disciplined strategy, running alongside his training partner and pacemaker Edwin Kipsaisak. The opening kilometer was covered in 2:44, followed by a relentless series of splits between 2:45 and 2:49. The sustained pace quickly discouraged any serious challenges from the younger contenders, who found themselves unable to disrupt Kamworor’s rhythm.

When Kipsaisak stepped aside after 8 kilometers, the decisive move had already been made. Kamworor passed 10K in 27:42, firmly in control. His surge between 16 and 17 kilometers, clocked in a punishing 2:42, broke the race open completely. From that point, victory was never in doubt.

“Actually, I knew I was going to win around 14K,” Kamworor said afterward. “I knew I had prepared well. I came here wanting to run a fast time, and Edwin did a great job pacing. It’s great to come back and win even faster.”

Behind him, Birhanu Balew of Bahrain ran strongly to secure second place in 58:23, while Kenya’s Gideon Rono impressed in his debut at the distance, finishing third in 58:38.

Kamworor’s journey back to the top has been anything but easy. Once the dominant force in global distance running—with three consecutive World Half Marathon titles, two World Cross Country championships, and two New York City Marathon victories—his career was nearly derailed in 2020 when he was struck by a motorbike during a solo training run. The injury required multiple surgeries and a lengthy rehabilitation, keeping him away from peak form for nearly three years.

Now fully recovered, Kamworor has returned to elite competition with renewed purpose. He finished second at the London Marathon in 2023 and has his sights set firmly on the marathon once again.

“I’m satisfied that I’m fully recovered now,” he said. “It’s very satisfying to win here again. Now I will go home and prepare for London in April. It will be very tough competition, but that’s what I like. My personal best is 2:04, but I believe I can go faster.”

Looking further ahead, Kamworor has set his ultimate goal on the Olympic Marathon at the 2028 Los Angeles Games. If selected, he would be nearing 36—but history shows that experience can triumph. Portuguese legend Carlos Lopes famously won Olympic marathon gold at age 38.

Women’s Race: Anley Wins Impressive Debut

The women’s race unfolded without an official pacemaker, placing the burden of pace-setting on the athletes themselves. Tanzania’s Magdalena Shauri courageously led much of the race but paid the price in the closing kilometers.

With just two kilometers remaining, Ethiopia’s Asmarech Anley and Melknat Wudu surged past the fading leader. Anley, making her half marathon debut, showed remarkable composure to take the win in 67:22.

“I realized I could win with a kilometer to go,” Anley said. “The times would have been faster with a pacemaker, but it doesn’t matter because I won.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor Returns to Ras Al Khaimah, Chasing Redemption on the Course That Launched His Career](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14155)

Thirteen years after announcing himself to the world on the roads of Ras Al Khaimah, [Geoffrey Kamworor](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor) returns to the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon this Saturday with renewed purpose, hard-earned resilience, and the belief that his best running may still lie ahead.

Few athletes in modern distance running have endured such dramatic highs and devastating setbacks. Kamworor’s victory here in 2013 marked his first major senior triumph and began a remarkable stretch of dominance. He went on to win three consecutive World Half Marathon titles and twice captured the World Cross Country Championships, establishing himself as one of the most versatile and formidable distance runners of his generation. His half marathon world record of 58:01, set in Copenhagen in 2019, remains one of the defining performances in road racing history. He also conquered the marathon stage, winning the New York City Marathon twice with commanding authority.

![Image 206](https://mybestruns.com/street/641503264b0a4c0a1ed6c457846138ce7ee7b8573687de60b12b1aa760248761.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

One of Kamworor’s most unforgettable moments came at the 2016 World Half Marathon Championships in Cardiff. After falling at the start and being trampled by competitors, he rose, regrouped, and delivered a stunning comeback victory.

![Image 207](https://mybestruns.com/street/b56c2befc644faaba5200072d771f1067fea3d4e7aee5b7148a549213b911fc1.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

“In Cardiff, it was wet and I slipped at the start,” Kamworor recalled. “Nobody tripped me. It was hard running through the crowd, but the fall made me more determined.”

That determination would be tested even further. In 2020, during the isolation of the COVID-19 pandemic, Kamworor’s career was nearly derailed when he was struck from behind by a motorcycle while training in Eldoret.

“I fractured my tibia and couldn’t run for six months,” he said. “When I started running again, my body was still out of balance and I kept getting injured. It took me over three years to be able to run properly.”

His return has been gradual but encouraging. In 2023, Kamworor stunned observers by finishing second at the London Marathon in a personal best of 2:04:23, proving his resilience on the global stage. He followed that performance with a marathon victory in Rotterdam last year, finishing just ten seconds slower than his London breakthrough.

Now 33, Kamworor brings both experience and renewed confidence back to Ras Al Khaimah.

“I think I’m training as well as ever,” he said. “I remember this flat, fast course from when I won in 2013. I’m just grateful to be back running without problems.”

Age is no barrier for distance runners at the highest level. History offers powerful examples, including Portugal’s Carlos Lopes, who won Olympic marathon gold at 37, and Romania’s Constantina Dita, who claimed Olympic marathon victory at 38. Kamworor hopes to add his own chapter to that legacy.

Strong Rivals Await on a Fast Course

Kamworor will face formidable competition. Ethiopia’s Jemal Mekonen enters with a personal best of 58:33, while Kenya’s Brian Kibor has run 58:39. Ethiopia’s Amedework Walelegn (58:40) and several rising talents add further depth to a field built for speed.

A Race Built on Speed and Records

Since its debut in 2007, the Ras Al Khaimah Half Marathon has earned global respect as one of the fastest half marathons in the world. Sammy Wanjiru’s 58:53 in the inaugural race set the tone, and the women’s race has been particularly historic. Mary Keitany (65:50), Peres Jepchirchir (64:52), and Ababel Yeshaneh (64:31) all set world records here, cementing the race’s reputation.

The flat, fast roads around Al Marjan Island once again promise ideal conditions for world-class performances.

### [How One Tribe in Kenya Came to Dominate Global Distance Running](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14033)

There may be no statistic in all of sports more astonishing than this one.

The Kalenjin, an ethnic group—often referred to as a tribe—in Kenya, make up about 13.4% of the country’s population, roughly 6.3 million people. On a global scale, they represent about one out of every 1,000 people worldwide.

![Image 221](https://mybestruns.com/street/31fd23f24578a76f6fc0580d9093e935c038cda98d42eefe81cdfdd0126b8ac7.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Yet this small community has produced an overwhelming share of the world’s greatest distance runners.

![Image 222](https://mybestruns.com/street/e23d62d8a509883c34d3fcc2300d64ea559616598580289fc6799ce1bc84e82a.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Their dominance has been so complete, and so sustained, that it has been described as“the greatest geographical concentration of achievement in the annals of sport.”And it is hard to argue otherwise.

From the Rift Valley to the World Stage

Most elite Kalenjin runners come from Kenya’s Rift Valley region, particularly areas such as Nandi, Elgeyo-Marakwet, Uasin Gishu, and Baringo, where elevations range from 2,000 to 2,400 meters (6,500–8,000 feet)above sea level.

Here, running is not a hobby—it is part of daily life.

Children grow up walking and running long distances, often on dirt roads. Training at altitude is the norm, not a strategy. And success stories are local and visible, creating a powerful cycle of belief and opportunity.

Champions Across Eras

The Kalenjin impact on global athletics stretches back more than half a century.

Kipchoge Keino, one of the pioneers of Kenyan distance running, won Olympic gold in the 1500 meters at the 1968 Mexico City Games and the 3000-meter steeplechase in 1972, helping place Kenyan runners on the world map.

Since then, Kenyan athletes—many of them Kalenjin—have dominated:

• The 3000-meter steeplechase, winning Olympic gold in nearly every Games since 1968

• The 5,000 meters and 10,000 meters at World Championships

• The marathon, particularly at the World Marathon Majors

Masters of the Marathon

Perhaps nowhere is this dominance more visible than in the marathon.

Kalenjin runners have repeatedly won and controlled races such as:

• Berlin Marathon

• London Marathon

• Chicago Marathon

• Boston Marathon

• New York City Marathon

These victories are not isolated moments—they are part of a long, uninterrupted pattern.

At the center of it all stands Eliud Kipchoge, widely regarded as the greatest marathon runner in history. A member of the Kalenjin community, Kipchoge has:

• Won two Olympic marathon gold medals(2016, 2021)

• Set a world record of 2:01:09 at the Berlin Marathon

• Become the first human to run 26.2 miles in under two hours

He is not an exception. He is the most refined expression of a system that has been producing champions for generations.

Why This One Tribe?

No single explanation tells the whole story, but several factors come together in the Rift Valley:

• Geography:High altitude, rolling terrain, and ideal training conditions

• Physiology:Exceptional running economy and efficient biomechanics

• Culture:Running as a respected path to success and opportunity

• Environment:Group training, competition, and long-term development from a young age

Together, these elements have created something unmatched in sport.

A Phenomenon Without Parallel

Great athletes come from everywhere. But nowhere else has such a small, specific populationproduced such sustained global dominance across events, generations, and decades.

Not sprinting.

Not swimming.

Not cycling.

Not soccer.

Only distance running.

From the highland paths of the Rift Valley to Olympic podiums and marathon finish lines around the world, the story of the Kalenjin remains one of the most extraordinary achievements in human performance.

And it is still being written.

Lucy Scott, from Bishop’s Stortford in Hertfordshire, completed the seven marathons over an 18-month stretch: Tokyo, Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago, New York City, and Sydney. She secured the honor on November 2 when she crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon, making her the “youngest Seven Star athlete” to date.

![Image 225](https://mybestruns.com/street/8efa56c4ab066e6aa7891ab01b1d469b175cc36baf13e2406b0f67f99ac6b649.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

“If I can get a place, I would love to do that,” she said.

His early splits showed controlled aggression:15:12 at 5K,30:25 at 10K, and 1:05:20 at halfway. Through 30K, he was still moving well in 1:33:02, but the final 10 kilometers through Central Park tested even the marathon master, bringing him home in 2:14:36.

Though not among his fastest times, this was a run filled with purpose and legacy. For Kipchoge, New York was never about breaking records — it was about embracing one of the sport’s most iconic stages and completing his journey across all six World Marathon Majors.

At 40 years old, the Kenyan legend has now conquered every major marathon city, further solidifying his place as the face of modern distance running. "Many at age 40 have run much faster but this is still very respectable," says KATA founder Bob Anderson.

One of the most anticipated starts in marathon history arrives this Sunday as Eliud Kipchoge, the two-time Olympic marathon champion and widely regarded as the greatest marathoner of all time, makes his debut at the TCS New York City Marathon (NYC Marathon).

The Big Picture

![Image 244](https://mybestruns.com/street/96d764bf26012370ecdf3f3d61944a94fd7ca2968bc46a880bdb060c61a87684.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

At 40 years old, Kipchoge has already built an extraordinary legacy: Olympic gold medals in 2016 (Rio) and 2020 (Tokyo), a world-record marathon time of 2:01:09 in Berlin 2022, and a historic sub-2-hour marathon effort in Vienna 2019 (1:59:40 – though not ratified).

![Image 245](https://mybestruns.com/street/93075bcc50df05415b42b72ae300f0a1fd8a1bbe0e000842857b4fe2a61fd0cd.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Why It Matters

• Legacy:Finishing NYC would give Kipchoge the coveted “six-star” AWMM medal for running all six of the premier majors.

• New challenge:The NYC course is markedly different from the flat, fast courses of Berlin or London. It’s undulating, uses bridges, and traverses the five boroughs—a true test of both physical and mental strength.

• Age and motivation:While Kipchoge remains in top shape, he acknowledges the impact of time and says this race is as much about meaning and experience as it is about finishing fast.

The Competition & Conditions

Kipchoge enters a stacked elite field. He’ll face defending champion Abdi Nageeye of the Netherlands, former NYC winners Evans Chebet and Albert Korir, and several rising stars with sub-2:04 personal bests.

What to Watch

• Will Kipchoge go for a bold win or focus on completing this final major?

• How will the unique challenges of NYC—bridges, hills, and roaring crowds—affect his pacing and strategy?

• Could this race mark the close of his competitive marathon career—or the beginning of a new chapter as ambassador and mentor?

Sunday’s race isn’t just another marathon for Eliud Kipchoge. It’s a long-awaited chapter in a legendary career—one that may see him conquer the final major, inspire millions, and reaffirm his enduring message:No human is limited.

### [Susanna Sullivan — The Teacher Who Runs Among the World’s Best Set to run NYC Sunday](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=13968)

American marathoner[Susanna Sullivan](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Susanna+Sullivan)continues to prove that world-class athleticism and everyday life can coexist. A sixth-grade math and science teacher from McLean, Virginia, Sullivan has quietly become one of the top American women in marathon history — balancing the classroom with 120-mile training weeks and remarkable consistency on the roads.

From Humble Beginnings to World Class

![Image 248](https://mybestruns.com/street/2efa509b71da10aeca45997943b7972cdbafeaea5697f8ddf8ad48ff1fab16cf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Born May 13, 1990, in West Palm Beach, Florida, and raised in Virginia, Sullivan’s early success came at George Mason High School, where she earned multiple state titles in cross-country and track. After competing at the University of Notre Dame, she battled injuries and fatigue but never lost her love for the sport.

![Image 249](https://mybestruns.com/street/e45aeea130e4e9df3fecc19d6a664f52952e160adec7b130191cbd23e46f1ded.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Her marathon debut came in 2015 at Grandma’s Marathon in Minnesota, where she clocked 2:35:37 for 9th place. Over the next decade, she quietly built momentum, cutting time from race to race. The breakthrough arrived in 2024 at the Chicago Marathon, where she finished 7th overall — and first American — in 2:21:56, a personal best that placed her among the top ten fastest U.S. women of all time.

Fourth at the 2025 World Championships in Tokyo

![Image 250](https://mybestruns.com/street/2a25e5d83c171aa4693c1b63120529834b561b4cf240e52bf24e5dfa51db4ea1.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

On September 14, 2025, Sullivan delivered one of her finest performances at the World Athletics Championships Marathon in Tokyo, finishing fourth in 2:28:17.

Under sweltering heat and high humidity, Sullivan courageously led much of the race, setting the pace through 25 kilometers before the eventual medalists pulled away. Her performance — the top American finish — underscored her strength, tactical intelligence, and resilience on one of the sport’s biggest stages.

It also marked a full-circle comeback. Two years earlier, at the 2023 World Championships, Sullivan fractured her kneecap mid-race and limped home in 58th place. Her return to the top five in Tokyo symbolized perseverance and renewed confidence.

![Image 251](https://mybestruns.com/street/67d069035f3d5a3494bdf6dd513ee472e1149137b23d4b6e01a7a6561ce6d780.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

The Balance of Two Worlds

While most professional runners build their lives around training, Sullivan still starts her mornings in the classroom. She teaches sixth-grade advanced math and science, grading papers and designing lessons between workouts.

“Running gives me perspective,” she has said in interviews. “It keeps me grounded. Teaching reminds me there’s more to life than splits and finish times.”

Her ability to balance two demanding worlds has made her an inspiration for runners who juggle careers, families, and athletic dreams.

On to New York

Next up, Sullivan is set to compete in the 2025 TCS New York City Marathon on Sunday, November 2. She enters as one of the leading Americans to watch in a stacked international field that includes Olympians and major-marathon champions.

After her stellar run in Tokyo, many eyes will be on how she handles the challenging hills and bridges of New York — a course that rewards experience and toughness rather than speed alone. Few embody those traits better than Sullivan.

Lessons from Her Journey

• Patience and perseverance— her steady rise from 2:35 to 2:21 shows the value of long-term commitment.

• Balance— proof that excellence isn’t limited to full-time athletes.

• Resilience— recovering from injuries and setbacks only to climb higher.

• Leadership— both in the classroom and in leading a world championship field

Career Highlights

• Marathon PR:2:21:56 – Chicago (2024)

• World Championships Tokyo (2025):4th Place, 2:28:17

• London Marathon (2023):10th Place, 2:24:27 (top American)

• Cherry Blossom 10-Mile (2022):Champion, 52:32

• Half Marathon PR:1:08:59 – January 2025

A Runner to Watch

Susanna Sullivan’s story reminds us that greatness doesn’t always come from perfect conditions or full-time focus. Sometimes it comes from a quiet classroom in Virginia, where a teacher grades homework — and then goes out to train like one of the best marathoners in the world.

Her journey is far from over, and as she lines up in New York, she represents not just American distance running but every runner chasing balance, progress, and purpose — one mile at a time.

When Koichi Kitabatake steps onto the starting line of the 2025 TCS New York City Marathon on November 2, he will make history as the oldest competitor in the field — at 91 years old.

The runner from Kanagawa, Japan, didn’t start running until long after most people retire. In fact, he only took up the sport at age 74, after finishing a long career as a telecommunications specialist. Four years later, at 78, he ran his first marathon — and he hasn’t stopped since.

![Image 254](https://mybestruns.com/street/d607ca06fe1d2de35df8b6bd48ea213e63d82e9444e18d9683c6c2262b77a650.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Running Into His 90s

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
Long before he conquered world cross-country championships, dominated the half-marathon distance and lifted the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) trophy, [Geoffrey Kamworor](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor) was a young Kenyan student with an ambitious dream that had little to do with running: becoming a [lawyer](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=lawyer).
![Image 2](https://mybestruns.com/street/de57be259ad5f2aa804935a23c35ae7bb6b49b6ec295d0ed68325e1b13b71303.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Growing up in Keiyo South, Kamworor developed the discipline that would later define his extraordinary athletic career. His daily routine involved running approximately five kilometres to school and another five kilometres back home. What might have seemed like an ordinary journey for a schoolboy was quietly laying the foundation for a future in international distance running.
![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/808283ce83ea90fb69283ae3a63fb6cc12becf4782bc79b9156f109324db53df.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
He attended Chepsamo Primary School before proceeding to Lelboinet Secondary School, where he combined his education with a growing passion for athletics. At the time, his ambitions extended beyond the track and roads. He wanted to pursue a career in law, and that dream eventually brought him an opportunity to study at a college in the United States.
