### [Susanna Sullivan — The Teacher Who Runs Among the World’s Best Set to run NYC Sunday](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=13968)
Fourth at the 2025 World Championships in Tokyo
![Image 250](https://mybestruns.com/street/2a25e5d83c171aa4693c1b63120529834b561b4cf240e52bf24e5dfa51db4ea1.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
On September 14, 2025, Sullivan delivered one of her finest performances at the World Athletics Championships Marathon in Tokyo, finishing fourth in 2:28:17.
Under sweltering heat and high humidity, Sullivan courageously led much of the race, setting the pace through 25 kilometers before the eventual medalists pulled away. Her performance — the top American finish — underscored her strength, tactical intelligence, and resilience on one of the sport’s biggest stages.
It also marked a full-circle comeback. Two years earlier, at the 2023 World Championships, Sullivan fractured her kneecap mid-race and limped home in 58th place. Her return to the top five in Tokyo symbolized perseverance and renewed confidence.
![Image 251](https://mybestruns.com/street/67d069035f3d5a3494bdf6dd513ee472e1149137b23d4b6e01a7a6561ce6d780.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The Balance of Two Worlds
While most professional runners build their lives around training, Sullivan still starts her mornings in the classroom. She teaches sixth-grade advanced math and science, grading papers and designing lessons between workouts.
“Running gives me perspective,” she has said in interviews. “It keeps me grounded. Teaching reminds me there’s more to life than splits and finish times.”

### [Susanna Sullivan — The Teacher Who Runs Among the World’s Best Set to run NYC Sunday](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=13968)
Her ability to balance two demanding worlds has made her an inspiration for runners who juggle careers, families, and athletic dreams.
On to New York
Next up, Sullivan is set to compete in the 2025 TCS New York City Marathon on Sunday, November 2. She enters as one of the leading Americans to watch in a stacked international field that includes Olympians and major-marathon champions.
After her stellar run in Tokyo, many eyes will be on how she handles the challenging hills and bridges of New York — a course that rewards experience and toughness rather than speed alone. Few embody those traits better than Sullivan.
Lessons from Her Journey
• Patience and perseverance— her steady rise from 2:35 to 2:21 shows the value of long-term commitment.
• Balance— proof that excellence isn’t limited to full-time athletes.
• Resilience— recovering from injuries and setbacks only to climb higher.
• Leadership— both in the classroom and in leading a world championship field
Career Highlights
• Marathon PR:2:21:56 – Chicago (2024)
• World Championships Tokyo (2025):4th Place, 2:28:17
• London Marathon (2023):10th Place, 2:24:27 (top American)
• Cherry Blossom 10-Mile (2022):Champion, 52:32
• Half Marathon PR:1:08:59 – January 2025
A Runner to Watch
Susanna Sullivan’s story reminds us that greatness doesn’t always come from perfect conditions or full-time focus. Sometimes it comes from a quiet classroom in Virginia, where a teacher grades homework — and then goes out to train like one of the best marathoners in the world.
Her journey is far from over, and as she lines up in New York, she represents not just American distance running but every runner chasing balance, progress, and purpose — one mile at a time.

### [At 91, Koichi Kitabatake Will Be the Oldest Runner in the 2025 New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=13965)
When Koichi Kitabatake steps onto the starting line of the 2025 TCS New York City Marathon on November 2, he will make history as the oldest competitor in the field — at 91 years old.
The runner from Kanagawa, Japan, didn’t start running until long after most people retire. In fact, he only took up the sport at age 74, after finishing a long career as a telecommunications specialist. Four years later, at 78, he ran his first marathon — and he hasn’t stopped since.
![Image 254](https://mybestruns.com/street/d607ca06fe1d2de35df8b6bd48ea213e63d82e9444e18d9683c6c2262b77a650.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
This year’s race will mark his 34th marathon, including two previous finishes in New York City. Kitabatake has flown across the world to participate in marathons on nearly every continent, proving that passion and discipline know no age limits.
Running Into His 90s
![Image 255](https://mybestruns.com/street/3ab25a75abc9eaf4b26f6e9578ceb610fb81fb7584b30cb8eaa1b933cf6d6266.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
As he prepares for the 26.2-mile journey through all five boroughs of New York City, Kitabatake shared with the Daily Mail some of his daily habits that keep him strong — both physically and mentally — well into his 90s.

### [At 91, Koichi Kitabatake Will Be the Oldest Runner in the 2025 New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=13965)
“I do a short workout and stretching every morning for about half an hour,” he said. “Then I run four to six miles twice a week, depending on how I feel.”
It’s a simple but powerful routine — one that underscores his belief in consistency over intensity.
Beyond the physical benefits, Kitabatake says running has transformed his outlook on life.
“Running has changed how I see things,” he told the Daily Mail. “It helps me stay positive and keeps my mind healthy.”
A Source of Inspiration
Kitabatake’s story has inspired countless others, especially those who feel it’s “too late” to start something new. His steady approach, humility, and unwavering commitment to movement highlight the broader spirit of the marathon itself — endurance, courage, and the celebration of life at every age.
As thousands line up in Staten Island to begin the 2025 TCS New York City Marathon, Kitabatake will stand among them — proof that age is just a number, and that the human spirit, when fueled by purpose, can keep running forever.

### [2027 Could Bring Unprecedented Heat, Raising New Concerns for Marathon Runners Worldwide](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15441)

The global running community could face a formidable challenge in [2027](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2027), as forecasts of a potentially powerful El Niño raise concerns about rising temperatures and the impact of extreme heat on marathon performances.

![Image 2](https://mybestruns.com/street/21525fef106f0f5e518948f3b7ac7c7a59c2dc7f609cbf843c1a3df2621fa9d4.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

With long-distance runners increasingly chasing personal bests on the world's biggest stages, the prospect of another exceptionally warm year has placed race-day weather firmly in the spotlight. For marathoners, even a modest rise in temperature can make the difference between a record-breaking performance and a difficult battle to reach the finish line.

![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/c649899eb4ea226a094d35c54188897ee0ecd5f22a51cbcb024dd442b8785c9e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

At the centre of the concern is the [Pacific Ocean](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Pacific+Ocean), where developing El Niño conditions could influence global temperatures. Forecasts have raised the possibility of an unusually strong event, although its eventual intensity and the precise effects on temperatures around the world remain uncertain.

El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon characterised by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures across parts of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. It can alter weather patterns across different regions, while its warming influence can contribute to higher global temperatures. The full impact depends on the strength of the event and how it interacts with other climate factors.

![Image 4](https://mybestruns.com/street/d0a9667bdea6ce04007f6323709b90066c76c7bf750a06efd1f2fbddbd1d21b0.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

The timing is particularly important. Global temperatures have often responded strongly in the year following a major El Niño, meaning 2027 could face an increased risk of challenging heat. However, whether it ultimately surpasses the existing global temperature record will depend on evolving ocean conditions, atmospheric patterns and human-caused climate change.

![Image 5](https://mybestruns.com/street/46b631cd0e12734e6118d1811afa82002a59f6f038f8de1a680ce25c9ce4a1e2.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

For marathon runners, the implications are significant. Scientific research has repeatedly shown that warmer conditions can reduce endurance performance, increase physiological strain and make it more difficult to maintain a planned race pace over 42.195 kilometres.

An analysis of seven North American marathons illustrates how substantially conditions can influence elite performances. Researchers found that leading male runners finished approximately 1.7 per cent slower relative to course records under the coolest conditions examined. In the warmest category, that difference increased to around 4.5 per cent.

For an athlete capable of running a marathon in 2:05:00, a slowdown of that magnitude could translate into several additional minutes on the clock. At the elite level, where races are frequently decided by seconds, such a difference can determine whether a runner achieves a personal best, secures a podium finish or misses a major performance target.

The consequences can be even more noticeable among recreational athletes, who often spend considerably longer exposed to the conditions.

A separate analysis by researchers at the University of Chicago, examining approximately 4.7 million marathon finishing times, highlighted the substantial effect of temperature on runners across different ability levels. The findings suggested that the typical participant could lose roughly 19 minutes when racing in temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, compared with conditions in the 40s. In the 80s Fahrenheit, the estimated time penalty rose to approximately 33 minutes.

These figures underline why marathon preparation involves much more than mileage, speed sessions and strength training. Temperature, humidity, direct sunlight and the body's ability to regulate heat can all influence how effectively a runner sustains an effort over the full distance.

Many marathon performances are achieved in cool conditions, with temperatures of approximately 4°C to 10°C often considered favourable for endurance running. As temperatures climb beyond that range, the body must devote more resources to cooling itself, potentially increasing cardiovascular strain and making a previously comfortable pace harder to maintain.

However, there is no universal temperature at which every marathon runner begins to slow down. Individual fitness, acclimatisation, humidity, wind, course exposure and race strategy all influence performance. A cool, overcast morning can produce very different outcomes from a sunny, humid day, even when the thermometer shows similar readings.

### [Cancer Survivor Brandon Throop Returns To Toronto Marathon In Hospital Gown For Third World Record Bid](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15440)

For [Brandon Throop](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Brandon+Throop), running a marathon in a hospital gown is about far more than chasing a place in the [Guinness World Records](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Guinness+World+Records). It is a deeply personal tribute to the medical team that helped save his life, a celebration of survival, and an opportunity to give back to the institution that stood beside him during one of the darkest chapters of his life.

![Image 8](https://mybestruns.com/street/f29108f8a11d11c189a98e7ad107e25370003868a0c2a06a0f60240f82ca748e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

In 2022, Throop was 35 years old, a father of two, and facing a life-changing diagnosis of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. His journey soon led him to [Princess Margaret Cancer Centre](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Princess+Margaret+Cancer+Centre) in Toronto, Canada, where he underwent chemotherapy and began a difficult battle against the disease.

![Image 9](https://mybestruns.com/street/544aaad28b469831ffc670d6b1f0afed09ba7cece4e33f54484abd893edf14de.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

The treatment that helped him fight cancer also left him physically weakened. For someone who had spent much of his life running, even the simplest movements became unexpectedly challenging. After completing treatment, climbing a single flight of stairs could leave him coughing and struggling to catch his breath.

However, rather than allowing the experience to define the limits of his future, Throop began rebuilding his strength one small step at a time. He started by running once around his neighbourhood block before gradually increasing the distance as his body recovered. What began as a modest attempt to regain his fitness eventually developed into an extraordinary mission with a purpose extending far beyond the finish line.

![Image 10](https://mybestruns.com/street/609ed787d02e0efaf2f9b8e1f2b60b1718ea68e0b9bbf56ffa21a91b509d4949.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Now, more than three years after becoming cancer-free, Throop is preparing to return to the [TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=TCS+Toronto+Waterfront+Marathon) on Sunday, October 18, 2026, for another attempt at the Guinness World Record for the fastest marathon completed while wearing a hospital gown.

This will be his third attempt to claim the record, following two determined performances in previous editions of the Toronto race. In 2023, he completed the marathon in 2:55:59 before returning in 2024 to improve his time to 2:55:01. Despite his progress, the record remained just out of reach.

The current benchmark stands at 2:50:12, established by Evan Ubene at the same Toronto Waterfront Marathon in 2022. To make history this time, Throop will need to improve significantly on his previous performances and take more than five minutes off his best hospital-gown marathon.

Yet the significance of Sunday's race cannot be measured by finishing time alone.

Throop's larger objective is to raise funds for the Princess Margaret Cancer Foundation, supporting the cancer research and care that played such an important role in his own recovery. He has already raised more than $137,000 toward his $150,000 fundraising target, bringing him within reach of a goal that could help support further advances in cancer treatment.

Every kilometre he covers in the distinctive hospital gown carries a message of gratitude to the people who cared for him and hope for patients whose journeys are only beginning. His challenge transforms a gruelling 42.195-kilometre race into a public expression of appreciation for the doctors, nurses, researchers and other healthcare professionals working to improve the lives of people affected by cancer.

The timing of this year's marathon makes the occasion even more meaningful. The race falls just days from the anniversary of his first chemotherapy session in 2022, bringing him back to a period that profoundly changed his life. Returning to the streets of Toronto now, healthy enough to pursue another marathon, offers a powerful reminder of how far he has travelled since those difficult days.

For Throop, choosing Toronto has never been simply about finding the fastest course on which to break a record. Although other marathons might offer different racing conditions, the Toronto Waterfront Marathon holds a significance that no alternative venue could easily replace. The course takes him past Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, the institution where he received treatment, while family members and friends who supported him throughout his illness are there to witness his journey.

It is a route that connects his past to his present: the hospital where he fought for his health, the streets where he now tests his endurance, and the people who helped him keep moving forward when the road ahead was uncertain.

His hospital gown is therefore much more than an unusual racing outfit. It is a symbol of the vulnerability he experienced as a patient, the strength he rediscovered through running, and his determination to turn a deeply personal struggle into something that benefits others.

As he prepares for his third record attempt, the challenge remains considerable. The existing mark of 2:50:12 demands an average pace of approximately four minutes per kilometre, a formidable task even without the physical discomfort and practical challenges of racing in a hospital gown.

Nevertheless, Throop has already demonstrated that his mission can make a difference regardless of the result on the clock. His previous attempts brought attention to cancer care, while his ongoing fundraising efforts have generated substantial support for the foundation that represents an important part of his personal story.

On Sunday, he will once again take his place among thousands of runners, carrying a message that reaches well beyond the marathon course. Whether he finally breaks the world record or falls short for a third time, his presence will stand as a reminder that recovery can open doors to remarkable achievements and that gratitude can become a powerful force for helping others.

For Brandon Throop, the finish line represents more than a sporting ambition. It is an opportunity to honour the people who helped him survive, support the research that may give other families more time together, and show what can be possible after a life-altering diagnosis.

The record is still waiting. But with more than $137,000 already raised toward his fundraising goal, Throop has another reason to consider his mission a success before the starting gun even sounds.

On the streets of Toronto, the hospital gown is returning with a purpose: to celebrate survival, give back to the people who helped save a life, and turn every step into hope for someone else.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)

Long before he conquered world cross-country championships, dominated the half-marathon distance and lifted the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) trophy, [Geoffrey Kamworor](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor) was a young Kenyan student with an ambitious dream that had little to do with running: becoming a [lawyer](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=lawyer).

![Image 14](https://mybestruns.com/street/de57be259ad5f2aa804935a23c35ae7bb6b49b6ec295d0ed68325e1b13b71303.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Growing up in Keiyo South, Kamworor developed the discipline that would later define his extraordinary athletic career. His daily routine involved running approximately five kilometres to school and another five kilometres back home. What might have seemed like an ordinary journey for a schoolboy was quietly laying the foundation for a future in international distance running.

![Image 15](https://mybestruns.com/street/808283ce83ea90fb69283ae3a63fb6cc12becf4782bc79b9156f109324db53df.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

He attended Chepsamo Primary School before proceeding to Lelboinet Secondary School, where he combined his education with a growing passion for athletics. At the time, his ambitions extended beyond the track and roads. He wanted to pursue a career in law, and that dream eventually brought him an opportunity to study at a college in the United States.

What began as a modest race through Central Park, with a handful of determined runners and a budget of just $1,000, has evolved into one of the most prestigious and sought-after marathons in the world. When the inaugural New York City Marathon took place in 1970, the entry fee was just $1. Organised by the New York Road Runners, the race was held entirely within Central Park, far removed from the enormous crowds, international attention and commercial scale that define the event today.

![Image 30](https://mybestruns.com/street/cb333999ed07e06d10edcf37e5452882364cbb7336ebf8347871bb079ae7bfbf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

The first champion was Gary Muhrcke, a New York City firefighter whose victory remains one of the most memorable stories from the race's early years. According to accounts of the inaugural edition, Muhrcke had finished a night shift before entering the competition shortly before the start. He went on to win in approximately 2:31, securing his place in the marathon's history.

The inaugural race also featured Nina Kuscsik, the only woman in the field. She started the event but withdrew after becoming ill, meaning no woman finished that first edition. Kuscsik would later become an important figure in the campaign for women's inclusion in competitive distance running.

Over the years, the New York City Marathon expanded beyond Central Park, eventually developing into the iconic five-borough journey that takes runners through Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Manhattan. Its transformation helped turn the race into a celebration of athletic achievement, community spirit and the extraordinary diversity of New York City.

Today, the marathon attracts elite athletes chasing victories and records, recreational runners pursuing personal milestones, charity participants raising funds for important causes, and thousands of international visitors eager to experience one of running's most celebrated events.

![Image 74](https://mybestruns.com/street/5ffa31af8295f395e0aff49642712e51130387366364addc2bf2c316bd3b7edc.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Her life was cut short at a time when her career was flourishing, leaving behind a legacy that continues to resonate with athletes, fans and the wider community.

For Kenya, a country whose identity is deeply intertwined with distance-running success, Tirop represented a remarkable generation of female athletes taking the sport to new heights. Her achievements on the track, across country and on the roads had already secured her place among the country's outstanding distance runners.

![Image 75](https://mybestruns.com/street/f77fa5828a0aeb325862244b31913486d927b332f71bf5f757228761f9169abf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Five years later, the sadness of her loss remains inseparable from the extraordinary story of what she accomplished in her short but memorable career.

A Champion Who Rose to the Top at 19

Tirop announced herself on the global stage in spectacular fashion at the 2015 World Athletics Cross Country Championships in Guiyang, China. At only 19, she won the senior women's race, becoming the youngest champion in the event since Zola Budd in 1985.

Her victory demonstrated not only her natural ability but also the composure and determination that would become defining features of her running career.

She subsequently established herself among the world's leading track athletes, winning bronze medals in the women's 10,000 metres at the 2017 World Athletics Championships in London and the 2019 edition in Doha.

Those back-to-back podium finishes confirmed her consistency at the highest level and underlined her ability to compete against the strongest distance runners in the world.

Tirop also demonstrated considerable versatility at the Tokyo 2020 Olympic Games, held in 2021, where she finished fourth in the women's 5,000 metres. Although she narrowly missed the podium, her performance reinforced her reputation as one of Kenya's most accomplished emerging distance-running talents.

A World Record That Made History

Just weeks before her death, Tirop delivered one of the defining performances of her career.

![Image 76](https://mybestruns.com/street/c78d43c7e9431cc77d4c0c7a69212a2bb6f64a57b712e93e9359780084f1438e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

On September 12, 2021, she clocked an astonishing 30:01 to win the women's 10km road race at the adizero Road to Records event in Herzogenaurach, Germany.

Her performance broke the then women's-only world record by 28 seconds, establishing a new benchmark for the distance. The record was subsequently ratified by World Athletics. It was aremarkable achievement that placed her name among the legends of distance running. Although her record has since been broken, the greatness of her achievement remains untouched, and no change in the record books can diminish the extraordinary talent, courage and determination she displayed that day. Time may bring new champions and faster performances, but it can never erase the mark she left on athletics.

In a race that demanded patience, tactical awareness and an exceptional finishing effort, Tirop broke away from compatriot Sheila Chepkirui during the closing stages and powered towards the finish line.

The performance was a remarkable demonstration of her endurance and competitive instinct. It also offered a glimpse of what might have followed had she been given more years to develop her career.

Her final competitive appearance came on October 3, 2021, when she finished second in a 10km race in Geneva, Switzerland. Ten days later, the world learned of her death.

The timing made the tragedy particularly difficult to comprehend: an athlete who had just rewritten the record books and was still competing at the highest level was suddenly gone.

![Image 77](https://mybestruns.com/street/96776c2a38ffe92e203c98190e24001e4c1d47d376c5bd46c7feef1ad83b81ce.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

A Tragedy That Reached Far Beyond Sport

Tirop's death was not simply the loss of an elite athlete. It also brought renewed international attention to violence against women and the need to create safer environments in which women and girls can live, train and pursue their ambitions.

Her story became a painful reminder that medals, records and international recognition cannot shield someone from violence in their private life.

In the years since her death, her name has continued to feature in efforts to promote women's empowerment, athlete welfare and the prevention of gender-based violence. Initiatives associated with her legacy, including Agnes Tirop Angels, reflect the continuing determination to transform grief into meaningful action.

Her story remains especially significant within athletics, where the pursuit of excellence must go hand in hand with respect for athletes' safety, dignity and wellbeing.

Five Years Later, Her Legacy Endures

For young runners who dream of representing Kenya on the international stage, Tirop's career remains an example of what dedication, talent and courage can achieve.

She rose from a promising young athlete to a world champion, a two-time World Championships medallist and a world-record holder. She excelled across different distances and surfaces, leaving an impressive body of achievements before reaching her 26th birthday.

Yet her legacy cannot be measured by statistics alone. It also lies in the conversations her death continues to inspire, the women whose safety must be protected and the determination to ensure that sporting success is never separated from human dignity.

Five years on, Agnes Tirop is remembered not only for the records she set or the medals she won, but also for the future that was taken from her.

Her achievements remain part of Kenya's rich athletics history, while her story continues to call for a world in which women can pursue their dreams without fear of violence.

Agnes Tirop's life was tragically short, but her impact reaches far beyond the finish line. Her achievements will remain in the record books, her memory will endure in the hearts of athletics fans, and her legacy will continue to inspire generations to come.

For fast runners, meeting the published standard can provide a much more certain path to the start line.

Berlin is also heavily sought after. The BMW Berlin Marathon uses a lottery for the majority of runners, while qualifying performances can provide another route into the race. With its fast course and reputation for producing world-class times, demand remains enormous every year.

International runners can also use official tour operators, although these packages generally cost more because they are tied to travel arrangements.

For runners chasing the Six Star Medal, the biggest lesson is simple: do not depend on the lottery alone.

By the finish, he had rewritten the history books with a breathtaking world record of 2:00:35.

Kiptum improved Eliud Kipchoge’s previous world record by 34 seconds, becoming the first athlete in history to officially break the 2:01 barrier in a record-eligible marathon.

![Image 194](https://mybestruns.com/street/eacc796a55e9a32d214d97a136a77187518c7b402af8cfcb4c3cf4cf85977904.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

![Image 195](https://mybestruns.com/street/225136d87ffb781fe257f7cb7053c718e7664bc764aea955ed3c0f70f7a2305f.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Tragically, that future would never unfold.

On February 11, 2024, just four months after his historic Chicago victory, Kiptum died in a road accident in Kenya alongside his Rwandan coach, Gervais Hakizimana. He was only 24 years old.

The loss sent shockwaves through the athletics world.

Today, three years after that unforgettable October morning in Chicago, 2:00:35 remains far more than a number on a record list.

It represents the extraordinary talent of a young athlete who appeared to be only at the beginning of his journey. It represents courage, ambition and a fearless approach to the marathon. And, perhaps most poignantly, it represents a chapter of greatness that ended far too soon.

Kelvin Kiptum gave the world one of the greatest marathon performances ever witnessed.

Three years later, the memory of that incredible morning remains alive.

Gone far too soon, but never forgotten.

![Image 233](https://mybestruns.com/street/12413240599ee9c1859b7b3b7f7fa683f7e05a7c9997d36e865c0052b7fa2888.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

The 2026 edition continued that long tradition, with roughly 30,000 runners taking part across the various events of Marathon Weekend. Yet even with favourable weather this year, the decision to move the race reflects a longer-term concern. Organisers are looking beyond a single race morning and considering how changing weather patterns could affect the event in the years ahead.

For runners, the move could eventually become one of the most important changes in the marathon's modern history. A later October date offers the possibility of cooler racing conditions while preserving the course, the atmosphere and the traditions that have made Twin Cities Marathon a fixture on the American running calendar.

For more than four decades, the first Sunday of October provided a familiar date for thousands of runners preparing to take on the Twin Cities course.

That tradition has now reached its final chapter.

From 2027, the Twin Cities Marathon will arrive later in the fall — opening a new era for a race whose history remains firmly connected to the streets of Minneapolis and St. Paul.

### [7 Packing Tips for Your First Time Traveling For a Race](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15391)

Traveling for a race is the perfect excuse to turn a running weekend into an adventure. Perhaps you’re heading to the [Tokyo Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/TokyoMarathon?b=prz&details=Y)⁠ and already thinking about the sushi and ramen you’ll enjoy afterward. Or maybe your next finish line is beside the beach.

Between training, booking a hotel and planning what to explore, packing can become an afterthought. Then race morning arrives, and your favorite socks are still at home, your race information is buried in your suitcase and your water bottle is nowhere to be found.

A little organization before departure can make the entire trip smoother. These seven packing tips will help you arrive ready to run and enjoy the weekend.

1. Pack Your Race-Day Outfit in Your Carry-On

Keep your race-day clothing and essentials in your carry-on. Pack your running top, shorts or tights, socks, sports bra if needed, and the small items you depend on during a race. If your checked luggage is delayed, your key gear will still be with you.

![Image 240](https://mybestruns.com/street/5c6a74501acac9b0ede92d94316cdfa0b4cdf306eb1a8ff130a06ab99f4b0028.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Fold your race outfit together or place it in a packing pouch so everything is easy to find. A smaller zip pouch can hold accessories. Knowing exactly where your race kit is means one less thing to worry about when you arrive.

2. Wear Your Running Shoes on the Plane

Your running shoes deserve the same attention as your race outfit. Wearing them on the plane keeps them out of checked luggage and leaves more room in your suitcase.

Choose a familiar pair you have already used in training. Race weekend is not the time to discover that new shoes rub or fit differently than expected. If you prefer to travel in another pair, keep your race shoes in your carry-on.

![Image 241](https://mybestruns.com/street/e69995b49a9f8387df3a425267e0e7bfdd5cf1fd3f9dcf4c2ee037e9c24fb131.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

3. Bring a Spacious Bag for Your Gear

A race trip often requires more than running clothes. Add a jacket, recovery clothes, snacks and accessories, and your packing list grows quickly. A spacious duffel with sturdy handles and useful pockets can keep those extras organized and serve as a day bag at your destination.

Think about what you’ll do beyond race day. A hike may call for trail shoes and a light layer. If pickleball is part of your plans, you may want a paddle and extra clothes.

The same thinking applies when choosing your bag. If you’re planning a few games on the court during the trip, consider [pickleball tour and duffel bags](https://pickleballnation.com/collections/pickleball-bags-and-backpacks)⁠. A backpack may be more practical for hiking or exploring on foot. Choose a bag that suits your itinerary, and check your airline’s size and weight limits before packing.

4. Organize Your Bib and Race Documents

Keep your identification, registration confirmation and race instructions together. A slim document pouch works well for paper copies, while a dedicated folder on your phone can keep digital information easy to access.

Download important details before leaving home, including the race map, confirmation email and packet pickup instructions. Save copies you can open without an internet connection.

If you already have your bib, keep it flat and protected. Otherwise, check where and when you need to collect it and what identification the organizer requires. Handling these details in advance helps keep the pre-race scramble to a minimum.

5. Take Familiar Snacks with You

Race travel can disrupt your usual eating routine. Your preferred breakfast may be unavailable, and the hotel buffet may not offer what you normally eat before a run.

Bring the bars, gels and electrolyte products you have already used in training. Your [runner’s diet](https://www.medicalnewstoday.com/articles/runners-diet)⁠ shouldn’t become a vacation guessing game.

Count what you’ll need for travel and race day, then pack a little extra. Keep some familiar snacks in your carry-on and bring enough race fuel for your planned strategy. Check destination rules before carrying food across international borders.

6. Always Have a Water Bottle

Busy travel days can make it easy to forget your usual drinking habits. A reusable water bottle is a simple item that deserves a place on your packing list.

Carry it empty through airport security, then fill it where drinking water is available. Keep it handy during your journey and when heading out for packet pickup or other race activities.

Staying hydrated is also part of [caring for your body while traveling](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php/7021)⁠. If an electrolyte mix is already part of your routine, pack your usual product. Having familiar supplies nearby makes it easier to maintain your normal habits while traveling.

7. Pack Layers for Changing Weather

A mild forecast doesn’t always reflect how it will feel while waiting at the starting line early in the morning. Pack a lightweight layer you have already worn while running.

A zip jacket or long-sleeve top can help you stay comfortable before the start. Decide in advance whether you’ll carry it during the race or leave it at an official bag check, following the organizer’s instructions.

For colder conditions, familiar gloves and other tested gear can help. Review this guide to [running in cold weather](https://mybestruns.com/What_to_Wear_for_Running_in_Cold_Weather.html)⁠, then check the forecast again before departure and once more before race morning so you can make any final adjustments.

Thoughtful packing helps you get more out of a destination race. Keep essential gear close, choose a bag that works for your plans and organize your documents before you leave. With those details handled, you can spend less time searching through your suitcase and more time enjoying the run—and everything that comes afterward.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
Long before he conquered world cross-country championships, dominated the half-marathon distance and lifted the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) trophy, [Geoffrey Kamworor](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor) was a young Kenyan student with an ambitious dream that had little to do with running: becoming a [lawyer](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=lawyer).
![Image 2](https://mybestruns.com/street/de57be259ad5f2aa804935a23c35ae7bb6b49b6ec295d0ed68325e1b13b71303.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Growing up in Keiyo South, Kamworor developed the discipline that would later define his extraordinary athletic career. His daily routine involved running approximately five kilometres to school and another five kilometres back home. What might have seemed like an ordinary journey for a schoolboy was quietly laying the foundation for a future in international distance running.
![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/808283ce83ea90fb69283ae3a63fb6cc12becf4782bc79b9156f109324db53df.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
He attended Chepsamo Primary School before proceeding to Lelboinet Secondary School, where he combined his education with a growing passion for athletics. At the time, his ambitions extended beyond the track and roads. He wanted to pursue a career in law, and that dream eventually brought him an opportunity to study at a college in the United States.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
However, the young Kenyan faced a defining decision: follow the academic path he had envisioned or commit himself fully to the sport that was beginning to reveal his remarkable potential. Kamworor chose athletics, a decision that would ultimately place his name among the most accomplished distance runners of his generation.
![Image 4](https://mybestruns.com/street/a94c34052d38330fd293c08402206cd4d7a39c33946639bdb76ca84e0ab123e7.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
His transformation from a promising schoolboy into an international contender began gathering momentum in 2010, when he joined the GSC training camp in Kaptagat. His development accelerated rapidly, and within a short period, an opportunity to compete in Finland exposed him to a higher level of international competition.
Still only 17, he reportedly competed nine times during that trip, demonstrating an impressive ability to adapt to the demands of competitive racing. Breaking the eight-minute barrier for 3,000 metres was an early indication of the talent that would eventually carry him to the highest levels of distance running.
![Image 5](https://mybestruns.com/street/84282c8c1c650ab6ffe7062ef243eacc858a034f27f3ff8005541232e23d4bd3.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
His breakthrough on the international stage followed in March 2011, when he captured the junior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Punta Umbría, Spain. That victory announced the arrival of a young athlete whose future would extend far beyond the junior ranks.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
Kamworor was not simply a runner with speed. He possessed the endurance, tactical intelligence and competitive determination required to succeed across different distances and racing surfaces. As his career developed, those qualities became the hallmarks of an athlete capable of challenging the world's best.
Cross country became one of the foundations of Kamworor's international success. In 2015, he won the senior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Guiyang, China, confirming his status as one of the leading distance runners in the world. Two years later, he returned to the top of the podium in Kampala, Uganda, defending his senior world cross-country crown in front of a home crowd. Winning consecutive senior world titles placed him in an elite category and demonstrated his remarkable command of the demanding discipline.
On the roads, however, Kamworor established an equally impressive legacy. He won the World Half Marathon Championships in Copenhagen in 2014, Cardiff in 2016 and Valencia in 2018, becoming a three-time champion at the distance. His achievements reflected a rare combination of strength, speed and race management, enabling him to prevail against formidable international opposition.
The half marathon became one of his signature events, but Kamworor's ambitions were never confined to a single discipline. He continued to demonstrate his versatility on the track, winning silver in the men's 10,000 metres at the 2015 World Athletics Championships in Beijing, China. From the grass of cross-country courses to the roads of major international races and the track of a global championship, he repeatedly demonstrated that his talent could flourish wherever the competition took him.
Among Kamworor's most memorable achievements are his victories at the New York City Marathon in 2017 and 2019. Winning one of the world's most celebrated marathons requires exceptional endurance, but winning it twice demands much more: tactical patience, resilience and the ability to navigate a demanding course against a deep international field.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
Kamworor demonstrated those qualities in both victories, establishing a special connection with the New York race and adding the marathon to an already remarkable collection of honours. His success in the American city also illustrated his ability to move successfully between distances. An athlete celebrated for his cross-country and half-marathon dominance had shown that he could also conquer the 42.195-kilometre marathon, one of the most demanding challenges in road racing.
Now, as he sets his sights on another New York campaign, the Kenyan star has an opportunity to strengthen his legacy further. A third men's open-division victory would place him among a very select group of athletes to have won the prestigious race three times. Such a milestone would be more than another addition to his trophy cabinet; it would reinforce the story of a runner whose competitive range has extended across nearly every major discipline in distance running.
Behind Kamworor's achievements lies a training environment built around discipline, consistency and high-level competition. Working under the guidance of renowned coach Patrick Sang, he has trained alongside some of Kenya's most celebrated athletes, including marathon great Eliud Kipchoge and middle- and long-distance superstar Faith Kipyegon.
Sharing a training environment with athletes of such calibre provides a demanding daily standard. Yet Kamworor has built his own identity through a career defined by major championship victories and sustained success across different racing distances. His journey has also included difficult periods and setbacks, reminding the running world that even the most accomplished champions must continually work to return to their best. His longevity at the elite level reflects the importance of patience, dedication and the willingness to keep pursuing new goals.
For aspiring athletes in Kenya, his story offers an important lesson: extraordinary achievements are often built through ordinary routines repeated consistently over many years. Those five-kilometre journeys to school and back were not glamorous. They did not come with cheering crowds, television cameras or medals. Yet they formed part of the foundation of a career that would eventually take him to the world's biggest running stages.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
Kamworor's story is ultimately about a choice that changed the direction of his life. The young student who once imagined himself arguing cases in a courtroom instead built his reputation by answering the toughest questions on the running track and roads. His achievements speak for themselves: world cross-country titles, three world half-marathon crowns, a global 10,000-metre silver medal and two New York City Marathon victories.
He may never have pursued the legal career he once envisioned, but his athletic record tells a compelling story of ambition, sacrifice and extraordinary accomplishment. His pursuit of another New York triumph offers a fresh chapter in a career that has already crossed the boundaries between cross country, track and road racing.
For Geoffrey Kamworor, the courtroom was a dream he left behind. The world of distance running became the stage on which he built his name. And while the law lost a prospective lawyer, athletics gained a champion whose achievements have helped define an era of Kenyan distance running.

### [From $1 To $358: How The New York City Marathon Became A Global Running Phenomenon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15437)
What began as a modest race through Central Park, with a handful of determined runners and a budget of just $1,000, has evolved into one of the most prestigious and sought-after marathons in the world. More than five decades later, the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) tells a remarkable story of how distance running has grown from a grassroots sporting event into a global spectacle.
![Image 9](https://mybestruns.com/street/bacec4114b3d54670c15a184e950b0e7ddb43de9849a87f97fe568b1a68fdecf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
When the inaugural New York City Marathon took place in 1970, the entry fee was just $1. Organised by the New York Road Runners, the race was held entirely within Central Park, far removed from the enormous crowds, international attention and commercial scale that define the event today.
![Image 10](https://mybestruns.com/street/cb333999ed07e06d10edcf37e5452882364cbb7336ebf8347871bb079ae7bfbf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Of the 127 registered participants, only 55 completed the race. Yet, despite its modest beginnings, the event laid the foundation for a marathon that would eventually capture the imagination of runners from every corner of the world.

### [From $1 To $358: How The New York City Marathon Became A Global Running Phenomenon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15437)
The first champion was Gary Muhrcke, a New York City firefighter whose victory remains one of the most memorable stories from the race's early years. According to accounts of the inaugural edition, Muhrcke had finished a night shift before entering the competition shortly before the start. He went on to win in approximately 2:31, securing his place in the marathon's history.
The inaugural race also featured Nina Kuscsik, the only woman in the field. She started the event but withdrew after becoming ill, meaning no woman finished that first edition. Kuscsik would later become an important figure in the campaign for women's inclusion in competitive distance running.
Over the years, the New York City Marathon expanded beyond Central Park, eventually developing into the iconic five-borough journey that takes runners through Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Manhattan. Its transformation helped turn the race into a celebration of athletic achievement, community spirit and the extraordinary diversity of New York City.
Today, the marathon attracts elite athletes chasing victories and records, recreational runners pursuing personal milestones, charity participants raising funds for important causes, and thousands of international visitors eager to experience one of running's most celebrated events.

For Hassan, however, the priority is no longer the immediate challenge of another marathon. The Dutch star has built her reputation through resilience, adaptability and a willingness to take on some of the toughest challenges in distance running. Recovering fully and returning to structured training will be essential as she considers her next competitive objectives.

### [New York City Marathon Unveils Special 50th-Anniversary Finisher Medal](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15396)
The [TCS New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=TCS+New+York+City+Marathon) is preparing to mark a major milestone in its history, and runners crossing the finish line on November 1 will take home a medal designed to celebrate five decades of the iconic five-borough course.
![Image 28](https://mybestruns.com/street/ecae9cb993c4827b205bb11a5919baf3fdbe053825f791ed62866f0de9a54720.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
[New York Road Runners (NYRR)](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+Road+Runners+%28NYRR%29) has unveiled the [official 2026 finisher medal](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=official+2026+finisher+medal), commemorating the 50th anniversary of the course that transformed the race after it moved beyond Central Park in 1976. The anniversary also marks 50 years since NYRR first introduced a finisher medal for the event.
The new medal combines elements of New York City and the marathon into a distinctive sculptural design. An abstract skyline spreads outward in a sunburst pattern, while the five bridges encountered along the marathon route are incorporated into the design, creating a visual connection between the race and the city through which it travels.
![Image 29](https://mybestruns.com/street/ba1ecfbebe54362af387eb1b68e3706f36b79a7a67e7053989de2d0eecd2a988.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

### [New York City Marathon Unveils Special 50th-Anniversary Finisher Medal](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15396)
At the heart of the concept is an unbroken circular skyline, symbolising the five boroughs coming together as one. It reflects one of the defining characteristics of the New York City Marathon: a single 26.2-mile journey that connects Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Manhattan.
The 2026 medal will be produced in zinc with an electroplated gold finish and measures 3.5 inches across, making it slightly larger than the standard medal in recognition of the anniversary. Despite the larger overall size, the central medallion remains 2.12 inches, the same measurement used for the 2025 edition.
The ribbon also pays tribute to the race's history, drawing inspiration from the visual style of the 1970s. It features the marathon logo, the 50th-anniversary emblem and references to all five boroughs, completing a design that blends the event's past with its present.
For thousands of runners, the medal will represent far more than simply a race souvenir. It will be a lasting reminder of the miles covered through one of the world's most recognisable cities and of the personal achievement of reaching the finish line in Central Park.
NYRR chief marketing and digital officer Juliette Morris said the design was created to capture the unique character of the marathon, from the atmosphere of New York City to the shared experience that brings runners and spectators together every year.
As the 2026 edition approaches, the special medal adds another layer of significance to a race already steeped in history. For those who complete the journey on November 1, it will serve as a tangible symbol of both their individual achievement and the 50-year legacy of the modern New York City Marathon.

### [Kenenisa Bekele Withdraws From Berlin Marathon After Achilles Injury](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15327)
Kenenisa Bekele’s much-anticipated return to the [BMW Berlin Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=BMW+Berlin+Marathon) has been abruptly cancelled after the Ethiopian distance-running legend suffered an injury to his left Achilles tendon during one of his final training sessions.
![Image 43](https://mybestruns.com/street/92bb94a8d88b7eef734b24fca958dd630df6c657aa31a746bfa6bf925d823766.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The 44-year-old Bekele was due to return to competitive action on Sunday, September 27, after being added to the elite field only last week. His late inclusion had generated enormous excitement, with fans looking forward to seeing one of the greatest distance runners in history back on one of the courses where he has produced some of his most memorable performances.
However, the injury has forced Bekele to withdraw just days before the race.
![Image 44](https://mybestruns.com/street/f9bc67e61212fd52ce701ec32ff6219d320188dd29ad74148e40ab8688f341e2.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

In 2016, he stormed to victory in 2:03:03 before returning three years later to produce one of the greatest marathon performances of his career, clocking 2:01:41 in 2019. That performance left him just two seconds short of Eliud Kipchoge’s then-world record of 2:01:39.

### [Kenenisa Bekele Withdraws From Berlin Marathon After Achilles Injury](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15327)
His 2:01:41 remains one of the fastest marathon performances ever recorded, and Berlin has long been a special stage in Bekele’s extraordinary career.
This year’s appearance was also expected to mark another chapter in his remarkable longevity. Bekele entered the race as a 44-year-old and had been targeting another strong performance after previously setting a masters marathon world record of 2:04:15 at the 2024 London Marathon, a mark he established at the age of 41.
Instead, his preparations have ended in disappointment.
Bekele has not completed a marathon since the Paris 2024 Olympic Marathon, where he finished 39th in 2:12:24. He subsequently entered the 2025 New York City Marathon but did not finish.
His withdrawal is another frustrating setback for a legendary athlete whose career has repeatedly been interrupted by injuries but who has continued to produce extraordinary performances well beyond the age at which many elite distance runners have retired.
For now, Berlin will have to wait for another Bekele appearance.
The Ethiopian legend will not be on the start line this Sunday, but his legacy on the Berlin streets remains firmly etched in marathon history.

![Image 51](https://mybestruns.com/street/4be03cb14e3dd0328f98a3077e606f8f55c0af21f11d9005d99c38fcd0d3c24b.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
In the women’s race, all eyes will be on [Tigst Assefa](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Tigst+Assefa) as the Ethiopian superstar returns to the course where she produced one of the most remarkable marathon performances in history. Assefa clocked 2:11:53 in Berlin in 2023, setting a world record at the time and establishing a course record that still stands.
![Image 52](https://mybestruns.com/street/eca84645e3b691369c59e2575e7ed009b803461b94e5c40fd19ca6be92c7cbaa.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

### [Tigst Assefa, Rosemary Wanjiru And Gabriel Geay Headline A Star-Studded Berlin Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15325)
Assefa, a two-time Berlin Marathon champion, will face defending champion [Rosemary Wanjiru](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Rosemary+Wanjiru), who returns to the German capital looking to retain her title. Wanjiru won the 2025 edition in 2:21:05 after previously finishing second in Berlin in 2022 in 2:18:00. Her personal best of 2:16:14 came at the 2023 Tokyo Marathon.
Wanjiru’s challenge will be particularly intriguing given the depth of the Ethiopian contingent. Bedatu Hirpa enters with a 2:18:27 personal best, followed by Dera Dida at 2:18:32, Zeineba Yimer at 2:18:47, Bosena Mulatie at 2:19:00, Misgane Alemayehu at 2:19:08 and Bekelech Gudeta at 2:19:39.
Kenya will also have another strong presence through Evaline Chirchir, whose 2:20:33 personal best places her among the leading women on the start list.
The Berlin Marathon’s reputation for producing fast times adds another layer of intrigue to an already stacked field. With a flat course, long stretches of uninterrupted running and a history of world records, the German capital has consistently provided elite athletes with the ideal conditions to test the limits of marathon performance.
Beyond the headline names, the race will also offer an opportunity for several contenders to make their mark on one of the biggest stages in road running. With experienced marathoners and ambitious challengers sharing the start line, the battle for the podium is expected to unfold at a demanding pace from the opening kilometres through the final stages of the race.
With Assefa returning to the scene of her historic 2023 run, Wanjiru arriving as the defending champion and a deep international cast lining up across both races, Berlin is once again set for a weekend of world-class marathon racing.
Three days out, the stage is set. The fast Berlin streets are waiting.

### [New York City Marathon Makes First Course Change in 15 Years](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15322)
The [TCS New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=TCS+New+York+City+Marathon) is set for a small but significant change to its iconic 26.2-mile course, with runners facing a revised section in the [Bronx](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Bronx) between Miles 20 and 21.
![Image 56](https://mybestruns.com/street/1936f9c4ddcb81f2a6318668a43f8a3258c6e4f5dedf2d2dac5807d0770bcefc.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
For 15 years, every New York City Marathon runner passed through the exact same stretch of the Bronx around Mile 20, navigating a short loop that surrounded a neighborhood supermarket and a 24-hour laundromat for much of race day. This November, that familiar loop will disappear.
![Image 57](https://mybestruns.com/street/07436f3fad13077b64b5db3e62de1d38e3117daf68206f1199d03f5681bbcbaf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
New York Road Runners (NYRR) is making its first course change to the marathon in 15 years. Instead of looping near East 140th Street, runners will head north on Alexander Avenue, turn onto Third Avenue and then cut south on 138th Street toward the Madison Avenue Bridge.

### [New York City Marathon Makes First Course Change in 15 Years](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15322)
The adjustment removes two turns from the Bronx section, reducing the number from seven to five. While that may sound insignificant for a race covering 26.2 miles, the change comes at a point when runners are already deep into the marathon and every turn, road surface and change in rhythm can become more noticeable.
![Image 58](https://mybestruns.com/street/dee421746c00314bfab71315f1f23f5cb01e237877ad3c36a10fa4f29ea4a7ba.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
However, the primary reason for the change is not to make the course faster or help runners shave seconds from their finishing times.
Bronx resident Jennifer Alicea told The New York Times that the previous route made it extremely difficult to reach her only nearby grocery store on marathon day. NYRR's Metellus, who grew up in the Bronx, described the affected blocks as food deserts and saw the course's required recertification as an opportunity to address the problem.
The timing also carries added significance. This year marks 50 years since the New York City Marathon expanded beyond Central Park in 1976, becoming the five-borough race that has since grown into one of the world's most famous marathons.
The route will still cover the same 26.2 miles through New York's five boroughs, but the Bronx experience will be slightly different. For elite athletes, two fewer turns could mean a smoother rhythm during the crucial closing stages. For thousands of recreational runners, the bigger difference may be felt by the communities living along the course rather than on the race clock.
The New York City Marathon has long been celebrated not only for its elite competition but also for the connection between the race and the communities it passes through. The latest adjustment reflects that relationship, showing how even an established course can evolve while preserving the character of the event.
So, two fewer turns, the same five boroughs and the same 26.2 miles — but potentially one less headache for residents of the Bronx.

![Image 56](https://mybestruns.com/street/1936f9c4ddcb81f2a6318668a43f8a3258c6e4f5dedf2d2dac5807d0770bcefc.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
For 15 years, every New York City Marathon runner passed through the exact same stretch of the Bronx around Mile 20, navigating a short loop that surrounded a neighborhood supermarket and a 24-hour laundromat for much of race day. This November, that familiar loop will disappear.
![Image 57](https://mybestruns.com/street/07436f3fad13077b64b5db3e62de1d38e3117daf68206f1199d03f5681bbcbaf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

### [New York City Marathon Makes First Course Change in 15 Years](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15322)
The adjustment removes two turns from the Bronx section, reducing the number from seven to five. While that may sound insignificant for a race covering 26.2 miles, the change comes at a point when runners are already deep into the marathon and every turn, road surface and change in rhythm can become more noticeable.
![Image 58](https://mybestruns.com/street/dee421746c00314bfab71315f1f23f5cb01e237877ad3c36a10fa4f29ea4a7ba.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
However, the primary reason for the change is not to make the course faster or help runners shave seconds from their finishing times.
Bronx resident Jennifer Alicea told The New York Times that the previous route made it extremely difficult to reach her only nearby grocery store on marathon day. NYRR's Metellus, who grew up in the Bronx, described the affected blocks as food deserts and saw the course's required recertification as an opportunity to address the problem.
The timing also carries added significance. This year marks 50 years since the New York City Marathon expanded beyond Central Park in 1976, becoming the five-borough race that has since grown into one of the world's most famous marathons.
The route will still cover the same 26.2 miles through New York's five boroughs, but the Bronx experience will be slightly different. For elite athletes, two fewer turns could mean a smoother rhythm during the crucial closing stages. For thousands of recreational runners, the bigger difference may be felt by the communities living along the course rather than on the race clock.
The New York City Marathon has long been celebrated not only for its elite competition but also for the connection between the race and the communities it passes through. The latest adjustment reflects that relationship, showing how even an established course can evolve while preserving the character of the event.
So, two fewer turns, the same five boroughs and the same 26.2 miles — but potentially one less headache for residents of the Bronx.

![Image 118](https://mybestruns.com/street/95227a0f364e1d87cf49dc8e320154f7b5c8294e5b97ce4bcd9047488e9ae328.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Just behind that group is Japan’s Kengo Suzuki (2:04:56), Italy’s Yemaneberhan Crippa (2:05:18), Kenya’s Edward Cheserek (2:05:24) and Japan’s Ryota Kondo (2:05:39). Ireland’s Peter Lynch (2:06:08), Great Britain’s Patrick Dever (2:06:18), Australia’s Haftu Strintzos (2:06:20) and Britain’s Jack Rowe (2:07:47) further strengthen a field that possesses extraordinary depth.
The American contingent is just as fascinating. Alongside Mantz and Talbi are Ryan Ford (2:05:46), Joe Klecker (2:05:56), Casey Clinger (2:08:43), Sam Chelanga (2:08:50), JP Flavin (2:09:17), Jared Ward (2:09:25), Turner Wiley (2:09:27), Andrew Colley (2:09:33), Robert Miranda (2:09:40) and Joel Reichow (2:09:56).

### [New York Marathon Set For Blockbuster Showdown As America’s Two Fastest Men Collide](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15097)
The depth continues with Aidan Troutner (2:10:23), JP Trojan (2:10:39), Paul Chelimo (2:10:55), Stephen Jones (2:11:17), Mo Bati (2:12:29), Aidan Reed (2:13:58), Owen Ritz (2:14:19), Merga Gemeda (2:15:12), Alec Baldwin (2:15:38) and Ryan Cutter (2:17:24). Australia’s James Nipperess (2:15:03) and Lesotho’s Kamohelo Mofolo (2:08:50) are also on the start list.
Three athletes will make their marathon debuts in New York: Sweden’s Andreas Almgren, Kenya’s Patrick Kiprop and American Ahmed Muhumed. Almgren, in particular, brings tremendous track credentials into his first attempt at 26.2 miles after winning the European 10,000m title in Birmingham in a championship-record 27:23.44.
The numbers tell the story of just how deep this field is. Ten men have personal bests faster than the existing New York City Marathon course record of 2:04:58, set by Tamirat Tola in 2023. Remarkably, Tola himself is not entered, nor is Alexander Mutiso, who finished runner-up to Kipruto in last year’s dramatic race.
For Mantz and Talbi, however, the stakes extend beyond the American record books. No American man has won the New York City Marathon since Meb Keflezighi in 2009, meaning the American contingent will arrive carrying a 17-year wait for another homegrown champion. Mantz and Talbi will have to overcome a formidable international field if either is to end that drought.

### [New York Marathon Set For Blockbuster Showdown As America’s Two Fastest Men Collide](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15097)
New York’s course will add another layer of difficulty. The bridges, sharp turns, rolling sections and notoriously demanding final miles toward Central Park have humbled some of the world’s fastest marathoners. Raw personal-best times will matter, but so will patience, positioning, tactical intelligence and the ability to produce a decisive move when the race reaches its most unforgiving stages.
With the official American record-holder, the fastest American by clock time, a defending champion, multiple 2:04 marathoners and a host of world-class contenders all converging on the Big Apple, the 2026 New York City Marathon has the ingredients of a classic.
On November 1, the streets of New York could become the setting for another extraordinary chapter in marathon history.

### [Tegla Loroupe Embarks On 840-Kilometre Peace Run From Kakuma To Nairobi](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15083)
Ambassador [Tegla Chepkite Loroupe](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Tegla+Chepkite+Loroupe) has embarked on an extraordinary [840-kilometre](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=840-kilometre) run from [Kakuma Refugee Camp](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Kakuma+Refugee+Camp) in Turkana County to [Uhuru Park](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Uhuru+Park) in Nairobi, turning a seven-day endurance challenge into a powerful campaign for peace, education, inclusion and greater awareness of the experiences and aspirations of refugees.
![Image 122](https://mybestruns.com/street/f6c0bd454740e847255f291ec4538ac4e16e2d3c7acf0c7377aec07936648a2d.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Loroupe is undertaking the journey alongside 28 refugees, with the initiative designed to shine a light on the challenges facing refugee communities in Kakuma and Dadaab while promoting stronger relationships between refugees and their host communities.
![Image 123](https://mybestruns.com/street/393bc370d13b06c74f3ba63dd29a0ce372aed4267ca5f67acc4e898391502bf5.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
For Loroupe, the run represents far more than a test of endurance. It is an extension of a mission she has pursued for years—using sport as a platform to promote peace, opportunity, education and inclusion for people whose lives have been affected by displacement.

### [Tegla Loroupe Embarks On 840-Kilometre Peace Run From Kakuma To Nairobi](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15083)
Reflecting on the early days of advocating for refugee inclusion in sport and development, Loroupe said it was deeply meaningful to see Yiech Pur Biel continue that mission. Biel, who grew up in Kakuma Refugee Camp and went on to represent the Refugee Olympic Team, will lead the team at the Youth Olympic Games in Senegal this year.
![Image 124](https://mybestruns.com/street/f312f7b0b340fc3c629d358d780eca099421f1f8648e0a7b4da6499baa5436fe.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
“Reflecting on the early days of advocating for refugee inclusion in sports and development, it means so much to see Yiech Pur Biel carry that mission forward — this year, he’ll lead the Refugee Olympic Team at the Youth Olympic Games in Senegal. I’m taking on an 840km journey over seven days, running from Kakuma Refugee Camp to Uhuru Park in Nairobi alongside 28 refugees. Every kilometre of this run is a reminder: displacement doesn’t have to mean the end of a dream. Everyone deserves the chance to pursue theirs,” Amb. Tegla Loroupe said.
![Image 125](https://mybestruns.com/street/f4bc362f01a154ae56a8ba5cd4b35dffc712870e23355dd8390615cb26eb1d72.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The message captures the heart of the initiative. By running alongside refugees rather than simply speaking about their experiences, Loroupe is seeking to bring their stories, ambitions and hopes closer to the national conversation.

### [Tegla Loroupe Embarks On 840-Kilometre Peace Run From Kakuma To Nairobi](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15083)
Her journey also reflects the remarkable transformation of her own life from elite athlete to global advocate. Born on 9 May 1973, Loroupe established herself as one of Kenya’s most accomplished long-distance runners before devoting much of her influence to peacebuilding, education, women's rights and humanitarian causes.
![Image 126](https://mybestruns.com/street/479806038d048b20500e5393f1815f3b1bea864ccd909b4a37c14d1e1f6ebcef.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
During her illustrious career, she held world records over 25 and 30 kilometres and became the first African woman to hold the women's marathon world record. She also became a three-time world half-marathon champion and made history as the first African woman to win the New York City Marathon, claiming the prestigious race twice.
Her victories extended to several of the world's major marathons, including London, Rotterdam, Hong Kong, Berlin and Rome, cementing her reputation as one of the outstanding distance runners of her generation.
Yet Loroupe's influence today extends well beyond her achievements on the road. Through the Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation and other initiatives, she has continued to champion peaceful coexistence and opportunities for communities affected by conflict and displacement.
The 840-kilometre journey now gives that mission a physical form. From Kakuma to Nairobi, every kilometre is intended to carry a message of hope while drawing attention to the potential of refugees when they are given access to education, sport, opportunity and a supportive community.
The participation of 28 refugees makes the journey even more significant. Their presence transforms the run from a symbolic campaign into a collective expression of resilience, allowing those directly affected by displacement to become part of the story being told.

### [Tegla Loroupe Embarks On 840-Kilometre Peace Run From Kakuma To Nairobi](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15083)
As Loroupe and her fellow runners make their way towards Uhuru Park over seven days, the distance will inevitably test their physical strength. But the greater purpose lies beyond the finish line: reminding Kenya and the wider world that being displaced does not mean being without dreams.
For Loroupe, every stride is therefore a statement of possibility—a call for peace, inclusion and education, and a powerful reminder that with the right opportunities, refugees can move beyond survival and pursue the futures they envision.

### [From Shark Attack Survivor to New York City Marathon Finisher: Ali Truwit's Extraordinary Journey of Courage and Resilience](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14896)
Some victories are measured by finish times. Others are defined by the obstacles overcome simply to reach the starting line.
For American Paralympic swimmer [Ali Truwit](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Ali+Truwit), completing the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) represented far more than covering 26.2 miles. It was the culmination of an extraordinary journey of survival, resilience, and unwavering determination that began with a life-altering shark attack just two years earlier.
![Image 129](https://mybestruns.com/street/8112546f7a444a2f5eee29dc55aa5cb262179b96de95ea565d789400f564a403.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
On a crisp November morning in 2025, Truwit crossed the iconic finish line wearing a carbon-fibre running blade, fulfilling a promise she had made while recovering in a hospital bed after losing her lower left leg. The emotional milestone marked another remarkable chapter in one of the most inspiring comeback stories in modern sport.
The road to that unforgettable finish began only days after Truwit celebrated a major personal achievement. In May 2023, she completed her first marathon in Copenhagen alongside her mother. Just ten days later, while enjoying a graduation trip to Turks and Caicos with former Yale swimming teammate Sophie Pilkinton, tragedy struck.
While the pair were snorkelling, a shark attacked Truwit, severely injuring her left leg. Displaying remarkable courage, the two swam approximately 55 metres back to their boat, where Pilkinton—then a medical student—quickly applied a tourniquet that stopped the bleeding and ultimately saved Truwit's life.
Doctors were forced to amputate her lower left leg on her 23rd birthday.

### [From Shark Attack Survivor to New York City Marathon Finisher: Ali Truwit's Extraordinary Journey of Courage and Resilience](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14896)
![Image 130](https://mybestruns.com/street/60182ea28dcbec09b201b2c96b35b47844e8b704ee2161e222ca8662ac6351b0.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Even in the darkest moments of recovery, Truwit's determination never disappeared. Reflecting on having recently completed her first marathon, she joked with one of the first responders that at least she had managed to run a marathon before the attack. The responder's simple but powerful reply would remain with her throughout rehabilitation: "You'll run another one."
Those words became a source of hope during the long and demanding road back.
![Image 131](https://mybestruns.com/street/8453df5e269fa1e38d0c2decf96df3c87ee036f4a16018159372af4552595ba9.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Only weeks after surgery, Truwit began learning to walk on a prosthetic limb before gradually returning to the swimming pool. The process was anything but straightforward. The water that had once been her sanctuary became a source of painful memories, yet she refused to allow fear to define her future.
Her relentless work ethic soon produced extraordinary results.
Less than 16 months after the attack, Truwit represented the United States at the Paris 2024 Paralympic Games, producing a sensational performance to claim both silver and bronze medals. Standing on the Paralympic podium was a powerful reminder of how far she had come in such a short period, and she dedicated those achievements to everyone who had helped save her life.
Still, another dream remained unfinished.

### [From Shark Attack Survivor to New York City Marathon Finisher: Ali Truwit's Extraordinary Journey of Courage and Resilience](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14896)
The New York City Marathon carried deep personal significance. It was not merely another endurance event but a symbolic return to the city where her life had changed forever. On November 2, 2025, she lined up in Staten Island accompanied by 13 family members and close friends, all proudly representing her nonprofit foundation, Stronger Than You Think. Among them was Pilkinton, the friend whose quick thinking had preserved her life on that unforgettable day in the Caribbean.
Together, they covered every mile of the marathon before celebrating an emotional finish that Truwit later described as being "over the moon."
Completing a marathon on a carbon-fibre running blade presents challenges far beyond those faced by able-bodied runners. The prosthetic demands greater strength from the hips, core, and remaining leg while requiring exceptional balance, coordination, and endurance. Truwit's preparation combined months of disciplined training, patience, and mental resilience as she effectively taught herself how to run again.
Her story extends well beyond medals and marathon finishes.
Inspired by her own recovery, Truwit founded Stronger Than You Think, a nonprofit organisation dedicated to helping individuals overcome physical and financial barriers following limb loss. Recognising that sports prosthetics can cost tens of thousands of dollars and are often not covered by insurance, the foundation provides financial assistance for prosthetic devices, supports water-safety education, and promotes opportunities within Paralympic sport.
The organisation has already helped provide more than 11 prosthetic limbs, delivered nearly $200,000 in direct support, and funded over 4,000 hours of water-safety lessons benefiting more than 700 young people.
Throughout her journey, Truwit has remained refreshingly honest about the emotional challenges that continue to accompany recovery. She has openly acknowledged that healing is an ongoing process and that grief can still come in waves. Rather than portraying an effortless comeback, she has demonstrated that resilience is built through persistence, even on the hardest days.
