Some victories are measured by finish times. Others are defined by the obstacles overcome simply to reach the starting line.
For American Paralympic swimmer [Ali Truwit](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Ali+Truwit), completing the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) represented far more than covering 26.2 miles. It was the culmination of an extraordinary journey of survival, resilience, and unwavering determination that began with a life-altering shark attack just two years earlier.
![Image 129](https://mybestruns.com/street/8112546f7a444a2f5eee29dc55aa5cb262179b96de95ea565d789400f564a403.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
On a crisp November morning in 2025, Truwit crossed the iconic finish line wearing a carbon-fibre running blade, fulfilling a promise she had made while recovering in a hospital bed after losing her lower left leg. The emotional milestone marked another remarkable chapter in one of the most inspiring comeback stories in modern sport.
The road to that unforgettable finish began only days after Truwit celebrated a major personal achievement. In May 2023, she completed her first marathon in Copenhagen alongside her mother. Just ten days later, while enjoying a graduation trip to Turks and Caicos with former Yale swimming teammate Sophie Pilkinton, tragedy struck.
While the pair were snorkelling, a shark attacked Truwit, severely injuring her left leg. Displaying remarkable courage, the two swam approximately 55 metres back to their boat, where Pilkinton—then a medical student—quickly applied a tourniquet that stopped the bleeding and ultimately saved Truwit's life.
Doctors were forced to amputate her lower left leg on her 23rd birthday.

### [From Shark Attack Survivor to New York City Marathon Finisher: Ali Truwit's Extraordinary Journey of Courage and Resilience](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14896)
![Image 130](https://mybestruns.com/street/60182ea28dcbec09b201b2c96b35b47844e8b704ee2161e222ca8662ac6351b0.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Even in the darkest moments of recovery, Truwit's determination never disappeared. Reflecting on having recently completed her first marathon, she joked with one of the first responders that at least she had managed to run a marathon before the attack. The responder's simple but powerful reply would remain with her throughout rehabilitation: "You'll run another one."
Those words became a source of hope during the long and demanding road back.
![Image 131](https://mybestruns.com/street/8453df5e269fa1e38d0c2decf96df3c87ee036f4a16018159372af4552595ba9.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Only weeks after surgery, Truwit began learning to walk on a prosthetic limb before gradually returning to the swimming pool. The process was anything but straightforward. The water that had once been her sanctuary became a source of painful memories, yet she refused to allow fear to define her future.
Her relentless work ethic soon produced extraordinary results.
Less than 16 months after the attack, Truwit represented the United States at the Paris 2024 Paralympic Games, producing a sensational performance to claim both silver and bronze medals. Standing on the Paralympic podium was a powerful reminder of how far she had come in such a short period, and she dedicated those achievements to everyone who had helped save her life.
Still, another dream remained unfinished.

### [From Shark Attack Survivor to New York City Marathon Finisher: Ali Truwit's Extraordinary Journey of Courage and Resilience](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14896)
The New York City Marathon carried deep personal significance. It was not merely another endurance event but a symbolic return to the city where her life had changed forever. On November 2, 2025, she lined up in Staten Island accompanied by 13 family members and close friends, all proudly representing her nonprofit foundation, Stronger Than You Think. Among them was Pilkinton, the friend whose quick thinking had preserved her life on that unforgettable day in the Caribbean.
Together, they covered every mile of the marathon before celebrating an emotional finish that Truwit later described as being "over the moon."
Completing a marathon on a carbon-fibre running blade presents challenges far beyond those faced by able-bodied runners. The prosthetic demands greater strength from the hips, core, and remaining leg while requiring exceptional balance, coordination, and endurance. Truwit's preparation combined months of disciplined training, patience, and mental resilience as she effectively taught herself how to run again.
Her story extends well beyond medals and marathon finishes.
Inspired by her own recovery, Truwit founded Stronger Than You Think, a nonprofit organisation dedicated to helping individuals overcome physical and financial barriers following limb loss. Recognising that sports prosthetics can cost tens of thousands of dollars and are often not covered by insurance, the foundation provides financial assistance for prosthetic devices, supports water-safety education, and promotes opportunities within Paralympic sport.
The organisation has already helped provide more than 11 prosthetic limbs, delivered nearly $200,000 in direct support, and funded over 4,000 hours of water-safety lessons benefiting more than 700 young people.
Throughout her journey, Truwit has remained refreshingly honest about the emotional challenges that continue to accompany recovery. She has openly acknowledged that healing is an ongoing process and that grief can still come in waves. Rather than portraying an effortless comeback, she has demonstrated that resilience is built through persistence, even on the hardest days.

### [Paul Tergat Backs Kenya’s Ambitious Bid to Host World Athletics Championships](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14683)
Kenyan athletics icon [Paul Tergat](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Paul+Tergat) has thrown his weight behind Kenya’s ambitious campaign to host the [World Athletics Championships](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=World+Athletics+Championships) in 2029 describing the nation as the true heartbeat of global distance running.
![Image 143](https://mybestruns.com/street/a795061f3329ff8c85d95538b5631ba5d8dc6348ddd7b1c730da11b24de27589.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
In a passionate message shared on X Space, the former marathon world record holder called on the international athletics community to experience the culture, heritage, and unmatched talent that have made Kenya one of the most dominant forces in the history of the sport.
![Image 144](https://mybestruns.com/street/9c831d53515e462f259b9dc0c3a7c0b7dc11090c7ff30771e122aea3794df219.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
“Kenya is inviting the world to experience running at its source,” Tergat said. “From the soil that produces legends, from communities where athletics is lived, breathed, and passed through generations.”
His remarks arrive at a time when Kenya is intensifying efforts to secure hosting rights for one of athletics’ most prestigious global events — a move that would mark a historic milestone for both the country and the African continent.

### [Paul Tergat Backs Kenya’s Ambitious Bid to Host World Athletics Championships](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14683)
Few figures embody Kenya’s running excellence more than Tergat himself. The legendary distance runner became the first Kenyan man to set a marathon world record after producing a groundbreaking performance of 2:04:55 at the Berlin Marathon 2003. His record stood until 2007 and cemented his place among the greatest marathoners in history.
![Image 145](https://mybestruns.com/street/54a4012169ca6f590982fd8659773658e805c72cf6efecfef99c7b39c759c14a.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Before conquering the roads, Tergat had already established an extraordinary legacy in cross country running. Between 1995 and 1999, he achieved one of the sport’s rarest feats by winning five consecutive World Cross Country long-race titles, dominating an era filled with elite competition.
On the track, Tergat was renowned for his unforgettable rivalry with Ethiopian great Haile Gebrselassie. The Kenyan star captured Olympic silver medals in the 10,000m at both the 1996 Atlanta Games and the 2000 Sydney Olympics, while also earning silver medals at the 1997 and 1999 World Championships. Many of those races were decided in dramatic final laps, with Tergat and Gebrselassie pushing each other to historic performances.
His success extended beyond the track and marathon scene. Tergat claimed back-to-back IAAF World Half Marathon titles in 1999 and 2000 before later winning the prestigious 2005 New York City Marathon, further solidifying his reputation as one of the most versatile distance runners of his generation.

### [Paul Tergat Backs Kenya’s Ambitious Bid to Host World Athletics Championships](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14683)
Away from competition, Tergat has remained deeply influential in Kenyan sport and athletics administration. He previously served as President of the National Olympic Committee of Kenya (NOC-K) and founded the Sports Personality of the Year Awards (SOYA), an initiative that continues to celebrate and recognize sporting excellence across the country.
![Image 146](https://mybestruns.com/street/e002e5f1e18d5fcde5a06a43b51f3acd7fee314848f3225e62b173554204168d.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
For decades, Kenya has remained synonymous with excellence in middle- and long-distance running, producing generations of champions who have rewritten world records, conquered Olympic podiums, and elevated the nation’s reputation on the global sporting stage. From the high-altitude training camps of the Rift Valley to packed road races across the world, Kenyan athletics has evolved into more than just sport — it is part of the country’s identity.
Tergat believes hosting the championships would offer the world an opportunity to witness firsthand the environment that shapes elite athletes. Beyond the competition itself, he emphasized the cultural significance of Kenyan running communities, where young athletes grow up inspired by local heroes and where endurance running is deeply woven into everyday life.
The bid also represents Africa’s growing desire to host more major international sporting events. While African athletes have consistently dominated global athletics for generations, the continent has rarely been given the opportunity to stage the sport’s biggest championships. Kenya’s proposal is therefore seen as both symbolic and transformative for athletics worldwide.
Tergat’s endorsement adds significant weight to the campaign. Widely regarded as one of the greatest distance runners in history, the Kenyan legend remains a respected voice within international athletics circles. His support reflects the confidence many within the sport have in Kenya’s ability to deliver a memorable and globally impactful championship.

### [Paul Tergat Backs Kenya’s Ambitious Bid to Host World Athletics Championships](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14683)
If successful, the championships would not only showcase elite competition but also spotlight Kenya’s rich sporting heritage, passionate fans, and deep-rooted connection to athletics — offering the world a chance to experience the birthplace of countless running legends.

When Kipsaisak stepped aside after 8 kilometers, the decisive move had already been made. Kamworor passed 10K in 27:42, firmly in control. His surge between 16 and 17 kilometers, clocked in a punishing 2:42, broke the race open completely. From that point, victory was never in doubt.

“Actually, I knew I was going to win around 14K,” Kamworor said afterward. “I knew I had prepared well. I came here wanting to run a fast time, and Edwin did a great job pacing. It’s great to come back and win even faster.”
Behind him, Birhanu Balew of Bahrain ran strongly to secure second place in 58:23, while Kenya’s Gideon Rono impressed in his debut at the distance, finishing third in 58:38.
Kamworor’s journey back to the top has been anything but easy. Once the dominant force in global distance running—with three consecutive World Half Marathon titles, two World Cross Country championships, and two New York City Marathon victories—his career was nearly derailed in 2020 when he was struck by a motorbike during a solo training run. The injury required multiple surgeries and a lengthy rehabilitation, keeping him away from peak form for nearly three years.

### [How One Tribe in Kenya Came to Dominate Global Distance Running](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14033)
There may be no statistic in all of sports more astonishing than this one.
The Kalenjin, an ethnic group—often referred to as a tribe—in Kenya, make up about 13.4% of the country’s population, roughly 6.3 million people. On a global scale, they represent about one out of every 1,000 people worldwide.
![Image 221](https://mybestruns.com/street/31fd23f24578a76f6fc0580d9093e935c038cda98d42eefe81cdfdd0126b8ac7.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Yet this small community has produced an overwhelming share of the world’s greatest distance runners.
![Image 222](https://mybestruns.com/street/e23d62d8a509883c34d3fcc2300d64ea559616598580289fc6799ce1bc84e82a.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Their dominance has been so complete, and so sustained, that it has been described as“the greatest geographical concentration of achievement in the annals of sport.”And it is hard to argue otherwise.
From the Rift Valley to the World Stage
Most elite Kalenjin runners come from Kenya’s Rift Valley region, particularly areas such as Nandi, Elgeyo-Marakwet, Uasin Gishu, and Baringo, where elevations range from 2,000 to 2,400 meters (6,500–8,000 feet)above sea level.
Here, running is not a hobby—it is part of daily life.

### [How One Tribe in Kenya Came to Dominate Global Distance Running](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14033)
Children grow up walking and running long distances, often on dirt roads. Training at altitude is the norm, not a strategy. And success stories are local and visible, creating a powerful cycle of belief and opportunity.
Champions Across Eras
The Kalenjin impact on global athletics stretches back more than half a century.
Kipchoge Keino, one of the pioneers of Kenyan distance running, won Olympic gold in the 1500 meters at the 1968 Mexico City Games and the 3000-meter steeplechase in 1972, helping place Kenyan runners on the world map.
Since then, Kenyan athletes—many of them Kalenjin—have dominated:
• The 3000-meter steeplechase, winning Olympic gold in nearly every Games since 1968
• The 5,000 meters and 10,000 meters at World Championships
• The marathon, particularly at the World Marathon Majors
Masters of the Marathon
Perhaps nowhere is this dominance more visible than in the marathon.
Kalenjin runners have repeatedly won and controlled races such as:
• Berlin Marathon
• London Marathon
• Chicago Marathon
• Boston Marathon
• New York City Marathon
These victories are not isolated moments—they are part of a long, uninterrupted pattern.
At the center of it all stands Eliud Kipchoge, widely regarded as the greatest marathon runner in history. A member of the Kalenjin community, Kipchoge has:
• Won two Olympic marathon gold medals(2016, 2021)
• Set a world record of 2:01:09 at the Berlin Marathon
• Become the first human to run 26.2 miles in under two hours
He is not an exception. He is the most refined expression of a system that has been producing champions for generations.
Why This One Tribe?
No single explanation tells the whole story, but several factors come together in the Rift Valley:
• Geography:High altitude, rolling terrain, and ideal training conditions
• Physiology:Exceptional running economy and efficient biomechanics
• Culture:Running as a respected path to success and opportunity

### [How One Tribe in Kenya Came to Dominate Global Distance Running](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14033)
• Environment:Group training, competition, and long-term development from a young age
Together, these elements have created something unmatched in sport.
A Phenomenon Without Parallel
Great athletes come from everywhere. But nowhere else has such a small, specific populationproduced such sustained global dominance across events, generations, and decades.
Not sprinting.
Not swimming.
Not cycling.
Not soccer.
Only distance running.
From the highland paths of the Rift Valley to Olympic podiums and marathon finish lines around the world, the story of the Kalenjin remains one of the most extraordinary achievements in human performance.
And it is still being written.

### [How One Tribe in Kenya Came to Dominate Global Distance Running](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14033)
There may be no statistic in all of sports more astonishing than this one.
The Kalenjin, an ethnic group—often referred to as a tribe—in Kenya, make up about 13.4% of the country’s population, roughly 6.3 million people. On a global scale, they represent about one out of every 1,000 people worldwide.
![Image 221](https://mybestruns.com/street/31fd23f24578a76f6fc0580d9093e935c038cda98d42eefe81cdfdd0126b8ac7.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Yet this small community has produced an overwhelming share of the world’s greatest distance runners.
![Image 222](https://mybestruns.com/street/e23d62d8a509883c34d3fcc2300d64ea559616598580289fc6799ce1bc84e82a.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Their dominance has been so complete, and so sustained, that it has been described as“the greatest geographical concentration of achievement in the annals of sport.”And it is hard to argue otherwise.
From the Rift Valley to the World Stage
Most elite Kalenjin runners come from Kenya’s Rift Valley region, particularly areas such as Nandi, Elgeyo-Marakwet, Uasin Gishu, and Baringo, where elevations range from 2,000 to 2,400 meters (6,500–8,000 feet)above sea level.
Here, running is not a hobby—it is part of daily life.

### [How One Tribe in Kenya Came to Dominate Global Distance Running](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14033)
Children grow up walking and running long distances, often on dirt roads. Training at altitude is the norm, not a strategy. And success stories are local and visible, creating a powerful cycle of belief and opportunity.
Champions Across Eras
The Kalenjin impact on global athletics stretches back more than half a century.
Kipchoge Keino, one of the pioneers of Kenyan distance running, won Olympic gold in the 1500 meters at the 1968 Mexico City Games and the 3000-meter steeplechase in 1972, helping place Kenyan runners on the world map.
Since then, Kenyan athletes—many of them Kalenjin—have dominated:
• The 3000-meter steeplechase, winning Olympic gold in nearly every Games since 1968
• The 5,000 meters and 10,000 meters at World Championships
• The marathon, particularly at the World Marathon Majors
Masters of the Marathon
Perhaps nowhere is this dominance more visible than in the marathon.
Kalenjin runners have repeatedly won and controlled races such as:
• Berlin Marathon
• London Marathon
• Chicago Marathon
• Boston Marathon
• New York City Marathon
These victories are not isolated moments—they are part of a long, uninterrupted pattern.
At the center of it all stands Eliud Kipchoge, widely regarded as the greatest marathon runner in history. A member of the Kalenjin community, Kipchoge has:
• Won two Olympic marathon gold medals(2016, 2021)
• Set a world record of 2:01:09 at the Berlin Marathon
• Become the first human to run 26.2 miles in under two hours
He is not an exception. He is the most refined expression of a system that has been producing champions for generations.
Why This One Tribe?
No single explanation tells the whole story, but several factors come together in the Rift Valley:
• Geography:High altitude, rolling terrain, and ideal training conditions
• Physiology:Exceptional running economy and efficient biomechanics
• Culture:Running as a respected path to success and opportunity

### [How One Tribe in Kenya Came to Dominate Global Distance Running](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14033)
• Environment:Group training, competition, and long-term development from a young age
Together, these elements have created something unmatched in sport.
A Phenomenon Without Parallel
Great athletes come from everywhere. But nowhere else has such a small, specific populationproduced such sustained global dominance across events, generations, and decades.
Not sprinting.
Not swimming.
Not cycling.
Not soccer.
Only distance running.
From the highland paths of the Rift Valley to Olympic podiums and marathon finish lines around the world, the story of the Kalenjin remains one of the most extraordinary achievements in human performance.
And it is still being written.

A 20-year-old British runner has officially become the youngest person in history to complete all seven World Marathon Majors and earn the coveted Seven Star Medal, Abbott World Marathon Majors announced.
Lucy Scott, from Bishop’s Stortford in Hertfordshire, completed the seven marathons over an 18-month stretch: Tokyo, Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago, New York City, and Sydney. She secured the honor on November 2 when she crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon, making her the “youngest Seven Star athlete” to date.
![Image 225](https://mybestruns.com/street/8efa56c4ab066e6aa7891ab01b1d469b175cc36baf13e2406b0f67f99ac6b649.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

![Image 226](https://mybestruns.com/street/d7deeb6474e70c5c49f8d0b3611d34c5f90fe7529c03f5da3d2de77710f2c9f6.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Introduced in 2016, the Six Star Medal originally honored runners who completed the six established majors. The series expanded in November 2024 with the addition of the Sydney Marathon, creating the Seven Star Medal Scott has now earned.

### [How One Tribe in Kenya Came to Dominate Global Distance Running](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14033)
Children grow up walking and running long distances, often on dirt roads. Training at altitude is the norm, not a strategy. And success stories are local and visible, creating a powerful cycle of belief and opportunity.
Champions Across Eras
The Kalenjin impact on global athletics stretches back more than half a century.
Kipchoge Keino, one of the pioneers of Kenyan distance running, won Olympic gold in the 1500 meters at the 1968 Mexico City Games and the 3000-meter steeplechase in 1972, helping place Kenyan runners on the world map.
Since then, Kenyan athletes—many of them Kalenjin—have dominated:
• The 3000-meter steeplechase, winning Olympic gold in nearly every Games since 1968
• The 5,000 meters and 10,000 meters at World Championships
• The marathon, particularly at the World Marathon Majors
Masters of the Marathon
Perhaps nowhere is this dominance more visible than in the marathon.
Kalenjin runners have repeatedly won and controlled races such as:
• Berlin Marathon
• London Marathon
• Chicago Marathon
• Boston Marathon
• New York City Marathon
These victories are not isolated moments—they are part of a long, uninterrupted pattern.
At the center of it all stands Eliud Kipchoge, widely regarded as the greatest marathon runner in history. A member of the Kalenjin community, Kipchoge has:
• Won two Olympic marathon gold medals(2016, 2021)
• Set a world record of 2:01:09 at the Berlin Marathon
• Become the first human to run 26.2 miles in under two hours
He is not an exception. He is the most refined expression of a system that has been producing champions for generations.
Why This One Tribe?
No single explanation tells the whole story, but several factors come together in the Rift Valley:
• Geography:High altitude, rolling terrain, and ideal training conditions
• Physiology:Exceptional running economy and efficient biomechanics
• Culture:Running as a respected path to success and opportunity

### [How One Tribe in Kenya Came to Dominate Global Distance Running](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14033)
• Environment:Group training, competition, and long-term development from a young age
Together, these elements have created something unmatched in sport.
A Phenomenon Without Parallel
Great athletes come from everywhere. But nowhere else has such a small, specific populationproduced such sustained global dominance across events, generations, and decades.
Not sprinting.
Not swimming.
Not cycling.
Not soccer.
Only distance running.
From the highland paths of the Rift Valley to Olympic podiums and marathon finish lines around the world, the story of the Kalenjin remains one of the most extraordinary achievements in human performance.
And it is still being written.

### [20-Year-Old Becomes Youngest Ever to Earn the Seven Star Medal](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14001)
A 20-year-old British runner has officially become the youngest person in history to complete all seven World Marathon Majors and earn the coveted Seven Star Medal, Abbott World Marathon Majors announced.
Lucy Scott, from Bishop’s Stortford in Hertfordshire, completed the seven marathons over an 18-month stretch: Tokyo, Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago, New York City, and Sydney. She secured the honor on November 2 when she crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon, making her the “youngest Seven Star athlete” to date.
![Image 225](https://mybestruns.com/street/8efa56c4ab066e6aa7891ab01b1d469b175cc36baf13e2406b0f67f99ac6b649.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Scott, a history student at the University of Nottingham, only began running in 2024. “It’s the best thing I’ve ever done,” she said.
![Image 226](https://mybestruns.com/street/d7deeb6474e70c5c49f8d0b3611d34c5f90fe7529c03f5da3d2de77710f2c9f6.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Introduced in 2016, the Six Star Medal originally honored runners who completed the six established majors. The series expanded in November 2024 with the addition of the Sydney Marathon, creating the Seven Star Medal Scott has now earned.

![Image 227](https://mybestruns.com/street/0d77ae1296805cbbae191bf1223771afc6fb5c6d57c80637692021c3854569a2.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Despite having no previous running experience, Scott took up the sport during her first year at university. Her debut marathon came in 2024 at the TCS London Marathon, where she raised £7,685 for The Essex Disabled Sport Foundation.
She credits her father, John Scott, as her inspiration. He had been pursuing the Six Star Medal before the Covid pandemic, but injuries prevented him from completing Tokyo and Boston. Lucy has since carried his dream forward, with her parents traveling the world to cheer her on at every finish line.
![Image 228](https://mybestruns.com/street/30b68a5f55950f25dd6186fb60495e72280f24a92ac593204d65e266e9d9b3ea.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
“I think they’ve loved the experience as much as I have,” she said.
Looking ahead, Scott plans to run her third London Marathon in April 2026—“if I can balance university and fundraising,” she noted. She also hopes to pursue the proposed Nine Star Medal, which Abbott World Marathon Majors is considering adding by including Cape Town and Shanghai.
“If I can get a place, I would love to do that,” she said.

### [Susanna Sullivan — The Teacher Who Runs Among the World’s Best Set to run NYC Sunday](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=13968)
American marathoner[Susanna Sullivan](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Susanna+Sullivan)continues to prove that world-class athleticism and everyday life can coexist. A sixth-grade math and science teacher from McLean, Virginia, Sullivan has quietly become one of the top American women in marathon history — balancing the classroom with 120-mile training weeks and remarkable consistency on the roads.
From Humble Beginnings to World Class
![Image 248](https://mybestruns.com/street/2efa509b71da10aeca45997943b7972cdbafeaea5697f8ddf8ad48ff1fab16cf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Born May 13, 1990, in West Palm Beach, Florida, and raised in Virginia, Sullivan’s early success came at George Mason High School, where she earned multiple state titles in cross-country and track. After competing at the University of Notre Dame, she battled injuries and fatigue but never lost her love for the sport.
![Image 249](https://mybestruns.com/street/e45aeea130e4e9df3fecc19d6a664f52952e160adec7b130191cbd23e46f1ded.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Her marathon debut came in 2015 at Grandma’s Marathon in Minnesota, where she clocked 2:35:37 for 9th place. Over the next decade, she quietly built momentum, cutting time from race to race. The breakthrough arrived in 2024 at the Chicago Marathon, where she finished 7th overall — and first American — in 2:21:56, a personal best that placed her among the top ten fastest U.S. women of all time.

### [Susanna Sullivan — The Teacher Who Runs Among the World’s Best Set to run NYC Sunday](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=13968)
Fourth at the 2025 World Championships in Tokyo
![Image 250](https://mybestruns.com/street/2a25e5d83c171aa4693c1b63120529834b561b4cf240e52bf24e5dfa51db4ea1.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
On September 14, 2025, Sullivan delivered one of her finest performances at the World Athletics Championships Marathon in Tokyo, finishing fourth in 2:28:17.
Under sweltering heat and high humidity, Sullivan courageously led much of the race, setting the pace through 25 kilometers before the eventual medalists pulled away. Her performance — the top American finish — underscored her strength, tactical intelligence, and resilience on one of the sport’s biggest stages.
It also marked a full-circle comeback. Two years earlier, at the 2023 World Championships, Sullivan fractured her kneecap mid-race and limped home in 58th place. Her return to the top five in Tokyo symbolized perseverance and renewed confidence.
![Image 251](https://mybestruns.com/street/67d069035f3d5a3494bdf6dd513ee472e1149137b23d4b6e01a7a6561ce6d780.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The Balance of Two Worlds
While most professional runners build their lives around training, Sullivan still starts her mornings in the classroom. She teaches sixth-grade advanced math and science, grading papers and designing lessons between workouts.
“Running gives me perspective,” she has said in interviews. “It keeps me grounded. Teaching reminds me there’s more to life than splits and finish times.”

### [Susanna Sullivan — The Teacher Who Runs Among the World’s Best Set to run NYC Sunday](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=13968)
Her ability to balance two demanding worlds has made her an inspiration for runners who juggle careers, families, and athletic dreams.
On to New York
Next up, Sullivan is set to compete in the 2025 TCS New York City Marathon on Sunday, November 2. She enters as one of the leading Americans to watch in a stacked international field that includes Olympians and major-marathon champions.
After her stellar run in Tokyo, many eyes will be on how she handles the challenging hills and bridges of New York — a course that rewards experience and toughness rather than speed alone. Few embody those traits better than Sullivan.
Lessons from Her Journey
• Patience and perseverance— her steady rise from 2:35 to 2:21 shows the value of long-term commitment.
• Balance— proof that excellence isn’t limited to full-time athletes.
• Resilience— recovering from injuries and setbacks only to climb higher.
• Leadership— both in the classroom and in leading a world championship field
Career Highlights
• Marathon PR:2:21:56 – Chicago (2024)
• World Championships Tokyo (2025):4th Place, 2:28:17
• London Marathon (2023):10th Place, 2:24:27 (top American)
• Cherry Blossom 10-Mile (2022):Champion, 52:32
• Half Marathon PR:1:08:59 – January 2025
A Runner to Watch
Susanna Sullivan’s story reminds us that greatness doesn’t always come from perfect conditions or full-time focus. Sometimes it comes from a quiet classroom in Virginia, where a teacher grades homework — and then goes out to train like one of the best marathoners in the world.
Her journey is far from over, and as she lines up in New York, she represents not just American distance running but every runner chasing balance, progress, and purpose — one mile at a time.

### [At 91, Koichi Kitabatake Will Be the Oldest Runner in the 2025 New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=13965)
When Koichi Kitabatake steps onto the starting line of the 2025 TCS New York City Marathon on November 2, he will make history as the oldest competitor in the field — at 91 years old.
The runner from Kanagawa, Japan, didn’t start running until long after most people retire. In fact, he only took up the sport at age 74, after finishing a long career as a telecommunications specialist. Four years later, at 78, he ran his first marathon — and he hasn’t stopped since.
![Image 254](https://mybestruns.com/street/d607ca06fe1d2de35df8b6bd48ea213e63d82e9444e18d9683c6c2262b77a650.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
This year’s race will mark his 34th marathon, including two previous finishes in New York City. Kitabatake has flown across the world to participate in marathons on nearly every continent, proving that passion and discipline know no age limits.
Running Into His 90s
![Image 255](https://mybestruns.com/street/3ab25a75abc9eaf4b26f6e9578ceb610fb81fb7584b30cb8eaa1b933cf6d6266.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
As he prepares for the 26.2-mile journey through all five boroughs of New York City, Kitabatake shared with the Daily Mail some of his daily habits that keep him strong — both physically and mentally — well into his 90s.

### [At 91, Koichi Kitabatake Will Be the Oldest Runner in the 2025 New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=13965)
“I do a short workout and stretching every morning for about half an hour,” he said. “Then I run four to six miles twice a week, depending on how I feel.”
It’s a simple but powerful routine — one that underscores his belief in consistency over intensity.
Beyond the physical benefits, Kitabatake says running has transformed his outlook on life.
“Running has changed how I see things,” he told the Daily Mail. “It helps me stay positive and keeps my mind healthy.”
A Source of Inspiration
Kitabatake’s story has inspired countless others, especially those who feel it’s “too late” to start something new. His steady approach, humility, and unwavering commitment to movement highlight the broader spirit of the marathon itself — endurance, courage, and the celebration of life at every age.
As thousands line up in Staten Island to begin the 2025 TCS New York City Marathon, Kitabatake will stand among them — proof that age is just a number, and that the human spirit, when fueled by purpose, can keep running forever.

### [2027 Could Bring Unprecedented Heat, Raising New Concerns for Marathon Runners Worldwide](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15441)
The global running community could face a formidable challenge in [2027](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2027), as forecasts of a potentially powerful El Niño raise concerns about rising temperatures and the impact of extreme heat on marathon performances.
![Image 2](https://mybestruns.com/street/21525fef106f0f5e518948f3b7ac7c7a59c2dc7f609cbf843c1a3df2621fa9d4.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
With long-distance runners increasingly chasing personal bests on the world's biggest stages, the prospect of another exceptionally warm year has placed race-day weather firmly in the spotlight. For marathoners, even a modest rise in temperature can make the difference between a record-breaking performance and a difficult battle to reach the finish line.
![Image 3](https://mybestruns.com/street/c649899eb4ea226a094d35c54188897ee0ecd5f22a51cbcb024dd442b8785c9e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
At the centre of the concern is the [Pacific Ocean](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Pacific+Ocean), where developing El Niño conditions could influence global temperatures. Forecasts have raised the possibility of an unusually strong event, although its eventual intensity and the precise effects on temperatures around the world remain uncertain.
El Niño is a natural climate phenomenon characterised by warmer-than-average sea surface temperatures across parts of the central and eastern equatorial Pacific. It can alter weather patterns across different regions, while its warming influence can contribute to higher global temperatures. The full impact depends on the strength of the event and how it interacts with other climate factors.

![Image 4](https://mybestruns.com/street/d0a9667bdea6ce04007f6323709b90066c76c7bf750a06efd1f2fbddbd1d21b0.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The timing is particularly important. Global temperatures have often responded strongly in the year following a major El Niño, meaning 2027 could face an increased risk of challenging heat. However, whether it ultimately surpasses the existing global temperature record will depend on evolving ocean conditions, atmospheric patterns and human-caused climate change.
![Image 5](https://mybestruns.com/street/46b631cd0e12734e6118d1811afa82002a59f6f038f8de1a680ce25c9ce4a1e2.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
For marathon runners, the implications are significant. Scientific research has repeatedly shown that warmer conditions can reduce endurance performance, increase physiological strain and make it more difficult to maintain a planned race pace over 42.195 kilometres.
An analysis of seven North American marathons illustrates how substantially conditions can influence elite performances. Researchers found that leading male runners finished approximately 1.7 per cent slower relative to course records under the coolest conditions examined. In the warmest category, that difference increased to around 4.5 per cent.
For an athlete capable of running a marathon in 2:05:00, a slowdown of that magnitude could translate into several additional minutes on the clock. At the elite level, where races are frequently decided by seconds, such a difference can determine whether a runner achieves a personal best, secures a podium finish or misses a major performance target.
The consequences can be even more noticeable among recreational athletes, who often spend considerably longer exposed to the conditions.

### [2027 Could Bring Unprecedented Heat, Raising New Concerns for Marathon Runners Worldwide](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15441)
A separate analysis by researchers at the University of Chicago, examining approximately 4.7 million marathon finishing times, highlighted the substantial effect of temperature on runners across different ability levels. The findings suggested that the typical participant could lose roughly 19 minutes when racing in temperatures in the 70s Fahrenheit, compared with conditions in the 40s. In the 80s Fahrenheit, the estimated time penalty rose to approximately 33 minutes.
These figures underline why marathon preparation involves much more than mileage, speed sessions and strength training. Temperature, humidity, direct sunlight and the body's ability to regulate heat can all influence how effectively a runner sustains an effort over the full distance.
Many marathon performances are achieved in cool conditions, with temperatures of approximately 4°C to 10°C often considered favourable for endurance running. As temperatures climb beyond that range, the body must devote more resources to cooling itself, potentially increasing cardiovascular strain and making a previously comfortable pace harder to maintain.
However, there is no universal temperature at which every marathon runner begins to slow down. Individual fitness, acclimatisation, humidity, wind, course exposure and race strategy all influence performance. A cool, overcast morning can produce very different outcomes from a sunny, humid day, even when the thermometer shows similar readings.

For [Brandon Throop](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Brandon+Throop), running a marathon in a hospital gown is about far more than chasing a place in the [Guinness World Records](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Guinness+World+Records). It is a deeply personal tribute to the medical team that helped save his life, a celebration of survival, and an opportunity to give back to the institution that stood beside him during one of the darkest chapters of his life.
![Image 8](https://mybestruns.com/street/f29108f8a11d11c189a98e7ad107e25370003868a0c2a06a0f60240f82ca748e.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
In 2022, Throop was 35 years old, a father of two, and facing a life-changing diagnosis of non-Hodgkin lymphoma. His journey soon led him to [Princess Margaret Cancer Centre](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Princess+Margaret+Cancer+Centre) in Toronto, Canada, where he underwent chemotherapy and began a difficult battle against the disease.
![Image 9](https://mybestruns.com/street/544aaad28b469831ffc670d6b1f0afed09ba7cece4e33f54484abd893edf14de.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The treatment that helped him fight cancer also left him physically weakened. For someone who had spent much of his life running, even the simplest movements became unexpectedly challenging. After completing treatment, climbing a single flight of stairs could leave him coughing and struggling to catch his breath.

However, rather than allowing the experience to define the limits of his future, Throop began rebuilding his strength one small step at a time. He started by running once around his neighbourhood block before gradually increasing the distance as his body recovered. What began as a modest attempt to regain his fitness eventually developed into an extraordinary mission with a purpose extending far beyond the finish line.
![Image 10](https://mybestruns.com/street/609ed787d02e0efaf2f9b8e1f2b60b1718ea68e0b9bbf56ffa21a91b509d4949.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Now, more than three years after becoming cancer-free, Throop is preparing to return to the [TCS Toronto Waterfront Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=TCS+Toronto+Waterfront+Marathon) on Sunday, October 18, 2026, for another attempt at the Guinness World Record for the fastest marathon completed while wearing a hospital gown.
This will be his third attempt to claim the record, following two determined performances in previous editions of the Toronto race. In 2023, he completed the marathon in 2:55:59 before returning in 2024 to improve his time to 2:55:01. Despite his progress, the record remained just out of reach.
The current benchmark stands at 2:50:12, established by Evan Ubene at the same Toronto Waterfront Marathon in 2022. To make history this time, Throop will need to improve significantly on his previous performances and take more than five minutes off his best hospital-gown marathon.
Yet the significance of Sunday's race cannot be measured by finishing time alone.

Throop's larger objective is to raise funds for the Princess Margaret Cancer Foundation, supporting the cancer research and care that played such an important role in his own recovery. He has already raised more than $137,000 toward his $150,000 fundraising target, bringing him within reach of a goal that could help support further advances in cancer treatment.
Every kilometre he covers in the distinctive hospital gown carries a message of gratitude to the people who cared for him and hope for patients whose journeys are only beginning. His challenge transforms a gruelling 42.195-kilometre race into a public expression of appreciation for the doctors, nurses, researchers and other healthcare professionals working to improve the lives of people affected by cancer.
The timing of this year's marathon makes the occasion even more meaningful. The race falls just days from the anniversary of his first chemotherapy session in 2022, bringing him back to a period that profoundly changed his life. Returning to the streets of Toronto now, healthy enough to pursue another marathon, offers a powerful reminder of how far he has travelled since those difficult days.
For Throop, choosing Toronto has never been simply about finding the fastest course on which to break a record. Although other marathons might offer different racing conditions, the Toronto Waterfront Marathon holds a significance that no alternative venue could easily replace. The course takes him past Princess Margaret Cancer Centre, the institution where he received treatment, while family members and friends who supported him throughout his illness are there to witness his journey.
It is a route that connects his past to his present: the hospital where he fought for his health, the streets where he now tests his endurance, and the people who helped him keep moving forward when the road ahead was uncertain.
His hospital gown is therefore much more than an unusual racing outfit. It is a symbol of the vulnerability he experienced as a patient, the strength he rediscovered through running, and his determination to turn a deeply personal struggle into something that benefits others.

For Brandon Throop, the finish line represents more than a sporting ambition. It is an opportunity to honour the people who helped him survive, support the research that may give other families more time together, and show what can be possible after a life-altering diagnosis.
The record is still waiting. But with more than $137,000 already raised toward his fundraising goal, Throop has another reason to consider his mission a success before the starting gun even sounds.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
Long before he conquered world cross-country championships, dominated the half-marathon distance and lifted the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) trophy, [Geoffrey Kamworor](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geoffrey+Kamworor) was a young Kenyan student with an ambitious dream that had little to do with running: becoming a [lawyer](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=lawyer).
![Image 14](https://mybestruns.com/street/de57be259ad5f2aa804935a23c35ae7bb6b49b6ec295d0ed68325e1b13b71303.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Growing up in Keiyo South, Kamworor developed the discipline that would later define his extraordinary athletic career. His daily routine involved running approximately five kilometres to school and another five kilometres back home. What might have seemed like an ordinary journey for a schoolboy was quietly laying the foundation for a future in international distance running.
![Image 15](https://mybestruns.com/street/808283ce83ea90fb69283ae3a63fb6cc12becf4782bc79b9156f109324db53df.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
He attended Chepsamo Primary School before proceeding to Lelboinet Secondary School, where he combined his education with a growing passion for athletics. At the time, his ambitions extended beyond the track and roads. He wanted to pursue a career in law, and that dream eventually brought him an opportunity to study at a college in the United States.
headings: ### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)

chunks.text:
### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
However, the young Kenyan faced a defining decision: follow the academic path he had envisioned or commit himself fully to the sport that was beginning to reveal his remarkable potential. Kamworor chose athletics, a decision that would ultimately place his name among the most accomplished distance runners of his generation.
![Image 16](https://mybestruns.com/street/a94c34052d38330fd293c08402206cd4d7a39c33946639bdb76ca84e0ab123e7.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
His transformation from a promising schoolboy into an international contender began gathering momentum in 2010, when he joined the GSC training camp in Kaptagat. His development accelerated rapidly, and within a short period, an opportunity to compete in Finland exposed him to a higher level of international competition.
Still only 17, he reportedly competed nine times during that trip, demonstrating an impressive ability to adapt to the demands of competitive racing. Breaking the eight-minute barrier for 3,000 metres was an early indication of the talent that would eventually carry him to the highest levels of distance running.
![Image 17](https://mybestruns.com/street/84282c8c1c650ab6ffe7062ef243eacc858a034f27f3ff8005541232e23d4bd3.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
His breakthrough on the international stage followed in March 2011, when he captured the junior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Punta Umbría, Spain. That victory announced the arrival of a young athlete whose future would extend far beyond the junior ranks.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
Kamworor was not simply a runner with speed. He possessed the endurance, tactical intelligence and competitive determination required to succeed across different distances and racing surfaces. As his career developed, those qualities became the hallmarks of an athlete capable of challenging the world's best.
Cross country became one of the foundations of Kamworor's international success. In 2015, he won the senior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Guiyang, China, confirming his status as one of the leading distance runners in the world. Two years later, he returned to the top of the podium in Kampala, Uganda, defending his senior world cross-country crown in front of a home crowd. Winning consecutive senior world titles placed him in an elite category and demonstrated his remarkable command of the demanding discipline.
On the roads, however, Kamworor established an equally impressive legacy. He won the World Half Marathon Championships in Copenhagen in 2014, Cardiff in 2016 and Valencia in 2018, becoming a three-time champion at the distance. His achievements reflected a rare combination of strength, speed and race management, enabling him to prevail against formidable international opposition.
The half marathon became one of his signature events, but Kamworor's ambitions were never confined to a single discipline. He continued to demonstrate his versatility on the track, winning silver in the men's 10,000 metres at the 2015 World Athletics Championships in Beijing, China. From the grass of cross-country courses to the roads of major international races and the track of a global championship, he repeatedly demonstrated that his talent could flourish wherever the competition took him.
Among Kamworor's most memorable achievements are his victories at the New York City Marathon in 2017 and 2019. Winning one of the world's most celebrated marathons requires exceptional endurance, but winning it twice demands much more: tactical patience, resilience and the ability to navigate a demanding course against a deep international field.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
Kamworor demonstrated those qualities in both victories, establishing a special connection with the New York race and adding the marathon to an already remarkable collection of honours. His success in the American city also illustrated his ability to move successfully between distances. An athlete celebrated for his cross-country and half-marathon dominance had shown that he could also conquer the 42.195-kilometre marathon, one of the most demanding challenges in road racing.
Now, as he sets his sights on another New York campaign, the Kenyan star has an opportunity to strengthen his legacy further. A third men's open-division victory would place him among a very select group of athletes to have won the prestigious race three times. Such a milestone would be more than another addition to his trophy cabinet; it would reinforce the story of a runner whose competitive range has extended across nearly every major discipline in distance running.
Behind Kamworor's achievements lies a training environment built around discipline, consistency and high-level competition. Working under the guidance of renowned coach Patrick Sang, he has trained alongside some of Kenya's most celebrated athletes, including marathon great Eliud Kipchoge and middle- and long-distance superstar Faith Kipyegon.
Sharing a training environment with athletes of such calibre provides a demanding daily standard. Yet Kamworor has built his own identity through a career defined by major championship victories and sustained success across different racing distances. His journey has also included difficult periods and setbacks, reminding the running world that even the most accomplished champions must continually work to return to their best. His longevity at the elite level reflects the importance of patience, dedication and the willingness to keep pursuing new goals.
For aspiring athletes in Kenya, his story offers an important lesson: extraordinary achievements are often built through ordinary routines repeated consistently over many years. Those five-kilometre journeys to school and back were not glamorous. They did not come with cheering crowds, television cameras or medals. Yet they formed part of the foundation of a career that would eventually take him to the world's biggest running stages.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
Kamworor's story is ultimately about a choice that changed the direction of his life. The young student who once imagined himself arguing cases in a courtroom instead built his reputation by answering the toughest questions on the running track and roads. His achievements speak for themselves: world cross-country titles, three world half-marathon crowns, a global 10,000-metre silver medal and two New York City Marathon victories.
He may never have pursued the legal career he once envisioned, but his athletic record tells a compelling story of ambition, sacrifice and extraordinary accomplishment. His pursuit of another New York triumph offers a fresh chapter in a career that has already crossed the boundaries between cross country, track and road racing.
For Geoffrey Kamworor, the courtroom was a dream he left behind. The world of distance running became the stage on which he built his name. And while the law lost a prospective lawyer, athletics gained a champion whose achievements have helped define an era of Kenyan distance running.

### [Geofry Kipchumba Returns To Defend Amsterdam Crown As World-Class Men’s And Women’s Fields Target History](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15438)
The [TCS Amsterdam Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=TCS+Amsterdam+Marathon) is set for an exciting showdown on Sunday, 18 October, with an outstanding international field preparing to challenge the course records, pursue personal bests and compete for victory on one of Europe’s most prestigious marathon stages.
![Image 21](https://mybestruns.com/street/eb8d3816a3274868be8a924326614ca1afe06b6de1ebe40127097ccfa48aa227.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The 2026 edition promises compelling competition in both the men’s and women’s races. Kenya and Ethiopia will feature prominently among the leading contenders, with experienced champions, emerging talents and athletes making their marathon debuts all bringing ambitious targets to Amsterdam.
In the men’s race, defending champion [Geofry Toroitich Kipchumba](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geofry+Toroitich+Kipchumba) returns with the course record firmly in his sights after producing a remarkable performance last year.
![Image 22](https://mybestruns.com/street/90ce64981bbdcc2ceba4696ee36703519b485ead3ee05d4dded9478724ace50d.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Kipchumba stormed to victory in 2:03:30 at the 50th edition of the race, establishing a new Amsterdam course record and the fastest marathon time ever recorded on Dutch soil. His return offers an opportunity to improve on that achievement, although a formidable field stands between him and another memorable victory.
headings: ### [Geofry Kipchumba Returns To Defend Amsterdam Crown As World-Class Men’s And Women’s Fields Target History](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15438)

chunks.text:
### [Geofry Kipchumba Returns To Defend Amsterdam Crown As World-Class Men’s And Women’s Fields Target History](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15438)
The Kenyan is not the only athlete arriving with the potential to challenge the record. Ethiopia’s Haymanot Alew has a marathon personal best of 2:03:31, recorded in Berlin, leaving him just one second outside the existing course record. The 2026 Egmond Half Marathon winner will be among the athletes hoping to turn that narrow gap into history on Amsterdam’s streets.
Another major contender is Ethiopia’s Tsegaye Getachew, a two-time Amsterdam champion who won the race in 2022 and 2024 before finishing second in 2025 with a personal best of 2:04:18. His familiarity with the course and previous success make him an important presence in a race expected to feature an intense battle among the leading men.
The depth of the field is underlined by the presence of 10 athletes who have recorded marathon times below 2:05, according to the race organisers. With several runners capable of sustaining an exceptional pace, the contest could develop into a demanding tactical battle in which positioning, endurance and the ability to respond to late-race attacks will prove decisive.
Kenya’s Isaia Kipkoech Lasoi is another athlete attracting attention ahead of the race, although his challenge comes with a different question. The half-marathon specialist will make his marathon debut after establishing an impressive personal best of 58:10 over 21.0975 kilometres.
His speed over the half-marathon distance provides an intriguing indication of his potential, but the full marathon presents an entirely different test. How effectively he manages his energy beyond the halfway point and adapts to the demands of 42.195 kilometres will be among the most interesting aspects of his first appearance at the distance.

While the men prepare to attack the 2:03:30 course record, the women’s race has its own compelling storyline, with four Ethiopian athletes arriving with personal bests faster than 2:20.
[Aynalem Desta](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Aynalem+Desta), the defending champion, returns after winning last year’s 50th edition in a personal best of 2:17:37. Her familiarity with the course and experience of winning in Amsterdam place her among the leading contenders as she seeks to defend her title.
![Image 24](https://mybestruns.com/street/48cba3cfce51cbef58f1e604d0b44c16a605e3b16d61c795923d13f218ddd722.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
However, Desta faces a formidable challenge from compatriot Meseret Belete Tola, the 2023 Amsterdam champion, whose personal best stands at 2:18:21. Belete’s previous success in the Dutch capital adds another layer of intrigue to a race featuring multiple athletes with the credentials to contend for victory.

### [Geofry Kipchumba Returns To Defend Amsterdam Crown As World-Class Men’s And Women’s Fields Target History](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15438)
Ethiopia’s Mestawut Fikir Truneh also brings considerable experience and a strong personal best of 2:18:48, recorded when she finished second at the 2024 Berlin Marathon. Meanwhile, compatriot Buze Diriba arrives with a best of 2:19:34, ensuring that the Ethiopian challenge extends well beyond the two former Amsterdam champions.
The international depth continues with Bahrain’s Desi Jisa Mokonin, Ethiopia’s Yeshi Kalayu Chekole and Eritrea’s Nazret Weldu Gebrehiwet, all of whom have recorded performances close to the two-hour-and-20-minute barrier.
Sweden’s Abeba Aregawi, a former world champion over 1,500 metres, adds another fascinating dimension to the contest. Aregawi set a Swedish marathon record of 2:23:12 on her debut earlier this year and will now face another major test as she continues her transition from track running to the marathon.
With the women’s course record standing at 2:16:52, the question is whether the leading contenders can produce the performance required to challenge it. Desta’s personal best of 2:17:37 already places her within striking distance, while Belete, Fikir and Diriba will be looking to turn their own ambitions into competitive results.
![Image 25](https://mybestruns.com/street/ef7576ded676610880fda0f1bccdc6e5d4019ee38128969bb5ea78fa45416151.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Beyond the elite fields, the athletes’ comments at the pre-race press conference have provided a glimpse into the different approaches they will bring to Sunday’s contest.
Kenya’s Nicholas Kipkorir expressed confidence in his return to Amsterdam, describing the city as a second home and believing that his familiarity with the environment could help him deliver his best performance.

### [Geofry Kipchumba Returns To Defend Amsterdam Crown As World-Class Men’s And Women’s Fields Target History](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15438)
“I love Amsterdam. It feels like my second home, and I know that will help me run my best time,” Kipkorir said.
His compatriot Geofry Kipchumba has set his sights on achieving another personal best while also fighting for victory. His ambition reflects the competitive spirit surrounding the men’s race, where the defending champion and several challengers are expected to target fast times.
“I’m going for another personal best and the win,” Kipchumba said.
Ethiopia’s Aynalem Desta is equally determined to build on her previous success in Amsterdam. Having won last year’s race in a personal best of 2:17:37, she will be aiming to deliver another strong performance against a deep women’s field.
“I love the TCS Amsterdam Marathon. I’m happy with the race I ran here last year, and I want to perform even better this year,” Desta explained.
Fellow Ethiopian Mestawut Fikir Truneh emphasised the importance of patience and perseverance, qualities that often determine the outcome of a marathon when fatigue begins to affect even the strongest runners.
“A marathon requires patience. You must not give up hope until the very last moment. Keep going and never give up,” Fikir said.
Among the Dutch athletes, Mikky Keetels has established a clear objective: breaking the two-hour-and-30-minute barrier, with hopes of going even faster if conditions allow.
“I really want to run under 2:30, and secretly maybe even a little faster,” Keetels revealed.
Fellow Dutch runner Noah Schutte is concentrating on the closing stages of the race, when maintaining pace and fighting through fatigue can make the difference between achieving a target and falling short.
“I especially want to give everything in the final kilometres and keep fighting,” Schutte said.
For Khalid Choukoud, the race presents an opportunity to improve his personal best while continuing to demonstrate his competitiveness at the age of 40. Breaking 2:10 would represent a particularly significant achievement for the experienced Dutch marathoner.

### [Geofry Kipchumba Returns To Defend Amsterdam Crown As World-Class Men’s And Women’s Fields Target History](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15438)
“It would be great to improve my personal best. But if I run under 2:10 at the age of 40, that would be a great achievement too,” Choukoud said.
All these ambitions will converge on Sunday, when the athletes take on the streets of Amsterdam before finishing inside the iconic Olympic Stadium.
The defending champions will be under pressure to retain their titles, record holders will be challenged by determined rivals, and debutants will have the opportunity to discover what they can achieve over the full marathon distance.
For Kipchumba, the immediate target is to defend his crown and potentially lower the 2:03:30 course record. For Alew, it is an opportunity to bridge the one-second gap separating his personal best from the mark. Getachew will be seeking another victory, while Lasoi faces the challenge of translating his exceptional half-marathon speed into marathon success.
In the women’s race, Desta will attempt to defend her title against a field featuring former champions, major-marathon performers and several athletes capable of producing personal bests. With the 2:16:52 course record in sight, the leading women could also make a serious attempt to rewrite the record books.
One start line will unite these athletes, but their objectives are different. Some are pursuing victory, others are targeting personal records, and a select few have their sights set on history.
When the gun fires on 18 October, the preparation will be over and the real test will begin. Amsterdam is ready for a day of world-class marathon racing, with the possibility of new records adding even greater anticipation to an already compelling contest.

### [From $1 To $358: How The New York City Marathon Became A Global Running Phenomenon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15437)
What began as a modest race through Central Park, with a handful of determined runners and a budget of just $1,000, has evolved into one of the most prestigious and sought-after marathons in the world. More than five decades later, the [New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=New+York+City+Marathon) tells a remarkable story of how distance running has grown from a grassroots sporting event into a global spectacle.
![Image 29](https://mybestruns.com/street/bacec4114b3d54670c15a184e950b0e7ddb43de9849a87f97fe568b1a68fdecf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
When the inaugural New York City Marathon took place in 1970, the entry fee was just $1. Organised by the New York Road Runners, the race was held entirely within Central Park, far removed from the enormous crowds, international attention and commercial scale that define the event today.
![Image 30](https://mybestruns.com/street/cb333999ed07e06d10edcf37e5452882364cbb7336ebf8347871bb079ae7bfbf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Of the 127 registered participants, only 55 completed the race. Yet, despite its modest beginnings, the event laid the foundation for a marathon that would eventually capture the imagination of runners from every corner of the world.

### [From $1 To $358: How The New York City Marathon Became A Global Running Phenomenon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15437)
The first champion was Gary Muhrcke, a New York City firefighter whose victory remains one of the most memorable stories from the race's early years. According to accounts of the inaugural edition, Muhrcke had finished a night shift before entering the competition shortly before the start. He went on to win in approximately 2:31, securing his place in the marathon's history.
The inaugural race also featured Nina Kuscsik, the only woman in the field. She started the event but withdrew after becoming ill, meaning no woman finished that first edition. Kuscsik would later become an important figure in the campaign for women's inclusion in competitive distance running.
Over the years, the New York City Marathon expanded beyond Central Park, eventually developing into the iconic five-borough journey that takes runners through Staten Island, Brooklyn, Queens, the Bronx and Manhattan. Its transformation helped turn the race into a celebration of athletic achievement, community spirit and the extraordinary diversity of New York City.
Today, the marathon attracts elite athletes chasing victories and records, recreational runners pursuing personal milestones, charity participants raising funds for important causes, and thousands of international visitors eager to experience one of running's most celebrated events.

### [Frankfurt Assembles Fastest-Ever Men’s Field as Former Champion Meskerem Assefa Returns](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15436)
The 43rd Mainova Frankfurt Marathon is set for a fast edition on October 25, with the deepest men’s field in race history and the return of 2018 women’s champion Meskerem Assefa.
For the first time, four men on the start list have personal bests under 2:05, with another four having broken 2:07. German record-holder Amanal Petros leads the field at 2:04:03, setting up a showdown featuring three of Germany’s leading marathoners.
The women’s race also promises strong competition. Five entrants have run under 2:22, making it the second-deepest women’s field in Frankfurt history by that measure, behind only the 2025 edition, which featured six.
“Overall this is surely the fastest elite field we have ever assembled for the Mainova Frankfurt Marathon. I am very pleased that the German men are playing a major role and I expect a thrilling top-class race,” said Jo Schindler, who is in his 25th year as race director.
German Stars Lead the Men’s Challenge
European champion Petros tops the entry list, but the competition is close. Ethiopia’s Andualem Belay brings a personal best of 2:04:44, followed by Germany’s Samuel Fitwi at 2:04:45 and Richard Ringer at 2:04:47.
With just 44 seconds separating the personal bests of the four fastest entrants, the race offers the prospect of a competitive battle at the front.
Kenya’s Benard Biwott, who has run 2:05:25, leads the next group of contenders. Israel’s Haimro Alame and Ethiopians Antenayehu Dagnachew and Jiregna Geleta round out the eight men with personal bests under 2:07.
Assefa Returns to Face Yimer and Saina
Meskerem Assefa’s return adds a former champion to an already strong women’s field. Her participation had been uncertain because of visa requirements, but organizers have now secured the visa needed for her trip to Germany.

The 25-year-old was approaching the final stretch of the race when tragedy struck, cutting short a life filled with ambition, talent and promise.
![Image 36](https://mybestruns.com/street/a3d0147af9a05de82fc0febbf8f334c8a41992e0374bf8d58b7fd5e658d63c22.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The Seoul Race, a major city-centre running event, brought approximately 12,000 participants onto the streets of downtown Seoul. For thousands of runners, the occasion was an opportunity to challenge themselves and celebrate their shared passion for the sport. However, the event ended in tragedy following the incident involving Ji-won, whose death has sent shockwaves through South Korea's running community.
According to reports, Ji-won collapsed shortly before 9 a.m. at the 20.6-kilometre mark along Cheonggyecheon-ro, approximately 500 metres from the finish line of the 21.1-kilometre race. She was reportedly running near the front of the women's half marathon field when she suddenly fell.

Olympic marathon champion [Sifan Hassan](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Sifan+Hassan) of [the Netherlands](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=the+Netherlands) has officially withdrawn from the [2026 TCS New York City Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=2026+TCS+New+York+City+Marathon) after illness disrupted her preparations, ending hopes of seeing the versatile distance-running star return to one of the world’s most prestigious road races this autumn.
![Image 41](https://mybestruns.com/street/ff056ddb48590d9d5770aeba39b2968d8cbf9e31921bf90d9e503fe24646ab1c.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Hassan announced her decision on social media, explaining that sickness had slowed her training and left her short of the level of preparation she had hoped to achieve ahead of the November 1 race. The withdrawal is a setback for the Dutch star, who had been looking forward to returning stronger after her previous appearance in New York.
“I was so excited to come back stronger, but a sickness slowed down my training and I’m not where I wanted to be. Sometimes, things just don’t go as planned,” Hassan wrote.
Despite her disappointment, the Olympic champion also sent her best wishes to the athletes preparing to compete in New York, demonstrating her support for the wider running community even as she steps away from the competition.
Hassan, who holds a personal best of 2:13:44, ranks fifth on the women’s all-time marathon list. Her extraordinary range across track and road running has established her as one of the most versatile athletes of her generation, capable of competing at the highest level from shorter distances to the marathon.

### [From Olympic Gold To National Icon: Letsile Tebogo’s Legacy Reaches Botswana’s Currency](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15433)
Botswana’s sprint sensation [Letsile Tebogo](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Letsile+Tebogo) has achieved something few athletes can ever imagine: seeing his sporting legacy celebrated beyond the stadium and onto the nation’s currency.
![Image 46](https://mybestruns.com/street/d3d681e99653acd0f0d64564b71017491d3e637358a5a08133a21ecdc69cc48a.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The Olympic 200m champion has been featured on Botswana’s commemorative [50-pula banknote](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=50-pula+banknote), a powerful tribute to a young athlete whose remarkable achievements have elevated his country’s profile on the global athletics stage.
Tebogo made history at the Paris 2024 Olympic Games, storming to victory in the men’s 200 metres in an astonishing 19.46 seconds to claim Botswana’s first-ever Olympic gold medal. In doing so, he also became the first African man to win Olympic gold in the 200m, marking a landmark moment for African sprinting.
![Image 47](https://mybestruns.com/street/7a42424e1dbd3d37e2c7625b920999bdc1c5b5b62729820253ac3c3fec1559ce.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

The recognition of his achievements has now extended beyond the track. His appearance on Botswana’s commemorative 50-pula banknote, issued to mark the 50th anniversary of the Bank of Botswana, places his historic Olympic victory among the milestones being celebrated in the nation’s financial and cultural history. The note also recognises members of Botswana’s men’s 4×400m relay team, who secured silver at the Paris 2024 Olympics.
For a young athlete who has risen to the summit of world sprinting, the honour carries significance beyond its monetary value. From the Olympic track to the nation’s currency, Letsile Tebogo has become a powerful symbol of Botswana’s ambition, pride and sporting progress. His remarkable 19.46-second performance in Paris will forever remain a landmark in Olympic history, while his growing legacy continues to inspire athletes and fans far beyond his homeland.
For Botswana, this is more than a tribute to a champion. It is a celebration of a historic achievement, a symbol of national pride and a reminder that one extraordinary performance can leave a lasting mark on an entire nation.

For 24-year-old [Ethan Woodhead](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Ethan+Woodhead), travelling from [Guernsey](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Guernsey) in the [United Kingdom](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=United+Kingdom) to [Chicago](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Chicago) to run a marathon was already an adventure. What he did not anticipate was that thousands of kilometres from home, a city full of strangers would make him feel as though he had brought his entire support network with him.
![Image 50](https://mybestruns.com/street/d4e0ba7d2d3f345e2182d3175fe03ef3b9bd7a93418c2b2c1aafa6e8cd3b5d86.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Woodhead travelled more than 6,400 kilometres (approximately 4,000 miles) to compete in the Chicago Marathon, expecting to tackle the demanding 42.195-kilometre distance without friends or family members lining the streets to cheer him on. However, thanks to a thoughtful initiative from his uncle, Phil Woodhead, his race turned into an extraordinary story of community spirit and the power of running to bring people together.
Knowing that his nephew would be running far from home, Phil took to Facebook with a simple request to Chicago spectators: keep an eye out for Ethan, wearing bib number 2024, and give him some encouragement along the course.

The [Kenyan Athletics Training Academy (KATA)](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Kenyan+Athletics+Training+Academy+%28KATA%29) marked a significant milestone on Wednesday, October 14, 2026, with the successful staging of the 60th edition of its Time Trial Series in Thika, Kenya. Athletes took to the course across the 10km and 5km distances, testing their fitness and racing the clock in conditions characterised by relatively high temperatures and humidity.
![Image 55](https://mybestruns.com/street/0db0272d31a0cb15c9690f225b8aa77f68693fc792c5a197e8ec57e61c1627bf.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Despite the challenging weather, the runners delivered competitive performances, with [Kelvin Ng'ang'a](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Kelvin+Ng%27ang%27a) leading the men's 10km in 30:48. Charles Wanjora finished second in 30:55, while Erick Cheruiyot completed the top three in 31:02, as the leading trio crossed the finish line within 14 seconds of one another.
![Image 56](https://mybestruns.com/street/2dd440db95a574e88af5946bbac48f2a7f24c86003a63a6b53e9040a3cb75e55.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)

Unlike major championship races, where medals and titles dominate the conversation, time trials offer a different measure of success. Athletes can assess their pacing, endurance and ability to maintain their effort across a set distance. Coaches can also use the results to evaluate training progress and make adjustments ahead of future competitions.
Wednesday's warm, humid conditions added another variable to that assessment. Weather can influence how runners feel and perform, making it important to consider the conditions when interpreting times and comparing results across different editions.
For athletes working towards personal bests and improved performances in road races, track events and longer-distance competitions, these opportunities to test fitness remain an important part of the preparation process.
Reaching its 60th edition represents a notable milestone for the KATA Time Trial Series and its continuing role in the Thika running community. By bringing athletes together for regular, timed competition, the series offers a practical environment for tracking progress, building competitive experience and maintaining focus on long-term goals.
From Nganga's leading performance in the men's 10km to Ruth Maina's victory in the women's race and the shared finishing time in the 5km, the day's results provided another snapshot of athletes at different stages of their development.
As the runners return to training, the times recorded in this edition will serve as a reference point for their next phase of preparation. For some, the priority will be improving speed; for others, it will be strengthening endurance, refining pacing or preparing for upcoming races.
At KATA, the principle remains straightforward: show up, put in the work, test your fitness and let the stopwatch tell the story.
The 60th edition is now in the books, but for the athletes who took part, the next challenge has already begun.
