“In Cardiff, it was wet and I slipped at the start,” Kamworor recalled. “Nobody tripped me. It was hard running through the crowd, but the fall made me more determined.”
That determination would be tested even further. In 2020, during the isolation of the COVID-19 pandemic, Kamworor’s career was nearly derailed when he was struck from behind by a motorcycle while training in Eldoret.
“I fractured my tibia and couldn’t run for six months,” he said. “When I started running again, my body was still out of balance and I kept getting injured. It took me over three years to be able to run properly.”
His return has been gradual but encouraging. In 2023, Kamworor stunned observers by finishing second at the London Marathon in a personal best of 2:04:23, proving his resilience on the global stage. He followed that performance with a marathon victory in Rotterdam last year, finishing just ten seconds slower than his London breakthrough.
Now 33, Kamworor brings both experience and renewed confidence back to Ras Al Khaimah.
“I think I’m training as well as ever,” he said. “I remember this flat, fast course from when I won in 2013. I’m just grateful to be back running without problems.”
Age is no barrier for distance runners at the highest level. History offers powerful examples, including Portugal’s Carlos Lopes, who won Olympic marathon gold at 37, and Romania’s Constantina Dita, who claimed Olympic marathon victory at 38. Kamworor hopes to add his own chapter to that legacy.
Strong Rivals Await on a Fast Course
Kamworor will face formidable competition. Ethiopia’s Jemal Mekonen enters with a personal best of 58:33, while Kenya’s Brian Kibor has run 58:39. Ethiopia’s Amedework Walelegn (58:40) and several rising talents add further depth to a field built for speed.

### [American Depth Meets Global Firepower in Women’s Field for 130th Boston Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14081)
Headlining the U.S. squad is the full 2024 Olympic Marathon team:Emily Sisson,Fiona O’Keeffe, and Dakotah Popehn. Sisson enters as the American record holder at 2:18:29, while O’Keeffe is coming off a strong fourth-place finish at the 2025 New York City Marathon. Popehn posted a lifetime best of 2:24:21 at Chicago last fall.
Joining them is the entire U.S. team from the World Championships Marathon in Tokyo:Susanna Sullivan,Jess McClain, and Erika Kemp. McClain was the top American at Boston last year, finishing seventh in 2:22:43, while Kemp owns a personal best of 2:22:56, the fastest marathon ever run by a U.S.-born Black woman.
Annie Frisbie, eighth in Boston last year, returns after a fifth-place finish in New York, and Keira D’Amato, the former American record holder, will make her third Boston appearance. Veteran Sara Hallalso returns after a runner-up finish at the Houston Marathon in January.
Several Americans will make their Boston debuts, including Megan Sailor,Natosha Rogers, and Amanda Vestri, underscoring the breadth of U.S. talent now entering the marathon ranks.
Internationally, the challenge remains formidable. Defending champion Sharon Lokedi returns after her course-record 2:17:22 victory last year, joined by fellow Kenyans Irine Cheptai and Vivian Cheruiyot. Ethiopia is represented by Workenesh Edesa and Bedatu Hirpa, both proven winners on the global circuit.
Experience on Boston’s unforgiving course will be key for Calli Hauger-Thackery, who enjoyed a breakout 2025 season, and Kenya’s Mary Ngugi-Cooper, a five-time Boston top-ten finisher with a personal best of 2:19:25.

### [How One Tribe in Kenya Came to Dominate Global Distance Running](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14033)
There may be no statistic in all of sports more astonishing than this one.
The Kalenjin, an ethnic group—often referred to as a tribe—in Kenya, make up about 13.4% of the country’s population, roughly 6.3 million people. On a global scale, they represent about one out of every 1,000 people worldwide.
![Image 221](https://mybestruns.com/street/31fd23f24578a76f6fc0580d9093e935c038cda98d42eefe81cdfdd0126b8ac7.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Yet this small community has produced an overwhelming share of the world’s greatest distance runners.
![Image 222](https://mybestruns.com/street/e23d62d8a509883c34d3fcc2300d64ea559616598580289fc6799ce1bc84e82a.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Their dominance has been so complete, and so sustained, that it has been described as“the greatest geographical concentration of achievement in the annals of sport.”And it is hard to argue otherwise.
From the Rift Valley to the World Stage
Most elite Kalenjin runners come from Kenya’s Rift Valley region, particularly areas such as Nandi, Elgeyo-Marakwet, Uasin Gishu, and Baringo, where elevations range from 2,000 to 2,400 meters (6,500–8,000 feet)above sea level.
Here, running is not a hobby—it is part of daily life.

### [How One Tribe in Kenya Came to Dominate Global Distance Running](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14033)
Children grow up walking and running long distances, often on dirt roads. Training at altitude is the norm, not a strategy. And success stories are local and visible, creating a powerful cycle of belief and opportunity.
Champions Across Eras
The Kalenjin impact on global athletics stretches back more than half a century.
Kipchoge Keino, one of the pioneers of Kenyan distance running, won Olympic gold in the 1500 meters at the 1968 Mexico City Games and the 3000-meter steeplechase in 1972, helping place Kenyan runners on the world map.
Since then, Kenyan athletes—many of them Kalenjin—have dominated:
• The 3000-meter steeplechase, winning Olympic gold in nearly every Games since 1968
• The 5,000 meters and 10,000 meters at World Championships
• The marathon, particularly at the World Marathon Majors
Masters of the Marathon
Perhaps nowhere is this dominance more visible than in the marathon.
Kalenjin runners have repeatedly won and controlled races such as:
• Berlin Marathon
• London Marathon
• Chicago Marathon
• Boston Marathon
• New York City Marathon
These victories are not isolated moments—they are part of a long, uninterrupted pattern.
At the center of it all stands Eliud Kipchoge, widely regarded as the greatest marathon runner in history. A member of the Kalenjin community, Kipchoge has:
• Won two Olympic marathon gold medals(2016, 2021)
• Set a world record of 2:01:09 at the Berlin Marathon
• Become the first human to run 26.2 miles in under two hours
He is not an exception. He is the most refined expression of a system that has been producing champions for generations.
Why This One Tribe?
No single explanation tells the whole story, but several factors come together in the Rift Valley:
• Geography:High altitude, rolling terrain, and ideal training conditions
• Physiology:Exceptional running economy and efficient biomechanics
• Culture:Running as a respected path to success and opportunity

### [20-Year-Old Becomes Youngest Ever to Earn the Seven Star Medal](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=14001)
A 20-year-old British runner has officially become the youngest person in history to complete all seven World Marathon Majors and earn the coveted Seven Star Medal, Abbott World Marathon Majors announced.
Lucy Scott, from Bishop’s Stortford in Hertfordshire, completed the seven marathons over an 18-month stretch: Tokyo, Boston, London, Berlin, Chicago, New York City, and Sydney. She secured the honor on November 2 when she crossed the finish line at the New York City Marathon, making her the “youngest Seven Star athlete” to date.
![Image 225](https://mybestruns.com/street/8efa56c4ab066e6aa7891ab01b1d469b175cc36baf13e2406b0f67f99ac6b649.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Scott, a history student at the University of Nottingham, only began running in 2024. “It’s the best thing I’ve ever done,” she said.
![Image 226](https://mybestruns.com/street/d7deeb6474e70c5c49f8d0b3611d34c5f90fe7529c03f5da3d2de77710f2c9f6.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Introduced in 2016, the Six Star Medal originally honored runners who completed the six established majors. The series expanded in November 2024 with the addition of the Sydney Marathon, creating the Seven Star Medal Scott has now earned.

Among Kamworor's most memorable achievements are his victories at the New York City Marathon in 2017 and 2019. Kamworor's story is ultimately about a choice that changed the direction of his life. The young student who once imagined himself arguing cases in a courtroom instead built his reputation by answering the toughest questions on the running track and roads. His achievements speak for themselves: world cross-country titles, three world half-marathon crowns, a global 10,000-metre silver medal and two New York City Marathon victories.
He may never have pursued the legal career he once envisioned, but his athletic record tells a compelling story of ambition, sacrifice and extraordinary accomplishment. His pursuit of another New York triumph offers a fresh chapter in a career that has already crossed the boundaries between cross country, track and road racing.
For Geoffrey Kamworor, the courtroom was a dream he left behind. The world of distance running became the stage on which he built his name. And while the law lost a prospective lawyer, athletics gained a champion whose achievements have helped define an era of Kenyan distance running.

### [Geofry Kipchumba Returns To Defend Amsterdam Crown As World-Class Men’s And Women’s Fields Target History](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15438)
The [TCS Amsterdam Marathon](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=TCS+Amsterdam+Marathon) is set for an exciting showdown on Sunday, 18 October, with an outstanding international field preparing to challenge the course records, pursue personal bests and compete for victory on one of Europe’s most prestigious marathon stages.
![Image 21](https://mybestruns.com/street/eb8d3816a3274868be8a924326614ca1afe06b6de1ebe40127097ccfa48aa227.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
The 2026 edition promises compelling competition in both the men’s and women’s races. Kenya and Ethiopia will feature prominently among the leading contenders, with experienced champions, emerging talents and athletes making their marathon debuts all bringing ambitious targets to Amsterdam.
In the men’s race, defending champion [Geofry Toroitich Kipchumba](https://mybestruns.com/running-news.php?tag=Geofry+Toroitich+Kipchumba) returns with the course record firmly in his sights after producing a remarkable performance last year.
![Image 22](https://mybestruns.com/street/90ce64981bbdcc2ceba4696ee36703519b485ead3ee05d4dded9478724ace50d.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
Kipchumba stormed to victory in 2:03:30 at the 50th edition of the race, establishing a new Amsterdam course record and the fastest marathon time ever recorded on Dutch soil. His return offers an opportunity to improve on that achievement, although a formidable field stands between him and another memorable victory.

### [Geofry Kipchumba Returns To Defend Amsterdam Crown As World-Class Men’s And Women’s Fields Target History](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15438)
The Kenyan is not the only athlete arriving with the potential to challenge the record. Ethiopia’s Haymanot Alew has a marathon personal best of 2:03:31, recorded in Berlin, leaving him just one second outside the existing course record. The 2026 Egmond Half Marathon winner will be among the athletes hoping to turn that narrow gap into history on Amsterdam’s streets.
Another major contender is Ethiopia’s Tsegaye Getachew, a two-time Amsterdam champion who won the race in 2022 and 2024 before finishing second in 2025 with a personal best of 2:04:18. His familiarity with the course and previous success make him an important presence in a race expected to feature an intense battle among the leading men.
The depth of the field is underlined by the presence of 10 athletes who have recorded marathon times below 2:05, according to the race organisers. With several runners capable of sustaining an exceptional pace, the contest could develop into a demanding tactical battle in which positioning, endurance and the ability to respond to late-race attacks will prove decisive.
Kenya’s Isaia Kipkoech Lasoi is another athlete attracting attention ahead of the race, although his challenge comes with a different question. The half-marathon specialist will make his marathon debut after establishing an impressive personal best of 58:10 over 21.0975 kilometres.
His speed over the half-marathon distance provides an intriguing indication of his potential, but the full marathon presents an entirely different test. How effectively he manages his energy beyond the halfway point and adapts to the demands of 42.195 kilometres will be among the most interesting aspects of his first appearance at the distance.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
However, the young Kenyan faced a defining decision: follow the academic path he had envisioned or commit himself fully to the sport that was beginning to reveal his remarkable potential. Kamworor chose athletics, a decision that would ultimately place his name among the most accomplished distance runners of his generation.
![Image 16](https://mybestruns.com/street/a94c34052d38330fd293c08402206cd4d7a39c33946639bdb76ca84e0ab123e7.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
His transformation from a promising schoolboy into an international contender began gathering momentum in 2010, when he joined the GSC training camp in Kaptagat. His development accelerated rapidly, and within a short period, an opportunity to compete in Finland exposed him to a higher level of international competition.
Still only 17, he reportedly competed nine times during that trip, demonstrating an impressive ability to adapt to the demands of competitive racing. Breaking the eight-minute barrier for 3,000 metres was an early indication of the talent that would eventually carry him to the highest levels of distance running.
![Image 17](https://mybestruns.com/street/84282c8c1c650ab6ffe7062ef243eacc858a034f27f3ff8005541232e23d4bd3.jpg?i=1792160905&t=1792160905)
His breakthrough on the international stage followed in March 2011, when he captured the junior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Punta Umbría, Spain. That victory announced the arrival of a young athlete whose future would extend far beyond the junior ranks.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
Kamworor was not simply a runner with speed. He possessed the endurance, tactical intelligence and competitive determination required to succeed across different distances and racing surfaces. As his career developed, those qualities became the hallmarks of an athlete capable of challenging the world's best.
Cross country became one of the foundations of Kamworor's international success. In 2015, he won the senior men's title at the World Cross Country Championships in Guiyang, China, confirming his status as one of the leading distance runners in the world. Two years later, he returned to the top of the podium in Kampala, Uganda, defending his senior world cross-country crown in front of a home crowd. Winning consecutive senior world titles placed him in an elite category and demonstrated his remarkable command of the demanding discipline.
On the roads, however, Kamworor established an equally impressive legacy. He won the World Half Marathon Championships in Copenhagen in 2014, Cardiff in 2016 and Valencia in 2018, becoming a three-time champion at the distance. His achievements reflected a rare combination of strength, speed and race management, enabling him to prevail against formidable international opposition.
The half marathon became one of his signature events, but Kamworor's ambitions were never confined to a single discipline. He continued to demonstrate his versatility on the track, winning silver in the men's 10,000 metres at the 2015 World Athletics Championships in Beijing, China. From the grass of cross-country courses to the roads of major international races and the track of a global championship, he repeatedly demonstrated that his talent could flourish wherever the competition took him.
Among Kamworor's most memorable achievements are his victories at the New York City Marathon in 2017 and 2019. Winning one of the world's most celebrated marathons requires exceptional endurance, but winning it twice demands much more: tactical patience, resilience and the ability to navigate a demanding course against a deep international field.

### [Geoffrey Kamworor: The Lawyer He Never Became, The Distance Running Legend He Was Born To Be](https://mybestruns.com/rndlnk.php?dx=15439)
Kamworor demonstrated those qualities in both victories, establishing a special connection with the New York race and adding the marathon to an already remarkable collection of honours. His success in the American city also illustrated his ability to move successfully between distances. An athlete celebrated for his cross-country and half-marathon dominance had shown that he could also conquer the 42.195-kilometre marathon, one of the most demanding challenges in road racing.
Now, as he sets his sights on another New York campaign, the Kenyan star has an opportunity to strengthen his legacy further. A third men's open-division victory would place him among a very select group of athletes to have won the prestigious race three times. Such a milestone would be more than another addition to his trophy cabinet; it would reinforce the story of a runner whose competitive range has extended across nearly every major discipline in distance running.
Behind Kamworor's achievements lies a training environment built around discipline, consistency and high-level competition. Working under the guidance of renowned coach Patrick Sang, he has trained alongside some of Kenya's most celebrated athletes, including marathon great Eliud Kipchoge and middle- and long-distance superstar Faith Kipyegon.
Sharing a training environment with athletes of such calibre provides a demanding daily standard. Yet Kamworor has built his own identity through a career defined by major championship victories and sustained success across different racing distances. His journey has also included difficult periods and setbacks, reminding the running world that even the most accomplished champions must continually work to return to their best. His longevity at the elite level reflects the importance of patience, dedication and the willingness to keep pursuing new goals.
For aspiring athletes in Kenya, his story offers an important lesson: extraordinary achievements are often built through ordinary routines repeated consistently over many years. Those five-kilometre journeys to school and back were not glamorous. They did not come with cheering crowds, television cameras or medals. Yet they formed part of the foundation of a career that would eventually take him to the world's biggest running stages.

On November 1, the streets of New York could become the setting for another extraordinary chapter in marathon history.

Tegla Loroupe has been honoured as the 2016 UN Person of the Year in Kenya for her work in ensuring the participation of the refugee team at the Rio 2016 Olympic Games.

Loroupe, a former marathon world record holder who won marathons in London, New York and Berlin in her heralded career, was the Chef de Mission for the ten-member squad that made up the Refugee Olympic Team, the first to compete at the Games.

Loroupe's journey with refugees began in 2014 when she took her peace-building efforts to refugee camps in Kenya where she discovered a great interest in athletics among refugee communities.

In 2015, she petitioned the International Olympic Committee to give refugees a chance to advance in their athletics careers by taking part in the Olympics. She then established an athletics training camp for refugees in Ngong, in the outskirts of Nairobi, which is run by her Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation. The Foundation is one of the projects which is supported by the IAAF's 'Athletics' for a Better World' social responsibility programme. Her hope was to help produce Olympic talent that would unite the people of countries that are at war.

Her vision was realised this summer when the first Refugee Olympic Team was constituted, comprised of ten refugees from Syria, Congo, Ethiopia and South Sudan, providing a symbol of hope to the more than 65 million people globally who are currently displaced by conflict. Five of the team members came Kenya’s Kakuma refugee camp.

Speaking at the award ceremony in Nairobi, Loroupe emphasised the role that each and every individual in the community plays to ensure there is peace. “We do not want to see more refugees," she said. "It does not help us. We want them to go back home and become ambassadors of peace."

The UNHCR Kenya Deputy Representative, Mr. Wella Kouyou, said Loroupe reminds us that refugees are human beings with capacity and aspirations just like anybody else.

“With her efforts, Tegla challenges all of us to also do our part in finding durable solutions for refugees," Kayou said.

**The United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) for the IAAF**

In 2015, she petitioned the International Olympic Committee to give refugees a chance to advance in their athletics careers by taking part in the Olympics. She then established an athletics training camp for refugees in Ngong, in the outskirts of Nairobi, which is run by her Tegla Loroupe Peace Foundation. The Foundation is one of the projects which is supported by the IAAF's 'Athletics' for a Better World' social responsibility programme. Her hope was to help produce Olympic talent that would unite the people of countries that are at war.

Her vision was realised this summer when the first Refugee Olympic Team was constituted, comprised of ten refugees from Syria, Congo, Ethiopia and South Sudan, providing a symbol of hope to the more than 65 million people globally who are currently displaced by conflict. Five of the team members came Kenya’s Kakuma refugee camp.

Speaking at the award ceremony in Nairobi, Loroupe emphasised the role that each and every individual in the community plays to ensure there is peace. “We do not want to see more refugees," she said. "It does not help us. We want them to go back home and become ambassadors of peace."

The UNHCR Kenya Deputy Representative, Mr. Wella Kouyou, said Loroupe reminds us that refugees are human beings with capacity and aspirations just like anybody else.

“With her efforts, Tegla challenges all of us to also do our part in finding durable solutions for refugees," Kayou said.

**The United Nations Refugee Agency (UNHCR) for the IAAF**

## Summary

The 2020 UN Security Council (SC) elections concluded during a historical period defined by the global COVID-19 pandemic. As officials scrambled to organise a socially distanced election, the final stage of the campaigns was forced into the digital realm. To bolster candidate states’ chances of being elected to the SC, digital diplomacy became the primary mode of communication. Here we focus on the SC campaigns of Canada, Ireland and Kenya, which were defined by ‘digital celebrity diplomacy’. U2 and Celine Dion supported the national campaigns of Ireland and Canada, while Kenya drew on the recognition of a number of celebrity athletes to bolster its campaign’s national brand. Thus, we explore the convergence of celebrity and digital diplomacy in these SC campaigns, contributing to new understandings of the use of celebrity in transforming the projection and reception of strategic narratives when integrated with digital diplomacy during the global COVID-19 pandemic.

As the Canadian International Development Minister Karina Gould argued, ‘it [the global pandemic] just demonstrates why it is important for Canada to sit on the UN Security Council. That campaign carries on, but in a different way’.[5](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESwwEB6zswFWeQ_UxkIw-te4UPBpWtkQO0HUuIoAAQZlK1mnIc2MTbjFwv3yhrWnyT9Dxy3PHZvbENwydjVgPc77hRRFl29slCygGp2v14ly0xxUGW1QOI5yqasGLNxp-l0e-IcDTEiemZkJn-upPduLpuR34jAp41qDgn85_1NOeMjBuCCoeqt_N2vRBlwZFuv26T1PJ9YAqLwD_x7VvjsaruhgrePekV1PuSuws6MLRTLDVna31hnvPkFz-dEFNvXCmjvuY&gsessionid=TWzY7GWuFKiKtcliyOYwb9o_D78qy-5O_xD-kcwyG0gWAmxPQ6Zu1A#FN000005) Other candidates also recognised the need to adopt new modes of campaigning. The Deputy Head of Norway’s SC campaign, Meena Syed, stated that ‘the pandemic has obviously changed our campaign and the working methods of the entire Foreign Service’, and ‘this has not been the time to focus on traditional campaigning’.[6](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESwwEB6zswFWeQ_UxkIw-te4UPBpWtkQO0HUuIoAAQZlK1mnIc2MTbjFwv3yhrWnyT9Dxy3PHZvbENwydjVgPc77hRRFl29slCygGp2v14ly0xxUGW1QOI5yqasGLNxp-l0e-IcDTEiemZkJn-upPduLpuR34jAp41qDgn85_1NOeMjBuCCoeqt_N2vRBlwZFuv26T1PJ9YAqLwD_x7VvjsaruhgrePekV1PuSuws6MLRTLDVna31hnvPkFz-dEFNvXCmjvuY&gsessionid=TWzY7GWuFKiKtcliyOYwb9o_D78qy-5O_xD-kcwyG0gWAmxPQ6Zu1A#FN000006) Ireland’s Ambassador to the UN Geraldine Byrne Nason stressed Ireland’s dedication to support ‘the role of the UN in leading the global response to the pandemic’.[7](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESwwEB6zswFWeQ_UxkIw-te4UPBpWtkQO0HUuIoAAQZlK1mnIc2MTbjFwv3yhrWnyT9Dxy3PHZvbENwydjVgPc77hRRFl29slCygGp2v14ly0xxUGW1QOI5yqasGLNxp-l0e-IcDTEiemZkJn-upPduLpuR34jAp41qDgn85_1NOeMjBuCCoeqt_N2vRBlwZFuv26T1PJ9YAqLwD_x7VvjsaruhgrePekV1PuSuws6MLRTLDVna31hnvPkFz-dEFNvXCmjvuY&gsessionid=TWzY7GWuFKiKtcliyOYwb9o_D78qy-5O_xD-kcwyG0gWAmxPQ6Zu1A#FN000007)

Digital diplomacy therefore became the primary mode of communication, representation and signalling in the final weeks of the UN elections campaign. Our focus in this article is on the digital celebrity aspects of the SC campaigns of Canada, Ireland and Kenya, all of which employed celebrities to attract global support for their candidacies.[8](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESwwEB6zswFWeQ_UxkIw-te4UPBpWtkQO0HUuIoAAQZlK1mnIc2MTbjFwv3yhrWnyT9Dxy3PHZvbENwydjVgPc77hRRFl29slCygGp2v14ly0xxUGW1QOI5yqasGLNxp-l0e-IcDTEiemZkJn-upPduLpuR34jAp41qDgn85_1NOeMjBuCCoeqt_N2vRBlwZFuv26T1PJ9YAqLwD_x7VvjsaruhgrePekV1PuSuws6MLRTLDVna31hnvPkFz-dEFNvXCmjvuY&gsessionid=TWzY7GWuFKiKtcliyOYwb9o_D78qy-5O_xD-kcwyG0gWAmxPQ6Zu1A#FN000008) More specifically, we explore the use of celebrity in the strategic narratives that informed the national campaigns, rather than assessing the role of such campaigns in actually achieving a seat on the SC.

Underpinning our article is also the premise that the boundaries between popular culture, world politics, celebrity and digital communication are becoming increasingly blurry, producing new digital practices in global politics.[9](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESwwEB6zswFWeQ_UxkIw-te4UPBpWtkQO0HUuIoAAQZlK1mnIc2MTbjFwv3yhrWnyT9Dxy3PHZvbENwydjVgPc77hRRFl29slCygGp2v14ly0xxUGW1QOI5yqasGLNxp-l0e-IcDTEiemZkJn-upPduLpuR34jAp41qDgn85_1NOeMjBuCCoeqt_N2vRBlwZFuv26T1PJ9YAqLwD_x7VvjsaruhgrePekV1PuSuws6MLRTLDVna31hnvPkFz-dEFNvXCmjvuY&gsessionid=TWzY7GWuFKiKtcliyOYwb9o_D78qy-5O_xD-kcwyG0gWAmxPQ6Zu1A#FN000009) The use of celebrity and the reception of this aspect of the campaigns in the media[10](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESwwEB6zswFWeQ_UxkIw-te4UPBpWtkQO0HUuIoAAQZlK1mnIc2MTbjFwv3yhrWnyT9Dxy3PHZvbENwydjVgPc77hRRFl29slCygGp2v14ly0xxUGW1QOI5yqasGLNxp-l0e-IcDTEiemZkJn-upPduLpuR34jAp41qDgn85_1NOeMjBuCCoeqt_N2vRBlwZFuv26T1PJ9YAqLwD_x7VvjsaruhgrePekV1PuSuws6MLRTLDVna31hnvPkFz-dEFNvXCmjvuY&gsessionid=TWzY7GWuFKiKtcliyOYwb9o_D78qy-5O_xD-kcwyG0gWAmxPQ6Zu1A#FN000010) makes the 2020 SC elections an interesting case to explore. It can tell us about the representation of states’ strategic narratives and marketing strategies during a time of global crisis.[11](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESwwEB6zswFWeQ_UxkIw-te4UPBpWtkQO0HUuIoAAQZlK1mnIc2MTbjFwv3yhrWnyT9Dxy3PHZvbENwydjVgPc77hRRFl29slCygGp2v14ly0xxUGW1QOI5yqasGLNxp-l0e-IcDTEiemZkJn-upPduLpuR34jAp41qDgn85_1NOeMjBuCCoeqt_N2vRBlwZFuv26T1PJ9YAqLwD_x7VvjsaruhgrePekV1PuSuws6MLRTLDVna31hnvPkFz-dEFNvXCmjvuY&gsessionid=TWzY7GWuFKiKtcliyOYwb9o_D78qy-5O_xD-kcwyG0gWAmxPQ6Zu1A#FN000011) Our study, moreover, shows how celebrity diplomacy both complements and challenges traditional forms of statecraft and diplomacy.[12](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESwwEB6zswFWeQ_UxkIw-te4UPBpWtkQO0HUuIoAAQZlK1mnIc2MTbjFwv3yhrWnyT9Dxy3PHZvbENwydjVgPc77hRRFl29slCygGp2v14ly0xxUGW1QOI5yqasGLNxp-l0e-IcDTEiemZkJn-upPduLpuR34jAp41qDgn85_1NOeMjBuCCoeqt_N2vRBlwZFuv26T1PJ9YAqLwD_x7VvjsaruhgrePekV1PuSuws6MLRTLDVna31hnvPkFz-dEFNvXCmjvuY&gsessionid=TWzY7GWuFKiKtcliyOYwb9o_D78qy-5O_xD-kcwyG0gWAmxPQ6Zu1A#FN000012)

We draw upon scholarship on the employment of celebrity to add strength and visibility to global justice campaigns.[13](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESwwEB6zswFWeQ_UxkIw-te4UPBpWtkQO0HUuIoAAQZlK1mnIc2MTbjFwv3yhrWnyT9Dxy3PHZvbENwydjVgPc77hRRFl29slCygGp2v14ly0xxUGW1QOI5yqasGLNxp-l0e-IcDTEiemZkJn-upPduLpuR34jAp41qDgn85_1NOeMjBuCCoeqt_N2vRBlwZFuv26T1PJ9YAqLwD_x7VvjsaruhgrePekV1PuSuws6MLRTLDVna31hnvPkFz-dEFNvXCmjvuY&gsessionid=TWzY7GWuFKiKtcliyOYwb9o_D78qy-5O_xD-kcwyG0gWAmxPQ6Zu1A#FN000013) In particular, we interrogate states’ use of celebrity in acquiring more influence within the UN and the role of celebrity in making national digital diplomacy more visible. – all three campaigns studied here were visual in their projection.[15](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESwwEB6zswFWeQ_UxkIw-te4UPBpWtkQO0HUuIoAAQZlK1mnIc2MTbjFwv3yhrWnyT9Dxy3PHZvbENwydjVgPc77hRRFl29slCygGp2v14ly0xxUGW1QOI5yqasGLNxp-l0e-IcDTEiemZkJn-upPduLpuR34jAp41qDgn85_1NOeMjBuCCoeqt_N2vRBlwZFuv26T1PJ9YAqLwD_x7VvjsaruhgrePekV1PuSuws6MLRTLDVna31hnvPkFz-dEFNvXCmjvuY&gsessionid=TWzY7GWuFKiKtcliyOYwb9o_D78qy-5O_xD-kcwyG0gWAmxPQ6Zu1A#FN000015) We argue that the national campaigns of the three countries reflected the projection of national strategic narratives, expressed in improvised efforts[16](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESwwEB6zswFWeQ_UxkIw-te4UPBpWtkQO0HUuIoAAQZlK1mnIc2MTbjFwv3yhrWnyT9Dxy3PHZvbENwydjVgPc77hRRFl29slCygGp2v14ly0xxUGW1QOI5yqasGLNxp-l0e-IcDTEiemZkJn-upPduLpuR34jAp41qDgn85_1NOeMjBuCCoeqt_N2vRBlwZFuv26T1PJ9YAqLwD_x7VvjsaruhgrePekV1PuSuws6MLRTLDVna31hnvPkFz-dEFNvXCmjvuY&gsessionid=TWzY7GWuFKiKtcliyOYwb9o_D78qy-5O_xD-kcwyG0gWAmxPQ6Zu1A#FN000016) to orchestrate identity narratives that centred on their dedication to the UN.[17](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESwwEB6zswFWeQ_UxkIw-te4UPBpWtkQO0HUuIoAAQZlK1mnIc2MTbjFwv3yhrWnyT9Dxy3PHZvbENwydjVgPc77hRRFl29slCygGp2v14ly0xxUGW1QOI5yqasGLNxp-l0e-IcDTEiemZkJn-upPduLpuR34jAp41qDgn85_1NOeMjBuCCoeqt_N2vRBlwZFuv26T1PJ9YAqLwD_x7VvjsaruhgrePekV1PuSuws6MLRTLDVna31hnvPkFz-dEFNvXCmjvuY&gsessionid=TWzY7GWuFKiKtcliyOYwb9o_D78qy-5O_xD-kcwyG0gWAmxPQ6Zu1A#FN000017) In the Canadian and Irish cases, the campaigns were fronted by celebrities known to mass audiences – Irish rock star Bono and Canadian pop singer Celine Dion. However, Kenya drew on celebrity sport stars to support its campaign. These national campaigns, we propose, are suggestive of an emergent normalisation of celebrity diplomacy through digital channels.

First, we reflect on the character of digital diplomacy, drawing upon scholarship in the field. We then identify a close relationship between popular culture and world politics and locate celebrity within that nexus. This is followed by an unpacking of the key features of celebrity diplomacy to capture the increasingly close relationship between celebrity and digital and traditional diplomacy in global politics. We then discuss our material and our strategic narrative approach to the analysis of national SC campaigns. This is followed by an analysis of the national UN campaigns, including identifying their location within popular culture and global power relations. To conclude, we argue that the combined use of celebrity endorsement and digital diplomatic tools in national SC campaigns can contribute to the projection of states’ strategic narratives. Moreover, we posit that a successful SC campaign increasingly relies on nation branding to project identity narratives, and that the celebrity – digital diplomacy nexus can be an effective way to do this.

## 2 Digital Diplomacy

Governments, international organisations (IO s) and non-governmental organisations (NGO s) employ digital methods to signal and represent their global commitments to mass audiences. Digital technology is also used to brand the nation, its people and its government, offering opportunities to explore its normative ambitions in global politics.[18](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESwwEB6zswFWeQ_UxkIw-te4UPBpWtkQO0HUuIoAAQZlK1mnIc2MTbjFwv3yhrWnyT9Dxy3PHZvbENwydjVgPc77hRRFl29slCygGp2v14ly0xxUGW1QOI5yqasGLNxp-l0e-IcDTEiemZkJn-upPduLpuR34jAp41qDgn85_1NOeMjBuCCoeqt_N2vRBlwZFuv26T1PJ9YAqLwD_x7VvjsaruhgrePekV1PuSuws6MLRTLDVna31hnvPkFz-dEFNvXCmjvuY&gsessionid=TWzY7GWuFKiKtcliyOYwb9o_D78qy-5O_xD-kcwyG0gWAmxPQ6Zu1A#FN000018) media.[19](https://www.google.com/goto?url=CAESwwEB6zswFWeQ_UxkIw-te4UPBpWtkQO0HUuIoAAQZlK1mnIc2MTbjFwv3yhrWnyT9Dxy3PHZvbENwydjVgPc77hRRFl29slCygGp2v14ly0xxUGW1QOI5yqasGLNxp-l0e-IcDTEiemZkJn-upPduLpuR34jAp41qDgn85_1NOeMjBuCCoeqt_N2vRBlwZFuv26T1PJ9YAqLwD_x7VvjsaruhgrePekV1PuSuws6MLRTLDVna31hnvPkFz-dEFNvXCmjvuY&gsessionid=TWzY7GWuFKiKtcliyOYwb9o_D78qy-5O_xD-kcwyG0gWAmxPQ6Zu1A#FN000019)
